campaign.title: RugPalace closing down sale
campaign.text: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots: 'CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! 70% off all handmade rugs before we shut our doors forever.' The campaign has run continuously for 14 months; company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly, and the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged. Radio spot adds 'last weekend, we mean it this time'.

detected_practices: persistent 'closing down' claim with no actual cessation of trade (running 14 months)
false urgency / perpetual 'final days' and 'last weekend' scarcity claims
fake reference prices — 'pre-sale' prices never actually charged (misleading discount of 70%)
generative AI used in campaign creation
personalisation/targeting of consumers
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is general adult consumers in the EU. Broad outdoor and radio reach means the campaign is not strictly age-gated, though no specific targeting of minors is indicated.
triage.summary: A multi-channel (web, radio, outdoor) retail campaign for RugPalace advertising a '70% off closing down sale' that has run continuously for 14 months despite no actual cessation of trade, ongoing monthly restocking, and reference prices that were never charged. It declares use of generative AI and personalisation/targeting, and features aggressive false-urgency and misleading-discount claims.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign expressly declares that generative AI was used to create campaign assets (web homepage, banners, radio spots). Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable, detectable format. Any AI-generated visuals or audio (e.g. radio spot voice/audio, homepage imagery, copy) used in this multi-channel campaign fall within scope, and the submission gives no indication the marking obligation is satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm which assets are AI-generated and ensure they carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) as delivered by the generative AI provider. Retain documentation from the AI tool vendor evidencing that outputs are marked and detectable as artificially generated, and verify the marking survives the export/publishing pipeline for web, radio and outdoor formats.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign is highly deceptive and uses false-urgency tactics, and it declares personalisation/targeting. Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that use manipulative or deceptive techniques to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm. However, on the stated facts the deception is human-authored advertising copy and the fake urgency is not shown to be produced or driven by an AI system, nor is there evidence of an AI-driven targeting technique impairing informed decision-making to the level of 'significant harm'. The prohibition threshold is therefore not established; the deception is properly addressed under UCPD. Flagged for awareness in case the declared personalisation is in fact AI-driven behavioural manipulation, which would require re-assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days!
findings.recommendation: Clarify how the declared personalisation/targeting operates. If AI is used to time or tailor these urgency/scarcity messages to exploit individual users' decision-making, obtain a detailed description and re-assess against the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition; ensure no AI-driven manipulative technique is deployed. Separately, resolve the underlying misleading claims (this is primarily a UCPD matter).

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core problems (perpetual "closing down" claim, false urgency, and never-charged reference prices) are misleading-practice issues governed by the UCPD, not the AI Act. Within the AI Act, the only clearly engaged obligation is Art. 50(2) marking of AI-generated assets, because the submission declares use of generative AI in campaign creation. There is no indication of deep fakes, synthetic likenesses, or AI-driven manipulation meeting the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition threshold, and Art. 50(4) is not engaged on the stated facts.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/targeting of EU consumers typically involves automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal preferences, interests and behaviour, which meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling. This brings the campaign within the scope of the GDPR profiling regime even though the ad copy itself contains no data-collection element.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document whether the personalisation relies on profiling of identifiable individuals; if so, map the data flows and treat all downstream GDPR profiling obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection) as applicable.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising/profiling requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — generally consent or a documented, balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The submission provides no evidence of any lawful basis for the declared targeting, so it is not demonstrable that the processing is lawful.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the lawful basis for the targeting. If relying on legitimate interests, complete and retain a Legitimate Interests Assessment; where consent is required (e.g. tracking cookies/ePrivacy), obtain valid, freely given consent before processing.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) requires processing to be lawful, fair and transparent. Profiling-based targeting conducted without clear disclosure to consumers, and embedded in a campaign built on demonstrably deceptive claims (perpetual 'closing down', never-charged reference prices), raises fairness and transparency concerns about how personal data is used to deliver those messages.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the personalisation is disclosed to consumers and that data is not used to amplify misleading messaging. Correct the underlying deceptive claims and provide clear, accurate information about the personalisation applied.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: If the web channel collects personal data (e.g. tracking for targeting, or any sign-up/lead-generation flow) the controller must provide Art. 13 information at the point of collection — identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and information about profiling. The submission describes personalisation but shows no privacy notice, so this obligation is likely engaged and not evidenced as satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: web homepage
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at every point where personal data is collected on the web property, expressly covering the personalisation/profiling purpose and the right to object to direct marketing.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Where personal data is used for direct marketing, including profiling for that purpose, data subjects have an absolute right under Art. 21(2)-(3) to object, and must be explicitly informed of that right at the latest at first communication. No opt-out mechanism or notice of this right is evidenced in the campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Present the right to object to direct marketing clearly and separately at first contact, and provide an easy, always-available mechanism to opt out of marketing and associated profiling.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Art. 22 is engaged only if the personalisation involves solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects (e.g. automated individualised pricing or exclusion from offers). The campaign text advertises a flat '70% off' to all, so there is no evidence of qualifying automated decision-making, but it should be ruled out.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm the personalisation does not include solely-automated individualised pricing or offer eligibility; if it does, apply Art. 22 safeguards (explicit consent basis, meaningful human intervention, right to contest).

verdicts.notes: The campaign is primarily a misleading-advertising case (UCPD territory) delivered via web, radio and outdoor — none of which, as described, contains a data-collection point or privacy notice. GDPR is engaged only through the declared use of personalisation/targeting of EU consumers, which typically constitutes profiling and triggers lawful-basis, transparency and right-to-object obligations. The submission provides no evidence of consent, privacy notices or how targeting is implemented, so findings are framed as risks requiring verification rather than confirmed breaches. No special-category data or minor targeting is indicated in the text.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The campaign's web homepage/storefront banner uses false-urgency and false-scarcity design tactics — a perpetual 'Final days!' / 'last weekend, we mean it this time' deadline that has run 14 months, plus a 70% reduction against reference prices that were never charged. Deploying such deceptive elements in an online interface to materially distort consumers' ability to make free and informed decisions is the type of dark pattern DSA Art. 25 prohibits. Applicability is scope-limited: Art. 25 binds 'providers of online platforms' (services disseminating third-party content to the public), and RugPalace's own storefront website likely does not qualify, so this conduct is chiefly caught by the UCPD. Flagged because the deceptive online-interface design squarely engages the Art. 25 concept.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days!
findings.recommendation: Remove the false and perpetual urgency/scarcity design from the web interface: only display genuine, time-limited deadlines and honest reference prices (lowest price in the prior 30 days). If any part of the campaign is served through an online platform interface RugPalace controls or operates, ensure the interface does not manipulate choice. Note that the UCPD applies to this conduct regardless of DSA platform scope.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign declares use of personalisation/targeting on web. DSA Art. 26(1) requires ad-transparency (identifiability as an ad, advertiser identity, payer, and main targeting parameters) — but this obligation falls on the online platform presenting the advertisement, not on the advertiser (RugPalace). If RugPalace's targeted ads are served through a third-party online platform, that platform must meet Art. 26(1); RugPalace should supply the necessary advertiser/targeting information to enable it.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Where personalised ads are placed on third-party online platforms, provide those platforms with the advertiser identity, payer information and targeting parameters they need to satisfy their DSA Art. 26(1) transparency obligations, and ensure ads are clearly identifiable as advertising.

verdicts.notes: The manipulative false-urgency messaging ("Final days!", "last weekend, we mean it this time") and never-charged reference prices are deployed on RugPalace's web homepage/storefront, which engages the deceptive-design concept behind DSA Art. 25 (prohibition of dark patterns). However, the DSA's Art. 25 and Art. 26 obligations bind "providers of online platforms" — services that store and disseminate third-party information to the public — and a retailer's own e-commerce/storefront website generally does not meet that definition. The same conduct is therefore primarily governed by the UCPD (dark patterns rules apply "without prejudice to" the UCPD, which is covered by another agent). No sensitive-data-based ad targeting (Art. 26(3)), no minor-targeted profiling ads (Art. 28), and no VLOP ad-repository (Art. 39) obligations are engaged on the facts. DSA relevance is limited and scope-dependent.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claim of ceasing trade
findings.rationale: Annex I point 15 prohibits, in all circumstances, claiming the trader is about to cease trading when this is not the case. Company filings show no cessation of trade, the campaign has run continuously for 14 months, and new stock arrives monthly — establishing the 'closing down' / 'shut our doors forever' claim is false. This is a per se blacklisted practice requiring no proof of consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! ... before we shut our doors forever.
findings.recommendation: Immediately cease all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging across web, radio and outdoor. Only use cessation-of-trade language if a genuine, documented decision to close has been made, with a defined and honoured end date.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits, in all circumstances, falsely stating a product is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. The offer has run continuously for 14 months while repeatedly asserting 'Final days' and 'last weekend, we mean it this time' — a demonstrably false time limitation designed to pressure consumers. Per se blacklisted.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Remove all false deadline and 'final days'/'last weekend' claims. Any time-limited offer must have a genuine end date that is actually enforced and not perpetually renewed.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6(1)(d) treats as misleading a practice that deceives the average consumer regarding the existence of a specific price advantage. The 'pre-sale' reference prices were never actually charged, so the advertised 70% reduction is fictitious and misrepresents the true price advantage, likely causing consumers to make a purchase they otherwise would not.
findings.evidence_quote: 70% off all handmade rugs
findings.recommendation: Base any advertised discount on the genuine lowest price actually charged in the 30 days before the reduction (consistent with the Price Indication Directive). Withdraw the 70% claim unless it can be substantiated against real prior selling prices.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of relentless, persistent false-deadline pressure sustained across web, weekly radio and outdoor for 14 months can constitute undue influence under Arts. 8-9, significantly impairing the average consumer's freedom of choice through timing and persistence. This reinforces the blacklisted findings as an aggressive-practice dimension of the same conduct.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the high-pressure, artificially urgent framing entirely; present offers with accurate, non-coercive information so purchase decisions are made freely.

verdicts.notes: The RugPalace campaign engages multiple UCPD blacklist ("per se" prohibited) practices. It advertises a "closing down" sale that has run for 14 months with no cessation of trade and monthly restocking (Annex I point 15), pushes false urgency through perpetual "final days"/"last weekend, we mean it this time" messaging (Annex I point 7), and claims a "70% off" discount against reference prices that were never actually charged (Art. 6 misleading action on price advantage). These are among the most clear-cut violations under the Directive, all prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer impact.

report.executive_summary: This "RugPalace closing down sale" campaign runs a fake permanent closing-down sale across web, radio and outdoor. The critical problem is that the core claims are simply false: the shop has been "closing down" for 14 months with no actual plans to shut, new stock arrives every month, and the "70% off" is measured against reference prices you never actually charged. Under EU consumer law (UCPD) these are among the most serious, blacklisted practices — falsely claiming to cease trading and using fake "final days/last weekend" urgency are prohibited in all circumstances, no matter how it affects consumers. On top of that, your declared use of personalisation triggers GDPR duties (a lawful basis, privacy notice, and a right to opt out of marketing) that you have not yet evidenced, and your declared use of generative AI means any AI-made visuals or audio must carry machine-readable "AI-generated" marking under the AI Act. The false-urgency web design also mirrors the "dark patterns" the DSA targets. Bottom line: the campaign is very likely unlawful in its current form and should be stopped and rebuilt around truthful claims before it runs again.
recommendations: STOP immediately: remove all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging across web, radio and outdoor. These are per se prohibited (UCPD Annex I point 15) unless you have a genuine, documented, dated decision to close and honour it.

Remove all false-urgency claims ('Final days!', 'last weekend, we mean it this time'). Any time-limited offer must have a real end date that is actually enforced and not perpetually renewed (UCPD Annex I point 7).

Withdraw the '70% off' claim unless it can be substantiated against the genuine lowest price actually charged in the 30 days before the reduction (UCPD Art. 6 / Price Indication Directive). Reference prices you never charged cannot be used.

Confirm which assets are AI-generated and ensure they carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) that survives export to web, radio and outdoor formats; retain vendor documentation evidencing the marking (AI Act Art. 50(2)).
Document a valid lawful basis for the personalisation/targeting of EU consumers — consent where required (e.g. tracking cookies), or a documented Legitimate Interests Assessment (GDPR Art. 6).

Provide a clear privacy notice at every web data-collection point covering the profiling purpose, and present the absolute right to object to direct marketing with an easy opt-out at first contact (GDPR Arts. 13 and 21).
Confirm the personalisation does not involve solely-automated individualised pricing or offer eligibility; if it does, apply Art. 22 safeguards (GDPR).

Where personalised ads run on third-party online platforms, supply the advertiser identity, payer and targeting parameters those platforms need for ad-transparency, and ensure ads are clearly identifiable as advertising (DSA Art. 26). Ensure any interface you control does not use manipulative dark-pattern design (DSA Art. 25).

Clarify how personalisation operates; if AI is used to time or tailor urgency/scarcity messages to individual users, re-assess against the AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative/deceptive AI techniques.

campaign.title: RugPalace closing down sale
campaign.text: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots: 'CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! 70% off all handmade rugs before we shut our doors forever.' The campaign has run continuously for 14 months; company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly, and the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged. Radio spot adds 'last weekend, we mean it this time'.

detected_practices: Perpetual 'closing down' / going-out-of-business claim (14 months, no actual cessation of trade)
False urgency / 'final days' and 'last weekend, we mean it this time' scarcity messaging
Fake reference pricing ('70% off', pre-sale prices never actually charged)
Misleading '70% off all handmade rugs' discount claim
Generative AI used in campaign content
Personalisation/targeting of advertising
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is general adult consumers, so minors are not the primary audience; however radio, outdoor and web homepage are broadcast/public channels that could incidentally reach minors. Declared personalisation/targeting means personal data is processed (GDPR) and the online web/personalised elements plus intermediary distribution may engage DSA advertising-transparency obligations. The most severe issues are the misleading "closing down" and fake-reference-price practices under the UCPD (Annex I blacklisted and misleading practices).
triage.summary: A multi-channel (web, radio, outdoor) EU consumer campaign for RugPalace promoting a "closing down / everything must go" sale with 70% discounts and heavy false-urgency messaging. Company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly, the "sale" has run continuously for 14 months, and the reference prices were never actually charged — strongly indicating misleading commercial practices and false discount/scarcity claims. The submitter declares use of generative AI and personalisation/targeting.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The advertiser confirms generative AI is used to produce campaign assets (web homepage content, radio spot audio, and likely banner imagery/copy). Under Art. 50(2), providers/deployers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The submission provides no indication that any AI-generated visuals, audio or copy carry machine-readable provenance marking, so the transparency obligation appears engaged and unsatisfied as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify every asset produced or manipulated with generative AI and ensure each carries machine-readable AI-provenance marking (e.g., C2PA/content credentials or equivalent watermarking) at the point of generation. Document the marking pipeline with the AI tool provider and retain evidence that outputs are detectable as artificially generated.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Art. 50(4) requires disclosure where AI generates/manipulates content constituting a deep fake (realistic depiction of real persons, places or events) or generates public-interest text. The campaign is retail advertising for rugs with no indication of deep fakes, synthetic influencers presented as real, or public-interest text, so this obligation does not appear engaged. Flagged only so that, if any AI-generated realistic imagery of real persons or synthetic 'testimonial' figures were added, disclosure would become mandatory.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm no AI-generated content depicts real or realistic persons/events or synthetic endorsers presented as authentic. If such content is introduced, add a clear disclosure that the content is artificially generated or manipulated.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign uses deceptive and manipulative messaging (perpetual 'closing down', fake reference prices, false urgency). Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems deploying purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and are reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Here the deception appears to be human-authored marketing copy rather than a technique deployed by an AI system, and there is no evidence of 'significant harm' in the Art. 5 sense; the core misleading-practice issues are matters for the UCPD. Flagged for awareness because if the declared generative AI or personalisation were used to algorithmically time or tailor these manipulative messages to distort consumer decisions, the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition could be triggered.
findings.evidence_quote: last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Verify whether generative AI or the declared personalisation/targeting is used to algorithmically optimise or time the urgency/scarcity messaging toward exploiting consumer decision-making. If so, cease AI-driven deployment of the deceptive messaging, as this risks the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition in addition to the underlying UCPD violations. Otherwise, resolve the misleading claims themselves under UCPD.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce content (web banners, radio spots, likely imagery/audio). This engages the AI Act's transparency obligation in Art. 50(2) requiring machine-readable marking of AI-generated synthetic content; the submission gives no indication this marking is in place. The deep-fake/public-interest-text disclosure under Art. 50(4) does not appear engaged (no synthetic likenesses of real persons or public-interest text). The manipulative/deceptive nature of the campaign is real but is human-authored marketing copy and is properly a UCPD matter; the Art. 5(1)(a) AI-prohibition is engaged only marginally and is flagged for awareness, since there is no evidence the deception is deployed by an AI system causing significant harm. The severe misleading-practice issues fall to the UCPD agent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personalisation/targeting is declared, so personal data is processed to select and reach recipients. Art. 5(1)(a) requires that processing be fair, not only lawful and transparent. Using profiling to deliver advertising that is demonstrably false (14-month 'closing down' with no cessation of trade, reference prices never charged) means personal data is processed to manipulate data subjects with deceptive content, undermining the fairness principle regardless of the separate UCPD deception assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! 70% off all handmade rugs before we shut our doors forever.
findings.recommendation: Do not use profiling/targeting to distribute advertising whose underlying claims are false. Correct the misleading creative and ensure any personalised delivery serves accurate, non-deceptive messaging so that the processing meets the fairness standard.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/targeting of advertising constitutes profiling: automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal preferences/interests and target individuals with tailored ads. This brings the campaign squarely within GDPR's scope and is the trigger for the lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations below.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling logic used for targeting, categories of data and inferences, and confirm none rely on special-category (Art. 9) attributes. Maintain records of processing for this activity.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising/profiling requires a valid lawful basis — generally consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign material provides no indication of any lawful basis for the targeting, so the requirement is engaged but not evidenced as satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the lawful basis for the targeting: obtain valid consent where required (e.g. cookies/tracking under ePrivacy) or complete and retain a legitimate-interests balancing test. Do not proceed with targeting until a lawful basis is confirmed.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected (e.g. via the web homepage / tracking for personalisation), Art. 13 requires the controller to provide identity, purposes, lawful basis, retention, data-subject rights and information about profiling at the point of collection. The material shows no such privacy information, so the transparency obligation is engaged and unmet as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at every point of personal-data collection (web homepage/tracking and any sign-up), covering purposes, lawful basis, retention, recipients, and the existence of profiling and rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Processing personal data for direct marketing, including related profiling, triggers an absolute right to object. The campaign material shows no opt-out/objection mechanism, so the obligation to facilitate objection is engaged but not evidenced.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, explicit and free mechanism to object to direct marketing and marketing-related profiling, clearly presented at first contact, and honour objections immediately.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of personalisation/targeting, so personal data processing and profiling (Art. 4(4)) are engaged, triggering GDPR obligations. The submitted material is advertising creative only and gives no evidence of a lawful basis, privacy notice, opt-out, or consent mechanism, so several obligations are engaged but unverified. The most GDPR-specific concern is fairness: personal data is being used to target consumers with systematically deceptive "closing down"/fake-discount content, which conflicts with the Art. 5(1)(a) fairness principle. The core deception itself is primarily a UCPD/DSA matter and is not double-counted here.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign declares use of personalisation/targeting and runs on the web homepage. Where such advertising is served via third-party online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires those platforms to ensure recipients can identify in real time that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters (with a way to change them). This obligation binds the platform provider rather than RugPalace as advertiser, but RugPalace must supply the advertiser-identity and payer information the platform needs to comply. The submitted material does not establish that RugPalace itself is an online-platform provider, so no direct breach by RugPalace is shown.
findings.evidence_quote: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots
findings.recommendation: Where the campaign is placed as paid advertising on third-party online platforms, ensure accurate advertiser-identity and 'paid for by' data are provided so the platform can meet its Art. 26(1) transparency labelling. Confirm whether RugPalace operates any service that qualifies as an 'online platform' under the DSA; if not, Art. 26 does not apply to it directly.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The persistent false-urgency and 'closing down' messaging on the web homepage is precisely the kind of deceptive/manipulative design that Art. 25 prohibits when embodied in an online platform's interface. However, Art. 25 applies to 'providers of online platforms' designing their online interfaces; a trader's own promotional website is generally not an 'online platform' in the DSA sense, and the same conduct is directly caught by the UCPD (Annex I points 7 and 15), which applies to all traders. Flagged for context only; the operative prohibition here is under the UCPD, assessed by another agent.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days!
findings.recommendation: Treat the false-urgency/closing-down conduct as a UCPD matter and remediate there. Only if RugPalace operates a DSA online platform/interface would Art. 25 impose an independent obligation — in that case remove the deceptive urgency framing from the interface design.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's advertising-transparency (Art. 26), recommender (Art. 27) and dark-pattern (Art. 25) obligations bind providers of online platforms and online interfaces, not advertisers/traders as such. RugPalace here is a rug retailer running storefront, radio, outdoor and its own web homepage campaign — the material does not establish that RugPalace operates an "online platform" (a hosting service disseminating third-party content to the public) or a VLOP, so the direct DSA obligations largely do not attach to this advertiser. The substantive misleading/false-urgency and fake-reference-pricing conduct is squarely a UCPD matter (covered by another agent). Two contextual points are worth flagging: if this campaign is distributed as paid advertising on third-party online platforms, those platforms' Art. 26 labelling/targeting-parameter duties are engaged; and the declared personalisation combined with the false-urgency messaging could constitute deceptive interface design (Art. 25) to the extent RugPalace's own web homepage qualifies as an online interface it operates.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claim of ceasing trade
findings.rationale: Annex I point 15 prohibits, in all circumstances, claiming the trader is about to cease trading when this is not the case. The campaign has run continuously for 14 months, company filings show no cessation of trade, and new stock arrives monthly — proving the 'closing down / shut our doors forever' claim is false. This is a blacklisted practice, unfair per se with no need to prove consumer detriment.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! ... before we shut our doors forever
findings.recommendation: Immediately cease all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging across web, radio and outdoor. Only use going-out-of-business language if there is a genuine, documented cessation of trade with a firm end date, and remove it once trading continues.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits falsely stating a product is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. Repeated 'final days' and 'last weekend, we mean it this time' deadlines across a 14-month continuous campaign are manifestly false time-limited claims designed to pressure consumers. This is a blacklisted practice, unfair in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Remove all false deadline and 'final days/last weekend' language. Only advertise a time-limited offer where the end date is genuine and honoured; do not restart or extend a 'final' deadline once it has passed.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers misleading actions regarding price and the existence of a specific price advantage. The 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged, so the advertised '70% off' is a fictitious discount that deceives the average consumer about a price advantage and induces a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. (The reference-price rule under the Price Indication Directive Art. 6a further requires the lowest price in the prior 30 days.)
findings.evidence_quote: 70% off all handmade rugs
findings.recommendation: Base any discount claim on the genuine lowest price actually charged in the preceding 30 days. Discontinue '70% off' unless it can be substantiated against real prior selling prices, and retain documentary evidence of those prices.

verdicts.notes: The RugPalace campaign contains multiple clear UCPD breaches, two of them blacklisted practices prohibited in all circumstances. The "closing down / everything must go / shut our doors forever" messaging run for 14 months with no cessation of trade and monthly restocking is a textbook false ceasing-trade claim (Annex I point 15). The perpetual "final days / last weekend, we mean it this time" deadlines are false urgency (Annex I point 7). The "70% off" claim against reference prices never actually charged is a misleading action on price advantage (Art. 6). These are high-confidence, high-severity findings requiring the campaign to be halted and rebuilt.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises a "closing down / everything must go / shut our doors forever" sale with "70% off" and "final days / last weekend, we mean it this time" urgency. The problem is that the sale has run continuously for 14 months, the business is not actually closing, new stock arrives monthly, and the "before" prices used to calculate the 70% discount were never charged. These facts make two of the claims outright illegal in all circumstances under EU consumer law: falsely claiming you are about to cease trading, and falsely claiming an offer is only available for a very limited time. The fake reference pricing is a separate misleading practice on price. On top of the consumer-law breaches, the declared use of personalisation means personal data is being processed to push demonstrably false messaging (a fairness problem under GDPR, with no evidenced lawful basis, privacy notice or opt-out), and the declared use of generative AI triggers AI Act transparency/marking obligations that are not shown to be met. The core issue is the deception itself — the campaign cannot be fixed cosmetically and must be stopped and rebuilt around truthful claims. Overall verdict: critical, do not continue running as-is.
recommendations: STOP the campaign now across web, radio and outdoor. The 'closing down / shut our doors forever' messaging is a blacklisted practice (UCPD Annex I point 15) that is illegal in all circumstances — no consumer harm needs to be proven. Only use closing-down language if there is a genuine, documented cessation of trade with a firm end date.

Remove all false-urgency language ('Final days', 'last weekend, we mean it this time'). Repeated deadlines over a 14-month campaign are a second blacklisted practice (UCPD Annex I point 7). Only advertise a time-limited offer when the deadline is real and honoured, and never restart a 'final' deadline.

Discontinue the '70% off' claim unless it can be substantiated against genuine prior selling prices. Under EU price-indication rules, discounts must reference the lowest price actually charged in the preceding 30 days. Retain documentary proof of real prior prices before making any discount claim.

Fix the personalisation/GDPR gaps before any relaunch: document a valid lawful basis for targeting (consent or a legitimate-interests assessment), publish a clear privacy notice at every data-collection point, and provide an easy opt-out from marketing and profiling. Never use targeting to distribute false messaging — that breaches the fairness principle.

Address AI Act transparency: identify every asset produced with generative AI and ensure outputs carry machine-readable AI-provenance marking. Confirm no AI or personalisation is being used to algorithmically time/optimise the deceptive urgency messaging. Document the marking pipeline.
If the campaign is placed as paid ads on third-party online platforms, supply accurate advertiser-identity and 'paid for by' data so the platform can meet its DSA Art. 26 transparency labelling.
Rebuild the campaign from scratch around truthful, substantiated claims and have it re-reviewed before going live; the deception is structural, not a labelling fix.

campaign.title: RugPalace closing down sale
campaign.text: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots: 'CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! 70% off all handmade rugs before we shut our doors forever.' The campaign has run continuously for 14 months; company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly, and the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged. Radio spot adds 'last weekend, we mean it this time'.

detected_practices: going-out-of-business / closing-down sale claim
false urgency ('Final days', 'last weekend, we mean it this time')
perpetual sale (running 14 months with monthly new stock, no cessation of trade)
fake reference pricing (pre-sale prices never actually charged)
misleading discount claim (70% off)
generative AI use in campaign
personalisation/targeting
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers; no specific indication minors are targeted, though radio/outdoor are broad-reach channels. UCPD strongly engaged (closing-down sale that never closes, false urgency, fake reference pricing likely breaching Annex I blacklist item 15 and the Price Indication Directive). GDPR engaged via declared personalisation/targeting. AI Act transparency obligations engaged via declared generative AI use. DSA included as the campaign runs on web/online channels and may involve intermediary/platform advertising.
triage.summary: RugPalace runs a continuous 'closing down / everything must go' sale that has persisted for 14 months despite no cessation of trade and monthly new stock, using false urgency ('final days', 'last weekend, we mean it this time') and reference prices that were never actually charged. The campaign spans web, radio and outdoor channels targeting general EU adult consumers, and declares use of generative AI and personalisation/targeting. This presents strong indicators of misleading and unfair commercial practices, plus data-processing and AI-transparency concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares that generative AI is used to produce campaign assets deployed across web banners, homepage and weekly radio spots (synthetic image, audio and/or text). Under Art. 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The submission gives no indication that any such marking is applied to the AI-generated assets, so the obligation is engaged and appears unmet as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm which campaign assets (banner visuals, homepage graphics/copy, radio audio) are AI-generated and ensure each carries machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., C2PA/watermarking) so it is detectable as artificially generated. Obtain and document confirmation from the AI-tool provider that outputs are marked; where the tool does not mark them, apply provenance metadata before publication and retain evidence for compliance records.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Art. 50(4) requires deployer disclosure only where AI generates/manipulates content constituting a deep fake (realistic depiction of real persons, places or events) or generates text on matters of public interest. The campaign material shows no synthetic real-person likeness, celebrity endorsement, realistic manipulated footage, or public-interest text, so this obligation is not squarely engaged on the facts. Flagged so that if any AI-generated realistic imagery of real people or synthetic 'testimonial' voices are in fact used, a clear AI-generation disclosure must be added.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Verify the AI-generated assets contain no deep-fake elements (synthetic likenesses of real persons, realistic manipulated video/audio, fabricated testimonials). If any are present, add a clear and prominent disclosure that the content was artificially generated or manipulated, at the point of exposure.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign uses deceptive false-urgency and fake closing-down messaging that materially distorts consumer decisions. Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that deploy manipulative or deceptive techniques to distort behaviour, but on the current facts the deception is human-authored ad copy and there is no evidence that an AI system is the mechanism producing the manipulation. The prohibition is therefore only marginally implicated; the misleading-practice dimension is properly addressed under UCPD. Flagged in case AI-driven personalisation is used to time or tailor these urgency cues to individuals.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Document how generative AI and the declared personalisation/targeting are actually used. If AI is used to adaptively time, tailor or intensify urgency/scarcity cues to exploit individual behaviour, reassess against the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition and cease any such AI-driven manipulative deployment; otherwise keep records showing AI is limited to asset generation, not behaviour-distorting persuasion.

verdicts.notes: The campaign expressly declares use of generative AI ("Declared use of generative AI: yes") across web banners, homepage and radio spots, which engages the AI Act's transparency/marking obligations for synthetic content (Art. 50(2)). Nothing in the submission indicates the AI-generated assets carry machine-readable provenance marking or any AI-generation disclosure. There is no evidence of deep fakes or synthetic real-person likenesses (so Art. 50(4) is not squarely engaged), and the deceptive/urgency elements are human-authored ad copy handled under UCPD rather than an AI-driven manipulative system under Art. 5(1)(a). Overall the AI Act exposure is a transparency-marking gap that is readily fixable.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/targeting of consumers on the web channel is automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (preferences, behaviour) and therefore constitutes profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This is the definitional trigger bringing the campaign within GDPR's profiling regime.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document what data is used for the targeting and confirm whether behavioural/segmentation profiling occurs, so the downstream lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations can be mapped and evidenced.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — generally consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign declares targeting but the material provides no lawful basis, consent flow, or LIA, so lawfulness of the processing is not demonstrated.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Establish and record a lawful basis for the targeting: implement GDPR-compliant consent capture (with ePrivacy consent for any web tracking/cookies) or complete and retain a legitimate-interest assessment before running personalised ads.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected on the web for targeting, Art. 13 requires that at the point of collection the controller provide identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and information about profiling. The campaign material contains no privacy information at the point of collection, so this transparency obligation is engaged and not shown to be met.
findings.evidence_quote: web homepage
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at every data-collection point on the web property (homepage, any forms/tracking), disclosing purposes, legal basis, retention and the existence of profiling, in line with Arts. 12 and 13.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct marketing triggers the absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3): consumers must be able to opt out of the targeting at any time, and this right must be explicitly presented. The campaign describes no opt-out or objection mechanism for the personalisation.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Present the right to object to direct-marketing profiling clearly and separately at the first communication and provide an easy, always-available opt-out that halts personalised targeting when exercised.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged through the campaign's declared use of personalisation/targeting, which on the web channel constitutes profiling of individuals (Art. 4(4)). The campaign text describes no lawful basis, no transparency/privacy notice at the point of data collection, and no direct-marketing opt-out mechanism, so the relevant obligations (Arts. 6(1), 13, 21) cannot be shown to be satisfied as described. There is no indication of special-category data, minor-targeting, or solely-automated decisions with legal/significant effect, so no critical GDPR breach is evident from the text; the primary unlawfulness of this campaign lies in pricing/urgency claims under UCPD, outside GDPR scope. These are documentation/design gaps to verify rather than proven breaches.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign declares personalisation/targeting and runs on the web. IF any part of the campaign is disseminated as advertising on a third-party online platform (social network, marketplace, ad network), that platform must ensure each ad is identifiable as an ad, discloses the advertiser and payer, and provides meaningful information on the main targeting parameters. As described, however, RugPalace advertises on its own homepage/banners and via radio/outdoor, which are not intermediary online platforms, so Art. 26(1) is not triggered on the current facts.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm the actual placement channels. If the ads run on any online platform, ensure ad-labelling, advertiser/payer identity and targeting-parameter disclosures are delivered by the platform in real time. If placement stays on the trader's own site/radio/outdoor, document that DSA Art. 26(1) is out of scope.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) flatly bans platform advertising targeted via profiling on GDPR Art. 9 special-category data. The campaign discloses targeting but gives no indication that sensitive attributes (health, religion, etc.) are used, and no online-platform placement is evidenced. Flagged only so the boundary is confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Verify that no targeting segments rely, directly or by inference, on special-category data. This is a hard prohibition for any platform-served ad regardless of consent.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The false-urgency and deceptive 'closing-down' messaging would constitute deceptive/manipulative interface design if presented within an online platform's interface (DSA Art. 25). However, Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms operating their own interfaces, not a rug retailer's marketing copy on its own site/radio/outdoor. The same conduct is squarely addressed under the UCPD (Art. 5 and Annex I) for all traders, which is another agent's remit. No DSA platform hook is established here.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... 'last weekend, we mean it this time'
findings.recommendation: Treat the perpetual 'closing-down'/false-urgency messaging as a UCPD matter. For DSA purposes, only if RugPalace operates or advertises within an online-platform interface should the deceptive-design analysis under Art. 25 be applied to that interface.

verdicts.notes: On the facts as submitted, the DSA is not clearly engaged. The DSA's advertising-transparency (Art. 26(1)), sensitive-data targeting ban (Art. 26(3)), recommender transparency (Art. 27), dark-patterns rule (Art. 25) and ad-repository duty (Art. 39) all attach to "providers of online platforms" (and, for Art. 39, VLOPs). The campaign is described as running on RugPalace's own storefront banners, homepage, radio and outdoor — a trader's own business website is not an intermediary "online platform," and there is no indication the ads are served on a third-party platform/VLOP. The deceptive "closing-down"/false-urgency conduct is real but is captured by the UCPD for all traders; under the DSA specifically it only bites if platform placement exists, which is not evidenced. Findings below are conditional flags to confirm the applicability boundary and cover the DSA angle should platform channels be added.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claim of ceasing trade
findings.rationale: Annex I point 15 prohibits in all circumstances claiming the trader is about to cease trading when this is not the case. The campaign has run continuously for 14 months, company filings show no cessation of trade, and new stock arrives monthly — so the 'closing down / shut our doors forever' claim is false. This is a per se blacklisted practice requiring no assessment of consumer effect.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! ... before we shut our doors forever.
findings.recommendation: Cease all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging immediately. Such claims may only be used if the business is genuinely and imminently ceasing to trade, with a definite end date and no ongoing restocking.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits in all circumstances falsely stating that a product will only be available on particular terms for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. The 'final days' and 'last weekend, we mean it this time' messaging has been repeated across a 14-month continuous run, making the limited-time claim demonstrably false. This is a per se blacklisted practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Remove all 'final days' / 'last weekend' / recurring deadline messaging. Only advertise a time-limited offer where the deadline is genuine and the terms actually expire on that date.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 makes a practice misleading where it deceives the average consumer as to the existence of a specific price advantage or the manner of price calculation, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Advertising '70% off' against 'pre-sale' reference prices that were never actually charged fabricates the price advantage, so the discount claim is false. (This also engages Price Indication Directive 98/6/EC Art. 6a on the lowest prior 30-day price, handled outside UCPD.)
findings.evidence_quote: 70% off all handmade rugs ... the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged
findings.recommendation: Base any discount claim on a genuine prior selling price that was actually charged — ideally the lowest price applied in the 30 days before the reduction. Discontinue references to fictitious 'pre-sale' prices and retain evidence substantiating every price-advantage claim.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 sets the general prohibition of unfair commercial practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer. The sustained perpetual-sale scheme, combining a false closing-down narrative, false urgency and fabricated reference pricing, is unfair as a whole and captured by the general clause even beyond the specific blacklisted items.
findings.evidence_quote: The campaign has run continuously for 14 months; company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly
findings.recommendation: Redesign the campaign to reflect the trader's genuine commercial situation — an ongoing business with real promotional offers — rather than a fictional liquidation, ensuring overall compliance with professional diligence.

verdicts.notes: This campaign presents multiple clear UCPD violations, including two blacklisted practices prohibited in all circumstances. A "closing down / everything must go" sale that has run continuously for 14 months while the trader has not ceased trading and receives new stock monthly is a false claim of ceasing to trade (Annex I point 15). The recurring "final days"/"last weekend, we mean it this time" messaging is a false urgency claim (Annex I point 7). The "70% off" against reference prices that were never charged is a misleading action on price advantage (Art. 6). No proof of substantiation exists in the material; the deception clearly can distort consumers' transactional decisions.

report.executive_summary: This "RugPalace closing down sale" campaign runs a perpetual liquidation narrative across web, radio and outdoor: it claims the store is closing forever, that it's the "final days"/"last weekend," and advertises "70% off." In reality the campaign has run continuously for 14 months, filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly, and the "pre-sale" reference prices were never actually charged. These are not grey areas — the "closing down" and "final days" claims are per se banned practices under the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (Annex I blacklist), and the fake "70% off" discount is a misleading action on price. This is the dominant, campaign-ending problem: the messaging must stop before the campaign can run at all. Secondary issues are readily fixable compliance gaps: because you declared generative AI, AI-generated assets likely need machine-readable "AI-generated" marking under the AI Act; and because you declared personalisation/targeting, you need a lawful basis, a privacy notice at data-collection points, and an opt-out under GDPR. The DSA is not triggered on the facts described (own website/radio/outdoor, not a third-party platform), but would apply if you place these ads on social networks or ad networks. Overall verdict: do not run this campaign as written.
recommendations: STOP immediately: remove all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging. This is a blacklisted practice (UCPD Annex I point 15) unless the business is genuinely and imminently closing with a fixed end date and no restocking.

STOP immediately: remove all 'final days', 'last weekend, we mean it this time' and recurring-deadline messaging. Repeating a 'limited time' claim over 14 months is a blacklisted false-urgency practice (UCPD Annex I point 7). Only advertise a deadline that is genuine and actually expires.

Fix the discount claim: base any '70% off' or similar on a real prior selling price that was actually charged (ideally the lowest price in the 30 days before the reduction, per Price Indication Directive Art. 6a). Drop the fictitious 'pre-sale' reference prices and keep evidence for every price claim.
Redesign the campaign to reflect reality: an ongoing business running genuine promotions, not a fictional liquidation.

AI Act: confirm which assets (banner visuals, homepage copy, radio audio) are AI-generated and ensure each carries machine-readable provenance marking so it is detectable as artificially generated; get written confirmation from your AI tool provider or apply the marking yourself before publication.
GDPR: establish and document a lawful basis for the web personalisation/targeting (consent flow or a legitimate-interest assessment, plus ePrivacy consent for cookies/tracking).

GDPR: add a clear, layered privacy notice at every web data-collection point disclosing purposes, legal basis, retention, rights and the existence of profiling (Arts. 12-13), and provide an easy, always-available opt-out from marketing profiling (Art. 21).

If you plan to place these ads on any third-party online platform (social/marketplace/ad network), ensure platform ad-transparency (advertiser/payer/targeting disclosure), confirm no special-category-data targeting, and avoid dark-pattern interface design under the DSA.
Verify AI-generated assets contain no deep-fake elements (synthetic real-person likenesses, fabricated testimonial voices); if any exist, add a prominent AI-generation disclosure.

campaign.title: FlashSale mattress countdown
campaign.text: Own-brand webshop promotion for the CloudRest mattress. Every product page shows a red banner: 'HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41' with a live countdown, and 'Only 3 left in stock!'. The countdown resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns, and stock is not actually limited (fulfilment is made-to-order with 2,000+ units weekly capacity). Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.

detected_practices: countdown timer (fake/resetting urgency)
false scarcity claim ('Only 3 left in stock!')
false deadline / recurring 'last chance, tonight only' messaging
persistent false urgency across web and email
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers; no evidence minors are specifically targeted. Email campaign implies collection/processing of email addresses (personal data), so GDPR consent/marketing-communication rules should be checked despite no declared personalisation.
triage.summary: Own-brand webshop promotion for the CloudRest mattress using a resetting countdown timer and a false 'Only 3 left' scarcity claim despite unlimited made-to-order capacity, plus weekly 'last chance, tonight only' emails. The urgency and scarcity claims are demonstrably false, raising clear misleading/aggressive commercial practice concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The weekly email blast constitutes processing of personal data (recipients' email addresses) for direct marketing. Under Art. 6(1), and consistent with ePrivacy rules referenced there, unsolicited email marketing to consumers generally requires prior consent (or the narrow soft opt-in for existing customers). The campaign text does not establish any lawful basis for the recipient list, so it is unclear whether the mailing is lawful.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Document a valid lawful basis for the email list: obtain prior opt-in consent, or rely on the ePrivacy 'soft opt-in' only for existing customers marketing similar products, and retain records evidencing that basis for each recipient.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct-marketing email must give the recipient an easy, always-available way to object (unsubscribe), and objection must be honoured immediately and permanently. The recurring weekly mailing engages the absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3), but the campaign text does not mention any unsubscribe mechanism or suppression handling.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, one-click unsubscribe link in every email and honour objections immediately by adding addresses to a permanent suppression list so no further Thursday blasts are sent.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: If email addresses are collected via the webshop (e.g. at checkout or a sign-up form), Art. 13 requires that recipients be told at the point of collection about the controller's identity, the direct-marketing purpose and legal basis, retention, and their rights including the right to object. The submission does not show that this information is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Own-brand webshop promotion for the CloudRest mattress
findings.recommendation: Ensure the sign-up/checkout point where emails are captured presents a concise privacy notice (or link) covering identity, marketing purpose, legal basis, retention period and the right to object under Art. 21.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged only through the recurring email blast, which processes email addresses (personal data) for direct marketing. There is no personalisation, profiling, special-category data, or child targeting, so most GDPR provisions are not implicated. The campaign text is silent on the lawful basis, transparency information, and opt-out mechanism for the email channel; these obligations are engaged but cannot be confirmed as met, so they warrant attention rather than a confirmed breach. The core misleading/urgency issues fall under UCPD, not GDPR.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: A resetting countdown timer falsely states that the sale/price will only be available for a very limited time. Because the deadline is never real (it perpetually renews), this is precisely the fake countdown timer that Annex I point 7 blacklists to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of an informed choice. It is prohibited in all circumstances with no case-by-case assessment required.
findings.evidence_quote: HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41' with a live countdown ... The countdown resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns
findings.recommendation: Remove the resetting countdown entirely. Only display a timer if it reflects a genuine, single, non-renewing deadline that is honoured (the price actually changes when it expires). If there is no real deadline, do not display any countdown.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The stock claim is false: fulfilment is made-to-order with 2,000+ units weekly capacity, so availability is effectively unlimited. Falsely stating a product is available for a very limited time / in very limited quantity to pressure an immediate decision is a blacklisted practice under Annex I point 7 (expressly covering false 'only X left' stock claims), prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: Only 3 left in stock!
findings.recommendation: Delete the 'Only 3 left in stock!' message. Do not display any stock-scarcity indicator unless it reflects the true, real-time available quantity. For made-to-order products with ample capacity, no scarcity messaging is justifiable.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The weekly repetition of 'last chance, tonight only' falsely represents each Thursday as a genuine final opportunity when the same offer recurs indefinitely. This is a false statement that the product is available on particular terms for a very limited time, blacklisted under Annex I point 7 regardless of consumer impact.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday
findings.recommendation: Stop describing a recurring weekly promotion as 'last chance' or 'tonight only'. Use accurate framing (e.g., 'weekly offer') and only use finality language for a genuinely one-off, non-repeating deadline.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Independently of the blacklist, these claims contain false information regarding the availability of the product and the existence of a limited-time price advantage, and are likely to cause the average consumer to take a transactional (purchase) decision they would not otherwise have taken. This is a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Only 3 left in stock!'. The countdown resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns, and stock is not actually limited
findings.recommendation: Ensure all availability, deadline and price-advantage statements are truthful and substantiated. Base any urgency messaging on real, verifiable facts about stock and offer duration.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of a perpetually resetting timer, permanent false scarcity, and weekly 'last chance, tonight only' emails applies sustained, artificial time pressure across channels. Such persistent, high-pressure tactics can constitute undue influence that significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice under Arts. 8-9, particularly given the manufactured and relentless nature of the pressure.
findings.evidence_quote: persistent false urgency across web and email
findings.recommendation: Remove the coordinated, recurring pressure tactics. Any genuine promotional urgency should be occasional, truthful, and not reinforced by artificial resetting or repeated false deadlines across web and email.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys demonstrably false urgency and scarcity claims: a countdown timer that resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns, an "Only 3 left in stock!" message despite unlimited made-to-order capacity (2,000+ units/week), and weekly "last chance, tonight only" emails. These are per se prohibited under UCPD Annex I point 7 (blacklisted false limited-availability claims), with no need to assess consumer-harm thresholds. The same conduct also constitutes a misleading action (Art. 6) and, given its persistent cross-channel pressure, engages the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9). Multiple critical violations are present.

report.executive_summary: Your FlashSale campaign for the CloudRest mattress uses two urgency tactics that are outright banned under EU consumer law: a countdown timer that secretly resets to three hours (so the "deadline" is never real) and an "Only 3 left in stock!" message even though you can make 2,000+ units a week to order. The weekly "last chance, tonight only" email repeats the same false-finality problem. These are on the EU's blacklist of practices that are illegal in all circumstances (UCPD Annex I, point 7) — no defence or context assessment applies, so they carry the highest risk. Separately, the same conduct is a misleading action and, taken together across web and email, edges into aggressive, high-pressure selling. There is also a secondary, lower-priority issue: the weekly email blast needs a proper legal basis (consent or the customer soft opt-in), a privacy notice at sign-up, and a working one-click unsubscribe — none of which are documented. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. Bottom line: the campaign cannot run in its current form and needs the fake timer and stock claims removed before launch.
recommendations: Immediately remove the resetting countdown timer. Only show a timer if it reflects a single, genuine, non-renewing deadline that is actually honoured (the price truly changes when it expires); otherwise show no timer at all.
Delete the 'Only 3 left in stock!' message. For a made-to-order product with 2,000+ units/week capacity, no scarcity claim is justifiable — only ever display real-time true stock levels.
Stop framing a recurring weekly promotion as 'last chance' or 'tonight only'. Use accurate wording such as 'weekly offer'; reserve finality language for genuinely one-off deadlines.
Eliminate the coordinated cross-channel pressure so that any remaining urgency is occasional and truthful, avoiding artificial reinforcement between web and email.

findings.rationale: The campaign prominently markets AI while the deployer declares no generative AI in the campaign assets. The campaign's deceptive elements (guaranteed/risk-free returns, fabricated testimonials, fake economist quote, inflated social proof) are human-crafted marketing copy properly addressed under UCPD/DSA, not by the AI Act — which regulates AI systems, not the truthfulness of claims. The product "AI trading signals" is a marketed product feature, not an AI system deployed to manipulate consumers, and the deployer declares no generative AI. The single AI-Act-relevant risk is a latent Art. 50(4) transparency obligation: the fabricated endorsement of a real TV economist runs in a video (YouTube pre-roll) channel, so if that likeness/voice were produced or manipulated with AI it would be an undisclosed deep fake.
