Financial/investment claims and misleading endorsements make vulnerable audiences a concern. Note: declaration of 'no AI' contradicts the campaign copy touting 'AI signals' — flag for AI Act specialist to assess whether AI is genuinely used or the claim is itself misleading. No personalisation/targeting or personal data collection declared, so GDPR is not clearly engaged, but the fabricated endorsement and false claims strongly engage UCPD, DSA (advertising transparency/illegal-content on platforms), and AI Act (misleading AI claims).
triage.summary: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll campaign for a 499 EUR crypto trading course promising guaranteed, risk-free returns via 'AI signals', supported by fabricated testimonials, invented customers, a false celebrity economist endorsement and inflated student numbers. The campaign contains multiple hallmark misleading and aggressive commercial practices targeting EU consumers around a high-risk financial product. Despite the declaration of no AI use, the product itself markets 'AI signals', so AI-related claims warrant review.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: If the fabricated endorsement of the real TV economist is realised through AI-generated or AI-manipulated image, audio or video (a deep fake of an identifiable real person), the deployer must disclose that the content is artificially generated/manipulated under Art. 50(4). An undisclosed synthetic likeness of a real public figure endorsing a product squarely engages this obligation. Because the campaign declares 'no generative AI', the medium of the fabrication is unclear and must be verified; a purely textual invented quote would not, by itself, trigger Art. 50(4) but would still be misleading under UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Confirm how the economist endorsement was produced. If any AI-generated/manipulated audio, image or video of the real person is used, cease it (it is also a false endorsement) — but at minimum add a clear, prominent disclosure that the depiction is artificially generated/manipulated. Reconcile the 'no AI' declaration with the actual assets.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: If the invented testimonial personas, images or copy were produced with generative AI (synthetic images/text presented as real customers), Art. 50(2) requires the outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign describes fabricated personas, so if generative AI produced them the marking obligation applies. The submission's 'no AI' declaration is inconsistent with the AI-heavy nature of the assets and must be clarified.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented
findings.recommendation: Audit the origin of all testimonial imagery and copy. Where any asset is AI-generated, apply machine-readable provenance/marking as required by Art. 50(2) (in addition to removing the fabricated/unverifiable testimonials, which are independently unlawful). Update the campaign's AI-use declaration to reflect reality.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition targets AI systems that deploy manipulative or deceptive techniques to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm. The promoted 'AI signals' trading tool, marketed to consumers as risk-free/guaranteed for a high-risk financial product, could — if the AI system itself operationally deceives or manipulates users into harmful financial decisions — fall within this prohibition. On the current text the manipulation appears to reside in human-authored ad copy rather than in the AI system's operation, so this is flagged for monitoring rather than as a confirmed breach. Significant financial harm to consumers is the relevant harm threshold.
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Obtain details of the 'AI signals' system: what it does, the claims made in-product, and whether it is designed/used to nudge users toward harmful trading decisions. If the AI system itself deploys deceptive/manipulative techniques causing significant financial harm, it is prohibited under Art. 5(1)(a) and cannot be marketed or used.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core misleading/aggressive practices (guaranteed returns, fake testimonials, fabricated endorsement, false social proof) are primarily UCPD/DSA matters. The AI Act is engaged only conditionally: the ads tout "AI signals" (product claim) and use fabricated assets (invented testimonials, stock-photo personas, a fabricated celebrity quote) that MAY have been AI-generated/manipulated, which would trigger Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking and Art. 50(4) deep-fake/synthetic-content disclosure. The declaration of "no generative AI" conflicts with the "AI signals" copy and prevents confirming whether Chapter II transparency duties apply — this must be clarified. The Art. 5 prohibitions are not clearly engaged as described, because the manipulative content is human-authored ad copy rather than an AI system deployed to distort behaviour, though the point warrants monitoring.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The landing page is an online interface that deceives and manipulates recipients through fabricated testimonials, invented customers, stock-photo personas and a false expert endorsement, materially distorting users' ability to make a free and informed purchasing decision. Combined with 'guaranteed'/'RISK-FREE' claims contradicted by buried 'results may vary' fine print, this is a deceptive interface design squarely within the Art. 25 prohibition of dark patterns.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course.
findings.recommendation: Remove all fabricated testimonials, invented customer names/stock photos and the fake TV-economist endorsement. Only display genuine, verifiable customer statements and real, authorised endorsements. Eliminate the contradiction between headline guarantees and disclaimer fine print by removing the unsubstantiated 'guaranteed'/'risk-free' claims entirely.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Ads presented on an online platform (YouTube) must let recipients clearly identify, in real time, that the content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The campaign relies on editorial-style testimonials and a purported expert recommendation that blur commercial intent; the advertiser must ensure the platform receives accurate information (advertiser identity, paid-for status) so the ad is unambiguously identifiable as such.
findings.evidence_quote: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads for a 499 EUR crypto trading course
findings.recommendation: Ensure the campaign is served through the platform's ad system with clear 'advertisement' labelling and truthful advertiser identity, and that no landing-page content masquerades as independent editorial or third-party endorsement. Supply the platform with accurate 'paid by / on behalf of' information.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The content is high-risk 'get-rich-quick' investment material distributed on a platform with no robust age gating, so minors could plausibly be reached. Art. 28's specific ban targets profiling-based advertising to minors; since the campaign declares no profiling or personalised targeting, the core prohibition is not clearly triggered, but the reachability of minors and the duty to ensure a high level of safety for minors warrant attention.
findings.evidence_quote: YouTube pre-roll ads
findings.recommendation: Confirm no profiling or behavioural targeting is used (which would trigger the Art. 28(2) ban if minors are reached with reasonable certainty). Apply available platform age-appropriate delivery controls and exclude audiences that cannot be verified as adults for this high-risk financial product.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs paid ads on an online platform (YouTube pre-roll) and drives to a landing page, so the DSA is engaged. The most directly applicable provision is Art. 25 (prohibition of dark patterns): the landing page uses fabricated testimonials, invented customer names, a fake celebrity-economist endorsement and contradictory fine print, all designed to deceive and materially distort users' ability to make free and informed decisions. Ad-transparency (Art. 26(1)) is engaged as an obligation, but is chiefly platform-facing; the disguised, editorial-style deceptive content still undermines identifiability. The Art. 26(3)/Art. 28 profiling-ad bans are not clearly triggered because no profiling or personalised targeting is declared, though minors reachability is worth noting.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: The trader admits to inventing consumer testimonials (invented names, stock photos, fabricated results) and fabricating an expert endorsement quote. Submitting or misrepresenting false consumer reviews/endorsements to promote a product is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances — no unfairness balancing is required.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Remove all invented testimonials and the fabricated economist quote entirely. Only use genuine reviews from real, verifiable customers who actually purchased the course, with steps in place to confirm authenticity. Any expert endorsement must be real, authorised in writing, and accurately quoted.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: Presenting a well-known economist as recommending the course when this is fabricated creates a false impression of endorsement/approval by a recognised authoritative person. Falsely claiming endorsement is a per se prohibited blacklist practice.
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Delete the fabricated endorsement. Do not imply recommendation or approval by any named expert, body or authority unless you hold documented, authorised proof of a genuine endorsement.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Describing a crypto trading product as 'RISK-FREE' with 'guaranteed' returns and a specific 40x profit in 90 days is false/deceptive about the main characteristics and results of the product. Crypto investment is inherently high-risk and returns cannot be guaranteed; the claim is likely to cause consumers to make a transactional decision (buying the 499 EUR course) they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days — our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Remove all 'risk-free', 'guaranteed returns' and specific profit-multiplier claims. Investment marketing must present balanced, substantiated information and prominent risk warnings; do not promise or imply any guaranteed or specific financial outcome.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: A small-print 'results may vary' disclaimer cannot correct headline claims of guaranteed, risk-free returns; material risk information is provided in an unclear, untimely and inadequate manner while the dominant message remains deceptive. Material information the average consumer needs (real risk of loss, absence of any guarantee, basis for the 50,000 figure) is omitted or hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: Fine print says results may vary
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, prominent risk disclosure at the point of the claim, not buried in fine print. Disclaimers cannot contradict the main message — the main message itself must be truthful. Substantiate or remove the '50,000 students' figure.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The '50,000 students' figure is used as social proof to influence purchase. Given the campaign's admitted fabrication of other social-proof elements, this unverified/inflated figure deceives consumers about the popularity and track record of the product — a main characteristic influencing the transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Join 50,000 students
findings.recommendation: Only state student numbers that are true and can be evidenced. If the figure cannot be substantiated, remove it.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Framing a high-risk financial product as guaranteed and risk-free, aimed at people wanting to make money quickly and potentially reaching financially vulnerable individuals, applies undue influence that can materially impair consumers' freedom of choice. Combined with the get-rich-quick funnel structure this edges toward an aggressive practice.
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Avoid pressure/undue-influence framing that exploits consumers' desire for quick financial gain. Present the product neutrally with honest risk information and no coercive 'guaranteed wealth' messaging.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort economic behaviour, including of credulous or financially vulnerable audiences (Art. 5(3)) who may be reached by unrestricted YouTube/search distribution of get-rich-quick content. The cumulative deception reinforces overall unfairness.
findings.evidence_quote: crypto trading course
findings.recommendation: Re-design the campaign to meet professional-diligence standards for financial promotions, ensure it does not exploit credulous/vulnerable groups, and apply appropriate audience safeguards for a high-risk investment product.

verdicts.notes: This campaign contains multiple hallmark unfair commercial practices, several of which are blacklisted per se prohibitions under Annex I that are unlawful in all circumstances (fabricated testimonials/endorsements). The core "guaranteed / risk-free returns" and "250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days" claims are misleading actions under Art. 6 that a boilerplate "results may vary" disclaimer cannot cure. Combined with a fabricated expert endorsement, invented customers and an unverifiable "50,000 students" figure, the campaign is very likely unfair. High-pressure, guaranteed-profit framing of a high-risk financial product also raises aggressive-practice and vulnerable-audience concerns.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets a 499 EUR crypto trading course using "guaranteed", "risk-free" returns and a "250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days" promise, backed by invented customer testimonials, stock-photo personas, an unverified "50,000 students" figure and a fabricated endorsement from a real TV economist. As currently described, it cannot run in the EU. Multiple elements are outright banned in all circumstances under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I): fake testimonials/endorsements and falsely claiming an expert's approval. The "risk-free/guaranteed returns" claims are misleading actions under the UCPD that a small-print "results may vary" disclaimer cannot fix. The deceptive landing page also amounts to a prohibited "dark pattern" under the Digital Services Act, and the paid ads must be clearly and truthfully labelled as advertising. Finally, your "no AI" declaration conflicts with the "AI signals" product claim and the fabricated assets — if any testimonial images or the economist endorsement were AI-generated, the AI Act requires disclosure/marking (and a synthetic likeness of a real person is separately unlawful). Bottom line: this is a high-legal-exposure, get-rich-quick funnel that needs to be rebuilt from the ground up before it can be published.
recommendations: STOP the campaign in its current form — several elements are per se prohibited (banned in all circumstances) and cannot be published while present.
Delete the fabricated TV-economist endorsement entirely. Any expert endorsement must be genuine, documented and authorised in writing (UCPD Annex I points 4 & 23c — critical).

Remove ALL invented testimonials, made-up customer names and stock-photo personas (e.g. 'Marta from Sevilla'). Only use verifiable statements from real customers who actually bought the course (UCPD Annex I point 23c — critical).

Remove every 'RISK-FREE', 'guaranteed returns' and specific profit-multiplier claim (e.g. '250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days'). Replace with balanced, substantiated messaging and prominent risk warnings at the point of claim — a 'results may vary' disclaimer does NOT cure this (UCPD Arts. 6 & 7 — critical/high).
Substantiate or delete the '50,000 students' figure; only claim numbers you can evidence (UCPD Art. 6 — high).
Fix the deceptive landing-page design so it no longer manipulates purchase decisions; the page must not masquerade as independent editorial or third-party endorsement (DSA Art. 25 — high).

Reconcile your 'no generative AI' declaration with the 'AI signals' product claim and the fabricated assets. Audit the origin of all testimonial imagery and the economist depiction; if any were AI-generated/manipulated, apply required marking/disclosure — and note a synthetic likeness of a real person is separately unlawful (AI Act Art. 50(2)/(4)).
Ensure the search and YouTube ads are served through the platforms' ad systems with clear 'advertisement' labelling and truthful advertiser identity (DSA Art. 26).
Confirm no profiling/behavioural targeting is used and apply age-appropriate delivery controls so this high-risk financial content is not served to minors (DSA Art. 28).
Obtain and document full details of the 'AI signals' tool; if the system itself deceives or manipulates users into harmful trading decisions it may be a prohibited practice (AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)).

Re-design the funnel to meet professional-diligence standards for financial promotions and avoid pressure/undue-influence framing that exploits people's desire for quick gains or targets vulnerable audiences (UCPD Arts. 5, 8-9).

campaign.title: CryptoMasterclass — guaranteed returns funnel
campaign.text: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads for a 499 EUR crypto trading course: 'Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days — our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed. Join 50,000 students.' Landing page shows testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course. Fine print says results may vary.

detected_practices: guaranteed returns claim
risk-free investment claim
unrealistic income/earnings claims
fabricated testimonials with stock photos and invented names
fake celebrity endorsement (fabricated TV economist quote)
misleading 'results may vary' fine print contradicting headline claims
social proof claim ('Join 50,000 students')
AI-generated trading signals promoted
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'adults interested in investing,' but no age-gating is described and YouTube pre-roll/search ads can reach minors, so under-18 reach cannot be excluded. The declared 'no personalisation' is contradicted by the funnel/ad-platform context, which typically involves behavioural targeting and ad-delivery data — GDPR flagged conservatively. Declared 'no generative AI' is inconsistent with the promoted 'AI signals' and likely AI-generated/synthetic promotional content; AI Act flagged for verification.
triage.summary: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll campaign for a 499 EUR crypto trading course making guaranteed, risk-free return promises alongside fabricated testimonials and a fake celebrity endorsement, contradicted only by fine print. The campaign advertises AI trading signals and runs on search/video platforms targeting EU consumers.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: A fabricated endorsement attributed to a real, identifiable public figure is precisely the deep-fake / synthetic-likeness scenario Art. 50(4) targets. The campaign declares 'no generative AI', but a fabricated quote from a named real economist strongly suggests synthetically created or manipulated likeness/statement content. If this quote (or any accompanying image/audio/video of the economist) was AI-generated or AI-manipulated, the deployer must clearly disclose that it is artificially generated. No such disclosure is described.
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Verify the origin of the celebrity quote and any associated media. If it is AI-generated/manipulated, it must be clearly disclosed as artificially generated. Best practice: remove the fabricated endorsement entirely, since an invented endorsement of a real person is independently unlawful regardless of AI disclosure.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: If the testimonial imagery, personas or copy were produced with a generative AI system, Art. 50(2) requires the provider to mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format as artificially generated. The declaration of 'no generative AI' is inconsistent with the fabricated nature of these assets, so AI generation cannot be excluded and marking obligations may be unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month')
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether testimonial images/text are AI-generated. If so, ensure machine-readable synthetic-content marking is applied and retained. Note that fabricated testimonials presented as real consumers are unlawful under consumer law irrespective of AI marking, so removal is the safer course.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign promotes an AI-based trading-signal system with guaranteed/risk-free framing. Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that deploy manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting behaviour and likely to cause significant harm. If the promoted 'AI signals' system itself generates deceptive outputs (e.g., presenting fabricated 'guaranteed' predictions) that impair investors' informed decision-making and cause financial harm, the prohibition could be engaged. On the facts, the deception is largely in human-authored ad copy, so this is flagged for verification rather than as a confirmed AI-driven manipulation.
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the underlying AI signals system produces or presents deceptive risk-free/guaranteed outputs to users. Ensure the AI system does not generate misleading assurances of guaranteed returns; substantiate or remove such claims and clearly communicate genuine risk of loss.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems exploiting vulnerabilities arising from age or a specific economic situation to distort behaviour causing significant harm. The offer appeals to people seeking quick financial gains (potentially those in financial distress) and, per triage, under-18 reach cannot be excluded. If the promoted AI system is used to target or tailor this offer to such vulnerable groups, the prohibition could be engaged. As described the targeting is not AI-driven ('no personalisation' declared), so this is a verification flag only.
findings.evidence_quote: Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days
findings.recommendation: Confirm no AI system is used to identify or target financially vulnerable individuals or minors with this high-risk investment offer. Implement age-gating and exclude vulnerability-based targeting; avoid any AI-driven optimisation toward users in financial distress.

verdicts.notes: The AI Act's obligations attach to actual AI systems and AI-generated/manipulated content. The campaign declares "no generative AI" but promotes "AI signals" and contains fabricated assets (invented testimonials with stock photos, a fabricated celebrity quote) whose provenance is unverified. Whether the AI Act bites depends on verification: if the fabricated endorsement/testimonials are AI-generated or deep fakes, Art. 50(4)/(2) transparency and marking duties apply, and if any AI system is used to deploy the deceptive persuasion, Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition could be engaged. The core misleading-advertising harm here is primarily a UCPD matter; AI Act findings are flagged for verification rather than as confirmed breaches.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle requires that personal data be processed fairly and transparently. Any personal data collected on a landing page whose entire persuasive context is built on fabricated testimonials, invented identities and a fake endorsement is obtained through a deceptive environment, undermining the fairness and transparency of processing. The declared 'no personalisation' further conflicts with the ad-platform funnel context, suggesting hidden tracking inconsistent with transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated/deceptive content and ensure that any data captured in the funnel is collected in a truthful, transparent context; provide a clear, accurate account of who collects data and why at every collection point.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll delivery, plus a conversion funnel, typically involve behavioural/ad-delivery data and tracking that require a valid lawful basis (consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment). The submission declares no personalisation yet the funnel/ad-platform context contradicts this, and no lawful basis for any tracking or lead processing is described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: no
findings.recommendation: Map all personal-data processing in the campaign (ad measurement, retargeting pixels, landing-page tracking, lead capture) and document a valid Art. 6(1) basis for each; obtain consent for any non-essential tracking and reconcile the 'no personalisation' declaration with actual ad-platform behaviour.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: A sales funnel for a paid course will capture personal data (e.g. sign-up/lead/checkout details). Article 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller's identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights (including any profiling) be provided. No such transparency information is described anywhere in the campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads for a 499 EUR crypto trading course
findings.recommendation: Add a layered privacy notice at every data-collection point (lead forms, checkout) covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights, including any profiling/automated decision-making.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The campaign runs on search and YouTube pre-roll with no age-gating described, so reach of under-16s (Art. 8 threshold, subject to national lowering to 13) cannot be excluded. If consent is used to process data of a child via this information-society-service funnel, parental consent and reasonable age-verification efforts are required; none are described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults interested in investing
findings.recommendation: Implement age-assurance/age-gating before data collection, exclude under-age reach in ad-platform settings, and put parental-consent mechanisms in place should the service ever collect data from users below the applicable digital-consent age.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Audience segmentation, ad delivery optimisation and retargeting on search/video platforms typically constitute profiling under Art. 4(4). Because profiling is likely present despite the 'no personalisation' declaration, the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency about profiling, right to object) are engaged and must be addressed.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: search, video
findings.recommendation: Assess whether ad delivery/retargeting amounts to profiling; if so, disclose it in the privacy notice, secure the correct lawful basis, and ensure the campaign does not silently profile individuals contrary to the 'no personalisation' declaration.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Where the funnel leads to direct-marketing processing (e.g. follow-up emails to captured leads or retargeting), data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and related profiling. The campaign describes no opt-out or objection mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy opt-out from direct marketing and related profiling in all communications and honour objections immediately across all systems.

verdicts.notes: The campaign does not describe an explicit data-collection flow, but as a paid search/YouTube pre-roll funnel driving to a sales landing page for a 499 EUR course, it necessarily involves personal-data processing (ad-delivery/behavioural data and landing-page lead capture). The declared "no personalisation" is inconsistent with the ad-platform funnel context, and no lawful basis, transparency notice, or age-gating is described. GDPR risks centre on lawfulness/fairness/transparency (Arts. 5(1)(a), 6(1), 13/12), likely profiling (Art. 4(4)), and unmitigated potential reach of minors (Art. 8). Findings are conservative because the collection mechanics are not fully specified in the submission.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The declared audience is adults, but no age-gating or age-assurance is described and YouTube pre-roll/search ads are accessible to minors, so under-18 reach cannot be excluded. Art. 28 requires online platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security and prohibits profiling-based ads to recipients reasonably known to be minors. A 499 EUR high-risk crypto trading product with 'guaranteed'/'risk-free' framing reaching unverified minors sits squarely within the minors-protection concern; any behavioural ad delivery that captures minors would breach the profiling ban.
findings.evidence_quote: adults interested in investing
findings.recommendation: Apply platform age-gating / audience-exclusion controls to restrict delivery to verified adults, disable any profiling-based delivery, and configure the campaign so it cannot be served to recipients who may be minors; document the age-assurance measures used on YouTube and search.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires recipients to be able to identify, clearly and unambiguously, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. Presenting fabricated third-party endorsements and invented testimonials within a platform ad obscures the true commercial nature and the identity of the party behind the message, undermining the transparency the platform must ensure. The advertiser must supply accurate advertiser/payer information and must not disguise paid promotion as independent editorial recommendation.
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Ensure all ad creatives are clearly identifiable as advertising on whose behalf they run, remove the fabricated endorsement and invented testimonials, and provide the platform with accurate advertiser and payer details so the required Art. 26(1) disclosures are truthful.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits online-platform interfaces that deceive or manipulate recipients or materially impair informed decision-making, including disguised advertising and false hierarchy of information. Where the campaign runs inside the VLOP ad experience, prominent 'guaranteed'/'risk-free' claims paired with contradicting, de-emphasised fine print and disguised testimonial content reflect the deceptive-design pattern Art. 25 targets. (The substantive misleading-claim assessment is primarily UCPD.)
findings.evidence_quote: Fine print says results may vary
findings.recommendation: Give material qualifications equal prominence to headline claims within the ad experience, and avoid presenting paid promotional content in a form that disguises its commercial nature or manipulates the recipient's decision.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: YouTube is a designated VLOP, so under Art. 39 the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach will be published in a public ad repository. The campaign's claims and any targeting will be subject to public and regulator scrutiny via the repository.
findings.evidence_quote: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads
findings.recommendation: Assume every creative and targeting parameter will be publicly archived; ensure all archived ad content is truthful and defensible before launch.

verdicts.notes: The DSA binds providers of online platforms rather than advertisers directly, but this campaign runs on YouTube (a designated VLOP) and paid search, so several DSA obligations are engaged in the ad-delivery context. The most substantive DSA concern is minors protection (Art. 28): the ad promotes a high-risk financial product with no described age-gating on channels that reach under-18s. Ad transparency (Art. 26(1)) and dark-pattern (Art. 25) obligations are engaged where fabricated endorsements and disguised testimonial content sit inside the platform ad experience, and Art. 39 means the ad and its targeting will be publicly archived. The core deceptive-claim issues (guaranteed returns, fake endorsement, fine print) are primarily UCPD matters handled by another agent.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Claiming a 499 EUR crypto trading course delivers 'risk-free' and 'guaranteed' returns is false information about the main characteristics and results of the product. Crypto trading is inherently volatile and cannot be risk-free or guaranteed; the claim deceives the average consumer about benefits/results and is likely to cause a transactional decision (paying 499 EUR) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Remove all 'risk-free' and 'guaranteed returns' language entirely. Investment/trading education must include prominent, truthful risk warnings and must not promise specific or guaranteed financial outcomes.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: A specific 40x-in-90-days earnings projection is an unsubstantiated and misleading claim about the results achievable, deceiving consumers about the product's main characteristics and likely distorting their purchasing decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days
findings.recommendation: Delete unrealistic income/earnings projections. Do not present specific return figures unless independently substantiated and typical; educational products should not advertise investment performance at all.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Fabricating consumer testimonials using stock photos and invented names, and a fabricated quote attributed to a well-known TV economist, is submitting/commissioning false consumer reviews and endorsements and misrepresenting endorsements. This is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month')
findings.recommendation: Remove all fabricated testimonials and the fabricated celebrity quote. Only use genuine, verifiable testimonials from real consumers who used the product, with their consent, and no invented or synthetic identities.

findings.title: Blacklist: unverified consumer reviews
findings.rationale: Presenting invented reviews as if submitted by real consumers who used the product, with no reasonable steps taken to verify they originate from genuine customers, is a blacklisted practice.
findings.evidence_quote: names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month')
findings.recommendation: Only publish reviews after implementing a genuine verification process confirming the reviewer actually purchased/used the course; remove all unverified or fictitious reviews.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: Presenting a fabricated endorsement from a well-known economist falsely claims the course has been endorsed/recommended by a recognised authority when it has not. This false endorsement claim is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated economist endorsement immediately. Only cite endorsements that are genuine, documented, and made with the endorser's authorisation.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: A buried 'results may vary' disclaimer that directly contradicts the prominent headline claims of 'guaranteed' and 'risk-free' returns provides material information in an unclear, untimely and hidden manner, and does not cure the misleading headline. This is a misleading omission/obscuring of material information.
findings.evidence_quote: Fine print says results may vary
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on fine-print disclaimers to offset headline claims. Material risk information must be equally prominent, and the headline claims must be truthful in their own right rather than corrected by fine print.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The '50,000 students' social-proof figure, presented alongside fabricated testimonials and false claims, is an unsubstantiated claim about the product's take-up that may deceive consumers about its popularity and credibility unless it can be verified.
findings.evidence_quote: Join 50,000 students.
findings.recommendation: Substantiate the student count with verifiable records before use, or remove it. Ensure all social-proof figures are accurate and evidenced.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Taken as a whole, the campaign is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer (and of credulous/inexperienced would-be investors as a vulnerable group under Art. 5(3)) by combining false guarantees with fabricated proof. The general unfairness safety-net applies to the overall funnel design.
findings.evidence_quote: guaranteed returns funnel
findings.recommendation: Redesign the campaign so that it meets professional diligence: truthful performance representation, genuine evidence, prominent risk disclosures, and no manipulative funnel tactics exploiting inexperienced investors.

verdicts.notes: This crypto-course campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including several outright blacklisted (Annex I) practices that are unfair in all circumstances regardless of consumer effect. The core "risk-free" and "guaranteed returns" claims are false/deceptive under Art. 6 for an inherently volatile investment product, and the invented testimonials with stock photos and a fabricated celebrity endorsement are blacklisted fake reviews/endorsements (points 23b/23c/4). A boilerplate "results may vary" disclaimer cannot cure headline claims that are literally false and contradicted by the fine print (Art. 7). Overall a high-risk, likely-illegal campaign requiring substantial redesign or withdrawal.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes a 499 EUR crypto trading course on Google Search and YouTube using "risk-free" and "guaranteed returns" claims, a promise to turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days, invented customer testimonials with stock photos, and a fabricated endorsement from a real TV economist. As submitted, it cannot run legally in the EU. The most serious problems are consumer-protection breaches: promising guaranteed/risk-free returns for a volatile product is a misleading action, and the fake testimonials and fabricated celebrity endorsement are "blacklisted" practices that are illegal in all circumstances — no disclaimer or fine print can fix them. On top of that, running to a broad audience with no age controls on YouTube/Search creates minors-protection and profiling risks under the DSA and GDPR, and the "no personalisation / no AI" declarations don't match a paid ad-funnel context, so data handling and any AI-generated assets need verification. The fabricated economist quote may also trigger AI Act deep-fake disclosure duties if it was AI-generated. Bottom line: this campaign should not launch in its current form and needs a fundamental rebuild, not tweaks.
recommendations: Do not launch. The campaign contains illegal-in-all-circumstances practices (fake testimonials, invented reviewer identities, and a fabricated celebrity endorsement) that must be removed entirely before anything else.

Delete all 'risk-free' and 'guaranteed returns' claims and the '250 EUR to 10,000 EUR in 90 days' projection. Educational trading products must not promise specific or guaranteed financial outcomes and must carry prominent, truthful risk warnings.

Remove the fabricated economist quote and all invented testimonials/stock-photo personas. Only use genuine, verified, consented testimonials from real customers, and only cite endorsements that are documented and authorised.
Stop relying on fine print. A buried 'results may vary' line does not cure false headline claims — any material qualifications must be truthful and equally prominent.
Substantiate or remove the '50,000 students' figure with verifiable records.

Add age-gating/audience exclusions so the ads cannot be served to minors on YouTube and Search, and disable any profiling-based delivery (required under DSA Art. 28 for this high-risk financial product).

Reconcile the 'no personalisation' and 'no generative AI' declarations with reality: map all data collection in the funnel (ad pixels, retargeting, lead/checkout forms), document a valid GDPR lawful basis, add a proper privacy notice and marketing opt-out, and confirm whether any creatives were AI-generated (which would trigger AI Act marking/disclosure duties).
Assume all creatives and targeting will be publicly archived in YouTube's VLOP ad repository — everything published must be truthful and defensible.
Recommended path: withdraw and fully rebuild the campaign around honest performance claims, real evidence, and clear risk disclosure, or seek legal review before any relaunch.

campaign.title: SlimTea 14-day detox — influencer push

Copy: 'Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE. The SlimTea 14-day detox flushes out toxins, melts belly fat while you sleep and cures bloating for good — I lost 6kg without changing anything else! Use my code LENA20.' No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere. Landing page repeats the fat-melting and cure claims with before/after photos.

detected_practices: undisclosed paid influencer partnership (no #ad / paid-partnership label)
contractual requirement to hide advertising nature ('no ad markers')
unsubstantiated health claims (detox, flushes toxins, cures bloating)
weight-loss / fat-melting efficacy claims ('melts belly fat while you sleep', 'lost 6kg')
before/after transformation photos
misleading disease/cure claim ('cures bloating for good')
discount/promo code (LENA20)
endorsement / testimonial marketing
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is women 18-35, but the informal 'Girls' framing and open TikTok/Instagram distribution mean minors (16-17 and younger) are plausibly reached. No AI use declared or evident. Although personalisation is declared as 'no', social-platform advertising and the discount-code tracking typically involve personal data processing, so GDPR is included as plausibly engaged.
triage.summary: A weight-loss "detox tea" campaign run via paid fitness influencer posts on Instagram/TikTok targeting women 18-35 in the EU, with the influencer contractually required to hide the advertising nature (no #ad markers). It makes strong health and slimming claims (detox, flushes toxins, melts belly fat while sleeping, cures bloating, 6kg loss) supported by before/after photos, both in posts and on the landing page.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The discount/affiliate code and landing page enable redemption and conversion tracking, which typically processes personal data (device identifiers, click/redemption events). The declaration of 'no personalisation' combined with tracking infrastructure creates a risk of covert or opaque data collection, and the deliberately hidden advertising nature ('no ad markers') undermines the fairness and transparency principle: consumers cannot understand the commercial data context in which any collection happens.
findings.evidence_quote: Use my code LENA20.
findings.recommendation: Map all data flows behind the code (affiliate networks, pixels, platform conversion APIs) and confirm each is disclosed and fairly processed; ensure the landing page carries a clear, accessible privacy notice at the point of any data collection.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: If the landing page collects any personal data (order/lead form, code redemption, cookies/pixels), Art. 13 requires that the controller's identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights be provided at the point of collection. The submitted material shows a marketing landing page with no evidence of the required information layer.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page repeats the fat-melting and cure claims with before/after photos.
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, layered Art. 13 privacy notice at every collection point (landing page forms, checkout, tracking consent banner), covering purposes and legal basis for any tracking tied to the LENA20 code.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Social-platform ad delivery and discount-code conversion tracking require a valid lawful basis (consent for tracking cookies/pixels under ePrivacy, or a documented legitimate-interest assessment). The campaign asserts no personalisation yet relies on trackable codes and paid social distribution; no lawful basis is evidenced, so the processing that supports the campaign may lack a valid Art. 6 basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: no
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for each processing operation (ad measurement, code tracking, retargeting audiences if any); obtain prior consent for any non-essential tracking technologies and record it.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: The campaign centres on weight loss, detox and a digestive 'cure'. If platform targeting, custom audiences, or code-based segmentation infer or use health-related interests to reach recipients, that constitutes processing of special-category (health) data, which is prohibited under Art. 9 absent explicit consent (and separately banned for platform ad targeting under DSA Art. 26(3)). Even engagement/lookalike audiences built on such health-themed interactions raise this risk.
findings.evidence_quote: melts belly fat while you sleep and cures bloating for good — I lost 6kg
findings.recommendation: Confirm no ad targeting, custom/lookalike audiences, or interest segments derive from health-related attributes; if any health inference is involved, cease it — explicit consent is required and such profiling-based ads are separately prohibited on platforms.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The informal 'Girls' framing plus open TikTok/Instagram distribution to a large follower base means the content plausibly reaches minors (under 16). Where consent is the basis for processing data of children via information society services, Art. 8 requires parental consent and reasonable age-verification for children below the applicable age threshold. No age-gating or verification is evident for any data collection triggered by the campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE.
findings.recommendation: Assess whether minors are reached and whether any data collection (code redemption, forms, tracking) captures children's data; implement age assurance and, where the age threshold is not met, parental-consent mechanisms or exclude minors from data-processing flows.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged indirectly. The campaign is a paid influencer/social push using a trackable discount code (LENA20) and a landing page — activities that typically involve personal data processing (platform ad delivery, click/conversion tracking, code redemption) even though "personalisation/targeting" is declared as "no". The campaign text supplies no privacy information, no lawful-basis or consent mechanism, and openly reaches an audience that plausibly includes minors on a health/weight-loss (special-category) theme. These are risks requiring clarification of the actual data flows rather than confirmed breaches, since the submitted material describes ad creative rather than the sign-up/tracking backend.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, in a clear, unambiguous manner and in real time, that content presented on the platform is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is shown. The influencer content is paid advertising (4,000 EUR per post) yet carries no paid-partnership or ad label, and the contract's 'no ad markers' requirement actively prevents the disclosure and the platform's built-in paid-partnership tooling from working. This defeats the real-time ad-identification the transparency regime is designed to guarantee.
findings.evidence_quote: No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Enable the platform's native paid-partnership / branded-content disclosure on every SlimTea post and add a clear #ad / #paidpartnership label; remove the contractual 'no ad markers' clause so the advertisement status and advertiser identity are unambiguously identifiable in real time.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions, expressly including disguised advertisements. Instructing the influencer to present paid promotional content as authentic personal opinion with no ad markers is a disguised-ad tactic that manipulates followers into treating an advertisement as independent endorsement.
findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'
findings.recommendation: Present the promotion transparently as advertising: drop the 'authentic tone, no ad markers' instruction and ensure the commercial nature is prominent and not concealed within organic-looking personal narrative, so followers can recognise it as an ad.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires appropriate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors on platforms accessible to them, and bans presenting ads based on profiling of users known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign uses open distribution on youth-heavy platforms with informal 'Girls' framing, so minors are plausibly reached. As the campaign declares no personalisation/profiling, the profiling-ad ban is not clearly triggered as described, but the aggressive weight-loss/detox messaging reaching minors raises minor-protection concerns.
findings.evidence_quote: the informal 'Girls' framing and open TikTok/Instagram distribution mean minors (16-17 and younger) are plausibly reached
findings.recommendation: Apply age-appropriate audience settings and exclude minors from delivery; do not use any profiling-based targeting where recipients may be minors, and avoid youth-directed framing ('Girls') for weight-loss content that reaches under-18 audiences.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as paid advertising on Instagram/TikTok but is contractually structured to hide its advertising nature ("authentic tone, no ad markers", no #ad/paid-partnership label). This directly engages DSA advertising-transparency and dark-pattern rules: while Arts. 25/26/28 bind the platforms, the advertiser's deliberate concealment defeats the real-time ad-identification the platform must ensure and constitutes disguised advertising. Because the campaign declares no personalisation/profiling, the profiling-specific bans (Art. 26(3) special-category targeting, Art. 28(2) profiling ads to minors) are not clearly triggered as described, though minors are plausibly reached and warrant caution.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: This is paid promotional content presented as the influencer's independent, authentic editorial opinion with no identification of its commercial nature. Using media/editorial-style content to promote a product that the trader has paid for, without making that clear, is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances. The contractual clause requiring 'no ad markers' shows the concealment is deliberate.
findings.evidence_quote: paid 4,000 EUR per post, contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers' ... No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere
findings.recommendation: Require a clear, prominent disclosure on every post (e.g. 'Paid partnership'/#ad label at the start of the caption and via the platform's branded-content tool). Remove the contractual 'no ad markers' clause; contracts must mandate disclosure, not prohibit it.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice where it is not apparent from context is a misleading omission. The material connection (a paid €4,000/post partnership plus a personalised discount code) is material information the average consumer needs to weigh the endorsement, and it is hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers' ... No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere
findings.recommendation: Disclose the material connection clearly and up-front in each post and on the landing page (paid partnership + affiliate/discount-code relationship), in an unambiguous and timely manner before the consumer engages with the content.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Falsely claiming a product can cure illnesses, dysfunction or malformations is prohibited in all circumstances. A tea claiming to 'cure' a bodily dysfunction (bloating) permanently is a false cure claim; such claims for a food/supplement cannot be substantiated and are blacklisted. 'Flushes out toxins' compounds the unsupported medical framing.
findings.evidence_quote: cures bloating for good
findings.recommendation: Remove all cure/treat/medical claims entirely ('cures bloating for good', 'flushes out toxins', 'detox'). Food supplements may not carry disease-cure claims; any permitted health claim must be authorised under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: These are false/unsubstantiated claims about the product's main characteristics and results, capable of causing the average consumer to purchase. 'Melts belly fat while you sleep' and a specific '6kg without changing anything else' outcome, reinforced by before/after photos, deceive consumers about efficacy the product cannot deliver.
findings.evidence_quote: melts belly fat while you sleep and cures bloating for good — I lost 6kg without changing anything else
findings.recommendation: Remove unsubstantiated slimming/efficacy claims and the specific weight-loss figure. Do not present before/after photos as typical results. Only make claims that are truthful and backed by robust evidence; add mandatory context for any lawful health claim.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign is contrary to professional diligence and is distributed openly on TikTok/Instagram with informal 'Girls' framing, so minors and body-image-vulnerable young women are plausibly reached. Under Art. 5(3), the aggressive weight-loss messaging must be assessed from the perspective of that vulnerable group, whose behaviour it is likely to materially distort.
findings.evidence_quote: Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE
findings.recommendation: Apply age-gating/audience controls to avoid reaching minors, avoid exploiting body-image insecurities, and ensure the overall practice meets professional diligence once the misleading and undisclosed elements above are corrected.

verdicts.notes: This detox-tea influencer campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including two blacklisted "in all circumstances" practices. It is a paid influencer promotion deliberately stripped of any ad disclosure (Annex I point 11; Art. 7), and it makes an explicit disease/cure claim ("cures bloating for good") (Annex I point 17). The efficacy and testimonial claims (fat-melting while sleeping, 6kg loss, before/after photos) are unsubstantiated misleading actions under Art. 6, and the informal "Girls" framing on open TikTok/Instagram distribution raises the Art. 5(3) vulnerable-consumer concern. Overall a high-risk, likely-unlawful campaign requiring substantial rework.

report.executive_summary: This campaign pays influencer @LenaFitLife €4,000/post to promote SlimTea as authentic personal opinion with no ad disclosure, while making dramatic weight-loss and health claims. As designed, it breaks EU consumer law in two ways that are banned outright, no exceptions: (1) it hides that the posts are paid advertising ("authentic tone, no ad markers", no #ad/paid-partnership label), and (2) it claims the tea "cures bloating for good", which is a prohibited disease/cure claim for a food product. On top of these, the "melts belly fat while you sleep" and "6kg without changing anything else" claims plus before/after photos are unsubstantiated and misleading. The DSA reinforces the disclosure problem, treating the hidden-ad structure as a dark pattern and requiring clear real-time ad labelling. The "Girls" framing on TikTok/Instagram plausibly reaches minors and body-image-vulnerable young women, raising minor-protection and vulnerable-consumer concerns. GDPR risks also arise because the LENA20 code and landing page likely track users and collect data with no privacy notice or lawful basis in evidence. Verdict: this campaign cannot run in its current form and needs substantial rework before launch.
recommendations: Remove the 'cures bloating for good' claim and all disease/cure and 'flushes out toxins'/'detox' medical framing entirely — these are prohibited outright for a food product and cannot be fixed with a disclaimer.

Add clear, prominent paid-partnership disclosure on every post (e.g. #ad plus the platform's branded-content/paid-partnership tool at the start of the caption) and on the landing page; delete the contractual 'authentic tone, no ad markers' clause and instead require disclosure.

Delete unsubstantiated efficacy claims — 'melts belly fat while you sleep', the specific '6kg without changing anything else' figure, and before/after photos presented as typical results; only make truthful claims backed by robust evidence and, for any health claim, one authorised under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006.
Apply age-gating and audience controls to exclude minors, and drop the youth-directed 'Girls' framing for weight-loss content given the vulnerable-consumer and minor-protection risks.

Map all data flows behind the LENA20 code and landing page (affiliate pixels, conversion tracking), publish a clear layered privacy notice at every collection point, document a lawful basis, and obtain prior consent for non-essential tracking.

Confirm no ad targeting, custom or lookalike audiences derive from health-related attributes; any health-based profiling must cease as it is special-category data and prohibited for platform ad targeting.
Do not launch until the two blacklisted practices (hidden advertising and the cure claim) and the misleading efficacy claims are fully remediated and legally re-reviewed.

triage.summary: Paid influencer campaign on Instagram/TikTok for a "SlimTea 14-day detox" targeting women 18-35 in the EU, using fitness influencer @LenaFitLife. The campaign features undisclosed paid endorsement (no #ad label, contract requires hiding ad markers), aggressive and likely unsubstantiated health/weight-loss claims (detox, fat-melting, cures bloating), before/after imagery, and an affiliate code.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The affiliate discount code is an attribution/tracking mechanism: when a user applies it (on the landing page or at checkout) personal data is processed to attribute the conversion to @LenaFitLife and pay her commission. This processing requires a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis. The submission gives no indication that a lawful basis has been identified or documented for the tracking/attribution processing generated by the code and landing page.
findings.evidence_quote: Use my code LENA20.
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for the data processing triggered by the affiliate code and landing-page interactions (e.g., contract necessity for order fulfilment, consent for any cookies/analytics used to attribute the code). Ensure any ePrivacy consent for tracking technologies is obtained before setting non-essential trackers.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The landing page is a point of personal-data collection (code redemption, likely purchase/sign-up and analytics). Under Art. 13 the controller must supply, at the point of collection, its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. Nothing in the submission indicates that this transparency information is presented on the landing page.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page repeats the fat-melting and cure claims with before/after photos.
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, accessible privacy notice at every collection point on the landing page and checkout covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients (including the influencer/affiliate network), retention periods and data-subject rights, linked before any data is submitted.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The GDPR fairness and transparency principle requires that data subjects understand who is processing their data and why. A campaign designed so the commercial/advertising nature is deliberately concealed ('no ad markers') creates an environment in which any data collection following the deceptive endorsement (via the LENA20 code and landing page) is not fair or transparent to the data subject, undermining Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'
findings.recommendation: Disclose the commercial nature of the endorsement and ensure that any data collected off the back of it is accompanied by honest, prominent information about the controller and purposes, so the processing is fair and transparent.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: A 280k-follower fitness account on TikTok/Instagram realistically reaches users under 16. If personal data is collected from those users through the landing page or code redemption on the basis of consent, Art. 8 requires that consent be given/authorised by a parent for children below the applicable age threshold (16, or 13-15 where a Member State has lowered it), with reasonable verification efforts. The submission shows no age-gating or parental-consent mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: fitness influencer @LenaFitLife (280k followers
findings.recommendation: Implement age verification/age-gating on the landing page and any sign-up flow; where consent is the basis and users are below the national digital-consent age, obtain and verify parental consent before processing, or restrict data collection from minors.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: The campaign concerns weight loss and bodily/health matters. The campaign declares no targeting, so there is no evidence health attributes were actually used to select the audience; however, if this product were ever promoted by inferring or using users' health status / weight-management interest to build or target the audience, that would process special-category (health) data under Art. 9, which is prohibited absent an exception such as explicit consent. Flagged as a forward-looking risk given the sensitive subject matter, not a confirmed breach on the current text.
findings.evidence_quote: flushes out toxins, melts belly fat while you sleep and cures bloating for good
findings.recommendation: Ensure no audience segment, custom/lookalike audience, or inference based on health, weight or body-image interest is used to deliver this campaign; if any health-related segmentation is contemplated, it is barred for platform ad targeting and would otherwise require explicit consent under Art. 9.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares no personalisation and no AI, so the core GDPR risks (targeted/profiled advertising, sensitive-data targeting) are not confirmed by the material itself — those data-driven targeting issues fall primarily to the DSA agent. However, the campaign clearly involves personal-data processing that engages GDPR: an affiliate/attribution code ('LENA20') and a landing page that plausibly collect and process personal data of visitors, a realistic minor audience, and health/body-image subject matter. The main findings are engaged obligations (lawful basis, transparency at point of collection, child consent) whose satisfaction cannot be verified from the submitted text, plus a latent Art. 9 risk if health attributes are ever used to reach this audience. None can be confirmed as a hard violation on the text alone.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The DSA requires that recipients can identify, clearly and unambiguously, that content presented on an online platform is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. This is paid promotional content (4,000 EUR per post) placed on Instagram/TikTok with no ad identifier. The advertiser's deliberate suppression of ad markers defeats the platform's Art. 26(1) transparency obligation and leaves the ad unidentifiable as such in real time.
findings.evidence_quote: No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Require the influencer to use the platforms' built-in paid-partnership / branded-content disclosure tools and a clear label (e.g. '#ad', 'Paid partnership with SlimTea') on every post and on the landing page, so recipients can identify the commercial nature and the advertiser in real time.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online-interface content in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions; disguised advertisements are an express example. Contractually engineering the post to appear as an organic, authentic personal endorsement while removing all ad markers is a disguised-ad dark pattern that manipulates the audience into treating a paid ad as genuine peer testimony.
findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'
findings.recommendation: Remove the contractual clause prohibiting ad markers. Rewrite the brief to mandate honest, prominent disclosure of the paid relationship so the content is not presented in a deceptive/manipulative manner; align creative with transparent-advertising standards.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The audience realistically includes minors on TikTok/Instagram, so Art. 28's minor-protection framework is contextually relevant. However, Art. 28(2) specifically bans ads presented on the basis of PROFILING using minors' personal data, and the campaign declares no personalisation/targeting or profiling. On the facts provided the prohibition is not triggered; flagged for awareness only.
findings.evidence_quote: women 18-35
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the platform that no profiling-based ad delivery is used for this campaign. If any behavioural/profiled ad delivery is later added, exclude users identifiable as minors, and treat the body-image/weight-loss content as sensitive for younger audiences (primarily a UCPD/GDPR matter).

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on Instagram and TikTok, which are online platforms (indeed VLOPs) subject to the DSA. The core DSA-relevant tactic is a deliberately disguised paid advertisement: the influencer post carries no ad label and the contract requires "authentic tone, no ad markers." This undermines the DSA ad-transparency framework (Art. 26(1)) and constitutes a disguised-advertising dark pattern (Art. 25). Note that most DSA duties bind the platform rather than the advertiser directly, but the advertiser's design of undisclosed content directly obstructs those obligations. findings.rationale: The award emblem and gold laurel badge were 'designed in-house' for an award that does not exist, yet are displayed as if they were an independent quality/award mark. Displaying a trust or quality mark (or equivalent award seal) without having obtained the necessary authorisation is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 2 — self-designed 'award' emblems presented as independent are the textbook example.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025', a gold laurel badge
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'European Water Quality Award 2025' wording and the gold laurel award seal entirely. Only display award or quality marks that are genuinely conferred by an independent body and for which written authorisation to display exists.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The campaign claims certification by the 'EU Institute of Hydration', a body that does not exist. The fictitious 'European Water Quality Award' likewise falsely implies endorsement by a body.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration'

findings.title: Misleading actions

If presented as an endorsement by a professional body it could also engage the Annex I point 4 blacklist.
findings.evidence_quote: '#1 recommended by dentists'

findings.recommendation: Adopt a claims-substantiation process ensuring every trust signal, award and endorsement is verified against genuine independent sources before publication; treat Art. 5 professional-diligence compliance as a baseline for all future PureFlow marketing.

The dentist claim is a separate misleading-action problem because it dresses up an unrepresentative internal survey as professional endorsement. Lead your marketing with the genuinely substantiated filtration performance figures that match your lab reports — this is your legitimate, defensible selling point.

This presents strong indicators of misleading advertising, hidden pricing, and subscription-trap dark patterns. Account creation implies personal data processing, and app-store/display distribution engages platform-level advertising and dark-pattern rules.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. The account-creation step is embedded in an onboarding flow deliberately designed to obscure the commercial reality (hidden pricing, omitted terms). Collecting personal data inside a manipulative, deceptive flow undermines the fairness and transparency principle, because the data subject is not put in a position to understand the true context in which they are handing over their data and entering a paid relationship.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Redesign the onboarding so that data collection occurs in a fair, transparent context: present pricing and subscription terms clearly and prominently before or at the point of account creation, and ensure the data-processing context is not distorted by deceptive design.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Account creation collects personal data directly from the data subject, triggering the Art. 13 duty to provide, at the point of collection, the controller's identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights. The campaign describes a sign-up flow focused on capturing users and converting a trial, with no indication that any of this mandatory information is surfaced at account creation.
findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at the account-creation screen covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights, and link it prominently rather than burying it.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information addressed to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear, plain language. The same design pattern that hides pricing in 'small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen' and omits key terms from the confirmation email signals that any privacy-related information in this flow is unlikely to meet the intelligibility and accessibility standard; transparency information delivered via the same obscured channels would not be genuinely accessible.
findings.evidence_quote: Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel
findings.recommendation: Ensure any privacy/data information given at sign-up and in follow-up emails is prominent, legible (not small grey text) and written in clear plain language, and confirm the confirmation email links to accessible privacy information.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The supervisor flagged that minors could potentially be reached. However, the campaign is declared for general adult consumers and a PDF scanner utility is not an information-society service directed at children, so Art. 8 (child's consent) is not clearly engaged on the current facts. Flagged only so the marketer verifies age-appropriate handling if any minors in fact create accounts.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: general adult consumers
findings.recommendation: Confirm the app is not directed at children and consider a light age-assurance/self-declaration step at account creation; if minors are foreseeably reached, apply Art. 8 parental-consent requirements for users under the applicable age threshold (13-16).

verdicts.notes: The campaign is primarily a consumer-pricing/deception matter, but it does engage GDPR because account creation after install involves collecting personal data and the app sends a confirmation email. The transparency deficit and the manipulative design of the data-collection flow are the main GDPR risks; the "minors potentially reached" triage signal is not substantiated by the campaign text (declared audience is general adults), so it is flagged only as informational.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing online interfaces that deceive or manipulate users or materially impair their ability to make free and informed decisions, and expressly covers forced continuity and making cancellation harder than subscription. The onboarding flow combines all three: (1) forced continuity via a trial that silently converts to a recurring €11.99/week charge; (2) obscured material information by burying the price in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen; and (3) obstruction of cancellation by omitting the recurring charge and cancellation method from the confirmation email.
