findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is distributed as app-store and display advertising, which engages the Art. 26(1) requirement that ads on online platforms be clearly and unambiguously identifiable as advertisements with advertiser identity available. The submitted material shows no failure of ad labelling itself, so this is noted only for awareness; the misleading 'free' content is addressed primarily under dark-pattern/UCPD analysis.
findings.evidence_quote: App-install ads: 'ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!'
findings.recommendation: Ensure the app-install and display placements carry the platform's standard ad label and correct advertiser/paid-for identity, and confirm the platform surfaces the required real-time ad-transparency information for these creatives.

verdicts.notes: The ScanGenius onboarding and post-install experience presents a textbook forced-continuity dark pattern under DSA Art. 25: a "free"-marketed app whose 3-day trial silently auto-converts to €11.99/week, with the price buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and cancellation instructions omitted from the confirmation email. This design impairs users' ability to make free and informed decisions and makes cancellation harder than subscription. The app-store/display ad channels engage Art. 26(1) transparency, but nothing in the material indicates the ads fail to be identifiable as advertisements, so that is flagged only for awareness. The minor-profiling ban (Art. 28) and sensitive-data ad ban (Art. 26(3)) are not engaged, as the campaign declares no targeting/profiling and an adult audience.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits describing a product as 'free' in all circumstances where the consumer must pay anything beyond unavoidable response/delivery costs. Here the app converts a 3-day trial into a recurring €11.99/week subscription, so the product is not free at all. This is a blacklisted practice presumed unfair regardless of consumer impact, and the app-store title repeating 'Free' compounds it.
findings.evidence_quote: ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!
findings.recommendation: Stop describing the app or its title as 'free' or '100% FREE'. Label it accurately, e.g. 'Free 3-day trial, then €11.99/week' with the recurring price shown up front. Remove 'No hidden costs' entirely unless there genuinely are none.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits false information deceiving the average consumer about the price or manner of price calculation. Claiming '100% FREE' and 'No hidden costs' is objectively false because the app auto-charges €11.99/week, and this deception causes consumers to download and create an account — a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs.
findings.recommendation: Correct all creative so price claims are truthful; disclose the €11.99/week recurring charge and the trial-to-paid conversion prominently in the ad and store listing before the consumer acts.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent

The recurring price (€11.99/week), the fact the trial auto-converts, and the cancellation method are all material. Burying the price in small grey text on the fourth screen (untimely and unclear) and omitting the recurring charge and cancellation instructions from the confirmation email are classic misleading omissions.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen. App store listing repeats 'Free' in the title. Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.
findings.recommendation: Present the full price, billing frequency, trial-conversion date and clear cancellation instructions prominently at the point of sign-up and repeat them in the confirmation email. Avoid low-contrast/small type; make the paid terms at least as prominent as the 'free' claim.

verdicts.notes: The ScanGenius campaign markets a PDF scanner as "100% FREE" while in fact the app requires payment of €11.99/week after a 3-day trial. This is a classic misleading 'free' claim and subscription-trap pattern targeting general EU adult consumers. Mandatory account creation means personal data is collected.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Mandatory account creation collects personal data at the point of sign-up. Art. 13 requires the controller to provide, at the moment of collection, its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention periods and data-subject rights. The described onboarding flow (three screens plus a price screen, then account creation) contains no reference to any privacy notice or these mandatory disclosures, so the information obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Present a concise, layered privacy notice at or before the account-creation step covering controller identity, processing purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients and data-subject rights (with a link to the full policy). Do not proceed with account creation until this information is accessible.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires that personal data be processed fairly and transparently, not through deception. Here the collection of personal data (account creation) is embedded in a funnel built on a materially misleading 'free/no hidden costs' claim with the price buried in small grey text. Collecting data inside a deceptive commercial context undermines the fairness of the processing under Art. 5(1)(a), independently of the pricing law issues.
findings.evidence_quote: 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the data-collection step is presented in a truthful, non-deceptive interface: display the recurring price and trial terms clearly before sign-up, and keep privacy information separate, clear and honest so consumers understand what they are agreeing to and why their data is collected.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any processing needs a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Forcing account creation to use an app advertised as free raises the question of whether the associated data collection is genuinely necessary for the (contractual) service or exceeds what is required. If the account is not strictly necessary to deliver the scanning function, contract cannot be the basis and consent/legitimate interests would need justification. As described, no lawful basis is documented.
findings.evidence_quote: After install, the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Document a specific lawful basis for each processing purpose. Collect only data necessary to provide the service (data minimisation); avoid making account creation mandatory where the core function does not require it, and record the basis relied on.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: The confirmation email indicates the app sends communications to registered users. If marketing or other non-essential consent is bundled into the mandatory account-creation step, consent is not 'freely given' and performance of the service must not be conditional on consent that is not necessary (Art. 7(4)). Consent must also be as easy to withdraw as to give; a flow that obstructs cancellation signals weak withdrawal mechanisms.
findings.evidence_quote: Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.
findings.recommendation: Separate any marketing/analytics consent from the account sign-up so it is optional and unbundled, use clear affirmative opt-in, and provide an equally easy withdrawal/unsubscribe mechanism (including a working unsubscribe link and cancellation route in emails).

verdicts.notes: Although the submission declares no personalisation and no generative AI, mandatory account creation means personal data is collected from general EU adult consumers, engaging the GDPR. The dominant risks are transparency: the campaign describes no privacy notice / Art. 13 information at the point of sign-up, and the data collection is embedded in a deliberately deceptive "100% FREE" onboarding funnel, undermining the lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle. There is also a lawful-basis question over compelling account creation for an app presented as free, and a potential conditionality issue if marketing consent is bundled into mandatory sign-up. Findings are limited to GDPR; the misleading-'free' and subscription-trap issues fall to the UCPD/DSA agents.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Presenting the €11.99/week recurring price only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen gives disproportionate prominence to the 'free'/download choice while obscuring the material cost information. Where this flow is presented via or in conjunction with an online platform (e.g. the app store), Art. 25's prohibition on dark patterns is engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Disclose the recurring €11.99/week price and trial-to-paid conversion clearly, prominently and up front (equal visual weight to the 'free' claim), on the first screen where the subscription is offered — not buried in grey text on a later screen.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Omitting the recurring charge and any cancellation instructions from the confirmation email, combined with a frictionless sign-up, indicates a forced-continuity / obstruction-of-cancellation pattern. Art. 25 expressly prohibits making cancellation harder than subscription. On platform-mediated interfaces this constitutes a dark pattern.
findings.evidence_quote: Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.
findings.recommendation: Include in the confirmation email the recurring amount, billing frequency, next charge date and a clear, one-step cancellation path, ensuring cancellation is at least as easy as subscribing.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's post-install onboarding and subscription flow engage the DSA Art. 25 prohibition on dark patterns / deceptive interface design: the €11.99/week price is buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen (false hierarchy / obscuring material choices), and the confirmation email omits any cancellation route, which points to cancellation being made harder than subscription — an example expressly named in Art. 25. DSA applicability depends on whether the relevant interfaces are operated by/through 'online platforms' (the app store and display ad network qualify as platforms; the app's own onboarding screens may not by themselves), so this is a risk rather than a clear breach. The underlying misleading 'free' claim is primarily a UCPD matter handled separately.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits, in all circumstances, describing a product as 'free' or 'without charge' where the consumer has to pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of responding/delivery. Here the product is expressly advertised as '100% FREE' with 'No hidden costs', but using it beyond a 3-day trial requires paying €11.99/week on an auto-renewing subscription. The 'free' descriptor is therefore materially false and blacklisted per se — no consumer-harm test is required.
findings.evidence_quote: ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!
findings.recommendation: Stop describing the app as '100% FREE' / 'No hidden costs'. Use accurate framing such as 'Free 3-day trial, then €11.99/week — cancel anytime' with the price and recurrence shown with equal prominence to the word 'free', in both the ad creative and the app-store title.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 (misleading actions) covers false information or deception about the price, the manner of price calculation and the existence of a price advantage that causes the consumer to take a transactional decision (installing, creating an account) they would not otherwise have taken. Repeating 'Free' in the store title while the real proposition is a €11.99/week recurring charge deceives the average consumer about price and induces the install/sign-up decision.
findings.evidence_quote: App store listing repeats 'Free' in the title.
findings.recommendation: Remove 'Free' from the app-store title. Ensure all price references accurately state the recurring price, billing frequency and that the trial auto-converts, so that no reasonable consumer is misled about the true cost.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 (misleading omissions) is engaged where material information the average consumer needs is omitted, hidden, or provided in an unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely manner. The subscription price, billing frequency, auto-conversion of the trial and the cancellation method are all material. Presenting the price only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen hides/obscures it, and omitting the recurring charge and cancellation route from the confirmation email withholds material pre- and post-contract information at the point the consumer needs it.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen. ... Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.
findings.recommendation: Disclose all material terms (price €11.99/week, weekly recurrence, trial auto-renewal date, and how to cancel) clearly and prominently before account creation and before the trial begins, and repeat them in the confirmation email together with a clear cancellation link/instructions.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, Art. 5 treats a practice as unfair where it is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the average consumer's economic behaviour. The overall subscription-trap design — a 'free' hook, mandatory account creation, buried pricing and an uninformative confirmation email — combines to distort the transactional decision beyond any single provision. This is a backstop where the specific breaches (points 20, Arts. 6 and 7) do not already fully capture the cumulative unfairness.

verdicts.notes: The ScanGenius campaign markets a PDF app as "100% FREE" with "no hidden costs", yet the app in fact requires account creation and locks users into a €11.99/week auto-renewing subscription after a 3-day trial. This is a textbook misuse of "free" (blacklisted under Annex I point 20, prohibited in all circumstances), compounded by misleading price/price-advantage claims (Art. 6) and material omission of the recurring charge and cancellation route (Art. 7). report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises ScanGenius as a "100% FREE PDF scanner" with "no hidden costs," but the app actually forces account creation and locks users into a €11.99/week auto-renewing subscription after a 3-day trial — with the price buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and no mention of the charge or cancellation route in the confirmation email. Calling a paid product "free" is an outright prohibited practice under EU consumer law (it is on the UCPD blacklist, banned in all circumstances, with no defence available). On top of that, the buried pricing and misleading store title are misleading actions and omissions, and the obscured price plus hard-to-cancel design are classic dark patterns under the Digital Services Act. Because the mandatory sign-up collects personal data inside this deceptive funnel, there are also GDPR transparency and lawful-basis concerns. This is not fixable with minor disclosure tweaks — the core "free" claim and the subscription-trap flow must be reworked before launch. The overall verdict is critical: the campaign should not run in its current form.

findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Here data is collected within a deceptive onboarding flow: users are told the app is '100% FREE' while account creation enrols them toward a recurring charge whose terms are buried in 'small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen', and the confirmation email omits the recurring charge. Collecting account/billing data under such misleading pretences breaches the fairness and transparency limb of Art. 5(1)(a): the data subject cannot understand the true nature of the relationship for which their data is being processed.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Align the data-collection context with reality: clearly and prominently disclose the paid subscription and pricing before account creation, and ensure the confirmation email transparently sets out the processing and the commercial terms. findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: The app makes use of the utility conditional on forced account creation. If any processing beyond what is strictly necessary to perform the requested service (e.g. marketing or ancillary processing) is bundled into that mandatory account step and relies on consent, Art. 7(4) requires that performance of a service not be made conditional on consent to processing that is not necessary for it, and any consent must be freely given, distinguishable and as easy to withdraw as to give. The forced account gate is a risk indicator, though the text does not confirm which specific processing is bundled.
findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation

verdicts.notes: The campaign forces account creation after install and sends a confirmation email, so it clearly involves collection and processing of personal data (at minimum identity/email and subscription/billing data). This engages the GDPR transparency/fairness principle and the Art. 13 information duty; no special-category data, profiling, or minor-targeting is evident, so the higher-risk provisions are not triggered on the facts given.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The onboarding flow is designed to materially distort users' ability to make a free and informed decision: a headline '100% FREE' claim, the recurring price obscured in small grey text on the fourth screen, an auto-converting trial (forced continuity), and complete omission of cancellation information in the confirmation email. Art. 25 expressly covers giving more prominence to certain choices, obscuring material terms and making cancellation harder than subscription. This is precisely the forced-continuity / obstruction-of-cancellation dark pattern the provision prohibits, insofar as the app's interface falls within the DSA's 'online platform' scope; where it does not, the identical conduct is caught by the UCPD.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms

findings.evidence_quote: App-install ads: 'ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!'
findings.recommendation: Ensure display/app-install creatives carry clear advertiser identification and do not obscure their commercial nature, and cooperate with the hosting platforms' ad-labelling and transparency mechanisms.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core problem — a "100% FREE" claim that hides an auto-converting €11.99/week subscription, with the price buried in small grey text and no cancellation information provided — is a textbook deceptive-design / forced-continuity pattern of the kind DSA Art. 25 targets. The main DSA caveat is scope: Art. 25 binds "providers of online platforms" in the design of their own interfaces, so its direct application depends on whether ScanGenius's onboarding flow qualifies as an online-platform interface; where it does not, the same conduct falls to the UCPD (covered by another agent). The app-store/display distribution also engages platform advertising-transparency duties (Art. 26(1)), though these are primarily obligations on the hosting platform. No profiling, sensitive-data targeting, minor-targeting or recommender-system practices are present, so Arts. 26(3), 27, 28 and 39 do not apply.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits in all circumstances describing a product as 'free' where the consumer must pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of responding/delivery. Here the app is marketed as '100% FREE' with 'No hidden costs', yet using it requires an account and enrols the user in a 3-day trial that auto-converts to €11.99/week. This is precisely the blacklisted scenario of a 'free' offer / free trial converting to a paid subscription without clarity — a per se violation requiring no case-by-case unfairness assessment. The explicit 'No hidden costs' assertion aggravates the deception given the price is in fact hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!
findings.recommendation: Stop describing the app as '100% FREE' / 'No hidden costs'. Either make the app genuinely free of charge, or replace the claim with an accurate description such as '3-day free trial, then €11.99/week — cancel anytime' displayed with equal prominence to the headline in every ad and the app-store title.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Repeating 'Free' in the app-store title independently reproduces the blacklisted misuse of 'free' under Annex I point 20, since the product is not free — it requires a €11.99/week paid subscription to use. The prominent, repeated placement reinforces the false impression at the decisive install-decision point.
findings.evidence_quote: App store listing repeats 'Free' in the title.
findings.recommendation: Remove 'Free' from the app-store title. If a free tier or trial genuinely exists, describe it accurately (e.g. 'free trial, then €11.99/week') rather than labelling the product 'Free'.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices that deceive the average consumer as to the price or manner of price calculation and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Claiming the product is '100% FREE' with 'No hidden costs' while it in reality costs €11.99/week is false information about price that induces the install and account-creation decision. This is a misleading action on top of the blacklist breach.
findings.evidence_quote: 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all pricing claims are truthful and complete. State the recurring price, billing frequency, trial length and the fact that the trial auto-renews to a paid subscription, at the point the consumer decides to install/subscribe.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 treats it as a misleading omission where material information (price, recurring nature, auto-conversion of the trial, how to cancel) is hidden or provided in an unclear, unintelligible or untimely manner. Placing the €11.99/week price only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen — after the consumer has already installed and created an account — is untimely and obscured presentation of material information. The confirmation email compounds this by omitting the recurring charge and cancellation method entirely.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Disclose the full price, billing cadence, renewal terms and cancellation route clearly and prominently before the consumer commits (ideally in the ad and on the first subscription screen), using legible contrast and size. Include the recurring charge amount and step-by-step cancellation instructions in the confirmation email.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The omission of the recurring charge and cancellation instructions from the confirmation email is a distinct misleading omission of material post-purchase information the average consumer needs to manage the subscription and avoid an unwanted charge, reinforcing the subscription-trap effect.
findings.evidence_quote: Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.
findings.recommendation: Add to the confirmation email a clear statement of the amount (€11.99/week), the date the trial ends and first charge occurs, and a direct link/instructions to cancel.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive a practice that, through undue influence, impairs consumer choice — including imposing onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights such as making cancellation burdensome. The combination of a very short 3-day trial window, forced account creation, price concealment and absence of any cancellation information in the confirmation email creates onerous barriers to avoiding the charge and cancelling, contributing to a subscription-trap that impairs free and informed decision-making.
findings.evidence_quote: starts a 3-day trial that converts to €11.99/week unless cancelled
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, clearly signposted cancellation path (at least as easy as sign-up), send a reminder before the trial converts, and ensure the trial length and cancellation deadline are conspicuous so consumers can genuinely exercise their right to avoid the charge.

verdicts.notes: The campaign advertises a "100% FREE" PDF scanner that in fact forces account creation and enrols users in an €11.99/week subscription after a 3-day trial, with the price buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and no cancellation information in the confirmation email. This engages a per se blacklisted practice (misuse of 'free', Annex I point 20), plus misleading actions on price (Art. 6), misleading omission of material cost/cancellation information (Art. 7), and aggressive practice through cancellation obstruction (Arts. 8-9). Multiple critical/high findings.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises ScanGenius as a "100% FREE" PDF scanner with "No hidden costs," but the app actually forces account creation and enrols users in a 3-day trial that auto-converts to €11.99/week, with the price hidden in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and no cancellation information in the confirmation email. Calling the product "free" when it in fact costs money is a per se banned practice under EU consumer law (the "misuse of free" blacklist) — meaning it is illegal outright, with no room for a case-by-case defence. On top of that, the buried pricing, auto-renewing trial and missing cancellation details are classic "subscription trap" / dark-pattern conduct that breaches rules on misleading actions and omissions, aggressive practices and prohibited deceptive interface design. The forced account creation and confirmation email also trigger data-protection duties (no privacy notice, no transparency at the point of data collection), and processing personal data inside a deceptive flow undermines the fairness principle. The AI Act does not apply. Overall this is a high-exposure campaign that cannot run in its current form — it needs substantive redesign, not cosmetic tweaks.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (notably full payment card details) is collected within a flow that misrepresents the transaction as free while the recurring 49.99 EUR/month purpose is buried. Processing personal/payment data obtained through a materially misleading interface breaches the requirement that data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Fairness is a self-standing GDPR obligation independent of the underlying consumer-law deception.
findings.evidence_quote: 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Make the actual purpose and consequence of providing card data unambiguous at the point of collection: state clearly, adjacent to the card fields, that the card will be charged 49.99 EUR/month after 5 days unless cancelled. findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting card and account data, Art. 13 requires the controller to provide, in an accessible way, its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, retention and data-subject rights. Relegating the true purpose (funding a recurring subscription) to page-3/footer terms means the point-of-collection information is not effectively provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout requires full card details; page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription
findings.recommendation: Present a layered privacy notice at checkout covering controller identity, processing purposes (including retention of card data for recurring billing), legal basis, retention period, and data-subject rights, including the right to object to direct marketing — before card details are submitted.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: A 'personalised' plan implies automated processing of user data to evaluate personal aspects (fitness goals, body metrics, preferences), which meets the definition of profiling. The submission declares no personalisation/targeting, so either profiling occurs without being disclosed/assessed, or the personalisation claim is unfounded. Undisclosed profiling of personal data lacks the required transparency and lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE
findings.recommendation: Reconcile the discrepancy: if plans are individualised from user data, document the profiling, disclose it under Art. 13, and secure an appropriate lawful basis (Art. 6). If no personalisation actually occurs, remove the 'personalised' claim.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Building a personalised fitness/coaching plan typically requires health-related inputs (weight, fitness level, health conditions/goals), which are special-category health data. Processing such data is prohibited unless explicit consent (or another Art. 9(2) exception) is obtained; the funnel shows no explicit-consent mechanism for health data.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE
findings.recommendation: If any health/fitness data is collected to generate the plan, obtain freely given, specific, informed and explicit consent for health-data processing separate from the general terms, and record the Art. 9(2) exception relied upon.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Each processing activity (card data for recurring billing, any personalisation, any marketing) needs a valid lawful basis. Where consent is relied on it must be validly obtained, and where contract is relied on the processing must be genuinely necessary — difficult to sustain when the recurring-billing purpose is concealed and the transaction is misrepresented as free.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout requires full card details
findings.recommendation: Map each processing purpose to a specific lawful basis and ensure the recurring-billing purpose is transparently presented so any contract/consent basis is valid; do not bundle marketing or personalisation into the payment step without a distinct lawful basis.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: If personal data is used for direct marketing (including any personalised offers or follow-up communications), the data subject has an absolute right to object, and must be explicitly informed of this right at the latest at first communication, presented clearly and separately.
findings.evidence_quote: personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy-to-use opt-out from direct marketing and profiling for marketing purposes, and present the right to object explicitly and separately at sign-up/first contact.

verdicts.notes: The funnel collects personal data (full payment card details, and inputs for a "personalised" plan) inside a deceptive "FREE" flow that hides the 49.99 EUR/month subscription in page-3/footer terms. This undermines the GDPR fairness and transparency principle and the point-of-collection information obligation, since data subjects hand over card data without transparent notice that it funds a recurring charge. The "personalised plan" claim contradicts the declared "no personalisation" and must be reconciled: if genuine, it likely involves profiling and probable health-data processing (Art. 4(4)/9/22) needing explicit consent; if not, the data-processing purpose disclosure is misleading. No minor-targeting concern given the declared 25-55 audience.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 expressly prohibits interfaces that make cancellation harder than subscription and that repeatedly request a choice already made. Sign-up happens instantly online with card details, but cancellation is confined to phone-only, business-hours contact and gated behind three mandatory retention counter-offers — a paradigmatic forced-continuity / obstruction-of-cancellation dark pattern that materially impairs the consumer's ability to make a free decision. (Scope caveat: Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms operating their online interfaces; applicability depends on whether the FitCoach funnel qualifies as an in-scope online platform.)
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Provide a cancellation path at least as easy as sign-up — a self-service online cancel button available 24/7 in the same interface where the subscription was purchased. Remove the mandatory three-counter-offer gate so cancellation is processed on first request without obstruction or nagging.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing interfaces that deceive or give more prominence to certain choices, materially distorting informed decisions. Repeating 'FREE' 11 times while confining the 49.99 EUR/month recurring charge to a footer terms link / page 3 is a deceptive prominence and information-hiding design pattern that impairs free and informed decision-making at the point of entering card details.
findings.evidence_quote: 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Present the recurring price (49.99 EUR/month), the 5-day auto-conversion date and cancellation method with equal visual prominence to the word 'FREE', adjacent to the call-to-action and the card-entry field, not hidden in footer terms. Reduce misleading repetition of 'FREE'.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign runs on social platforms; DSA Art. 26(1) requires that each ad be identifiable in real time as an advertisement with advertiser identity and targeting parameters. This obligation falls primarily on the hosting platform rather than the advertiser, and nothing in the campaign text indicates the ad is disguised as non-advertising, so no breach by the marketer is evident — flagged only for context.
findings.evidence_quote: Display and social ads: 'Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE
findings.recommendation: Ensure ads are delivered via the platforms' official paid-ad channels so they carry the required 'advertisement' labelling and advertiser identity, rather than any format that could obscure their commercial nature.

verdicts.notes: The FitCoach funnel exhibits textbook dark-pattern design that DSA Art. 25 explicitly names: obstruction of cancellation (making cancellation harder than sign-up), false prominence of the "FREE" choice while burying paid subscription terms, and nagging retention counter-offers. The main DSA scope caveat is that Art. 25 binds "providers of online platforms" in the operation of their own interfaces; if the FitCoach landing/checkout page is the trader's own website rather than an in-scope online platform, the identical conduct is nonetheless caught by UCPD (assessed separately). Art. 26(1) ad-transparency and the sensitive-data/minor targeting bans are largely obligations on the hosting social platforms and are not clearly breached by the advertiser as described. Overall this is a strong dark-pattern risk that should be remediated regardless of the platform-scope question.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits in all circumstances describing a product as 'free' where the consumer must pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of delivery. Here the offer is billed as '100% FREE' but auto-converts into a 49.99 EUR/month subscription after a 5-day window. The recurring subscription charge is plainly not a delivery cost, so the 'FREE' claim is a blacklisted misuse. Repeating 'FREE' 11 times while the real cost sits only in footer terms aggravates this.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.
findings.recommendation: Stop describing the offer as 'FREE'. Either make the welcome kit genuinely free of any post-trial charge, or prominently label it as a paid trial (e.g. '5-day trial then 49.99 EUR/month') with the recurring price shown with equal prominence to '1.95 EUR shipping'. Remove the '100% FREE' and repeated 'FREE' claims.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The price and the existence of a recurring subscription commitment are material information the average consumer needs before deciding. Providing it only on 'page 3 of the terms' / a footer link is an untimely, unclear and hidden disclosure, while the headline screams 'FREE'. This is a misleading omission under Art. 7, which the concept graph flags for auto-converting free trials with obscured terms.
findings.evidence_quote: page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days unless cancelled ... the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the 49.99 EUR/month price, the 5-day trigger, and the auto-renewal at the point of decision — in the ad creative and above the checkout button — not buried in linked terms. Ensure the consumer sees total cost and renewal terms before entering card details.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers deception about price and the manner of price calculation, and about the existence of a price advantage. Presenting the plan as costing only 1.95 EUR shipping while concealing a 49.99 EUR/month charge creates a false overall impression of price likely to cause consumers to transact when they otherwise would not. The 'personalised FitCoach plan' claim is also potentially a false statement about the product's main characteristics, given the submission declares no personalisation/targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Present a truthful, complete price up front. Substantiate or drop the 'personalised' claim: if plans are not genuinely tailored to the individual, do not call them 'personalised'. Align the advertised characteristics with what is actually delivered.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive any practice that, through undue influence or onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights, impairs the consumer's freedom of choice. Restricting cancellation to phone-only during business hours, combined with a mandatory three-counter-offer retention script, imposes onerous barriers and applies pressure to keep a subscription many enrolled in believing it was 'free'. This significantly impairs the consumer's ability to exit.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, non-obstructive cancellation route matching the ease of sign-up (online self-service, at least as simple as enrolment). Remove mandatory multi-step retention counter-offers before a cancellation is honoured; a single optional retention message at most, with immediate cancellation on request.

verdicts.notes: The FitCoach funnel engages multiple UCPD prohibitions. Most seriously, it misuses "FREE" (Annex I point 20 — a blacklisted per se prohibition) because consumers pay far more than delivery: a 49.99 EUR/month subscription auto-starts after 5 days. It also constitutes a misleading omission (Art. 7) by burying the subscription in footer/page-3 terms, a misleading action (Art. 6) on price and on the "personalised" claim, and an aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9) through onerous phone-only cancellation with mandatory retention counter-offers. These are strong, clearly evidenced violations.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets a "100% FREE" FitCoach trial that actually auto-enrols consumers into a 49.99 EUR/month subscription after 5 days, with the real cost buried in footer/page-3 terms while "FREE" appears 11 times on the landing page. This is a serious, clear-cut problem. Calling it "FREE" when the consumer ends up paying a recurring charge is a per se banned practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I) — a violation regardless of intent or context. On top of that, hiding the price is a misleading omission, the phone-only cancellation with mandatory retention counter-offers is an aggressive/dark-pattern practice, and collecting full card details inside a deceptive flow breaches GDPR's fairness and transparency duties. There is also a contradiction to fix: you declared "no personalisation," yet the ad promises a "personalised plan," which likely implies profiling and possibly health-data processing that carries its own consent obligations. As designed, this funnel is very likely unlawful in the EU and should not launch in its current form. The core deceptive "FREE" claim and the obstructed cancellation are the highest-priority fixes.

Add a layered privacy notice at the point of card collection covering controller identity, processing purposes (including retention of card data for recurring billing), legal basis, retention period, and data-subject rights, including a clear opt-out from direct marketing.
Do not launch the campaign until the 'FREE' claim, price disclosure, and cancellation obstruction are corrected; these represent likely per se and high-severity violations under UCPD, DSA and GDPR.

The campaign declares no AI and no personalisation, yet advertises a "personalised" plan — the personalisation claim and card/checkout data collection warrant a GDPR review. UCPD is central given misleading omissions of material price/subscription info and aggressive cancellation barriers; DSA applies to the online platform/ad delivery on display and social channels. AI Act not engaged based on declared and observed facts.
triage.summary: A free-trial funnel for FitCoach that heavily advertises a "100% FREE" personalised plan for a 1.95 EUR shipping fee, while concealing enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription disclosed only in footer/page-3 terms. Cancellation is deliberately obstructed (phone-only, business hours, mandatory counter-offers). The pattern strongly indicates misleading/aggressive commercial practices and a subscription trap.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (full payment card details, identity/contact data) is collected in a checkout framed as free/'just shipping', while the real purpose of capturing the card — enabling a recurring 49.99 EUR/month charge — is concealed in footer/page-3 terms. Processing personal data obtained through a materially misleading interface is neither fair nor transparent, breaching the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.' Checkout requires full card details
findings.recommendation: Present the true purpose of collecting card details (recurring subscription billing) clearly and prominently at the point of collection, on the same screen as the payment form, before the consumer submits card data. Do not use a misleading 'free/shipping only' framing to capture data for a different processing purpose.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: GDPR requires that at the point of collecting personal data the controller provide, in an accessible form, the purposes and legal basis of processing (here, storing the card for recurring billing), controller identity, retention and data-subject rights. Relegating the material processing purpose to a footer/page-3 terms link means the required information is not provided at the point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at the checkout point of collection covering controller identity, that card data will be retained and re-used for recurring monthly charges, the legal basis, retention period, and how to exercise rights — do not bury it behind a single footer link.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Article 12 requires information about processing to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible using clear and plain language. Disclosing the key data-use/billing information only on 'page 3 of the terms' fails the easy-accessibility and clarity requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription
findings.recommendation: Surface the processing/billing information in plain language and prominently in the sign-up flow, not deep within multi-page terms; use clear headings and avoid burying material terms.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Storing and re-using payment card data to charge a recurring subscription needs a valid lawful basis. If relied on as consent, the consent is not informed or unambiguous because the recurring-billing purpose is hidden; if relied on as contract necessity, the consumer has not been clearly informed that they are entering a paid contract. The lawful basis for the card-retention/recurring-charge processing is therefore not validly established as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout requires full card details; page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days unless cancelled
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a clear lawful basis for storing the card and processing recurring charges, and ensure the consumer is transparently informed of and agrees to that purpose before card data is submitted (e.g., an explicit, unbundled affirmative step acknowledging the paid subscription).

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The ad promises a 'personalised' plan while the campaign declares no personalisation/profiling. If personalisation is real, it likely involves automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (fitness goals, preferences, potentially health-related attributes), which is profiling under Art. 4(4) and must be disclosed. If it is not real, no profiling occurs but the claim is inaccurate. Either way this discrepancy warrants review and, if profiling exists, transparency about it.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Clarify whether the plan is genuinely personalised. If any profiling of the individual occurs, disclose it in the Art. 13 notice (existence and logic of profiling) and establish a lawful basis; if not, remove or qualify the 'personalised' claim.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: A personalised fitness/coaching plan may involve collecting health- or fitness-related data, which can constitute special-category data under Art. 9 requiring explicit consent. The campaign text does not evidence such collection in the funnel, so this is flagged only for awareness of downstream data intake.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: If the onboarding/plan generation collects health, weight, medical or fitness-condition data, treat it as special-category data: obtain explicit consent and apply Art. 9 safeguards.

verdicts.notes: The funnel collects personal data (full card details and enrolment/identity data) at checkout, so GDPR is engaged even though no AI or targeting is declared. The main GDPR concerns are fairness and transparency: card data is captured under a "100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping" pretext while the true processing purpose (storing the card for a recurring 49.99 EUR/month charge) and the terms are hidden in footer/page-3 links, undermining Art. 5(1)(a), Art. 12/13 transparency and any valid consent under Art. 6(1). The "personalised plan" claim also sits inconsistently with the declared no-personalisation, indicating either a false claim or undisclosed profiling that would trigger profiling-transparency duties.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces so as to materially distort users' ability to make free decisions, and expressly targets 'making cancellation harder than subscription' and obstruction of cancellation. Here enrolment is a frictionless online checkout, but cancellation is confined to phone calls during business hours and gated behind three mandatory retention counter-offers — a textbook forced-continuity / obstruction dark pattern that impairs the user's ability to exit the contract as easily as they entered it.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Provide an online cancellation mechanism at least as easy as sign-up (e.g. a one-click 'cancel subscription' button in the account area), available at all times, and remove mandatory retention scripts and counter-offer barriers that obstruct the exit path.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits interfaces that deceive or manipulate by giving disproportionate prominence to certain information/choices and by hiding material information. Repeating 'FREE' 11 times while relegating the recurring 49.99 EUR/month charge (starting after 5 days) to a footer link and page 3 of the terms creates a false visual hierarchy that manipulates the transactional decision — a deceptive-design dark pattern in the platform/landing interface.
findings.evidence_quote: 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the auto-renewing 49.99 EUR/month price, the 5-day trigger and the auto-renewal at the same visual level and adjacency as the 'FREE' claim and directly next to the payment/consent action, with equal prominence; obtain explicit affirmative acknowledgement of the paid subscription before capturing card details.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Where these display and social ads are served on online platforms, DSA Art. 26(1) requires each ad be clearly identifiable as an advertisement with the advertiser's identity and meaningful targeting-parameter information available in real time. The obligation rests primarily on the platform, but the campaign relies on that transparency framework; nothing in the submission indicates non-compliant labelling, so this is flagged for awareness rather than as a breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Display and social ads: 'Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.'
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ads are delivered with proper platform ad labelling and correct 'paid for by / on behalf of' advertiser identification (FitCoach), and that any targeting parameters disclosed by the platform accurately reflect the campaign setup.

verdicts.notes: The FitCoach funnel engages DSA Art. 25 (prohibition of dark patterns) on two distinct fronts: (1) forced-continuity design where cancellation is deliberately made harder than sign-up (phone-only, business hours, mandatory retention counter-offers) — a scenario Art. 25 expressly names; and (2) a deceptive interface hierarchy that gives overwhelming prominence to "FREE" (11 times) while burying the material 49.99 EUR/month auto-renewing subscription in footer/page-3 terms. DSA Art. 25 applies to online-platform interfaces; to the extent FitCoach delivers the checkout/landing experience through its own platform interface the prohibition applies directly, and platform-delivered ad experiences (display/social) engage Art. 26 transparency. The same conduct is squarely covered by the UCPD for all traders (assessed by that agent); DSA adds the platform-interface prohibition layer.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits in all circumstances describing a product as 'free' when the consumer must pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of responding/delivery. Here the offer is a free trial that auto-converts to a 49.99 EUR/month subscription after 5 days, and the checkout captures full card details specifically to charge that recurring fee. The '100% FREE' claim (repeated 11 times) is therefore a blacklisted misuse of 'free' — the plan is not free at all; it is a paid subscription obscured behind a small shipping charge.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.
findings.recommendation: Stop describing the plan as '100% FREE'. Present it accurately, e.g. '5-day trial, then 49.99 EUR/month unless cancelled', with the recurring price shown up front and given at least equal prominence to any 'trial' language. Only use 'free' where nothing beyond genuine, unavoidable delivery cost is payable.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The existence, price and manner of calculation of the recurring charge, and the negative-option (auto-renewal) nature of the offer, are material information the average consumer needs before deciding to hand over card details. Confining it to page 3 of the terms and a footer link — while 'FREE' appears 11 times — hides material information and presents it in an unclear and untimely manner, in breach of Art. 7. This distorts the transactional decision to enrol.
findings.evidence_quote: page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days unless cancelled ... the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link
findings.recommendation: Disclose the 49.99 EUR/month price, the 5-day conversion date, the auto-renewal mechanism and how to cancel clearly and prominently at the point of decision (on the ad and immediately at checkout, adjacent to the payment fields), not buried in footer/page-3 terms. Require an explicit, informed opt-in acknowledgement of the recurring charge before card capture.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive any practice that, through undue influence, imposes onerous or disproportionate non-contractual barriers on a consumer wishing to exercise contractual rights (including terminating a contract). Restricting cancellation to a phone line available only during business hours, combined with a mandatory three-counter-offer retention script that impedes and pressures the consumer before the request is processed, creates exactly such onerous barriers and coercive pressure, especially given sign-up is a frictionless online click.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Offer a cancellation method at least as easy as sign-up — e.g. a one-click online cancellation available 24/7 in the account or via the same channel used to subscribe. Remove the mandatory retention counter-offers as a precondition to processing cancellation; honour cancellation requests promptly without pressure tactics.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits deceiving the average consumer about a product's main characteristics. The ad promotes a 'personalised' plan, yet the campaign declares no personalisation is used. If the plan is not in fact individually tailored, the 'personalised' claim is false/unsubstantiated and likely to cause consumers to enrol who would not otherwise have done so.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Only claim the plan is 'personalised' if it is genuinely individualised and you can substantiate how. Otherwise remove or qualify the word (e.g. 'a fitness plan') so the described main characteristic matches what is actually delivered.

verdicts.notes: The FitCoach free-trial funnel engages the UCPD on multiple fronts, including a blacklisted (per se prohibited) practice. Describing the plan as "100% FREE" when it silently converts to a 49.99 EUR/month subscription and captures full card details is a misuse of 'free' (Annex I point 20) and a misleading omission of the price/subscription terms (Art. 7). The phone-only, business-hours cancellation with mandatory retention counter-offers is an aggressive practice via onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights (Arts. 8-9), and the unsubstantiated "personalised" claim is a misleading action (Art. 6). Overall this is a classic subscription-trap pattern that is likely unlawful under the Directive.

report.executive_summary: The FitCoach funnel advertises a "100% FREE" plan for a 1.95 EUR shipping fee, but silently signs users up for a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days, with the paid terms hidden in a footer link and on page 3 of the terms. This is a textbook "subscription trap" and carries serious, likely-unlawful compliance problems. The most severe is a per se prohibited practice under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive: calling something "free" when the consumer must pay a recurring charge is blacklisted and unlawful in all circumstances — no context or defence applies. On top of that, the buried pricing is a misleading omission, the phone-only/business-hours cancellation with mandatory three-offer retention scripts is an aggressive practice and a prohibited "dark pattern" under the DSA, and the "personalised" claim contradicts your own declaration of no personalisation. Capturing full card details under a "free/shipping only" pretext also breaches GDPR transparency and fairness rules, and undermines any valid legal basis for storing the card for recurring billing. This campaign should not run in its current form. The good news is these issues are fixable, but they require genuine redesign, not cosmetic tweaks.
recommendations: STOP calling the plan '100% FREE'. This is a blacklisted practice under UCPD Annex I point 20 and is unlawful regardless of any disclaimers. Replace with an accurate description, e.g. '5-day trial, then 49.99 EUR/month unless cancelled', shown up front.

Disclose the recurring price (49.99 EUR/month), the 5-day auto-conversion date and the auto-renewal mechanism prominently on the ad and directly adjacent to the payment fields at checkout — with equal visual prominence to any trial/free language. Do not bury this in footer or page-3 terms.

Require an explicit, unbundled affirmative opt-in acknowledging the paid subscription BEFORE capturing card details, and use that same-screen disclosure to establish transparency and a valid GDPR legal basis for storing the card for recurring charges.

Replace the cancellation process: provide an online, self-service cancellation at least as easy as sign-up (e.g. one-click in the account area), available 24/7. Remove the mandatory three-offer retention script as a precondition to cancelling — this is both an aggressive practice (UCPD) and a prohibited dark pattern (DSA Art. 25).

Resolve the 'personalised' claim contradiction: either the plan is genuinely individualised (substantiate it and disclose any profiling under GDPR) or remove the word. As declared 'no personalisation', the current claim is likely a misleading action.

Provide a proper layered privacy notice at the point of card collection covering controller identity, that the card is retained and re-used for monthly billing, the legal basis, retention period and data-subject rights (GDPR Arts. 12/13).
If onboarding collects health, weight or fitness-condition data, treat it as special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 and obtain explicit consent with appropriate safeguards.
Ensure the display/social ads carry correct platform ad labelling and advertiser identification (DSA Art. 26).

Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing. 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.

Despite declaring no personalisation, the offer promises a 'personalised' plan and collects payment/fitness data, so personal data processing is engaged (transparency/consent, fitness data may be health-adjacent). 'FREE'/hidden-subscription and dark-pattern cancellation are strong misleading action/omission and aggressive-practice concerns under UCPD.
triage.summary: A 'free trial' funnel that advertises a personalised FitCoach plan as 100% FREE (mentioned 11 times) while concealing enrolment into a EUR 49.99/month subscription in footer/page-3 terms, auto-starting after 5 days. Cancellation is deliberately obstructed (phone-only, business hours, mandatory retention counter-offers). Collects full payment card and health/fitness-related personal data at checkout.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (card details and fitness/personalisation inputs) is collected within a deliberately deceptive funnel: 'FREE' appears 11 times while the EUR 49.99/month auto-enrolment is concealed in footer/page-3 terms. Collecting and using personal data to operate a funnel that misleads the data subject about the true nature and cost of the processing/relationship breaches the fairness and transparency principle, which requires processing to be fair and not deceptive irrespective of the separate consumer-law analysis.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.
findings.recommendation: Ensure that at the point personal data is collected, the true commercial context (paid recurring subscription, price, start date) is disclosed clearly and prominently so that data is not obtained under materially misleading pretences. Align the data-collection flow with a genuinely fair presentation of the offer.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The campaign collects personal data (payment card data and personalisation/fitness inputs) at checkout but shows no Article 13 information at the point of collection — controller identity, purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention periods, data subject rights and (given the 'personalised plan') information about any profiling. The only linked information is buried footer/page-3 terms, which is not a substitute for a layered privacy notice presented at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout requires full card details
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at the checkout/sign-up point covering all Art. 13 items (identity/contact of controller, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, rights, and any profiling), rather than relying solely on footer terms links.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information relating to the processing and the offer is not concise, transparent, intelligible or easily accessible: material terms are pushed to page 3 of the terms and a footer link. Art. 12 requires information addressed to data subjects to be provided in an easily accessible form using clear and plain language; burying it defeats that requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link
findings.recommendation: Surface data-processing and offer information in a clear, easily accessible manner near the point of data entry using plain language; avoid burying material information in footer links or deep terms pages.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Building a 'personalised' fitness plan from user data is automated processing to evaluate personal aspects (health, fitness, personal preferences) and therefore meets the definition of profiling under Art. 4(4). Notably the campaign declares 'no personalisation/targeting', yet the copy advertises a personalised plan — an internal inconsistency that means profiling may be occurring without being acknowledged or governed.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Clarify and document whether personalisation/profiling actually occurs. If the plan is personalised from user data, treat it as profiling: document it, disclose it, and ensure a valid lawful basis and Art. 13 profiling information are in place.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing personal data to generate a personalised plan and to run the subscription requires a valid lawful basis. None is disclosed. Personalisation/profiling based on user-supplied data generally requires consent or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment; contract necessity would not obviously cover profiling that goes beyond what the user requested. Absent any stated basis, lawfulness is not demonstrated.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the lawful basis for each processing purpose (contract for the subscription; consent or a documented LIA for personalisation/profiling), and disclose it in the privacy notice.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: A personalised fitness/coaching plan is likely to involve data concerning health or health-adjacent data (fitness levels, body metrics, goals). Processing such special-category data is prohibited unless an Art. 9(2) exception — in a marketing/personalisation context typically explicit consent — applies. The campaign shows no explicit consent mechanism, and the deceptive funnel makes valid explicit consent unlikely.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the personalisation inputs constitute health data. If so, obtain freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous explicit consent (Art. 9(2)(a)) via a clear, unbundled mechanism, and do not condition it on the deceptive free-trial framing.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: To the extent consent is relied on for personalisation/marketing, Art. 7 requires that withdrawing consent be as easy as giving it. The asymmetric, phone-only, business-hours-only, friction-laden cancellation design signals a broader intent to obstruct withdrawal/opt-out, which is inconsistent with the Art. 7 easy-withdrawal condition and the fairness of any consent obtained through this flow.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, online self-service mechanism to withdraw consent and to cancel, at least as easy as the sign-up, and remove the mandatory retention-friction steps for consent withdrawal.

verdicts.notes: The funnel processes personal data (full payment card details and fitness/personalisation data used to build a "personalised FitCoach plan") within a deceptive free-trial/subscription-trap flow. This engages GDPR on multiple fronts: the fairness and transparency principle is undermined by collecting data inside a misleading "100% FREE" context with material terms buried; Art. 13 information does not appear to be provided at the point of collection; the "personalised" plan built on fitness data constitutes profiling requiring a disclosed lawful basis (and, as health-adjacent data, likely explicit consent under Art. 9). Despite the declaration of "no personalisation," the campaign copy itself advertises a personalised plan, creating an inconsistency that must be resolved.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits in all circumstances describing a product as 'free' if the consumer has to pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of delivery. Here the offer is described as '100% FREE' and 'FREE' appears 11 times, yet the consumer is enrolled into a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that auto-starts after 5 days. That recurring charge is not an unavoidable delivery cost, so calling the plan 'free' is a blacklisted (per se) unfair practice regardless of consumer effect.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.
findings.recommendation: Stop describing the plan as '100% FREE'. If a genuine trial is offered, present the recurring 49.99 EUR/month price with equal or greater prominence at the point of the 'free' claim (e.g. 'Free 5-day trial, then 49.99 EUR/month unless cancelled'). Remove or drastically reduce repeated 'FREE' messaging that contradicts the true cost.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the average consumer needs, or providing it in an unclear or untimely manner. The recurring 49.99 EUR/month price, the 5-day auto-conversion, and the cancellation mechanism are all material information. Burying them on 'page 3 of the terms' and a footer link, while the headline shouts 'FREE', means the material terms are hidden and presented untimely, distorting the transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days unless cancelled ... the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the total cost, the auto-renewal trigger date, and how to cancel clearly and up-front on the ad and landing page, adjacent to the offer and before card details are collected — not solely in footer/page-3 terms. Use a plain-language pre-checkout summary the consumer must see.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers misleading actions regarding price or the manner of its calculation and the existence of a price advantage. Fronting only a 1.95 EUR shipping fee while the real cost is 49.99 EUR/month (drip pricing) creates a false overall impression of the price and of a 'free' advantage, likely causing consumers to take a transactional decision (handing over card details) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping
findings.recommendation: State the full price the consumer will actually pay, including the recurring subscription, in the same visual context as the '1.95 EUR shipping' and any 'free' claim, so the total cost is not misrepresented.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive any practice that, through undue influence or onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights, impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Restricting cancellation to phone-only during business hours (while sign-up is instant online) and forcing consumers through three mandatory retention counter-offers before a cancellation is processed creates onerous, disproportionate barriers to exercising the right to cancel, pressuring consumers to remain subscribed.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Provide a cancellation route at least as easy as sign-up (e.g. one-click online cancellation available 24/7). Remove mandatory retention counter-offers as a precondition to processing cancellation; any retention offer must be optional and must not delay or obstruct the cancellation.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour. The overall design of the funnel — a 'free' hook, hidden recurring cost, silent 5-day auto-conversion, and obstructed cancellation — combines into a subscription trap that falls below the standard of professional diligence and materially distorts behaviour, reinforcing the specific-provision findings above.
findings.evidence_quote: the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link
findings.recommendation: Redesign the funnel so the whole customer journey is transparent and fair: honest headline, prominent price and auto-renewal disclosure, affirmative consent to the paid subscription, and a symmetric, easy cancellation path.

verdicts.notes: This "free trial" funnel raises serious UCPD concerns. The prominent "100% FREE" claim (11×) is a blacklisted misuse of 'free' because the consumer is in fact enrolled in a EUR 49.99/month subscription — a per se prohibited practice under Annex I point 20. The concealment of the subscription cost in footer/page-3 terms is a misleading omission (Art. 7) and the price presentation is a misleading action (Art. 6). The deliberately obstructed, phone-only cancellation with mandatory retention counter-offers is likely an aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9), reinforced by the general fairness safety-net (Art. 5). Multiple provisions are engaged with at least one clear blacklist violation.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises a fitness plan as "100% FREE" (repeated 11 times) for only €1.95 shipping, while actually enrolling consumers into a €49.99/month subscription that auto-starts after 5 days — with the true cost buried in footer/page-3 terms and cancellation restricted to phone-only during business hours behind three mandatory retention offers.
