The most serious problem: calling the plan "free" when consumers must pay a recurring subscription is a per se prohibited practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I, point 20) — banned in all circumstances, no defence available. On top of that, the hidden pricing is a misleading action/omission, and the obstructed cancellation is likely an aggressive practice. Separately, the funnel collects payment and fitness data (likely health data) inside this deceptive flow, breaching GDPR's fairness and transparency principles, with no proper privacy notice at collection and an internal contradiction (the campaign declares "no personalisation" yet advertises a "personalised plan"). The overall verdict is critical: the campaign cannot run in its current form and needs a fundamental redesign, not cosmetic tweaks.
recommendations: STOP using '100% FREE' / 'FREE' language. Because consumers must pay a €49.99/month subscription, calling the plan 'free' is a blacklisted, per se illegal practice (UCPD Annex I point 20) — this alone blocks the campaign from running. Reframe honestly, e.g. 'Free 5-day trial, then €49.99/month unless cancelled.'

Disclose the full price, the 5-day auto-conversion date, and how to cancel clearly and prominently on the ad and landing page — adjacent to the offer and before any card details are collected. Do not rely on footer links or page-3 terms.
Require affirmative, informed consent to the paid subscription at checkout (e.g. an unbundled tick showing '€49.99/month after 5 days'), rather than defaulting consumers into it.

Fix the cancellation path: provide an online, 24/7 self-service cancellation at least as easy as sign-up, and remove the mandatory three retention counter-offers as a precondition to cancelling (aggressive-practice risk under UCPD Arts. 8-9).

Resolve the personalisation contradiction: the campaign declares 'no personalisation' but sells a 'personalised plan.' Confirm whether profiling occurs; if fitness/body data is used, treat it as health data (special category) and obtain valid explicit consent (GDPR Art. 9) — which cannot be validly given inside a deceptive funnel.

Add a clear, layered privacy notice at the point of data collection covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients, data-subject rights and any profiling (GDPR Arts. 12-13).
Document a lawful basis for each processing purpose (contract for the subscription; consent/LIA for personalisation) before launch.
Treat this as a full funnel redesign, not a copy edit — re-submit for review once the offer framing, pricing disclosure, consent, cancellation, and data-collection flows are all corrected.

campaign.title: FlyGreen — carbon neutral flights
campaign.text: Airline brand campaign across OOH, social and in-app banners: 'Fly 100% CARBON NEUTRAL. Every FlyGreen ticket is climate-positive — you fly, the planet wins.' The claim rests entirely on purchasing unverified forestry offsets covering an estimated 8% of per-flight emissions; no lifecycle data, no methodology page, no third-party verification. The green leaf logo and 'planet-positive' tagline appear on all fares including long-haul.

detected_practices: absolute environmental claim ('100% carbon neutral')
climate-positive / 'planet-positive' claim
unsubstantiated green claim (offsets cover only ~8% of emissions)
reliance on unverified forestry carbon offsets
no methodology, lifecycle data or third-party verification
green imagery/leaf logo used across all fares including long-haul (greenwashing)
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is general consumers with no targeting; social and app channels mean minors could plausibly be reached even if not the intended audience. Core risk is misleading vague and unsubstantiated environmental claims under the UCPD (Annex I and forthcoming greenwashing rules). DSA is included because social/platform advertising raises transparency and dissemination obligations for online intermediaries. No generative AI declared and no personalisation/personal data declared, so AI Act and GDPR are not obviously engaged based on the submission.
triage.summary: An airline brand campaign across OOH, social and in-app banners promoting flights as '100% carbon neutral' and 'climate-positive', where the claim rests on unverified forestry offsets covering only ~8% of per-flight emissions with no lifecycle data, methodology or third-party verification. This is a textbook greenwashing / misleading environmental claim case applied across all fares including long-haul. Distributed to general consumers, including via social platforms.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The social and in-app banner elements are advertisements presented via online platforms, engaging DSA Art. 26(1). For each such ad, recipients must be able to identify in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf/by whom it is paid. The submission describes only creative and claims and gives no indication that the ads will carry the required ad-identification and advertiser-identity information; the advertiser must ensure this information is supplied so the platform can meet its obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: Airline brand campaign across OOH, social and in-app banners
findings.recommendation: Ensure the FlyGreen social and in-app placements are delivered through official ad channels with the platform's paid-ad label, and that the advertiser identity and paying entity are correctly declared to the platform so the mandatory 'who paid / on whose behalf' disclosures appear. Do not disguise the ads as organic/editorial content.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If any of the social placements run on a Very Large Online Platform, DSA Art. 39 requires that VLOP to keep a public ad repository containing the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. The unsubstantiated '100% carbon neutral' / 'climate-positive' claim, resting on offsets covering only ~8% of emissions with no verification, will therefore be publicly archived and open to regulator, competitor and NGO scrutiny for the retention period.
findings.evidence_quote: Fly 100% CARBON NEUTRAL. Every FlyGreen ticket is climate-positive
findings.recommendation: Assume every platform ad will be permanently and publicly archived: only run environmental claims that can be substantiated with lifecycle data, disclosed methodology and third-party verification, since the archived creative cannot later be quietly withdrawn.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Delivery via social and in-app channels means minors may plausibly be reached. However, DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits only advertisements based on profiling of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. Because the campaign declares no profiling, targeting or personal-data use, the specific ban is not engaged; contextual, non-profiled ads reaching minors do not breach Art. 28(2). Flagged for awareness only.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: no
findings.recommendation: Keep these placements strictly contextual/non-profiled. If any future optimisation, lookalike or behavioural targeting is introduced, re-assess against Art. 28(2), which bans profiling-based ads to users reasonably known to be minors regardless of consent.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core legal risk (misleading/unsubstantiated environmental claims) sits under the UCPD, not the DSA. Under the DSA, the campaign engages the advertising-transparency regime because it is distributed as paid ads on social platforms and in-app banners: each ad must be clearly identifiable as an ad, with the advertiser/payer identifiable (Art. 26(1)), and if it runs on a VLOP it will be publicly archived in an ad repository where the unverified '100% carbon neutral' claim will be exposed to scrutiny (Art. 39). No profiling or sensitive-data targeting is declared, so the bans in Art. 26(3) and Art. 28 (profiling-based ads to minors) are not triggered even though minors may be incidentally reached via contextual placements.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The claims '100% carbon neutral' and 'climate-positive' are false/deceptive as to a main characteristic (environmental benefits/results) of the flights. In reality the offsets cover only an estimated 8% of per-flight emissions, so the flight is far from carbon neutral and cannot be 'climate-positive'. 'You fly, the planet wins' asserts a net benefit that is factually impossible for an aviation product whose emissions are 92% unabated. Such deceptive environmental claims are likely to cause the average consumer to book a flight they would otherwise avoid, distorting a transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Fly 100% CARBON NEUTRAL. Every FlyGreen ticket is climate-positive — you fly, the planet wins.
findings.recommendation: Remove the absolute and net-positive claims ('100% carbon neutral', 'climate-positive', 'you fly, the planet wins'). Do not describe the product as carbon neutral or climate-positive while ~92% of emissions are unabated. Any residual environmental claim must be accurate, specific and reflect actual verified reductions (e.g. exact percentage of emissions covered by verified offsets), and must not overstate benefits.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The environmental claim is presented without any of the material information the average consumer needs to assess it: the offset methodology, the scope/percentage of emissions actually covered, lifecycle emissions data, and independent verification. Omitting or hiding this substantiation renders the claim misleading by omission, especially where the headline claim ('100% carbon neutral') strongly implies robust substantiation that does not exist.
findings.evidence_quote: no lifecycle data, no methodology page, no third-party verification
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, accessible substantiation: publish a methodology page, disclose that offsets cover only ~8% of per-flight emissions and the residual unabated share, cite recognised standards and independent third-party verification, and link this prominently from all ad assets. If robust substantiation cannot be provided, the claim must not be made.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Applying green leaf imagery and a 'planet-positive' tagline uniformly across all fares, including high-emission long-haul flights whose offset coverage is negligible, is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour by creating an overall impression of environmental soundness the product does not possess. This engages the Art. 5 general fairness safety-net where the practice is not fully captured by the specific misleading rules.
findings.evidence_quote: The green leaf logo and 'planet-positive' tagline appear on all fares including long-haul.
findings.recommendation: Stop using blanket green imagery/'planet-positive' branding across all fares, particularly long-haul. Restrict any environmental signalling to what is accurate and verified per product, and adopt a professional-diligence review process for all environmental claims before publication.

verdicts.notes: This is a textbook greenwashing case under the UCPD. The campaign makes absolute, unqualified environmental claims ("100% carbon neutral", "climate-positive", "you fly, the planet wins") that are objectively false or misleading: the claim rests on unverified forestry offsets covering only ~8% of per-flight emissions, so the flights are neither carbon neutral nor climate-positive. These deceptive claims about a main characteristic of the product violate Art. 6 (misleading actions). The absence of any lifecycle data, methodology or third-party verification is a misleading omission of material substantiation information under Art. 7. Applying green branding uniformly across all fares including long-haul reinforces the deception and breaches the Art. 5 professional-diligence standard. Under the CJEU/CPC case law and the incoming Empowering Consumers Directive (2024/825), generic "carbon neutral"-type claims of this kind are treated as unfair; offset-based neutrality claims of this severity are high-risk.

report.executive_summary: The FlyGreen campaign markets flights as "100% carbon neutral" and "climate-positive" ("you fly, the planet wins") across OOH, social and in-app channels. This is a textbook greenwashing problem: the neutrality claim rests on unverified forestry offsets that cover only about 8% of per-flight emissions, leaving roughly 92% unabated — so the flights are neither carbon neutral nor climate-positive. These absolute, unsubstantiated environmental claims are likely to breach the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (misleading actions under Art. 6, misleading omissions under Art. 7, and the general fairness standard under Art. 5), which is the campaign's core and most serious legal exposure. Applying green-leaf imagery and "planet-positive" branding uniformly across all fares, including high-emission long-haul, makes the deception worse. There is also a secondary, lower-level DSA issue: the paid social and in-app placements must carry proper ad-identification and advertiser/payer disclosures, and if run on a very large platform the misleading creative will be permanently and publicly archived in an ad repository open to regulator, competitor and NGO scrutiny. GDPR and the AI Act are not engaged. Verdict: do not run this campaign in its current form — the environmental claims must be corrected or removed before publication.
recommendations: Do not publish the campaign as drafted. Remove the absolute and net-positive claims — '100% carbon neutral', 'climate-positive', and 'you fly, the planet wins' — as they are false while ~92% of per-flight emissions are unabated (UCPD Art. 6, critical).
Stop applying the green-leaf logo and 'planet-positive' tagline uniformly across all fares, especially long-haul, where offset coverage is negligible (UCPD Art. 5).

If any environmental claim is retained, make it accurate and specific: state that verified offsets cover only ~8% of per-flight emissions and disclose the unabated residual, rather than implying overall neutrality.

Publish a linked methodology page with lifecycle emissions data, recognised offset standards and independent third-party verification, and link it prominently from all ad assets; if this substantiation cannot be provided, do not make the claim at all (UCPD Art. 7).
Introduce a professional-diligence sign-off process reviewing all environmental claims against the UCPD and the incoming Empowering Consumers Directive (2024/825) before publication.

For the social and in-app placements, deliver via official paid-ad channels with the platform's paid-ad label and correct advertiser/payer identity so DSA Art. 26(1) transparency is met; do not disguise ads as organic content.

Assume any ad run on a very large online platform will be permanently and publicly archived (DSA Art. 39) — only run creative that is fully substantiated, as archived versions cannot be quietly withdrawn.

Keep social/in-app placements strictly contextual and non-profiled; if behavioural, lookalike or optimisation targeting is later added, re-assess against DSA Art. 28(2) (ban on profiling-based ads to minors).

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation and behavioural retargeting are automated processing of personal data to target individuals, i.e. profiling under Art. 4(4). Any such processing requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Behavioural advertising to consumers generally requires consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment; here no lawful basis is identified, and given the sensitive purpose (payday lending) and vulnerable audience a legitimate-interest balancing test would be very difficult to pass, pointing towards a consent requirement that is not evidenced.

For behavioural ad targeting obtain freely given, specific, informed opt-in consent (and note ePrivacy consent for cookies/trackers), or conduct and record a legitimate-interest assessment — recognising that targeting financially distressed consumers for high-cost credit is unlikely to survive a balancing test.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting people by their 'economic situation' (financial difficulty) is expressly within the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling. This means the full profiling regime (lawful basis, transparency, right to object, Art. 22 safeguards) applies, and the profiling evaluates a personal aspect of vulnerable individuals.
