findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring that a customer is pregnant from purchase history is processing of health data — a special category under Art. 9 — even though it is inferred rather than declared. Art. 9 prohibits such processing unless a specific exception (e.g. explicit consent) applies. Here enrolment is silent and there is no explicit consent, so the prohibition is breached.
findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring pregnancy/health status for marketing unless you first obtain separate, explicit, granular opt-in consent specifically covering the use of health inferences for targeted messaging; otherwise remove health-derived signals (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) from audience-building entirely.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous via a clear affirmative action. Silent automatic enrolment and a vague notice referring only to 'personalised offers' cannot constitute valid consent — and for Art. 9 data explicit consent is required, which is entirely missing.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Implement an unbundled, affirmative opt-in (no pre-ticked boxes, no silent enrolment) that specifically names the health inference and the prenatal/baby marketing purpose before any enrolment occurs.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: All processing needs a valid Art. 6 lawful basis. Email/app-push direct marketing and profiling generally require consent (or, at most, a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment which cannot cover Art. 9 data). No lawful basis is evident and legitimate interest cannot lawfully justify silent processing of sensitive health inferences for marketing.
findings.evidence_quote: A pharmacy chain mines loyalty-card purchase histories
findings.recommendation: Document a valid lawful basis before processing; for health-inference marketing the only viable basis is explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a) combined with Art. 6(1)(a). Do not rely on legitimate interest for this processing.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle prohibits covert data collection and misleading privacy information. Silently deriving a pregnancy inference and describing it only as 'personalised offers' is covert and unfair processing, breaching Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Make the profiling and health-inference activity fully transparent at the point of collection and stop describing sensitive-data-driven targeting with a vague euphemism.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at collection the controller disclose the purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights, and the existence of profiling. A notice mentioning only 'personalised offers' omits the pregnancy/health inference, the profiling logic, the legal basis and the rights — failing the information duty.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the privacy notice to specifically state that purchase data is used to infer life-stage/health status for targeted marketing, the legal basis (explicit consent), retention period, recipients, and how to object/withdraw.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear plain language. A euphemistic reference to 'personalised offers' that conceals sensitive-data profiling is not transparent or intelligible about what actually happens.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Use clear, plain-language disclosures that a reasonable customer would understand describe pregnancy/health inference and baby-product targeting.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of purchase data to predict health/life-stage and segment customers squarely meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling, triggering the associated transparency, lawful-basis and objection obligations that are not satisfied here.
findings.evidence_quote: automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience and receive personalised emails and app pushes
findings.recommendation: Treat the audience-building as profiling: document it, disclose it, ground it in explicit consent, and honour objection rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and related profiling. Nothing in the campaign indicates an easy, communicated opt-out from the profiling and messaging, so this obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, one-click objection/opt-out in every email and app-push and honour it immediately for both messaging and the underlying profiling.

verdicts.notes: The campaign infers pregnancy (health data, an Art. 9 special category) from loyalty-card purchase histories and uses it to target individuals — the core prohibited processing under GDPR Art. 9, which requires explicit consent that is plainly absent here ("Enrolment is silent"). The processing also lacks a valid lawful basis (Art. 6), fails the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and the specific information duties (Arts. 12-13, since the notice mentions only "personalised offers"), constitutes profiling (Art. 4(4)) with no evident objection mechanism (Art. 21), and the shared-household exposure of sensitive inferences aggravates the fairness breach. This is a high-risk, likely-unlawful campaign as described.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data (GDPR Art. 9), including health data derived by inference. Enrolling customers into a 'Growing Family' audience by inferring pregnancy from purchase histories and then serving them personalised prenatal/baby advertising is precisely profiling-on-health-data ad targeting, and the ban applies regardless of consent. This is a substantive breach IF the delivery channel (the pharmacy's app serving app-push ads) is an online platform under the DSA; for pure email/1:1 push the DSA's platform scope may not attach, so severity is set to high rather than critical pending confirmation of the delivery interface.
findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience and receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products
findings.recommendation: Do not use inferred pregnancy or any GDPR Art. 9 attribute (directly or via purchase-history proxies) to determine who receives advertising. If the app is or may be treated as an online platform, remove health-inference from all ad-targeting parameters entirely — consent cannot cure the DSA Art. 26(3) prohibition. Base any prenatal/baby messaging on explicit opt-in self-declaration rather than silent inference.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28(2) bans presenting profiling-based advertisements to recipients the provider is aware with reasonable certainty are minors, and Art. 28(1) requires a high level of privacy/safety for minors on platforms accessible to them. Shared-household loyalty accounts mean profiling-based prenatal/baby ads (and the sensitive pregnancy inference) may reach minors who use the account. If delivered via a platform interface, this engages Art. 28; severity is medium because it is contingent on both platform scope and on minors actually being reachable through the shared account, which the campaign does not confirm.
findings.evidence_quote: Household members sharing the account also see the campaign.
findings.recommendation: Where a shared or household account may be used by minors, suppress profiling-based advertising to that account and avoid exposing sensitive life-stage inferences through shared interfaces. Implement account-holder verification / individual profiles so profiled messaging is not shown to unidentified account users who may be minors.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that, for each advertisement on a platform, recipients can identify in a clear and unambiguous manner that it is an ad and meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that it is presented to them, and how to change them. Silent enrolment with only a vague 'personalised offers' reference provides no meaningful disclosure of the targeting parameters (pregnancy inference from purchase history). This obligation is engaged only if the messaging is presented as advertising on an online platform; for direct email/push the transparency requirements arise chiefly under GDPR/UCPD, hence low severity here.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'.
findings.recommendation: If any of this is served through a platform interface, provide clear, real-time ad-transparency notices per Art. 26(1): identify the content as advertising, disclose the main targeting parameters (that they were selected based on purchase-history inference), and offer an accessible way to change/opt out of those parameters.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's advertising rules (Arts. 25–28) apply to providers of online platforms. As described, this campaign is delivered via direct email and app-push from a pharmacy chain to its own loyalty-card holders — 1:1 direct marketing that likely falls outside the "advertising presented on an online platform" concept, so the DSA may not be the primary instrument (GDPR Art. 9 and the UCPD are more directly engaged). However, if the pharmacy's app qualifies as an online platform, or if any of this targeting/personalisation is served through a platform interface, two DSA prohibitions are squarely implicated in substance: the ban on ads based on profiling using special-category (health) data, and the ban on profiling-based ads reaching minors via shared accounts. Findings are flagged with this scope contingency.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The average consumer is not told that their loyalty-card purchase history (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) is being mined to infer pregnancy and drive the messaging they receive. The commercial intent and the material basis for the targeting are hidden and disclosed only in an unclear, ambiguous way ('personalised offers'). Under Art. 7 this is a misleading omission: the consumer lacks material information needed to make an informed decision about whether to accept pregnancy-based marketing. The lack of transparency about who receives it (shared household accounts) compounds the omission.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, timely, upfront disclosure of the specific data-driven basis and commercial nature of the enrolment before sending life-stage messaging: state that purchase history is used to infer life stage, name the audience, and offer an easy, prominent opt-in/opt-out. Replace vague 'personalised offers' wording with specific, intelligible information about what triggers the messaging.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The primary audience is a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (consumers inferred to be pregnant), and the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group under Art. 5(3). Silent enrolment combined with emotionally resonant messaging ('Week by week, we're with you') aimed at this group is capable of materially distorting economic behaviour and is arguably contrary to professional diligence, functioning as the fairness safety-net where the specific rules leave gaps.
findings.evidence_quote: loyalty-card holders inferred as pregnant
findings.recommendation: Apply heightened care when targeting sensitive life-stages: obtain genuine informed opt-in, avoid manipulative emotional framing, and document a professional-diligence assessment showing the campaign does not exploit the group's heightened sensitivity. Consider excluding health-inferred audiences from automatic enrolment altogether.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Repeated email and app-push messaging keyed to an emotionally sensitive life-stage could amount to undue influence exploiting a consumer's situation if it is persistent and inescapable, which can render a practice aggressive under Arts. 8-9. On the current facts persistence/harassment is not clearly established, so this is flagged as a lower-level risk rather than a likely breach.
findings.evidence_quote: receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products ('Week by week, we're with you')
findings.recommendation: Set frequency caps, honour easy unsubscribe/mute for the audience, and avoid intensifying cadence around emotionally charged moments so the messaging cannot be characterised as harassment or undue influence.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD chiefly through misleading omission / hidden commercial intent: consumers are silently enrolled into a health-inference-driven marketing audience with only a vague "personalised offers" notice, so the material basis and commercial nature of the messaging is not made transparent (Art. 7). Because the audience is a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (consumers inferred as pregnant) receiving emotionally resonant messaging, the general fairness safety-net (Art. 5, assessed from the average member of the vulnerable group) is also engaged. No blacklisted (Annex I) practice is clearly present on the facts, and the consent/special-category-data aspects fall to GDPR/DSA. Aggressive-practice concerns are flagged at a lower level pending evidence of persistence.

report.executive_summary: This campaign silently enrols pharmacy loyalty-card holders into a "Growing Family" audience by inferring pregnancy from their purchases (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) and then sends them prenatal and baby marketing via email and app-push. The core problem is that inferring pregnancy is processing of health data, which GDPR treats as a special category requiring explicit, opt-in consent — and here enrolment is silent with only a vague "personalised offers" notice, so there is no lawful basis and no valid consent. This is a likely unlawful, high-exposure campaign as designed, not a fixable-around-the-edges issue. On top of GDPR, the same health-based profiling triggers a DSA advertising prohibition if the app counts as an online platform (consent cannot cure that ban), and raises added risk of reaching minors through shared household accounts. Under consumer law (UCPD), hiding the fact that purchase history drives the targeting is a misleading omission, made worse because pregnant consumers are a vulnerable group receiving emotionally charged messaging. In short: the campaign cannot go live in its current form. You must either obtain genuine explicit opt-in for health-based targeting or stop building audiences from health-related purchases altogether.
recommendations: Stop the silent enrolment immediately: do not build the 'Growing Family' audience from pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits or any purchase-derived health signal unless and until you have separate, explicit, granular opt-in consent that specifically names the pregnancy/health inference and the baby-product marketing purpose. Pre-ticked boxes and silent auto-enrolment do not count.
If you cannot secure genuine explicit consent, remove health-derived signals from audience-building entirely and base any prenatal/baby messaging only on customers who self-declare and opt in.

Rewrite the privacy notice and messaging in clear plain language: state that purchase history is used to infer life-stage/health status for targeted marketing, name the legal basis (explicit consent), retention, recipients, and how to object or withdraw. Drop the euphemistic 'personalised offers' wording.

Treat the DSA health-targeting ban (Art. 26(3)) as a hard stop if the pharmacy app is or may be an online platform — consent does not cure it. Confirm the app's DSA status before relying on it as a channel; if in scope, do not use any Art. 9 attribute or purchase-history proxy to decide who sees ads.

Fix the shared-household exposure: suppress profiling-based messaging and sensitive inferences on shared/household accounts and introduce individual profiles or account-holder verification so a pregnancy inference is never shown to unidentified users, who may include minors.
Add a clear, one-click opt-out in every email and app-push and honour it immediately for both the messaging and the underlying profiling (GDPR Art. 21 absolute right to object to direct marketing).
Apply frequency caps and avoid intensifying cadence around emotionally charged moments; avoid manipulative framing (e.g. 'Week by week, we're with you') aimed at a vulnerable group.
Before any relaunch, run and document a DPIA and a professional-diligence/fairness assessment given the sensitive audience, and have legal sign-off on the lawful basis.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing

findings.title: Definition of consent

findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing

findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy opt-out in every email and app-push and at enrolment; on objection, immediately stop all profiling and marketing for that individual.

findings.title: Definition of profiling

verdicts.notes: This campaign infers pregnancy — health data under GDPR Art. 9 — from loyalty-card purchases (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) and silently enrols customers into a 'Growing Family' audience for personalised marketing. findings.rationale: Consumers are not told that their loyalty-card purchase histories (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) are being mined to infer pregnancy and silently enrol them into a marketing audience. findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes the RoboPets toy line to children aged 6-11 on YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world, using influencer-voiced videos and daily in-game pop-ups that tell kids to get their parents to buy the product. As written, it cannot be run lawfully. The most serious problem is a clear-cut breach of EU consumer law: the copy directly tells children to buy and to pester their parents to buy — this is banned outright, with no exceptions, under the UCPD "blacklist." On top of that, the daily urgency-driven pop-ups and purchase-linked in-game rewards (500 RoboCoins) amount to aggressive, manipulative "dark pattern" tactics that exploit young children, breaching both the UCPD and the Digital Services Act's minor-protection rules. There are also significant data-protection gaps: the campaign targets children far below the GDPR consent age with no parental-consent mechanism, age verification, lawful basis, or child-friendly privacy notice described, and the "no personalisation" claim has not been verified against how the platforms actually deliver these pop-ups and ads. The AI Act is not engaged. Bottom line: do not launch in its current form — the core creative concept needs to be rebuilt, not just tweaked.
recommendations: STOP — do not launch this campaign in its current form. The direct exhortation to children to buy, and to persuade their parents to buy, is prohibited outright under UCPD Annex I point 28 and is not fixable with disclaimers.

Remove all copy that instructs children to buy or to ask/tell their parents to buy (e.g. 'tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW', 'Ask them today, don't wait'). Reframe messaging to be purely informational and directed at the purchasing adult.

Delete the daily Roblox pop-ups and the purchase-linked reward mechanic (the 500 RoboCoins for ordering the Mega Pack). Any paid product must be offered only to adults via proper age-gating, with no exhortation, urgency, repetition or peer-pressure ('before your friends get theirs') aimed at children.

Ensure every video and in-game placement is unmistakably labelled as advertising in a form a 6-11 year-old can recognise, with RoboPets identified as the advertiser; do not present the animator's endorsement as independent content.

Before any data-processing features run for this age group, confirm the lawful basis under GDPR, implement verifiable parental consent and reasonable age verification, and provide a layered, child-friendly privacy notice at the point of data collection. If no compliant mechanism exists, do not run account-linked pop-ups or reward features for children.

Verify the 'no personalisation/targeting' declaration in writing with both platforms and audit the actual delivery mechanics — profiling-based advertising to known minors is flatly banned under DSA Art. 28(2), and behavioural/engagement data may be in use despite the declaration. Correct the declaration if any tracking is found.
Do not introduce any 'limited time' or 'while stocks last' claims; in a child-directed context, drop urgency framing entirely.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data

findings.evidence_quote: Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!

This engages GDPR obligations around children's consent (Art. 8), the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), and child-appropriate transparency (Arts. 12-13). findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign is deliberately delivered on online platforms accessible to (and here specifically targeting) minors aged 6-11. Art. 28 requires providers to put in place appropriate measures ensuring a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors and to design child-reaching experiences in an age-appropriate way. Daily nagging pop-ups that pressure child players to procure a purchase and dangle an in-game currency reward are the opposite of a safety-oriented, age-appropriate design and expose minors to commercial pressure they cannot reasonably resist. Additionally, Art. 28 bans advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors; the declared audience is expressly children, so any profiling-based delivery would be prohibited outright.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'
findings.recommendation: Redesign the child-facing platform experience to meet Art. 28: remove recurring purchase-pressure pop-ups aimed at child players, eliminate purchase-linked reward incentives directed at minors, and adopt an age-appropriate design that does not commercially pressure children. Confirm in writing that no profiling/behavioural targeting is used to deliver these ads to the child audience, and document the age-assurance and safety measures applied on both platforms.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that manipulates or materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, and expressly captures repeatedly requesting an action (nagging). 'Daily pop-ups' repeatedly prompting child players to trigger a purchase, reinforced with urgency ('tonight') and a virtual-currency reward ('unlock 500 RoboCoins') tied to buying, is a nagging/manipulative design pattern that impairs free decision-making — an effect that is especially severe against a 6-11 audience.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Remove the repeated daily purchase prompts and the reward-for-purchase mechanic from the in-game interface. Any in-world commercial messaging should be non-repetitive, clearly separated from gameplay rewards, and must not exploit the interface to steer children toward transactions.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content presented on the platform is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. An influencer/animator-voiced promotional script and a branded Roblox 'world' blur the line between editorial/entertainment content and advertising (disguised advertising), making it difficult — particularly for children aged 6-11 — to recognise the material as a paid advertisement for RoboPets.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator)
findings.recommendation: Ensure clear, prominent, child-comprehensible ad disclosure on all video and in-game placements (e.g. unambiguous 'Advert'/'Paid promotion for RoboPets' labelling), identify the advertiser on whose behalf the content is presented, and verify the hosting platforms surface the required ad-identification information for each placement.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is delivered to children aged 6-11 via online platforms (YouTube Kids, Roblox branded world), squarely engaging the DSA's minor-protection and interface-design rules. The daily nagging pop-ups pressuring child players to trigger a purchase, combined with a virtual-currency reward tied to buying, are classic manipulative design directed at a vulnerable audience (Art. 25) and are incompatible with the high level of safety Art. 28 requires for platforms accessible to minors. The disguised, influencer-voiced advergame format also raises ad-identifiability concerns under Art. 26(1). The "no personalisation" declaration should be independently verified, as any profiling-based ad delivery to these known minors would independently breach Art. 28.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 prohibits, in all circumstances, including in an advertisement a direct exhortation to children to buy, or to persuade their parents/other adults to buy, the advertised product. The video script — voiced for a declared audience of children 6-11 — does exactly this ('tell your mum and dad to buy you one'), as does the Roblox pop-up ('Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight'). This is a blacklisted practice requiring no case-by-case unfairness assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Remove all pester-power and direct-purchase exhortations aimed at children. Child-facing creative must not instruct children to buy or to ask parents to buy. If a purchase message is needed, direct it to the parent/adult audience through channels not targeted at children, and strip imperative buy-language from child-directed video and in-game content.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: This in-game pop-up is a second, distinct instance of the same blacklisted practice: a direct exhortation to child players to persuade their parents to buy, reinforced with an in-game virtual-currency reward tied to the purchase, delivered as recurring daily prompts to children. Falls squarely within Annex I point 28.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!
findings.recommendation: Remove the purchase-linked exhortation and the reward-for-purchase mechanic from child-facing in-game pop-ups. Do not condition in-game rewards (RoboCoins) on children procuring a parental purchase.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign applies undue influence and pressure — urgency language ('RIGHT NOW', 'tonight', 'don't wait'), social-pressure framing ('before your friends get theirs'), daily repeated pop-ups, and a purchase-linked reward — to an audience of children whose freedom of choice is readily impaired. Taken together (timing, persistence, exploitation of credulity) this is likely an aggressive commercial practice that materially distorts children's transactional behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the urgency/pressure and social-comparison framing and the daily repetition of prompts. Any surviving product information for children must be non-pressurising and must not exploit the credulity or peer-pressure susceptibility of young children.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (here children, due to age and credulity) to be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. The overall design — child-credibility endorsement, urgency, reward incentives — is contrary to professional diligence and likely materially distorts the economic behaviour of children 6-11, reinforcing the specific breaches above as an overarching fairness failure.
findings.evidence_quote: They're SO cool — tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW
findings.recommendation: Re-conceive the campaign so it meets professional-diligence standards for child audiences: no exploitation of credulity, no purchase pressure, and independent legal/child-marketing sign-off before any child-directed launch.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the commercial intent of a practice to be clearly identifiable where not apparent from context. Content voiced by a popular kids' animator and embedded inside a branded Roblox 'world' can blur advertising and entertainment for young children, who are less able to recognise commercial intent. If the advertising nature and any material connection with the creator are not clearly and age-appropriately disclosed, this is a misleading omission / hidden commercial intent.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator)
findings.recommendation: Ensure the commercial/advertising nature is unmistakably and age-appropriately signalled in the video and in the Roblox world, and disclose the material connection with the animator/creator. Note that clearer disclosure does not cure the Annex I point 28 breaches, which must be removed regardless.

verdicts.notes: This child-directed campaign contains a textbook per-se violation of UCPD Annex I point 28: it directly exhorts children (aged 6-11) both to buy and to persuade their parents to buy, prohibited in all circumstances. The high-pressure, repeated ('daily pop-ups') and incentive-backed ('500 RoboCoins') messaging directed at a highly credulous audience also engages the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9) and the general/vulnerable-group safety net (Art. 5). There is a secondary risk that the influencer-voiced content and branded Roblox world do not adequately disclose commercial intent to children (Art. 7).

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes the RoboPets toy line to children aged 6-11 via YouTube Kids videos and a branded Roblox world. As written, it contains a clear-cut illegal practice: both the video script ("tell your mum and dad to buy you one") and the Roblox pop-ups ("Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight") directly tell children to buy or to pester their parents to buy — this is banned outright under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I, point 28), with no room for a case-by-case defence. On top of that, the daily nagging pop-ups, urgency language ("RIGHT NOW", "tonight"), peer-pressure framing, and a virtual-currency reward tied to a purchase amount to aggressive and manipulative "dark pattern" practices that regulators treat especially harshly when aimed at young children (UCPD Arts. 5, 8-9; DSA Arts. 25, 28). Even though you declared "no personalisation," delivering per-player daily pop-ups almost certainly processes children's personal data, triggering GDPR obligations around verifiable parental consent, age verification, and child-friendly transparency (GDPR Arts. 5, 8, 12-13) — none of which are currently described. The influencer/animator-voiced content and branded game world also risk failing to make the advertising nature clear to children (DSA Art. 26; UCPD Art. 7). This campaign cannot launch in its current form; the core mechanics require redesign, not just relabelling.
report.recommendations: Do not launch this campaign in its current form — the direct "ask your parents to buy" messaging is a per-se illegal practice under EU law and must be removed before anything goes live.

The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'

direct exhortation to children to pester parents to purchase ('Get your parents to order the Mega Pack')
urgency/pressure cues aimed at children ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'before your friends get theirs')
influencer/endorsement by popular kids' animator
in-game daily pop-up advertising to child players
purchase incentive tied to in-game reward (500 RoboCoins for Mega Pack purchase)
social pressure / fear-of-missing-out targeting minors
advergaming in a branded Roblox world
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is children 6-11; content is placed on YouTube Kids channels and a Roblox branded world, so the actual reached audience is overwhelmingly minors. Direct exhortations to children to purchase and to pester parents are per se prohibited under UCPD Annex I point 28. Despite the 'no personalisation' declaration, both YouTube and Roblox involve processing of children's personal data; GDPR (Art. 8 children's consent, profiling/advertising to minors) and DSA (prohibition on advertising based on profiling of minors, and platform obligations for minors' protection) should be reviewed. AI Act flagged as not engaged based on the declared absence of generative AI and no apparent AI system in use, though the 'no AI' declaration should be verified by the specialist team.
triage.summary: Marketing campaign for the RoboPets collectible toy line delivered via YouTube Kids videos and a branded Roblox world, explicitly targeting children aged 6-11 in the EU. The creatives directly exhort children to buy or to pressure their parents to buy, using urgency and social-pressure cues, plus in-game pop-ups offering virtual-currency rewards for purchases. Although generative AI and personalisation are declared as not used, the campaign operates on platforms that process minors' data and is directed at children.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The entire declared audience falls below the GDPR Art. 8 threshold (16, or as low as 13 under national law). The campaign runs on YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world — information society services offered directly to children — and delivers personalised interactions such as 'daily pop-ups to child players'. Where consent is the legal basis, processing of these children's data is lawful only with verified parental consent, and the controller must make reasonable efforts to verify it. Nothing in the submission shows any parental-consent or age-verification mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: children 6-11
findings.recommendation: Before launch, confirm the lawful basis for processing child users' data on both platforms. Where consent is relied upon, implement verified parental consent for under-16s (or the applicable national age) with reasonable age-verification measures, and document these in the campaign's data-processing records; if no valid basis exists, do not process the children's data.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Serving daily targeted pop-ups to identified child players and delivering child-directed content on YouTube Kids involves processing children's personal data. The 'no personalisation/targeting' declaration is inconsistent with pushing individualised daily prompts to child players, raising fairness and transparency concerns. Processing of children's data that is not clearly, fairly and transparently disclosed — especially to a highly vulnerable child audience — breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Reconcile the 'no personalisation' declaration with the actual in-game pop-up delivery; map exactly what child data is processed to serve these pop-ups. Ensure processing is fair (no exploitation of children's vulnerability) and that any tracking used to deliver the pop-ups is transparently disclosed and lawful.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: GDPR Art. 12 requires that information provided to data subjects be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear and plain language, in particular where addressed to a child. A campaign directed wholly at 6-11 year-olds on YouTube Kids and Roblox must provide any privacy information in a child-appropriate form. The submission contains no indication that child-appropriate transparency information about data processing is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: voiced by a popular kids' animator
findings.recommendation: Provide child-appropriate, plain-language privacy information (and parent-facing notices) covering any data processing arising from the campaign on both platforms, presented at the relevant point in the child/parent journey.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any processing of the child players' personal data to deliver the campaign requires a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis. For children this is constrained: legitimate interest is difficult to rely on for advertising to young minors, and consent must satisfy Art. 8. The submission asserts no personalisation but does not identify any lawful basis for the processing that platform delivery to identified child players entails.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: no
findings.recommendation: Document and justify the Art. 6(1) lawful basis for every processing activity in the campaign. For advertising-related processing of under-13/under-16 children, rely on verified parental consent rather than legitimate interest, and complete a documented balancing/DPIA before launch.

verdicts.notes: The campaign targets children aged 6-11 in the EU on YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world — both information society services that process minors' personal data. Every child in the declared audience is below the GDPR Art. 8 age threshold (13-16), so any consent-based processing requires verified parental consent, which the "no personalisation" declaration neither addresses nor evidences. The child-directed in-game "daily pop-ups" and the fairness/transparency obligations for information provided to children are also engaged. The declaration of "no targeting" does not remove GDPR exposure because campaign delivery on these platforms necessarily involves processing children's data; the lawful basis, parental-consent, and child-appropriate transparency positions must be documented.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Repeated daily pop-ups nagging child players to trigger a purchase, combined with urgency cues ('RIGHT NOW', "don't wait", 'before your friends get theirs') and a reward tied to buying (500 RoboCoins for the Mega Pack), are manipulative interface/communication design (nagging + FOMO + purchase incentive) that materially distorts and impairs the ability of recipients — here children, an especially vulnerable group — to make free and informed decisions. This falls squarely within the dark-pattern prohibition of Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'
findings.recommendation: Remove the repeated daily purchase pop-ups and the reward-for-purchase mechanic aimed at children, and strip urgency/FOMO cues ('RIGHT NOW', "don't wait", 'before your friends get theirs'). Do not link in-game virtual-currency rewards to real-money purchases in a child audience. Any interface elements must not nag, pressure or steer child players toward transactions.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign is placed on online platforms accessible to (and here specifically directed at) minors aged 6-11. Art. 28 requires a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors and age-appropriate design, and prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. Although personalisation is declared 'no', the campaign is knowingly minor-directed and must be verified as free of any profiling-based ad delivery; the aggressive, pester-power and FOMO content is not age-appropriate design consistent with the protection duty.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for the RoboPets collectible toy line on YouTube Kids channels and a Roblox branded world
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document that no profiling/behavioural targeting is used to deliver these ads to the child audience (coordinate with the platform providers, who bear the primary Art. 28 obligation). Redesign creatives to meet age-appropriate standards: no exhortations to buy or to pester parents, no pressure/urgency tactics directed at children. Obtain assurance that placement respects the platforms' minor-protection measures.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Advergaming within a branded Roblox world and influencer-voiced video content risk blurring the boundary between editorial/entertainment content and advertising. Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and unambiguously in real time, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. Immersive branded-world experiences and animator-voiced promotions directed at young children — who have limited ability to recognise commercial intent — are especially likely to fail this identifiability requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator)
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad unit and the branded Roblox experience carries a clear, prominent, child-comprehensible 'advertisement/sponsored' label identifying RoboPets as the advertiser, disclosed in real time. Ensure influencer/animator content is unambiguously marked as advertising. Coordinate with the platforms on ad-labelling implementation.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world explicitly directed at children aged 6-11, engaging several DSA provisions. The daily in-game pop-ups and FOMO/urgency cues aimed at child players are manipulative interface design (Art. 25); the campaign's placement on minor-accessible platforms engages the minors-protection and profiling-ad ban regime (Art. 28); and the advergaming and influencer-voiced formats risk disguised advertising that is not clearly identifiable as such (Art. 26(1)). Note that some DSA duties bind the platform providers directly, but the marketer's design choices create direct exposure and should be remediated.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 prohibits, in all circumstances, including in an advertisement a direct exhortation to children to buy the advertised product or to persuade their parents/other adults to buy it for them. The declared audience is children 6-11, the content sits on YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world, and the script explicitly tells children to get their parents to buy the toy. This is a per-se (blacklisted) violation requiring no assessment of consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Remove all imperatives directing children to purchase or to ask/pressure parents to purchase. Rewrite creative so it does not exhort the child to buy or to nag adults; any purchase call-to-action must be addressed to adults through adult-facing channels, not embedded in child-directed content.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: The Roblox pop-up is a second, independent direct exhortation to child players to get their parents to purchase, additionally sweetened with an in-game virtual-currency reward conditioned on the purchase. This falls squarely within the Annex I point 28 blacklist and the reward mechanic intensifies the pester pressure it creates.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!
findings.recommendation: Delete the pop-up entirely, or at minimum remove any instruction to get parents to buy and any purchase-conditioned reward. Do not tie in-game rewards (RoboCoins) to real-money purchases in content served to children.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Even setting aside the blacklist, stacking urgency ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait') and social-pressure/FOMO cues ('before your friends get theirs'), plus daily repeated pop-ups, aimed at 6-11 year-olds amounts to undue influence exploiting the credulity and limited critical capacity of children, likely to distort their economic behaviour and pressure a transactional decision. This engages the aggressive-practices prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Strip urgency, deadline and social-pressure language from child-facing creative and cease the daily recurring pop-ups. Assess pressure tactics from the perspective of an average child in the target group, not an average adult.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires practices likely to distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group — here children, due to age and credulity — to be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. The overall design (child channels, animator voice, urgency, purchase-linked rewards) is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts children's behaviour, engaging the general fairness safety-net alongside the specific blacklist entries.
findings.evidence_quote: children 6-11
findings.recommendation: Apply an age-appropriate, professional-diligence review to the whole campaign concept, not just individual lines, ensuring no element materially distorts the economic behaviour of children in the 6-11 group.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice where not apparent from context. Advergaming within a branded Roblox world and content voiced by a 'popular kids' animator' can blur the line between entertainment and advertising for young children, who may not recognise the commercial intent. If the promotional nature is not clearly and age-appropriately disclosed, this is a misleading omission / hidden commercial intent.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently label all promotional content as advertising in a way children can understand, ensure the influencer/animator content carries an unambiguous ad disclosure, and make the commercial nature of the Roblox branded world and pop-ups obvious to child users.

verdicts.notes: This child-directed campaign contains textbook per-se prohibited practices under the UCPD. The video and in-game scripts directly exhort children aged 6-11 to buy the product and to pester their parents to buy it — a practice banned in all circumstances under Annex I point 28. Additional concerns arise under Arts. 8-9 (aggressive/undue-influence tactics exploiting children's credulity) and Art. 7 (hidden commercial intent in advergaming pop-ups and influencer-voiced content, which is not obviously advertising to a child). No fairness defence is available for the blacklisted conduct; the creative must be rewritten.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes the RoboPets toy line to children aged 6-11 on YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world, using scripts that tell kids to get their parents to buy the toy "right now" and daily in-game pop-ups that reward children with virtual coins for pushing a purchase. The single most serious problem is that the creative directly tells children to buy the product and to pester their parents to buy it — a practice that is banned outright in the EU under the UCPD blacklist (Annex I, point 28), with no defence available. On top of that, the urgency and social-pressure cues ("before your friends get theirs"), the daily nagging pop-ups, and the purchase-linked RoboCoins reward amount to aggressive and manipulative practices (UCPD Arts. 8-9 and DSA Art. 25 dark patterns) aimed at a highly vulnerable audience. The campaign also blurs advertising and entertainment (advergaming and an animator's voice) without clear child-comprehensible ad labelling, raising disguised-advertising issues under DSA Art. 26 and UCPD Art. 7. Because every user is a child below the GDPR age-of-consent threshold and the "daily pop-ups to child players" contradict the "no personalisation" declaration, there are also unresolved GDPR issues around lawful basis, verified parental consent, and child-appropriate transparency. The AI Act is not engaged. In short: the campaign cannot launch in its current form — the child-purchase exhortations are per-se illegal and the creative must be fundamentally rewritten, not just tweaked.
recommendations: Do not launch as-is. Remove every instruction that tells children to buy the product or to ask/pressure their parents to buy it, in both the video scripts and the Roblox pop-ups — this is a per-se prohibited practice (UCPD Annex I, point 28) with no fairness defence.
Delete the daily Roblox purchase pop-ups entirely, and remove the RoboCoins-for-purchase reward mechanic; never tie in-game virtual-currency rewards to real-money purchases in child-directed content.

Strip all urgency, deadline and social-pressure/FOMO language ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'before your friends get theirs') from any child-facing creative to eliminate aggressive/dark-pattern exposure (UCPD Arts. 8-9; DSA Art. 25).
Move any purchase call-to-action to adult-facing channels only; child-directed content should never contain a buy prompt.

Add clear, prominent, child-comprehensible 'advertisement/sponsored' labelling to all creative, the branded Roblox world, and the animator-voiced videos so the commercial intent is unmistakable (DSA Art. 26; UCPD Art. 7).

Reconcile the 'no personalisation/targeting' declaration with the 'daily pop-ups to child players' — map exactly what child data is processed, confirm no profiling-based ads are served to known minors (DSA Art. 28), and correct the submission if targeting is in fact occurring.

Establish and document a GDPR lawful basis for any processing of child users' data; where consent is relied on, implement verified parental consent and reasonable age-verification for under-16s (or applicable national age) per Art. 8, plus child-appropriate, plain-language privacy notices (Arts. 12, 6).

Have a professional-diligence, age-appropriate compliance review of the whole reworked concept — not just individual lines — before resubmission, and coordinate ad-labelling and minor-protection measures with YouTube and Roblox.

campaign.title: FlexiPure joint supplement
campaign.text: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure capsules: 'Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days — or your money back. Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers. Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently. Order today and end your arthritis forever.' Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference. Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.

detected_practices: health claim (cure arthritis in 30 days)
disease cure/reversal claim (diabetes reversal bundle)
unsubstantiated efficacy statistic ('97% cure rate' with no study reference)
before/after X-ray imagery as proof
'clinically proven' claim without evidence
conspiracy framing ('doctors don't want you to know')
money-back guarantee
encouraging discontinuation of prescribed medication
cross-sell/upsell at checkout
AI-generated content
personalisation/behavioural targeting
triage.audience_notes: Target audience is adults 50+ with chronic joint pain — a vulnerable group under UCPD (health condition, potential for exploitation). Claims about curing disease and discontinuing prescription painkillers are especially harmful for this cohort. No indication minors are targeted or likely reached.
triage.summary: Web and social campaign for the FlexiPure joint supplement targeting vulnerable adults 50+ with chronic joint pain, making aggressive unsubstantiated medical cure claims (curing arthritis, reversing joint damage, diabetes reversal) supported by unreferenced statistics and before/after X-ray imagery, and encouraging users to abandon prescribed medication. It declares use of generative AI and personalised targeting, and includes upsell/cross-sell mechanics at checkout. The health/vulnerability targeting and personalisation raise significant consumer-protection, data-protection and platform-content concerns.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign uses declared AI-driven personalisation/targeting to reach a group defined by age (50+) and by a health condition/disability (chronic joint pain) — a vulnerable group under Art. 5(1)(b). It combines this with false cure claims and encouragement to discontinue prescribed painkillers, which materially distorts purchasing and health-related behaviour in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm (worsened disease, harm from stopping medication). Where an AI system is the vehicle for exploiting that vulnerability, this is a prohibited practice, not merely a regulated one.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes ... Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI targeting/personalisation to reach this audience with these messages. Remove all content urging discontinuation of prescription medication and all cure/reversal claims. If any AI personalisation is retained, ensure it cannot be configured to exploit age- or health-based vulnerability, and document a vulnerability-impact assessment before deployment.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Where the declared AI system drives the persuasion/targeting, deploying purposefully deceptive techniques (false 'clinically proven' cure claims, conspiracy framing, fabricated '97% cure rate') that appreciably impair the target's ability to make an informed decision and cause a purchase they would not otherwise make, in a manner likely to cause significant harm, engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative/deceptive AI techniques. Engagement depends on the extent to which AI (vs. human copywriting) drives the deceptive persuasion, hence medium.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days ... Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently
findings.recommendation: Ensure any AI-driven persuasion/optimisation does not deploy deceptive tactics; strip the deceptive and conspiracy-framed claims from AI-generated or AI-optimised assets, and keep AI optimisation limited to lawful, substantiated messaging.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares generative-AI-produced content. Under Art. 50(2), providers/deployers of AI systems generating synthetic image, text (or other) content must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated. There is no indication the AI-generated copy or imagery (including the before/after X-ray visuals if synthetic) carries such marking.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Apply machine-readable provenance/AI-generation marking (e.g., C2PA-style metadata) to all generative-AI outputs used in the campaign, and keep records of which assets were AI-generated. Note that synthetic 'before/after X-ray' imagery presented as proof may also constitute deep-fake/deception concerns to be addressed separately.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of both generative AI and AI-driven personalisation/targeting, which brings it squarely within the AI Act. Most seriously, AI is used to target and persuade a vulnerable group (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain) with cure claims and encouragement to abandon prescribed medication — engaging the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on exploiting age/health-related vulnerabilities in a way reasonably likely to cause significant harm, and overlapping with the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive/manipulative AI techniques. Separately, AI-generated campaign assets (and any synthetic imagery) trigger the Art. 50(2) marking obligation. Note that the substantiation/health-claim and consumer-protection dimensions are for the UCPD/DSA/GDPR agents.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: The campaign targets an audience defined by a health condition (chronic joint pain / arthritis) and declares use of personalisation/targeting. Segmenting or targeting people using a health status — directly or via inferred/proxy attributes — involves processing of special-category health data, which is prohibited under Art. 9 unless a specific exception (in a marketing context, the data subject's explicit consent) applies. Nothing in the submission indicates explicit consent has been obtained, so the processing is presumptively unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Do not build or target audience segments based on health conditions (joint pain, arthritis, diabetes) unless you have collected the data subject's explicit, granular Art. 9 consent for that specific purpose. Prefer contextual advertising (e.g. placement on relevant content) rather than targeting individuals inferred to have a health condition, and document the legal basis relied upon.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). For ordinary personalisation this is typically consent or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment; where the targeting relies on health data (as here) only explicit consent will suffice. The submission provides no indication that any lawful basis has been identified or documented.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis for the personalisation/profiling before launch. Given the health-data dimension, obtain explicit consent via a clear, unbundled opt-in and retain records demonstrating it; if legitimate interest is claimed for any non-sensitive personalisation, complete and retain a legitimate-interests assessment.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/behavioural targeting is automated processing used to evaluate personal aspects (health, preferences, behaviour) of individuals and therefore meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling. This is definitional context that triggers the associated obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Treat the personalisation activity as profiling and ensure the full profiling-related compliance stack applies: lawful basis, Art. 13 transparency about profiling, and Art. 21 opt-out mechanisms.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The campaign drives users to a landing page and checkout where personal data will be collected (orders, upsells) and where personalisation/profiling occurs. Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, users be told the controller's identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, their rights, and the existence of profiling/automated decision-making. There is no indication this information is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever.
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at the point of data collection (landing page and checkout) covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention periods, data-subject rights, and the existence and logic of any profiling used for targeting.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that health-based profiling of a vulnerable audience be transparent and fair. Targeting individuals by inferred health status while making aggressive claims, without transparent disclosure of the data processing and targeting logic, undermines fairness and transparency in the processing of their personal data.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Ensure the data processing underlying the targeting is transparent (disclose that targeting is based on health-related inferences and how it is done) and fair to this vulnerable cohort; avoid covert tracking or inference and give users meaningful control over the personalisation.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Where personal data is processed for direct marketing, including profiling for such marketing, data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time and the processing must then stop. Every marketing communication and profiling operation must facilitate this opt-out.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy-to-use opt-out from direct marketing and marketing profiling in every communication and on the site, and ensure objections are honoured immediately and completely.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalisation/targeting and explicitly targets "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain" — targeting an audience by health condition (arthritis/joint pain). Under GDPR this means processing (including inference) of special-category health data, which is prohibited unless explicit consent applies (Art. 9), and the personalisation constitutes profiling requiring a valid lawful basis (Art. 4(4)/Art. 6(1)). Transparency and fairness obligations (Art. 5(1)(a), Art. 13) are also engaged at the point of data collection/checkout. The submission gives no indication that explicit consent, a lawful basis, or the required information notices are in place, so material GDPR risk is present. (Note: the misleading health/cure claims themselves are primarily a UCPD/DSA matter and are not assessed here except insofar as they rely on health-data processing.)

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The campaign is delivered on social platforms and explicitly uses personalisation/targeting to reach an audience segmented by a health condition (chronic joint pain / arthritis). Health status is a special category of personal data under GDPR Art. 9. DSA Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling that uses such special-category data — directly or by inference — regardless of any consent obtained. Targeting sufferers of a specific chronic illness therefore falls squarely within the prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Remove all targeting parameters that segment on or infer health status/medical conditions. Do not use audiences built on 'joint pain', 'arthritis', 'chronic pain' or lookalikes/proxies derived from them. Reach the audience only through non-sensitive criteria (e.g., broad contextual placement) so no profiling ad on the platform relies on Art. 9 data.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: As a paid social-platform advertising campaign, each ad must let recipients identify in a clear, concise, unambiguous, real-time manner that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, plus meaningful information on the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submission gives no indication these disclosures are provided, and AI-generated creative can further obscure commercial/advertiser identity.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: Web, Social
findings.recommendation: Ensure every social placement carries the platform's standard 'ad/sponsored' labelling with the correct advertiser and payer identity, and that the platform surfaces the main targeting parameters and controls. Verify the AI-generated content does not disguise the ad's commercial nature.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If any of the social placements run on a Very Large Online Platform, the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach will be entered into a public ad repository. The aggressive unsubstantiated medical claims and health-based targeting would then be publicly archived and open to regulator, researcher and journalist scrutiny, amplifying enforcement exposure.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days
findings.recommendation: Assume public archiving on VLOPs: only run claims and targeting that can withstand public and regulatory scrutiny. Correct the substantiation and targeting issues before launch rather than relying on ephemerality.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: If the checkout interface steers users toward the add-on bundle through deceptive or manipulative design (e.g., pre-selected/sneaked-in items, false prominence, obstruction), that would constitute a prohibited dark pattern in online interface design under DSA Art. 25. On the evidence available the design details are unknown, so this is flagged for verification; the substantive deception in the claims is primarily a UCPD matter.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle
findings.recommendation: Ensure the upsell is presented neutrally with an equally prominent decline option, no pre-ticked add-ons, and no confirm-shaming. Confirm the checkout does not sneak the 'diabetes reversal' bundle into the basket.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on social platforms with declared personalisation/targeting to an audience defined by a health condition ("adults 50+ with chronic joint pain"). This engages the DSA's prohibition (Art. 26(3)) on presenting ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special-category (health) data — a hard ban that consent cannot cure. Standard platform-ad transparency obligations (Art. 26(1)) also apply, and if placed on a VLOP the ad and its targeting parameters will be publicly archived (Art. 39), exposing the unsubstantiated claims to scrutiny. Dark-pattern concerns (Art. 25) are noted but are more squarely addressed under UCPD.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: FlexiPure is a capsule/supplement, yet the campaign claims it CUREs arthritis, reverses joint damage 'permanently' and ends arthritis 'forever'. The checkout also cross-sells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle. Falsely claiming a product can cure illnesses is a blacklisted practice prohibited in all circumstances, irrespective of whether consumers are actually misled. Supplements cannot lawfully claim to cure arthritis or reverse/reverse diabetes.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days
findings.recommendation: Remove all curative/reversal claims entirely ('cure arthritis', 'reverses joint damage permanently', 'end your arthritis forever', 'diabetes reversal'). Supplements may only carry authorised health claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006; no cure or disease-treatment claims are permitted.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The '97% cure rate' and 'Clinically PROVEN' claims, together with before/after X-ray imagery presented as proof, are unsubstantiated efficacy/'main characteristics' claims with no cited study. Presenting false or unverifiable performance data that would cause the average consumer to purchase constitutes a misleading action regarding the product's benefits and results.
findings.evidence_quote: a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: Delete unsubstantiated statistics and 'clinically proven' wording unless supported by adequate, referenced, methodologically sound evidence held on file before publication. Remove before/after X-ray imagery unless it derives from a genuine, verifiable clinical study that is properly cited.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign uses undue influence and exploitation of the audience's misfortune (chronic pain in adults 50+) — urging discontinuation of prescribed medication and using conspiracy framing ('Doctors don't want you to know') and pressure ('Order today and end your arthritis forever') to distort the transactional decision of a vulnerable group. This constitutes an aggressive practice that impairs free choice and risks serious health harm.
findings.evidence_quote: Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers
findings.recommendation: Remove all messaging encouraging discontinuation of prescribed medication, the conspiracy/'doctors don't want you to know' framing, and high-pressure exhortations. Include a statement advising consumers not to stop prescribed treatment without consulting a doctor.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The declared target audience is a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (age and physical infirmity) under Art. 5(3). The combination of cure claims and pressure tactics is contrary to professional diligence and likely materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average member of that group, engaging the general unfairness safety-net over and above the specific prohibitions.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Reassess the entire campaign from the perspective of a vulnerable member of the target group; eliminate practices that exploit their health condition and ensure all claims and design meet professional diligence standards.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: Referencing doctors/medical authority in this framing implies a medical/institutional standing for the product it does not have, while the '97% cure rate' and 'clinically proven' claims suggest scientific/clinical endorsement without any identified study or approving body. To the extent it conveys unfounded approval or endorsement by a medical or scientific body, it engages the blacklist prohibition on false claims of endorsement.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough
findings.recommendation: Remove any implication of medical, clinical or institutional endorsement. Only reference approval/endorsement where a named body has genuinely granted it and the terms of that approval are complied with.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Material information the consumer needs (the source, methodology and existence of the alleged clinical evidence, and the terms of the 'money-back guarantee') is omitted or presented in an unclear/untimely manner. Failing to provide the substantiating study and the guarantee conditions is a misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: Where any performance figure or 'clinically proven' claim is retained, disclose the underlying study reference clearly; set out the full, transparent conditions of the money-back guarantee at the point of the claim.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including a clear blacklisted practice. Most seriously, it falsely claims a food supplement cures arthritis (and cross-sells a "diabetes reversal" bundle), which is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17. It further makes unsubstantiated "clinically proven"/"97% cure rate" efficacy claims (Art. 6 misleading actions), uses aggressive tactics exploiting a vulnerable audience of chronically ill adults 50+ (Arts. 5 and 8-9), and its "doctors don't want you to know" framing and lack of study reference implicate false endorsement and misleading omission concerns. Immediate removal/reworking of the health claims is required.

report.executive_summary: This campaign for FlexiPure joint supplement cannot run in anything close to its current form — it breaches multiple EU laws, several of them outright bans that no amount of disclaimers or consent can fix. The most serious problem is the claim that a supplement can "cure" arthritis (and a "diabetes reversal" upsell): claiming a product cures illness is a blacklisted, always-prohibited practice under consumer law, and the "clinically proven"/"97% cure rate" figures and before/after X-rays have no supporting study. The campaign also urges people to throw away prescribed painkillers and uses "doctors don't want you to know" pressure tactics aimed at chronically ill older adults — aggressive and unfair practices that risk real health harm. On top of that, targeting people by a health condition (joint pain/arthritis) is flatly banned for social-platform ads under the DSA and requires explicit consent under GDPR, which is not evidenced. Because AI drives the targeting and persuasion of a vulnerable group with false cure claims, this likely crosses into a prohibited AI practice under the AI Act, and AI-generated content/imagery is not marked as required. In short: multiple critical, non-fixable-by-tweaking violations. The campaign must be stopped and fundamentally rebuilt, not patched.
recommendations: Do not launch. Remove every curative/reversal claim immediately — 'cure arthritis', 'reverses joint damage permanently', 'end your arthritis forever' and the 'diabetes reversal' bundle. Claiming a supplement cures disease is banned outright (UCPD Annex I pt 17); supplements may only use authorised health claims under Reg. 1924/2006.

Delete all content urging people to stop prescribed medication ('thrown away their prescription painkillers') and the 'doctors don't want you to know' conspiracy framing and 'order today' pressure — these are aggressive practices exploiting a vulnerable audience and risk serious health harm. Add a note advising consumers not to stop prescribed treatment without consulting a doctor.

Stop targeting or segmenting the audience by health condition. Health-based ad targeting on social platforms is flatly prohibited under DSA Art. 26(3) and cannot be cured by consent. Use only broad/contextual placement, and exclude 'joint pain'/'arthritis'/'chronic pain' audiences, lookalikes and proxies.

Do not use AI personalisation/targeting to reach this vulnerable group with these messages — AI-driven exploitation of an age/health-vulnerable audience with false cure claims likely constitutes a prohibited AI practice (AI Act Art. 5). Conduct and document a vulnerability-impact assessment before any AI personalisation is retained.

Remove the '97% cure rate', 'clinically proven' wording and the before/after X-ray images unless backed by genuine, referenced, methodologically sound clinical evidence held on file before publication.

Mark all AI-generated text and imagery in machine-readable format (e.g. C2PA metadata) per AI Act Art. 50(2), and treat synthetic X-ray 'proof' images as a deception risk — do not present fabricated imagery as clinical evidence.

Establish a lawful GDPR footing before any data collection: obtain explicit Art. 9 consent for any health-based processing (or drop it), document an Art. 6 lawful basis, and provide a clear Art. 13 privacy notice plus an easy direct-marketing opt-out at the landing page and checkout.

Ensure DSA ad-transparency compliance: every social placement must carry clear 'ad/sponsored' labelling with correct advertiser/payer identity, and the checkout upsell must be neutral (no pre-ticked items, equally prominent decline, no confirm-shaming). Assume ads will be publicly archived on large platforms and open to regulator scrutiny.

campaign.title: FlexiPure joint supplement
campaign.text: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure capsules: 'Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days — or your money back. Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers. Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference. Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.
