triage.audience_notes: Declared target is adults 50+ with chronic joint pain — a vulnerable audience under UCPD due to age and medical condition, heightening scrutiny of misleading health claims and personalised targeting. No indication minors are targeted.
triage.summary: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure joint capsules making aggressive, unsubstantiated medical claims (guaranteed 30-day arthritis 'cure', permanent joint reversal, '97% cure rate' with no source, before/after X-rays) and encouraging users to abandon prescription painkillers, plus a cross-sell 'diabetes reversal' bundle. It uses generative AI and personalised targeting aimed at an older, chronically ill and therefore vulnerable audience. The material raises serious misleading/aggressive practice, health-claim, AI-content, and data-processing concerns.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign declares AI-driven personalised targeting explicitly aimed at older adults with a chronic health condition — a group vulnerable due to age and disability/illness. The messaging is designed to materially distort their purchasing and health behaviour ('thrown away their prescription painkillers', 'end your arthritis forever'). Steering vulnerable people to abandon prescribed medication in reliance on an unproven 'cure' is reasonably likely to cause significant (physical health) harm, which is the harm element Art. 5(1)(b) requires. If an AI system performs or optimises this targeting, the practice falls within the prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... yes [use of personalisation/targeting]
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI systems to target or optimise delivery of this messaging to elderly / chronically ill audiences. Exclude health-condition and age-based vulnerability signals from AI targeting models, and remove all content encouraging discontinuation of prescription medication. Document that no AI personalisation exploits age/health vulnerability before any EU launch.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Where the declared generative AI / personalisation acts as an AI system deploying purposefully deceptive techniques (conspiracy framing, fabricated '97% cure rate', false 'clinically PROVEN' claims) that appreciably impair the audience's ability to make an informed decision and cause a decision they would not otherwise take with a reasonably likely significant-harm effect, Art. 5(1)(a) is engaged. The deceptive character is clear; the AI-system nexus needs confirming.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently
findings.recommendation: Ensure no AI system is used to generate or amplify deceptive persuasion (fabricated statistics, false authority/conspiracy framing). Remove the deceptive claims entirely; if AI generates campaign copy, gate outputs so they cannot assert unsubstantiated medical efficacy or manipulate informed decision-making.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The advertiser declares generative AI is used to produce campaign assets. As a deployer/provider of AI-generated synthetic image, text or video content, outputs must be marked in a machine-readable, detectable format under Art. 50(2). Nothing in the submission indicates such marking is applied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated assets (copy, images, video, audio) carry machine-readable provenance/marking identifying them as artificially generated, and confirm the generation tool applies compliant marking. Retain records of which assets are AI-generated.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: If the before/after X-ray images are AI-generated or AI-manipulated to appear as authentic medical evidence of real patient outcomes, they are manipulated realistic content whose synthetic nature must be disclosed under Art. 50(4). Presenting fabricated 'authentic' medical imagery without disclosing manipulation breaches the transparency obligation (and compounds the deception harm relevant to Art. 5).
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure
findings.recommendation: Verify whether the X-ray images are AI-generated/manipulated. If so, clearly disclose that they are artificially generated/manipulated — or, given they are used as fabricated medical proof, remove them entirely. Do not present synthetic imagery as genuine clinical evidence.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares both generative-AI content and AI-driven personalised targeting of a vulnerable audience (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain), which engages several AI Act provisions. Most seriously, using an AI system to personalise deceptive health messaging that urges an elderly, chronically ill audience to abandon prescription medication risks the Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) prohibitions on manipulative/deceptive AI and AI exploiting age- and health-related vulnerabilities, because the reasonably likely effect is significant (health) harm. In addition, any AI-generated copy and — especially — the before/after X-ray 'proof' images trigger the Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking and Art. 50(4) manipulated-content disclosure obligations. Several conclusions depend on facts not stated (whether the targeting/generation is done by an in-scope AI system and whether the X-rays are AI-generated), so these are flagged as risks to verify.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Targeting a declared audience defined by a medical condition (chronic joint pain / arthritis) means processing data revealing health status — a special category under Art. 9 — whether the attribute is known or inferred. Such processing is prohibited unless a specific exception applies. Health-based marketing targeting rarely qualifies, and explicit consent for using health data to serve ads is not evidenced anywhere in the campaign. The 'diabetes reversal' upsell compounds this by revealing/inferring a further health condition.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Do not segment or target audiences using health conditions (arthritis, joint pain, diabetes) or proxies for them. If any health-based targeting is genuinely intended, it must rest on a valid Art. 9 exception — realistically only explicit, granular, freely-given opt-in consent specifically for using health data to serve personalised ads, documented and separable from other consents. Prefer contextual (non-health) targeting instead.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalised targeting to evaluate/predict aspects concerning health and personal interests constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This brings the campaign within the GDPR profiling regime (lawful basis, transparency, objection), and because the profiling analyses health it is particularly high-risk.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Map and document the profiling logic used for this campaign, conduct a DPIA given the sensitive-data and vulnerable-audience risk, and ensure a lawful basis and safeguards are in place before any profiling of this audience proceeds.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis (typically consent, or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment). Where health data is involved, an Art. 9 condition is also required on top. The campaign provides no indication of any lawful basis or consent capture for the targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid Art. 6(1) basis for the profiling/targeting (consent is realistic here given the sensitivity), and pair it with an Art. 9 condition. Do not rely on legitimate interests for health-based ad targeting.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent relied on to lawfully target based on health must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous and — for Art. 9 data — explicit. Bundled or pre-ticked consent does not qualify. Nothing in the campaign shows a compliant consent mechanism, so reliance on consent as described would fail the standard.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Implement a standalone, explicit opt-in for health-based personalisation with clear plain-language explanation of what health data is used and why; keep it unbundled from purchase, newsletter or other consents, and record it.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The landing page and checkout collect personal data (orders, and likely tracking for the declared personalisation) but no privacy information, purposes, legal basis, retention or profiling disclosures are indicated. Art. 13 requires this information at the point of collection, including information about profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at every data-collection point (landing page, checkout, any sign-up), covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and the existence of profiling/automated targeting.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that data subjects understand and can reasonably expect the processing. Using an older, chronically ill audience's health status for targeted advertising without transparent disclosure — combined with misleading claims — undermines fairness and transparency of the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the personalisation is transparent and fairly presented to the data subject, avoid covert tracking, and align the data-processing disclosures with what users would reasonably expect; correcting the misleading claims also reduces fairness risk.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: As a direct marketing campaign using profiling, data subjects have an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, including related profiling. The campaign shows no opt-out/objection mechanism for the targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure capsules
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, always-available mechanism to object to direct marketing and profiling (e.g., clear opt-out in ads and communications), and honour objections by ceasing processing for that purpose immediately.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalised targeting of "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain" and a "diabetes reversal" cross-sell — meaning audiences are segmented using health status, a special category of personal data. This engages GDPR Art. 9's prohibition (processing lawful only under a narrow exception such as explicit consent), and also triggers profiling, lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations. On the facts described, no valid Art. 9 basis, consent mechanism, or transparency information is evidenced, so a violation is likely absent significant additional controls. (ePrivacy/DSA/UCPD dimensions are covered by other agents.)

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The campaign explicitly personalises/targets an audience defined by a health condition (chronic joint pain / arthritis). Under DSA Art. 26(3), providers of online platforms shall not present advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data referred to in GDPR Art. 9, which include health data. Targeting people because of a chronic illness — whether by direct segmentation or by inference (e.g. arthritis/joint-pain interest signals) — is prohibited for social-platform ads regardless of consent. The social channel makes this a live DSA platform-advertising issue.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Remove all targeting that relies on or infers a health condition. For the social component, restrict audience definition to non-sensitive parameters (e.g. broad demographics or contextual placement on relevant content) and do not use health-status, arthritis, joint-pain, medication or diabetes interest segments. Document the targeting parameters to demonstrate no Art. 9 data is used, directly or by proxy.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives, manipulates or materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, including giving undue prominence to certain choices and pressuring conversions. The combination of manufactured urgency ('Order today'), fear/conspiracy framing ('Doctors don't want you to know'), and a checkout-stage upsell to an unrelated 'diabetes reversal' bundle can amount to deceptive/manipulative interface design steering vulnerable users toward decisions they would not otherwise freely make. (Applies to owned platform interfaces; equivalent conduct for all traders is separately covered by UCPD.)
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever ... Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.
findings.recommendation: Remove false urgency cues and coercive/conspiracy framing from the landing page and checkout. Ensure the checkout upsell is a neutral, clearly separate opt-in (no pre-ticked boxes, no confirm-shaming) and does not exploit the audience's medical condition to pressure purchases.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that ads on online platforms be identifiable in real time as advertisements, disclose on whose behalf and who paid for them, and provide meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submission gives no indication that the social placements will carry clear ad labelling, advertiser identity, or targeting-parameter disclosure.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: Web, Social ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure each social placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement, identifies FlexiPure as advertiser/payer, and surfaces the main targeting parameters with a way for recipients to adjust them, in line with the platform's DSA ad-transparency features.

verdicts.notes: This social/web campaign engages the DSA primarily through its personalised targeting of "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain" — targeting on a health condition (a GDPR Art. 9 special category), which DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits for platform advertising regardless of consent. Secondary DSA concerns arise from manipulative interface tactics (urgency, conspiracy framing, checkout upsell) potentially amounting to dark patterns under Art. 25, and from platform ad-transparency obligations under Art. 26(1). Note that misleading/false health claims themselves fall primarily to UCPD and are reported by that agent.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: FlexiPure is a joint supplement, not a licensed medicine. Claiming it will 'CURE arthritis' and 'reverses joint damage permanently' / 'end your arthritis forever' is a claim that the product cures an illness. Falsely claiming a product can cure illnesses is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17 — no consumer-perception or materiality test applies.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days
findings.recommendation: Remove all curative, reversal and 'forever/permanent' claims for the supplement. Supplement claims must be limited to authorised health claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006; do not present the product as curing, reversing or ending arthritis.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: A 'diabetes reversal' bundle repeats the same blacklisted false cure/treatment claim for a second serious chronic illness, again prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'diabetes reversal' claim entirely; do not market any bundle as reversing or curing diabetes.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The '97% cure rate', 'clinically PROVEN', and before/after X-ray imagery convey false/unverifiable information about the product's main characteristics, benefits and results, deceiving the average consumer and causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take (Art. 6). Efficacy statistics and clinical proof presented without any substantiation are misleading actions.
findings.evidence_quote: a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: Withdraw the unsubstantiated statistic and 'clinically proven' wording and the X-ray imagery unless backed by verifiable, referenced, properly-conducted clinical evidence that supports the exact claim; even then, curative claims remain prohibited under Annex I point 17.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Presenting efficacy figures and 'clinically proven' assertions while omitting the study source, methodology and any qualifying information deprives the average consumer of material information needed to assess the claim, constituting a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: If any substantiation exists, disclose the study source, sample and methodology clearly and prominently. Absent that, remove the claim rather than presenting figures without material context.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The conspiracy framing, the exhortation that 'Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers', and 'Order today and end your arthritis forever' apply undue influence on a clearly vulnerable audience (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain) by exploiting their medical condition and encouraging abandonment of prescribed medication, impairing free and informed choice. Under Art. 5(3) fairness is assessed from the perspective of the average member of this vulnerable group, aggravating the aggressive-practice risk.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough
findings.recommendation: Remove conspiracy framing, urgency pressure and any encouragement to discontinue prescription medication. Do not exploit the audience's illness; include a clear statement to consult a healthcare professional and not to stop prescribed treatment.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average member of the identified vulnerable group (age and physical infirmity, Art. 5(3)). Encouraging chronically-ill older adults to abandon prescription painkillers in favour of an unproven supplement falls below the standard of care expected of a trader.
findings.evidence_quote: Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers
findings.recommendation: Reframe the campaign to comply with professional diligence: substantiated, non-curative claims only, no encouragement to stop medical treatment, and messaging appropriate to a health-vulnerable older audience.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including a clear blacklisted practice. Claiming a food supplement is "clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis" and "reverses joint damage permanently" is a false cure claim prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17. Layered on top are misleading actions (Art. 6) via the unsubstantiated "97% cure rate" and before/after X-rays, misleading omissions (Art. 7) as no study is referenced, and aggressive practices (Arts. 8-9) exploiting a vulnerable 50+ chronically-ill audience — heightening scrutiny under Art. 5(3). The "diabetes reversal" upsell repeats the cure violation.

report.executive_summary: The FlexiPure campaign markets a food supplement as a proven cure for arthritis ("Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days", "reverses joint damage permanently", "97% cure rate") and adds a "diabetes reversal" upsell at checkout. Claiming a supplement cures illness is an outright banned practice under EU consumer law (UCPD blacklist) — it is prohibited in all circumstances, no exceptions, and applies to both the arthritis and diabetes claims. This campaign cannot launch in the EU in anything close to its current form and needs a fundamental rebuild, not tweaks.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities

The messaging exploits that vulnerability by urging sufferers to abandon effective treatment ('Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers') in favour of an unproven supplement. findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... use of personalisation/targeting: yes

If any AI targeting is retained, ensure it cannot exploit health/age vulnerability and cannot steer users toward harmful health decisions; obtain a documented harm assessment.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Where the declared generative AI and personalisation systems are used to deploy purposefully deceptive/manipulative content (fabricated '97% cure rate', conspiratorial 'doctors don't want you to know' framing, permanence claims) that impairs the target's ability to make an informed decision and causes them to take decisions they would not otherwise take (buying, stopping medication), the practice engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on AI-based deceptive/manipulative techniques causing significant harm.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently
findings.recommendation: Remove deceptive and manipulative claims and do not operationalise them through AI-driven persuasion/personalisation. Any AI system used in the campaign must not deploy deceptive techniques that distort consumer decisions; substantiate all claims and drop conspiratorial framing.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce content. Under Art. 50(2), synthetic audio/image/video/text outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated. Nothing in the submission indicates that AI-generated campaign assets carry the required provenance marking.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all generative-AI-produced campaign assets (copy, images, video) are marked in a machine-readable/provenance format identifying them as AI-generated, and document that the marking is applied at output.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: If the before/after X-ray images (or any realistic imagery) are AI-generated or AI-manipulated to appear as authentic medical evidence, they constitute deep-fake/manipulated content whose artificial generation must be disclosed under Art. 50(4). Given generative AI is declared and the imagery purports to depict real medical outcomes, disclosure is required and is absent as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images
findings.recommendation: Confirm the provenance of the X-ray imagery. If AI-generated or manipulated, clearly disclose that it is artificially generated/manipulated (and note it does not depict real patient results); otherwise remove imagery that misrepresents clinical efficacy.

verdicts.notes: The campaign explicitly declares use of generative AI and AI-driven personalised/behavioural targeting, aimed at a group vulnerable by age (50+) and health condition (chronic joint pain). The AI-driven targeting is deployed to push deceptive medical cure claims that encourage abandoning prescription medication — a mechanism likely to materially distort behaviour and cause significant health harm, engaging the Art. 5(1)(b) and Art. 5(1)(a) prohibitions. Separately, the declared generative-AI content and the before/after X-ray imagery trigger the Art. 50(2) marking and Art. 50(4) disclosure/deep-fake obligations, which are not addressed as described.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Targeting/personalising advertising to people defined by 'chronic joint pain' (arthritis) means processing data revealing a health condition — a special category under Art. 9. Even where the health status is inferred rather than declared, building or using a 'chronic joint pain' audience segment processes health data. Art. 9 prohibits this unless a specific exception applies, and the only realistic marketing exception is the data subject's explicit consent, which is not evidenced. The 'diabetes reversal' upsell further reinforces health-status inference/segmentation.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Do not build or target audience segments on the basis of health conditions (arthritis/joint pain, diabetes) or their proxies. If any health-based targeting is genuinely intended, obtain prior explicit (Art. 9(2)(a)) consent that is separate, specific and documented; otherwise restrict targeting to non-sensitive criteria. Note that for platform advertising such targeting is separately banned under DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of consent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/behavioural targeting to a defined health-and-age audience is automated processing to evaluate and predict personal aspects (health, preferences, behaviour) and therefore constitutes profiling within the Art. 4(4) definition, triggering the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling logic and audience-building parameters, and ensure each downstream obligation (lawful basis, Art. 13 information, Art. 21 opt-out) is met before running personalised targeting.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — in practice consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment. Where health data is involved, legitimate interest is not available and only explicit consent will do. The submission shows no lawful basis for the personalised targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Establish and document the lawful basis before processing. For any health-related segmentation this must be explicit consent (Art. 6 in combination with Art. 9(2)(a)); for non-sensitive personalisation, either consent or a completed legitimate-interest assessment with a balancing test.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that data subjects are not misled about how their data is used and that collection/tracking is not covert. A campaign that segments on health status and runs behavioural targeting must be transparent about it; combining sensitive-data processing with manipulative, deceptive marketing content also undermines the 'fairness' limb of Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure capsules
findings.recommendation: Ensure the privacy notice and consent flow clearly and honestly disclose all data collection, tracking technologies and health-based targeting; avoid covert tracking and ensure the surrounding marketing does not deceive users about data use.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The landing page and checkout collect personal data (orders, and any lead/tracking data for the personalised campaign). At the point of collection the controller must provide Art. 13 information: identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data subject rights, and information about profiling. Nothing indicates such notice is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever.
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at every point of data collection (landing page forms, checkout, tracking consent) covering all Art. 13 items, including the existence of profiling/personalised targeting and how to object.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct marketing and related profiling trigger an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). Recipients of the personalised campaign must be able to opt out of direct-marketing profiling at any time, and be informed of that right explicitly at the latest at first contact.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Implement and clearly signpost an easy, no-cost opt-out from direct marketing and marketing profiling; present the right to object explicitly and separately at first contact and in every communication.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalisation/behavioural targeting and explicitly targets "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain" — i.e. it segments audiences by a health condition. Under GDPR this is processing of special-category (health) data (Art. 9), which is prohibited absent explicit consent, and it constitutes profiling (Art. 4(4)) requiring a lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) and transparency (Arts. 5(1)(a), 13). Nothing in the submission indicates a valid lawful basis, explicit consent, or transparency at the point of collection. These are the GDPR-specific risks; the misleading/aggressive health claims themselves are for other regulations.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The campaign is delivered on social platforms with declared personalised/behavioural targeting to an audience defined by a health condition (chronic joint pain). Chronic joint pain / arthritis is health data, a special category under GDPR Art. 9. DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling that uses such special-category data — whether the health attribute is used directly or by inference — and this prohibition applies regardless of any consent. An advertiser instructing platforms to target on this basis directly causes a prohibited ad presentation.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Remove all targeting that uses or infers health status. Do not segment or target social/web ads on 'joint pain', 'arthritis', or equivalent health interest/inference categories. Restrict targeting to non-sensitive parameters (e.g. broad contextual placement) and confirm with each platform that no special-category profiling is applied to the campaign.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: As a paid campaign presented on online platforms, each advertisement must let recipients identify, clearly and in real time, that it is an ad, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submission provides no indication these disclosures are in place, so the Art. 26(1) transparency obligation is engaged and not demonstrably satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: Web, Social ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure every placement is clearly labelled as advertising, names the advertiser/beneficiary and payer, and surfaces the main targeting parameters with a way to change them — typically via the platform's native ad-disclosure and 'why am I seeing this ad' tooling. Verify labelling is applied to all social and web ad units.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The landing/checkout experience combines high-pressure urgency with an upsell for an unrelated 'diabetes reversal' bundle. If the interface gives undue prominence to accepting the upsell, obscures the choice, or otherwise impairs a free and informed decision, this could constitute a prohibited dark pattern under Art. 25. The submission lacks interface detail, so this is flagged as attention rather than a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever ... Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.
findings.recommendation: Design the checkout so add-ons like the upsell bundle are presented neutrally (equal prominence for decline/accept, no pre-ticked boxes, no confirm-shaming, no repeated nagging). Review the landing page and checkout flow against the DSA dark-patterns criteria before launch.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on social platforms with declared personalisation/targeting to an audience defined by health status ("adults 50+ with chronic joint pain"). Under the DSA this most seriously engages the Art. 26(3) prohibition on presenting profiling-based ads using GDPR Art. 9 special-category (health) data — a flat ban regardless of consent. Art. 26(1) ad-transparency obligations are also engaged and not evidenced. Art. 25 (dark patterns) is a lower-confidence flag around the urgency/upsell design. Minors are not the target, so Art. 28 and Art. 39 are not assessed as breaches.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: A food supplement is claimed to cure and permanently reverse arthritis. Claiming a product can cure illness is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17, irrespective of any evidence. The checkout 'diabetes reversal' bundle is a second, independent false cure claim caught by the same prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days ... this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently. Order today and end your arthritis forever.
findings.recommendation: Remove all disease cure/prevention/reversal claims entirely ('cure arthritis', 'end your arthritis forever', 'reverses joint damage permanently', 'diabetes reversal'). Supplements may only carry authorised health claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 and must not claim to cure, treat or prevent disease.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'order today' framing manufactures urgency to elicit an immediate decision. If tied to any false limited-time availability it is blacklisted under Annex I point 7; combined with the cure framing it pressures a vulnerable audience into an uninformed transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever.
findings.recommendation: Remove artificial urgency cues unless a genuine, truthful and clearly-substantiated time limit exists; never combine deadline pressure with health-outcome promises.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The '97% cure rate' statistic, 'Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers', and the before/after X-ray imagery are unsubstantiated factual claims about the product's main characteristics and results that are likely to deceive the average consumer and cause a transactional decision. Art. 6 covers exaggerated/unsubstantiated efficacy and results claims; the burden of substantiation lies on the trader.
findings.evidence_quote: a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: Delete unverifiable statistics and medical imagery, or replace with only claims backed by cited, robust and legally-permissible evidence. Do not use X-ray images that imply clinical efficacy the product does not have.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The conspiratorial 'doctors don't want you to know' framing and encouragement to abandon prescription medication amount to undue influence that exploits the misfortune (chronic pain) of a health-compromised audience, impairing free and informed choice — an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9. The health/age vulnerability heightens the assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough ... Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers.
findings.recommendation: Remove conspiratorial claims and any suggestion that consumers discontinue prescribed medication. Avoid pressure tactics that exploit the audience's medical condition.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign explicitly targets a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (older adults in chronic pain). Under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that vulnerable group, lowering the threshold at which the misleading and aggressive elements above materially distort economic behaviour. Acts as the fairness safety-net reinforcing the specific breaches.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Reassess the entire campaign against the vulnerable-consumer standard; the exploitation of the audience's health condition and credulity must be eliminated, not merely toned down.

verdicts.notes: The FlexiPure campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including at least two per-se blacklisted practices (Annex I). The core "clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis" / "reverses joint damage permanently" / "diabetes reversal" messaging is a false cure claim prohibited in all circumstances (Annex I point 17), and the campaign is otherwise saturated with misleading actions (Art. 6), aggressive undue-influence tactics exploiting a vulnerable audience (Arts. 5(3), 8-9), and blacklisted false urgency (Annex I point 7). This is a high-severity, likely-unlawful campaign requiring substantial removal/rework of claims, not minor fixes.

report.executive_summary: The FlexiPure campaign markets a food supplement with claims that it is "clinically proven to cure arthritis" and "reverses joint damage permanently," plus a checkout upsell promising "diabetes reversal." These are illegal disease-cure claims that are banned outright in the EU for supplements — no amount of evidence can make them lawful. On top of that, the campaign urges vulnerable older people in chronic pain to stop taking their prescription medication, uses fake statistics ("97% cure rate"), before/after X-ray images with no study, and conspiratorial "doctors don't want you to know" framing — all of which are misleading and aggressive practices that exploit a vulnerable audience. Because you target people by a health condition (chronic joint pain) using AI-driven personalisation, you also breach the DSA's flat ban on ads targeted with health data (which no consent can cure), and GDPR rules on processing special-category health data. The declared use of generative AI adds further problems: AI must not exploit health/age vulnerability or deploy deceptive persuasion, and AI-generated content (including any synthetic X-rays) must be labelled. In short, this is not a campaign that can be fixed with tweaks — the core proposition is unlawful and must be fundamentally rebuilt.
recommendations: STOP the campaign as-is — do not launch or continue. The central cure/reversal claims ('cure arthritis in 30 days', 'end your arthritis forever', 'reverses joint damage permanently', 'diabetes reversal') are blacklisted disease-cure claims banned in all circumstances under UCPD Annex I point 17. Remove them entirely.

Remove all content that encourages people to stop taking prescription medication ('thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers') — this is aggressive, exploits a vulnerable audience, and risks serious health harm.

Delete the '97% cure rate' figure and the before/after X-ray images. Unverifiable statistics and imagery implying clinical efficacy are misleading actions; use only authorised health claims backed by cited, robust evidence under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006.
Remove the conspiratorial 'doctors don't want you to know' framing and the artificial 'order today' urgency.

Stop targeting or segmenting audiences by health condition (arthritis/joint pain, diabetes) or any proxy for it. The DSA bans health-data-based ad targeting on platforms regardless of consent, and GDPR treats this as prohibited special-category processing without explicit consent.

If any personalisation is retained, restrict it to non-sensitive criteria, establish and document a lawful basis, provide a clear privacy notice at every data-collection point, and offer an easy opt-out from marketing profiling.
Ensure any AI-driven targeting cannot exploit age/health vulnerability or steer users toward harmful health decisions; obtain a documented harm assessment before using AI in this campaign.
Label all generative-AI-produced assets as AI-generated in a machine-readable format; if the X-ray images are AI-generated or manipulated, this must be clearly disclosed (or the images removed).

Redesign the checkout so the upsell is presented neutrally — no pre-ticked boxes, confirm-shaming, or repeated nagging — and ensure every ad placement is clearly labelled with advertiser, payer and targeting information.
Re-run the entire reworked campaign past legal/compliance review against the vulnerable-consumer standard before any launch.

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads
campaign.text: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'. The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.

detected_practices: Impersonation of official/government authority (fake coat-of-arms emblem, national colours, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' styling)
Failure to identify the trader in the advertisement
Buried/obscured disclaimer ('not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey)
Charging €49 for a service that is publicly available for free
False urgency ('before the deadline')
Generative AI used in ad creative production
Targeting of vulnerable (low-income) consumers
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is low-income households — a potentially vulnerable group under UCPD Art. 5(3), heightening the misleadingness assessment. Although the submitter declares 'no personalisation/targeting', the stated targeting of low-income households and delivery via display/search platforms likely involves ad-targeting mechanics and personal data processing, so GDPR is flagged for verification. DSA is engaged via online advertising transparency and trader identification/traceability obligations on platforms and intermediaries. The 'no personalisation' declaration should be independently verified rather than relied upon.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'), leading to a private site charging €49 for a publicly free application, with the non-affiliation disclaimer buried in tiny grey text and no trader identification in the ads. The campaign uses generative AI in its creative and explicitly targets vulnerable low-income households. This presents strong indicators of misleading/aggressive commercial practices and exploitation of consumer vulnerability.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Generative AI is declared to have produced the ad creative (the government-bulletin styling, coat-of-arms-like emblem, national-colour imagery and copy). Art. 50(2) requires that outputs of AI systems generating synthetic image/text/audio/video be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The submission gives no indication that the AI-generated assets carry any provenance marking, and the transparency need is heightened because the synthetic imagery is used to fabricate the appearance of an official government notice.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets (images and copy) embed machine-readable provenance/marking (e.g., C2PA content credentials or equivalent watermarking) as produced by the generative-AI provider; obtain written confirmation from the AI tool/provider that outputs are marked, and retain records of which assets were AI-generated.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The ad deploys deceptive techniques (impersonating an official government notice, false urgency) with the effect of materially distorting consumers' decisions and causing significant harm (paying €49 for a publicly free application). Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits deceptive techniques deployed via an AI system that impair informed decision-making. As declared, AI was used only to produce the creative rather than as a system operating the deceptive/manipulative technique, so this is a conditional risk rather than a clear breach — but if the AI system is used to generate, optimise or personalise deceptive persuasion at scale, the prohibition could be directly engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI systems to generate, optimise or target deceptive/impersonating persuasion. Remove the official-notice framing entirely; if any AI system is used to select, tailor or optimise ad delivery or messaging, document that it is not deploying manipulative/deceptive techniques likely to distort behaviour and cause harm.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign explicitly targets low-income households — a group vulnerable due to their economic situation — with a practice reasonably likely to cause significant (financial) harm (€49 charge for a free service). Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits an AI system that exploits such economic-situation vulnerability to materially distort behaviour. The submitter declares 'no personalisation/targeting', so as described the exploitation appears human-directed rather than executed by an AI system; the prohibition would be directly engaged only if an AI system performs the vulnerability-based targeting. This should be independently verified given the audience declaration conflicts with the stated targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Verify whether any AI system performs audience selection/optimisation toward low-income or financially distressed users; if so, discontinue that targeting. Given the vulnerable audience and financial harm, avoid AI-driven targeting of economic-vulnerability signals altogether and document the ad-delivery mechanics to substantiate the 'no personalisation' declaration.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI in its creative production, which engages the AI Act's transparency regime. The primary AI-Act exposure is Art. 50(2): AI-generated visuals/copy should carry machine-readable provenance marking, and nothing in the submission indicates this is done. The deceptive government-impersonation and vulnerable-audience targeting are serious, but under the AI Act the Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) prohibitions attach to an AI *system* that deploys the manipulative technique or performs the exploitative targeting; here AI is declared only for creative production and targeting is declared as "no personalisation," so those prohibitions are engaged only as conditional/verification risks rather than clear breaches. The core misleadingness and vulnerability-exploitation issues fall primarily to UCPD/DSA/GDPR agents.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data collected through the €49 application form is obtained in a deceptive context: consumers are led to believe they are dealing with a government energy-subsidy authority, when they are handing data to an unidentified private trader, with the only corrective disclosure buried in 7pt grey text. Data obtained by deception/impersonation cannot be processed 'fairly and in a transparent manner' as required by Art. 5(1)(a). The misleading framing infects the lawfulness and fairness of the entire processing operation.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' ... The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Do not collect any personal data under government-impersonating branding. Remove the coat-of-arms emblem, national colours and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' styling, and clearly identify the private trader before any data entry so that the data subject understands who is actually collecting and processing their data.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at the point of collecting personal data the controller provide, as a minimum, its identity and contact details, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The campaign concealing the trader's identity (in the ads, and effectively at the portal where affiliation is denied only in 7pt grey) means the data subject cannot know who the controller is when submitting a €49 application. This obstructs the mandatory identity and transparency disclosures owed at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at the application form containing the controller's true identity/contact details, processing purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights — legibly, not in 7pt grey — before the user submits personal data or payment.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. Presenting the single most material clarification about the controller's true (non-governmental) nature in 7pt grey footer text is the opposite of easily accessible, undermining the transparency of any accompanying privacy information collected at the portal.
findings.evidence_quote: 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present all data-protection and identity information in clearly legible size, colour and placement (not buried in small grey footer text), using plain language, so data subjects can readily understand who is processing their data and why.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Applications for energy-subsidy eligibility from low-income households commonly require data that reveals or infers special-category information (e.g. health conditions or disability qualifying for support, and other socio-economic vulnerability indicators). Processing such Art. 9 data is prohibited absent a specific exception such as explicit, informed consent. Explicit consent cannot be validly obtained where the collection context is deceptive and the controller is concealed, so any special-category processing here risks lacking a valid Art. 9 exception.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility
findings.recommendation: Before designing the application flow, assess whether any collected fields reveal or infer special-category data; if so, either avoid collecting it or ensure a valid Art. 9 exception (typically explicit, freely given, informed consent) obtained in a transparent, non-deceptive context with the true controller identified.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any processing of the applicant's personal data needs a valid Art. 6 legal basis. Where the processing is presented under a false government identity, neither consent (not freely/informed given) nor legitimate interests (a deceptive commercial purpose is unlikely to survive the balancing test against the vulnerable data subject's interests) is readily available, casting doubt on whether a lawful basis exists for the data collected via the portal.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6 legal basis for the application processing, disclosed at the point of collection under the trader's true identity; abandon the impersonation, since deceptive framing prevents both valid consent and a defensible legitimate-interests basis.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's main GDPR exposure arises at the point of data collection: the linked "energy-subsidy-portal.eu" collects personal data via a paid subsidy application while impersonating a government body and concealing the trader's identity. This makes any processing unlikely to be fair and transparent (Art. 5(1)(a)), and the Art. 12/13 obligations (identity of the controller, purposes, legal basis at collection) cannot be satisfied where the ad and site deliberately obscure who is behind them. Subsidy-eligibility applications from low-income households can also reveal special-category data (e.g. health/disability), engaging Art. 9. There is no evidence in the text of targeting/profiling being used, so profiling provisions are not affirmatively engaged, but the "no personalisation" claim should be independently verified by the platform-transparency (DSA) reviewer.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, for each ad presented on an online platform, in a clear and unambiguous manner and in real time, that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. These display/search ads not only omit the trader's identity but actively masquerade as a government 'OFFICIAL NOTICE', so recipients cannot recognise them as commercial advertising from a private company. This defeats the core transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad clearly and prominently identifies that it is a paid advertisement and names the trader ('energy-subsidy-portal.eu' / the operating company) on whose behalf it is presented, using the platform's ad-disclosure and 'paid by' fields; remove all official-government styling that obscures the commercial and trader identity.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions, including disguised advertisements and false hierarchy that hides material information. The ads impersonate an official government bulletin (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'), the crucial 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer is buried in 7pt grey text, and 'before the deadline' manufactures false urgency — a combination that steers vulnerable low-income users into paying €49 for a publicly free service.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Remove the deceptive official-government styling (emblem, national colours, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'); give the non-affiliation and paid-service disclosures equal prominence to the main claim (not 7pt grey); disclose the €49 fee and the free public alternative up front; and drop unsubstantiated deadline-urgency cues.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA advertising-transparency and dark-pattern regimes. Ads delivered via display/search platforms fail to identify the advertising nature and the trader on whose behalf they are shown (Art. 26(1)), and the creative is designed to deceive — disguised as an official government notice with a buried 7pt grey non-affiliation disclaimer and false urgency (Art. 25). Provisions on sensitive-data targeting, recommender transparency, minors and VLOP ad repositories are not supported by the facts as described.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads present a private company's commercial offer as an official government notice — national colours, a coat-of-arms emblem and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' styling falsely convey that the trader/service is authorised or endorsed by a public body when the site is expressly 'not affiliated with any government'. This is exactly the 'fake government affiliation, official-looking notices' scenario blacklisted under Annex I point 4 and is prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government/official styling: no national colours, no coat-of-arms or state emblem, no 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing. Make clear from the outset, prominently, that this is a paid private commercial service unconnected to any public authority.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying a coat-of-arms-like state emblem the trader is not authorised to use is the unauthorised display of an official quality/authority mark, blacklisted under Annex I point 2 and prohibited in all circumstances. It manufactures a false badge of official standing.
findings.evidence_quote: a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Remove the coat-of-arms-like emblem entirely and use only the company's own clearly-branded, non-official marks.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads fail to identify the commercial intent and the trader's identity. Under Art. 7, failing to make the commercial nature apparent and omitting the trader's identity are misleading omissions of material information the consumer needs — here made worse because the government styling actively disguises the commercial intent. The €49 charge and free public alternative are also material facts hidden from the ad.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader in every ad, label the content unmistakably as a commercial advertisement, and disclose upfront the €49 fee and that the underlying application is available for free from the public authority.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Charging €49 for a service (submitting a subsidy application) that is publicly available for free, while presenting it as an official eligibility check, deceives the average consumer as to the nature of the service, its price/price advantage and the trader's authority, causing a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise take — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: State plainly that the application can be submitted free of charge directly to the government, describe exactly what the €49 buys, and drop any implication that payment is required for eligibility or that the service is official.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing manufactures urgency to elicit an immediate decision. If no genuine binding deadline applies to using this paid service (the free public application route is unaffected by any private 'deadline'), this is a false limited-time claim blacklisted under Annex I point 7. At minimum the deadline claim is misleading absent substantiation.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove the deadline/urgency framing unless a genuine, verifiable statutory deadline exists and is accurately described, and clarify that any deadline relates to the public scheme, not to the trader's paid service.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign is explicitly aimed at low-income households — a group made vulnerable by their economic situation, particularly regarding energy subsidies. Under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group, heightening the misleadingness assessment. Exploiting financial distress with an official-looking notice contravenes professional diligence and materially distorts these consumers' economic behaviour, engaging the general unfairness prohibition as a safety-net over the specific breaches.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not target vulnerable low-income consumers with pressure or official-mimicry tactics; ensure the offer is fair, transparent and genuinely valuable given a free public alternative exists, and apply heightened clarity standards for this audience.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The only corrective disclosure is provided in an unclear, untimely and obscured manner — 7pt grey text in the footer, after the misleading impression is created. Under Art. 7 material information provided unintelligibly or untimely is treated as omitted, so this buried disclaimer does not cure the deception.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present the non-affiliation statement prominently and up front (in the ad itself and at the top of the landing page), in legible size and contrast, before any call to action or payment step.

verdicts.notes: This campaign presents multiple serious UCPD breaches. Its core mechanic is impersonating an official government energy-subsidy notice to sell a €49 service for an application that is publicly free — a false endorsement/affiliation claim (blacklisted Annex I point 4) reinforced by an unauthorised coat-of-arms-style emblem (Annex I point 2). It also uses false urgency, hides its commercial intent and the trader's identity, and buries the sole corrective disclosure in 7pt grey — all engaging Arts. 6, 7 and 5, aggravated by the explicit targeting of low-income (vulnerable) consumers under Art. 5(3). Several practices are blacklisted, i.e. unfair in all circumstances regardless of actual consumer effect.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads dressed up as an official government bulletin — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-style emblem and "OFFICIAL NOTICE" wording — to drive low-income households to a private site that charges €49 for an energy-subsidy application that is actually free from the government. This is the single most serious problem: falsely claiming government affiliation and displaying an official-looking emblem are practices that are banned outright under EU consumer law (UCPD blacklist), regardless of intent or effect. On top of that, the ads don't identify who is really behind them, the only "not affiliated with any government" disclaimer is hidden in 7pt grey text, and the "before the deadline" wording invents false urgency — all classic misleading and dark-pattern tactics that also breach the Digital Services Act. Because people hand over personal data (and pay) while believing they're dealing with the government, the data collection is also unlawful and untransparent under the GDPR, with added risk if the application captures sensitive information from vulnerable applicants. The declared use of generative AI adds a transparency obligation (AI-generated assets should be marked), and the AI Act's manipulation/vulnerability prohibitions could be engaged if AI is used to target or optimise this deception. In its current form the campaign cannot be run: it is deceptive by design and targets a vulnerable audience. Fixing the small print will not save it — the core "official notice for a free-but-charged service" mechanic must be abandoned.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as designed. The government-impersonation-for-a-free-service model is unlawful at its core and cannot be fixed by adjusting disclosures.

Remove ALL official/government styling immediately: no national colours, no coat-of-arms or state-emblem imagery, and no 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing. These specific elements are blacklisted (banned in all circumstances) under the UCPD.

Tell users plainly and up front — in the ad itself and at the top of the landing page — that this is a paid private commercial service, unconnected to any public authority, and that the application can be submitted for free directly to the government.
Clearly identify the trader in every ad and label the content unmistakably as a paid advertisement, using the platform's 'paid by'/ad-disclosure fields (DSA Art. 26).
Disclose the €49 fee and exactly what it buys before any call to action; give the non-affiliation statement equal prominence to the main message (never 7pt grey).
Drop the 'before the deadline' urgency wording unless a genuine, verifiable statutory deadline exists and is accurately described as relating to the public scheme, not your service.
Stop targeting low-income/vulnerable households with pressure or official-mimicry tactics; heightened fairness standards apply to this audience.

Before collecting any personal data, provide a clear, legible privacy notice at the form with the real controller's identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights (GDPR Arts. 12/13), and establish a valid Art. 6 basis under the trader's true identity.

Assess whether the application collects special-category data (e.g. health/disability) and, if so, either avoid it or obtain valid explicit consent in a transparent, non-deceptive context (GDPR Art. 9).

Ensure all AI-generated assets carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) per AI Act Art. 50(2), and confirm no AI system is used to target or optimise the deceptive messaging toward vulnerable users (AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)/(b)).

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads
campaign.text: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'. The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.
