triage.audience_notes: Explicitly targets low-income households — a potentially vulnerable audience under UCPD Art. 5(3), heightening the seriousness of the deceptive/impersonation practices. No indication minors are specifically targeted.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording) to funnel low-income users to a private site charging €49 for a publicly free application. The ads fail to identify the trader and bury a 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer in 7pt grey text. Generative AI is declared for the creative, and the site collects personal data via the paid application, targeting a vulnerable audience.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Generative AI is declared for the ad creative (display/search assets, likely including the coat-of-arms-like emblem and copy). Under Art. 50(2), providers of generative AI systems must ensure synthetic image/text outputs are marked in a machine-readable, detectable format. The campaign gives no indication that the AI-generated assets carry any provenance/machine-readable marking, so the transparency obligation appears unmet as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets (images, emblem, copy) carry machine-readable provenance/watermark marking (e.g. C2PA/SynthID or equivalent) as generated by the provider's system, and retain records demonstrating the marking. Confirm with the generative-AI provider that Art. 50(2) marking is applied to every output used in the campaign.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign uses AI-generated content and explicitly targets low-income households — a group vulnerable due to a 'specific social or economic situation', the exact category in Art. 5(1)(b). The AI-generated official-looking notice materially distorts their behaviour by inducing payment of €49 for a service that is publicly free, which is reasonably likely to cause significant (financial) harm to precisely this financially vulnerable group. This engages the prohibition on AI exploiting economic-situation vulnerabilities.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy AI-generated deceptive creative against a group targeted because of low income. Remove the low-income targeting for this deceptive framing, eliminate the government-impersonation elements, and ensure the offer does not induce vulnerable users into paying for a free service. Legal review of Art. 5 prohibition exposure is strongly advised before launch.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI-generated creative deploys deceptive techniques (impersonating an official government bulletin, false urgency) with the effect of materially distorting consumer behaviour — impairing informed decision-making and causing users to pay €49 for a publicly free application, i.e. reasonably likely significant financial harm. Where such deceptive content is produced/deployed via an AI system, Art. 5(1)(a) is engaged. The fit is arguable (the deception is human-designed, with AI as the generation tool), so flagged as an elevated risk rather than a definitive prohibited-practice breach.
findings.evidence_quote: 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Cease using AI to generate deceptive government-impersonation creative. Remove the 'OFFICIAL NOTICE', national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem and false 'deadline' urgency. Obtain a documented Art. 5 assessment confirming the AI-generated content does not deploy deceptive techniques capable of distorting behaviour to consumers' detriment.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The AI-generated creative manipulates official state imagery (a coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours) to appear authentically governmental, and the text purports to inform the public on a matter of public interest (2026 energy subsidy eligibility). Where AI-generated/manipulated image or public-interest text is deployed to appear authentic, Art. 50(4) disclosure of artificial generation may be engaged in addition to the Art. 50(2) marking obligation. Flagged as low given the marginal 'deep fake' fit for a synthetic emblem.
findings.evidence_quote: a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: If any AI-generated imagery is designed to appear as authentic official/government content, disclose clearly and prominently that it is artificially generated (Art. 50(4)) — or, preferably, remove the state-emblem imagery entirely, which is the underlying deception. Ensure any public-interest text is not passed off as an authentic government communication.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI for the ad creative, which engages the AI Act's transparency obligations for synthetic content (Art. 50). The AI-generated creative is styled as an official government notice and deployed to deceive low-income households into paying €49 for a publicly free application, which raises serious concerns under the Art. 5 prohibitions on deceptive AI techniques (5(1)(a)) and AI exploiting economic-situation vulnerabilities (5(1)(b)). The clearest, immediately actionable gap is the absence of any machine-readable marking of the AI-generated assets (Art. 50(2)); the Art. 5 prohibitions are flagged as elevated risks because the AI-generated content is the vehicle for a deceptive practice causing financial harm to a vulnerable group. UCPD/DSA deception and trader-identification issues are handled by other agents.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data submitted through the 'energy subsidy' application is obtained under a false pretence that the site is an official/state channel. Data collected via impersonation of a public authority, with the trader's identity and non-affiliation concealed, cannot be said to be processed fairly or transparently. The deceptive government-notice framing is the operative mechanism inducing the data subject to disclose their data, directly violating the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application ... ads do not identify the trader ... 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Cease the impersonation framing entirely. Data collection must occur under the trader's true identity, with prominent, honest disclosure that the service is a private, paid intermediary not affiliated with any government, presented before the user submits any personal data.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data via the application form, the controller must provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights at the point of collection. A trader that refuses to identify itself and disguises itself as a government body cannot satisfy the Art. 13 identity and purpose disclosure obligations; the buried 7pt disclaimer is not concise, intelligible or easily accessible information about who is actually collecting the data and why.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at the point of collection stating the true controller identity, contact details, the processing purposes (paid application-handling service), the legal basis, recipients, retention period, and data-subject rights, in plain and prominent language rather than as a buried footer.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any lawful basis relied on (e.g. consent to process the application, or contract) is undermined because it is built on deception: the data subject believes they are dealing with a government body, not entering a paid private contract. Consent or contract 'agreed' under a materially false impression of the counterparty and service does not provide a sound legal basis for processing the personal data submitted.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Re-establish processing on a valid basis by first removing the deception, then obtaining freely given, informed agreement/consent based on accurate information about the private, paid nature of the service before any personal data is processed.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information addressed to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. A key disclosure that undercuts the entire deceptive premise, rendered in 7pt grey footer text, fails the accessibility and intelligibility requirements that also govern how privacy and identity information must be communicated to users whose data is being collected.
findings.evidence_quote: 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Surface all material information about the controller and the service at least as prominently as the primary offer, using legible font size, sufficient contrast and clear placement before data submission.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is primarily a UCPD/DSA/AI Act deception case, but it also engages GDPR because a private company collects personal data through a paid 'energy subsidy' application obtained by impersonating an official government portal. Personal data collected under a false pretence of state affiliation is not processed fairly or transparently (Art. 5(1)(a)), and consumers cannot receive accurate controller-identity and purpose information at the point of collection (Art. 13) when the trader hides its identity and its non-governmental nature in 7pt grey text. The deceptive framing also undermines any valid lawful basis (Art. 6). Findings assume, as the description implies, that data is collected via the paid application form.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each advertisement presented on an online platform, recipients can identify in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. These display and search ads fail to identify the trader at all, and by masquerading as an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' government bulletin they also obscure that the content is a commercial advertisement. This defeats both the advertiser-identity and ad-identification limbs of the transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad clearly and prominently discloses the identity of the trader (the private company operating energy-subsidy-portal.eu) and that it is a paid advertisement, in real time and in a form recipients can readily see — not buried in a 7pt footer. Remove any styling that implies the ad is an official government communication.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The ad is a disguised advertisement — a recognised dark pattern (deceptive design that materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions) under the DSA Art. 25 framework, reinforced by the hidden 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer in 7pt grey. The false 'before the deadline' urgency compounds the manipulation. Note Art. 25 primarily binds providers of online platforms in how they design and operate their interfaces; the advertiser's own deceptive creative is more directly captured by UCPD. The finding is flagged so platform-facing exposure is understood.
findings.evidence_quote: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin ... 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Redesign the creative so it is not disguised as official/state communication: remove national colours, the coat-of-arms-like emblem and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing; surface the 'not affiliated with any government' statement at legible size and prominence; and drop unsubstantiated deadline urgency. This also reduces the risk of platforms rejecting the ads as deceptive interface content.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as display and search ads on online platforms, engaging DSA advertising-transparency rules. The most direct DSA issue is Art. 26(1): the ads "do not identify the trader," so recipients cannot see on whose behalf the ad is presented or who paid for it. The disguised "official notice" styling also engages the DSA dark-patterns framework (Art. 25), though that provision principally binds platform providers' interface design rather than the advertiser; the deceptive-creative core is primarily a UCPD matter handled by another agent. Art. 26(3) (special-category targeting), Art. 28 (minors) and Arts. 27/39 (platform-operator obligations) are not engaged on the declared facts.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads present a private company as an official government body/notice, implying approval, endorsement or authorisation by a public authority that does not exist — the site itself admits it is 'not affiliated with any government'. This is precisely the blacklisted 'fake government affiliation, official-looking notices' practice, prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer impact.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government/official framing: delete the 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording, national colours and any state-notice styling. The ad must not claim, state or imply any governmental approval, endorsement or affiliation. Clearly present the offer as a commercial service by a named private trader.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Using a coat-of-arms-like emblem to imply state/official status is displaying an equivalent of a quality/trust mark or official symbol without authorisation, which is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances. It reinforces the false impression of independent official backing.
findings.evidence_quote: a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Remove the coat-of-arms-like emblem and any insignia resembling official state or EU symbols. Use only the trader's own clearly commercial branding, and do not display any mark implying official certification or authorisation.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing manufactures artificial time pressure to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of the opportunity to make an informed choice (e.g. to discover the application is free and available directly). If no genuine, accurately stated deadline applies to this paid service, it is a blacklisted false-urgency practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove urgency/deadline messaging unless a specific, genuine and accurately disclosed deadline exists and is stated. Do not use deadlines to pressure users away from checking the free public route.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Charging €49 for a service that is publicly free, while presenting it as an official eligibility check, deceives the average consumer as to the existence and nature of the service and its price/value, causing a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently state upfront that the €49 fee is for an optional private assistance service, that the underlying application is available free of charge from the relevant authority, and provide the free official route. Ensure the price and what it buys are transparent before any commitment.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads fail to identify the trader and its commercial intent, and the crucial 'not affiliated with any government' clarification is hidden in 7pt grey footer text — material information provided in an unclear, untimely and obscured manner. Under Art. 7 the commercial intent must be apparent and material information (trader identity, that the service is paid and privately offered) cannot be hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trading company (name/legal identity) in the ads and landing page, make the commercial nature obvious at first contact, and give the 'not affiliated with any government' statement equal prominence to the headline — not buried in 7pt grey. Disclose price and the free alternative at the same level of prominence.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice explicitly targets low-income households, a group whose economic behaviour is particularly likely to be distorted by an official-looking energy-subsidy notice and time pressure. Under Art. 5(3) the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of this vulnerable group, which aggravates the seriousness of the misleading/impersonation conduct and confirms the practice is contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting a vulnerable low-income audience with deceptive official-notice framing. Even after removing government styling, ensure the offer is genuinely fair, transparent and does not exploit financial vulnerability; consider whether charging for a free public service is a legitimate offer at all.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is a textbook impersonation scam under the UCPD: government-styled "OFFICIAL NOTICE" ads with national colours and a coat-of-arms-like emblem imply state endorsement/affiliation to funnel users to a private site charging €49 for a publicly free application. Multiple Annex I "blacklist" practices (prohibited in all circumstances, without any case-by-case assessment) are clearly present — false endorsement by a public body (point 4), unauthorised official emblem/mark (point 2) and false urgency (point 7) — plus misleading action (Art. 6) and misleading omission/hidden trader identity (Art. 7). The explicit targeting of low-income households aggravates the assessment under Art. 5(3).

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads dressed up as an official government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-style emblem and an "OFFICIAL NOTICE" about 2026 energy subsidy eligibility — to funnel low-income households to a private site charging €49 for an application that is free from the authorities. This is, in substance, a government-impersonation scheme, and it triggers the most serious category of consumer-law breach: several practices here are on the EU "blacklist" of tactics banned outright, with no room for argument (fake official endorsement, unauthorised official emblem, and false deadline urgency). On top of that, the ads never say who the trader is and hide the "not affiliated with any government" disclaimer in 7pt grey text, which breaches ad-transparency and misleading-omission rules. Because it targets a financially vulnerable group and uses AI-generated creative to do so, it also engages the AI Act's prohibitions on deceptive and vulnerability-exploiting AI, plus missing AI-content marking. Collecting personal data through a fake official portal further breaches GDPR fairness, transparency and lawful-basis requirements. The bottom line: this campaign cannot be fixed with cosmetic tweaks and must not launch in its current form — the core concept (charging for a free public service behind a government disguise) is likely unlawful.
report.recommendations: ["Do not launch this campaign. The government-impersonation concept triggers EU blacklisted practices (banned in all circumstances) and the AI Act deception/vulnerability prohibitions — these cannot be remediated by wording changes.

The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.

triage.audience_notes: Explicitly targets low-income households, a financially vulnerable group under UCPD Art. 5(3) — deceptive urgency and fake official framing are especially likely to distort their decisions. Users likely to submit personal data and payment info on the portal; ad platform intermediary obligations and misleading-advertising rules (DSA) are engaged. AI Act flagged for declared generative AI use (potential transparency/manipulation concerns).
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') to funnel low-income users to a private site charging \u20ac49 for a publicly free application, with a barely-legible non-affiliation disclaimer and no trader identification. Generative AI was declared as used in creating the material. The campaign shows strong hallmarks of misleading/deceptive commercial practices exploiting a vulnerable audience.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Generative AI was declared as used to create the campaign assets, which include a synthetic coat-of-arms-like emblem, government-styled visuals and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' copy. Art. 50(2) requires providers of generative AI systems to ensure synthetic image/text outputs are marked in a machine-readable, detectable format as artificially generated. Nothing in the campaign indicates such marking is present, and the synthetic official-looking emblem is precisely the kind of AI output the marking obligation is designed to make detectable.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated visuals and text used in the ads carry machine-readable AI-provenance/watermark metadata (e.g. C2PA/SynthID-style marking) as produced by the generative system, and retain documentation that the marking was applied. Note this is separate from — and does not cure — the misleading official-impersonation problems flagged under UCPD/DSA.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The AI-generated material is designed to appear as an authentic official communication on a matter of public interest (2026 energy subsidy eligibility). Where a deployer uses AI to generate/manipulate image content that would falsely appear authentic, or text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, Art. 50(4) requires clear disclosure that the content is artificially generated/manipulated. The fake emblem and official-notice framing are candidates for this disclosure duty, reinforcing that the artificial nature must not be concealed.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: If AI-generated imagery/text is retained, add a clear, prominent human-readable disclosure that the content is AI-generated and is not an official government communication. Better: discontinue the official-notice styling entirely, since disclosure will not cure the underlying impersonation problem.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems deploying purposefully deceptive techniques with the effect of materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm. Generative AI here produced deceptive creative (false officialdom, false urgency) directing users to pay €49 for a free service — potentially significant financial harm. However, the prohibition targets AI systems that manipulate through their operation; on the facts the manipulation is human-designed content creation rather than an AI system autonomously distorting behaviour, so this is flagged as a contextual risk rather than a clear breach.
findings.evidence_quote: OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy generative AI (or any tool) to produce deceptive official-impersonation or false-urgency creative. Remove the fake official framing and the 'before the deadline' urgency, which are the elements that could bring AI-driven persuasion within the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities arising from a specific economic situation to materially distort behaviour in a way likely to cause significant harm. The campaign deliberately targets an economically vulnerable group and is likely to cause them real financial harm (€49 for a free application). The prohibition, however, is triggered by an AI system exploiting the vulnerability; personalisation/targeting is declared 'no' and no AI targeting system is described, so the strict trigger is not clearly met — flagged for attention given the AI-generated content dimension.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Avoid deploying AI-based targeting or AI-generated persuasion aimed at financially vulnerable audiences for this offer. If any AI system is used to select or tailor delivery to low-income households, reassess against Art. 5(1)(b) before running; and eliminate the exploitative €49-for-free-service proposition.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to create ad material that mimics an official government bulletin (coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, "OFFICIAL NOTICE" copy). Under the AI Act this squarely engages the Art. 50 transparency obligations for synthetic content: AI-generated images/text must carry machine-readable provenance marking (Art. 50(2)), and content generated to appear as public-interest information may require deployer disclosure (Art. 50(4)). The Art. 5 prohibitions (manipulative AI techniques; exploitation of the economically vulnerable low-income audience) are contextually relevant and worth flagging, but on the facts the deception is human-designed and no AI system is described as autonomously targeting or manipulating users (personalisation declared "no"), so those are raised as attention points rather than clear breaches. The core deception/urgency/impersonation issues fall primarily under UCPD/DSA and are handled by those agents.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed fairly and transparently. Here users are induced to hand over subsidy-application personal data and payment details under a false impression that they are dealing with a government authority. Collecting personal data through a deliberately deceptive frame — where the trader impersonates officialdom and hides its identity — is the paradigm of unfair, non-transparent data collection this principle prohibits. Fairness under Art. 5(1)(a) is breached at the moment of collection regardless of what the site later does.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove the official/government framing and impersonation entirely; collect data only under an accurate, non-deceptive presentation that makes clear the data subject is dealing with a private commercial operator, so that any personal data obtained is processed fairly and transparently.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires the controller's identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights to be provided when personal data is collected. The trader is not identified in the ads and the only identity-adjacent statement on the site is a 7pt grey 'not affiliated with any government' line. There is no described privacy notice at the point where the €49 application (and its personal/payment data) is collected, so the controller's identity and mandatory information are not properly provided to data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, complete Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of data collection: identify the actual controller (company name, contact/DPO), the purposes and lawful basis, recipients, retention periods and data-subject rights, prominently and before any personal data or payment is submitted.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. Burying the single most decision-relevant clarification in 7pt grey footer text is the opposite of easily accessible and intelligible presentation, and it signals that any privacy-related disclosures are likely presented in the same obscured, non-transparent manner.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present all data-subject information (and the affiliation clarification) in a legible size and prominent position using plain language, so it is genuinely accessible before the user provides personal data or payment.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any processing of the personal data submitted through the portal needs a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Because the data is obtained through deceptive inducement, consent (Art. 6(1)(a)) could not be freely given or informed, and a legitimate-interest basis (Art. 6(1)(f)) is unlikely to survive a balancing test given the deceptive framing and the exploitation of a financially vulnerable audience. The campaign as described gives no indication of a valid basis for processing the collected data.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis for processing the application data; if relying on consent, ensure it is freely given and informed under a truthful, non-deceptive presentation, and conduct a legitimate-interest assessment that accounts for the audience's vulnerability.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is primarily a misleading-advertising/impersonation matter (UCPD/DSA/AI Act), but it also engages GDPR because it funnels users into submitting personal data (energy-subsidy application details) and payment information on 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu'. The deceptive government framing means personal data is obtained through a controller whose identity is concealed at the point of inducement, undermining the fairness and transparency principle and the Art. 13/12 information duties. The campaign text does not describe any privacy notice, lawful basis, or controller identity, so these are risks flagged on the described facts rather than confirmed breaches of the portal's back-end practices. Note: this is not personalised/profiled targeting (declared 'no'), so Arts. 4(4)/22/21 are not primarily engaged; audience selection is a vulnerability/UCPD concern.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients of ads on online platforms can identify, clearly and in real time, that the content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. These paid display and search ads do neither: they are dressed as a government notice and omit any advertiser identity, so the platform-level transparency obligation is not met as described.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ads are clearly labelled as advertising and disclose the actual trader's legal name and that it is a private commercial service, prominently within the ad creative itself (not only in the site footer). Provide accurate advertiser identity to the ad platform so it can meet its Art. 26(1) disclosure duties.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Styling paid ads as a government bulletin with national colours and a coat-of-arms-like emblem, combined with a non-affiliation disclaimer hidden in 7pt grey, is deceptive interface/communication design that materially distorts recipients' ability to make a free and informed decision (disguised advertisement / false hierarchy of information). This is exactly the manipulative design Art. 25 prohibits, and it is aggravated by the false 'deadline' urgency and targeting of low-income households.
findings.evidence_quote: OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove all government/official framing (national colours, emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'), drop the artificial deadline unless a genuine statutory deadline is stated accurately, and surface the 'not affiliated with any government' statement in equal prominence to the headline in legible size so the interface no longer deceives users.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs paid display and search ads that (a) fail to identify the trader on whose behalf they are presented and (b) are deliberately disguised as an official government bulletin. Both engage core DSA advertising-transparency and dark-pattern rules. Art. 26(1) is not satisfied as described (no trader identity), and the "OFFICIAL NOTICE"/fake-emblem framing with a concealed disclaimer is a disguised-advertisement dark pattern under Art. 25. Art. 26(3)/28 are not engaged (no sensitive-data profiling declared, no minors); Art. 39 applies only if these run on a designated VLOP, in which case archived ad records would expose the concealed trader identity.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads are deliberately dressed as an official government communication (coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') to make consumers believe the private trader is affiliated with, endorsed or authorised by a public body. This is a per se prohibited practice regardless of consumer effect. The 7pt grey 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer does not cure a blacklisted practice.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government-imitating elements: the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, and the phrase 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'. The ad must make clear it is from a private company with no government affiliation, prominently and up-front — not in a concealed footer.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying a coat-of-arms-like emblem evoking an official/state quality or authority mark without authorisation is a per se prohibited display of a trust/quality mark or equivalent. The emblem functions as an unauthorised official seal signalling legitimacy and endorsement.
findings.evidence_quote: national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the emblem entirely. Do not use any badge, seal or emblem that could be mistaken for an official or governmental mark unless properly authorised.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads omit material information — the identity of the trader and the commercial intent of the practice — and present the material as an official government notice, so the commercial (paid application-assistance) intent is not apparent from context. Consumers cannot make an informed decision without knowing they are dealing with a private fee-charging company. The non-affiliation disclaimer in 7pt grey is provided in an unclear/untimely manner and does not remedy the omission.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader (company name) in the ads themselves and disclose the commercial nature of the offer up-front and legibly. Make the €49 fee and the non-affiliation statement prominent, not buried in tiny grey footer text.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The overall presentation deceives the average consumer about the nature of the service and its price advantage: it implies an official eligibility check, while in fact charging €49 for a service that is publicly free. This misleads on the trader's identity/qualifications and on price/price calculation, and is likely to cause a transactional decision (paying €49) the consumer would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: State honestly and prominently that the underlying application is free through the official channel, that the company is a private paid intermediary, and what the €49 buys. Do not present the service as an official eligibility check.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing invokes time pressure to elicit an immediate decision. To the extent no genuine, verifiable deadline applies to the €49 service (or the deadline is presented in a way that pressures immediate payment), this is a false/artificial urgency claim, which is per se prohibited. Combined with the vulnerable audience, it deprives consumers of opportunity for informed choice.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove urgency framing unless a genuine, accurate and clearly specified deadline exists and relates to the actual official application; never use a deadline to pressure payment for the private service.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign is expressly aimed at low-income households, a clearly identifiable group vulnerable due to their economic situation. Under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group, for whom fake official framing, false urgency and a €49 charge for a free service are especially likely to materially distort economic behaviour. This aggravates every other finding and is contrary to professional diligence as a fairness safety-net.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not exploit the financial vulnerability of low-income households. If any legitimate service is offered, ensure it is transparent, fairly priced, clearly non-governmental, and free of pressure tactics; consider whether charging for a freely available public service is defensible at all.

verdicts.notes: This campaign shows multiple clear UCPD breaches, including blacklisted (per se prohibited) practices. Ads impersonate an official government notice using a coat-of-arms-like emblem and national colours to falsely imply government affiliation/endorsement (Annex I points 4 and 2), while a private trader charges €49 for a publicly free application. Commercial intent and trader identity are concealed (Art. 7), the 'official notice' framing and price are misleading actions (Art. 6), and 'before the deadline' creates false urgency (Annex I point 7). Because the campaign explicitly targets financially vulnerable low-income households, the aggressive/vulnerability lens of Art. 5(3)/Arts. 8-9 aggravates the assessment.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads disguised as an official government bulletin — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem and "OFFICIAL NOTICE" copy — to push low-income households to a private site (energy-subsidy-portal.eu) that charges €49 for a subsidy application that is publicly free. This is not a borderline case: it hits the EU consumer-law "blacklist" of practices that are banned outright, meaning they are illegal regardless of how consumers actually react. Specifically, it falsely implies government approval/endorsement, displays an unauthorised official-style emblem, conceals that it is a paid ad from a private trader, invents deadline urgency, and misleads on price — all aggravated by deliberately targeting a financially vulnerable audience. The tiny 7pt grey "not affiliated with any government" footer does not fix any of this; hidden disclaimers cannot cure a blacklisted practice. On top of the consumer-law breaches, the ads violate DSA advertising-transparency and dark-pattern rules, collect personal and payment data unfairly and without proper notice under GDPR, and the AI-generated official-looking assets trigger AI Act synthetic-content marking obligations. The verdict is that this campaign cannot run in its current form — it must be fundamentally redesigned, not tweaked.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as designed. The core concept — impersonating an official government notice to sell a free service — is per se illegal under UCPD Annex I and cannot be made compliant with disclaimers or edits.</recommendation>

Remove ALL government-imitating elements immediately: the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, and the phrase 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'. These trigger blacklisted practices (false endorsement and unauthorised official mark).

Seriously reconsider charging €49 for a service that is publicly free to a low-income audience. If any legitimate intermediary service is offered, state up-front and prominently that the underlying application is free through the official channel and exactly what the €49 buys.

Identify the actual trader (legal company name) clearly and up-front within the ad creative itself, and label the ads as advertising, so recipients know it is a paid ad from a private company (required by DSA Art. 26 and UCPD Art. 7).

Remove the 'before the deadline' urgency framing unless a genuine, accurately specified statutory deadline exists and relates to the real official application — never to pressure payment for the private service.
Bring all disclosures out of the 7pt grey footer: the non-affiliation statement and any privacy information must be legible and prominent, in plain language, before any data or payment is submitted.

If any personal or payment data is collected, provide a complete GDPR Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of collection (controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights) and establish a valid, documented lawful basis under a truthful presentation.
Ensure any AI-generated visuals and text carry machine-readable AI-provenance marking (AI Act Art. 50(2)); note this does not cure the impersonation problem and is a secondary, technical fix only.
Have compliance/legal sign off on the redesigned campaign before relaunch given the critical exposure and the targeting of a vulnerable group.

campaign.title: You've WON — iPhone giveaway retargeting
campaign.text: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.' Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked. Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page. A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'.

detected_practices: false prize/win claim
fake 'you've won' giveaway
phantom prize (no draw, no stock)
countdown timer / false urgency (15 minutes)
bait-and-switch verification fee (4.99 EUR)
hidden subscription trap (39 EUR/month VIP club on separate terms page)
fake progress bar / simulated verification
behavioural retargeting
SMS blast marketing
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'general consumers'; no age-gating means minors can plausibly be reached, especially via display retargeting and SMS. Personal data is clearly involved (retargeting profiles, phone numbers, payment/verification data), engaging GDPR and ePrivacy for the SMS marketing. The campaign is a textbook aggressive/misleading practice under UCPD (banned 'prize' and subscription-trap tactics on the Annex I blacklist), and its online distribution and likely payment fraud characteristics engage the DSA. No generative AI declared or evident, so the AI Act is not obviously engaged.
triage.summary: A deceptive display/SMS campaign falsely telling every visitor they have won an iPhone 16 Pro, using false urgency and a small 'verification shipping' fee to enrol users in a hidden 39 EUR/month subscription, with no real prize draw or stock. It relies on behavioural retargeting and SMS blasts to general EU consumers, combining a phantom prize, subscription trap, and simulated verification bar.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The entire data-processing operation is built on a deliberate deception: personal data (retargeting identifiers, phone numbers, payment data) is collected and used under a false 'you've won an iPhone' pretext, with a fake progress bar simulating verification. Processing personal data on the back of a fabricated prize and hidden subscription trap cannot be 'fair' or 'transparent' as required by the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked.
findings.recommendation: Cease the deceptive prize framing entirely. Personal data may only be collected and processed for genuine, accurately described purposes with truthful information about what happens to the data; a campaign whose premise is false cannot be brought into GDPR compliance and should be withdrawn.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: SMS direct marketing and behavioural retargeting/profiling require a valid lawful basis — for SMS marketing generally prior consent (ePrivacy Art. 13), and for behavioural profiling either consent or a balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign describes mass 'SMS blasts' and retargeting with no indication of any lawful basis, and the deceptive context makes legitimate interests unbalanceable.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Do not send marketing SMS or run behavioural retargeting without a documented, valid lawful basis — prior opt-in consent for SMS marketing and for tracking/profiling. Maintain records demonstrating the basis for each processing purpose before launch.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent obtained in this flow cannot be valid: it is not 'freely given, specific and informed' because users are deceived about the purpose (a fake prize) and steered by false urgency into a hidden 39 EUR/month subscription. Consent extracted through deception and dark patterns does not meet the Art. 4(11) standard.
findings.evidence_quote: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping
findings.recommendation: Rebuild any consent capture as a clear, unbundled, affirmative opt-in with accurate information about the actual purposes (marketing, subscription, profiling), free of deceptive prize framing and artificial time pressure.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point personal data is collected (SMS number, payment/verification data), the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights, including any profiling. Burying material terms on a separate page and collecting data under a prize pretext means the required Art. 13 information is not provided transparently at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: described on a separate terms page
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at the actual point of data collection covering all Art. 13 items, including that data is used for retargeting/profiling and for enrolling users in a paid subscription. Do not relegate material processing information to a separate terms page.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting to serve tailored ads constitutes profiling — automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict a person's interests and behaviour. This engages the GDPR profiling regime (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights), which the campaign does not address.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups
findings.recommendation: Treat the retargeting as profiling: document lawful basis, disclose it in the Art. 13 notice, and ensure the profiling can be objected to at any time.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time to direct marketing and related profiling. Mass SMS marketing must offer an easy opt-out mechanism; the campaign as described provides no indication of any opt-out/objection route in the SMS or retargeting.
findings.evidence_quote: SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, functioning opt-out in every marketing SMS (e.g. STOP mechanism) and honour objections to profiling immediately, ceasing all direct-marketing processing on request.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: With no age-gating, minors can plausibly be reached via display retargeting and SMS. If consent is the basis for processing data of children in this information-society-service context, parental consent and reasonable age-verification efforts are required for under-16s (or the Member State threshold), which the campaign makes no provision for.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience is 'general consumers'
findings.recommendation: Implement age assurance to exclude or specially protect minors, and obtain verifiable parental consent where data of children below the applicable age threshold would otherwise be processed on a consent basis.

verdicts.notes: This deceptive display/SMS campaign processes personal data (behavioural retargeting profiles, phone numbers, payment/verification data) and squarely engages GDPR. The core problem is that data is processed unfairly and non-transparently under a fraudulent "you've won" pretext, without any evident lawful basis or valid consent for SMS marketing and profiling, and with no transparency information at collection. Several GDPR obligations are likely breached; the fraudulent framing also makes any purported consent invalid (not freely given, specific or informed).

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: A simulated verification/progress bar that fabricates a non-existent process is a deceptive interface that materially distorts the recipient's ability to make a free and informed decision, exactly the conduct DSA Art. 25 prohibits. Combined with the false 15-minute countdown and forced-continuity subscription, the interface manipulates users into paying.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fake progress bar and all simulated 'verification' UI, remove the false countdown, and never use interfaces that fabricate a process or state. Any genuine payment or consent flow must reflect the true state of the transaction.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Hiding a recurring 39 EUR/month subscription on a separate terms page while presenting the transaction as a small 'verification shipping' fee is forced continuity / obscured material choice — a dark pattern under Art. 25 that impairs informed decision-making and typically also makes cancellation harder than sign-up.
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the recurring subscription, its price and cancellation terms prominently at the point of payment with affirmative opt-in, and make cancellation at least as easy as enrolment. Do not enrol users in any subscription as a by-product of a 'shipping' payment.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The 15-minute deadline is a false urgency tactic attached to a non-existent prize ('Every visitor wins; there is no draw'). Fabricated urgency that pressures a decision is a manipulative interface design under DSA Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: Claim within 15 minutes
findings.recommendation: Remove the artificial countdown/deadline. Only present time limits that are genuine and truthfully described.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Where these retargeting ads are presented on an online platform, Art. 26(1) requires each ad to be clearly and unambiguously identifiable as an advertisement, with the advertiser/payer identity and meaningful information about the targeting parameters. Disguising a paid ad as a personal 'prize notification' defeats ad-transparency and hides the advertiser identity and targeting logic.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro!'
findings.recommendation: Label platform-served ads clearly as advertising, disclose on whose behalf and who paid for them, and provide accessible information on the main targeting parameters and how to change them.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign relies on behavioural retargeting to 'general consumers' with no age-gating, so minors are plausibly reached. DSA Art. 28 prohibits presenting profiling-based advertising to recipients the platform is aware with reasonable certainty are minors and requires a high level of protection for minors. Profiled/retargeted ads reaching minors would breach this ban.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visitor 'wins'
findings.recommendation: Ensure no profiling-based/retargeted ads are served to users who are or may reasonably be minors; implement age-assurance measures on the platforms used and exclude minors from behavioural targeting for this campaign.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If any of the display advertising is served on a Very Large Online Platform, the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach will be published in a public ad repository under Art. 39, exposing the deceptive prize claims and targeting to regulatory and public scrutiny.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Assume ads will be publicly archived; ensure all creative, advertiser data and targeting can withstand scrutiny — which this campaign in its current deceptive form cannot.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages several DSA provisions where distributed on online platforms. Most seriously, the interface design (fake "checking your prize... verified!" progress bar, false 15-minute countdown, and a 39 EUR/month subscription buried on a "separate terms page") is deceptive/manipulative design squarely within the DSA Art. 25 prohibition on dark patterns. The undisclosed, disguised nature of the retargeting ads engages the ad-transparency duty in Art. 26(1), and behavioural retargeting with no age-gating engages the ban on profiling-based ads to minors in Art. 28. Art. 25 and Art. 26/28 apply specifically to providers of online platforms; the marketer should ensure compliance both directly and via the platforms it uses.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 31 prohibits in all circumstances creating the false impression that the consumer has won a prize when in fact there is no prize, or where claiming it is subject to paying money or incurring a cost. Here every visitor 'wins', there is no draw and no phones are stocked (so there is no prize at all), and claiming it requires paying a 4.99 EUR fee. This is a per se blacklisted false prize claim on both limbs.
findings.evidence_quote: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.
findings.recommendation: Cease the 'you've won' messaging entirely. A prize promotion is lawful only if a genuine prize exists, a real draw takes place, and claiming it is not conditional on any payment. This concept cannot be made compliant without being redesigned as a genuine, cost-free promotion.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits in all circumstances falsely stating that a product/offer is available only for a very limited time in order to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of the opportunity to make an informed choice. The 15-minute countdown is artificial (there is no genuine prize or deadline) and exists solely to pressure immediate payment. This is a per se blacklisted false urgency claim.
findings.evidence_quote: Claim within 15 minutes
findings.recommendation: Remove the artificial 15-minute countdown. Any time limit must reflect a genuine, truthful constraint; a manufactured deadline designed to force a snap decision is prohibited.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices containing false information or deceiving the average consumer about the existence or main characteristics of the product, and about price. The 'verified!' progress bar falsely represents that a legitimate verification/selection process is occurring, and the '4.99 EUR verification shipping' label misrepresents the true price and nature of the transaction (which is actually enrolment in a paid subscription). These false representations cause a transactional decision the consumer would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'
findings.recommendation: Remove all simulated verification/'checking your prize' UI elements and any framing of the charge as mere 'verification shipping'. All representations must be truthful about what the consumer is actually buying and paying for.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the consumer needs, or providing it in an unclear or untimely manner. The recurring 39 EUR/month subscription is the true, dominant cost of the transaction, yet it is buried on a separate terms page while the consumer is led to believe they are paying only 4.99 EUR to claim a prize. Concealing this material cost and the ongoing commercial nature of the offer is a misleading omission (a classic subscription-trap).
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the full recurring price (39 EUR/month), billing frequency, and cancellation terms prominently and up-front, at the point and moment of the payment decision, in the same interface — not on a separate page. In this campaign, however, the underlying prize premise is itself unlawful, so disclosure alone will not cure it.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices that, through undue influence or pressure, materially impair the average consumer's freedom of choice. Combining a false 'you've won' trigger, a coercive 15-minute deadline, persistent retargeting popups and SMS blasts creates high-pressure, undue influence that pushes consumers into an immediate payment and subscription commitment they would not otherwise make.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the high-pressure elements (false win trigger, artificial deadline, persistent nagging). Given the practice is already per se prohibited under Annex I, the campaign should not proceed in any form resembling this design.

verdicts.notes: This campaign is a textbook cluster of practices banned outright under the UCPD Annex I blacklist. It falsely tells every recipient they have won an iPhone (a phantom prize with no draw and no stock) that can only be claimed by paying a 4.99 EUR fee within an artificial 15-minute deadline, then enrols them in a hidden 39 EUR/month subscription disclosed only on a separate terms page, reinforced by a simulated "verified!" progress bar. These are per se prohibited (Annex I points 31 and 7) and additionally constitute misleading actions, misleading omissions, and aggressive practices under Arts. 6-9. Multiple critical violations; no legitimate cure is possible short of abandoning the concept.

report.executive_summary: This campaign tells every recipient they have "won" an iPhone 16 Pro, pressures them to pay a 4.99 EUR "verification shipping" fee within 15 minutes, then silently enrols them in a 39 EUR/month "VIP club" buried on a separate terms page — all reinforced by a fake "verified!" progress bar. There is no draw, no prize and no stock, so the entire premise is a fabrication. This is not a borderline case: it triggers outright, per se bans under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I: false prize claims and false urgency), the DSA's prohibition on dark patterns, and multiple GDPR principles (unfair/deceptive processing, no lawful basis, invalid consent, no transparency). The core concept is a subscription-trap scam and cannot be made compliant by tweaking disclosures — it must be abandoned. Running it risks regulatory enforcement, fines, and potential fraud exposure across all EU markets. The overall verdict is critical / non-compliant.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign. The 'you've won' framing is a phantom prize with a paid claim condition — banned outright under UCPD Annex I point 31 and cannot be cured by any disclosure.

Abandon the underlying concept entirely: there is no draw, no prize and no stock, so no version of this messaging can be made lawful. Redesign from scratch as a genuine, truthful promotion if you want a prize element.
Remove the artificial 15-minute countdown (per se banned false urgency under UCPD Annex I point 7).
Remove the fake 'checking your prize... verified!' progress bar and all simulated verification UI (misleading action under UCPD Art. 6 and a prohibited dark pattern under DSA Art. 25).

Stop the hidden subscription trap: never enrol users in a 39 EUR/month charge as a by-product of a 'shipping' fee. Any genuine subscription must show full recurring price, billing frequency and cancellation terms up-front at the point of payment, with affirmative opt-in and easy cancellation.
Do not send marketing SMS or run behavioural retargeting without documented, valid prior opt-in consent; the deceptive framing means any consent captured here is invalid under GDPR.
Provide a clear privacy notice at the point of data collection (GDPR Art. 13) and a working opt-out (STOP) in every marketing SMS.
Implement age assurance to exclude minors from behavioural/retargeted advertising (DSA Art. 28, GDPR Art. 8).
Ensure platform-served ads are clearly labelled as advertising with advertiser identity and targeting disclosure (DSA Art. 26); assume all creative will be publicly archived and scrutinised.
Seek legal review before any relaunch — the current design exposes the business to enforcement action and potential fraud liability across the EU.

campaign.title: You've WON — iPhone giveaway retargeting
