Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked. Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page. A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'.

detected_practices: false prize/winning claim ('you've WON')
fake lottery/giveaway with no actual draw
everyone 'wins' — guaranteed fake prize
countdown/urgency pressure ('claim within 15 minutes')
hidden subscription trap (39 EUR/month VIP club buried on separate terms page)
small upfront fee to unlock hidden recurring charges ('4.99 EUR verification shipping')
fake progress bar / fabricated verification animation
behavioural retargeting
SMS blasts / direct marketing
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'general consumers' with no age gating; SMS blasts and display retargeting can reach minors, so minors are plausibly reached. Prize-based lures are especially manipulative toward vulnerable and younger users.
triage.summary: A fraudulent 'iPhone giveaway' campaign run via display retargeting popups and SMS blasts, where every visitor is falsely told they have won a prize that does not exist and pressured to pay a small 'verification' fee within 15 minutes. Paying secretly enrols users in a 39 EUR/month subscription disclosed only on a separate terms page, aided by a fake progress bar. This is a textbook deceptive/aggressive practice with a subscription trap, using behavioural retargeting and SMS marketing on EU general consumers.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (phone numbers, retargeting identifiers) is collected and processed within a fabricated prize scheme using a fake progress bar ('checking your prize... verified!'). Processing personal data in an inherently deceptive context, where the stated purpose (awarding a prize) is false, breaches the requirement that data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. The user cannot understand the true purpose of the processing (enrolment in a paid subscription and marketing).
findings.evidence_quote: Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked.
findings.recommendation: Cease the deceptive scheme entirely. Any legitimate data collection must state the real purpose truthfully and fairly at the point of collection, with no fabricated verification or prize narratives.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: SMS direct marketing and behavioural retargeting each require a valid lawful basis — in practice prior consent for SMS marketing (ePrivacy) and consent/legitimate-interest for behavioural tracking. The campaign shows no indication of any lawful basis, freely given consent, or legitimate-interest assessment; the 'SMS blasts' phrasing suggests untargeted, non-consented mass messaging.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any processing: obtain prior, specific opt-in consent for SMS marketing and for behavioural retargeting cookies/identifiers, and retain proof of consent.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent obtained through this flow cannot be freely given, specific, informed or unambiguous: users are deceived into a payment via a fake prize and a hidden 39 EUR/month subscription buried on a separate terms page. Consent to processing/marketing obtained via such dark-pattern deception fails the Art. 4(11) standard.
findings.evidence_quote: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping
findings.recommendation: Redesign so that any consent to data processing or marketing is unbundled from payment, clearly presented (not on a separate buried page), and given by a genuine affirmative action free of deception or coercion.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct marketing (SMS and retargeting-based profiling) triggers the data subject's absolute right to object. The campaign describes no opt-out mechanism in the SMS messages or retargeting flow, so the facilitation of the right to object appears absent.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, functioning opt-out (e.g. STOP keyword for SMS and an easy mechanism to object to retargeting) in every communication, and honour objections immediately by ceasing marketing processing.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting personal data (phone number, payment, retargeting identifiers), the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and rights. The campaign discloses key terms only on a separate buried page and provides no proper Art. 13 notice, so mandatory transparency information is not provided at the point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: described on a separate terms page
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, accessible privacy notice at the point of data collection identifying the controller, all processing purposes (including the subscription and retargeting), legal basis, and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: With no age gating, SMS blasts and display retargeting can reach minors, and prize lures are especially manipulative toward younger users. Where consent is the basis for information society services likely to reach children, processing minors' data below the applicable age threshold requires verifiable parental consent and reasonable verification efforts — neither of which is present.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: general consumers
findings.recommendation: Implement age verification/gating and, where minors may be reached, obtain and verify parental consent; do not process children's data on the basis of consent that cannot meet Art. 8 requirements.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting of individuals constitutes profiling within Art. 4(4), which brings the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) into scope for this campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Treat the retargeting as profiling: ensure it rests on a valid basis, is disclosed in the privacy notice, and is subject to an easy objection mechanism.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data (phone numbers for SMS blasts, behavioural retargeting profiles) of EU consumers within a fundamentally deceptive scheme. This engages GDPR most acutely through the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and lawful-basis requirements: SMS direct marketing and behavioural retargeting require a valid basis (consent), and there is no indication of consent, transparency notices, opt-out mechanisms, or age gating. Because minors are plausibly reached and the entire data-collection context is fraudulent, several obligations are likely breached.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The interface combines a fabricated win claim, a fake verification progress bar, and an artificial 15-minute countdown to deceive and pressure users, then enrols them in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' disclosed only on a separate terms page. This is deceptive and manipulative interface design that materially distorts the user's ability to make a free and informed decision, including forced-continuity/hidden-subscription tactics — precisely the conduct Art. 25 prohibits.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'
findings.recommendation: Cease the campaign in its current form. Remove the fake progress bar, the false 'you've WON' framing, and the artificial deadline. Any subscription must be presented up front with the recurring 39 EUR/month price and cancellation terms as prominently as the sign-up, with no obstruction to cancellation.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The retargeting popups are advertisements presented through online platform interfaces, but they are disguised as a personal prize notification with no advertiser identity, no indication they are advertising, and no disclosure of the paid subscription behind them. Art. 26(1) requires recipients to identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an ad, on whose behalf it is presented, and the main targeting parameters.
findings.evidence_quote: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro!
findings.recommendation: Clearly label the placement as an advertisement, identify the advertiser and payer, and disclose the main parameters used to target the recipient and how to change them. Remove the disguised 'prize' framing that conceals the commercial and subscription nature of the offer.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign uses behavioural retargeting (profiling-based ads) against a 'general consumers' audience with no age gating, so minors are plausibly reached. Art. 28 prohibits presenting profiling-based advertisements to recipients reasonably known to be minors and requires age-appropriate protection; profiled prize-lure ads without age assurance run a serious risk of reaching and manipulating minors.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Do not serve profiling/retargeting-based ads to users who may be minors. Implement age-assurance measures and exclude minors from profiled targeting; given the prize-lure design, avoid delivering this content to audiences that cannot be reliably confirmed as adults.

verdicts.notes: This "iPhone giveaway" retargeting campaign engages the DSA insofar as it is delivered through online platform interfaces (retargeting popups). It is a textbook dark pattern under Art. 25: a fabricated win notice, a fake "verified" progress bar, an artificial 15-minute deadline, and a hidden 39 EUR/month subscription trap disclosed only on a separate terms page — design that deceives and materially impairs users' ability to make free, informed decisions, including forced continuity. The disguised commercial/subscription intent also undermines Art. 26(1) advertising transparency, and profiling-based retargeting reaching an ungated "general consumer" audience implicates the Art. 28 ban on profiled ads to minors. Note: Arts. 25/26/28 bind providers of online platforms; the advertiser's exposure depends on the delivery surface, but the design is non-compliant on any platform that operates these interfaces.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: Creating the false impression that the consumer has won a prize when there is in fact no prize, and/or making claiming it subject to paying money, is prohibited in all circumstances. The campaign concedes 'Every visitor wins; there is no draw and no phones are stocked' and requires a 4.99 EUR payment to 'claim' — a textbook Annex I point 31 breach on both limbs (no prize + payment required).
findings.evidence_quote: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.
findings.recommendation: Cease this practice entirely. Do not represent that consumers have won a prize unless a genuine, verifiable prize exists, is actually awarded through a real draw, and can be claimed without any payment or cost. There is no compliant version of a 'won a prize that doesn't exist / pay to claim' message.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Falsely stating that a product/offer is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of an informed choice is blacklisted. Since there is no genuine prize or draw, the 15-minute window is a fabricated deadline designed purely to pressure payment.
findings.evidence_quote: Claim within 15 minutes
findings.recommendation: Remove artificial countdown/deadline messaging. Any time limit stated to consumers must correspond to a genuine, truthful limitation on a real offer.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: A won/prize item is presented as costing the consumer nothing beyond delivery, but the 4.99 EUR labelled 'verification shipping' is not a genuine unavoidable delivery cost of a real prize — no phones are stocked — and it in fact acts as a gateway to a hidden 39 EUR/month charge. Describing something as won/free while extracting payment beyond genuine delivery cost is blacklisted.
findings.evidence_quote: you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! ... just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping
findings.recommendation: Do not describe any item as won/free where the consumer must pay anything other than the genuine unavoidable cost of collection/delivery of a real product. Eliminate the 'verification shipping' fee construct.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The recurring 39 EUR/month subscription is material information that the consumer needs to make an informed decision. Burying it on a separate terms page while the headline promises a won prize for 4.99 EUR hides the true cost and commercial reality, constituting a misleading omission and a subscription trap. The transactional decision (paying 4.99 EUR) is induced without the key price information.
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the full recurring cost (39 EUR/month), its nature, duration and cancellation terms clearly, prominently and up front — adjacent to the price and before payment — with affirmative, informed opt-in. However, given the false-prize core this offer cannot simply be 'fixed' by disclosure; the underlying scheme must be withdrawn.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The fabricated verification animation gives false information about the existence and nature of the prize and the process, deceiving the average consumer as to the main characteristics of what is being offered and causing a transactional decision (payment) they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'
findings.recommendation: Remove any fabricated 'verification' or 'checking your prize' animations. Do not simulate processes or confirmations that do not reflect a genuine, truthful state of affairs.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of an artificial 15-minute deadline, repeated SMS blasts and retargeting popups, and the manufactured excitement of a 'win' applies undue influence and pressure that significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and pushes them into an immediate payment. Assessed via Art. 5(3) it is especially manipulative toward younger/credulous users who may be reached.
findings.evidence_quote: Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate high-pressure time limits and repeated urgency-driven solicitations. Allow consumers time and clear information to make a free, informed decision without coercive framing.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Repeated SMS blasts and retargeting popups risk constituting persistent and unwanted solicitations by remote media. As described, the campaign shows no evidence of prior consent or respect for opt-out, and 'blasts' implies volume/repetition characteristic of the prohibited practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Ensure all SMS/remote marketing is sent only to consumers who have given valid prior consent, cap frequency, and immediately cease contact on objection/opt-out. (Consent lawfulness itself sits under ePrivacy/GDPR.)

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a fairness safety-net, the scheme is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average consumer, and is especially likely to distort the behaviour of credulous/younger consumers plausibly reached by untargeted SMS and display. It confirms the overall unfairness of the practice beyond the specific prohibitions engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked.
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the campaign. A scheme built on a non-existent prize and a concealed subscription cannot be brought into compliance and should not run.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including several blacklisted (per se prohibited "in all circumstances") practices. The core mechanic — telling every visitor they have "WON" a prize that does not exist and requiring payment to claim it — is squarely blacklisted under Annex I point 31. The fake 15-minute deadline (Annex I point 7), the effectively "free" prize costing money (point 20 read with Art. 7), and the fabricated verification progress bar (Arts. 6/7) compound the deception, while the whole scheme also breaches the aggressive-practices rules and the general fairness clause. This is a clear, serious violation profile warranting the highest severity.

report.executive_summary: This campaign tells every recipient they have "won" an iPhone 16 Pro that does not exist, pressures them with a fake 15-minute countdown and a bogus "verifying your prize" animation, charges a 4.99 EUR "shipping" fee to claim it, and then quietly enrols them into a 39 EUR/month subscription disclosed only on a separate terms page. This is not a borderline case: it hits some of the most serious prohibitions in EU consumer law. Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive it triggers multiple blacklisted practices that are banned outright in all circumstances — most notably the false-prize claim (Annex I, point 31) — meaning there is no version of this that can be made compliant. It also breaches the Digital Services Act ban on dark patterns and the rules on advertising transparency and protection of minors, and the GDPR's fairness, lawful-basis and consent requirements because personal data (phone numbers and retargeting profiles) is collected inside a fraudulent scheme with no valid consent, notice, or opt-out. The overall verdict is critical: this campaign must not run and cannot be "fixed" — it must be withdrawn entirely. Only the AI Act is not engaged; every other assessed regime shows likely serious violations.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign, and immediately halt it if already live. The core mechanic — claiming everyone has won a prize that does not exist and charging to claim it — is a per se prohibited practice under UCPD Annex I point 31 and cannot be remedied by better wording or disclosure.

Remove the fake 'you've WON' framing, the fabricated 'checking your prize... verified!' progress bar, and the artificial 15-minute countdown. These are deceptive/aggressive practices (UCPD Arts. 6-9) and DSA Art. 25 dark patterns.

Eliminate the hidden subscription trap: no legitimate offer may bury a recurring 39 EUR/month charge on a separate terms page. Any genuine paid product must show the full recurring price, duration and cancellation terms up front, adjacent to the payment step, with an affirmative informed opt-in.
Drop the '4.99 EUR verification shipping' construct — you cannot describe an item as won/free while extracting a fee that is not the genuine delivery cost of a real product (UCPD Annex I point 20).

For any future legitimate marketing: obtain valid prior opt-in consent for SMS and for behavioural retargeting, provide a proper privacy notice at the point of collection, include a working STOP/opt-out in every message, and stop treating 'blasts' as acceptable (GDPR Arts. 5, 6, 13, 21; ePrivacy).

Implement age assurance / gating before serving any profiling-based ads. As designed, minors can be reached, which breaches the DSA Art. 28 ban on profiled ads to minors and GDPR Art. 8 children's-consent rules; prize lures are especially manipulative toward young users.
For any legitimate ads delivered via online platforms, label them clearly as advertising, identify the advertiser/payer, and disclose the main targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26).
Have legal/compliance sign off on any replacement campaign before relaunch, given the multiple blacklisted practices and cross-regulatory exposure (UCPD, DSA, GDPR).

campaign.title: You've WON — iPhone giveaway retargeting

Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked. Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page. A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'.

detected_practices: false 'you've won a prize' claim (no draw, no phones stocked)
fake urgency countdown ('claim within 15 minutes')
hidden subscription trap (39 EUR/month VIP club buried on separate terms page)
small upfront charge to enrol in recurring subscription (4.99 EUR 'verification shipping')
fake progress bar / deceptive UI ('checking your prize... verified!')
behavioural retargeting
SMS marketing blasts
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'general consumers' via display and SMS with no age gating, so minors can plausibly be reached. Personalisation/targeting is declared, and SMS blasts plus retargeting rely on personal data (phone numbers, tracking identifiers/behavioural profiles), engaging GDPR and ePrivacy consent concerns. The deceptive tactics and dark patterns strongly engage the UCPD (misleading and aggressive practices, false 'you have won a prize' item on the UCPD blacklist) and the DSA (online interface dark patterns / deceptive design). No generative AI declared or apparent, so AI Act not flagged.
triage.summary: A deceptive prize-scam campaign using retargeting popups and SMS blasts that falsely tells every visitor they have won an iPhone, then uses fake urgency and a fake verification progress bar to induce a small 'shipping' payment that secretly enrols them in a 39 EUR/month subscription. This exhibits clear aggressive/misleading commercial practices, a subscription trap, dark-pattern UI, and behavioural targeting of general EU consumers.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (phone numbers, tracking identifiers, behavioural profiles) is collected and used to deliver marketing built on a demonstrably false premise. Processing personal data in furtherance of a knowingly deceptive scheme breaches the core principle that data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently — consumers are misled about the true purpose (enrolling them in a paid subscription), which is neither fair nor transparent.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked.
findings.recommendation: Cease the deceptive prize framing entirely. Data may only be processed where the stated purpose is truthful; disclose the real purpose of any data collection and ensure processing is fair and non-manipulative.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: SMS direct marketing and behavioural retargeting each require a valid lawful basis. SMS marketing generally requires prior consent (ePrivacy Art. 13), and behavioural profiling for ads requires consent or a valid legitimate-interest balancing. Nothing in the campaign evidences a lawful basis; consent obtained via a deceptive prize claim would not be a valid basis, and legitimate interest cannot justify processing embedded in a scam.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any SMS or retargeting processing — for SMS, obtain genuine prior opt-in consent; for behavioural profiling, either obtain consent or complete a defensible legitimate-interest assessment. Do not rely on data gathered through the deceptive flow.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent for marketing/tracking gathered in this flow cannot be 'freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous.' The user is deceived about what they are agreeing to (a 39 EUR/month subscription buried on a separate page) and pressured by a false win and fake countdown, so consent is neither informed nor freely given.
findings.evidence_quote: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping
findings.recommendation: Redesign consent collection so it is separate from any payment/enrolment, uses clear affirmative action, is unbundled, and clearly and truthfully states what data is processed and for what purpose.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to demonstrate valid consent, that consent requests be clearly distinguishable and in plain language, and that essentials not be hidden. Burying the material subscription terms on a separate page and bundling enrolment into a 'verification shipping' payment fails these conditions and defeats the ability to demonstrate valid consent.
findings.evidence_quote: enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page
findings.recommendation: Present all material terms and any consent request in a clearly distinguishable, plain-language form at the point of collection; keep consent unbundled from payment and make withdrawal as easy as giving it.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data (e.g., phone numbers, tracking identifiers), the controller must provide its identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and any profiling information at the point of collection. The campaign shows no such privacy information; the true purpose is actively concealed behind the fake prize.
findings.evidence_quote: SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, accurate Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of data collection, including controller identity, the real purposes (marketing, subscription enrolment), legal basis, retention and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time to direct marketing and related profiling. SMS blasts and behavioural retargeting are direct marketing/profiling, yet the campaign provides no described opt-out mechanism (e.g., STOP for SMS, opt-out from profiling).
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, functioning opt-out in every SMS (e.g., 'reply STOP') and an easy mechanism to object to profiling/retargeting; honour objections immediately and suppress the contact from further marketing.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The behavioural retargeting relies on automated processing of personal data to analyse and predict consumers' interests/behaviour, which meets the definition of profiling and triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups
findings.recommendation: Treat the retargeting as profiling and ensure all profiling-related obligations (lawful basis, Art. 13 transparency including profiling info, and Art. 21 objection) are satisfied.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: With display and SMS delivery to a general audience and no age gating, minors can plausibly be reached. Where consent is the basis for information-society-service processing offered to children, processing is lawful only for children of at least 16 (or the lower national threshold), with parental consent and reasonable verification below that age — none of which is provided here.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: general consumers
findings.recommendation: Implement age-gating/age-assurance and, where minors could be reached, obtain and verify parental consent before processing, or exclude minors from the campaign entirely.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data (phone numbers for SMS blasts; tracking identifiers/behavioural profiles for retargeting) entirely within a deceptive prize-scam framing. Because the whole premise is a fabrication ("Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked"), the processing cannot be lawful, fair or transparent, and any consent obtained through such deception is invalid. SMS direct marketing without demonstrable prior consent, absent opt-out facilitation, and behavioural profiling of a general audience with no age gating compound the exposure. Several GDPR obligations are engaged and, as described, likely breached.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: A fabricated verification/progress bar that simulates a genuine prize-verification process is deceptive interface design that manipulates recipients and materially distorts their ability to make a free and informed decision, exactly the conduct DSA Art. 25 prohibits for online platforms.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fake progress bar and any simulated verification. Interfaces must not fabricate processes or states that do not exist; only display genuine, truthful status indicators.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Presenting a 4.99 EUR 'verification shipping' charge while hiding the recurring 39 EUR/month enrolment on a separate terms page is a forced-continuity / sneaking dark pattern under Art. 25 — giving prominence to the trivial charge and obscuring the material recurring commitment, impairing free and informed choice.
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page
findings.recommendation: Disclose the full recurring price (39 EUR/month), billing frequency and how to cancel with equal prominence at the point of payment, before any charge; make cancellation at least as easy as sign-up.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The 15-minute countdown is false urgency: there is no genuine draw and no phones stocked, so the deadline is fabricated to pressure decisions — a manipulative interface tactic within the scope of DSA Art. 25 (as well as the urgency/scarcity concept it governs).
findings.evidence_quote: Claim within 15 minutes
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the artificial countdown. Any time limit shown must be genuine and truthful; do not use fabricated deadlines to pressure users.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Behaviourally retargeted advertising presented via platform interfaces must be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, disclose on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, and give meaningful information about the main targeting parameters. The disguised 'you've won' prize messaging does none of this and is not labelled as advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Where ads appear on an online platform, label them clearly as advertisements in real time, identify the advertiser/payer, and provide accessible information about the targeting parameters and how to change them.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Display and SMS retargeting to 'general consumers' with no age gating means minors can plausibly be reached, and the campaign relies on behavioural profiling/tracking identifiers. DSA Art. 28 bans profiling-based advertising to recipients who are minors and requires appropriate protection measures where interfaces are accessible to minors.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: general consumers
findings.recommendation: Implement age-assurance or exclude minors from profiling-based targeting; ensure no behaviourally targeted ads are served to users reasonably known to be minors, and apply age-appropriate safeguards.

verdicts.notes: The campaign exhibits textbook deceptive-design / dark-pattern tactics that DSA Art. 25 prohibits: a fake verification progress bar, a false "you've won" prize claim, artificial urgency, and a subscription trap where recurring 39 EUR/month terms are buried on a separate page while a small 4.99 EUR charge is presented as mere "shipping" — materially distorting users' ability to make free and informed decisions. Behavioural retargeting also engages DSA ad-transparency (Art. 26(1)) and, given no age gating on display/SMS to "general consumers", the ban on profiling-based ads to minors (Art. 28). DSA Arts. 25–28 obligations attach specifically to providers of online platforms; applicability depends on whether the interfaces are operated on/by such a platform, but where they are, the design is very likely non-compliant.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: The campaign creates the false impression that the consumer has won a prize when in fact 'every visitor wins', there is no draw and no phones are stocked, and claiming the 'prize' is conditioned on paying 4.99 EUR. This is exactly the conduct blacklisted under Annex I point 31 — false prize claims where there is no prize and/or claiming it requires paying money. It is prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.
findings.recommendation: Cease the campaign entirely. Do not represent that a consumer has won a prize unless a genuine prize exists, has been fairly awarded, and can be claimed without any payment beyond genuine unavoidable costs.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 15-minute deadline is an artificial countdown designed to elicit an immediate decision and deprive the consumer of time to make an informed choice. Since there is no genuine prize or genuine time-limited availability, this is a false urgency/limited-time claim blacklisted under Annex I point 7 and prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: Claim within 15 minutes
findings.recommendation: Remove all artificial deadlines and countdowns. Only use time limits that reflect genuine, verifiable availability constraints.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: The iPhone is presented as a won/free prize, yet the consumer must pay 4.99 EUR framed as 'verification shipping' plus enrolment in a 39 EUR/month club. A charge labelled 'verification' is not a genuine unavoidable delivery cost, so describing the item as an effectively free prize while extracting payment engages the Annex I point 20 prohibition on misuse of 'free'/no-charge framing.
findings.evidence_quote: you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping
findings.recommendation: Do not present any product as a free or won prize when the consumer must pay a 'verification' fee or is enrolled in a paid subscription. Only genuine, unavoidable delivery costs may be charged for a genuinely free item.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The fake progress bar and 'verified!' state falsely represent that a legitimate prize-verification process has occurred, and the whole message deceives the average consumer as to the existence and nature of the offer and the price they will pay, causing a transactional decision (paying 4.99 EUR) they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fake progress bar and any 'verified' indicators. Never simulate processes or checks that do not actually take place.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The material fact that payment enrols the consumer in a recurring 39 EUR/month subscription is hidden on a separate terms page and omitted from the primary offer message. Failing to give this material price/contractual information clearly and timely is a misleading omission under Art. 7 and constitutes a subscription trap.
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page.
findings.recommendation: Disclose all recurring charges, the full price, billing frequency, and cancellation rights clearly and prominently at the point of the offer and before payment — not buried on a separate page.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of relentless retargeting popups, SMS blasts and a 15-minute deadline applies undue pressure and time pressure that significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice, pushing them into an immediate transactional decision. This engages the aggressive-practices prohibition in Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected
findings.recommendation: Stop the high-pressure retargeting and SMS blasting combined with artificial deadlines. Marketing must not coerce or unduly influence consumers into immediate decisions.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall scheme is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts consumer economic behaviour; because it is untargeted display/SMS with no age gating, it may also reach credulous or vulnerable consumers, who are assessed under Art. 5(3). The practice is fundamentally unfair.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked.
findings.recommendation: Abandon the deceptive prize mechanic entirely and adopt an honest offer that meets the standard of professional diligence, with particular care not to exploit vulnerable or credulous recipients.

verdicts.notes: This is a fraudulent prize-scam campaign that engages multiple UCPD "blacklist" prohibitions (unfair in all circumstances) as well as the general misleading, aggressive and omission provisions. The core "you've WON an iPhone" claim is false (no draw, no phones stocked) and conditioned on payment — a per-se prohibited false prize claim. It is compounded by false urgency, a deceptive "verified!" progress bar, a hidden 39 EUR/month subscription trap, and misuse of an effectively "free" prize framing. Nearly all findings are critical because they fall within Annex I, which is banned outright regardless of consumer impact.

report.executive_summary: This campaign tells every recipient they have "won" an iPhone 16 Pro and pressures them to pay a 4.99 EUR "verification shipping" fee within 15 minutes. In reality there is no draw, no phones exist, and paying secretly signs the person up to a 39 EUR/month "VIP club" hidden on a separate page. A fake progress bar that "verifies" the non-existent prize completes the deception. This is not a borderline marketing issue — it is a prize scam that breaks EU consumer law outright. It triggers several of the UCPD "blacklist" practices that are banned in all circumstances (false prize claims, false urgency, misuse of "free"), plus misleading and aggressive-practice rules, DSA dark-pattern prohibitions, and multiple GDPR breaches around unlawful SMS/retargeting data use and invalid consent. Because the entire premise is fabricated, no wording tweak can fix it; the campaign must be stopped, not adjusted. Running it as described exposes the business to enforcement action, heavy fines, and likely fraud liability.
recommendations: Stop this campaign immediately and do not launch it in any form — the false prize mechanic is banned outright under EU law and cannot be salvaged by editing the copy.
Never claim a consumer has won a prize unless a genuine prize exists, has been fairly awarded, and can be claimed without any payment; remove the 4.99 EUR 'verification shipping' charge entirely.
Remove the fake 'checking your prize... verified!' progress bar and any simulated verification — never display processes or states that do not actually occur.
Eliminate the 15-minute countdown and all artificial urgency; only show deadlines that reflect genuine, verifiable constraints.

Abandon the hidden subscription trap. If you offer any paid subscription, disclose the full 39 EUR/month price, billing frequency and cancellation method with equal prominence at the point of payment, and make cancelling as easy as signing up.
For any future SMS marketing, obtain genuine prior opt-in consent and include a working opt-out (e.g. 'reply STOP') in every message; do not use data gathered through the current deceptive flow.
For behavioural retargeting, establish a documented lawful basis, provide a complete privacy notice at the point of collection, label ads clearly as advertising, and honour objections to profiling.
Implement age-gating/age-assurance so minors are excluded from profiling-based targeting and are not exposed to the campaign.
Have legal/compliance review any replacement promotion before launch, given the fraud and multi-regulation exposure here.

campaign.title: GrandDraw 'You have won' mailer
campaign.text: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up.' The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.

detected_practices: false 'guaranteed winner' prize claim
advance-fee / pay-to-claim scheme
artificial deadline / false urgency (7-day forfeiture)
no verifiable draw terms
processing/insurance fee exceeding actual prize value
misleading representation of a prize (voucher vs €2,500)
targeting vulnerable elderly consumers
triage.audience_notes: Declared as general adult consumers but skews elderly, a recognised vulnerable group under UCPD Art. 5(3); average-consumer benchmark should be adjusted to the vulnerable target. No indication minors are targeted or reached.
triage.summary: A prize-draw mailer (email and postal) telling recipients they are a "guaranteed winner" of a €2,500 prize but demanding a €29.90 advance fee within 7 days to release winnings, where the draw has no verifiable terms and the actual prize is a low-value voucher worth less than the fee. This is a classic misleading/aggressive advance-fee prize scam that skews toward elderly consumers. UCPD is squarely engaged (banned practices: falsely stating a prize can be won, and creating an impression of having won while requiring payment); GDPR applies as postal/email addresses are processed and the campaign relies on 'selected' address data.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (postal/email address) is processed to deliver a communication that is deliberately deceptive — a false 'guaranteed winner' claim used to extract an advance fee. Processing personal data as the vehicle for a fraudulent/misleading solicitation cannot be 'fair' and the message is not 'transparent' about who is processing the data or why. This breaches the core lawfulness-fairness-transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize
findings.recommendation: Cease using recipients' personal data for a deceptive prize solicitation. Any legitimate marketing must be truthful, clearly identify the sender/controller, and state the genuine purpose of the communication.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Sending unsolicited direct marketing requires a valid lawful basis; for email direct marketing prior consent is generally required (Art. 6(1) read with ePrivacy). The addresses were 'selected' with no indication of consent or a documented, balanced legitimate-interest basis, and legitimate interest cannot support processing that is unlawful/deceptive in purpose. No valid legal basis appears to exist.
findings.evidence_quote: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any marketing: obtain prior opt-in consent for email marketing, and for postal marketing conduct and record a legitimate-interest assessment based on lawfully sourced data. Do not process 'selected' address lists absent this.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is used to contact individuals, the controller must provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The mailer identifies no controller, gives no privacy information and no verifiable terms, so the Art. 13 information obligations are not met at (or before) the point of use.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms
findings.recommendation: Include a clear privacy notice with the controller's identity and contact details, purpose and legal basis of processing, data source, retention period and how to exercise data-subject rights, in every communication.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: This is a direct marketing communication, so recipients have an absolute right to object to further marketing, which must be actively facilitated. The mailer provides no opt-out/objection mechanism and instead pressures recipients into further engagement, failing the Art. 21(2)-(3) obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy, cost-free way to object to/opt out of direct marketing in every message (e.g. unsubscribe link and postal opt-out), honour objections immediately, and maintain a suppression list.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data (postal and email addresses) to send unsolicited direct marketing built entirely on deception ("guaranteed winner" prize scam). Under GDPR this engages the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), the requirement for a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) — noting email direct marketing generally needs prior consent — the obligation to provide identity/purpose/rights information (Art. 13), and the absolute right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21). As described, none of these obligations appear satisfied: the sender is not identified, no privacy information or opt-out is offered, addresses were "selected" without an apparent lawful basis, and the entire message is misleading, which is per se incompatible with fair and transparent processing.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 31 prohibits in all circumstances creating the false impression that the consumer has won a prize when claiming it is subject to paying money or incurring a cost. The mailer states the recipient is the 'GUARANTEED WINNER' but requires a €29.90 fee to 'release' the prize. This is a per-se banned practice; no case-by-case materiality assessment is needed. The 'draw has no verifiable terms' and the actual prize is a voucher worth less than the fee, reinforcing that there is effectively no genuine prize.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Do not run this campaign. A lawful prize promotion cannot condition receipt of a genuine prize on any payment or cost. Remove the fee entirely and only claim a win where the recipient has actually won a real, verifiable prize under published, verifiable terms.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits falsely stating that an offer is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision and deprive the consumer of the opportunity to make an informed choice. The 7-day forfeiture deadline is an artificial, fabricated urgency device attached to a fictitious 'win', designed to rush recipients into paying before they can scrutinise the (non-existent, unverifiable) draw terms.
findings.evidence_quote: pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated forfeiture deadline. Any time limit in a genuine promotion must reflect real terms and must not be used to pressure an immediate payment.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 (misleading actions) is engaged: the communication contains false information about the existence and main characteristics of the 'prize' and its value. Recipients are led to believe they have won €2,500 when the item actually sent is a low-value 'prize catalogue voucher' worth less than the €29.90 fee, and the price/consideration relationship is deceptive. This causes a transactional decision (paying the fee) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize
findings.recommendation: Do not represent a €2,500 win where the real benefit is a low-value voucher. All prize descriptions and values must be accurate and substantiated; the net cost/benefit to the consumer must not be misrepresented.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 (misleading omissions) is engaged: material information a consumer needs — the actual identity/value of the item, the true nature of the 'fee', the real terms of the draw, and the odds/basis of 'selection' — is hidden or absent, and the true commercial intent (selling a low-value voucher for €29.90) is disguised as prize administration.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.
findings.recommendation: Disclose clearly and prominently the true nature and value of what is provided, the full terms of any promotion, and the genuine commercial purpose. Do not label a purchase price as a 'processing and insurance fee'.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 (aggressive practices) are engaged through undue influence and pressure: a coercive forfeiture threat combined with a payment demand significantly impairs freedom of choice and prompts a payment the consumer would not otherwise make. The impact is aggravated because the audience skews elderly — a clearly identifiable vulnerable group under Art. 5(3) — so the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group.
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the pressure/forfeiture mechanic and the payment demand. Given the audience skews elderly, avoid any high-pressure framing; assess all messaging against the vulnerable-consumer benchmark under Art. 5(3).

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 provides the general fairness safety-net, and Art. 5(3) requires assessment from the perspective of the average member of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group where the practice is likely to distort their behaviour. The campaign is contrary to professional diligence and targets a base that skews elderly (age/credulity vulnerability), materially distorting their economic behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER
findings.recommendation: Treat the elderly-skewing audience as a vulnerable group and calibrate any future promotion to that benchmark; ensure the practice as a whole meets professional diligence — in this case, the practice cannot be salvaged and should be withdrawn.

verdicts.notes: This mailer is a textbook advance-fee prize scam and squarely engages the UCPD, most seriously the Annex I blacklist. It creates the false impression the recipient has won a €2,500 prize while making the claim conditional on paying a €29.90 "processing and insurance fee" — prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 31. It compounds this with false/misleading representation of the prize (a low-value voucher worth less than the fee), a fabricated 7-day forfeiture deadline, and high-pressure/aggressive elements aimed at a consumer base that skews elderly (Art. 5(3) vulnerable group). Multiple independent, per-se violations are present.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is a classic advance-fee prize scam and cannot be made compliant with cosmetic edits — it must not be sent. It tells recipients they have "won" a €2,500 prize but demands a €29.90 "processing and insurance fee" to release it, while the item actually delivered is a voucher worth less than the fee. Telling consumers they've won a prize that requires payment to claim is banned outright in every circumstance under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I point 31) — no case-by-case defence is available. It is aggravated by fabricated urgency (the 7-day forfeiture threat), misrepresentation of the prize's value, and high-pressure tactics aimed at an audience that skews elderly, a legally recognised vulnerable group. Separately, using recipients' postal and email addresses to deliver a deceptive solicitation breaches core GDPR principles: there is no valid lawful basis, no sender/controller identification, no privacy information, and no way to opt out. The declared "no personalisation / no AI" status does not reduce the risk. Verdict: unlawful as designed; withdraw it entirely.
recommendations: Do not send this campaign in any form — the win-plus-fee structure is a per-se prohibited practice (UCPD Annex I point 31) that cannot be remedied by rewording.
Remove the €29.90 fee and the 'guaranteed winner' framing entirely; never condition receipt of a genuine prize on any payment or cost.
If any future prize promotion is run, publish genuine, verifiable draw terms and only claim a win where the recipient has actually won a real, accurately described and valued prize.
Delete the fabricated 7-day forfeiture deadline and all high-pressure language; calibrate any messaging to the vulnerable-consumer benchmark given the elderly-skewing audience.

Do not use 'selected' address lists — establish and document a valid GDPR lawful basis before any marketing (prior opt-in consent for email; a recorded legitimate-interest assessment on lawfully sourced data for post).
Include a compliant privacy notice in every communication: controller identity and contact details, purpose and legal basis, data source, retention period, and data-subject rights.
Provide a clear, free, easy opt-out/objection mechanism (unsubscribe link and postal opt-out) and maintain a suppression list.

Given the scam-like structure and elderly targeting, escalate to legal/compliance leadership and preserve records; a campaign of this nature risks regulatory enforcement and potential criminal fraud exposure.

campaign.title: GrandDraw 'You have won' mailer
campaign.text: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up.' The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.

detected_practices: false 'guaranteed winner' prize claim
advance-fee scam (processing/insurance fee to release prize)
unverifiable/undisclosed draw terms
artificial urgency / deadline (7 days or forfeit)
misleading prize value vs. actual voucher worth less than the fee
targeting vulnerable elderly consumers
triage.audience_notes: Audience skews elderly, a group with recognised vulnerability under the UCPD's average/vulnerable consumer standard; this heightens the aggressive-practice and misleading-practice concerns.
triage.summary: A prize-draw mailer sent by email and post claiming the recipient is a 'guaranteed winner' of a €2,500 prize but demanding an upfront €29.90 fee to release winnings that are actually only a voucher worth less than the fee, with unverifiable draw terms and a coercive 7-day forfeiture deadline. This matches classic misleading and aggressive commercial practices (a blacklisted 'false prize'/advance-fee scheme) aimed at general adult consumers skewing elderly. It involves collecting personal identity and payment data.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed fairly, lawfully and transparently. Here the recipient's identity data (and payment data) is solicited on a fabricated 'guaranteed winner' pretext where the 'draw' has no verifiable terms and the fee exceeds the actual voucher value. Collecting personal and payment data through a deceptive premise is processing that is neither fair nor lawful and breaches the core Art. 5(1)(a) principle, especially given the audience skews elderly (vulnerable data subjects).
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Do not collect any personal or payment data on a false or unverifiable prize premise. If a genuine promotion exists, present accurate, verifiable terms and collect only data that is necessary, on a lawful and non-deceptive basis; otherwise the data processing cannot be made compliant and the mailer must not be sent.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing personal data for direct marketing requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis; unsolicited email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (with ePrivacy). The campaign discloses no consent, no legitimate-interest assessment, and no source of the recipient list. Sending marketing email/mail to individuals (skewing elderly) without any identified lawful basis is processing without a valid legal ground.
findings.evidence_quote: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any send: prior opt-in consent for the email channel, and a demonstrable, list-provenance-backed basis for postal contacts. Retain records of consent/basis and the data source. Without a lawful basis, cease the processing.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data (identity confirmation and payment/insurance details) the controller must, at the point of collection, provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights. The mailer requests identity and payment data while providing none of this mandated Art. 13 information.
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, accessible privacy notice at the point any data is collected: controller identity and contact details, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention period, and data-subject rights (including the right to object and to complain to a supervisory authority).

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires that information to data subjects be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear, plain language. A mailer whose promotional terms are unverifiable and which omits any transparent privacy communication fails the intelligibility/transparency standard, and the deceptive framing actively undermines the data subject's ability to understand how their data will be used — a concern heightened for an elderly audience.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms
findings.recommendation: Communicate all data-related information (and the promotion's terms) transparently in clear plain language, without misleading framing, so recipients can understand who is processing their data, why, and how to exercise their rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct-marketing communication must inform recipients of, and facilitate, the absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing. The mailer contains only a coercive forfeiture deadline and no opt-out or objection mechanism, so the Art. 21(2)-(3) right is not brought to the recipient's attention or facilitated.
findings.evidence_quote: or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, easy-to-use opt-out/objection mechanism in every marketing communication (e.g. unsubscribe link for email, freepost/telephone opt-out for mail) and honour objections immediately by suppressing the individual from further marketing.

verdicts.notes: This is a direct-marketing communication (email + postal mailer) that processes personal data (recipient names/addresses) and actively solicits further personal data — identity confirmation and payment/card details — on a demonstrably false "guaranteed winner" premise. Under GDPR this engages the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) because the data is obtained through deception, the lawful-basis requirement (Art. 6(1)) since unsolicited email direct marketing generally requires prior consent and none is evident, and the transparency-at-collection duties (Arts. 12/13) since the mailer discloses no controller identity, purpose, legal basis, retention or data-subject rights while demanding identity and payment data. No opt-out/right-to-object mechanism (Art. 21) is provided. Findings below.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: This is the paradigm case of the Annex I point 31 blacklist item: creating the false impression the consumer has won a prize where claiming it is subject to paying money or incurring a cost. The 'guaranteed winner' framing combined with a mandatory €29.90 'processing and insurance fee' to release the prize is prohibited in all circumstances, with no need to prove consumer harm. The fact that the 'prize' is actually only a voucher worth less than the fee further confirms there is no genuine prize.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Do not run this campaign. Any prize promotion must not require any payment to claim the prize; remove the fee entirely and, if any prize draw is genuine, publish verifiable terms and ensure the advertised prize actually exists and is delivered without cost to the consumer.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The mailer contains false information about the existence and main characteristics of the 'product'/prize and its value. The 'draw' has no verifiable terms and the €29.90 fee exceeds the value of the voucher actually sent, so the €2,500 prize and 'winner' status are deceptive as to the existence of the benefit and the price/value relationship, causing consumers to take a transactional decision (paying the fee) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize
findings.recommendation: Cease making unsubstantiated prize and value claims. Only advertise benefits that genuinely exist, are accurately valued, and are backed by verifiable, publicly available promotion terms.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The mailer omits and obscures material information a consumer needs to make an informed decision: the true nature and low value of the 'prize' (a voucher), the absence of verifiable draw terms, the identity/conditions of the promotion, and the fact that the payment exceeds what is received. Hiding these material facts is a misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.
findings.recommendation: Disclose all material information clearly and prominently — the true prize, its actual value, complete and verifiable draw terms and eligibility, the promoter's identity, and any costs — before any consumer engages.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The coercive 7-day forfeiture deadline applies undue pressure to elicit an immediate payment decision, significantly impairing the consumer's freedom of choice through undue influence. This is aggravated because the audience skews elderly, a vulnerable group under Art. 5(3), whose behaviour is more readily distorted by such pressure combined with the false win claim.
findings.evidence_quote: pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Remove the artificial forfeiture deadline and all high-pressure payment demands. Genuine promotions should allow ample time and must never condition a 'prize' on urgent payment.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The deadline manufactures false urgency — falsely stating the offer/prize is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision and deprive the consumer of a proper opportunity to make an informed choice. Given the 'draw' has no verifiable terms, the deadline is artificial and blacklisted per se.
findings.evidence_quote: within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Eliminate any false or artificial time limits and forfeiture threats. Only communicate genuine, verifiable deadlines tied to real, lawful promotion terms.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Beyond the specific blacklist items, the practice breaches the general fairness prohibition and engages the Art. 5(3) vulnerable-consumer standard: the campaign is designed to distort the economic behaviour of an identifiable group vulnerable by reason of age and credulity. It is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts their transactional decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: general adult consumers, skews elderly
findings.recommendation: Withdraw the campaign entirely. Any consumer-facing promotion targeting or foreseeably reaching elderly consumers must be assessed against the more protective vulnerable-consumer standard and must be free of deception and pressure.

verdicts.notes: This mailer is a textbook blacklisted advance-fee prize scam. It creates the false impression that the recipient has won a €2,500 prize while making release conditional on paying a €29.90 fee — a per-se prohibited practice under UCPD Annex I point 31 requiring no case-by-case assessment. It is also compounded by misleading actions/omissions (fee exceeds actual voucher value; no verifiable draw terms), an aggressive coercive deadline, and heightened concern because the audience skews elderly (Art. 5(3) vulnerable-consumer standard). Multiple critical violations are present.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is an advance-fee prize mailer that tells recipients they are the "guaranteed winner" of a €2,500 prize but demands a €29.90 fee within 7 days to release it — while the actual "prize" is only a voucher worth less than the fee, and the draw has no verifiable terms. This is one of the practices that EU consumer law bans outright, in all circumstances, with no need to prove anyone was harmed: conditioning a "prize" on a payment is a blacklisted false prize scam under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. It is further aggravated by false urgency, a coercive forfeiture deadline, misleading value claims, and the fact that it targets an audience skewing elderly, who are treated as vulnerable consumers under the law. On top of the consumer-law breaches, collecting recipients' identity and payment details on this deceptive basis violates core GDPR principles (fair, lawful and transparent processing) and lacks any valid lawful basis, privacy notice, or opt-out. The AI Act and DSA do not apply. This campaign cannot be made compliant with cosmetic edits — it must not be sent.
report.recommendations: Do not send this campaign in any form — the "pay a fee to release your prize" mechanic is prohibited outright under EU consumer law and exposes the business to enforcement, penalties and potential fraud liability.
