advance fee required to claim prize (banned practice)
no verifiable draw terms
artificial urgency / countdown deadline (7 days)
forfeiture-to-runner-up pressure tactic
misrepresentation of prize value (fee exceeds voucher value)
targeting of vulnerable/elderly consumers
triage.summary: A prize-draw mailer claiming the recipient is a 'guaranteed winner' of €2,500 but demanding a €29.90 advance 'processing/insurance' fee to release a prize that is actually a low-value voucher, with no verifiable draw terms and a coercive 7-day forfeiture deadline. This is a textbook misleading/aggressive practice — likely an outright banned 'you have won a prize, pay to claim' practice under the UCPD blacklist — that appears designed to exploit elderly consumers. Personal data (postal/email addresses selected as 'winner') is processed, and no AI or targeting is declared.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Here recipients' addresses are processed to operate a scheme built on a false 'guaranteed winner' claim, a fictitious draw with 'no verifiable terms', and an advance fee for a low-value voucher. Using personal data as the vehicle for a deceptive and exploitative scheme (targeting elderly consumers) is inherently unfair processing and breaches the fairness principle, independent of the separate UCPD deception.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize
findings.recommendation: Do not process consumers' contact data to operate a deceptive prize scheme. Any legitimate promotion must rest on truthful, verifiable draw terms and must not use personal data to mislead or pressure recipients; abandon the 'guaranteed winner / pay-to-claim' construct entirely.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Art. 6(1) requires a valid lawful basis for processing, and unsolicited email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (with ePrivacy). The campaign declares no personalisation and gives no indication of consent or any pre-existing relationship; addresses appear to have been 'selected' from an unspecified source. There is no evident lawful basis for sending unsolicited marketing email to these recipients.
findings.evidence_quote: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected
findings.recommendation: Only send email direct marketing to recipients who have given valid prior consent (or fall within a narrow soft opt-in from a genuine prior transaction). Document the source and lawful basis for every address in the mailing list, and suppress addresses without a demonstrable basis.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at the point of collecting/using personal data the controller disclose its identity, the purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, and data-subject rights. The mailer identifies no controller, no privacy information, and no basis for how the recipient's address was obtained or will be used, leaving data subjects unable to understand or exercise their rights.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms
findings.recommendation: Include a clear privacy notice with the identity and contact details of the data controller, the purposes and lawful basis for processing, retention period, and how to exercise data-subject rights, in every email and postal communication.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) gives an absolute right to object to direct marketing, and every direct-marketing communication must facilitate that opt-out. This mailer is direct marketing but provides no mechanism to object or unsubscribe; the only 'action' offered is paying a fee, which does not satisfy the obligation to enable and inform recipients of their opt-out right.
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, free and easy opt-out mechanism to every marketing message (e.g. unsubscribe link in email, opt-out address in postal mail) and honour objections immediately by ceasing all direct marketing to that individual.

verdicts.notes: The mailer processes personal data (postal and email addresses "selected" as winners) for direct marketing without any indication of a lawful basis, transparency information, or opt-out. Because the underlying scheme is a deceptive "you have won, pay to claim" construct, the processing itself appears to breach the fairness and transparency principle. Unsolicited email marketing to addresses of unknown provenance also lacks the consent/legitimate-interest basis GDPR requires, and no controller identity or data-subject rights are disclosed. Findings are graded on the GDPR obligations engaged; the underlying deception is primarily a UCPD matter handled separately.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: This is the paradigm case blacklisted in all circumstances: creating the false impression the consumer has won a prize where claiming it is subject to paying money. The 'guaranteed winner' framing combined with a mandatory €29.90 fee to 'release' winnings — where the actual item is a low-value voucher costing less than the fee — falls squarely within Annex I point 31, which admits no defence and no need to prove consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Do not run this campaign. Any genuine prize promotion must impose no cost or payment whatsoever to claim the prize; remove the fee entirely and only send a genuine unconditional win notice, or withdraw the 'you have won' framing altogether.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The artificial 7-day deadline with 'forfeiture to the runner-up' manufactures a false time-limited condition designed to elicit an immediate decision and deprive the consumer of opportunity to make an informed choice. As the 'draw has no verifiable terms', the deadline and forfeiture claim are not genuine, engaging the Annex I point 7 blacklist prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Remove all countdown/forfeiture pressure language; any time limits in a legitimate promotion must be genuine, verifiable and stated in published terms.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The mailer misrepresents the existence and nature of the prize (a €2,500 'GrandDraw prize') and its value/price relationship: the consumer pays €29.90 for a voucher worth less than the fee. This false information about the main characteristics and value of the 'prize' causes a transactional decision (paying the fee) the consumer would not otherwise take — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent
findings.recommendation: Accurately describe what is actually provided (a low-value voucher) and its real value; do not describe it as a €2,500 prize or imply the consumer receives net value from paying.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Material information the consumer needs — the identity/terms of the draw, odds, how the 'winner' was 'selected', what the voucher actually is and its real value, and that the fee exceeds that value — is omitted or hidden, and the commercial (revenue-raising) intent is disguised as a prize notification. This constitutes a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, complete promotion terms (organiser identity, selection basis, actual prize description and value, all costs) up front; disclose the true commercial nature of the communication.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of coercive deadline, loss-framing ('forfeited to the runner-up'), and exploitation of an audience that 'skews elderly' amounts to undue influence that significantly impairs the average (vulnerable) consumer's freedom of choice, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take — an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9, assessed from the perspective of the vulnerable group per Art. 5(3).
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the pressure and loss-framing entirely; do not deploy prize-claim mechanics designed to exploit older or credulous recipients.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the practice is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (elderly/credulous recipients) under Art. 5, including Art. 5(3). Even if the specific blacklist points did not apply, the overall design of the mailer would be unfair.
findings.evidence_quote: general adult consumers, skews elderly
findings.recommendation: Reassess the entire concept against professional-diligence standards; a compliant prize promotion is unconditional, transparent, and not designed to exploit vulnerable recipients.

verdicts.notes: This mailer is a textbook per se prohibited practice under the UCPD. It creates the false impression the recipient has won a €2,500 prize while conditioning "release" on a €29.90 fee — the exact conduct banned in all circumstances by Annex I point 31. It compounds this with a false urgency/forfeiture deadline (Annex I point 7), misleading action on the true prize value (Art. 6), a misleading omission of verifiable draw terms (Art. 7), and an aggressive coercive tactic exploiting elderly consumers (Arts. 8-9 / Art. 5(3)). Multiple blacklisted, no-defence violations are present.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is a "you have won, now pay to claim" prize mailer that tells recipients they are the guaranteed winner of a €2,500 prize but demands a €29.90 fee to release it — while the item actually sent is a voucher worth less than the fee. This is one of the clearest examples of a practice that is banned outright under EU consumer law: no defence, no need to prove anyone was harmed. On top of that, the fake 7-day "forfeit to the runner-up" deadline, the concealed true value, and the deliberate targeting of an elderly audience add further serious breaches (misleading actions/omissions and aggressive practices). Separately, using people's postal and email addresses to run a deceptive scheme — with no lawful basis, no privacy information, and no opt-out — breaches data protection rules. In plain terms: this campaign cannot be fixed with edits; running it exposes you to regulatory enforcement, fines, and likely fraud liability. Do not send it.
report.recommendations: ["Do not run this campaign in any form. The core "guaranteed winner, pay a fee to claim" mechanic is banned outright under UCPD Annex I point 31 — there is no compliant version of pay-to-claim.", "If you want to run a genuine prize promotion, make it entirely free to claim (no processing, insurance, or any other fee) and only notify people who have actually won under published, verifiable draw terms.", "Remove all false urgency and loss-framing (the 7-day deadline and 'forfeited to the runner-up' language) — banned under Annex I point 7.", "Describe any prize or voucher accurately and at its real value; never present a low-value voucher as a €2,500 prize.", "Publish complete, honest promotion terms: organiser identity, how winners are selected, odds, the actual prize and its value, and any conditions.", "Stop deploying prize-claim tactics that exploit elderly or credulous recipients; assess concepts against a vulnerable-consumer standard.", "Fix the data-protection failures before any future mailing: only contact people with a valid lawful basis (prior consent for email marketing), document the source of every address, include a full privacy notice with the controller's identity, and provide a free, easy opt-out in every message.", "Given the likely fraud dimension, have legal/compliance review the underlying business model before any consumer contact resumes."]

campaign.title: HomeSecure winter blitz — purchased list
campaign.text: Email campaign for home alarm systems sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available). The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced. Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

detected_practices: purchased marketing list from data broker
email marketing without valid consent records
no unsubscribe/opt-out mechanism in emails
no reference to privacy policy
list upload to Meta/Google for lookalike audience creation
behavioural targeting via lookalike audiences
follow-up cold calls to non-openers using broker-appended phone numbers
fear/security-based advertising for home alarm systems
personalisation/targeting of consumers
triage.summary: A B2C email/social/phone campaign for home alarm systems sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker with no valid consent records, then uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences, with follow-up calls to non-openers. The campaign lacks unsubscribe mechanisms and any privacy policy reference, raising serious lawful-basis, consent, transparency, and ePrivacy/direct-marketing concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Direct e-mail marketing and profiling require a valid lawful basis. There are no consent records, the vague broker attestation ('opted-in somewhere in 2019') cannot demonstrate a lawful basis, and consent given to a broker for other purposes cannot lawfully be transferred to this controller. No legitimate-interest assessment is possible for unlawfully sourced data. Processing therefore has no valid Art. 6(1) basis.
findings.evidence_quote: sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Do not use the purchased list. Only market to individuals for whom you hold demonstrable, specific consent (or a properly documented lawful basis). Delete broker-sourced data lacking provenance and build a lawfully collected, consented list instead.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that the data subject consented. With no consent records at all, the accountability requirement is impossible to meet, and consent cannot be relied upon as a lawful basis for the email marketing to these addresses.
findings.evidence_quote: no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Retain auditable, granular consent records (who, when, what was consented to, wording shown). Absent such records, treat consent as non-existent and cease processing.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A generic broker 'opt-in somewhere in 2019' is neither specific to this controller/campaign nor informed, and cannot constitute valid consent under Art. 4(11).
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker
findings.recommendation: Obtain fresh, specific, informed opt-in consent naming your organisation and the marketing purpose before contacting any individual.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and it must be facilitated. Omitting an unsubscribe mechanism and relying on manual reply handling obstructs the right to object and fails to enable easy opt-out for both the emails and the profiling/lookalike processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a functioning, one-click unsubscribe link in every marketing email and a clear opt-out for phone contact, and honour objections immediately across all channels including the ad platforms.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading personal data to build lookalike audiences is automated processing to analyse/predict personal preferences and behaviour, i.e. profiling under Art. 4(4). This profiling of unlawfully sourced data has no valid basis and was not disclosed to data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Do not upload broker data to ad platforms. Only run custom/lookalike audiences using data subjects who have consented to such processing, and disclose the profiling at collection.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When processing personal data (including data obtained indirectly), the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients (e.g. Meta/Google), retention and data-subject rights, and information on profiling. None of this is provided at any point in the campaign, breaching the information duties (Arts. 13/14).
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete privacy notice covering all purposes (email, lookalike profiling, phone), recipients and rights, and link it in every communication; where data is obtained indirectly, notify data subjects within the required timeframe.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires transparency information to be concise, accessible and communicated to data subjects. No privacy information is made accessible in any channel, so the transparency communication obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Make an easily accessible, plain-language privacy notice available in every email, social ad and call script.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached: processing lacks a lawful basis, individuals are contacted (email and phone) using covertly appended broker data without their knowledge, and no transparency is provided — the essence of unfair and non-transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Cease processing broker-appended contact data; ensure all processing has a lawful basis, is disclosed to data subjects, and respects their reasonable expectations.

verdicts.notes: This campaign presents multiple serious GDPR breaches. It processes 400,000 addresses from a purchased broker list with no demonstrable lawful basis or valid consent (Arts. 6(1), 7, 4(11)), uploads that data to Meta/Google for lookalike profiling (Arts. 4(4), 6(1)), provides no unsubscribe/opt-out mechanism (Art. 21), and offers no transparency information or privacy policy at any stage (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13). Follow-up calls to non-openers compound the lack of lawful basis. The campaign is very unlikely to be defensible as described.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Meta and Google are online platforms (VLOPs) subject to DSA ad-transparency obligations. When they present these lookalike-targeted ads, each ad must let recipients identify in real time that it is an ad, on whose behalf it is shown, who paid, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. As the advertiser driving a custom/lookalike-audience campaign, HomeSecure must provide accurate advertiser-identity and targeting information so the platform can meet Art. 26(1); a campaign built on an opaque purchased list with no documented parameters undermines this transparency chain.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ad account discloses the true advertiser/payer identity to the platform, use the platforms' native paid-ad/label tools so ads are clearly identifiable as advertising, and be able to describe the main targeting parameters (custom/lookalike audience source) so the platform's Art. 26(1) disclosures are accurate. Do not run ads from a source that cannot be documented.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits platform ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including by inference. Home-security advertising and lookalike modelling from an undocumented data-broker list create a residual risk that the platform's profiling could correlate with sensitive attributes, though nothing in the campaign text shows special-category data is actually used as a targeting parameter. Flagged for awareness rather than as a likely breach.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the custom/lookalike audiences are not built on or optimised toward any GDPR Art. 9 attribute (health, ethnicity, religion, etc.), and document the audience-building parameters to demonstrate no sensitive-data profiling is involved.

verdicts.notes: The DSA principally binds providers of online platforms rather than advertisers, so most of this campaign's core defects (consent, unsubscribe, privacy policy, cold calls) fall under GDPR/UCPD/ePrivacy, not the DSA. However, the campaign uploads a purchased list to Meta and Google — very large online platforms — to build lookalike audiences, which engages DSA advertising-transparency rules that the advertiser must support. There is a residual, speculative risk under the Art. 26(3) ban on profiling with special-category data if the security/lookalike targeting infers sensitive attributes, but nothing in the campaign text shows Art. 9 categories are used. No minors are involved and no platform interface/dark-pattern design is described.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Recipients on a purchased broker list never solicited or opted into contact with this trader. Emailing them and then following up with phone calls to those who did not open — combined with emails that have 'no unsubscribe link' so recipients cannot signal refusal — amounts to a persistent, cross-channel solicitation that is unwanted (no valid consent, no opt-out possible). Annex I point 26 prohibits 'persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, fax, e-mail or other remote media' in all circumstances, and the marketing relevance expressly covers scripted re-contact of users and ignoring refusal. This is a per-se blacklisted practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Stop the follow-up call wave to non-openers and cease contacting individuals for whom no verifiable, specific consent to be contacted by this trader exists. Only re-contact recipients who have not objected and where a lawful direct-marketing basis and a working, one-click opt-out exist; cap contact frequency and honour any refusal immediately across all channels.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of unsolicited emails to a 400,000-address purchased list, the absence of any functioning opt-out mechanism, and a subsequent phone-call wave to non-openers creates persistence and onerous barriers to declining contact. Under Arts. 8-9 a practice is aggressive where, through undue influence or by making it burdensome to exercise the right to be left alone, it impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. The timing/persistence factor and the burdensome opt-out (manual replies only) are among the listed factors for aggressiveness.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, functioning, no-cost opt-out in every communication (unsubscribe link in email, do-not-call honouring on calls), suppress non-responders after the first contact rather than escalating to calls, and document that no high-pressure or misfortune-exploiting messaging (e.g. fear-based 'you are unsafe' framing) is used in the alarm-system copy.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's data-protection and consent failures fall mainly under GDPR/ePrivacy, but two UCPD hooks are engaged. The multi-channel push to a purchased list with no opt-out mechanism, followed by scripted phone re-contact of non-openers, engages the blacklist prohibition on persistent and unwanted solicitations (Annex I point 26) and the aggressive-practices provisions (Arts. 8-9). No misleading-content or blacklisted claims are evidenced beyond these; findings are scoped to solicitation conduct.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems to 400,000 email addresses bought from a data broker, uploads that same list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences, and follows up with phone calls to people who didn't open the emails. As designed, it is very likely unlawful and should not go out. The core problem is that you have no valid consent or lawful basis for any of these contacts — the broker's vague "opted-in somewhere in 2019" claim with no records cannot support marketing under GDPR. On top of that, the emails have no unsubscribe link and no privacy notice, and the phone follow-ups to non-openers count as persistent, unwanted solicitation that is banned outright under EU consumer law. Uploading the list to Meta/Google adds profiling and ad-transparency risks. The AI Act does not apply. In short: multiple critical GDPR breaches plus a per-se prohibited practice mean this campaign carries serious regulatory and fine exposure and needs to be stopped and rebuilt on a properly consented list.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as designed. Stop the purchased-list email send, the Meta/Google lookalike upload, and the phone follow-up wave to non-openers.</br>
Cancel the phone calls to non-openers immediately — this is a per-se prohibited 'persistent and unwanted solicitation' under UCPD Annex I point 26, banned in all circumstances.
Delete the broker-sourced data. With no consent records, you cannot demonstrate a lawful basis (GDPR Arts. 6, 7, 4(11)); consent given to a broker for other purposes cannot be transferred to you.

Rebuild your marketing on a lawfully collected, consented list: obtain fresh, specific, informed opt-in that names HomeSecure and the marketing purpose, and keep auditable records (who, when, wording shown).
Add a functioning one-click unsubscribe link to every email and honour opt-outs immediately across all channels; provide a clear do-not-call mechanism for phone contact.

Reference and link an accessible, plain-language privacy notice in every communication, covering all purposes (email, lookalike profiling, phone), recipients (Meta/Google), retention, rights and profiling (GDPR Arts. 12, 13/14).

Only run custom/lookalike audiences using data subjects who have consented to that processing; document the audience-building parameters and confirm no special-category (Art. 9) attributes are used, so platform DSA ad-transparency disclosures stay accurate.
Review call and email copy to ensure no fear-based or high-pressure 'you are unsafe' messaging that could constitute an aggressive practice under UCPD Arts. 8-9.

The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced. Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

detected_practices: purchased/broker-sourced marketing list
email marketing without consent records
no unsubscribe/opt-out link in emails
no privacy policy reference or transparency notice
uploading list to Meta/Google for lookalike audiences
behavioural targeting/lookalike audience building

triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is homeowners aged 30-65 across the EU; no minors expected, though a purchased broker list gives no reliable age verification. Consent provenance is unverifiable ('opted-in somewhere in 2019', no records).
triage.summary: A multi-channel (email, social, phone) home-alarm marketing campaign sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker with no valid consent records, then uploaded to Meta/Google to build lookalike audiences, with follow-up cold calls using broker-appended phone numbers. Emails lack any unsubscribe mechanism and reference no privacy policy. The campaign raises serious lawful-basis, consent, transparency and direct-marketing issues affecting EU consumers.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing 400,000 addresses (plus broker-appended phone numbers) for direct marketing requires a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis. Broker-purchased lists with no consent records provide no demonstrable consent, and legitimate interest cannot cure unsolicited electronic direct marketing where prior consent is the required basis (Art. 6(1) note references ePrivacy). No lawful basis is present for the email sends, the lookalike uploads, or the follow-up calls.
findings.evidence_quote: purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Do not send. Marketing personal data may only be used where a documented, valid lawful basis exists. Delete or quarantine the unverifiable broker list and rebuild from first-party opt-ins with retained consent records, or obtain contractual proof of GDPR-valid consent naming your organisation as recipient before any processing.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(1) requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that the data subject consented. 'Opted-in somewhere in 2019' with no records makes consent impossible to demonstrate. Art. 7(3) also requires withdrawal to be as easy as giving consent, which fails given the absent unsubscribe mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Maintain auditable consent records (who, when, what wording, what scope) for every recipient. Without such records, treat the list as having no consent and do not process it. Ensure a one-click withdrawal path is available in every message.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Valid consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A vague broker claim of an opt-in 'somewhere in 2019' does not evidence consent that was specific to this controller and this home-alarm marketing purpose, nor informed. Third-party list purchases almost never carry consent specific enough to be reused by the buyer.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker
findings.recommendation: Only rely on consent that is specific to your organisation and the actual purpose. Generic historical broker opt-ins do not qualify; re-permission the audience with a clear, purpose-specific opt-in or exclude them.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) grants an absolute right to object to direct marketing, and every marketing communication must facilitate an easy opt-out. Emails with no unsubscribe link, plus follow-up cold calls, fail to provide or respect this right. Manual reply handling is not an adequate, reliable opt-out mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a functioning, one-click unsubscribe in every email and an easy opt-out on calls, honour objections immediately across all channels (email, phone, and the Meta/Google audiences), and suppress objecting individuals from all lists.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Because the data was not obtained from the data subject directly (broker sourcing) and is used for new purposes, the controller must proactively provide Art. 13/14-type information: identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients (Meta/Google), retention, data-subject rights and any profiling. No privacy notice is provided at any point, so recipients receive none of this.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete privacy notice and reference it prominently in every email and call script, disclosing the controller identity, source of the data, purposes, legal basis, the Meta/Google recipients, retention period, and how to exercise objection and other rights.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires transparency information to be concise, accessible and communicated in clear language. With no privacy policy reference or accessible notice anywhere in the campaign, the transparency information is neither provided nor accessible to data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Make the privacy information easily accessible (linked in every message, plain language) so recipients can readily understand how their data is used and exercise their rights.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached: the data lacks a lawful basis, individuals are not informed, and their data is covertly repurposed to build lookalike audiences on Meta/Google — a use they were never told about and could not expect. This combination of unlawful, unfair and non-transparent processing directly offends Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Cease uploading and any lookalike-audience building from this data. Only process data lawfully, with a valid basis and full transparency about all recipients and purposes, before any onward sharing to advertising platforms.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading the list to build lookalike audiences constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4) — automated processing to evaluate and predict personal preferences/behaviour to expand targeting. This profiling inherits the lawful-basis (Art. 6), transparency (Art. 13) and objection (Art. 21) obligations, none of which are satisfied here.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Treat lookalike/audience-matching as profiling: establish a lawful basis, disclose it in the privacy notice, and honour objections. Absent valid consent for the underlying list, do not use it for profiling at all.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages GDPR at nearly every level and is very likely unlawful as described. Personal data (email addresses, appended phone numbers) is processed for direct marketing with no valid lawful basis: consent provenance is unverifiable and unrecorded, so neither the controller's demonstrability obligation nor the consent standard is met. Transparency obligations are ignored (no privacy notice, no information at any collection point), the right to object is not facilitated (no unsubscribe), and the list is repurposed for lookalike-audience profiling on Meta/Google without any basis. Multiple high/critical GDPR issues; the safest fix is to stop the campaign and remediate provenance and transparency before any send.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Building lookalike audiences on Meta and Google means presenting advertisements on online platforms, which triggers DSA Art. 26(1). Recipients must be able to identify in real time that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf and who paid for it, and receive meaningful information about the main targeting parameters used and how to change them. Where an advertiser supplies audience lists and lookalike parameters, it must ensure the platform is given accurate advertiser-identity and parameter information so these disclosures can be made; a list of unverifiable broker provenance run as a lookalike source undermines the platform's ability to disclose meaningful, lawful targeting parameters.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: When running the Meta/Google campaigns, complete the platforms' advertiser verification and 'paid for by' / advertiser-identity disclosures, ensure ads are clearly labelled as advertisements, and use only audience sources whose parameters can be lawfully and transparently disclosed. Do not seed lookalike audiences from a list with no consent records, as its targeting parameters cannot be lawfully substantiated for the Art. 26 disclosure.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is engaged only through the paid advertising leg of the campaign — uploading the purchased list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences constitutes platform advertising subject to Art. 26 transparency. The DSA's core Art. 26 obligations bind the platform providers rather than the advertiser directly, but the marketer must supply accurate advertiser-identity and targeting information to satisfy them, so this is flagged as an attention point. The email and cold-call legs, missing unsubscribe link, and unverifiable broker consent are chiefly GDPR/ePrivacy/UCPD matters and fall outside the DSA. Art. 26(3) (sensitive-data ad ban), Art. 28 (minors) and Art. 25 (dark patterns) are not supported by the campaign facts as described.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Cold-calling recipients who did not open the marketing email — using phone numbers they never provided to the trader (appended by a broker) and for which no consent records exist — is an unsolicited re-contact by remote media. Because the emails carry no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and no consent provenance is verifiable, recipients have no genuine way to signal refusal, so the multi-channel re-contact is 'unwanted' and, across email plus phone escalation, 'persistent'. This is the blacklisted practice of persistent and unwanted solicitations, prohibited in all circumstances, and there is no contractual-enforcement justification here.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Stop the phone follow-ups to non-openers on broker-appended numbers. Only contact individuals who have given verifiable, specific consent to marketing on that channel; include a clear, working one-click unsubscribe/opt-out in every email and an easy opt-out on calls; and maintain a suppression list so anyone who does not engage or who objects is not re-contacted.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The design escalates from unsolicited email to follow-up phone calls while providing no straightforward exit route (no unsubscribe link, opt-out only via manual replies). Persistent, multi-channel contact that removes an easy means to make the solicitations stop — pushed with fear-based home-security framing ('winter blitz') — can amount to undue influence/harassment that impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice, engaging the prohibition on aggressive commercial practices. This finding is closely related to the Annex I point 26 breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Provide a low-effort, immediately effective opt-out on every channel (email unsubscribe link and a do-not-call honouring process), cap contact frequency, and avoid pressure/fear framing so that recipients are not coerced into engaging by relentless or hard-to-escape solicitation.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Emails omit any reference to who is processing data and how, and give no clear opt-out information. While the commercial (alarm-sales) intent of the emails is apparent, the omission of material information consumers need to understand and control the contact is capable of engaging the misleading-omissions rule; the primary home for these transparency/consent defects, however, is the GDPR, so the UCPD weight is limited.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Include clear sender identity, purpose, and a link to the privacy policy/opt-out in every communication so that material information is not omitted or provided in an unclear or untimely manner.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's contact tactics engage the UCPD directly. Placing follow-up phone calls to non-openers on broker-appended numbers, combined with emails that offer no opt-out mechanism, fits the blacklisted practice of persistent and unwanted solicitations (Annex I point 26), which is prohibited in all circumstances. The same escalating, no-exit contact strategy, layered onto fear-based security framing, also risks being an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9. The underlying consent/lawful-basis and privacy-notice defects are chiefly GDPR matters and are left to that assessment.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems by email, social ads, and phone to 400,000 people on a list bought from a data broker with no consent records. As described, it is very likely unlawful and should not go out in its current form. The core problem is that you have no valid legal basis to contact these people: "opted-in somewhere in 2019" with no records does not count as consent under GDPR, so the email sends, the phone follow-ups, and the Meta/Google lookalike uploads all rest on nothing. On top of that, the emails have no unsubscribe link and no privacy notice, and cold-calling non-openers on broker-appended numbers is a blacklisted "persistent and unwanted solicitation" under consumer protection law — banned outright. Uploading the list to build lookalike audiences also creates advertising-transparency exposure on the platforms. There is no quick fix here; the list itself is the liability. Stop the campaign and rebuild from properly consented, first-party data before any send.
recommendations: Do not launch. Stop all planned email sends, phone follow-ups, and platform uploads using this list — the lack of verifiable consent makes every channel unlawful.</br>

Quarantine or delete the broker list. You cannot demonstrate valid, specific consent for any of the 400,000 contacts, and no legitimate-interest argument can rescue unsolicited electronic marketing. Rebuild the audience from first-party opt-ins with retained, auditable consent records (who, when, wording, scope).
Remove the list from Meta and Google and stop building lookalike audiences from it. This is profiling without a lawful basis and without transparency, and it cannot be used for ad targeting.
Stop the follow-up calls to non-openers entirely. Cold-calling on broker-appended numbers with no opt-out is a prohibited practice in all circumstances — this is a hard line, not a tuning issue.

Add a working one-click unsubscribe to every email and an easy opt-out on every call; honour objections immediately and suppress across all channels (email, phone, and the ad platforms). Manual reply handling is not adequate.

Add and prominently reference a complete privacy notice in every message and call script: controller identity, data source, purposes, legal basis, the Meta/Google recipients, retention period, and how to object and exercise rights.
Drop or soften fear-based 'winter blitz' framing and the escalating multi-channel pressure to avoid aggressive-practice exposure; cap contact frequency.

Before any future launch, complete platform advertiser verification and 'paid for by' disclosures, and only seed audiences from sources whose targeting parameters can be lawfully and transparently substantiated.

campaign.title: HomeSecure winter blitz — purchased list
campaign.text: Email campaign for home alarm systems sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available). The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced. Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

detected_practices: Purchased marketing list with no verifiable consent records
Email marketing to 400,000 addresses without valid consent
No unsubscribe/opt-out mechanism in emails
No privacy policy reference or transparency disclosure
Upload of list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
Data enrichment/appending of phone numbers by broker
Unsolicited follow-up phone calls to non-openers
Behavioural targeting/personalisation
Fear/security-based marketing angle (home alarm systems)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is homeowners aged 30-65 in the EU; no minors targeted, though age is unverified against a purchased list of uncertain provenance.
triage.summary: Multi-channel (email, social, phone) direct marketing campaign for home alarm systems targeting EU homeowners aged 30-65, using a 400,000-address list purchased from a data broker with no verifiable consent records. The list is uploaded to Meta and Google for lookalike audiences, emails lack any unsubscribe link or privacy policy reference, and broker-appended phone numbers are used for follow-up calls to non-openers. Serious GDPR/ePrivacy consent, transparency and opt-out concerns dominate, with DSA (platform ad targeting) and UCPD (unsolicited/aggressive persistent marketing) also engaged.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: All processing of the 400,000 addresses/phone numbers for email, calls and platform uploads requires a valid lawful basis. Email/phone direct marketing to individuals generally requires prior consent, and no consent records exist. A vague broker claim of 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' with no records does not establish consent, and legitimate interest cannot rescue e-marketing that lacks the consent required under ePrivacy. There is therefore no valid Art. 6(1) basis for any of the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Cease using the purchased list until a valid lawful basis is established. Do not send marketing without demonstrable, specific prior consent obtained by the controller; discard records for which consent cannot be evidenced.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Under Art. 7 the controller must be able to demonstrate that consent was given. Buying a list where the broker cannot supply consent records makes it impossible to meet this burden of proof, and the controller cannot rely on a third party's unsubstantiated assertion. The absence of any withdrawal mechanism (see Art. 21) also breaches the requirement that withdrawal be as easy as giving consent.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Obtain and retain granular consent records (who, when, wording, scope) for every recipient. Where records cannot be produced, treat consent as absent and suppress those contacts.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Consent supposedly given to an unspecified party 'somewhere in 2019' cannot be specific or informed as to this controller and this alarm-marketing purpose, so it does not qualify as valid consent capable of being relied on for this campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019'
findings.recommendation: Collect fresh consent directly, naming the controller and the specific marketing purposes and channels, before contacting any individual.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute and every marketing communication must facilitate a clear, easy opt-out. Emails with no unsubscribe mechanism, relying only on manual reply handling, fail to provide the accessible means to object required by Art. 21, and the same failure extends to the follow-up phone calls.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a functioning one-click unsubscribe link in every email and a clear opt-out on calls; honour objections immediately and suppress objectors across all channels and the platform audiences.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where data was not obtained from the data subject (bought list) the controller must still provide Art. 13/14 information — identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients (including Meta/Google), retention and rights. No privacy notice is referenced anywhere in the campaign, so data subjects receive none of the mandated information.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a full privacy notice at first contact (link in emails, disclosure on calls) covering controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, source of the data, and how to object/withdraw.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Marketing to people from a covertly acquired list, without informing them or offering opt-out, and re-using their data for lookalike modelling, is neither lawful, fair nor transparent and breaches the overarching principle in Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Rebuild the campaign around a transparent, consent-based data flow with clear notices and easy objection so that all processing is demonstrably lawful, fair and transparent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading the list to Meta and Google to generate lookalike audiences is automated processing to evaluate and predict personal preferences/behaviour, i.e. profiling under Art. 4(4). This profiling shares personal data with new recipients and requires its own lawful basis and transparency, which are absent here.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Do not upload the list for lookalike modelling absent a valid basis and disclosure; if pursued, document a lawful basis, name Meta/Google as recipients in the privacy notice, and provide an opt-out.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Broker-appended phone numbers used for follow-up calls are further direct-marketing processing of data the individuals never provided or consented to, with no means to object. This compounds the Art. 21 opt-out failure across an additional channel.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker
findings.recommendation: Stop calling numbers appended without consent; screen against national do-not-call registers, obtain consent where required, and offer an immediate opt-out on every call.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages GDPR at almost every step and multiple serious violations are likely. Direct marketing (email, phone, platform audiences) is conducted on a purchased 400,000-address list with no verifiable consent records, so there is no valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) and consent cannot be demonstrated (Arts. 4(11)/7). Data subjects were never informed (Arts. 5(1)(a), 13), there is no opt-out mechanism (Art. 21), and uploading the list for lookalike audiences constitutes further profiling without basis. Recommend halting the campaign on this list until a valid basis, transparency and opt-out are in place.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: By running lookalike-audience advertising on online platforms, the advertiser presents profiling-based ads whose targeting must satisfy DSA Art. 26(1): each ad must be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, disclose on whose behalf it is presented and who paid, and give recipients meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that they are targeted (and how to change them). A campaign built on an opaque purchased list and custom/lookalike audiences will struggle to provide the meaningful, accurate parameter disclosure Art. 26(1) requires.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the advertiser identity and payer are correctly configured in Meta/Google ad settings so the platforms' 'Why am I seeing this ad?' / paid-for-by disclosures are accurate, and that ads are clearly labelled. Only use audiences whose targeting parameters can be honestly and meaningfully described; a list with no consent records cannot underpin lawful custom/lookalike targeting.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Meta and Google are designated VLOPs, so any ads served through them are entered into a public ad repository under DSA Art. 39, including advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. This campaign's targeting — derived from a data-broker list with 'no consent records available' — will be publicly archived and open to scrutiny by regulators, journalists and researchers, materially amplifying regulatory and reputational exposure of the underlying unlawful-list issue.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Before launching any VLOP ad, confirm that the audience source, targeting parameters and advertiser/payer details are lawful and defensible, on the assumption they will be permanently and publicly disclosed in the platforms' ad repositories. Do not use the purchased list as a custom-audience/lookalike seed.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting platform ads based on profiling that uses GDPR Art. 9 special-category data. The declared targeting (homeowners aged 30-65) does not use sensitive attributes on its face, but a fear/security angle combined with an opaque broker list creates a residual risk that lookalike modelling could infer or proxy sensitive attributes. No evidence of actual sensitive-data targeting is present, so this is flagged only for awareness.
findings.evidence_quote: Email campaign for home alarm systems
findings.recommendation: When configuring lookalike/custom audiences, verify that no targeting parameters directly or indirectly rely on health, ethnicity, religion or other Art. 9 categories, and document that the seed audience and modelling exclude sensitive-attribute inference.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is engaged because the purchased 400,000-address list is uploaded to Meta and Google — both designated Very Large Online Platforms — to build lookalike (profiling-based) advertising audiences. This triggers platform advertising transparency obligations (Art. 26(1)) and public ad-repository archiving of the campaign's targeting parameters and reach (Art. 39). The core consent/opt-out/transparency failures sit under GDPR/ePrivacy and UCPD, but the platform-ad dimension carries genuine DSA exposure: targeting built on an unlawfully sourced list will be publicly scrutinisable, and there is a residual risk of inferred sensitive-attribute targeting. Minors and dark-pattern/recommender provisions are not engaged by the facts described.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Recipients are contacted by email and then re-contacted by telephone despite never having engaged with or requested the marketing, and with no opt-out mechanism to signal refusal. Annex I point 26 prohibits, in all circumstances, making persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone or e-mail where not justified to enforce a contractual obligation. Emailing 400,000 addresses with no consent records and then telephoning the non-openers is a scripted, cross-media re-contact of people who have not asked to be contacted and cannot easily stop it — the hallmark of a persistent and unwanted solicitation.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') ... Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Cease the phone follow-up to non-openers entirely. Only contact individuals who have provided verifiable, specific consent to that channel, include a working one-click unsubscribe/opt-out in every email, and suppress from all channels anyone who does not engage or who objects. Do not use non-engagement as a trigger for escalating to another channel.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: By removing any easy means to opt out ('replies handled manually', no unsubscribe link, no privacy policy) while escalating contact from email to unsolicited phone calls, the campaign creates onerous barriers to the consumer exercising the right to refuse further contact and applies persistent pressure across channels. Arts. 8-9 treat persistence, timing and onerous barriers to exercising rights as factors making a practice aggressive where they impair the average consumer's freedom of choice.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Provide a frictionless, clearly signposted opt-out in every communication and honour it immediately across all channels. Remove the multi-channel escalation logic and ensure no consumer must take burdensome manual steps (e.g. composing a reply email) to stop being contacted.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core failings (no lawful consent, no opt-out, no transparency) are primarily GDPR/ePrivacy matters. Under the UCPD, the salient issue is the persistent, multi-channel, unwanted contact structure: emails with no unsubscribe mechanism followed by phone calls to people who never engaged, with no viable way to refuse. This engages Annex I point 26 (blacklisted persistent/unwanted solicitations) and Arts. 8-9 (aggressive practices via onerous barriers to exercising the right to be left alone). The fear/security marketing angle alone is not, without more, an aggressive practice under the UCPD.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems by email, phone and social ads to 400,000 people whose contact details were bought from a data broker with no consent records ("opted-in somewhere in 2019"). As designed, it breaches EU law at almost every step. Under GDPR/ePrivacy there is no valid lawful basis or demonstrable consent to email, call or upload these people's data; the emails have no unsubscribe link and no privacy notice, so recipients are never informed and cannot object. Uploading the list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences is further profiling without a basis, and because both are Very Large Online Platforms the targeting will be permanently and publicly archived in ad repositories where regulators and journalists can scrutinise it. The escalation from unanswered emails to unsolicited phone calls to non-openers is a persistent, unwanted, cross-channel solicitation that is blacklisted outright under consumer law. In short, this is not a fixable-around-the-edges campaign — the underlying data source is unusable and the campaign should not launch on this list.
recommendations: Do not launch on this list. Stop all use of the purchased 400,000-record list for email, phone and platform uploads immediately — there is no valid lawful basis or consent, and no fix is possible while the data source is unlawful.
Delete or fully suppress any records for which the broker cannot supply granular consent evidence (who consented, when, exact wording, scope, channels). Treat unverifiable consent as no consent.

Cancel the phone follow-up to non-openers entirely — using non-engagement to escalate to another channel is a blacklisted, always-unlawful practice under consumer law. Screen any future calling against national do-not-call registers.
Remove the list from Meta and Google; do not use it as a seed for custom or lookalike audiences. Delete any audiences already built from it.
Rebuild future campaigns on a first-party, consent-based list: collect fresh, specific, informed consent that names your organisation as controller and the exact marketing purposes and channels.
Add a working one-click unsubscribe link to every email and a clear opt-out on any call, honoured immediately and across all channels — not manual reply handling.
Publish and reference a full privacy notice at first contact (controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients including any ad platforms, data source, retention, and how to object/withdraw).

If any platform advertising is pursued later, ensure advertiser/payer identity and targeting parameters are correctly configured and honestly describable, on the assumption they will be publicly disclosed in VLOP ad repositories.

campaign.title: FitBoost win-back blitz
campaign.text: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS ('Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'). Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice 'to understand churn'. The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly.

detected_practices: repeated win-back email sequence after unsubscribe (days 1,3,5,7,10)
post-unsubscribe SMS marketing
guilt-tripping / shaming copy ('give up on yourself')
unsolicited outbound phone calls to unsubscribed users
delayed unsubscribe processing ('up to 30 days') while sends continue
objection/opt-out requests routed to a monthly-reviewed mailbox (delayed handling)
behavioural personalisation/targeting of former subscribers
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults (former subscribers); no indication minors are targeted. Note that continued contact after unsubscribe raises ePrivacy/GDPR consent and right-to-object concerns, and the aggressive tactics raise UCPD aggressive/persistent-solicitation and unfair-practice concerns.
triage.summary: A win-back campaign targeting lapsed gym-app subscribers via email, SMS and phone that continues marketing after users unsubscribe, delays opt-out/objection processing (up to 30 days; monthly-reviewed mailbox), and uses emotionally manipulative, shaming copy. It involves personalisation of former subscribers' personal data and direct electronic marketing to adults in the EU, with no declared generative AI use.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Unsubscribing from marketing constitutes an objection to processing for direct-marketing purposes. Under Art. 21(2)-(3) this right is absolute and, once exercised, the personal data must no longer be processed for direct marketing. Continuing to send emails on days 1/3/5/7/10, two SMS, and outbound phone calls after the user has unsubscribed directly disregards a valid objection and processes personal data for the very purpose objected to.
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS
findings.recommendation: Suppress all marketing channels (email, SMS, phone) immediately and in real time upon unsubscribe. Remove the person from any active win-back sequence at the moment of opt-out rather than continuing scheduled sends; do not use unsubscribe as a trigger for further solicitation.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21 requires that once a data subject objects, processing for direct marketing must stop 'at any time' — effectively without undue delay. Routing objections to a mailbox reviewed only monthly means marketing continues for up to a month after a valid objection, failing to give the objection immediate effect.
findings.evidence_quote: objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly
findings.recommendation: Implement an automated, promptly processed objection/opt-out channel that suppresses marketing without undue delay (in practice, immediately). Do not rely on a manually, monthly-reviewed mailbox as the objection route.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(3) requires that it be as easy to withdraw consent as to give it, and withdrawal must take effect. A 30-day processing window during which marketing continues makes withdrawal ineffective and burdensome, undermining the validity of any consent relied on for the direct marketing and any related processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue
findings.recommendation: Make withdrawal/unsubscribe take effect immediately and stop all sends at once. Remove the '30 days' delay for suppression; if any residual technical delay is unavoidable, it should be minimal (hours) and no further marketing may be sent during it.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Once a user has unsubscribed, there is no valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) to continue direct-marketing contact. Outbound calls to unsubscribed users, even framed as churn research, use personal data for a purpose the user has opted out of and cannot be justified by legitimate interests given the user's clear objection, nor by contract or consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice 'to understand churn'
findings.recommendation: Cease calling users who have unsubscribed. If genuine, non-marketing churn research is desired, obtain fresh, specific consent and keep it strictly separate from marketing; respect any objection and do not contact users who have opted out.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) requires processing to be fair. Continuing to process contact data to send guilt-inducing, shaming messages to people who have already opted out, combined with a delayed/obscured suppression process, is unfair processing of their personal data.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'
findings.recommendation: Stop processing personal data to deliver manipulative/shaming content, especially to users who have opted out. Ensure post-unsubscribe communications, if any transactional ones are strictly necessary, are neutral and clearly not marketing.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural personalisation/targeting of former subscribers is profiling within Art. 4(4). Profiling related to direct marketing is expressly covered by the Art. 21 objection right, so any profiling must also cease on objection and requires a valid lawful basis and transparency.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling logic used for win-back targeting, ensure a valid lawful basis, provide transparency to data subjects, and ensure the profiling stops for anyone who has objected/unsubscribed.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: A gym/fitness app may hold data revealing health, fitness or physical activity that can constitute special-category (health) data under Art. 9. If win-back targeting or personalisation relies on such data, explicit consent or another Art. 9 exception is required. The campaign text does not confirm this, so it is flagged for verification rather than as a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers
findings.recommendation: Verify whether the win-back segmentation uses any health/fitness data (e.g., activity levels, workout history, body metrics). If so, ensure an Art. 9 legal basis (typically explicit consent) is in place and that such data is not used for marketing after objection.

verdicts.notes: The campaign continues direct marketing (email, SMS, phone) after users have unsubscribed and delays honouring opt-out/objection requests ("up to 30 days" while sends continue; a monthly-reviewed objection mailbox). This most seriously engages the absolute right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21) and the conditions for consent/withdrawal (Art. 7), with knock-on issues for lawful basis (Art. 6), fairness/transparency (Art. 5(1)(a)) and profiling (Art. 4(4)). Personal data of identifiable former subscribers is clearly involved. A likely violation of GDPR is present chiefly on the failure to give effect to objections/withdrawal promptly.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits in all circumstances persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, e-mail or other remote media, except to enforce a contractual obligation. Here the trader continues contacting users across three channels precisely because they have unsubscribed (i.e. clearly signalled they do not want contact). A scheduled multi-touch win-back sequence plus scripted re-contact by phone is the paradigm blacklisted conduct — unfair per se, with no need to prove consumer harm. Understanding churn is not enforcement of any contractual obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS ... call unsubscribed users twice
findings.recommendation: Suppress all marketing/win-back contact once a user unsubscribes. Remove the day 1/3/5/7/10 email cadence, the post-unsubscribe SMS, and the outbound 'understand churn' calls to unsubscribed users. If churn feedback is genuinely wanted, offer it as a single optional prompt on the unsubscribe page itself, not repeated outbound solicitations.
