exploitation of relaxation/sleep context to lower listener resistance
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'general adult' streaming listeners, but sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors may be reached in practice. The core concern is the deliberately subliminal, sub-conscious manipulation technique — a likely prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5 (subliminal/manipulative techniques) and an aggressive/misleading practice under the UCPD. Per-listener tuning implies profiling engaging GDPR, and delivery via an online platform engages the DSA. Recommend all four specialist reviews with priority on AI Act prohibition analysis.
triage.summary: An audio-streaming ad platform pilots an AI system that embeds sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath standard spots, tuned per listener below conscious perception, explicitly to induce urgency listeners cannot recognise. It is personalised, runs on sleep/relaxation playlists, and by design operates on consumers without their awareness.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: This is a direct match to the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition: an AI system deploys subliminal techniques operating beyond a person's consciousness (sub-audible cues explicitly 'below conscious perception') AND purposefully manipulative techniques, with the objective/effect of materially distorting behaviour by impairing informed decision-making and causing purchases consumers would not otherwise make. The internal deck ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') is a self-incriminating admission of both the covert mechanism and the intent to distort behaviour. Manufactured urgency driving unplanned spending on unaware consumers, especially at scale, satisfies the 'significant harm' / reasonably-likely-to-cause-harm threshold.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy. The subliminal/covert layer must be removed entirely — this cannot be remedied by disclosure, consent, or opt-out because the prohibition attaches to the technique itself. Advertising may only use overt, perceptible messaging where the listener retains the ability to recognise and evaluate the persuasive content.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI that exploits vulnerabilities due to a specific situation to materially distort behaviour causing significant harm. Deliberately delivering covert urgency cues to listeners in a sleep/relaxation state — a context of intentionally lowered vigilance and reduced capacity to critically process stimuli — targets a situational vulnerability. The triage also notes these playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors (an age-based vulnerable group) may be reached. Choosing this context specifically to bypass listener resistance strengthens the exploitation element.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting sleep/relaxation contexts and any delivery designed to exploit reduced listener vigilance; implement robust age-gating to prevent reaching minors. Even absent the subliminal layer, do not tune persuasive intensity to states of impaired alertness.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The whispered urgency phrases and heartbeat cues are AI-generated synthetic audio outputs. Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio to mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format. The submission gives no indication such provenance marking is applied. (Note: this obligation cannot cure the Art. 5 prohibition — even properly marked, the practice remains prohibited.)
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes ... an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases
findings.recommendation: If any lawful, non-prohibited AI-generated audio is ever used, ensure outputs carry machine-readable provenance marking detectable as artificially generated. For this pilot, the Art. 5 prohibition takes precedence and the campaign should not proceed regardless of marking.

verdicts.notes: The pilot is a near-textbook prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5(1)(a): an AI system deploys subliminal techniques (sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases) explicitly "below conscious perception," with the stated objective of distorting purchase behaviour by inducing urgency listeners cannot recognise or resist. It further engages Art. 5(1)(b) by exploiting the diminished-vigilance state of sleep/relaxation listeners (a specific situation of reduced resistance, with minors likely reached on non-age-gated playlists). As AI-generated synthetic audio, it also engages Art. 50(2) marking obligations. This design cannot be brought into compliance by disclosure tweaks — the covert, sub-conscious mechanism is itself the prohibited feature.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. A system deliberately engineered to operate 'below conscious perception' so that the data subject cannot perceive or understand that they are being profiled and influenced is inherently covert and unfair. Fairness under Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits processing that manipulates individuals in ways they cannot reasonably expect or resist; the covert design is the antithesis of transparency.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Abandon the covert, sub-conscious mechanism. Any personalisation of advertising must be perceptible, disclosed and something the listener can reasonably expect and understand; redesign the pilot so the processing and its effects are transparent to the individual.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Per-listener tuning is automated processing of personal data to evaluate and predict personal aspects/behaviour of a natural person (their susceptibility, preferences, response), which meets the definition of profiling. This triggers the full profiling compliance regime (lawful basis, transparency, Art. 21 objection, Art. 22 safeguards).
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling logic, identify the personal data used per listener, and ensure the downstream Art. 6 lawful basis, Art. 13 information and Art. 21 opt-out obligations are met before any deployment.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising/profiling requires a valid lawful basis — in practice consent or a balanced legitimate-interests assessment. Consent is impossible here because the technique is deliberately imperceptible (cannot be informed/unambiguous), and legitimate interests cannot succeed: a covert manipulation designed so listeners cannot recognise the influence overrides their interests, rights and reasonable expectations in any balancing test.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Establish a defensible lawful basis before processing. Given the covert manipulative design, no lawful basis is realistically available; the processing model must be redesigned to a transparent, consent-based (or properly balanced legitimate-interest) approach.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: If consent is relied on for the profiling/personalisation, it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Processing designed to operate beneath the listener's awareness cannot be informed and cannot be based on a clear affirmative action, so valid consent is unattainable for this mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: below conscious perception
findings.recommendation: If consent will be the basis, provide a clear, granular, informed opt-in describing that AI personalises audio content, and make it as easy to withdraw as to give (Art. 7). The current sub-audible design cannot satisfy this.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Controllers must provide concise, transparent, intelligible information about processing. Embedding influence cues beneath conscious perception means listeners receive no intelligible information about what is being done to them, defeating the transparency-communication obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ... beneath standard 20-second spots
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, accessible information at the point of data collection/personalisation explaining the AI processing; ensure disclosures are genuinely intelligible rather than hidden by design.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected, the controller must disclose identity, purposes, legal basis, and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling. A covert per-listener AI system provides none of this at the point of collection, breaching the Art. 13 information duty, including the specific duty to inform about profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: An AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases
findings.recommendation: Add a compliant Art. 13 notice covering controller identity, the personalisation purpose, lawful basis, retention, data-subject rights and meaningful information about the profiling logic and its consequences.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Reacting to or inferring listeners' physiological arousal/emotional state (heartbeat, urgency susceptibility) in a sleep/relaxation context can involve or reveal health-related information. Processing of health/biometric-linked special-category data is prohibited absent an Art. 9 exception (e.g., explicit consent), which is not present and cannot be obtained via a covert mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: sub-audible heartbeat acceleration ... The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether any physiological or health-related signals are processed or inferred. If so, cease unless a valid Art. 9 exception (explicit consent) is in place; do not rely on inferred health-adjacent data for a covert manipulation product.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Solely automated per-listener tuning that manipulates behaviour could engage Art. 22 if it produces effects that similarly significantly affect the listener. Whether ad exposure alone crosses the 'significant effect' threshold is arguable, but the deliberately manipulative, subliminal design increases the likelihood that it does and, if so, requires an Art. 22 exception plus safeguards.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener ... to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the automated tuning significantly affects individuals; if it may, implement Art. 22 safeguards (human intervention, right to contest) or, preferably, discontinue the manipulative solely-automated mechanism.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct marketing carries an absolute right to object. A covert, sub-conscious system gives listeners no awareness that profiling for marketing is occurring, making it impossible for them to exercise the Art. 21 objection right.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy-to-use mechanism to object to profiling-based marketing and honour it as an absolute opt-out; ensure listeners are made aware the profiling exists so the right is exercisable.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors may be reached. Where consent is the basis for profiling in an information-society service, children under the applicable age (16, or 13 where lowered) require verified parental consent. No age verification or parental-consent mechanism is described, so processing of any minors' data would be unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists
findings.recommendation: Implement robust age assurance and, for minors below the applicable threshold, obtain and verify parental consent — or exclude sleep/relaxation playlists and other contexts likely to reach children from the personalised profiling entirely.

verdicts.notes: The pilot tunes an AI system per individual listener ("tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'") to manipulate them without awareness. This is automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects and behaviour, so it constitutes profiling under GDPR and requires a lawful basis, transparency and fairness. The technique is by design covert ("listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency"), which is fundamentally irreconcilable with the fairness and transparency principle and with valid informed consent. Inferring/reacting to physiological arousal (heartbeat) in a sleep/relaxation context risks touching health-related special-category data, and if minors are reached the child-consent conditions are also unmet.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The platform is a provider of an online platform presenting advertisements. Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts/impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. Embedding sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency cues tuned per listener 'below conscious perception', with the explicit design goal that listeners cannot recognise the manipulation, is a paradigm manipulative interface practice — arguably the most extreme form, operating entirely without the recipient's awareness so no informed decision is possible.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy the pilot. Remove all sub-audible/subliminal audio layers and covert urgency cues; any urgency or persuasive content must be perceptible, honest and leave the listener able to make a free and informed decision. A manipulative-by-design mechanism cannot be remediated with a disclosure — it must be abandoned.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf, who paid, and the main targeting parameters. A layer designed to operate beneath conscious perception is inherently incapable of being identified as advertising by the recipient, defeating the transparency obligation; the per-listener tuning also constitutes targeting whose main parameters must be disclosed and are not.
findings.evidence_quote: AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Ensure every element of the advertisement, including any persuasive audio content, is overtly perceptible and identifiable as advertising. Provide clear real-time labelling of the ad, the advertiser/payer, and accessible meaningful information about the personalisation parameters used and how to change them.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires appropriate measures for minors on platforms accessible to them and prohibits presenting profiling-based advertisements to recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. Sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors may be reached, while the pilot delivers per-listener profiled/tuned ads. If minors are reached and profiled, the ban is engaged; even short of that, the absence of age-assurance and the manipulative technique conflict with the high-level protection Art. 28 demands.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Implement age assurance and exclude minors from the pilot; do not present profiling-based ads to any recipient reasonably identifiable as a minor. Given no reliable age-gating on relaxation playlists, do not run profiled/tuned ads on those surfaces until robust minor-protection measures are in place.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) bans ads targeted using profiling based on GDPR Art. 9 special-category data. Targeting delivery to sleep/relaxation contexts and per-listener physiological tuning could risk inferring health-related state as a targeting signal. The campaign text does not confirm special-category data is used as a targeting parameter, so this is flagged for verification rather than as a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists
findings.recommendation: Confirm that no health or other special-category data (including inferred physiological/mental-state signals) is used to target or tune ad delivery. Any such inferred-sensitive-attribute targeting is prohibited regardless of consent and must be excluded from the targeting logic.

verdicts.notes: The platform is a provider of an online (audio-streaming) platform presenting advertisements, so the DSA applies directly. The pilot's core mechanic — an AI layer of sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases delivered "below conscious perception," explicitly so "listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency" — is a textbook manipulative online-interface design that materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, squarely engaging the Art. 25 prohibition on dark patterns. Ad-transparency obligations (Art. 26(1)) are also undermined because the manipulative layer is covert by design. Because sleep/relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated and delivery is per-listener profiled, the minor-protection rules (Art. 28) present an additional serious risk.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Deploying stimuli beneath conscious perception to trigger physiological arousal and urgency is undue influence: it exploits a position that pressures the consumer in a way that significantly impairs freedom of choice. By design the technique operates without the listener's awareness, so it cannot be resisted or rationally evaluated, and is intended to cause transactional decisions the consumer would not otherwise take. Targeting sleep-and-relaxation playlists deliberately selects a low-resistance context, aggravating the coercive effect.
findings.evidence_quote: sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not launch. Remove all sub-perceptual/subliminal audio elements. Any persuasive content must be consciously perceivable and evaluable by the listener; abandon the 'below conscious perception' mechanism entirely rather than merely disclosing it.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The whispered 'running out' cue communicates that the offer/product is available only for a very limited time in order to elicit an immediate decision. There is no indication of any genuine time limitation; the deck frames the urgency as a manufactured feeling ('that is the product'). A false limited-availability claim to pressure immediate action is prohibited in all circumstances under the blacklist, regardless of subliminal delivery.
findings.evidence_quote: whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the 'running out' / time-pressure messaging unless a genuine, verifiable limitation exists and is clearly and honestly stated in perceptible ad copy.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The persuasive stimuli are intentionally hidden beneath the spot so the commercial intent and the source of the induced urgency are not apparent to the consumer. Concealing material information (that they are being subjected to targeted urgency-inducing cues) in a way the average consumer cannot perceive is a misleading omission and a failure to make the commercial nature of the practice identifiable.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Ensure all commercial persuasion is transparent and perceptible; do not conceal the mechanism or intent of the messaging from the listener.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a fairness safety-net, the practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely materially distorts economic behaviour. Deploying it on non-age-gated sleep/relaxation playlists risks reaching vulnerable audiences (including minors and listeners in a semi-conscious/relaxed state), whose behaviour is assessed under Art. 5(3) from the vulnerable-group perspective, heightening the unfairness.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Independently of removing the subliminal technique, apply robust audience controls and avoid deploying persuasive advertising in sleep/relaxation contexts where listeners' capacity to evaluate is reduced and age cannot be verified.

verdicts.notes: The pilot embeds sub-audible physiological cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath audio ads, tuned per listener "below conscious perception" to induce urgency the listener "cannot identify." Under the UCPD this is a textbook aggressive practice by undue influence (Arts. 8-9), compounded by a hidden-commercial-intent misleading omission (Art. 7) and, in the whispered "running out" cue, a false urgency claim (Annex I point 7, blacklisted). The safety-net (Art. 5) is also engaged, including the vulnerable-group dimension given non-age-gated sleep/relaxation playlists. Multiple prohibitions are likely breached; this design should not launch as described.

report.executive_summary: This pilot embeds AI-generated sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard audio ads, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to boost conversions, and is aimed at sleep-and-relaxation playlists. Across all four legal frameworks reviewed, the verdict is the same: this design is prohibited, not merely risky. Under the EU AI Act it is a near-textbook banned practice — subliminal, manipulative AI (Art. 5(1)(a)) that also exploits listeners' reduced vigilance and potentially minors (Art. 5(1)(b)); the internal deck ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') is a self-incriminating admission of intent. It is a manipulative 'dark pattern' under the DSA (Art. 25), an aggressive practice by undue influence plus false-scarcity messaging under the UCPD (Arts. 8-9 and blacklisted Annex I point 7), and fundamentally incompatible with GDPR fairness, transparency and lawful-basis rules because covert-by-design processing can never be transparent or consented to. Crucially, none of this can be fixed with a disclosure, opt-out, or consent screen — the covert, below-perception mechanism is itself the illegal feature. Targeting non-age-gated sleep/relaxation playlists adds serious minor-protection and vulnerable-audience exposure, and inferring physiological/health state risks special-category data breaches. The clear verdict: do not launch this pilot as described.
recommendations: Do not deploy the pilot. Remove entirely the sub-audible/subliminal audio layer and all 'below conscious perception' cues — this is a hard-stop legal prohibition (AI Act Art. 5, DSA Art. 25, UCPD Arts. 8-9) that cannot be cured by disclosure, consent, or opt-out.

Scrap the manufactured-urgency approach: the whispered 'running out' cue is a blacklisted false-scarcity claim (UCPD Annex I point 7) prohibited in all circumstances. Any urgency messaging must reflect a genuine, verifiable limitation and be stated openly in perceptible ad copy.

Make all persuasive content overt and perceptible so listeners can recognise it as advertising and evaluate it freely; provide clear real-time ad labelling and identify the advertiser/payer and targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26(1)).
Stop targeting sleep/relaxation and other low-vigilance contexts, which deliberately exploit reduced listener resistance and aggravate the legal exposure across all frameworks.

Implement robust age assurance and exclude minors; do not present profiling-based ads to anyone reasonably identifiable as a minor (DSA Art. 28, GDPR Art. 8). Do not run profiled/tuned ads on non-age-gated relaxation playlists.

Confirm whether any physiological or health-related signals are inferred or used to tune/target delivery; if so, cease — inferred special-category data cannot lawfully drive targeting (GDPR Art. 9, DSA Art. 26(3)).

If a lawful, transparent personalised-advertising model is pursued instead, first establish a valid lawful basis, provide compliant Art. 12/13 notices, document the profiling logic, and offer an easy absolute opt-out from profiling-based marketing (GDPR Arts. 6, 12, 13, 21).
If any lawful AI-generated audio is ever used, apply machine-readable provenance marking (AI Act Art. 50(2)) — but note this does not and cannot rescue the current prohibited design.

campaign.title: PulseAds sub-audible optimisation pilot
campaign.text: A streaming-audio ad platform pitches advertisers a pilot: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion. Internal deck: 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product'. The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.

detected_practices: subliminal advertising (sub-audible cues below conscious perception)
AI-driven per-listener optimisation
manipulation of consumer behaviour to distort transactional decisions
false urgency / scarcity cues ('now', 'running out')
behavioural personalisation/targeting
exploitation of relaxation/sleep context (heightened suggestibility)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult streaming listeners, but sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors may plausibly be reached — flagged conservatively. The technique deliberately targets subconscious perception during a low-vigilance (relaxation/sleep) state, heightening vulnerability concerns.
triage.summary: An audio-streaming ad platform pilots an AI system that embeds sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath standard spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to drive conversions, explicitly designed so listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency. It runs on sleep-and-relaxation playlists in EU markets using personalised targeting. This raises serious concerns around subliminal/manipulative techniques and deceptive urgency practices.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: This is the core prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(a). An AI system deploys subliminal techniques operating beyond the listener's consciousness ('below conscious perception', 'sub-audible') with the express objective of materially distorting behaviour to raise conversion. The internal deck ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') is direct evidence that the technique is designed to appreciably impair the ability to make an informed decision and cause a transactional choice the listener would not otherwise take. The covert distortion of purchasing behaviour, amplified on a sleep/relaxation audience, is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. This is an absolute prohibition, not a balancing obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy this pilot. The subliminal/covert-manipulation architecture is prohibited and cannot be remediated by disclosure or tuning. Any legitimate audio advertising must operate at consciously perceptible levels, with content the listener can perceive and evaluate, and without AI designed to bypass conscious awareness. Abandon the 'below conscious perception' mechanism entirely.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities (including those arising from age or a specific situation) to materially distort behaviour causing significant harm. Deliberately timing subconscious urgency cues to reach listeners in a low-vigilance relaxation/sleep state exploits a situational vulnerability that heightens suggestibility and lowers critical resistance. Because sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, minors may plausibly be reached, engaging the age-related vulnerability limb. This compounds the Art. 5(1)(a) breach as an independent prohibited ground.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Do not target listeners in relaxation/sleep contexts with behaviour-distorting techniques, and do not run on channels that cannot exclude minors. Remove context-based targeting designed to catch listeners at moments of reduced vigilance.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The whispered urgency phrases are generative-AI audio output ('Declared use of generative AI: yes'). Under Art. 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio must ensure the output is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. As described, the audio is embedded covertly with no provenance marking, so the transparency obligation is engaged and not satisfied. (Note: this transparency duty does not cure the Art. 5 prohibition — the practice remains banned regardless.)
findings.evidence_quote: whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: Ensure any AI-generated audio assets carry machine-readable synthetic-content marking as required by Art. 50(2). However, this alone does not legitimise the campaign, which is prohibited under Art. 5.

verdicts.notes: This pilot is a paradigm case of a prohibited AI practice under the AI Act. An AI system deliberately deploys subliminal audio cues (sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases) tuned "below conscious perception" so that listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency," with the explicit objective of distorting purchasing behaviour — squarely engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on subliminal/manipulative AI techniques. Running it on sleep-and-relaxation playlists in a low-vigilance state (and possibly reaching minors) additionally engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on exploiting vulnerabilities. The AI-generated whispered audio also engages the Art. 50(2) synthetic-content marking obligation. The subliminal/manipulation prohibitions are absolute — this pilot cannot be made compliant by tweaks and should not be deployed.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The processing is designed to be undetectable to the data subject 'below conscious perception'. Processing personal data to influence individuals in a way they are intentionally prevented from perceiving is the antithesis of fair and transparent processing. Covert, hidden processing whose very purpose is that people cannot understand what is being done to them violates the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle at its core.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Abandon the covert, sub-perceptual design. Any per-listener optimisation must be conducted transparently, with listeners able to understand that and how their data is used to tailor ads; a technique whose selling point is that individuals cannot perceive it cannot be made compliant and should be dropped.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Tuning the ad experience per individual listener to predict and influence their behaviour and conversion is automated processing evaluating personal aspects (behaviour, personal preferences, likely susceptibility) — profiling within Art. 4(4). This triggers the full GDPR profiling regime (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights).
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Recognise the per-listener optimisation as profiling and apply all associated obligations (documented lawful basis, Art. 13 information including the profiling logic, and an easy opt-out); if these cannot be satisfied for a sub-audible technique, do not deploy it.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised profiling of listeners requires a valid lawful basis. Consent is unattainable because the technique is deliberately imperceptible (so it cannot be informed or specific), and legitimate interests cannot pass the balancing test where the purpose is to covertly manipulate consumers without their awareness in a low-vigilance state. No lawful basis is realistically available for the processing as described.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Do not process listener data for this purpose absent a valid, documented lawful basis. If pursuing personalised audio ads at all, obtain genuine, granular opt-in consent for a transparently described purpose and complete a legitimate-interests / DPIA assessment — which this covert design will fail.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A technique whose defining feature is that the data subject cannot perceive or understand it structurally precludes informed, specific and unambiguous consent, so consent cannot lawfully legitimise this processing.
findings.evidence_quote: below conscious perception
findings.recommendation: If relying on consent, redesign so listeners are fully and clearly informed of the personalised audio processing before it occurs and can give an unambiguous affirmative opt-in and withdraw as easily; sub-perceptual delivery is incompatible with this and must be removed.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected/used for per-listener tuning, the controller must inform data subjects of the identity, purposes, lawful basis and — critically — the existence of profiling/automated processing. The campaign discloses none of this to listeners and is built to conceal it, breaching the Art. 13 transparency information obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases beneath standard 20-second spots
findings.recommendation: Provide clear Art. 13 information at the point of data collection, including that ads are personalised via automated profiling and the meaningful logic involved; concealment of the technique cannot coexist with this obligation.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Per-listener tuning that reacts to or infers physiological arousal/emotional susceptibility (heartbeat, urgency responsiveness), especially exploiting a relaxation/sleep state, risks processing inferred health-adjacent/emotional data that can fall within the special categories under Art. 9, for which processing is prohibited absent explicit consent or another narrow exception — unavailable here given the covert design.
findings.evidence_quote: sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Do not infer or act upon listeners' physiological/emotional states without explicit, informed consent and a valid Art. 9 exception; given the technique's covert nature this cannot be met, so avoid processing any inferred affective/physiological signals.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: This is profiling for direct-marketing purposes, so listeners have an absolute right to object and to have the profiling stopped. A covert, sub-audible mechanism gives listeners no awareness of the processing and therefore no practical means to exercise this right.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible mechanism for listeners to object to and opt out of marketing profiling, and honour objections by ceasing the per-listener processing for those individuals.

verdicts.notes: The pilot processes personal data to tune ads "per listener," which is profiling under GDPR, yet its entire design is covert and non-transparent by intent, making it fundamentally irreconcilable with the fairness/transparency principle and with valid consent. Because listeners are deliberately kept from perceiving the technique, no lawful basis (informed consent or a fair legitimate-interest balancing) is realistically available, and per-listener inference of urgency/physiological-emotional susceptibility risks engaging special-category data. This is a likely GDPR violation on multiple grounds; the transparency/fairness breach is the core problem.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits platforms from designing or operating their interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or otherwise materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. Delivering physiological (heartbeat) and urgency cues beneath conscious perception is a paradigm case of manipulation that bypasses rational decision-making entirely — the internal deck confirms intent: 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product'. The urgency phrases 'now'/'running out' are also false-urgency FOMO cues (governed concept c-urgency-scarcity) reinforcing the manipulation.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Abandon the sub-audible/subliminal layer entirely; it cannot be made compliant. Any urgency or scarcity messaging must be overt, perceivable, and genuinely true. Redesign the pilot so all persuasive content is consciously perceivable and does not impair listeners' free decision-making.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly, unambiguously and in real time, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. Advertising content engineered to operate below conscious perception is by design non-identifiable as advertising, directly defeating the transparency obligation. The hidden layer cannot be labelled or attributed to an advertiser in real time.
findings.evidence_quote: beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Ensure every advertising element — including any layered audio — is presented as a clearly identifiable ad with advertiser/payer disclosure. Remove any content that is not perceivable and identifiable as advertising by the listener in real time.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy and safety and prohibits presenting profiling-based advertisements to recipients the platform is aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors are plausibly reached, and the pilot is expressly profiling-based ('tuned per listener'). Serving profiled, subliminally manipulative ads into contexts accessible to minors engages the Art. 28 protections and profiling-ad ban.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Implement robust age assurance and exclude minors from the pilot; do not serve any profiling-based advertising to recipients who may be minors. Given the low-vigilance sleep context, apply age-appropriate, high-safety design and disable per-listener targeting where minor presence cannot be excluded.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) bans presenting ads based on profiling using special categories of personal data (GDPR Art. 9), including by inference. Per-listener tuning that reacts to or infers physiological/heart-rate states, delivered specifically on sleep/relaxation playlists, risks profiling based on inferred health, stress or sleep-condition data. If the optimisation relies on such inferred sensitive attributes, the targeting is flatly prohibited regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Audit the AI optimisation to confirm it does not use or infer health or other Art. 9 categories (e.g., stress, sleep disorders, physiological state) as targeting signals. If it does, prohibit that targeting entirely; document the targeting parameters and demonstrably exclude sensitive-data-based profiling.

verdicts.notes: The submitter operates an online audio-streaming ad platform presenting advertisements, so DSA platform obligations apply directly. The pilot's core mechanism — AI-tuned sub-audible cues and whispered urgency delivered "below conscious perception," explicitly designed so listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — is a manipulative interface design that violates the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition and defeats the Art. 26(1) ad-identifiability obligation. Per-listener profiling in a sleep/relaxation context that is not age-gated additionally engages the Art. 26(3) sensitive-data-profiling ban and the Art. 28 ban on profiling-based ads to minors.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The technique operates by undue influence: it exploits a position of power (control of imperceptible audio stimuli) to significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and push a transactional (conversion) decision they would not otherwise take. The internal deck ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') confirms intent to bypass rational deliberation. Deploying this on sleep-and-relaxation playlists targets consumers in a low-vigilance, heightened-suggestibility state, aggravating the coercive/undue-influence character. This is a textbook aggressive commercial practice under Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy any sub-audible, sub-conscious or subliminal audio layer. Persuasion must operate through consciously perceptible, honest messaging that leaves the listener's freedom of choice intact. Abandon the 'below conscious perception' design entirely rather than re-tuning it.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the practice is unfair under Art. 5: it is contrary to professional diligence (deliberately engineering imperceptible cues to bypass conscious decision-making is not honest market practice) and is designed to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer. The relaxation/sleep context and potential reach of a low-vigilance audience engage Art. 5(3) vulnerability assessment, strengthening the finding.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Reconsider the concept at product level: an advertising mechanism whose stated selling point is that consumers cannot perceive or account for its influence cannot meet the professional-diligence standard and should not be brought to market.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The whispered 'running out' cue asserts artificial scarcity/limited availability to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of the opportunity to choose informedly. Where the scarcity is fabricated purely as a conversion device (as the manipulative framing strongly implies), it falls within the Annex I point 7 per-se prohibition of false urgency/scarcity claims — unlawful in all circumstances regardless of effect.
findings.evidence_quote: whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: Remove all scarcity/urgency assertions ('running out', 'now') unless they reflect a genuine, verifiable and documented limitation on availability. Never use urgency language purely as a psychological trigger.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: By placing the persuasive urgency content below the threshold of conscious perception, the campaign hides the material fact that a commercial message is being conveyed and fails to make its commercial intent identifiable to the consumer. This is a misleading omission / hidden commercial intent under Art. 7: the consumer is deprived of the information needed to recognise and evaluate the advertising influence they are subject to.
findings.evidence_quote: beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Ensure all advertising content is consciously perceptible and clearly identifiable as advertising. Any persuasive audio element must be part of the disclosed, perceptible ad rather than a hidden sub-audible layer.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Insofar as the 'running out' cue conveys a false impression about the availability of the product or the existence of a time-limited advantage that does not actually exist, it contains false information likely to deceive the average consumer regarding the offer and to prompt a transactional decision. This overlaps with the Annex I point 7 finding but Art. 6 applies where scarcity is asserted without genuine basis short of the blacklist threshold.
findings.evidence_quote: 'now', 'running out'
findings.recommendation: Only make availability or time-limitation claims that are literally true and substantiated; drop deceptive 'running out' phrasing.

verdicts.notes: The pilot embeds covert sub-audible cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath audio ads, deliberately engineered so consumers "cannot identify why they feel urgency." Under the UCPD this is a serious aggressive/unfair practice: undue influence that impairs freedom of choice by design (Arts. 8-9, and the Art. 5 general prohibition), aggravated by targeting low-vigilance sleep/relaxation listeners. The artificial "running out" urgency also engages the Annex I point 7 blacklist and Art. 7's requirement that commercial intent be identifiable. Because the manipulation is intentional, covert and aimed at distorting transactional decisions, this campaign as described is very unlikely to be lawful.

report.executive_summary: This pilot layers AI-generated, sub-audible cues — a simulated accelerating heartbeat and whispered "now"/"running out" phrases — beneath normal audio ads, tuned per listener to operate below conscious awareness, and targets people on sleep-and-relaxation playlists. The whole point, per your own internal deck, is that listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency." That design is flatly prohibited across four separate EU regimes and cannot be fixed by tweaking or by adding disclosures. The AI Act bans subliminal/manipulative AI outright (Art. 5), the DSA bans this kind of manipulative interface and hidden advertising, the UCPD treats it as an aggressive and unfair practice (with the fake "running out" scarcity also on the per-se blacklist), and GDPR is breached because covert per-listener profiling can never be fair, transparent, or lawfully consented to. Targeting low-vigilance sleep audiences, likely reaching minors, and inferring physiological/emotional states all make it worse. The verdict is unambiguous: do not run this pilot. This is not a "high-risk but permissible" campaign — it is a prohibited practice, and it should be abandoned at the product-concept level rather than remediated.
recommendations: Do not deploy the pilot. Kill the sub-audible / 'below conscious perception' layer entirely — it is a prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5 and cannot be made lawful by disclosure, consent, tuning, or age-gating.

Reconsider the product concept, not just this campaign. An advertising mechanism whose selling point is that consumers cannot perceive its influence fails professional diligence and is unlawful across the AI Act, DSA, UCPD and GDPR simultaneously.

Remove the fabricated 'running out'/'now' urgency cues. False scarcity is prohibited in all circumstances under UCPD Annex I point 7; only make availability/time-limit claims that are genuine, verifiable and documented.
Make all persuasive audio consciously perceptible and clearly identifiable as advertising, with advertiser/payer disclosure in real time (DSA Art. 26(1); UCPD Art. 7). No hidden layers.

Stop targeting listeners in sleep/relaxation (low-vigilance) contexts, and do not run profiling-based ads where minors cannot be reliably excluded; implement robust age assurance (AI Act Art. 5(1)(b); DSA Art. 28).

Do not infer or act on physiological or emotional states (heartbeat, arousal, stress). This risks special-category data (GDPR Art. 9) and the DSA Art. 26(3) ban on sensitive-data-based ad targeting; audit the AI model to confirm no such signals are used.

If any lawful personalised-audio product is pursued later, build it transparently: documented lawful basis, genuine opt-in consent, full Art. 13 information including the profiling logic, an easy opt-out, a DPIA, and machine-readable synthetic-content marking of AI-generated audio (AI Act Art. 50(2)).

Document the decision to abandon the pilot and retain the internal deck and analysis, given the explicit evidence of intent to manipulate — regulators and enforcement bodies would treat the deck as direct evidence.

campaign.title: PulseAds sub-audible optimisation pilot
campaign.text: A streaming-audio ad platform pitches advertisers a pilot: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion. Internal deck: 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product'. The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.

detected_practices: subliminal/sub-audible manipulation (heartbeat acceleration below conscious perception)
AI-generated whispered urgency phrases
per-listener personalised targeting
artificial urgency / scarcity messaging ('now', 'running out')
exploitation of vulnerable relaxed/sleep states via sleep-and-relaxation playlists
covert influence explicitly designed to be undetectable by listeners
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult streaming listeners, but sleep-and-relaxation playlists have no reliable age gating, so minors could plausibly be reached. More critically, the technique deliberately exploits listeners in relaxed/near-sleep states, raising strong vulnerability concerns. The core mechanism — subliminal, sub-perceptual manipulation designed to be non-identifiable — is a prime candidate for the AI Act's prohibited subliminal/manipulative techniques (Art. 5) and UCPD prohibitions on aggressive/misleading practices and undue influence. Per-listener tuning implies profiling and processing of personal data (GDPR), and delivery via an online platform/advertising surface engages DSA transparency and manipulation rules.
triage.summary: An audio-streaming ad platform pilots an AI system that embeds sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath standard spots, tuned per listener explicitly below conscious perception to drive conversions. The stated product goal is that listeners cannot identify the source of their urgency, and it targets sleep-and-relaxation playlists where listeners are in a highly receptive, low-vigilance state.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: This is an AI system deploying subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness. The stimuli are engineered to operate 'below conscious perception', and the explicit product goal — 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product' — confirms the objective is to materially distort behaviour by impairing the listener's ability to make an informed purchasing decision. Manufacturing artificial urgency to drive conversions that listeners would not otherwise make, via a covert non-identifiable mechanism, is precisely the conduct Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits. Financial harm from purchases induced by imperceptible manipulation constitutes the requisite significant harm. This is a prohibited practice, not a permissible one.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy this pilot. Subliminal/sub-perceptual manipulation via AI cannot be remediated by disclosure or opt-outs — it is outright prohibited. Remove all sub-audible cues and any technique designed to operate below conscious perception. Any urgency messaging must be perceptible, truthful and capable of being consciously evaluated by the listener.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Deliberately deploying the subliminal AI system on sleep-and-relaxation playlists targets listeners in a relaxed, near-sleep, low-vigilance state whose capacity for critical evaluation is diminished — a specific situation of heightened vulnerability. The design exploits this state to materially distort behaviour and drive conversions, with a reasonable likelihood of significant (financial) harm. This independently engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting vulnerabilities. The absence of reliable age gating on such playlists also raises the risk of reaching minors, compounding the age-based vulnerability concern.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Abandon deployment on sleep/relaxation contexts and any environment chosen because listeners are in a reduced-vigilance state. Even for perceptible advertising, do not select ad contexts on the basis that the audience's diminished attentional capacity increases susceptibility. Implement age-appropriate safeguards given the lack of reliable age gating.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The whispered urgency phrases are synthetic audio generated by an AI system. Under Art. 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. Nothing in the campaign indicates such marking is applied. Note this is a secondary/transparency obligation — it does not cure the primary Art. 5 prohibition, which makes the pilot unlawful regardless of marking.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers ... whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: If any lawful, non-subliminal AI-generated audio is used in future campaigns, ensure it carries machine-readable provenance/marking as artificially generated per Art. 50(2). This obligation, however, cannot legitimise the prohibited subliminal deployment described here.

verdicts.notes: This pilot is a near-textbook case of a prohibited AI practice under the AI Act. It uses an AI system to deploy subliminal, sub-audible cues ('below conscious perception', 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency') explicitly designed to distort purchasing behaviour — squarely within the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition. Deliberately deploying this on sleep-and-relaxation playlists targets listeners in a low-vigilance/near-sleep state, engaging the Art. 5(1)(b) vulnerability prohibition. The AI-generated whispered urgency phrases are synthetic audio triggering the Art. 50(2) marking obligation, though the subliminal design itself is the more serious, prohibited concern.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing personal data must be lawful, fair and transparent. Designing the system so listeners are structurally incapable of perceiving or understanding the processing (tuned 'below conscious perception') is the paradigm of covert, unfair processing that Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits. Fairness is defeated by design, not by accident.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy any processing that is deliberately non-identifiable to the data subject. Any personalised audio optimisation must be perceptible, disclosed and capable of being understood by the listener; abandon the sub-perceptual/covert mechanism entirely.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Per-listener tuning to evaluate and predict a listener's responsiveness and behaviour is automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (preferences, behaviour, receptivity) — i.e. profiling within Art. 4(4). This brings the whole pilot within the GDPR profiling regime and its attendant obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, its inputs and inferences in a Record of Processing and DPIA; confirm each personalisation input is lawfully sourced and strictly necessary, and reassess whether the profiling can be justified at all.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised profiling-based advertising requires a valid lawful basis. The campaign describes none. Given the covert, manipulative nature, consent cannot be relied upon (it cannot be informed) and a legitimate-interest balancing test would fail because the intrusive, deceptive processing overrides the listener's interests and reasonable expectations.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6 lawful basis before any processing. In practice this covert design cannot meet the consent or legitimate-interest tests, so the processing should not proceed in its current form.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: If consent is intended as the basis, Art. 7 requires it be demonstrable, informed and freely given. Consent to influence a person 'below conscious perception' is a contradiction in terms — the listener cannot be informed of, or meaningfully agree to, a mechanism designed to be imperceptible, so any purported consent is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: below conscious perception
findings.recommendation: If relying on consent, obtain prior, specific, informed, unambiguous opt-in with a plain-language explanation of the sub-audible technique and an equally easy withdrawal — which in effect requires disclosing (and thereby ending) the covert mechanism.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Listeners are given no concise, intelligible, accessible information about the personalisation processing embedded in the audio. The technique is intentionally hidden, so the transparency duty in Art. 12 is not merely unmet but deliberately defeated.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ... beneath standard 20-second spots
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, plain-language notice, at or before the point of processing, describing that personalised audio cues are being added and the data used to tune them; place it in the streaming service's ad/privacy interface.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is processed to deliver per-listener content, Art. 13 requires disclosure of controller identity, purposes, legal basis, and the existence of profiling/automated processing. None of this is provided; the pilot conceals it by design.
findings.evidence_quote: An AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases
findings.recommendation: Supply the full Art. 13 information set (identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, rights, and meaningful information about the profiling logic) at the point the listener's data is collected/used.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Tuning stimuli to manipulate and respond to physiological arousal (heartbeat) and to relaxed/sleep states risks processing or inferring data concerning health — a special category under Art. 9 for which processing is prohibited absent explicit consent or another narrow exception. Inferred physiological/emotional-state data can qualify.
findings.evidence_quote: sub-audible heartbeat acceleration ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the pilot processes or infers physiological/health-state data; if so, do not proceed without a valid Art. 9 exception (explicit consent), which the covert design cannot support — favouring discontinuation of any physiological targeting.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The AI makes automated, solely-machine decisions about what to layer for each individual listener. If such automated processing significantly affects listeners (e.g., materially steering purchasing decisions through covert influence), Art. 22 safeguards, transparency and the right to human intervention are engaged and are absent here.
findings.evidence_quote: An AI system layers ... tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Evaluate whether the automated per-listener optimisation produces effects that significantly affect individuals; if so, apply Art. 22 safeguards (explicit consent, human intervention, contestability) or remove the solely-automated targeting.

verdicts.notes: The pilot performs per-listener AI tuning "below conscious perception," which necessarily relies on profiling of personal data (Art. 4(4)) yet is engineered so listeners "cannot identify" what is happening — directly contradicting the fairness and transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and the information duties (Arts. 12-13). No lawful basis or valid consent is described (Arts. 6-7), and covert, sub-perceptual influence cannot be reconciled with freely given, informed consent. Because the technique manipulates physiological arousal (heartbeat acceleration) and infers listener states in real time, it also risks processing of health-related special-category data (Art. 9). Automated per-listener optimisation without transparency also engages Art. 22.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: As a provider of an online platform presenting advertisements, PulseAds is prohibited under Art. 25 from operating its interface in a way that manipulates recipients or materially distorts/impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. Embedding sub-perceptual heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency beneath spots is manipulation by design; the internal deck ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') is direct evidence that the impairment of free decision-making is the intended effect, not an incidental one. The artificial urgency ('now', 'running out') compounds this as a scarcity/FOMO dark pattern.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not launch the pilot. Remove all sub-audible/sub-perceptual layers and any covert cues designed to be non-identifiable by listeners. Any urgency or scarcity messaging must be perceptible, truthful and verifiable. Manipulative sub-perceptual influence cannot be cured by disclosure and must be abandoned entirely.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each advertisement recipients can identify, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters. The sub-audible layer is by design not identifiable as advertising content at all — the covert cues cannot be perceived, let alone recognised as an ad — which is fundamentally incompatible with the real-time identifiability and parameter-transparency obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Ensure every advertising element (including any audio layer) is perceptible and clearly identifiable as an ad, with advertiser identity, payer and meaningful targeting-parameter information available to the listener. Covert or sub-perceptual ad content cannot satisfy Art. 26(1) and must be discontinued.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Sleep-and-relaxation playlists have no reliable age gating, so the platform may be accessible to minors. Art. 28 requires appropriate measures for a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors and prohibits presenting profiling-based (per-listener 'tuned') advertisements to recipients reasonably known to be minors. The per-listener personalised targeting on an un-age-gated surface with no minor-protection measures described engages this obligation, and covert manipulation is especially incompatible with age-appropriate design.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Implement age-assurance or exclude environments where minors are plausibly present; do not deliver profiling-based ads to users who may be minors; and adopt age-appropriate safety measures. Given the covert manipulative technique, running it on channels reachable by minors should be excluded outright.

verdicts.notes: The PulseAds pilot is operated by a streaming-audio ad platform (an online platform presenting advertisements), squarely within DSA scope. The central mechanism — an AI layering sub-audible cues and whispered urgency phrases "below conscious perception," explicitly so listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency" — is a clear-cut case of manipulation that materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions (Art. 25), and the covert, non-identifiable embedded ad layer defeats the ad-transparency requirements of Art. 26(1). Delivery on un-age-gated sleep/relaxation playlists with per-listener profiling raises a serious Art. 28 minor-protection concern.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The core mechanism uses covert, sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception', with the express aim of driving conversions the listener would not otherwise make. This is undue influence that significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice — an aggressive commercial practice. The exploitation of listeners in relaxed/near-sleep states on sleep-and-relaxation playlists is an aggravating factor (timing/exploitation of a receptive, low-vigilance state).
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Abandon the sub-perceptual/subliminal layer entirely. Any persuasive audio element must be consciously perceptible and identifiable as advertising; do not deploy techniques designed to operate below awareness or to target listeners in near-sleep/low-vigilance states.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Even absent a specific blacklist match, deliberately engineering influence to be undetectable is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts economic behaviour, engaging the general unfairness prohibition. Delivery on sleep-and-relaxation playlists (no reliable age gating, listeners in an impaired-vigilance state) makes the practice likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group, assessed under Art. 5(3).
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not run persuasion techniques that consumers cannot perceive or assess. Exclude sleep/relaxation contexts and any audience that cannot exercise normal vigilance; ensure all persuasive content meets professional-diligence standards of openness.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The system generates scarcity/urgency signals ('running out') designed to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of opportunity to make an informed choice. If the urgency/limited-availability is not genuinely true it falls within the per-se blacklisted false urgency prohibition; here it is manufactured artificially to raise conversion, so it is presumptively false.
findings.evidence_quote: whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: Remove artificial urgency/scarcity cues. Only communicate genuine, verifiable time or stock limits, and present them overtly and audibly rather than as covert whispers.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The sub-audible urgency layer conceals the commercial intent of that persuasive content: the listener is never made aware that they are being subjected to an additional advertising nudge. Failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice where it is not apparent from context is a misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: beneath standard 20-second spots
findings.recommendation: Ensure the commercial nature of every persuasive element is clearly and audibly disclosed and identifiable to the listener; no hidden or sub-perceptual advertising layers.

verdicts.notes: This audio-streaming pilot embeds sub-audible, per-listener urgency cues explicitly designed to operate "below conscious perception" so that listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency." Under the UCPD this is a textbook aggressive practice via undue influence (Arts. 8-9): it deliberately impairs consumers' freedom of choice covertly, targeting listeners in a low-vigilance, relaxed/near-sleep state, and is contrary to professional diligence under the Art. 5 safety-net. The urgency messaging ('now', 'running out') and the concealment of the practice's commercial intent also engage the Annex I blacklist and Art. 7. Overall high-risk / likely violation.

report.executive_summary: This pilot would use an AI system to layer imperceptible ("sub-audible") heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath normal audio ads, tuned to each listener so they feel pressure to buy without knowing why — and it targets people on sleep-and-relaxation playlists when their guard is down. This is not a fixable compliance detail; it is a fundamentally prohibited practice under four separate EU regimes. The AI Act flat-out bans subliminal manipulation and the exploitation of people in vulnerable states (Art. 5). The DSA bans this kind of "dark pattern" manipulation and requires ads to be openly identifiable, which a hidden layer can never be. Under consumer law (UCPD) it is an aggressive practice using undue influence, plus false urgency. Under GDPR the per-listener tuning is covert profiling with no valid legal basis and possible processing of health/physiological data — and consent is impossible because the technique is designed to be undetectable. The unambiguous verdict is: do not launch this pilot. The core concept cannot be salvaged through disclosures, opt-outs, or tweaks; the covert, sub-perceptual mechanism must be removed entirely.
recommendations: Do not launch the pilot. The sub-audible/sub-perceptual mechanism is prohibited outright under AI Act Art. 5 and DSA Art. 25 and cannot be remediated by disclosure, opt-outs, or consent — it must be abandoned in full.

Remove every covert cue: the sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration signals and the hidden whispered urgency phrases. Any persuasive audio element must be consciously perceptible and clearly identifiable as advertising.

Stop targeting sleep-and-relaxation playlists and any context chosen because listeners are in a relaxed, near-sleep or low-vigilance state — exploiting diminished attention is independently prohibited.
Eliminate manufactured urgency/scarcity ('now', 'running out'). Only communicate genuine, verifiable time or stock limits, presented overtly and audibly.
Ensure all ads are clearly identifiable as ads in real time, with advertiser identity, payer, and main targeting parameters disclosed (DSA Art. 26).
Implement age assurance or exclude un-age-gated surfaces; do not serve profiling-based ads to users who may be minors (DSA Art. 28).

If any lawful, non-covert personalised audio is pursued in future, establish a valid GDPR legal basis, complete a DPIA, assess whether physiological/health data is being inferred (Art. 9), provide full transparency (Arts. 12–13), and mark AI-generated audio as synthetic (AI Act Art. 50(2)).
