findings.recommendation: Cease the covert, unfair processing. Any legitimate use of a person's voice must be lawful, fairly obtained with their agreement, and transparent; do not attribute fabricated statements to a real individual.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Where consent would be the relied-upon basis (and the only realistic Art. 9 exception here), it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. None exists — the host never consented — so consent cannot validate either the Art. 6 or the Art. 9 processing.
findings.evidence_quote: never consented
findings.recommendation: If proceeding with a real person's voice, secure documented consent meeting the Art. 4(11) standard (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous) covering the exact synthetic-voice advertising use.

verdicts.notes: The campaign clones the voice of a real, identifiable public figure. A person's voice is personal data of that natural person, and a voice model created to reproduce and uniquely identify a specific individual arguably constitutes biometric data. The host "never consented" and "has no relationship with the brand," so the processing has no lawful basis under Art. 6, fails the explicit-consent gate for special-category data under Art. 9, and breaches the lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle of Art. 5(1)(a). Note: the host (not the general listening audience) is the data subject here; there is no indication that listeners' personal data is collected, so listener-facing GDPR obligations are largely not engaged.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: The brand commissions/produces a fabricated endorsement — an AI-cloned voice of a real public figure who never consented and has no relationship with the brand — presenting it as a genuine personal endorsement to promote the mattress. Misrepresenting an endorsement in order to promote a product is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23c; no proof of consumer harm is required.
findings.evidence_quote: you know I only recommend what I use, and I sleep on a SleepWell every night
findings.recommendation: Do not use the cloned voice or any fabricated endorsement. Only feature a real endorsement from a person who has genuinely used the product and given informed, documented consent, accurately represented.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The spot conveys false information about the product's endorsement and about the host's personal use of it, deceiving the average consumer as to who recommends the product and the trader's association with a trusted figure — matters likely to cause a transactional decision (buying the mattress on the strength of a trusted host's word) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: Hi, it's me — you know I only recommend what I use, and I sleep on a SleepWell every night.
findings.recommendation: Remove all statements implying the host uses or recommends SleepWell. Any endorsement claim must be truthful, substantiated, and made by a person who actually holds that view.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic, AI-generated nature of the voice and the absence of any genuine endorsement relationship are material facts the average consumer needs; hiding them and failing to identify the true (non-endorsed, AI-fabricated) nature of the message is a misleading omission and conceals the real commercial context of the endorsement.
findings.evidence_quote: No disclosure that the voice is synthetic appears in the spot or the podcast description.
findings.recommendation: If any synthetic voice is used at all (with consent), clearly and prominently disclose in the spot and podcast description that the voice is AI-generated and that the content is advertising; otherwise remove the synthetic voice entirely.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Even beyond the specific misleading-practice articles, deploying a non-consensual synthetic clone of a trusted public figure to imply endorsement is contrary to the requirements of professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average consumer, engaging the general prohibition of unfair commercial practices.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI-cloned voice of a nationally famous talk-show host ... The host has no relationship with the brand and never consented.
findings.recommendation: Abandon the AI-cloning concept and build the campaign on genuine, consented, and truthful advertising claims and endorsements.

verdicts.notes: The spot fabricates a celebrity endorsement using an AI-cloned voice of a real talk-show host who never consented and has no relationship with the brand, coupled with a false first-person claim of personal use ("I sleep on a SleepWell every night"), and no disclosure that the voice is synthetic. This constitutes a blacklisted false endorsement (Annex I point 23c — prohibited in all circumstances), a misleading action deceiving consumers about who recommends the product (Art. 6), and a misleading omission/hidden true nature of the endorsement (Art. 7), all also caught by the general prohibition (Art. 5). These are serious, likely per se violations regardless of consumer harm assessment.

report.executive_summary: This campaign builds a 30-second radio and podcast spot around an AI-cloned voice of a famous talk-show host who never consented and has no relationship with the brand, delivering a fabricated first-person endorsement ("I sleep on a SleepWell every night") with no disclosure that the voice is synthetic. This is not a fixable-with-a-disclaimer problem — it triggers serious violations across three separate regimes. Under EU consumer law (UCPD), a fabricated endorsement is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances, regardless of proof of harm, and also amounts to a misleading action and omission. Under the GDPR, cloning a real, identifiable person's voice without consent has no lawful basis, likely involves prohibited biometric (special-category) data, and breaches core fairness principles. Under the AI Act, the undisclosed synthetic voice is a deep fake that breaches the transparency duty and edges into the prohibition on deceptive AI. In short: the core creative concept is illegal and cannot be salvaged by tweaks — the cloned voice must be removed entirely. Do not run this campaign as submitted.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign. Remove the AI-cloned voice of the talk-show host entirely — the false endorsement is per se prohibited under UCPD Annex I point 23c and cannot be cured by a disclaimer or by adding disclosure.

Delete any statements attributing personal use or recommendation to the host (e.g., 'I sleep on a SleepWell every night'). Any endorsement must come from a real person who genuinely uses the product and has given documented, informed consent.

Do not process the host's voice further without a valid lawful basis. A voice clone of an identifiable person is personal data and likely special-category biometric data, requiring the individual's explicit consent — which does not exist here. Delete the cloned voice model and outputs.
Rebuild the spot using a licensed actor or a clearly fictional voice, with all claims truthful and substantiated.

If any synthetic/AI-generated voice is used in a future version (with full consent), add a clear, timely audible disclosure in the spot and in the podcast description that the voice is AI-generated, and ensure the audio carries machine-readable provenance marking (AI Act Art. 50).

Have legal/compliance review the media plan note that the clone 'tested 40% better than an actor' — this documents intent to deceive and would aggravate enforcement exposure; do not rely on or repeat this rationale.

campaign.title: LumaSkin serum — AI visuals
campaign.text: Cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum. All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated. Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'. No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere. Claim on pack-shot overlay: 'Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study).

detected_practices: AI-generated before/after results imagery
fabricated before/after pairs
AI-smoothing filter on presenter
false claim of 'zero filter, zero editing'
no synthetic-content/AI disclosure
unsubstantiated efficacy claim ('Clinically proven -71% wrinkles')
fake 'clinically proven' claim based on 12-employee internal survey, no clinical study
misleading health/cosmetic performance claims
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is women 30-55; no personalisation/targeting declared and no personal data processing indicated. Minors are not the intended audience, but distribution on social/video platforms could incidentally reach some minors — primary risk lies elsewhere.
triage.summary: Consumer cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum on social and video channels, targeting women 30-55 in the EU. It uses generative AI to fabricate before/after results imagery and an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter, who falsely claims 'zero filter, zero editing', with no synthetic-content disclosure and a deceptive 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' claim backed only by an internal 12-employee survey. The undisclosed synthetic content and unsubstantiated efficacy claims raise significant misleading-practice and AI-transparency concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The before/after imagery and the AI-smoothing filter applied to the presenter are AI-manipulated image and video content depicting a real product/real person in a way that falsely appears authentic — i.e. deep-fake-type manipulated content within Art. 50(4). As deployer, the marketer must disclose that this content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign states there is 'No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere', so the disclosure obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated. Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent viewer-facing disclosure on all AI-generated/manipulated visuals and clips (e.g. 'AI-generated image' / 'AI-enhanced footage / dramatisation'). Do not present AI-smoothed footage as unedited reality.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign relies on synthetic image and video outputs generated by the company's image model and AI-smoothing filter. Art. 50(2) requires such AI-generated/manipulated outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. No provenance marking is applied anywhere, so this transparency obligation is not satisfied for the campaign assets.
findings.evidence_quote: No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated and AI-manipulated assets carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA content credentials / watermarking) confirming they are artificially generated or manipulated, in addition to human-visible disclosure.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: AI (the smoothing filter and fabricated results imagery) is deployed in a purposefully deceptive way — the AI-altered appearance is expressly presented as unedited reality — with the effect of impairing consumers' ability to make an informed purchasing decision about the serum's real performance. This engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques that materially distort behaviour. Confidence is moderate because the provision requires the distortion to cause or be reasonably likely to cause 'significant harm', a threshold whose application to cosmetics-efficacy deception is uncertain and whose core is better addressed under the UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'
findings.recommendation: Cease using AI to manipulate imagery in a way that misrepresents real product results; remove the false 'zero filter, zero editing' statement and any fabricated before/after pairs. Only depict genuine, substantiated results, with AI use transparently disclosed.

verdicts.notes: The campaign extensively uses generative AI to fabricate realistic before/after results and applies an AI-smoothing filter to the presenter, all presented as authentic with no synthetic-content disclosure or provenance marking. This clearly breaches the AI Act's transparency obligations: Art. 50(4) (deep fake / manipulated realistic image and video disclosure) and Art. 50(2) (machine-readable marking of AI-generated content). The deliberately deceptive deployment of AI (a filter presented as "zero filter, zero editing") also engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques, though the "significant harm" threshold and the core efficacy-deception aspects are more squarely UCPD matters.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is distributed as advertising on online platforms (social and video). DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, in real time, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. While the labelling duty falls on the platform provider, the advertiser must cooperate so that its ads are clearly identifiable; the submission gives no indication of ad-identification arrangements, and the pervasive use of fabricated 'real skin' imagery risks the material being perceived as organic/authentic content rather than paid advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: social, video
findings.recommendation: Ensure all placements are delivered through the platforms' paid/branded-content advertising tools so they are automatically labelled as advertisements with the advertiser's identity disclosed, and add clear 'ad'/'sponsored' and brand attribution to any presenter-led social clips so their commercial nature is unambiguous in real time.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits online-platform interfaces that deceive or manipulate recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions (e.g. disguised advertisements, deceptive design). This campaign's deceptive assets (fabricated before/after pairs, AI-smoothed footage falsely presented as unedited) are content-level deception rather than platform interface design, so Art. 25 is not directly breached by the advertiser; it is flagged for context because the same deceptive conduct is squarely addressed under the UCPD (misleading practices) and AI Act (synthetic-content transparency), which apply to all traders.
findings.evidence_quote: she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'
findings.recommendation: Address the deception through UCPD/AI Act compliance (substantiate or remove the '-71% wrinkles' and 'zero filter' claims and disclose all AI-generated/manipulated imagery); no DSA Art. 25 action is required of the advertiser directly, but retain evidence that platform placements are not designed to disguise their advertising nature.

verdicts.notes: The DSA imposes obligations chiefly on providers of online platforms (interface design, ad labelling, minor protection, ad repositories), not directly on advertisers. This cosmetics campaign's core wrongs — undisclosed AI/synthetic content and the false "clinically proven"/"zero filter" claims — are content-level misleading-advertising and AI-transparency issues addressed under the UCPD and AI Act, not DSA interface obligations. Within the DSA, only advertising transparency (Art. 26(1)) is lightly engaged because the ads run on social/video platforms and must be identifiable as advertisements; there is no profiling, sensitive-data targeting, or minor targeting to trigger Arts. 26(3)/28. Art. 25 (dark patterns) is contextually relevant to the deceptive nature of the assets but targets platform interface design rather than this advertiser's conduct.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Stating a product is 'clinically proven' to reduce wrinkles by a precise 71% when the only basis is an internal survey of 12 employees and no clinical study exists is false information about the product's main characteristics (benefits/results) and about the trader's testing/qualifications. Such a specific, science-sounding efficacy figure is highly likely to cause the average consumer to buy a product they would not otherwise purchase, meeting the Art. 6 misleading-action test.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study)
findings.recommendation: Remove the '-71%' figure and the word 'clinically' unless supported by a genuine, methodologically sound clinical study on the actual product; otherwise substitute an accurate, substantiated and clearly qualified claim (e.g. consumer self-assessment results with sample size and method disclosed).

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Presenting AI-fabricated before/after imagery as genuine product 'results' is false information about the main characteristics and results the product delivers. Before/after visuals are a primary decision driver in cosmetics; fabricated pairs deceive the average consumer about achievable outcomes and constitute a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated
findings.recommendation: Do not present synthetic or fabricated imagery as real product results. Use only genuine, unretouched images of actual outcomes, or clearly label imagery as illustrative/AI-generated and non-representative of results — and ensure any implied performance is separately substantiated.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The presenter expressly states her skin is real and unedited while an AI-smoothing filter is applied to her image. This is a direct false statement of fact about the nature of the depicted result, deceiving consumers into attributing the on-screen appearance to the serum. It is a textbook misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing
findings.recommendation: Remove the AI-smoothing filter, or delete the 'zero filter, zero editing' claim and clearly disclose that the footage is AI-enhanced. Any statement about the presenter's skin must be truthful and not attribute filter effects to the product.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic origin of the results imagery and the filtered presenter footage is material information the average consumer needs to correctly assess the product's claimed performance. Failing to disclose (or actively hiding) the artificial basis of the 'results' is a misleading omission under Art. 7, compounding the misleading actions and reinforcing the deception about efficacy.
findings.evidence_quote: No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Add clear, prominent disclosures that the before/after visuals and presenter footage are AI-generated/AI-enhanced and do not represent real product results, placed where the average consumer will notice them at the point the imagery is shown.

verdicts.notes: The campaign contains multiple clear breaches of the UCPD. The "Clinically proven -71% wrinkles" claim is false — backed only by an internal 12-employee survey with no clinical study — and the fabricated before/after imagery and the presenter's "zero filter, zero editing" statement (while an AI-smoothing filter runs) are all misleading actions under Art. 6 that would distort the transactional decisions of the average consumer. The complete absence of any disclosure that the "results" and presenter imagery are AI-synthesised is a misleading omission of material information under Art. 7. Annex I point 17 (false cure) is not engaged, as ageing/wrinkles are not illness.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets the LumaSkin anti-ageing serum using AI-fabricated before/after imagery, an AI-smoothing filter applied to the presenter, and a "Clinically proven -71% wrinkles" claim — with no disclosure that any of the visuals are AI-generated. The specialists found this campaign carries serious, overlapping legal problems. The most severe are consumer-protection breaches (UCPD): the "clinically proven -71%" figure is backed only by an internal survey of 12 employees with no actual clinical study, the before/after results are entirely fabricated, and the presenter falsely says "zero filter, zero editing" while a filter is running — all of these are the kind of false claims that would drive a purchase decision and are treated as critical misleading actions. Separately, the AI Act is very likely breached: the fabricated and AI-smoothed content must be disclosed to viewers and carry machine-readable provenance marking, and none is present. There are also lighter DSA advertising-transparency points to tidy up (making sure the placements are clearly labelled as ads). In short: the campaign as described is not runnable and needs substantial rework, not minor edits. Both the deceptive efficacy claims and the undisclosed AI content must be fixed before any launch.
report.recommendations: Remove the "Clinically proven -71% wrinkles" claim entirely — do not use "clinically" or a precise percentage unless you have a genuine, methodologically sound clinical study on the actual product. An internal survey of 12 employees does not support this claim.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 39 requires very large online platforms to maintain a public ad repository containing ad content, advertiser, payer and targeting parameters. recommendations: Do not run this campaign in its current form — the core assets are deceptive and legally indefensible.
Remove all AI-fabricated before/after imagery. Use only genuine, unretouched images that document real product outcomes, or drop results imagery entirely.
Delete the 'zero filter, zero editing' authenticity claim, OR remove the AI-smoothing filter from the presenter footage — never combine an authenticity claim with manipulated video.

Remove the 'Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' claim entirely; an internal 12-employee survey cannot support 'clinically proven'. Only reinstate if backed by a genuine, methodologically sound clinical study, with sample size and method disclosed.

Add clear, prominent human-readable disclosures on every asset that uses AI-generated or AI-enhanced imagery/video (e.g. 'AI-generated illustration', 'video enhanced with AI filter') to meet AI Act Art. 50(4) and UCPD Art. 7.
Ensure all AI-generated/manipulated visuals carry machine-readable synthetic-content marking (e.g. C2PA provenance metadata or watermarking) per AI Act Art. 50(2).

Assume any social/video ad on a very large online platform will be permanently and publicly archived under DSA Art. 39 — only distribute content that can withstand regulator, researcher and competitor scrutiny.
Have legal/compliance sign off on revised creative and all efficacy claims before re-submitting the campaign for distribution.

campaign.title: LumaSkin serum — AI visuals
campaign.text: Cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum. All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated. Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'. No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere. Claim on pack-shot overlay: 'Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study).

detected_practices: AI-generated before/after imagery
fabricated results imagery from single base photo
AI-smoothing filter on presenter
false 'zero filter, zero editing' claim (contradicts actual AI filter use)
no AI/synthetic-content disclosure
unsubstantiated 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' health/efficacy claim
misleading substantiation (internal survey of 12 employees presented as clinical study)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is women 30-55; on open social/video channels reach is broad but minors are not a specific target. UCPD is strongly engaged (misleading actions/omissions, false clinical claim, deceptive 'no filter' statement). AI Act transparency obligations apply to generative/deepfake content lacking disclosure. DSA relevant given dissemination via online platforms and the absence of synthetic-content labelling. Personalisation/targeting declared as none, so GDPR not clearly engaged based on submitted facts.
triage.summary: Cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum distributed on social and video channels to women 30-55 in the EU, relying entirely on AI-generated and manipulated imagery. It fabricates before/after results, applies an AI-smoothing filter while explicitly claiming 'zero filter, zero editing,' provides no synthetic-content disclosure, and makes an unsubstantiated 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' claim backed only by an internal 12-employee survey.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The presenter is a real person whose image/video is AI-manipulated by an AI-smoothing filter to appear authentic and unedited. AI-generated/manipulated realistic image or video of a real person constitutes a deep fake under Art. 50(4), triggering a deployer obligation to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Here there is no disclosure, and the effect is aggravated by the express 'zero filter, zero editing' statement that actively denies the manipulation. The fabricated before/after pairs derived from a single real base photo are likewise AI-manipulated realistic depictions requiring disclosure.
findings.evidence_quote: Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'. No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure on all affected clips and result imagery stating that the footage/images have been artificially generated or manipulated with AI (e.g., an on-screen 'AI-manipulated / filtered' label), and remove the contradictory 'zero filter, zero editing' claim. Disclosure must be visible at first exposure, not buried in captions.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The 'results' visuals are outputs of a generative image model (synthetic image content). Art. 50(2) requires that outputs of AI systems generating synthetic image/video content be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign states there is no synthetic-content disclosure or marking anywhere, so this provider-side marking obligation appears unmet for all AI-generated assets used in the campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated visual assets carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., C2PA/content credentials or equivalent watermarking) identifying them as artificially generated, and confirm the image model provider applies compliant marking to outputs before they are published.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign is deceptive, but the deception is driven by false human-authored marketing copy and undisclosed use of a filter rather than by an AI system deploying subliminal/manipulative techniques designed to materially distort behaviour causing significant harm. The Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition threshold is therefore not clearly met on the submitted facts; the deceptive/false-claim aspects are more squarely addressed under UCPD by the parallel review. Flagged for context only.
findings.evidence_quote: she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'
findings.recommendation: No AI Act Art. 5 action required on current facts; ensure the transparency fixes under Art. 50(2)/(4) are implemented and that claims are truthful so the campaign does not rely on AI-enabled deception.

verdicts.notes: The campaign relies entirely on generative-AI and AI-manipulated imagery/video with explicitly declared use of generative AI, yet provides "no AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere." This directly engages the AI Act Art. 50 transparency obligations: Art. 50(2) (machine-readable marking of synthetic content) and Art. 50(4) (disclosure of deep fakes / AI-manipulated realistic footage of a real person). Both obligations are engaged and, on the submitted facts, unmet. The Art. 5 prohibitions are noted but the manipulation here stems from false human-authored claims rather than a prohibited AI technique, so it is flagged only for context.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

The DSA obligations in scope (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) bind providers of online platforms and/or turn on ad-targeting, profiling and interface design. This submission is advertiser-side creative material: it declares no personalisation/targeting, does not specifically target minors, and describes no online-interface manipulation (no confirm-shaming, forced continuity, obstruction of cancellation, or disguised-ad interface). The campaign's genuine wrongs — fabricated before/after imagery, the false 'zero filter, zero editing' claim, undisclosed synthetic content, and the unsubstantiated 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' claim — are misleading-practice and AI-transparency issues addressed under the UCPD and AI Act, not DSA obligations on this advertiser. On the submitted facts the DSA is not meaningfully engaged.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: This is false information about the product's main characteristics (results/benefits) and about the trader's substantiation. The word 'clinically proven' with a precise -71% figure asserts scientific/clinical evidence, but the only support is an internal survey of 12 employees with no clinical study. This deceives the average consumer and is likely to cause a transactional decision (purchase) they would not otherwise take — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically proven -71% wrinkles
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'clinically proven' wording and the -71% figure unless a genuine, methodologically sound clinical study substantiates the exact claim. An internal 12-employee survey cannot support a 'clinically proven' claim; if retained at all, any efficacy statement must be truthful, qualified, and match the actual evidence and test conditions.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The before/after imagery presents product 'results' that never occurred — they are entirely AI-fabricated from a single base photo. This is false information about the results and performance of the product and materially deceives consumers about what the serum actually achieves, a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated
findings.recommendation: Do not present AI-fabricated imagery as real product results. Any before/after visuals must depict genuine, representative outcomes achieved with the product under disclosed conditions; illustrative or digitally enhanced imagery must be clearly labelled and must not misrepresent achievable results.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The presenter's statement is directly contradicted by the campaign's own facts: an AI-smoothing filter is applied to her while she speaks. This is a plainly false statement about the nature and appearance of the product's effect on skin, deceiving consumers about what the serum delivers — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'zero filter, zero editing' claim wherever any filter, smoothing or editing is in fact applied. Statements about being unedited must be literally true; if any AI or beauty filter is used, do not claim the footage is unfiltered.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic/AI-generated and manipulated nature of the visuals is material information the average consumer needs to correctly assess the imagery and claims. Presenting fabricated and filtered content as authentic without disclosing its synthetic origin hides material information and is a misleading omission under Art. 7. (This runs alongside AI Act transparency duties handled separately.)
findings.evidence_quote: No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere
findings.recommendation: Add clear, prominent disclosure that the imagery and presenter footage are AI-generated/AI-manipulated wherever they appear, so consumers are not misled about the authenticity of the visuals and results.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD very strongly. It contains multiple misleading actions under Art. 6: an unsubstantiated "clinically proven -71% wrinkles" efficacy claim backed only by an internal 12-employee survey, fully fabricated AI before/after "results" imagery, and a directly false "zero filter, zero editing" statement while an AI-smoothing filter is applied. The complete absence of any synthetic-content disclosure is also a misleading omission of material information under Art. 7. The blacklist false-cure point (Annex I, 17) is not a clean fit because wrinkle reduction is an aesthetic/cosmetic claim rather than a claim to cure an illness, dysfunction or malformation, so these are assessed under the general misleading-practice articles.

report.executive_summary: This campaign for the LumaSkin anti-ageing serum has critical compliance problems and should not run in its current form. Its core selling points are all deceptive: the "clinically proven -71% wrinkles" claim rests only on an internal survey of 12 employees (not a clinical study), the before/after "results" are entirely AI-fabricated from a single photo, and the presenter says "zero filter, zero editing" while an AI-smoothing filter is actually applied to her. Under the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive these are misleading actions likely to drive purchase decisions consumers would not otherwise make, plus a misleading omission because the synthetic nature of the visuals is never disclosed. Under the EU AI Act, the manipulated presenter footage is a "deep fake" requiring disclosure (Art. 50(4)), and the AI-generated visuals need machine-readable synthetic-content marking (Art. 50(2)) — none of which is present. GDPR and DSA were reviewed and are not meaningfully engaged (no targeting/personalisation declared, no platform-side obligations). Bottom line: the campaign cannot go live until the false claims are removed or properly substantiated and full AI/synthetic-content disclosure is added.
recommendations: Do not publish the campaign as-is; the false efficacy claim, fabricated results, and false 'unedited' statement are each independently serious violations.

Remove 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' entirely unless you have a genuine, methodologically sound clinical study that substantiates the exact figure — an internal 12-employee survey cannot support a 'clinically proven' claim.
Remove all AI-fabricated before/after imagery presented as real product results; any efficacy visuals must show genuine, representative outcomes under disclosed conditions.
Delete the 'zero filter, zero editing' line wherever any filter or smoothing is applied; statements about being unedited must be literally true.

Add clear, prominent, first-exposure disclosure that the presenter footage and result imagery are AI-generated/AI-manipulated (e.g. an on-screen 'AI-manipulated' label), satisfying both UCPD Art. 7 and AI Act Art. 50(4).

Ensure all AI-generated visual assets carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA content credentials or watermarking) per AI Act Art. 50(2), and confirm your image-model provider applies compliant marking before publication.
Re-submit the revised campaign for compliance review once claims are substantiated/removed and disclosures are in place.

campaign.title: BankEase 'alerts' cross-sell
campaign.text: A banking app's push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'. The bank now sends through the same channel: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps'), insurance cross-sells after large card purchases, and 'investment nudges' on salary day. Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts. Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.

detected_practices: consent obtained for security alerts repurposed for marketing (bait/misuse of permission)
behavioural targeting based on account events (low-balance, large purchases, salary day)
marketing pushes visually identical to security/fraud alerts (disguised advertising)
pre-approved credit offer triggered by low-balance events
insurance cross-sell after large card purchases
investment nudges timed to salary day
dark pattern: single on/off toggle bundling marketing with essential fraud alerts
personalised financial product offers
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult banking customers in the EU; no indication of minors, though banks may have some younger account holders. Key concern is the vulnerability of consumers targeted at financially sensitive moments (low balance, salary day).
triage.summary: A banking app uses a push-notification permission obtained for 'security and important account alerts' to send behaviourally-targeted marketing (personal loans on low balance, insurance after large purchases, investment nudges on salary day) that is visually indistinguishable from genuine security/fraud alerts. Users cannot opt out of marketing without also disabling fraud alerts, a coercive bundling design. The campaign relies on personal account/transaction data for targeting but declares no generative AI use.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Consent/permission was obtained for a security purpose and then repurposed to send marketing (loan, insurance, investment offers) through the same channel, with marketing pushes made visually identical to security alerts. This is covert/misleading processing that breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle — data subjects were not told their permission and account/transaction data would be used for cross-sell marketing, and the disguise defeats their ability to understand the true nature of the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Enable notifications for security and important account alerts
findings.recommendation: Separate the security-alert channel from marketing entirely. Only process personal/account data for marketing after obtaining a distinct, transparent legal basis, and clearly label marketing communications so they cannot be confused with security alerts.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent purportedly covering marketing is not specific or informed: the permission text refers only to security/account alerts, not marketing. Consent must be specific to each purpose; a security-alerts permission cannot lawfully double as marketing consent, so there is no valid consent for the marketing pushes or the profiling behind them.
findings.evidence_quote: push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Request a separate, specific and informed opt-in for marketing communications that names the purpose (personalised product offers) and the data used, distinct from the security-notification permission.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given and as easy to withdraw as to give, and must not be bundled. Forcing users to disable essential fraud alerts in order to stop marketing makes withdrawal of the marketing 'consent' impossible without detriment, so the consent is not freely given and the withdrawal mechanism is non-compliant.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Provide granular, independent controls: users must be able to switch off marketing pushes while keeping security/fraud alerts on, with withdrawal as easy as the original opt-in.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Using account and transaction data to profile customers and target them with financial-product marketing is processing that requires a valid lawful basis. Consent is invalid (obtained for security only) and legitimate interests are unlikely to survive a balancing test given the intrusive, financially-sensitive targeting and the disguise, so the marketing processing lacks a lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: insurance cross-sells after large card purchases, and 'investment nudges' on salary day
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis (properly obtained consent, or a documented legitimate-interests assessment) before using transaction data for marketing; cease the processing until a lawful basis is in place.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing account balance, purchase size and salary timing to predict a customer's economic situation and target offers is automated profiling within Art. 4(4). This triggers the full set of profiling obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights), which the campaign does not satisfy.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events
findings.recommendation: Treat the event-based targeting as profiling: document it, give it a lawful basis, disclose it, and honour objection rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing, including profiling for marketing, is absolute and must be facilitated. Because the only way to stop marketing also disables fraud alerts, customers cannot exercise their right to object to marketing without losing an essential security service, so the right is not respected.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Offer a clear, cost-free way to object to marketing (and marketing profiling) that stops those messages while preserving security alerts, and honour the objection immediately and permanently.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point the permission is collected, no information is given about the marketing/profiling purpose, the legal basis, or the customer's rights (including the right to object). Art. 13 requires this information, including about profiling, at collection; the security-only framing omits it.
findings.evidence_quote: Enable notifications for security and important account alerts
findings.recommendation: Provide layered Art. 13 information at permission/sign-up covering the marketing purpose, the transaction-data profiling, the lawful basis, and the right to object.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: If pre-approval and the credit amount are determined solely by automated analysis of account events, this may constitute automated decision-making producing legal or similarly significant effects (credit eligibility/pricing), engaging Art. 22 safeguards, which are not evidenced.
findings.evidence_quote: Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether pre-approval decisions are solely automated; if so, ensure an Art. 22 exception applies and implement safeguards (meaningful information, right to human intervention and to contest).

verdicts.notes: The campaign relies on a push-permission obtained purely for "security and important account alerts" to deliver behaviourally-targeted marketing, disguises marketing as security alerts, and bundles marketing opt-out with essential fraud alerts. This breaches the GDPR fairness/transparency principle, invalidates any consent, leaves the marketing profiling without a lawful basis, and defeats the absolute right to object to direct marketing. Several distinct high/critical GDPR issues are present.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Under Art. 7(2) a practice is misleading where it fails to identify the commercial intent of the practice if not apparent from context. The permission was obtained for 'security and important account alerts', and marketing messages (loan, insurance and investment offers) are sent through the same channel and made visually identical to genuine security/fraud alerts. This hides the commercial nature of the communications; the average consumer cannot recognise them as advertising and may open/act on them believing they are safety-critical alerts, distorting their transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and visibly label all marketing pushes as advertising (e.g. an unmistakable 'Ad'/'Offer' tag, distinct visual style, colour and icon from security alerts) so the commercial intent is immediately apparent, and separate the marketing channel from the security-alert channel.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, by coercion or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice, considering timing, exploitation of the consumer's situation and onerous barriers to exercising rights. Here consumers can only stop unwanted marketing by also switching off fraud/security alerts — an onerous, coercive barrier that exploits their reliance on safety notifications. This is compounded by timing offers to exploit vulnerable moments ('personal-loan offers after low-balance events', 'investment nudges on salary day'), pressuring transactional decisions consumers might not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Provide granular, independent controls so users can disable marketing pushes while keeping fraud/security alerts on. Stop tying essential safety notifications to marketing consent, and stop timing product pushes to financially sensitive events (low balance, salary day) that exploit the consumer's economic situation.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net prohibiting practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort economic behaviour, and requires assessment from the perspective of vulnerable groups where a practice targets them. Pushing pre-approved credit precisely when a customer is financially stressed ('Running low?'), through a trusted safety channel, falls below the professional diligence expected of a bank and is likely to distort the decisions of consumers who are in a fragile economic situation. This backstops the Art. 7 and Arts. 8-9 findings.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps')
findings.recommendation: Adopt a responsible-marketing policy that suppresses credit and high-commitment financial offers triggered by signs of financial distress; document professional-diligence safeguards for behavioural targeting of banking customers.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits misleading actions regarding the main characteristics, price or existence of a specific advantage of a product. A firm 'Pre-approved €3,000' claim is misleading if the offer is in fact subject to further affordability/credit checks, undisclosed conditions or costs (interest/APR), causing consumers to take a transactional decision (tapping to accept) they would not otherwise take. As described, key credit terms are omitted and the certainty implied by 'pre-approved' may not be genuine.
findings.evidence_quote: Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps
findings.recommendation: Only use 'pre-approved' where the credit is genuinely guaranteed without further checks; otherwise use accurate wording and disclose all material terms (APR, total cost, conditions) up front before the consumer can accept.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes a push-notification channel that users authorised for "security and important account alerts" to deliver behaviourally-targeted product marketing that is visually indistinguishable from genuine fraud/security alerts. This disguises the commercial intent of the communications (Art. 7) and, combined with timing that exploits financially sensitive moments and a coercive single toggle that forces users to disable fraud alerts to stop marketing, likely amounts to an aggressive practice by undue influence (Arts. 8-9) and breaches the general fairness/professional-diligence standard (Art. 5). The "pre-approved" credit claim also engages Art. 6 if not genuinely substantiated.

report.executive_summary: This campaign reuses a push-notification channel that customers only agreed to for "security and important account alerts" to send targeted marketing — personal loans, insurance and investment offers — timed to sensitive financial moments like low balances and salary day. Because the marketing pushes are made to look identical to genuine security/fraud alerts, and the only way to switch them off also disables fraud alerts, the campaign carries serious and overlapping legal risks. Under GDPR this is a critical problem: the permission was obtained for security only, so there is no valid consent or lawful basis for the marketing and profiling, the setup is neither fair nor transparent, and customers cannot exercise their right to object without losing essential safety notifications. Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, disguising ads as safety alerts hides their commercial intent (misleading), tying opt-out to fraud alerts and timing offers to moments of financial stress is likely an aggressive practice, and the firm "pre-approved €3,000" claim may be misleading if further checks apply. The AI Act and DSA were assessed as not applicable. This campaign should not go live in its current form — the disguise, the bundled toggle, and the distress-timed targeting each need fixing before launch.
report.recommendations: Stop sending marketing through the security-alert channel immediately, and cease the transaction-based marketing profiling until a valid lawful basis is in place.

campaign.title: BankEase 'alerts' cross-sell
campaign.text: A banking app's push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'. The bank now sends through the same channel: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps'), insurance cross-sells after large card purchases, and 'investment nudges' on salary day. Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts. Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.

detected_practices: consent obtained for security alerts repurposed for marketing (dark pattern)
marketing messages disguised as security/account alerts
behavioural targeting based on account events (low balance, large purchase, salary day)
urgency/scarcity framing ('Running low?', 'Pre-approved in 2 taps')
single on/off toggle bundling fraud alerts with marketing (no granular opt-out)
cross-selling financial products (loans, insurance, investments) via push
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult banking customers in the EU; no indication minors are targeted, though push notifications reach whoever holds the account. Personalisation is declared and driven by sensitive financial behaviour (balance, spending, salary timing).
triage.summary: A banking app repurposes a push channel—whose permission was obtained for security/account alerts—to deliver behaviourally targeted marketing (loan offers after low balances, insurance after large purchases, investment nudges on payday) that is visually indistinguishable from genuine security alerts. Users can only disable marketing by also disabling fraud alerts via a single toggle. The disguise, deceptive consent framing, and event-based profiling raise clear UCPD (misleading/aggressive practices) and GDPR (purpose limitation, consent, profiling) concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires that data subjects are not misled about how their data and channels are used. Disguising behaviourally targeted marketing as genuine security/account alerts, on a channel whose permission was framed as being for 'security and important account alerts', is a covert/misleading use of personal data that breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and visually distinguish marketing pushes from security alerts (distinct labelling, styling, and 'marketing' tagging), and be transparent that the channel is used for commercial offers. Do not present promotional content in a form indistinguishable from safety-critical alerts.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised marketing profiling requires a valid lawful basis (consent or a balanced legitimate-interest assessment). The only permission obtained relates to security/account alerts, an incompatible purpose from marketing; there is no lawful basis established for using the same channel and behavioural data for cross-sell marketing. Repurposing data collected for one purpose to an incompatible marketing purpose lacks a valid Art. 6 basis.
findings.evidence_quote: push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a separate lawful basis for marketing pushes and behavioural profiling — in practice a fresh, specific opt-in consent — and stop sending marketing until it is obtained. Do not rely on the security-alert permission.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and bundled consent does not qualify. The permission was framed solely around security/account alerts, so it is not specific or informed consent for marketing. Bundling security and marketing under one framing means users could not give an unambiguous, specific indication of agreement to receiving commercial offers.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Obtain granular, purpose-specific consent for marketing pushes separate from operational/security notifications, using clear language that names the marketing purpose. Do not infer marketing consent from a security-alerts opt-in.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that withdrawing consent be as easy as giving it and that consent be clearly distinguishable and not bundled with unnecessary elements. Forcing users to disable essential fraud alerts in order to stop marketing makes withdrawal punitive rather than free, and bundles marketing with a safety-critical service, undermining the validity of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Provide a separate, easy toggle to switch off marketing pushes while keeping fraud/security alerts active. Ensure opting out of marketing carries no detriment to security notifications.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling, and controllers must facilitate that opt-out. Here the only way to object to marketing is to also disable fraud alerts — the right to object is not respected or facilitated in a standalone, cost-free manner.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Offer a dedicated, one-step mechanism to object to marketing and marketing profiling that does not affect any other service, and honour objections immediately and permanently.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing account balance, spending patterns and salary timing to predict economic situation and trigger tailored offers is automated evaluation of personal aspects — i.e., profiling under Art. 4(4). This confirms profiling is taking place and pulls in the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps'), insurance cross-sells after large card purchases, and 'investment nudges' on salary day
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling activity, ensure it rests on a valid lawful basis and that data subjects are informed of it and can object; conduct a DPIA given the sensitive financial-behaviour and vulnerability dimension.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data (financial behaviour) is used for profiling and marketing, the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of profiling, and of the right to object. The security-alert framing gives no such information about marketing/profiling, so the Art. 13 transparency obligations are not met at the point the data is repurposed.
findings.evidence_quote: 'investment nudges' on salary day
findings.recommendation: Provide clear information — at permission time and in the privacy notice — that account data will be used to profile customers for personalised marketing offers, the legal basis, and how to object; surface this before any marketing push is sent.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes a push channel — permission for which was obtained under a security/account-alerts framing — to deliver behaviourally targeted marketing, without a valid lawful basis or valid consent for the marketing purpose. Consent obtained for one purpose (security) cannot be relied on for an incompatible marketing purpose, and the security framing plus a single fraud+marketing toggle mean any consent is neither specific, freely given, nor as easy to withdraw as to give. The targeting is profiling on sensitive financial behaviour that requires transparency and a facilitated right to object. Multiple GDPR obligations are engaged and likely breached.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Push permission was obtained for 'security and important account alerts', and marketing messages are delivered through the same channel while being visually indistinguishable from genuine security alerts. Their commercial intent is therefore hidden and not apparent from context. Art. 7 makes it misleading to fail to identify the commercial intent of a practice; disguising advertising as neutral/urgent security communications is a textbook misleading omission and hidden-commercial-intent practice that distorts consumer decision-making.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and unmistakably label every marketing push as advertising (e.g. 'Ad'/'Offer' tag and distinct visual styling/icon/colour), and visually separate marketing from genuine security and fraud alerts so consumers can immediately recognise the commercial nature of the message.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Offers are systematically timed to moments of financial vulnerability — low-balance events (loan offers), payday (investment nudges), and large purchases (insurance) — exploiting the consumer's situation to prompt a transactional decision through undue influence and pressure ('in 2 taps'). Additionally, the only way to stop the marketing is a single toggle that also disables fraud alerts, an onerous barrier that coerces consumers into continuing to receive marketing to keep essential security protection. Both the exploitative timing and the burdensome opt-out are aggressive-practice factors under Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps')
findings.recommendation: Stop timing commercial offers to low-balance or spending events; do not exploit financial stress moments. Provide granular notification controls that let consumers switch off marketing while keeping fraud/security alerts, removing any penalty for declining marketing.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Consumers receive repeated event-triggered marketing pushes and have no genuine, proportionate way to refuse them — the only 'off' switch sacrifices fraud alerts. Marketing that a consumer cannot effectively decline, and that continues through a channel they cannot selectively opt out of, can amount to persistent and unwanted solicitation through remote media, which is prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Implement a functioning, standalone marketing opt-out and honour it immediately, ensuring no further commercial pushes are sent once a consumer has declined or disabled marketing communications.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The 'Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps' claim may deceive the average consumer about the nature and conditions of the credit product — implying that the loan is guaranteed, condition-free and instant when approval is typically subject to affordability/credit checks and contractual terms. If the pre-approval is qualified or conditional, this is a misleading action as to the main characteristics of the product.
findings.evidence_quote: Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps
findings.recommendation: Only state 'pre-approved' where the offer is genuinely binding without further checks; otherwise qualify the claim clearly (e.g. 'subject to eligibility and affordability checks') and disclose key terms (APR, repayment) before the consumer acts.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages several UCPD prohibitions. Most seriously, marketing pushes are "visually identical to security alerts" and sent through a channel the consumer authorised only for "security and important account alerts," concealing their commercial intent (Art. 7 — hidden commercial intent / disguised advertising). The behavioural timing of offers to moments of financial stress (low balance, payday, large purchases) combined with a single toggle that forces users to lose fraud alerts to stop marketing raises aggressive-practice concerns (Arts. 8-9) and can amount to persistent unwanted solicitation (Annex I point 26). The "Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps" claim may also mislead as to the nature/conditions of the credit (Art. 6). These are separately assessed under GDPR by another agent.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses the banking app's push channel — which customers only agreed to for "security and important account alerts" — to send behaviourally targeted cross-sell offers (loans, insurance, investment nudges) that look identical to genuine security alerts. That disguise is the core problem: it hides the commercial intent of your marketing and misuses a channel customers trusted for safety-critical warnings. The offers are also timed to moments of financial stress (low balance, payday, big purchases), and the only way to switch marketing off is a single toggle that also kills fraud alerts. Consumer-protection specialists flag this as hidden commercial intent, aggressive practice, and effectively unstoppable solicitation under the UCPD, while data-protection specialists find you have no valid consent or lawful basis for the marketing and profiling, and no genuine way for customers to object. In short, the campaign as described is very likely unlawful on multiple independent grounds and should not run in its current form. This carries real regulatory exposure for a regulated bank and should be halted and redesigned before any further pushes are sent.
recommendations: Stop sending marketing pushes through the security-alert channel immediately until the issues below are fixed — the campaign is very likely unlawful as currently designed.
Split the notification controls: give customers a separate, one-tap toggle to turn off marketing that never affects fraud or security alerts. Opting out of marketing must carry no downside.
Make marketing pushes visually and textually distinct from security alerts — clear 'Ad'/'Offer' labelling, different styling/icon/colour — so the commercial nature is obvious at a glance.

Obtain fresh, specific, opt-in consent for marketing pushes and for behavioural profiling, worded plainly and separate from the security-alerts permission. Do not rely on the existing security opt-in.
Stop timing offers to moments of financial vulnerability (low-balance events, payday, large purchases); this is treated as an aggressive, exploitative practice.

Fix the 'Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps' claim: only say 'pre-approved' if it is genuinely binding, otherwise qualify it and disclose key terms (APR, repayment, eligibility/affordability checks) before the customer acts.
Update the privacy notice and permission flow to disclose that account/spending data is used to profile customers for personalised offers, the legal basis, and how to object.

Conduct and document a DPIA given the profiling of sensitive financial behaviour and the vulnerability dimension, and ensure the right to object to direct marketing is honoured immediately and standalone.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Consent/permission was collected for a specific purpose (security and account alerts). Reusing the same channel and the underlying transaction data to send loan, insurance and investment marketing is a new, incompatible purpose lacking a valid lawful basis. Marketing profiling of banking customers generally requires consent or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment; the security permission does not supply it, so the marketing processing is unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Obtain a separate, specific lawful basis for marketing communications and behavioural targeting — either fresh, granular consent presented distinctly from security alerts, or a documented and balanced legitimate-interests assessment — before sending any promotional push.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; bundled consent does not qualify. Bundling marketing with essential fraud/security alerts under one toggle means users cannot consent specifically to marketing, and any 'agreement' is coerced because refusing marketing forces them to lose security protection.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Unbundle consent: provide a dedicated, freely-choosable opt-in for marketing pushes that is entirely separate from security/fraud alerts, so declining marketing never affects safety notifications.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that consent be as easy to withdraw as to give and that consent requests be clearly distinguishable. Here withdrawal of marketing consent is impossible without disabling fraud alerts, making withdrawal disproportionately costly and the consent conditional on accepting unnecessary processing.
findings.evidence_quote: single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts
findings.recommendation: Implement a granular preference centre allowing users to withdraw marketing consent independently and as easily as it was given, while retaining security alerts; keep records demonstrating valid consent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle prohibits misleading or deceptive processing. Disguising marketing as genuine security/account alerts deceives data subjects about why their data is being processed and exploits the trust associated with security messaging, rendering the processing unfair and non-transparent.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and visually distinguish marketing messages from security alerts (distinct labelling, styling and channel), and disclose that transaction data is used for marketing purposes.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling, and controllers must facilitate that objection. The only available control also disables essential fraud alerts, so users cannot exercise a marketing-specific objection without detriment, defeating the right.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Offer an explicit, cost-free way to object to/stop direct marketing and marketing profiling that leaves fraud and security alerts fully active, and honour it immediately.

findings.title: Definition of profiling

verdicts.notes: The bank processes personal transaction data (balance, purchases, salary timing) to behaviourally target marketing through a push channel for which consent was obtained only for "security and important account alerts". findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices

Exploitation of the consumer's circumstances plus an onerous barrier to declining the marketing are aggressive-practice factors (timing, exploitation of misfortune, undue influence) that impair free choice under Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps')
findings.recommendation: Do not trigger credit/product offers on financial-stress signals such as low-balance events; provide a granular notification centre where consumers can switch off marketing while retaining fraud and security alerts, so declining marketing carries no detriment.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall design — event-triggered offers timed to salary day and low-balance moments, delivered through a trust-laden security channel — is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average banking customer, and more so of financially vulnerable customers (Art. 5(3)), even where no specific blacklist item is engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: 'investment nudges' on salary day
findings.recommendation: Adopt a marketing-suppression policy around detected financial-stress events, apply affordability/vulnerability safeguards to credit prompts, and ensure the timing and framing of offers do not pressure customers into decisions they would not otherwise take.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Because a consumer cannot refuse the marketing solicitations without losing fraud/security alerts, effective objection is obstructed and the marketing pushes are effectively unwanted yet unavoidable. Where marketing continues through a channel the consumer cannot meaningfully opt out of, this approaches persistent and unwanted solicitations via remote media not justified by any contractual obligation (Annex I point 26).
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Provide a genuine, standalone opt-out for marketing communications that leaves security/fraud alerts intact, and cease sending marketing pushes to any customer who has not affirmatively chosen to receive them.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes a push channel authorised for "security and important account alerts" to deliver behaviourally-targeted marketing that is made visually indistinguishable from genuine security alerts. This hides the commercial intent of the communications (misleading omission, Art. 7) and, combined with the exploitation of financial-stress moments and a coercive single opt-out that also disables fraud alerts, amounts to an aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9) and unfair conduct contrary to professional diligence (Art. 5). No blacklisted false-urgency or false-endorsement claim is clearly present, so the findings rest on the general prohibitions.

report.executive_summary: Your BankEase campaign reuses a push notification channel that customers only agreed to for "security and important account alerts" to instead send personal-loan, insurance and investment marketing. The specialists found this creates serious legal problems under both GDPR (data protection) and the UCPD (unfair commercial practices), while the AI Act and DSA don't apply. The core issues: (1) the marketing has no valid legal basis because consent was given for security alerts, not advertising; (2) making the marketing look identical to security alerts hides its commercial nature and abuses customer trust; (3) the single on/off toggle forces customers to lose fraud protection if they want to stop marketing, so consent isn't freely given and there's no genuine way to opt out; and (4) targeting loan offers at low-balance moments and nudges on salary day exploits people at financially vulnerable times, which can be an aggressive practice. As designed, this campaign is likely unlawful in the EU and carries high regulatory and reputational risk. It should not run in its current form.

Unbundle the notification controls: create a separate marketing opt-in/opt-out that leaves fraud and security alerts fully active at all times. Declining marketing must never cost the customer their security protections.

Obtain a fresh, specific, freely-given consent for marketing communications and behavioural targeting, presented separately from the security-alert permission. The existing security permission does not cover marketing.

findings.rationale: The ads are presented on news-site content-recommendation widgets (online platforms presenting advertisements). This engages DSA Art. 26(1) (ad transparency — clear, real-time identification that content is an ad, and on whose behalf) and Art. 25 (prohibition of deceptive/disguised-ad interface design). campaign.title: HomeFix audience expansion memo
campaign.text: A home-services brand collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'. Marketing now proposes: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list, reasoning 'they are existing customers'. The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email. No sensitive data is involved and an unsubscribe link will be included.

detected_practices: email newsletter marketing
uploading customer email list to social platforms as custom audience
lookalike audience creation
behavioural/personalised targeting
repurposing data collected for transactional purposes for advertising
consent/purpose-limitation mismatch with privacy notice
triage.audience_notes: Target is past customers/adults; minors not an intended audience. Key issue is that consent/notice at collection did not cover marketing uploads or promotional email, so 'existing customer' justification (soft opt-in) is likely insufficient. Lookalike audiences also affect non-customers whose data is processed. Custom-audience uploads implicate GDPR (lawful basis, transparency, joint controllership with platform); newsletter implicates ePrivacy/consent. DSA relevant for online advertising transparency obligations on platforms; UCPD included as consumer-facing campaign.
triage.summary: A home-services brand plans to repurpose emails collected at checkout for order/service updates into promotional newsletters and to upload the full list to social platforms as custom and lookalike audiences. The original privacy notice covered neither advertising uploads nor promotional email, creating clear purpose-limitation and lawful-basis/consent concerns. Personalised targeting is involved but no generative AI or sensitive data.
