findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Emails were collected under 'Receive order updates and service information' — a transactional/service purpose. Repurposing that list for a weekly promotional newsletter and for uploading to social platforms as custom and lookalike audiences are new advertising purposes for which no lawful basis has been established. Consent given for service messages does not extend to advertising, and the bare 'existing customer' justification is insufficient: any legitimate-interest basis would require a documented balancing test, and email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (ePrivacy). Custom-audience uploads to platforms create a further, un-based disclosure to a third party.
findings.evidence_quote: reasoning 'they are existing customers'
findings.recommendation: Do not proceed on the current footing. Either (a) obtain fresh, specific opt-in consent for promotional email and for sharing/uploading contact data to social platforms, or (b) complete and document a Legitimate Interests Assessment for any processing where LIA is genuinely available — noting email marketing to this list still needs a consent/soft opt-in basis. Segment the list to only those with a valid basis; suppress everyone else.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached where data collected for a narrow, clearly-stated service purpose is silently reused for advertising the individual would not reasonably expect. Reusing service-collection emails for promotional and social-platform advertising, absent any disclosure at collection, is unfair and non-transparent processing incompatible with the original purpose (purpose limitation).
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Treat the advertising use as a new purpose requiring a compatible lawful basis and prior notice. Update the privacy notice and provide clear information to affected individuals before any new processing begins; do not rely on the original service-only notice.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 required the controller, at collection, to disclose all purposes, the legal basis, and recipients (including social platforms as recipients/co-controllers). The notice disclosed only service purposes, so individuals were never informed their data could be used for promotional email or shared with social platforms for targeting — a transparency failure that must be remedied before the new processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Provide the missing Art. 13/14 information: the advertising purposes, the lawful basis relied upon, that data will be uploaded to named social platform(s) as recipients, and the right to object. Deliver this proactively to affected data subjects before starting the new processing.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Building lookalike audiences is automated processing to evaluate and predict personal preferences, interests and behaviour, and therefore constitutes profiling. It processes the customers' data for a purpose not covered by the original notice, and lookalike modelling also affects non-customers whose data is analysed by the platform to find 'similar' individuals — engaging profiling obligations and expanding the pool of affected data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Recognise custom/lookalike targeting as profiling requiring a valid basis and transparency. Do not build lookalikes without a lawful basis and disclosure; assess whether the profiling can be justified and document the roles/joint-controllership with the platform before proceeding.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling. An email unsubscribe link addresses only the newsletter channel; it does not enable objection to the custom-audience/lookalike processing on social platforms, and the right to object was never presented to individuals at collection. The right must be explicitly offered and effective across all marketing processing.
findings.evidence_quote: an unsubscribe link will be included
findings.recommendation: Explicitly inform recipients of the right to object at the first communication and provide an effective mechanism to opt out of both the newsletter and the social-platform audience processing (e.g. removal from uploaded audiences and suppression of future uploads), honouring objections immediately and absolutely.

verdicts.notes: The brand collected emails at checkout solely for "order updates and service information" and now proposes to reuse the same list for promotional newsletters and to upload it to social platforms for custom and lookalike audiences. The original purpose and privacy notice covered neither activity, so there is no valid lawful basis and a clear breach of the purpose-limitation, fairness and transparency principles. The "existing customer" reasoning does not cure the lawful-basis, transparency and profiling problems under the GDPR, and lookalike creation additionally processes personal data of non-customers.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Running custom-audience and lookalike ads on an online platform means each ad presented must, under DSA Art. 26(1), be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, disclose on whose behalf and who paid for it, and expose meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. While the transparency obligation falls on the platform, HomeFix as the advertiser must provide accurate advertiser-identity and payment information and ensure the targeting parameters (customer-list custom audience / lookalike) are declarable so the platform can meet its Art. 26(1) duties.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the correct advertiser (HomeFix) is named as the entity 'on whose behalf' and 'who paid' in the platform's ad settings, and configure campaigns so the platform can surface the targeting basis (uploaded customer list / lookalike) in its 'Why am I seeing this ad?' transparency panel. Do not obscure advertiser identity behind a third party.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting platform ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special-category data. The campaign explicitly involves no sensitive data and targets a general home-services customer list, so the prohibition is not triggered as described. Flagged for awareness: if lookalike modelling or audience segments ever come to rely on inferred sensitive attributes (e.g. health, ethnicity), Art. 26(3) would apply and prohibit that targeting regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: No sensitive data is involved
findings.recommendation: Keep audience definitions free of any GDPR Art. 9 attributes or proxies; periodically verify that custom-audience and lookalike segments are not built on inferred sensitive characteristics.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs paid targeted advertising on a social platform (custom audience + lookalike audiences), which engages the DSA online-advertising transparency regime — but most DSA obligations (Art. 26, 28, 39) fall on the platform provider rather than on HomeFix as advertiser. The one directly relevant hook is Art. 26(1) ad transparency: the advertiser must supply accurate identity/"who paid" data and the targeting must be disclosable to recipients. The prohibitions on sensitive-data profiling (Art. 26(3)) and profiling ads to minors (Art. 28) are not triggered here: the campaign declares no sensitive data and targets past customers/adults only. The core lawful-basis, purpose-limitation and consent problems belong to GDPR/ePrivacy, outside this regulation's scope.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The commercial intent of the data collection was not apparent to consumers: the checkout label presented collection as transactional/service communication only, while the actual intended use is promotional newsletters and uploading the list to social platforms for custom and lookalike advertising audiences. Under Art. 7, a practice is misleading where it fails to identify commercial intent that is not apparent from context and omits material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision. A consumer told they were signing up for 'order updates and service information' would not reasonably expect their contact data to be used to fuel advertising, so the commercial intent was hidden at the decisive moment.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Do not treat the transactionally-collected list as a marketing base. At the point of collection, clearly and separately identify any marketing/advertising purpose (e.g. a distinct, unbundled opt-in for promotional email and for sharing data with social platforms) so commercial intent is apparent before the consumer provides their data. For the existing list, only send marketing to contacts for whom a lawful, transparent marketing purpose was disclosed; otherwise re-permission them with a clear statement of the promotional and ad-audience use.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Weekly promotional emails to recipients who only signed up for service/order updates could become 'unwanted solicitations'. Annex I point 26 prohibits persistent and unwanted solicitations by email. As described the practice is not yet a breach — an unsubscribe link is included and there is no indication of contacting people who have refused — but sending frequent marketing to a list that never opted into marketing raises the risk, and any continued contact after an unsubscribe/objection would fall squarely within this blacklisted practice.
findings.evidence_quote: start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list
findings.recommendation: Honour unsubscribes and objections immediately and suppress those contacts across all channels including custom-audience uploads; cap frequency and ensure every recipient had a genuine opportunity to decline marketing. Never re-contact users who have opted out with win-back sequences.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's central defects — repurposing transactionally-collected emails for advertising uploads and newsletters without covering notice/consent — are primarily GDPR/ePrivacy matters handled by other agents. Under the UCPD specifically, the relevant issue is that the data was collected under a purely transactional framing ("Receive order updates and service information") that did not identify the commercial/advertising intent, engaging Art. 7 (hidden commercial intent / misleading omission). Annex I point 26 (persistent unwanted solicitations) is not currently breached because an unsubscribe link is provided and no ignoring of opt-outs is described, but the newsletter to a non-opted-in list is a latent risk if consumers object and contact continues.

report.executive_summary: This campaign proposes to reuse an email list — collected at checkout only for "order updates and service information" — for a weekly promotional newsletter and for uploading to social platforms to build custom and lookalike advertising audiences. The core problem is that none of these advertising uses were disclosed or consented to when the emails were collected, so there is no valid legal basis for them under GDPR. The "they're existing customers" justification does not fix this: promotional email generally needs prior consent (or a narrow soft opt-in), and uploading the list to social platforms is a new disclosure to a third party that customers never agreed to. There are also transparency and fairness failures (customers were never told, and were never offered the right to object), and building lookalikes counts as profiling that also pulls in non-customers. Under consumer-protection rules, framing the collection as purely transactional hid the real commercial intent. The DSA points are minor and mostly fall on the platform, and the AI Act does not apply. Verdict: do not proceed as planned — this needs a proper legal basis, fresh consent or a documented assessment, and updated notices before any of it goes ahead.
recommendations: Do not upload the existing list to social platforms or start the newsletter on the current footing — there is no lawful basis for either advertising use.</br>

Obtain fresh, specific, unbundled opt-in consent for (a) promotional email and (b) sharing/uploading contact data to social platforms; only market to contacts who have a valid basis and suppress everyone else.

If relying on legitimate interests where genuinely available, complete and document a Legitimate Interests Assessment first — but note that direct-marketing email still needs a consent or soft opt-in basis under ePrivacy.

The original privacy notice covered neither ad uploads nor marketing email, raising clear purpose-limitation and lawful-basis concerns despite an unsubscribe link. No generative AI or sensitive data is declared.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Each of the three proposed processing operations (ad-platform upload, lookalike creation, promotional email) needs a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis. The data was gathered only for transactional 'order updates and service information'; being an 'existing customer' is not itself a lawful basis. Uploading a customer list to a social platform and building lookalikes generally requires consent (or a carefully documented, and here dubious, legitimate-interest assessment that survives a balancing test), and email direct marketing generally requires prior consent under Art. 6 read with the ePrivacy regime. No such basis exists for these new purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list, reasoning 'they are existing customers'
findings.recommendation: Do not proceed until a lawful basis is established for each purpose: obtain fresh, specific opt-in consent for promotional email and for ad-platform/custom-audience uploads, or (if relying on legitimate interests where legally available) complete and document a legitimate-interest assessment. Custom-audience uploads and lookalikes in practice require consent — seek it before any upload.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that data not be processed in ways individuals were not informed of and would not reasonably expect. Collecting emails under a narrow 'order updates' framing and then covertly repurposing them for advertising and marketing is unfair and non-transparent, and conflicts with the purpose-limitation expectation set at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email
findings.recommendation: Only process the data for purposes compatible with, and disclosed in, the original notice. For the new advertising and marketing purposes, re-inform data subjects transparently and obtain an appropriate basis before processing; do not silently expand the scope.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller disclose all purposes and legal bases, recipients (e.g. the social platform receiving the uploaded list), and data-subject rights. The checkout notice disclosed only transactional purposes and named no advertising recipients, so the information obligation was not met for the intended marketing/advertising processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email
findings.recommendation: Update the collection-time privacy notice to list all intended purposes (promotional email, ad-platform uploads, lookalike modelling), the recipient social platforms, retention periods, and the right to object. Provide this information to the existing list before any new processing begins.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent captured at checkout was tied to 'order updates and service information' only. Consent must be specific and informed for each purpose; it cannot be stretched to cover advertising uploads or promotional newsletters that were not presented to the customer. There is therefore no valid consent for the new marketing purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Collect separate, granular, freely given opt-in consent specifically for promotional email and for custom-audience/lookalike advertising, using clear language distinguishable from the transactional sign-up. Record and be able to demonstrate this consent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Custom-audience matching and lookalike generation are automated processing used to evaluate and predict personal preferences and behaviour, meeting the definition of profiling. Profiling for marketing must rest on a lawful basis, be disclosed, and respect the data subject's rights — none of which is satisfied here.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Treat the custom-audience/lookalike activity as profiling: establish and disclose a lawful basis, inform data subjects that their data will be used for audience matching and modelling, and honour objections to this profiling.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling. An email unsubscribe link addresses only the newsletter channel; it does not enable objection to the custom-audience upload and lookalike profiling, and the right to object must be actively signposted (not just an unsubscribe footer). The opt-out also does not remedy the missing lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: an unsubscribe link will be included
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, explicit way to object to all direct-marketing processing, including removal from ad-platform custom audiences and exclusion from lookalike modelling, and clearly inform recipients of this right at the first communication and at collection — not only via an email unsubscribe link.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes email addresses collected at checkout under an "order updates and service information" notice for entirely new purposes — social custom-audience uploads, lookalike building, and weekly promotional email — none of which were disclosed at collection. This breaches core GDPR obligations on lawful basis (Art. 6(1)), the lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), the collection-time information duty (Art. 13), and the standard for valid consent (Art. 4(11)). Custom-audience and lookalike processing is profiling (Art. 4(4)) requiring its own basis, and while an unsubscribe link is provided, it does not cure the absence of a lawful basis and Art. 21 rights must still be respected. No special-category data or minors are involved, so Arts. 8 and 9 are not engaged.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Running ads via a social-platform custom audience and lookalikes is profiling-based platform advertising. DSA Art. 26(1) requires that each such ad be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, that the advertiser (and who paid) be identified, and that recipients get meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. While the operational obligation rests on the online platform, the advertiser must ensure its custom-audience/lookalike campaigns are set up so the platform can surface accurate advertiser identity and targeting-parameter disclosures. The custom-audience matching key (a customer email list) must be reflected honestly in the 'why am I seeing this ad' parameters.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Ensure social ads run under a correctly identified advertiser/payer account so the platform's Art. 26(1) disclosures (ad label, advertiser identity, 'why you're seeing this' targeting parameters) are accurate; do not use targeting configurations that obscure that a matched customer list is the basis for reaching the recipient. Confirm the platform's ad-transparency features are enabled for these EU campaigns.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is only lightly engaged by this campaign. The plan to upload a customer email list as a social custom audience and build lookalikes constitutes profiling-based platform advertising, which triggers the DSA Art. 26(1) ad-transparency regime (ad labelling, advertiser identity, and disclosure of the main targeting parameters). No sensitive-category targeting is declared (Art. 26(3) not engaged) and the audience is adults/past customers, not minors (Art. 28 not engaged). No owned recommender system, dark-pattern interface, or VLOP status is present, so Arts. 25, 27 and 39 do not apply. The substantive problems — purpose repurposing, absent lawful basis for the upload and for email marketing — are GDPR/UCPD matters for other agents.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Email addresses were obtained under a framing that presents only operational, service-related purposes and a privacy notice that 'mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email'. Using that contact for a weekly promotional newsletter and for social custom-audience/lookalike advertising means the commercial (marketing/advertising) intent behind the data collection was not made apparent to the consumer at the material time. Failing to identify commercial intent, and omitting material information a consumer needs before providing their data, is a misleading omission under Art. 7. This overlaps with GDPR transparency but is independently actionable as an unfair commercial practice where the concealed purpose could affect the consumer's decision to hand over their email.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on the checkout notice as a basis for promotional or ad-targeting use. Disclose the marketing purpose transparently and obtain a separate, clearly-labelled marketing opt-in at or before collection, so the commercial intent is apparent to the consumer. For any future collection, list advertising uploads and promotional email explicitly in the notice.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Recipients never signed up for marketing, so the promotional emails are, in substance, unsolicited. Annex I point 26 prohibits persistent and unwanted solicitations by email. As described, the practice does not clearly meet the blacklist threshold because a functional unsubscribe link is provided and there is no evidence of continued contact after an objection; the 'persistent' element and disregard of an opt-out are not present. It is flagged as a watch-point: if the weekly cadence continues to recipients who did not consent, or continues after opt-outs, it would move into prohibited territory.
findings.evidence_quote: start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list
findings.recommendation: Only email recipients who have given a valid marketing opt-in; honour unsubscribe/objection immediately and suppress opted-out contacts across all channels including custom audiences. Avoid win-back or re-contact sequences to anyone who has objected.

verdicts.notes: This campaign's core defects are data-protection ones (purpose limitation, lawful basis, ePrivacy consent for email marketing) handled by other agents. Under the UCPD specifically, the main angle is a possible misleading omission / hidden commercial intent: emails were collected under an operational framing ('Receive order updates and service information') that concealed any promotional or ad-targeting purpose, so consumers were not informed of the commercial intent at the point they handed over data. The blacklisted persistent-solicitation prohibition (Annex I point 26) is not clearly met because an unsubscribe link is offered and no post-objection re-contact is described. Overall a moderate UCPD concern that overlaps heavily with GDPR.

report.executive_summary: This campaign proposes to take email addresses that customers gave only for order updates and service information, and reuse them for three new purposes: uploading the list to social platforms as a custom audience, building lookalike audiences, and sending a weekly promotional newsletter. The core problem is that customers were never told about — and never agreed to — any marketing or advertising use of their data. Under GDPR this means you have no valid lawful basis for any of the three activities, and the plan breaches the transparency, purpose-limitation, and consent rules; "they are existing customers" is not a lawful basis, and email marketing plus custom-audience uploads generally require prior opt-in consent. The custom-audience and lookalike work also counts as profiling and triggers ad-transparency duties on the platform side (DSA). Separately, collecting the emails under a purely operational framing while intending to market to them is a potential misleading omission / hidden commercial intent under consumer-protection law (UCPD). An unsubscribe link and the absence of sensitive data do not fix these issues. Verdict: do not launch as designed — the personalisation/advertising elements need a proper legal basis and fresh, specific consent before proceeding.
recommendations: Do not upload the list, build lookalikes, or send the newsletter until each purpose has a valid lawful basis — being an existing customer is not sufficient.

Obtain fresh, specific, granular opt-in consent (separate from the original transactional sign-up) for (a) promotional email and (b) custom-audience/lookalike advertising uploads, and keep records to demonstrate that consent.
Only email and only include in custom audiences those contacts who have given valid marketing consent; suppress everyone else across all channels.

Update the collection-time privacy notice to disclose all marketing purposes, the recipient social platforms, retention periods, and the right to object, and re-inform the existing list before any new processing.

Provide an explicit, easy way to object to all direct marketing — including removal from ad-platform custom audiences and exclusion from lookalike modelling — not just an email unsubscribe link, and honour objections immediately across every channel.
Make the commercial/marketing intent clear at the point any future email is collected, so consumers are not misled about why their data is being requested (UCPD).

If you intend to rely on legitimate interests where legally available instead of consent, complete and document a legitimate-interest assessment first; note that custom-audience uploads and email marketing in practice generally require consent.

When ads do run, confirm the platform's DSA ad-transparency features are enabled and the campaigns run under a correctly identified advertiser/payer so ad labels, advertiser identity, and 'why you're seeing this' targeting disclosures are accurate.
Avoid any weekly cadence, win-back, or re-contact sequences to people who did not consent or who have opted out, to steer clear of the UCPD prohibition on persistent unwanted solicitations.

promotional email newsletter to existing customer list

triage.summary: A home-services brand proposes to repurpose customer emails collected at checkout (under a notice covering only 'order updates and service information') for advertising: uploading the list to social platforms as a custom audience, building lookalikes, and sending a weekly promotional newsletter. verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Data collected for 'order updates and service information' is being repurposed for advertising and promotional email without ever informing the data subjects. Processing personal data for purposes incompatible with, and undisclosed at, the point of collection breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle — the reuse is neither transparent (never notified) nor fair (used contrary to the reasonable expectations set by the collection notice).
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Do not reuse the checkout list for advertising or promotional email under the existing notice. Either (a) re-permission the list with a clear, specific opt-in for marketing/ad-platform sharing, or (b) restrict use to the originally stated purposes. Update the privacy notice to describe advertising uploads, lookalike creation and newsletters before any such processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Each proposed operation needs a valid legal basis. Uploading emails to social platforms as a custom audience and building lookalikes is disclosure/processing for personalised advertising that generally requires consent (or a demonstrable, balanced legitimate-interest assessment) — the bare fact that 'they are existing customers' is not itself a lawful basis, especially where the collection notice excluded these uses. Email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (ePrivacy soft opt-in requires similar products and a chance to object given at collection, which was not provided here). Lookalike audiences also process data of individuals who never consented at all.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list, reasoning 'they are existing customers'
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before processing: obtain GDPR-compliant consent for the social-platform upload/lookalike sharing and for marketing email, or complete and record a legitimate-interests assessment (recognising consent is the safer basis for ad-platform sharing). Halt the lookalike build absent a defensible basis for expanding beyond the known contacts.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Any consent captured at checkout was tied to transactional order/service updates, not marketing. Consent must be specific and clearly distinguishable per purpose; a transactional sign-up cannot be stretched to cover advertising uploads or promotional newsletters. The controller could not demonstrate valid consent for the new marketing purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Run a fresh, granular opt-in for each purpose (newsletter, social-audience sharing), in clear plain language, kept separate from the transactional service, with easy withdrawal. Retain records demonstrating each consent.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at collection the controller disclose all purposes and the legal basis, and recipients of the data. The notice named only order/service updates, so data subjects were not informed that their email could be shared with social platforms, used to build lookalikes, or used for promotional email. This information deficit means the later processing lacks the required transparency at source.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Provide compliant Art. 13 information covering the advertising and newsletter purposes, the legal basis, and that data will be shared with named social-media platforms as recipients — and give this information before, not after, the data is used for those purposes.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Building custom and lookalike audiences and behavioural targeting constitutes profiling — automated processing to evaluate/predict personal preferences and interests to target individuals with tailored ads. This confirms the activity engages the profiling regime (lawful basis, transparency and the right to object), heightening the significance of the basis and notice failures above.
findings.evidence_quote: build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list
findings.recommendation: Treat the targeting as profiling: document it in the privacy notice as such, secure the appropriate lawful basis for profiling-based advertising, and ensure it is covered by the objection/opt-out mechanisms.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing (including related profiling) is absolute and must be facilitated. An unsubscribe link addresses newsletter opt-out but does not, on its own, provide a way to object to the social-platform custom-audience/lookalike profiling, nor is the right explicitly and separately presented at the first communication as required.
findings.evidence_quote: an unsubscribe link will be included
findings.recommendation: Present the right to object to direct marketing explicitly and clearly at the point of first contact (Art. 21(4)), and provide an effective mechanism to stop not just emails but also the custom-audience/lookalike profiling — e.g. removing objecting individuals from uploaded audiences.

verdicts.notes: The brand collected emails at checkout under a notice covering only "order updates and service information" and now proposes to repurpose that data for advertising uploads to social platforms, lookalike expansion, and a weekly promotional newsletter. This is a purpose-limitation and lawful-basis mismatch: none of the marketing purposes were disclosed at collection, no consent was obtained for them, and lookalike audiences extend processing to non-customers who never had any relationship with the brand. An unsubscribe link does not cure the lack of a valid basis or the missing transparency. Findings are grounded in GDPR Arts. 5(1)(a), 6(1), 7, 13, 4(4) and 21.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(2) treats a practice as a misleading omission where it fails to identify the commercial intent of the practice when this is not apparent from the context. Here the consumer surrendered their email at checkout under a notice presenting the purpose as transactional/service ('order updates and service information'). The genuine commercial intent — building an advertising audience and sending promotional marketing — was not apparent at the point the data was obtained. Repurposing service-collected contact data for promotional messaging and ad-platform uploads means the commercial intent underlying the data collection was hidden from the average consumer, who reasonably understood they were only enabling service communications. This distorts the consumer's decision to hand over their contact details.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information' ... start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list ... The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on service-framed consent for marketing. At the point of collection, clearly and separately identify the commercial/marketing intent (e.g. a distinct, unbundled opt-in stating the email may be used for promotional newsletters and to build social advertising audiences). For the existing list collected under the service-only notice, re-permission the audience with a transparent notice that discloses the marketing and ad-upload purpose before using it for promotion, rather than repurposing it under 'they are existing customers'.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core problems (purpose limitation, lawful basis, transparency for advertising uploads and marketing email) are primarily GDPR/ePrivacy issues, which fall to other agents. Under the UCPD, one provision is genuinely engaged: Art. 7 on hidden commercial intent. Emails were collected at checkout under a notice framed purely as service/transactional ("order updates and service information"), so the commercial/marketing intent behind the collection was not made apparent to the consumer — yet the data is now to be used for a promotional newsletter and social advertising. The Annex I point 26 blacklist (persistent, unwanted solicitations) is NOT triggered as described, because an unsubscribe link is provided and there is no re-contact after objection; aggressive practices (Arts. 8-9) are likewise not engaged.

report.executive_summary: The campaign proposes reusing an email list collected at checkout for order/service updates to instead upload to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and send a weekly promotional newsletter. The core problem is that none of these marketing uses were disclosed or consented to when the emails were collected — the privacy notice only mentioned transactional order and service information. This creates a serious legal mismatch under GDPR: you lack a valid lawful basis and transparency for the marketing and ad-platform uses, and consent given for service updates cannot be stretched to cover advertising. Building lookalikes compounds the risk by extending processing to non-customers who never engaged with you at all. There is also a consumer-protection issue (UCPD) because the commercial intent behind collecting the emails was effectively hidden. An unsubscribe link and the "they're existing customers" reasoning do not cure any of these problems. The verdict is high risk — do not launch as designed; the list must be re-permissioned before it can be used for marketing or ad uploads.
recommendations: Do not proceed with the campaign as designed: halt the social-platform upload, lookalike build, and promotional newsletter to the existing list until a valid basis is in place.

Re-permission the existing list: send a compliant re-consent request obtaining granular, unbundled opt-ins separately for (a) the promotional newsletter and (b) sharing emails with named social platforms for custom audiences/lookalikes. Only contacts who opt in can be used.

Update the privacy notice to disclose the advertising uploads, lookalike creation, promotional email, the legal basis, and that data will be shared with named social-media platforms — and present this before any such processing, not after.

campaign.title: StyleHub marketplace checkout optimisation

Declining purchase protection shows 'I'll risk losing my order' as the only decline label. A pre-ticked 2.99 EUR 'carbon protection fee' and a 4.90 EUR 'service fee' are added at the final payment step only, not shown on product or cart pages. A/B test shows +18% attach rate.

Confirmshaming decline label for purchase protection ('I'll risk losing my order')
Pre-ticked add-on fee ('carbon protection fee')
Hidden/drip-priced fees revealed only at final payment step (carbon protection fee + service fee)
Non-transparent pricing (fees not shown on product or cart pages)
Potentially misleading 'carbon protection fee' environmental framing (possible greenwashing)
A/B testing to optimise attach rate
Dark patterns / manipulative choice architecture
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general EU consumers; a general-audience fashion marketplace can plausibly be accessed by minors, so specialist review should confirm. Newsletter opt-out implies email/consent processing, so GDPR is engaged despite the 'no personalisation' declaration. The DSA is engaged because StyleHub is an online marketplace with third-party sellers and its checkout deploys deceptive interface design (Art. 25 prohibition on dark patterns for platforms). AI Act not engaged given no use of AI/generative systems.
triage.summary: A fashion marketplace (third-party sellers, EU-wide) is testing checkout UX changes that use confirmshaming decline labels, a pre-ticked 'carbon protection fee', and additional fees revealed only at the final payment step rather than on product or cart pages. These are classic dark patterns raising misleading/aggressive practice, price-transparency and possible greenwashing concerns, on an online marketplace subject to the DSA's dark-pattern prohibition.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(3) requires that it be as easy to withdraw consent as to give it, and recital-79/EDPB guidance treats manipulative consent interfaces as undermining valid consent. A confirmshaming decline label that shames the user for opting out of marketing emails introduces emotional friction into the withdrawal/decline path, so the mechanism to refuse or withdraw marketing consent is not offered on an equal, neutral footing with acceptance.
findings.evidence_quote: The newsletter opt-out link now reads 'No thanks, I hate saving money'
findings.recommendation: Replace the shaming label with a neutral, factual option (e.g. 'No thanks' / 'Don't subscribe') presented with equal visual prominence to the opt-in, ensuring declining or withdrawing marketing consent is as easy and pressure-free as giving it.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be 'freely given' and the result of a genuine, unpressured choice. Deploying confirmshaming at the point of choosing to decline the newsletter manipulates the data subject's decision, casting doubt on whether any resulting opt-in constitutes freely given, unambiguous consent as defined in Art. 4(11).
findings.evidence_quote: The newsletter opt-out link now reads 'No thanks, I hate saving money'
findings.recommendation: Design the newsletter sign-up as an affirmative, unbundled opt-in with neutral accept/decline wording and no guilt-inducing framing, so that any recorded consent can be relied on as freely given and demonstrable.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing under Art. 21(2) is absolute and must be facilitated. Framing the opt-out with a shaming label rather than a clear, unimpeded mechanism creates friction that discourages exercise of this right at the point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: The newsletter opt-out link now reads 'No thanks, I hate saving money'
findings.recommendation: Ensure the direct-marketing opt-out/objection is presented clearly and neutrally at sign-up and in every communication, with no deterrent wording, so consumers can decline or object without friction.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires that personal data (here, marketing-email sign-up decisions) be processed fairly. Manipulative choice architecture that steers users into consenting to marketing by shaming those who decline is inconsistent with fair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The newsletter opt-out link now reads 'No thanks, I hate saving money'
findings.recommendation: Adopt neutral, balanced consent interface design so the data subject's marketing choice reflects a fair, transparent decision rather than one produced by manipulative UX.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged only through the newsletter opt-out mechanism, which implies email/marketing-consent processing. The confirmshaming opt-out label ("No thanks, I hate saving money") is a consent-related dark pattern that undermines the requirement that withdrawing consent / objecting to direct marketing be as easy, unambiguous and free of manipulation as giving it, and conflicts with the fairness/transparency principle. The pre-ticked fees and hidden pricing are pricing/consumer-protection matters (UCPD/DSA) and do not by themselves engage GDPR, as no personal-data processing is described in relation to them.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Confirmshaming: the decline option is framed with self-deprecating, emotionally loaded language to shame recipients out of exercising a free choice. DSA Art. 25 expressly prohibits designing online interfaces in a way that manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions; the KG dark-patterns concept lists confirm-shaming as a paradigm example.
findings.evidence_quote: The newsletter opt-out link now reads 'No thanks, I hate saving money'.
findings.recommendation: Use neutral, factual choice labels of equal prominence (e.g. 'No thanks' / 'Subscribe'). Remove guilt-inducing or emotionally coercive wording from decline options.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: A second confirmshaming instance combined with a false hierarchy of choices: the sole decline label frames the free choice to opt out as reckless and dangerous, manipulating the consumer's decision at checkout. findings.rationale: Sneaking a charge into the basket via a pre-ticked add-on that the consumer must actively notice and de-select is contrary to professional diligence and is designed to materially distort economic behaviour. The declared +18% attach rate is direct evidence the design distorts choices rather than reflecting genuine consumer demand. Combined with the confirmshaming and hidden fees, the overall checkout flow is an unfair practice caught by the Art. 5 safety net.
findings.evidence_quote: A pre-ticked 2.99 EUR 'carbon protection fee' ... A/B test shows +18% attach rate
findings.recommendation: Make all optional add-ons opt-in (unticked by default) with a neutral label and clear price. Do not rely on default selection to drive attach rate; measure genuine consumer intent, not manipulated defaults.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Confirmshaming decline labels use emotionally loaded, guilt-inducing wording that pressures and shames consumers out of the choice they would otherwise make, exerting undue influence that impairs freedom of choice and can cause a transactional decision (e.g. keeping purchase protection or subscribing) they would not otherwise take. Offering only a pejorative decline label, with no neutral option, heightens the coercive effect.

findings.recommendation: Replace pejorative/guilt-based decline labels with neutral, factual wording (e.g. 'No thanks' / 'Decline purchase protection'). Present accept and decline options with equal prominence and neutral framing so consumers can choose freely.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: By presenting product prices on product and cart pages without the mandatory service and carbon fees, the interface can deceive the average consumer as to the price and the manner in which it is calculated, potentially causing a transactional decision (starting checkout) not otherwise taken. This is secondary to the Art. 7 omission but the price presentation also risks being a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: a 4.90 EUR 'service fee' are added at the final payment step only
findings.recommendation: Ensure advertised prices reflect the actual total the consumer will pay, or clearly indicate that additional unavoidable fees apply and their amount, at the point the price is first shown.

verdicts.notes: The checkout UX engages several UCPD prohibitions. Drip pricing — revealing a 2.99 EUR carbon fee and 4.90 EUR service fee only at the final payment step — is a misleading omission of material price information under Art. 7. The pre-ticked add-on combined with confirmshaming decline labels and an admitted +18% attach rate indicates a practice contrary to professional diligence that materially distorts consumer choice (Art. 5), while the guilt-inducing/coercive decline labels amount to undue influence engaging Arts. 8-9. These are dark patterns that overlap with DSA Art. 25, but are independently unfair under the UCPD applicable to all traders.

report.executive_summary: This campaign changes the checkout flow on your EU fashion marketplace by adding guilt-based decline labels, a pre-ticked paid add-on, and fees that only appear at the final payment step. While the +18% attach rate looks like a win, three separate EU laws flag this as a likely violation. Under the DSA (Art. 25) and the UCPD, the pre-ticked "carbon protection fee," the hidden "service fee" (drip pricing), and the shaming decline labels ("I hate saving money", "I'll risk losing my order") are classic dark patterns that manipulate consumers rather than reflect genuine choice. Under the GDPR, the confirmshaming newsletter opt-out means any consent you collect is not "freely given" and is legally invalid. The A/B test result is actually evidence against you — it demonstrates the design deliberately distorts consumer decisions. As is, this campaign should not launch; the practices are unfair, non-compliant, and expose you to regulatory action across DSA, consumer-protection and data-protection regimes.
recommendations: Show all fees upfront: display the 2.99 EUR carbon fee and 4.90 EUR service fee inclusive in the price on product and cart pages — do not reveal them only at the final payment step. This is the single biggest fix (DSA Art. 25, UCPD Arts. 5-7).
Un-tick the carbon protection fee by default so it requires an explicit opt-in, and clearly label it as optional and separate from any genuinely mandatory charges.

Replace all guilt-based decline labels with neutral, symmetrical wording — e.g. 'Subscribe' / 'No thanks' for the newsletter, and 'No, continue without protection' for purchase protection — giving the decline option equal visual prominence.

Treat the newsletter consent as invalid under GDPR while the confirmshaming label is in place; only rely on consent collected through a neutral, freely-given interface, and keep records demonstrating this.
Re-run the A/B test on the compliant design and measure genuine consumer intent rather than manipulated defaults — do not use the +18% attach rate to justify the current flow.
Check whether minors can subscribe to the newsletter and, if so, add age-appropriate consent handling (GDPR Art. 8), as this is a general-audience EU service with no age gating.

report.executive_summary: This campaign adds urgency messaging to your hotel listings — viewer counts ("17 people are looking right now"), recent-booking counts ("Booked 43 times in the last 24 hours"), "In high demand!" labels, and "Only 1 room left at this price!" banners. Treat the 'Only 1 room left at this price!' scarcity banner and the viewer/booking counters as the highest priority — these hit the UCPD Annex I blacklist (false scarcity, point 7; misrepresented social endorsement, point 23c) and are per se illegal regardless of consumer impact.

campaign.title: TixNow 'from €25' concert tickets
campaign.text: Ticket seller advertises 'Arena tour tickets from €25!' across search and social. At checkout, a mandatory 'venue service fee' (€7.50), 'e-ticket delivery' (€2.90) and 'order processing' (€3.10) appear on the final step, raising the cheapest possible total to €38.50. The fees apply to every ticket and every delivery method. A 10-minute cart timer runs during checkout; the timer reflects a real inventory hold released at expiry.

drip pricing / hidden mandatory fees revealed at checkout
mandatory unavoidable fees (venue service fee, e-ticket delivery, order processing) that apply to every ticket regardless of delivery method
cheapest achievable total (€38.50) materially above advertised price

triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers, but concert/tour ticketing on search and social realistically reaches minors, so minor reach is treated as plausible. No generative AI is declared or evident, so the AI Act is not currently engaged. Personalisation/targeting is declared as 'no', but running ads on search and social platforms and processing checkout/order data still involves personal data (GDPR) and the platforms are intermediaries/VLOPs (DSA), so both are flagged. UCPD is the core regime given the headline vs. unavoidable-price gap; the countdown timer appears legitimate (real inventory hold) but should still be verified.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The described checkout necessarily collects personal data (order, contact, e-ticket delivery and payment details), which triggers the controller's obligation to provide Art. 13 information (identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights) at the point of collection. The campaign material does not describe such a notice; this is not evidence of a breach in a marketing submission, but it is the point where GDPR obligations attach.
findings.evidence_quote: At checkout, a mandatory 'venue service fee' (€7.50), 'e-ticket delivery' (€2.90) and 'order processing' (€3.10) appear on the final step
findings.recommendation: Ensure the checkout flow surfaces a clear, easily accessible privacy notice (or a prominent link to it) before or at the point personal and payment data are entered, covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis (contract for the ticket sale), recipients (e.g. venue, payment processor, e-ticket delivery), retention periods and data-subject rights.

verdicts.notes: The submitted material is an advertising/pricing matter (headline "from €25" vs. unavoidable €38.50 total) that primarily engages UCPD, not GDPR. The campaign explicitly declares no personalisation/targeting, and the text describes no consent flow, tracking, profiling, sign-up form, special-category data, or minor-directed consent collection — so no GDPR breach is substantiated by the material. GDPR is engaged only in the background because any concert-ticket checkout necessarily processes order, contact and payment data; the only responsible flag is an informational reminder to provide an Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of collection. Art. 8 (children's consent) is not engaged, as ticket sales rest on contract rather than a consent-based information society service.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: By placing paid advertisements on search and social online platforms, the campaign falls within the DSA advertising-transparency regime. Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. The obligation is primarily on the platform, but the advertiser must supply accurate identity/payer information and ensure placements are not disguised as organic content. triage.summary: A marketplace blender launch that systematically manipulates consumer reviews: buying 300 fake five-star reviews with fabricated verified-purchase badges, paying real customers only for 5-star reviews, displaying a misleading 4.9/5 rating and a self-created 'Customers' Choice' endorsement badge, and falsely reporting negative reviews as spam to have them removed. findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Emailing existing customers a promotional voucher offer is direct marketing that processes personal data (email address, identity, purchase link). Such email marketing generally requires a valid lawful basis — typically prior consent (ePrivacy Art. 13) or a carefully assessed legitimate interest. The submission declares no personalisation and gives no indication that customers consented to receive marketing emails or that a legitimate-interest balancing test was performed, so the processing lacks a demonstrable lawful basis as described.
findings.evidence_quote: email real customers offering a 20 EUR voucher only if they leave a 5-star review
findings.recommendation: Before sending, confirm and document a lawful basis: rely on the ePrivacy 'soft opt-in' only for the same/similar products where marketing consent was offered at collection, or obtain prior consent; otherwise do not send. Record the basis and only email customers on a valid marketing list.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute and every marketing communication must facilitate opt-out. The campaign describes a marketing email with no mention of an unsubscribe/opt-out mechanism or of screening the recipient list against prior objections/suppression lists.
findings.evidence_quote: email real customers offering a 20 EUR voucher only if they leave a 5-star review
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, functioning opt-out (unsubscribe) link in every marketing email, honour it immediately, and screen the send list against your existing suppression/objection records before dispatch.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Using customer contact data to solicit reviews under an undisclosed condition (payment only for 5-star ratings) that will then be presented to the public as genuine 'verified buyer' feedback is not fair or transparent processing of the customers' data, and the purpose of the outreach is not being communicated honestly to the data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: offering a 20 EUR voucher only if they leave a 5-star review (4 stars or below: no voucher)
findings.recommendation: Do not condition incentives on the rating given. If soliciting reviews, tell customers clearly and up front how their data and review will be used, keep any incentive unconditional and disclosed, and provide a privacy notice at the point of contact.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is used/collected for this marketing purpose, the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The campaign provides no indication that any such privacy information accompanies the customer email or the review/voucher process.
findings.evidence_quote: email real customers offering a 20 EUR voucher only if they leave a 5-star review
findings.recommendation: Provide or link a concise privacy notice in the marketing email covering controller identity, purpose, legal basis, retention and rights (including the right to object), in clear and plain language.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged because the campaign emails real customers a promotional offer, which is direct marketing involving processing of their personal data (email address, purchase history). The description gives no indication of a lawful basis/prior consent for this marketing email, no opt-out/right-to-object mechanism, and no transparency about the (undisclosed) purpose — namely a voucher conditioned on posting a 5-star review. The review-manipulation practices themselves are primarily UCPD/DSA matters; the GDPR findings below concern the customer-email data processing.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing, organising or operating an online platform interface in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions. Displaying a fabricated aggregate rating ('Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers') built on purchased and voucher-gated reviews, a self-created 'Customers' Choice' badge dressed up as an independent endorsement, and systematic suppression of genuine negative reviews together manipulate the product-page interface and the social-proof signals consumers rely on, materially distorting their purchasing decision. The direct addressee of Art. 25 is the platform provider rather than the seller, but this seller conduct is precisely the manipulative interface manipulation the provision targets and creates platform-level exposure.
findings.evidence_quote: Product page will display 'Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers' and a 'Customers' Choice' badge we designed ourselves. Negative reviews are reported for removal as 'spam' regardless of content.
findings.recommendation: Do not manipulate the product-page interface: remove the fabricated 4.9/5 rating, drop the self-designed 'Customers' Choice' badge (or clearly label it as a self-assessment, not an independent award), and stop filing false 'spam' reports against negative reviews — only report reviews that genuinely violate the platform's content policy. Let ratings and badges reflect authentic, unincentivised, verified consumer feedback so the interface does not distort consumer decision-making.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's review-manipulation tactics (fabricated 4.9/5 aggregate rating, self-designed 'Customers' Choice' badge presented as an endorsement, and false 'spam' reports to suppress negative reviews) are, in substance, deceptive/manipulative online-interface conduct of the kind DSA Art. 25 prohibits — they materially distort consumers' ability to make free and informed decisions on the marketplace product page. The important caveat is that Art. 25's direct duty-bearer is the *provider of the online platform*, not a seller/advertiser; KitchenPro is the latter. These practices are therefore primarily UCPD blacklist matters (points 23b/23c/2, covered by another agent), but they also expose the marketplace to Art. 25 exposure and mean the seller is inducing platform-interface manipulation. No paid-ad targeting, minors, special-category targeting, recommender-system or ad-repository issues are engaged, so Arts. 26–28/39 are not applicable.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Commissioning a review farm to submit false consumer reviews that do not originate from genuine purchasers is a blacklisted practice prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23c (submitting or commissioning false reviews to promote a product). The conditional voucher ('only if they leave a 5-star review') and reporting all negative reviews as 'spam' regardless of content additionally constitute misrepresenting/manipulating the body of consumer reviews (cherry-picking and suppressing negatives), also caught by 23c.

findings.recommendation: Do not purchase, commission or fabricate any reviews. Remove all bought reviews. Never condition an incentive on a specific star rating — any solicited review must be neutral, disclose the incentive, and accept all ratings. Stop reporting genuine negative reviews as spam; only remove content that genuinely breaches platform content policies.

findings.rationale: Attaching fabricated 'verified-purchase' badges to purchased reviews and displaying 'Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers' states that reviews originate from consumers who actually purchased/used the product without taking any reasonable and proportionate verification steps — indeed the badges are known fakes. findings.recommendation: Remove all 'verified' / 'verified buyers' labelling unless a genuine, documented verification process confirms each reviewer actually purchased the product. Do not attach verified-purchase badges to any review that is not verified.

findings.rationale: Displaying a self-created 'Customers' Choice' quality/award emblem presented as an independent endorsement is displaying a trust mark, quality mark or equivalent without the necessary authorisation — blacklisted in all circumstances under Annex I point 2 (which expressly covers self-designed 'customers' choice' or award emblems presented as independent).

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Sending marketing emails to a customer list is processing of personal data for direct marketing and requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis; e-mail direct marketing generally requires prior consent (or a narrow soft opt-in for existing customers for similar products). The campaign provides no indication that a lawful basis or valid consent for this email outreach exists.

Do not email customers who have not been captured under one of these bases.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct-marketing communication must respect and facilitate the absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing. The described email programme contains no reference to an opt-out/unsubscribe mechanism or to informing recipients of this right.

findings.recommendation: Include a clear, free and easy opt-out (unsubscribe) in every marketing email and honour objections immediately by suppressing the recipient from further marketing; explicitly present the right to object at the point of first contact.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data

findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that personal data not be used in ways detrimental or misleading to individuals. Using customers' contact data to orchestrate a rating-gating scheme that misleads other consumers is not a fair use of that data, undermining the fairness limb even where the deceptive-practice core is handled under UCPD/DSA.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core wrongdoing (fake reviews, fabricated verified-purchase badges, suppression of negative reviews, misleading rating claims) sits under UCPD/DSA, not GDPR. However, the campaign includes a genuine GDPR footprint: emailing "real customers" with a voucher offer is a direct-marketing operation processing personal data. Although the submission declares no personalisation, this direct marketing engages GDPR obligations on lawful basis, consent, transparency and the right to object, which the description gives no indication of satisfying. The incentivised solicitation is also relevant because personal data is used to induce commercially deceptive conduct, engaging the fairness principle.

The DSA provisions in scope (Arts. 25, 26, 26(3), 27, 28, 39) impose obligations on providers of online platforms / VLOPs, not on third-party sellers using a marketplace. KitchenPro is a merchant/trader manipulating review content on a platform it does not operate; it neither designs the platform interface (Art. 25) nor places platform advertising, engages in targeting/profiling (Art. 26/26(3)/28), operates a recommender system (Art. 27), or runs an ad repository (Art. 39). The review manipulation, fabricated verified-purchase badges, gated incentivised reviews, misleading 4.9/5 claim and self-made 'Customers' Choice' badge are prohibited practices, but they fall under the UCPD (e.g. Annex I points 23c, 23b, 2), which is another agent's remit. findings.recommendation: Remove the self-designed 'Customers' Choice' badge and any aggregate rating not derived from genuine, verifiable reviews. Marketplaces should note their Art. 25 duty not to operate interfaces that present such manipulated signals.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
