findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(4) requires that consent be freely given and that access to a service (member prices) not be conditioned on consent to processing that is not necessary for that service. Bundling four distinct purposes into one all-or-nothing consent, tied to the price benefit, removes genuine choice. None of the four purposes is necessary to provide loyalty pricing, so the conditionality strongly indicates consent is not freely given.
findings.evidence_quote: now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms. Declining any element means losing all member prices.
findings.recommendation: Unbundle consent into separate, granular opt-ins for each purpose (profiling, location push, partner sharing, external ad targeting); make each optional; and provide member prices without requiring consent to any non-essential processing.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; bundled consent covering multiple distinct purposes expressly does not qualify. Sharing with 60 unnamed partners also undermines the 'specific' and 'informed' requirements. As designed, the consent fails the definition and cannot serve as a valid legal basis.
findings.evidence_quote: a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Collect separate specific consents per purpose and name (or make readily accessible a list of) the recipient partners so the data subject can make an informed, unambiguous choice for each.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(3) requires withdrawal of consent to be as easy as giving it and without detriment. Penalising withdrawal by terminating the entire membership imposes a significant detriment that deters withdrawal and further evidences that the original consent was not freely given.
findings.evidence_quote: Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Allow withdrawal of any data-processing consent while preserving membership and, at minimum, core loyalty benefits; decouple continued membership from ongoing consent to non-essential processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising, cross-platform ad targeting, partner sharing and profiling generally require valid consent (or a carefully balanced legitimate interest). Because the consent here is very likely invalid under Arts. 4(11) and 7, the profiling, location push, partner sharing and external ad targeting would lack a lawful basis under Art. 6(1).
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis for each processing purpose; where consent is used it must be granular and unconditioned, otherwise reassess whether the processing can lawfully proceed at all.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is undermined where the only privacy-preserving option is quietly removed and members are steered into extensive data processing framed emotively as savings. This manipulative framing obscures the data trade-off and is unfair to data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Reinstate a genuine no/low-data membership option or clearly explain the data implications neutrally at the point of enrolment; avoid framing that hides the processing being consented to.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information about the processing must be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear plain language at the point of collection. Signage emphasising 'savings' while collecting consent for profiling, location tracking, 60-partner sharing and external ad targeting does not transparently communicate what is being consented to, and the in-store/app channels make full disclosure at the point of consent challenging.
findings.evidence_quote: In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'.
findings.recommendation: Present clear, layered privacy information (identity, all purposes, recipients, retention, rights) prominently at each consent moment in-store, in-app and by email, not just an emotive slogan.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that recipients of the personal data, the purposes and legal basis, retention and profiling information be provided at collection. Referring generically to '60 retail media partners' without identifying them or the categories/purposes fails the recipient-disclosure requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners'
findings.recommendation: Provide the identities or categories of the 60 partners, the specific purposes of sharing, retention periods, and information about profiling at the point of enrolment.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing purchase history to evaluate personal preferences and behaviour is profiling within the Art. 4(4) definition, confirming that the profiling-specific obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) are engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling
findings.recommendation: Document that purchase-history analysis is profiling and ensure all associated GDPR obligations are met.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including profiling for such marketing. The campaign as described offers no marketing/profiling opt-out short of losing all member prices or membership, which fails to facilitate the absolute right to object.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, no-detriment way for members to object to direct marketing and marketing-related profiling at any time while retaining membership.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Supermarket loyalty enrolment via app/in-store is realistically completed by households including minors, and app-based location push and profiling are information society services. Where a child under the applicable age (13-16) enrols and consent is the basis, parental consent and reasonable age-verification are required, which the all-adult framing does not address.
findings.evidence_quote: grocery shoppers, general adult
findings.recommendation: Introduce age assurance at enrolment and a parental-consent mechanism for users below the applicable age threshold before profiling or targeting their data.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch relies on a single combined consent covering four distinct processing purposes (purchase-history profiling, location-based push, sharing with 60 partners, external ad targeting), makes it non-granular, conditions member prices on accepting all elements, removed the former data-free tier, and cancels membership entirely if consent is withdrawn. These features cut directly against the GDPR conditions for valid consent (freely given, specific, granular, and as easy to withdraw as to give), the lawful-basis requirement for profiling/marketing, and transparency obligations. Consent as constructed is very likely invalid, meaning the processing lacks a lawful basis. Minors realistically reached by loyalty enrolment raise an additional Art. 8 concern.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign profiles members on purchase history and location and uses that data for behavioural ad targeting on external platforms. Because supermarket loyalty clubs and in-store/app channels are realistically accessed by households including minors (per triage), the advertiser may supply profiling-derived audience data that results in profiling-based ads being presented on third-party platforms to recipients who are minors. DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using minors' data. The advertiser cannot lawfully instruct or benefit from such targeting; feeding broad loyalty-derived segments into external platform ad targeting risks driving prohibited profiled ads to minors.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Exclude minors from all behavioural/profiling-based ad targeting fed to external platforms. Implement age gating on membership data used for ad targeting, contractually require retail-media partners and external platforms to suppress profiled ad delivery to anyone not reasonably certain to be an adult, and document that loyalty-derived targeting segments cannot reach minors.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Purchase-history profiling can directly reveal or allow inference of GDPR Art. 9 special-category data (e.g. health from pharmacy/medical/dietary items, religion from religious dietary staples, ethnicity from cultural foods). If such purchase-derived segments are shared with 60 retail-media partners and used to target ads on external platforms, those platforms would be presenting ads based on profiling using special categories of data, which DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits regardless of consent. The advertiser risks being the source of prohibited sensitive-attribute targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Prohibit and technically prevent the use of purchase-history-derived sensitive or proxy segments (health, religious/dietary, ethnic-food indicators) for any external-platform ad targeting. Filter special-category signals out of data shared with retail-media partners and obtain contractual assurances that shared segments will not be used to build sensitive-attribute ad targeting.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Where the loyalty programme results in the supermarket's advertisements being presented on external online platforms, those ads must be identifiable as advertisements, disclose on whose behalf they are shown and who paid, and provide meaningful information about the main targeting parameters. As advertiser, the supermarket must supply accurate advertiser-identity and parameter information so the hosting platform can meet Art. 26(1); opaque data sharing across 60 partners can undermine the traceability required for this transparency.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Ensure that ads placed on external platforms carry clear advertiser identity and payer information, and that the targeting parameters supplied are accurately documented so the platform can present the required 'main parameters' disclosure to recipients.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The bundled 'take-it-or-leave-it' consent and confirm-shaming framing ('Say YES to savings!') are textbook dark-pattern / manipulative interface design. However, DSA Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms in their interface design, and this conduct occurs in the supermarket's own first-party channels (in-store signage, own loyalty app, email), not on a hosting online platform. It is therefore primarily addressed under GDPR Art. 7 (freely given/granular consent) and the UCPD, not DSA. Flagged for context only.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices. In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'
findings.recommendation: Address the bundled-consent and confirm-shaming design under GDPR (granular, unbundled, freely given consent; withdrawal as easy as giving) and UCPD fairness rules. No direct DSA Art. 25 obligation arises for this advertiser unless the consent flow is operated on a qualifying online platform interface.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's substantive obligations (Arts. 25, 26, 28, 39) bind providers of online platforms/VLOPs, not advertisers directly. The submitter is a supermarket using first-party channels (in-store, own app, email), so it is not itself an "online platform" — the bundled-consent dark-pattern conduct falls to GDPR/UCPD rather than DSA Art. 25. DSA is engaged only indirectly through the declared "ad targeting on external platforms": as an advertiser buying profiling-based placements on third-party platforms, the campaign's targeting choices are constrained by the platforms' DSA duties, notably the ban on profiling-based ads to minors (Art. 28) and the ban on ads based on special-category data (Art. 26(3)), plus ad-transparency obligations (Art. 26(1)). Findings are risk/attention level, not direct violations by this advertiser.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The campaign is presented to consumers as an offer of 'savings', while the material information that enrolment requires an extensive, bundled data trade-off (profiling, location tracking, sharing with 60 third parties and cross-platform ad targeting) is not surfaced with equal prominence at the point of the enrolment decision. Emotive signage like 'Say YES to savings!' emphasises the benefit while hiding or providing in an unclear/untimely manner the material conditions the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision to join. That is a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices (up to 40% off staples) now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms. ... In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'
findings.recommendation: At every enrolment touchpoint (signage, app, email) disclose clearly, prominently and before the decision that member prices are conditional on accepting profiling, location tracking, sharing with named third parties and cross-platform ad targeting. Avoid benefit-only framing that omits the data cost; present benefit and conditions with equal prominence.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Removing the privacy-friendly option 'quietly' and not informing consumers that the only remaining route to member prices now carries a mandatory data trade-off hides material information about the changed nature of the offer. Consumers who previously could obtain member prices without data sharing are not told that this option no longer exists, affecting their informed transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Actively and transparently communicate the removal of the data-free tier and its consequences; ideally reinstate a genuine non-data (or granular-choice) path to core member prices so the removal does not operate as a hidden material change.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Making membership (and all member prices) contingent on accepting every processing purpose, and cancelling membership entirely upon withdrawal of consent, imposes an onerous, disproportionate penalty for exercising a right. Coupled with the 'up to 40% off staples' incentive on essential goods, this operates as undue influence that significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and pressures them into accepting terms they might otherwise decline, engaging the aggressive-practices prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices. ... Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Decouple exercise of data rights from continued access to the core loyalty benefit: allow consumers to withdraw consent to individual processing purposes (profiling, location, third-party sharing, cross-platform ads) while retaining membership and baseline member prices. Remove the all-or-nothing penalty structure.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Even where not fully caught by Arts. 6-8, the overall design — benefit-forward emotive framing, bundled consent, silent removal of the data-free option and a withdrawal penalty — functions as a manipulative/dark-pattern-style architecture contrary to professional diligence that is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average grocery shopper regarding enrolment. This is the general fairness safety-net for the combined effect of the tactics.
findings.evidence_quote: Say YES to savings!
findings.recommendation: Redesign the enrolment journey so choices are neutral and unpressured (no confirm-shaming, no false hierarchy between 'save' and privacy), grant granular consent, and ensure the average consumer can understand and decline data uses without losing the headline benefit.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The 'up to 40% off' member-price advantage is promoted as a straightforward saving, but the true 'price' of accessing it is extensive personal-data consent. If the price advantage is presented in a way that deceives the average consumer about the existence or real cost/nature of the price advantage, it risks being a misleading action as to the price advantage. This is a lower-confidence flag pending how the discount baseline and conditions are actually presented.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices (up to 40% off staples)
findings.recommendation: Ensure member-price claims are substantiated (genuine reductions against a proper reference price) and that the data-consent condition attaching to the price advantage is disclosed alongside the '% off' claim, so the price advantage is not presented misleadingly.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch is not itself a blacklisted (Annex I) practice, but it raises real UCPD concerns. The "Say YES to savings!" framing and the quiet removal of the data-free tier obscure the true nature of the exchange (member prices are paid for with extensive data consent), engaging Art. 7 (misleading omission) and the Art. 5 fairness safety-net. Cancelling membership entirely on consent withdrawal creates an onerous barrier to exercising a right that can amount to undue influence under Arts. 8-9. The GDPR consent-validity issues are for the GDPR agent; here the focus is on whether the average consumer is deceived or pressured in their transactional decision to enrol.

report.executive_summary: This campaign relaunches the SuperSave loyalty club so that member prices (up to 40% off staples) are only available if shoppers accept a single bundled consent covering four separate data uses: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and ad targeting on external platforms. As designed, this creates serious legal exposure. Under GDPR, the bundled all-or-nothing consent almost certainly is not "freely given" or "specific," which means the profiling, sharing and ad-targeting likely have no valid legal basis at all — a critical problem. Cancelling membership when someone withdraws consent, and quietly removing the old data-free tier, compound the risk and also raise consumer-protection concerns under the UCPD (misleading omission, aggressive/undue-influence practices, and confirm-shaming "Say YES to savings!" framing). The DSA does not bind you directly as a first-party advertiser, but feeding loyalty-derived segments to external platforms risks driving prohibited profiling-based ads to minors and ads built on sensitive purchase data. This campaign should not launch in its current form; it needs a redesign of the consent architecture before going live in the EU.
recommendations: Unbundle the consent: create separate, granular opt-ins for each of the four purposes (profiling, location push, partner sharing, external ad targeting), each independently optional and off by default.
Decouple member prices and membership from non-essential data consent — provide core loyalty pricing without requiring any of the four data uses. Reinstate a genuine no/low-data membership path.
Stop cancelling membership when consent is withdrawn. Make withdrawal as easy as giving consent and impose no detriment to membership or baseline member prices.

Fix the enrolment messaging: replace confirm-shaming 'Say YES to savings!' framing with neutral, prominent disclosure at every touchpoint (in-store, app, email) that member prices are (or are not) conditional on data uses, presented with equal prominence to the discount claim.
Disclose the 60 'retail media partners' by identity or clear categories, plus purposes, retention periods and profiling information, at the point of enrolment (GDPR Arts. 12-13).
Provide an easy, no-detriment opt-out from direct marketing and marketing-related profiling at any time while keeping membership (GDPR Art. 21).
Actively and transparently communicate the removal of the former data-free tier rather than doing it quietly (UCPD Art. 7).
Exclude minors from behavioural/profiling-based targeting fed to external platforms and add age assurance; contractually require partners to suppress profiled ad delivery to non-adults (DSA Art. 28).
Filter special-category and proxy segments (health, religious/dietary, ethnic-food indicators) out of data shared with partners and prohibit their use for external ad targeting (DSA Art. 26(3)).

Ensure any ads placed on external platforms carry accurate advertiser identity, payer and targeting-parameter information (DSA Art. 26(1)), and substantiate the 'up to 40% off' claim against a proper reference price (UCPD Art. 6).

Declining any element means losing all member prices. In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'. A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed. Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.

triage.summary: A supermarket loyalty relaunch conditions all member discounts on a single bundled consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and cross-platform ad targeting, with the previous data-free tier quietly removed. Consent is effectively forced (decline or withdraw = lose all member prices/membership), raising serious freely-given/granular consent and 'consent-or-pay' issues under GDPR, dark-pattern/manipulative framing concerns, and cross-platform behavioural ad targeting. No generative AI is declared or apparent.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific and unambiguous, and bundled consent expressly does not qualify. A single combined opt-in covering four distinct processing purposes deprives data subjects of granular choice, so no valid consent is obtained for any of the purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Unbundle the consent into separate, independently toggleable opt-ins for each purpose (profiling, location push, partner sharing, external ad targeting), each pre-set to off, so members can accept some and refuse others.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that consent not be conditional on processing unnecessary to the service and that withdrawal be as easy as giving. Tying core member pricing to unnecessary marketing/profiling consent, and making withdrawal trigger loss of membership, creates a detriment that renders consent not freely given and penalises withdrawal.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices. ... Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Decouple member prices from marketing/profiling consent; provide loyalty pricing based on data strictly necessary to run the scheme (contract basis), and ensure withdrawing marketing consent has no effect on membership or discounts.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle is undermined by quietly removing the privacy-friendly option and by 'Say YES to savings!' framing that nudges consent while hiding the data trade-off, creating an unfair imbalance and pressure inconsistent with fair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Reinstate a genuine data-minimising membership option, and present the data implications neutrally and prominently rather than through savings-only 'Say YES' framing so members can make an informed, unpressured choice.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Each processing purpose needs a valid lawful basis. If consent is the intended basis but is invalid (bundled/forced), the profiling, location processing, 60-partner sharing and external ad targeting lack any lawful basis under Art. 6(1); legitimate interests is unlikely to cover extensive cross-platform sharing and behavioural targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Map each purpose to a defensible lawful basis; rely on valid, granular consent for profiling/location/partner-sharing/external targeting, and document why any legitimate-interest reliance passes a balancing test.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing purchase history to evaluate personal preferences and behaviour for offers constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4), which triggers the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling
findings.recommendation: Recognise this activity as profiling, apply the heightened consent/transparency requirements, and ensure members are informed of the profiling and its consequences.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Grocery purchase histories can reveal or infer special-category data (e.g. health via dietary/medical products, religion via diet, pregnancy). Processing such data — including inferred attributes — is prohibited absent explicit consent or another Art. 9 exception, which a bundled generic consent cannot satisfy.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling
findings.recommendation: Screen out or safeguard purchases that reveal special-category data, or obtain separate explicit consent specifically for any such processing, and avoid building sensitive inferences for targeting.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection the controller must disclose the purposes, legal basis, recipients and profiling logic. A single 'Say YES' prompt referencing '60 retail media partners' without identifying recipients, retention or rights likely fails the Art. 13 information obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at sign-up identifying (or categorising with a linked list of) the 60 partners, purposes, retention periods, the profiling involved and how to exercise data-subject rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Members have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and related profiling without losing the underlying service. Structuring the scheme so that objecting/withdrawing ends membership frustrates this absolute right by attaching a penalty to it.
findings.evidence_quote: Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Allow members to object to direct marketing and marketing profiling at any time via an easy mechanism while retaining membership and member prices, and honour objections by ceasing the relevant processing.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch conditions all member prices on a single combined consent bundling four distinct purposes (purchase-history profiling, location push, sharing with 60 partners, cross-platform ad targeting), with declining or withdrawing consent meaning loss of all discounts/membership and the removal of the previously available data-free tier. This fails the freely-given, specific and granular requirements of valid consent (Arts. 4(11) and 7) and makes withdrawal punitive rather than as easy as giving. Extensive behavioural profiling and 60-partner sharing also raise lawful-basis, transparency, fairness and objection issues, and grocery purchase histories can reveal special-category (e.g. health) data.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: To the extent the loyalty enrolment and combined-consent choice is presented through the supermarket's app (an online interface), Art. 25 prohibits designing/operating that interface so as to deceive, manipulate or materially impair a recipient's free and informed decision. The 'Say YES to savings!' framing is confirm-shaming that gives disproportionate prominence to acceptance; combined with a single bundled consent where declining any element loses all member prices, and the quiet removal of the previously available data-free tier, the interface steers users toward consent rather than presenting a genuine free choice. These are recognised dark-pattern techniques (false hierarchy of choices, obstruction of the privacy-friendly option).
findings.evidence_quote: 'Say YES to savings!'
findings.recommendation: Redesign the app enrolment interface to present accept/decline options with equal prominence and neutral wording (remove 'Say YES to savings!' framing), unbundle the consent into separate granular toggles for profiling, location push, partner sharing and cross-platform targeting, and restore an equivalent low-data membership path so that declining is a real, unpenalised option. Ensure withdrawing consent is as easy as giving it and does not cancel core membership.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The campaign performs cross-platform behavioural ad targeting built on purchase-history profiling. Under Art. 26(3), the platforms presenting those ads may not target based on profiling using special-category data (GDPR Art. 9). Grocery purchase histories can reveal or allow inference of sensitive attributes (e.g. health via dietary/medical products, religion via dietary staples). The supermarket is the advertiser rather than the platform provider, so the prohibition binds the platform, but the advertiser's targeting parameters must not require or enable sensitive-data-based profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Contractually and technically ensure external-platform targeting audiences and custom-audience uploads exclude any parameters derived from special-category inferences from purchase history; document that targeting relies only on non-sensitive segments so partner platforms remain compliant with Art. 26(3).

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Triage flags that minors may be reached. Art. 28(2) bans profiling-based advertising to recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors on platforms accessible to minors. The supermarket is not itself the platform provider for the external-platform ads, but where the loyalty app or push offers are accessible to minors, profiling-based targeted offers to them would be impermissible. This is contextual context rather than a direct breach by this advertiser.
findings.evidence_quote: location-based push offers
findings.recommendation: Confirm that loyalty membership and profiling-based offers are restricted to adults, and configure external-platform campaigns to exclude under-18 audiences from any profiling-based ad targeting.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's operative marketing provisions bind providers of online platforms/interfaces. This supermarket is primarily an advertiser and operates its own loyalty app. The most directly relevant DSA hook is Art. 25 (dark patterns in online interface design), engaged by the app's manipulative consent flow ("Say YES to savings!", forced all-or-nothing bundling, quiet removal of the data-free tier). The ad-transparency, sensitive-data and minor-targeting bans (Arts. 26/28) largely bind the external platforms carrying the targeted ads rather than this advertiser, so they are contextual rather than direct violations here. The core consent/fairness issues are better addressed under GDPR and UCPD by the parallel agents.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The signage presents enrolment purely as a savings benefit while omitting the material information the average consumer needs to decide: that saying 'yes' means accepting purchase-history profiling, location-based push, sharing with 60 retail media partners and cross-platform ad targeting. Failing to make the true nature and commercial intent of the exchange (personal data traded for discounts, shared with 60 third parties) clear and timely is a misleading omission — material information provided in an unclear/untimely manner and the commercial/data-monetisation intent hidden behind a savings message.
findings.evidence_quote: Say YES to savings!
findings.recommendation: Replace the one-sided 'Say YES to savings!' prompt with a clear, upfront disclosure at the point of enrolment stating that member prices are conditioned on data processing and sharing with named categories of partners, itemising each purpose, so the average consumer can make an informed transactional decision before enrolling.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Considered as a whole, the design steers economic behaviour contrary to professional diligence: an all-or-nothing bundle, a positively-framed nudge, and the silent removal of the privacy-friendly tier that would otherwise have given consumers a genuine choice. This architecture is likely to materially distort the average consumer's decision to enrol and to consent, functioning as a dark pattern caught by the general fairness safety-net where not addressed by a more specific provision.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices. In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'. A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Reinstate a genuine data-minimising membership/pricing option (or unbundle so that essential loyalty pricing does not depend on non-essential profiling/sharing), present choices with equal prominence, and avoid confirm-shaming or one-sided framing so the club structure does not distort the enrolment decision.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Tying loss of the entire membership (and all accrued member prices) to any withdrawal of consent creates an onerous barrier to exercising a right and can operate as undue influence: the consumer is pressured to maintain consent to avoid a disproportionate detriment, significantly impairing free choice. Arts. 8-9 expressly treat onerous barriers to exercising contractual/withdrawal rights as an aggressive-practice factor.
findings.evidence_quote: Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Decouple consent withdrawal from membership status: allow members to withdraw consent to profiling/sharing/targeting while retaining membership and core member pricing, so exercising the right carries no disproportionate penalty.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch presents mainly a GDPR consent-bundling problem, but several design and communication choices independently engage the UCPD. The "Say YES to savings!" signage combined with an all-or-nothing bundled consent (decline any element = lose all discounts) and the quiet removal of the data-free tier is a manipulative design/dark pattern that omits the true data-for-discount trade-off (Arts. 5 and 7). Making withdrawal of consent cancel membership entirely is a candidate aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9). No blacklisted (Annex I) practice is clearly present, so this is a risk rather than a per se violation; the framing and the conditional structure should be corrected.

report.executive_summary: This campaign relaunches your loyalty club so that member prices require accepting a single, all-or-nothing consent covering four very different things: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and ad targeting on outside platforms. The core problem is that under GDPR this bundled consent is almost certainly invalid — consent must be freely given, specific and granular, and it can't be forced by threatening loss of all discounts. Making withdrawal cancel membership entirely, and quietly deleting the old data-free tier, compounds the risk and also raises consumer-protection issues under the UCPD (misleading omission of the true data-for-discount trade-off, and a pressuring/aggressive design). The "Say YES to savings!" framing in your app is a classic dark pattern that the DSA (Art. 25) prohibits for online interfaces. The AI Act does not apply here. As designed, the campaign should not launch — it carries a high likelihood of a GDPR enforcement finding and consumer-protection challenge across the EU. The good news: every issue is fixable with structural changes to how consent and pricing are linked.
recommendations: Unbundle the consent into separate, independently toggleable opt-ins (each defaulted off) for profiling, location push, 60-partner sharing, and external ad targeting, so members can accept some and refuse others (GDPR Arts. 4(11), 7).

Decouple member prices from marketing/profiling consent: run core loyalty pricing on the data strictly necessary to operate the scheme (contract basis), so declining or withdrawing marketing consent does NOT reduce discounts or cancel membership (GDPR Arts. 6, 7, 21).
Reinstate a genuine data-minimising membership tier equivalent to the one that was removed, so consumers have a real, unpenalised alternative (GDPR Art. 5(1)(a); UCPD Art. 5).
Ensure withdrawing consent is as easy as giving it and never terminates membership or accrued benefits — remove the 'withdrawal cancels membership' rule (GDPR Arts. 7, 21; UCPD Arts. 8-9).

Replace the one-sided 'Say YES to savings!' signage and app prompt with neutral, equally prominent accept/decline options that disclose upfront that prices are conditioned on data processing and sharing (UCPD Art. 7; DSA Art. 25).

Provide a layered privacy notice at sign-up identifying the 60 partners (or partner categories with a linked list), each purpose, retention periods, the profiling logic, and how to exercise data-subject rights (GDPR Art. 13).

Screen out or obtain separate explicit consent for any purchase data that could reveal special-category information (health, religion, pregnancy) and avoid building sensitive inferences for targeting (GDPR Art. 9).
Contractually and technically require external-platform audiences to exclude special-category-derived parameters and under-18 users from profiling-based targeting (DSA Arts. 26(3), 28).
Confirm loyalty membership and profiling-based offers are restricted to adults before launch.
