findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A single combined consent bundling four distinct processing purposes is not 'specific' and, per the definition, bundled consent does not qualify as valid consent. Data subjects cannot consent granularly to each purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Unbundle the consent into separate, independently toggleable opt-ins for each purpose (profiling, location push, third-party sharing, cross-platform ad targeting), each defaulting to off, with no purpose pre-selected.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(4) requires that when assessing whether consent is freely given, utmost account is taken of whether performance of a service is conditional on consent to processing not necessary for that service. Profiling, third-party sharing and cross-platform ad targeting are not necessary to provide member pricing, so conditioning all member prices on this consent makes it non-free ('pay-with-data'). Removing the previously available data-free tier reinforces the lack of a genuine free choice.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices.
findings.recommendation: Restore an equivalent-value membership/pricing tier that does not require consent to non-necessary marketing processing, so members have a genuine free choice; do not degrade core benefits for those who decline optional processing.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(3) requires that withdrawing consent be as easy as giving it and that withdrawal must be possible without detriment. Making withdrawal terminate the entire membership imposes a serious penalty that deters withdrawal and effectively negates the right, undermining the free and revocable nature of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Decouple consent withdrawal from membership status: allow members to withdraw any or all consents while retaining membership and core benefits; provide a withdrawal mechanism at least as easy as the enrolment opt-in.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling, sharing with 60 partners and cross-platform ad targeting each require a valid lawful basis. As the campaign relies on consent that is bundled, conditional and penalised on withdrawal, that consent is likely invalid, leaving the processing without a lawful basis. Legitimate interest is unlikely to justify large-scale sharing and cross-platform targeting given the individuals' reasonable expectations.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis for each processing operation; where consent is relied on, ensure it meets Arts. 4(11)/7. Name or categorise the 60 recipients and reassess whether the scope of sharing is proportionate.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle is engaged. Quietly removing the data-free tier and steering members via 'Say YES to savings!' framing while obscuring the data trade-offs constitutes unfair, non-transparent processing design (a consent dark pattern).
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose the change and the data implications of enrolment; avoid manipulative framing; present the choice neutrally so members understand what data is processed and can decline without confusion.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection controllers must inform data subjects of purposes, legal basis, recipients (or categories), retention and rights, including information about profiling. In-store signage reading only 'Say YES to savings!' does not convey this, and 60 unnamed partners is insufficiently specified for the recipient-disclosure obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners'
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at every collection point (in-store, app, email) identifying purposes, legal basis, retention, data-subject rights, the categories/identities of the 60 recipients, and the profiling logic.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time to direct marketing and profiling related to it. The design forces an all-or-nothing choice tied to membership rather than allowing an unconditional opt-out of direct-marketing profiling, which fails to facilitate this right.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, unconditional mechanism to object to direct-marketing profiling and location-based push offers at any time, without loss of membership or member prices, and honour it immediately.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of purchase history to predict preferences and target offers meets the definition of profiling, which triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) engaged above.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling
findings.recommendation: Treat the purchase-history analysis as profiling and ensure it complies with the lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations flagged in this assessment.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch is built on a single combined consent covering four distinct processing purposes (profiling, location-based push, sharing with 60 partners, cross-platform ad targeting), tied to core member pricing, with the data-free tier removed and withdrawal cancelling membership. This fails GDPR's freely-given, specific, granular and unbundled consent standard (Arts. 4(11), 7), the conditionality and withdrawal-parity rules (Art. 7), and the fairness/transparency principles (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13). Personalised profiling and data sharing also require a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) and must respect the absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). This is a high-severity GDPR compliance failure as described.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Where the enrolment/consent is presented through the app's online interface, the design deceives or manipulates recipients and materially distorts their ability to make a free and informed decision. It bundles distinct choices into one all-or-nothing 'YES', gives overwhelming prominence to acceptance ('Say YES to savings!' with a 40% price penalty for declining — confirm-shaming), removes the previously available data-free option, and obstructs withdrawal by making it cancel membership entirely (making 'cancellation' harder and penalised). These are the archetypal dark patterns Art. 25 prohibits.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices ... now require accepting a single combined consent ... Declining any element means losing all member prices. In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'. A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed. Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Redesign the app consent interface: unbundle each processing purpose into separate, equally prominent opt-ins with a genuine, penalty-free 'reject' path; restore or offer a data-minimal membership tier; present neutral (non-confirm-shaming) wording; and make consent withdrawal as easy as giving it without cancelling core membership. Do not give visual/wording prominence to acceptance over refusal.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign drives behavioural advertising delivered on external online platforms. Each such ad must let recipients identify in real time that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters (with a way to change them). As advertiser, the supermarket must supply this information so the platforms can meet Art. 26(1); the campaign as described gives no indication these disclosures are in place.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad placed on external platforms is clearly labelled as advertising, discloses the supermarket as advertiser/payer, and surfaces meaningful targeting parameters and controls. Provide platforms with the advertiser/payer identity and parameter data required by Art. 26(1).

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Purchase-history profiling of grocery data can directly or by inference reveal GDPR Art. 9 special categories (e.g. health from dietary/medical/pharmacy items, religion from food choices, potentially ethnicity). Presenting platform advertisements based on profiling that uses such special-category data — even inferred — is prohibited under Art. 26(3) regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling ... ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Exclude any special-category attributes (including proxies/inferences such as health-, religion- or ethnicity-linked purchase segments) from the profiles used to target platform advertising. Document and enforce filtering so no ad audience is built on Art. 9 data.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: A mass-market grocery app is plausibly accessible to and used by minors. If the platform presents profiling-based advertising (including personalised push offers) to recipients it is aware with reasonable certainty are minors, that is prohibited under Art. 28, which also requires appropriate measures for a high level of minors' privacy and safety.
findings.evidence_quote: location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Implement age-assurance/segmentation so no profiling-based ads or personalised push offers are delivered to users known or reasonably certain to be minors, and apply age-appropriate privacy-by-default settings in the app.

verdicts.notes: The supermarket operates a loyalty app with a consent/enrolment interface and drives cross-platform behavioural ad targeting, engaging the DSA where it acts as an online-platform interface provider and as an advertiser on external platforms. The bundled, all-or-nothing consent flow framed with "Say YES to savings!", combined with obstruction (withdrawal cancels membership) and quiet removal of the data-free tier, presents a strong DSA Art. 25 dark-patterns risk. Secondary risks arise under Art. 26(1) (ad transparency on external platforms), Art. 26(3) (profiling that could infer special-category data), and Art. 28 (profiled ads/push potentially reaching minors). Art. 39 (VLOP ad repositories) does not apply — the supermarket app is not a VLOP.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The real 'price' of the member prices is now the surrender of purchase-history profiling, location data, sharing with 60 retail media partners and cross-platform ad targeting. Presenting the offer as 'savings' via 'Say YES to savings!' while quietly removing the data-free alternative hides material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision — namely the extent of data processing that is the true condition of the discount and the loss of the no-data option. Providing this information unclearly or not at the decision point is a misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed
findings.recommendation: At the point of enrolment/consent (signage, app, email), clearly and prominently disclose in plain language the full scope of data processing that is the condition of member prices (profiling, location tracking, sharing with 60 named partners, external ad targeting), and transparently state whether any non-data or reduced-data membership option is available. Do not obscure the removal of the previous tier.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Bundling all processing purposes into a single take-it-or-leave-it consent, tying up to 40% price advantages on grocery staples to acceptance, and cancelling membership entirely on withdrawal of consent uses the threat of losing everyday savings to pressure consumers. This undue influence and the onerous barrier to exercising the right to refuse/withdraw can significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and cause them to consent to data processing they would not otherwise accept.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices
findings.recommendation: Decouple the price benefit from non-essential processing so consumers can obtain member prices without accepting profiling, 60-partner sharing and external ad targeting. Make refusing or withdrawing consent for optional purposes as easy and consequence-light as giving it, and stop conditioning continued membership on retention of consent for non-essential data uses.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The in-store signage frames the data-surrender decision purely as 'savings', a confirm-shaming / false-framing design that steers the consumer toward consent and away from the significant privacy trade-off. Assessed against professional diligence, this manipulative design is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average grocery shopper and functions as the general-clause safety net for the deceptive design not fully captured by Arts. 6-8. Because mass-market grocery channels can reach less sophisticated or vulnerable consumers, the distortion risk is heightened.
findings.evidence_quote: Say YES to savings!
findings.recommendation: Reframe the enrolment call-to-action neutrally so it does not present consent as an unambiguous benefit ('Say YES to savings!'); give equal visual prominence and equally easy pathways to the decline/opt-out option, and avoid confirm-shaming or loaded language in the consent interface.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch is primarily a GDPR consent matter, but its consumer-facing design engages the UCPD. The "Say YES to savings!" framing, the all-or-nothing bundling ("declining any element means losing all member prices"), the quiet removal of the data-free tier, and membership cancellation on withdrawal together constitute deceptive/manipulative design that steers consumers' economic behaviour. These are assessable under the general unfairness clause (Art. 5), as a misleading omission (Art. 7 — the true "data cost" and terms are obscured), and potentially as an aggressive practice through undue influence and onerous barriers (Arts. 8-9). No blacklisted (Annex I) practice is clearly present, so findings sit at high/medium rather than critical.

report.executive_summary: This campaign relaunches the SuperSave loyalty club by tying member prices (up to 40% off) to a single all-or-nothing consent that bundles four separate data uses: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and ad targeting on external platforms. As designed, it very likely breaches EU data protection law and consumer law, and carries significant online-platform (DSA) risk. The core problems are that the consent is bundled rather than granular, is not freely given because members lose all savings if they decline, cannot be withdrawn without losing membership, and the previous data-free tier was quietly removed. The "Say YES to savings!" framing plus removal of the no-data option amount to a dark pattern and a misleading/aggressive commercial practice that pressures shoppers into surrendering data. There is also inadequate disclosure of purposes, recipients and profiling, and a risk that grocery-based profiling infers sensitive traits or reaches minors. This is not a fixable-with-wording problem: the underlying structure ("pay with your data or lose your discount") needs to change. Overall verdict: high risk — do not launch in its current form.
recommendations: Unbundle the consent: provide separate, independently toggleable opt-ins for each purpose (profiling, location push, third-party sharing, cross-platform ad targeting), each defaulting to off and none pre-selected.

Restore an equivalent-value membership/pricing tier that does NOT require consent to non-essential marketing processing, so members keep member prices without accepting profiling, 60-partner sharing or external ad targeting.
Decouple consent withdrawal from membership: let members withdraw any or all consents while keeping membership and member prices, and make withdrawal as easy as giving consent.
Replace the 'Say YES to savings!' framing with neutral wording; give the decline/opt-out path equal visual prominence and equal ease, and remove confirm-shaming.

Clearly and prominently disclose (in-store, app, email) the full data implications of enrolment, including purposes, legal basis, retention, rights, and the categories or identities of the 60 recipients, and openly disclose that the data-free tier was removed / whether a reduced-data option exists.
Establish and document a valid lawful basis for each processing operation, and provide an easy, unconditional opt-out of direct-marketing profiling and location push without loss of membership.

For external-platform ads: ensure each ad is labelled as advertising, discloses the advertiser/payer and meaningful targeting parameters, and exclude any special-category attributes or proxies (health, religion, ethnicity inferred from purchases) from targeting.
Implement age assurance so no profiling-based ads or personalised push offers reach users who are known or reasonably certain to be minors.

campaign.title: MegaBasket sponsored search results
campaign.text: MegaBasket, an online marketplace with 40M EU users, sells 'Boosted Placement': paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile. Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.

detected_practices: Sponsored/paid ranking positioned as top search results
Advertising disclosure obscured (6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag, hover-only on desktop, absent on mobile)
Misleading ranking explanation ('ordered by relevance' when placement is paid)
Behavioural/inferred-attribute targeting by price sensitivity
Paid prominence in search results without clear disclosure
triage.summary: MegaBasket, a large EU online marketplace (40M users), sells 'Boosted Placement' that puts paid seller products in the top four search positions with disclosure that is effectively hidden (6pt hover-only tag on desktop, none on mobile) while telling users results are 'ordered by relevance'. It also targets users based on inferred price sensitivity. This raises concerns about deceptive/undisclosed advertising, misleading ranking transparency, and personal-data-driven behavioural targeting.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's price sensitivity is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict an aspect concerning the person's 'economic situation' and 'behaviour', which is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This is the threshold definition that pulls the practice into the GDPR regime.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Recognise price-sensitivity segmentation as profiling and document it in the RoPA; apply all downstream profiling obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights) below.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling of 40M EU users to derive price-sensitivity segments requires a valid lawful basis. Personalised-advertising profiling generally requires consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment; the campaign identifies no lawful basis and describes no consent mechanism or LIA. Processing without a demonstrable basis is unlawful under Art. 6(1).
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before running price-sensitivity targeting: obtain freely given, specific, informed opt-in consent, or complete and record a legitimate-interests assessment that weighs users' reasonable expectations (behavioural targeting on a marketplace is intrusive and hard to justify on LI alone). Do not deploy the segment until this is in place.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Deriving and acting on inferred economic attributes without informing users breaches the fairness and transparency limbs of Art. 5(1)(a). Users cannot reasonably expect that browsing behaviour is used to score their price sensitivity for seller targeting, and covert inference of economic vulnerability is inherently unfair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Make the inference and its use transparent at or before collection, and assess fairness — in particular avoid exploiting inferred price sensitivity in ways users would not expect (e.g. steering price-sensitive users toward higher-margin placements). Conduct a DPIA given large-scale profiling of 40M individuals.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data are collected and used to build price-sensitivity profiles, Art. 13 requires the controller to inform users at collection of the purposes, legal basis, recipients and the existence of profiling. Nothing in the campaign indicates users are told their data is used to infer price sensitivity for ad targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Provide layered, point-of-collection information disclosing that behavioural data is used to infer price sensitivity for advertising, the lawful basis relied on, that this is profiling, and how to object — linked from the privacy notice and the ad-settings surface.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information about processing (including profiling) to be concise, transparent and not misleading. Presenting outputs shaped by paid placement and price-sensitivity targeting as merely 'ordered by relevance' undermines the transparency of any profiling-related information provided to data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure any explanation of how results are ordered accurately reflects the use of profiling/targeting signals, using clear and plain language, and reconcile it with the Art. 13 profiling disclosure.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct-marketing/advertising purposes triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). The campaign provides no mechanism for users to object to or opt out of price-sensitivity profiling, and users must be explicitly informed of this right at the latest at first communication.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Implement an easily accessible, no-cost opt-out from advertising profiling (including price-sensitivity segmentation), honour it immediately and completely, and present the right to object explicitly and separately from other information.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket's ad system lets sellers target users by "inferred price sensitivity" — automated processing of personal data to predict a person's economic situation, i.e. profiling under GDPR Art. 4(4). This engages GDPR obligations on lawful basis (Art. 6(1)), fair/transparent processing (Art. 5(1)(a)), transparency about profiling (Art. 12/13) and the absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). The campaign discloses none of these safeguards, so the profiling is likely being run without a demonstrable lawful basis or the required transparency. (Ad-disclosure and ranking-transparency issues fall primarily under DSA/UCPD and are left to those agents.)

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each advertisement, recipients can identify in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. A 6pt light-grey tag that only appears on hover on desktop — and is entirely absent on mobile — does not make the paid nature clear, unambiguous or perceivable in real time. On mobile there is no disclosure at all. Meaningful information on who paid and the targeting parameters is also not provided.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a persistent, high-contrast, adequately sized 'Sponsored/Ad' label on every Boosted Placement listing on both desktop and mobile (not hover-dependent), together with accessible information on the advertiser/payer and the main targeting parameters and how to change them.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions; disguised advertisements are a recognised dark pattern. Making paid placements visually identical to organic results while hiding the disclosure gives paid choices undue prominence and disguises their commercial nature, distorting users' purchasing decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Redesign the search interface so paid placements are visually and functionally distinguishable from organic results with a clear, always-visible ad label; do not rely on interface design that blends paid and organic listings.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: Art. 27 requires platforms using recommender/ranking systems to set out in plain language the main parameters used and options to modify them. Stating results are 'ordered by relevance' when the top four positions are determined by payment misrepresents the main ranking parameters and omits that paid placement is a determinant, so the ranking transparency is inaccurate and misleading.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Update the ranking explanation to disclose that paid placement ('Boosted Placement') is a determining parameter for the top positions, describe the actual main parameters in plain language, and provide options for users to influence ranking (e.g. sort by genuine relevance/price).

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) prohibits ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories (health, religion, ethnicity, etc.). Inferred price sensitivity is not a special category of data, so on the facts as described this prohibition is not engaged. Flagged for completeness because inference-based targeting can, in some cases, act as a proxy that reveals special-category data; if price-sensitivity inferences are derived from or correlate with sensitive attributes, Art. 26(3) could apply.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Confirm that price-sensitivity inferences are not derived from or proxies for GDPR Art. 9 special categories; document the input signals to demonstrate no sensitive-data profiling underlies the targeting.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 39 requires very large online platforms (VLOPs) to maintain a public ad repository including ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. The DSA VLOP threshold is 45M average monthly EU users; at 40M MegaBasket is below the threshold and likely not a designated VLOP, so Art. 39 probably does not apply yet. It is flagged because the platform is near the threshold and would need to build an ad repository if designated.
findings.evidence_quote: an online marketplace with 40M EU users
findings.recommendation: Monitor EU user numbers against the 45M VLOP threshold; if approaching or designated, prepare a compliant public advertisement repository capturing Boosted Placement ads, payers and targeting parameters.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket is a large EU online marketplace and thus an "online platform" under the DSA, engaging the advertising- and interface-transparency regime. Its 'Boosted Placement' product presents paid seller listings that are visually indistinguishable from organic results with an effectively hidden label (6pt light-grey, hover-only on desktop, absent on mobile), while telling users results are "ordered by relevance." This engages Art. 26(1) (ad identifiability), Art. 25 (dark pattern / disguised advertising) and Art. 27 (recommender/ranking parameter transparency) — likely breaches. The inferred price-sensitivity targeting does not appear to use GDPR Art. 9 special categories, so the Art. 26(3) prohibition is likely not triggered (noted for completeness); Art. 39 applies only if MegaBasket is a designated VLOP (its 40M users are below the 45M threshold), flagged as info.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits hiding material information or providing it in an unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely manner, and expressly requires identifying the commercial intent of a practice where not apparent from context. The paid nature of the top four search positions is material information the average consumer needs to weigh those results correctly. A 6pt, low-contrast, hover-only label on desktop — and no label at all on mobile — means the commercial intent is not clearly identified and is effectively hidden. Paid prominence in search results is expressly treated as material information under the UCPD framework.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a clear, high-contrast, always-visible 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label on every boosted result on both desktop and mobile, in adequate font size and with sufficient colour contrast, without requiring hover. Ensure the label is present in real time for every paid placement.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 catches practices containing false information that deceive the average consumer as to the main characteristics of the product/service and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Stating results are 'ordered by relevance' when the first four positions are determined by payment, not relevance, is an affirmatively false statement about the ranking parameters. It deceives consumers into treating paid placements as the most relevant/best options, materially influencing purchase decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Correct the ranking explanation so it accurately discloses that top positions are paid placements (e.g. 'Sponsored results appear first; remaining results are ordered by relevance'). Never describe paid positions as relevance-based.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: Annex I point 11 blacklists using content to promote a product where a trader has paid, without making the paid promotion clear. While drafted for editorial media, its rationale — undisclosed paid content presented as independent — applies by analogy to paid search results presented as indistinguishable from organic listings. The absence of any effective disclosure means the paid promotion is not made clear, so the blacklisted advertorial-style concern is engaged, though the direct fit is weaker than Arts. 6-7.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Treat boosted placements as clearly identified paid promotions with prominent labelling so they are never presented as independent/organic content; this fix overlaps with the Art. 7 remedy.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Targeting by inferred price sensitivity is primarily assessed under GDPR (profiling/lawful basis) and DSA (ad-targeting transparency). Under the UCPD it is noted as context: the general fairness safety-net (Art. 5) and personalised-pricing disclosure obligations could be engaged if price-sensitivity inference were used to shape prices or offers in a way contrary to professional diligence. On the facts given (targeting of ads, not prices) no distinct UCPD breach is established, so this is flagged for information only.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: If price-sensitivity inference is ever used to personalise prices or offers rather than only ad targeting, disclose the personalisation to consumers and reassess against Art. 6(1)(d) and personalised-pricing disclosure rules.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket's 'Boosted Placement' sells the top four search positions to paying sellers while making the advertising nature effectively invisible (6pt light-grey hover-only 'promoted' tag on desktop, absent on mobile) and simultaneously tells users results are 'ordered by relevance'. This engages the UCPD on two strong grounds: failure to identify commercial intent / hidden advertising (Art. 7 misleading omission — a matter the CJEU and Consumer Protection Cooperation authorities treat as material), and an affirmatively false statement about the ranking basis (Art. 6 misleading action). Both are likely breaches. The inferred-price-sensitivity targeting is primarily a GDPR/DSA matter but is flagged for UCPD context. Annex I point 11 (advertorials) is arguably engaged by analogy but is a secondary/weaker fit for marketplace search grids.

report.executive_summary: The MegaBasket "Boosted Placement" campaign sells the top four search positions to paying sellers, presents them as visually identical to organic results, and tells users results are "ordered by relevance" while also letting sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity. This creates serious compliance problems across three areas. Under the DSA and the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, the near-invisible ad label (6pt grey, hover-only on desktop, absent on mobile) fails to make the paid nature clear, and the "ordered by relevance" claim is affirmatively false — both are likely breaches, and the blended design risks being treated as a prohibited dark pattern. Under the GDPR, inferring price sensitivity for 40M users is profiling that currently appears to run with no stated lawful basis, no transparency, and no way for users to object. The EU AI Act is not engaged, and the DSA's VLOP ad-repository and special-category ad-targeting rules are not triggered on the current facts (though the platform is close to the 45M VLOP threshold). Overall verdict: high risk — the campaign should not go live in its current form until the labelling, ranking-disclosure, and profiling-consent issues are fixed.
recommendations: Add a clear, high-contrast, always-visible 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label to every Boosted Placement on BOTH desktop and mobile — no hover requirement, adequate font size and contrast. This single fix addresses the strongest DSA (Art. 26), UCPD (Art. 7), and dark-pattern (DSA Art. 25) risks.

Correct the ranking explanation immediately: stop describing paid positions as 'ordered by relevance'. State plainly that the top positions are paid placements and describe the actual main ranking parameters (DSA Art. 27 / UCPD Art. 6).
Do not run price-sensitivity targeting until a valid GDPR lawful basis is in place — obtain freely given opt-in consent or complete and document a legitimate-interests assessment (GDPR Art. 6).

Make the price-sensitivity profiling transparent to users at the point of collection (purposes, that it is profiling, lawful basis) and add an easy, free opt-out honouring the absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling (GDPR Arts. 5, 12, 13, 21).
Conduct a DPIA covering the large-scale (40M user) profiling and record the price-sensitivity segmentation in the RoPA.
Redesign the search grid so paid placements are visually and functionally distinguishable from organic results, rather than blended (DSA Art. 25 dark-pattern risk).
Confirm and document that price-sensitivity inferences are not derived from or proxies for GDPR Art. 9 special categories, to keep clear of the DSA Art. 26(3) ad-targeting ban.
Monitor EU monthly active users against the 45M VLOP threshold; if approached or designated, build a compliant public ad repository (DSA Art. 39).
If price-sensitivity data is ever used to personalise prices or offers (not just ad targeting), disclose it and reassess under UCPD Art. 6(1)(d) and personalised-pricing rules.

campaign.title: MegaBasket sponsored search results
campaign.text: MegaBasket, an online marketplace with 40M EU users, sells 'Boosted Placement': paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile. Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.

detected_practices: Sponsored search results occupying top four grid positions
Paid placement visually near-indistinguishable from organic results
Advertising disclosure hidden (6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag on hover only, absent on mobile)
Misleading ranking explanation claiming 'ordered by relevance' while placement is paid
Behavioural targeting by inferred price sensitivity
Very large online platform (40M EU users)
triage.summary: MegaBasket, a large EU online marketplace (40M users), sells 'Boosted Placement' whereby paying sellers occupy the top four search grid positions that are visually near-identical to organic results, with advertising disclosure only appearing on desktop hover and absent on mobile, while ranking explanations misleadingly state results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity. The campaign raises concerns about undisclosed paid ranking, deceptive ranking transparency, and behavioural profiling of consumers.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's price sensitivity is automated processing of personal data to evaluate and predict personal aspects — specifically the individual's economic situation and behaviour — which is squarely within the definition of profiling. This classification is what triggers the substantive GDPR obligations below.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Recognise the price-sensitivity targeting feature as profiling and document it in the record of processing activities and DPIA, so the accompanying lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations are addressed.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling users by inferred price sensitivity for advertising requires a valid lawful basis. Such behavioural targeting generally needs freely given consent or a rigorously documented legitimate-interests assessment that survives the balancing test. The campaign describes no consent mechanism or LIA, so processing appears to lack a demonstrable lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before running price-sensitivity targeting: either obtain granular, opt-in consent for this profiling, or complete and retain a legitimate-interests assessment weighing the intrusiveness of inferring economic vulnerability against user expectations, with an easy opt-out.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that individuals are not misled about how their data drives outcomes. Profiling users by inferred price sensitivity while telling them results are merely 'ordered by relevance' is covert, unfair processing that obscures the role of paid placement and behavioural inference in what users see.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure ranking and ad-serving explanations honestly reflect that paid placement and profiling parameters (including inferred price sensitivity) influence results; remove or correct the 'ordered by relevance' statement so users are not misled about the processing of their data.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is used to build price-sensitivity inferences, Art. 13 requires the controller to inform users of the purposes, lawful basis, recipients (sellers as targeting parties) and the existence of profiling. The campaign shows no such information being provided at or before collection.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at the point of data collection that explains the price-sensitivity profiling, its purpose and lawful basis, that data feeds seller ad-targeting, and the user's rights including the right to object.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct-marketing purposes triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). Users must be able to opt out of the price-sensitivity profiling and its use for advertising at any time, and be explicitly informed of this right at the latest at first communication. The campaign describes no opt-out mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Implement a clear, easily accessible opt-out from price-sensitivity profiling and marketing use, present the right to object explicitly and separately in the interface, and ensure objecting users are excluded from the targeting system immediately.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket's ad system lets sellers target users by "inferred price sensitivity", which is automated profiling of an individual's economic situation and behaviour under GDPR Art. 4(4). This engages the requirements for a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)), transparency (Arts. 5(1)(a), 13), and the absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). The campaign text discloses none of these safeguards, and the platform's misleading "ordered by relevance" explanation compounds the fairness/transparency concern. Note: DSA ad-transparency/targeting rules and UCPD ranking-disclosure issues are covered by other agents.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, for each ad, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. A 6pt light-grey label shown only on desktop hover — and entirely absent on mobile — is neither clear, unambiguous, nor available in real time to the user viewing the results. Boosted Placement therefore fails the ad-identifiability obligation, especially on mobile where there is no disclosure at all.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a persistent, high-contrast, adequately sized 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label on every boosted result on both desktop and mobile (no hover requirement), and surface the paying seller's identity and the fact of payment for each placement.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Making paid placements visually identical to organic results — with disclosure hidden on hover and absent on mobile — is a disguised advertisement, an established dark pattern. Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an interface in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions. Presenting ads as if they were neutral relevance-ranked results distorts consumers' purchasing choices.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Redesign the search interface so paid and organic results are visually and structurally distinguishable (clear labelling, distinct styling/section), removing any design element that causes users to mistake paid placements for organic relevance rankings.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: Art. 27 requires online platforms using recommender systems to set out in plain language the main parameters used to rank results. Stating results are 'ordered by relevance' while the top four positions are in fact determined by payment misrepresents (and omits) a main ranking parameter — paid placement. The ranking explanation is therefore inaccurate and incomplete under Art. 27.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Update the ranking/recommender explanation to disclose in plain language that top positions are determined by paid placement (commercial consideration) alongside relevance, clearly separating paid from organic ranking criteria.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: With 40M EU users MegaBasket is above the VLOP threshold (45M average monthly recipients is the designation line; 40M is close and the platform is clearly at very-large scale), triggering Art. 39 obligations to maintain a public ad repository including ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. The Boosted Placement ads and their inferred-price-sensitivity targeting must be logged in such a repository if MegaBasket is designated a VLOP.
findings.evidence_quote: an online marketplace with 40M EU users
findings.recommendation: If designated (or once above the VLOP threshold), maintain a compliant public ad repository capturing each Boosted Placement ad's content, the paying seller, the payer, the targeting parameters (including price-sensitivity segments) and reach; ensure targeting practices can withstand this public scrutiny.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories (health, religion, sexual orientation, etc.). Inferred price sensitivity is not, in itself, a special category of data, so this targeting does not breach Art. 26(3) on the facts described. Flagged for context because if price-sensitivity inference draws on or acts as a proxy for special-category data, the prohibition would be engaged, and the targeting parameters must still be disclosed under Art. 26(1) and logged under Art. 39.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Confirm that the price-sensitivity inference does not use or proxy GDPR Art. 9 special-category data; disclose the price-sensitivity targeting parameter to recipients under Art. 26(1) and include it in the ad repository under Art. 39.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket is an online marketplace (an online platform, and at 40M EU users a very large online platform) presenting paid advertising in its search results, so the DSA advertising and interface-design rules apply directly. The design makes paid placement visually near-indistinguishable from organic results with an inadequate disclosure, and describes results as "ordered by relevance" — engaging Art. 26(1) (ad identifiability), Art. 25 (disguised-advertisement dark pattern) and Art. 27 (recommender-parameter transparency). Art. 39 ad-repository obligations are engaged as a VLOP; the price-sensitivity targeting is flagged for context but is not itself an Art. 26(3) breach since price sensitivity is not a GDPR Art. 9 special category.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Paid placement is a material fact and its commercial intent is not apparent from context, so it must be clearly identified. A 6pt light-grey label shown only on desktop hover, and entirely absent on mobile, does not make the advertising nature clear, intelligible and timely. This hides material information / provides it in an unclear, ambiguous and untimely manner, causing consumers to treat paid listings as neutral, relevance-based results — a misleading omission of commercial intent contrary to Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a persistent, high-contrast, adequately sized 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label on every paid listing, always visible (not hover-dependent) and shown identically on desktop and mobile, positioned so the average consumer immediately perceives the listing as advertising before interacting with it.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The top four positions are determined by payment ('Boosted Placement'), yet the platform tells consumers results are 'ordered by relevance'. This is false information about the main parameters and manner in which the offer is presented and ranked, deceiving the average consumer into believing top listings are the most relevant on the merits. It is likely to cause a transactional decision (clicking/buying the top items) they would not otherwise take — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Correct the ranking explanation to state truthfully that the leading positions are paid placements and describe the actual main ranking parameters; do not claim results are 'ordered by relevance' where payment determines position.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Making paid listings visually indistinguishable from organic ones is a disguised-advertisement / deceptive design practice contrary to professional diligence that materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average consumer. Where not fully caught by Arts. 6-7 it engages the Art. 5 general fairness safety-net (the dark-patterns concept expressly maps disguised ads to UCPD Arts. 5-9).
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Redesign the interface so paid and organic results are clearly and consistently distinguishable across all devices, avoiding false visual hierarchy that steers consumers toward paid listings under the impression they are neutral results.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: Annex I point 11 blacklists paid promotion presented as independent editorial content. Search-result placement is analogous paid promotion disguised as neutral platform output; while its primary anchor under the UCPD is Art. 7(2) (hidden commercial intent) rather than classic 'editorial media' advertorial, the same undisclosed-paid-promotion rationale is engaged and reinforces that disclosure is mandatory.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search
findings.recommendation: Treat the paid placement as advertising requiring unambiguous disclosure in all circumstances; ensure the sponsored nature is inseparable from the listing rather than concealed, consistent with the per-se prohibition on undisclosed paid promotion.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket sells top-four search placement that is visually near-identical to organic results, discloses the paid nature only via a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag on desktop hover and not at all on mobile, and tells users results are 'ordered by relevance'. Under the UCPD this is a disguised advertisement with hidden commercial intent (misleading omission, Art. 7) compounded by a false statement about the ranking criterion (misleading action, Art. 6), and functions as a deceptive interface design caught by the general unfairness prohibition (Art. 5). These are likely breaches that materially distort consumers' transactional decisions.

report.executive_summary: Your "Boosted Placement" product sells the top four search positions to paying sellers but makes those paid listings look identical to organic results — the only disclosure is a tiny 6pt grey "promoted" tag that appears on desktop hover and never on mobile — while telling shoppers results are "ordered by relevance." Three separate laws are triggered by this. Under the DSA and the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, this is a disguised advertisement with hidden commercial intent and a false ranking claim, which regulators treat as a deceptive "dark pattern" and a misleading practice that steers purchasing decisions. Under the GDPR, letting sellers target users by "inferred price sensitivity" is profiling of people's economic circumstances that currently has no stated lawful basis, no transparency notice, and no opt-out. As a very-large-scale marketplace (40M EU users) you also likely face DSA ad-repository obligations. None of these problems are cosmetic — they go to the core of how the product is designed and described. The campaign should not launch in its current form; fixing the disclosure, the "relevance" claim, and the profiling safeguards is required first.
recommendations: Add a persistent, high-contrast, adequately sized 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label to every paid listing, always visible (no hover) and shown identically on desktop and mobile — this single fix addresses the most serious DSA and UCPD breaches.

Stop describing results as 'ordered by relevance'. Update ranking/recommender explanations to state plainly that the top positions are paid placements, and describe the actual main ranking parameters (DSA Art. 27; UCPD Arts. 6-7).

Redesign the search grid so paid and organic results are visually and structurally distinguishable (distinct styling or a separate section), eliminating the false visual hierarchy that regulators classify as a prohibited dark pattern (DSA Art. 25).

Before running price-sensitivity targeting, establish and document a GDPR lawful basis — either granular opt-in consent or a retained legitimate-interests assessment — recognising this feature as profiling of users' economic situation.

Provide a clear layered privacy notice at data collection explaining the price-sensitivity profiling, its purpose, that it feeds seller targeting, and give users an easy, always-available opt-out (GDPR Arts. 13 and 21 right to object to marketing profiling).
Confirm the price-sensitivity inference does not use or act as a proxy for GDPR Art. 9 special-category data; if it does, targeting is outright prohibited under DSA Art. 26(3).

Given the 40M EU user base near the VLOP threshold, prepare a compliant public ad repository logging each Boosted Placement ad's content, paying seller, payer, targeting parameters (including price-sensitivity segments) and reach (DSA Art. 39).

campaign.title: MegaBasket sponsored search results
campaign.text: MegaBasket, an online marketplace with 40M EU users, sells 'Boosted Placement': paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile. Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.

detected_practices: paid sponsored search placements in top positions
advertising disclosure inadequate/absent on mobile ('promoted' tag not shown)
hidden/obscured 'promoted' label (6pt light-grey, hover-only on desktop)
misleading ranking explanation claiming 'ordered by relevance'
undisclosed advertising blended with organic results
behavioural targeting by inferred price sensitivity
profiling/inference of consumer characteristics
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult marketplace shoppers across the EU; no indication minors are specifically targeted, though a 40M-user general marketplace may incidentally reach some. DSA obligations are heightened given marketplace scale (potential VLOP threshold, and Article 26 ad/ranking transparency and Article 27 recommender transparency). Inferred price-sensitivity targeting engages GDPR profiling rules and possibly DSA restrictions on profiling-based ads. The concealed 'promoted' labelling and false 'relevance' claim engage UCPD prohibitions on misleading/hidden commercial communications (Annex I no. 11 - advertorial/hidden ads).
triage.summary: MegaBasket, a large online marketplace (40M EU users), sells 'Boosted Placement' where paid seller products occupy the top four search positions styled identically to organic results, with a 'promoted' tag that is barely visible on desktop and entirely absent on mobile, while ranking explanations falsely claim results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also targets users based on inferred price sensitivity. The campaign raises concerns around undisclosed/misleading advertising, ranking transparency, and behavioural profiling.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Inferring 'price sensitivity' from user behaviour is automated processing of personal data to evaluate and predict a personal aspect (economic situation / behaviour / preferences), squarely meeting the definition of profiling in Art. 4(4). This triggers the full profiling regime under GDPR.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Formally document the price-sensitivity inference as profiling, map the input signals and data flows, and treat it under the profiling obligations below (lawful basis, transparency, objection). Conduct a DPIA given the large-scale (40M users) behavioural profiling.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling users by inferred price sensitivity for ad targeting is personal-data processing that requires a valid lawful basis. The submission provides no evidence of consent or a completed legitimate-interests balancing test; behavioural advertising profiling of this kind generally requires consent or a carefully documented LIA, which is absent here.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis before enabling price-sensitivity targeting. If relying on consent, obtain freely given, specific, informed consent; if relying on legitimate interests, complete and retain a legitimate-interests assessment weighing the intrusiveness of inferring economic vulnerability.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle requires that data subjects understand how their data is used. Inferring price sensitivity to shape what users see, while telling them results are simply 'ordered by relevance', is a non-transparent and arguably unfair use of profiling that conceals the personalised, commercial nature of the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Ensure ranking and targeting explanations honestly reflect that placements are paid and that targeting uses inferred user characteristics; avoid framing that hides the profiling from users.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is used to build a price-sensitivity profile, Art. 13 requires the controller to inform users at collection about the purposes, legal basis and the existence of profiling. The submission gives no indication users are told their price sensitivity is inferred and used for ad targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy notice and just-in-time disclosures to clearly explain that behavioural data is used to infer price sensitivity for advertising, including the purposes, lawful basis, and the meaningful logic of the profiling.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct-marketing/advertising purposes is subject to an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). No opt-out from the price-sensitivity profiling and targeting is described.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Provide an easily accessible, functioning opt-out that stops profiling-based ad targeting (including the price-sensitivity inference) and inform users of this right at the point of first communication.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: If price-sensitivity inference were used to drive personalised pricing or automated exclusion from offers that significantly affects users, Art. 22 restrictions on solely-automated decisions would apply. As described the practice targets ad placement rather than setting individual prices, so this is flagged for monitoring rather than as a likely breach.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Confirm the inference is used only for ad targeting and not to set individualised prices or exclude users from offers; if it ever drives pricing/eligibility decisions, apply Art. 22 safeguards (explicit consent, human intervention, right to contest).

verdicts.notes: The campaign's ad system that lets sellers "target users by inferred price sensitivity" involves automated inference of an economic-situation attribute from personal data, which is profiling under GDPR Art. 4(4). Nothing in the submission establishes a lawful basis, transparency, or an opt-out mechanism for this profiling, engaging Arts. 6(1), 5(1)(a)/13 and 21. Note-only special-category (Art. 9) processing is not clearly present since price sensitivity alone is not a sensitive category, but the practice raises meaningful GDPR compliance risk. The hidden/misleading disclosure and ranking-transparency issues are primarily UCPD/DSA matters handled by other agents.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Boosted Placement products are advertisements presented on an online platform. Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf and who paid for it, plus the main targeting parameters. A 6pt light-grey label shown only on hover (desktop) and entirely absent on mobile does not allow real-time, unambiguous identification of the ad, and no advertiser/payer identity or targeting-parameter information is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a persistent, high-contrast, adequately sized 'Sponsored/Ad' label on every Boosted Placement result on both desktop and mobile (not hover-dependent), and make the seller/payer identity and the main targeting parameters accessible for each ad in real time.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing online interfaces that deceive or manipulate recipients or impair free and informed decisions; disguised advertisements are a recognised dark pattern. Styling paid placements identically to organic results, hiding the 'promoted' tag, and combining this with a false 'ordered by relevance' explanation materially distorts users' ability to distinguish ads from organic results and make informed choices.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Redesign the search interface so paid placements are visually and structurally distinct from organic results with prominent labelling, and remove any design element (concealed label, identical styling) that obscures the commercial nature of the top positions.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: The marketplace search ordering is a recommender system under the DSA. Art. 27 requires the main parameters of the ranking to be set out in plain language. Stating results are 'ordered by relevance' when the top four positions are determined by payment is inaccurate and omits paid placement as a decisive parameter, defeating the transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Update the ranking explanation to state plainly that the top positions are paid placements and disclose the actual main parameters (e.g. bid/payment plus relevance), and offer users any available options to modify the ranking.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: With 40M EU users, MegaBasket is likely to meet or approach the VLOP threshold (45M average monthly EU recipients). If designated as a VLOP, Art. 39 requires a public ad repository containing ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach for the Boosted Placement ads.
findings.evidence_quote: an online marketplace with 40M EU users
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP designation status; if designated (or upon reaching the threshold), implement a compliant public ad repository covering all Boosted Placement advertisements including targeting parameters and reach.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket's "Boosted Placement" is paid advertising presented on an online platform, so the DSA advertising and interface-design rules apply directly. The disclosure fails the Art. 26(1) standard (concealed/absent labels), the disguised-ad-plus-false-relevance design engages the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition, and the misleading "ordered by relevance" ranking explanation engages Art. 27 recommender transparency. Given 40M EU users, VLOP ad-repository obligations under Art. 39 may also apply. The inferred price-sensitivity targeting is a GDPR profiling issue but does not trigger the Art. 26(3) ban, which is limited to GDPR Art. 9 special-category data.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The commercial intent of the top-four placements is not apparent from context: paid results are styled identically to organic ones, and the paid nature is disclosed only via a 6pt light-grey label shown on hover on desktop and NOT AT ALL on mobile. Failing to identify commercial intent, and providing material information (that the placement is paid) in an unclear, ambiguous or non-existent manner, is a misleading omission under Art. 7. The paid/organic distinction is material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision, and on mobile it is entirely withheld.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a clear, prominent, always-visible advertising/paid-placement label on every boosted result across both desktop and mobile (not hover-dependent, adequate size and contrast). Ensure consumers can readily distinguish paid placements from organic results at first glance.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The ranking explanation affirmatively and falsely states results are 'ordered by relevance' when the first four grid positions are actually determined by payment ('Boosted Placement'). This is false information deceiving the average consumer as to the basis on which products are presented and their main characteristics/price advantage, likely causing a transactional decision (trusting/clicking a top result believed to be the most relevant) they would not otherwise take. It is a misleading action, not merely an omission.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Correct the ranking explanation to accurately state that top positions include paid placements and disclose the main parameters (including payment) that determine ranking order. Do not describe payment-driven positions as ordered by relevance.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: By close analogy to the Annex I point 11 blacklist prohibition on paid promotion presented as independent/editorial content without clear identification, MegaBasket presents paid seller placements in a form indistinguishable from organic (independent) results without making the paid nature clear. Presenting paid promotion as if it were neutral, unpaid ranking content, without clearly identifiable disclosure, falls squarely within the mischief the blacklist targets and is prohibited in all circumstances where present.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Make the paid nature of boosted placements clearly identifiable at the point of display on every device, so paid content is never presented as if it were independent/organic search output.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Targeting users by inferred price sensitivity engages the general fairness/professional-diligence safety-net where it materially distorts economic behaviour, but on the facts given this is primarily addressed under GDPR profiling and DSA ad-transparency rules rather than a standalone UCPD breach. Flagged for context; no clear UCPD violation established on the text alone.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Ensure price-sensitivity targeting does not result in misleading price presentations or personalised-pricing without disclosure; coordinate with GDPR/DSA assessments.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket sells top-four search placements styled identically to organic results, with a paid-placement label that is inadequate on desktop (6pt light-grey, hover-only) and entirely absent on mobile, while ranking explanations falsely state results are "ordered by relevance". This engages the UCPD prohibitions on misleading omissions/hidden commercial intent (Art. 7), misleading actions (Art. 6, the false relevance claim) and, by strong analogy, the Annex I blacklist on undisclosed paid promotion presented as independent content (point 11). The failure to identify paid ranking and the affirmatively false relevance statement are likely breaches, most acutely on mobile where no disclosure exists at all.

report.executive_summary: Your "Boosted Placement" product sells the top four search positions to paying sellers, but presents those paid results as if they were normal, relevance-ranked organic results. The core problem is disclosure: the "promoted" tag is tiny (6pt), grey, appears only on hover on desktop, and is completely absent on mobile — while your ranking explanation tells users results are "ordered by relevance," which is false for the paid positions. This combination is very likely to breach EU consumer law (UCPD misleading actions and omissions, and by analogy the Annex I blacklist on undisclosed paid promotion) and the DSA's advertising-transparency, dark-patterns and recommender-transparency rules. Separately, letting sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity is profiling under the GDPR, and the submission shows no lawful basis, no transparency, and no opt-out for it. With 40M EU users you are also near the VLOP threshold, which would trigger ad-repository obligations. The mobile experience is the sharpest risk, since paid placements there carry no disclosure at all. Overall this campaign should not go live in its current form; it needs meaningful design and disclosure changes before launch.
recommendations: Add a clear, always-visible, high-contrast 'Sponsored/Ad' label to every Boosted Placement result on BOTH desktop and mobile — never hover-dependent. This fixes the single most severe issue (critical UCPD Art. 7 / DSA Art. 26), which is worst on mobile where there is currently no disclosure at all.

Stop describing paid positions as 'ordered by relevance'. Correct the ranking explanation to state plainly that top positions are paid placements and disclose the actual main ranking parameters (UCPD Art. 6, DSA Art. 27).
Redesign the search grid so paid placements are visually and structurally distinct from organic results, removing the identical-styling dark pattern (DSA Art. 25).
For the Boosted Placement ads, expose the advertiser/payer identity and main targeting parameters in real time per ad (DSA Art. 26).

Before enabling price-sensitivity targeting, document it as profiling, establish and record a valid lawful basis (consent or a completed legitimate-interests assessment), and run a DPIA given large-scale (40M-user) behavioural profiling (GDPR Arts. 4(4), 6, 35).

Update privacy notices and just-in-time disclosures to explain that behavioural data is used to infer price sensitivity for advertising, and provide an easy, working opt-out from profiling-based targeting (GDPR Arts. 13, 21).

Confirm the price-sensitivity inference is used only for ad placement and never to set individual prices or exclude users from offers; if it ever affects pricing/eligibility, apply GDPR Art. 22 safeguards.

Confirm VLOP designation status; if designated or on reaching ~45M monthly EU recipients, build a compliant public ad repository for all Boosted Placement ads including targeting parameters and reach (DSA Art. 39).

campaign.title: DentaBright 'real smiles' video wall
campaign.text: A teeth-whitening brand's landing page features a 'Real customers, real smiles' video wall: twelve testimonial clips ('I tried everything, only DentaBright worked'). All twelve are paid actors reading scripts; two never used the product. On-screen text shows first names and cities. A small footer note says 'individual results may vary'; nothing indicates the testimonials are dramatised. Product claims themselves are within the substantiated range.

detected_practices: testimonials presented as 'real customers' but performed by paid actors
two endorsers who never used the product
undisclosed dramatised/scripted testimonials
misleading authenticity claim ('Real customers, real smiles')
on-screen display of first names and cities of purported customers
'individual results may vary' disclaimer without disclosing testimonials are staged
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is general adult consumers; testimonials are the persuasive core. Fake/undisclosed endorsements are a per-se misleading commercial practice under UCPD Annex I. GDPR is flagged because on-screen first names + cities are personal data (even if actors, their identifiers are displayed and any real-consumer data would raise consent/accuracy issues). DSA included because testimonial/endorsement authenticity and disclosure obligations apply to content disseminated via online platforms/social channels; note personalisation was declared 'no'.
triage.summary: A teeth-whitening brand's landing page presents a video wall of twelve 'Real customers, real smiles' testimonials that are in fact paid actors reading scripts, two of whom never used the product, with no disclosure that the endorsements are staged or paid. While the product claims are substantiated, the false representation of testimonials as genuine consumer experiences raises misleading/deceptive-practice concerns and involves the display of personal data (first names and cities of purported customers).

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: A first name combined with a city, displayed alongside a photographed/filmed individual, is personal data of an identifiable natural person. Publishing these identifiers in a public advertisement is 'processing' that requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Because the twelve individuals are paid actors, the lawful basis would normally be their consent via a model release/performance contract. Nothing in the text indicates such releases are missing, so this is a point to verify rather than an established breach.
findings.evidence_quote: On-screen text shows first names and cities.
findings.recommendation: Ensure each actor's talent/model-release contract expressly authorises use of their (real or stage) first name and city in this advertising context, covering the EU markets and channels used. Retain the releases as evidence of the Art. 6(1) lawful basis (consent/contract).

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed fairly and accurately-in-context. Displaying named, located individuals under the banner 'Real customers, real smiles' attaches a false 'genuine customer' narrative to those identifiers.
