findings.rationale: Profiling-based personalised pricing needs a valid lawful basis. A generic analytics-cookie banner does not cover using device/behavioural data to set individual prices, and legitimate interest is hard to sustain where the processing is covert and works to the consumer's economic disadvantage. As described, the pricing engine appears to lack any valid Art. 6(1) basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis specifically for personalised pricing. If relying on consent, obtain separate, specific consent for pricing personalisation; if relying on legitimate interest, complete and document a balancing test — noting covert, disadvantageous processing will likely fail it.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: To the extent consent is relied on, a generic analytics banner is neither specific nor informed as to profiling-based pricing. Bundled/generic consent does not qualify as freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous consent for a distinct purpose such as individual price setting.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Unbundle consent: present a distinct, clearly worded opt-in for pricing personalisation separate from analytics cookies, describing the purpose in plain language so consent is genuinely specific and informed.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: If consent is the chosen basis, Art. 7 requires the request to be clearly distinguishable and the controller to be able to demonstrate consent for the specific purpose. A generic banner bundling analytics with (undisclosed) pricing profiling fails these conditions and provides no demonstrable, withdrawable consent for the pricing use.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Provide a distinguishable consent request for pricing personalisation, log consent to demonstrate it, and make withdrawal as easy as giving consent, with clear effect on the price displayed.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The price a consumer is offered is determined solely by automated profiling. Where personalised pricing systematically disadvantages a group and affects the price of the transaction, it can constitute a decision that 'similarly significantly affects' the individual, engaging Art. 22, which requires an exception (e.g. explicit consent) plus safeguards. None of the Art. 22 conditions or safeguards appear to be met.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes.
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the pricing decision produces a significant effect; if so, rely on a valid Art. 22(2) exception (e.g. explicit consent), and implement safeguards — meaningful information about the logic, the ability to obtain human intervention, express a view, and contest the price.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Any information provided to data subjects must be transparent, intelligible and not misleading. The FAQ statement is the opposite of transparent about the real (profiling-based) reason prices differ, undermining the Art. 12 standard for clear and accurate information.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the FAQ and privacy communications in clear, plain, accurate language that explains that prices are personalised via profiling, so information provided to consumers is genuinely intelligible and not misleading.

verdicts.notes: The adaptive pricing engine processes personal data (device type, prior visit history, dwell time / "hesitation index") through automated means to evaluate individuals' behaviour and economic situation — this is profiling under GDPR Art. 4(4) and personalised pricing under the pricing-practices concept. The processing is covert (nothing on the site discloses it) and the FAQ actively misrepresents pricing as reflecting "live market availability," breaching the transparency/fairness principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and the information obligation (Art. 13). A generic analytics consent banner cannot provide a valid, specific and informed lawful basis for profiling-based pricing (Arts. 6(1), 4(11), 7), and the automated pricing decision may engage Art. 22. Multiple likely violations identified.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices that deceive the average consumer regarding the price or the manner in which the price is calculated and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The FAQ affirmatively attributes displayed prices to 'live market availability', but prices are in fact adjusted ±12% based on device type, prior visits and a behavioural 'hesitation index'. This is a false statement about the manner of price calculation likely to cause consumers to accept a quote (e.g. returning iOS users' systematically higher first quote) they might otherwise reject or shop around on. Because it is an active false representation rather than mere silence, it engages Art. 6, not only Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Remove or correct the FAQ statement. Do not attribute personalised prices to 'live market availability'. Accurately state that displayed prices may be individually adjusted and explain, in plain terms, the categories of factors used (e.g. device type, browsing history) so the price-calculation description is truthful.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision, or hiding it/providing it unclearly. That prices are personalised through automated profiling is material information (expressly recognised as a required disclosure for personalised pricing based on automated decision-making under the Consumer Rights Directive as amended by the Omnibus Directive). The site discloses nothing, so consumers cannot understand that the price shown is individually calculated rather than a standard/market price — a classic misleading omission of the commercial nature and basis of the price.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, prominent disclosure at the point the price is displayed (not buried) stating that the price has been personalised on the basis of automated processing, and explain the main parameters. Ensure the disclosure is timely (before the consumer decides) and intelligible to the average consumer.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The general fairness safety-net applies to practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort or are likely to distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer, where not fully caught by specific rules. Systematically presenting identifiable returning users a higher first quote based on inferred willingness to pay ('hesitation index'), combined with concealment of the mechanism, departs from the standard of professional diligence a consumer can reasonably expect from a travel agency and is likely to distort transactional decisions. This reinforces the Art. 6/7 findings and captures the exploitative design even where individual disclosures are added.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes.
findings.recommendation: Adopt a transparent, non-exploitative pricing policy: avoid pricing that targets inferred hesitation/vulnerability of specific users, document the professional-diligence basis for any personalisation, and ensure consumers can obtain a non-personalised or reference price for comparison.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is a B2C commercial practice within UCPD scope. Two significant issues arise: (1) undisclosed personalised/adaptive pricing is a misleading omission of material information under Art. 7, since personalised pricing based on automated profiling must be disclosed to consumers; and (2) the FAQ statement that prices "reflect live market availability" is a misleading action under Art. 6 because it affirmatively misrepresents the manner of price calculation, which is actually driven by device type, prior visits and a behavioural "hesitation index". The general fairness safety-net (Art. 5) is also engaged by systematically quoting higher first prices to identifiable returning users without disclosure. Blacklisted urgency/scarcity practices do not apply as no urgency messaging is used and prices are honoured as displayed.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses a pricing engine that secretly adjusts hotel prices by up to ±12% based on each visitor's device, past visits, and how long they hesitate — with returning iOS users systematically shown higher first quotes. The core problem is concealment: nothing on the site tells consumers prices are personalised, and the FAQ actively misstates that prices "reflect live market availability." This creates serious, overlapping legal exposure under both data protection and consumer law. Under GDPR, the profiling is covert, lacks a valid legal basis (a generic analytics cookie banner does not cover pricing personalisation), and breaches transparency and fairness rules, with a likely automated decision-making concern. Under the UCPD, the FAQ is a misleading action and the non-disclosure is a misleading omission — EU law specifically requires that personalised pricing based on automated processing be disclosed to consumers. The AI Act and DSA were assessed as not applicable. This is not a design tweak: as currently built and described, the campaign is likely unlawful on multiple counts and should not launch until the disclosure, consent, and pricing-logic issues are fixed.
recommendations: Do not launch (or immediately pause) the campaign as currently designed until the disclosure and consent issues below are resolved — the covert, disadvantageous personalisation carries likely violations under both GDPR and the UCPD.

Correct the false FAQ statement: stop attributing prices to 'live market availability' and accurately state that displayed prices may be individually personalised based on automated processing (UCPD Art. 6; GDPR Arts. 12/5(1)(a)).

Add a clear, prominent disclosure at the point the price is shown that prices are personalised via automated profiling, and explain the main parameters used (device type, prior visits, hesitation index) — this is a mandatory disclosure for automated personalised pricing (UCPD Art. 7; GDPR Art. 13).

Establish and document a valid GDPR lawful basis specifically for pricing personalisation. A generic analytics-cookie banner is insufficient; if using consent, obtain separate, unbundled, specific opt-in consent, and if relying on legitimate interest, complete a balancing test (noting covert, consumer-detrimental processing will likely fail it) (GDPR Arts. 6, 7, 4(11)).

Reconsider the exploitative design itself: pricing that targets inferred hesitation/willingness-to-pay of identifiable returning users may breach the general fairness standard even with disclosures. Offer a non-personalised reference price for comparison (UCPD Art. 5).

Assess whether the automated price constitutes a decision with a significant effect under GDPR Art. 22; if so, secure a valid exception (e.g. explicit consent) and implement safeguards — human intervention, the right to express a view and contest the price.
Document the processing in a record of processing activities and conduct a DPIA, given the systematic profiling of individuals with potential significant effects (GDPR Art. 4(4)).

campaign.title: AeroFly checkout add-ons
campaign.text: An airline's own booking flow pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking. The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen. Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'. No pressure language is used and all add-ons are genuine services.

detected_practices: pre-ticked/pre-selected optional add-ons at checkout
obscured deselection via collapsed accordions (dark pattern)
bundled total hiding itemised add-on costs until final screen
drip pricing / partitioned pricing ('Lisbon from €39' excluding pre-selected extras)
generative AI used in campaign content
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult EU consumers; no targeting/personalisation declared, but email channel implies processing of contact data. AI use is declared but its role (e.g. content generation) should be verified against transparency obligations. The pre-selection and hidden-deselection design should be assessed as a potential misleading/aggressive practice under UCPD Annex I (pre-ticked boxes) and Consumer Rights Directive Art. 22.
triage.summary: An airline booking flow pre-selects paid add-ons (cancellation cover, priority boarding, a carbon contribution) with deselection hidden behind collapsible accordions, showing only a bundled total until the final screen, while promo emails advertise the bare fare. Practices raise potential UCPD concerns around pre-ticked boxes, drip/partitioned pricing and dark patterns hindering informed consumer choice. Generative AI is declared and the email channel involves processing personal data.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Generative AI is declared and, on the facts, is used to produce campaign content (web page and promotional email copy such as 'Lisbon from €39'). Under Art. 50(2), providers/deployers of AI systems generating synthetic text, image, audio or video must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The submission gives no indication that any AI-generated assets carry provenance marking, so the obligation appears engaged and unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify which campaign assets (email/web copy, any images or audio) are AI-generated or AI-manipulated and ensure they carry machine-readable provenance/watermark marking in line with Art. 50(2). Document the generative-AI tooling and confirm its outputs embed detectable synthetic-content markers; retain evidence for audit.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The pre-selected add-ons, deselection hidden behind collapsed accordions and the bundled total that obscures itemised costs are textbook dark patterns that steer consumer choice. Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits manipulative/deceptive techniques only where they are deployed BY an AI system and are reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Nothing in the submission indicates the checkout interface is AI-driven (generative AI is declared for content only), and the potential harm (unwanted low-value add-ons) is unlikely to meet the 'significant harm' threshold. This is therefore flagged for context: if the steering/personalisation of the checkout were later found to be AI-powered, Art. 5(1)(a) would need re-assessment. The dark-pattern practices themselves fall under UCPD Arts. 5-9 / DSA Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Confirm the checkout pre-selection and accordion design is static UI logic, not AI-driven optimisation/personalisation. If any AI system dynamically steers defaults or nudges users, re-assess against Art. 5(1)(a). Regardless, remediate the dark-pattern design under the UCPD/DSA workstreams (default to unticked add-ons, transparent itemised pricing).

verdicts.notes: The campaign's AI Act exposure is narrow. Generative AI is declared and is used to produce marketing content (web/email copy), which engages the Art. 50(2) obligation to mark AI-generated outputs in a machine-readable format; nothing in the submission indicates this marking is applied, so it warrants attention. No conversational AI/chatbot is present (Art. 50(1) not applicable) and no deep fakes or synthetic personas are used (Art. 50(4) not applicable). The dark-pattern checkout design (pre-ticked add-ons, hidden deselection, drip pricing) is a serious concern but under UCPD/DSA, not the AI Act: Art. 5(1)(a) only bites where the manipulation is deployed by an AI system and causes significant harm, and the design here is not attributed to an AI system.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Sending promotional emails involves processing personal (contact) data for direct marketing, which requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1); email marketing generally requires prior consent (ePrivacy Art. 13). The campaign describes an email channel but does not state the lawful basis or that valid consent was obtained.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the promo email list (typically prior opt-in consent for existing/new subscribers, or the ePrivacy 'soft opt-in' for existing customers regarding similar products). Ensure records demonstrate valid consent where relied upon.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct marketing email must respect and facilitate the absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing (Art. 21(2)-(3)). The campaign material does not mention an unsubscribe/opt-out mechanism in the promo emails.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure each promo email contains a clear, functional, one-click unsubscribe/opt-out that is honoured immediately and results in suppression of the address for marketing purposes.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: The pre-ticked add-ons concern consent to purchase paid services, not consent to personal-data processing, so GDPR's prohibition on pre-ticked boxes for consent (Art. 4(11)) is not directly engaged. Flagged only to clarify scope: if any of these pre-selected boxes were also used to bundle consent to data processing/marketing, the pre-ticked/bundled-consent prohibition would apply and such consent would be invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution'
findings.recommendation: Verify that none of the pre-selected checkboxes double as consent to data processing, tracking or marketing. If they do, separate and un-tick any such consent, as pre-ticked or bundled consent does not constitute valid GDPR consent.

verdicts.notes: The core problematic mechanics of this campaign — pre-selected paid add-ons, hidden deselection via accordions, bundled/drip pricing — concern consent to a purchase/contract and are governed by UCPD, the Consumer Rights Directive and DSA, not by GDPR consent (Art. 4(11)/7), which concerns consent to personal-data processing. GDPR's genuine touchpoint is the email marketing channel: "Promo emails" involve processing of contact data and thus require a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1), typically prior consent under ePrivacy) and a facilitated right to object/opt-out (Art. 21). The submission does not describe the consent basis or an unsubscribe mechanism, so these are flagged for verification rather than as confirmed breaches. No personalisation/profiling is declared and generative AI is used only for content, so Arts. 4(4)/22 are not engaged.

The DSA marketing provisions (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) apply to providers of intermediary "online platforms" (and Art. 39 specifically to VLOPs). This campaign is an airline's own booking flow and its own promotional emails — a first-party trader operating its own e-commerce interface, not an online-platform/hosting intermediary presenting third-party content or ads. Although the pre-ticked add-ons, accordion-hidden deselection and bundled/drip pricing are textbook deceptive-design tactics, DSA Art. 25 explicitly applies "without prejudice to the UCPD, which covers the same conduct for all traders"; for a first-party trader this conduct is a UCPD / Consumer Rights Directive matter (handled by other agents), not a DSA one. No online-platform, VLOP, recommender-system or platform-advertising elements are present, so the DSA is not engaged.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The itemised costs of the pre-selected add-ons (Cancellation Cover €14.99, Priority Boarding €9.99, €2 carbon contribution) are hidden behind collapsed accordions and merged into a single bundled total until the last screen. This omits/hides material price information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision and provides it in an untimely, unclear manner — the paradigm of a misleading omission of hidden costs under Art. 7. Pre-selection means silence results in extra charges the consumer may not have chosen.
findings.evidence_quote: The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen.
findings.recommendation: Present all add-ons as unticked (opt-in) by default and display each add-on's price as a clearly itemised line in the running total from the moment it is offered, not only on the final screen. Ensure the total payable, broken down by item, is visible before the consumer commits.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Headlining the bare fare of €39 while the booking flow then pre-selects paid extras that inflate the amount actually payable is partitioned/drip pricing. It deceives the average consumer about the price and the manner in which the price is calculated, and is likely to cause a transactional decision (starting the booking) they might not otherwise take. That the extras are genuine services does not cure the misleading impression created by the headline price combined with default-on add-ons.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure advertised headline fares reflect the price a consumer will actually pay through the default flow, i.e. do not pre-select paid extras. If optional extras exist, they must be genuinely optional (opt-in) so that the €39 figure remains achievable and accurate.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Combining default pre-selection with an obstructive interface that forces the consumer to open each accordion and untick separately imposes onerous barriers to declining unwanted charges. This design can amount to undue influence that significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and pushes them toward paying for extras they did not actively choose, engaging the aggressive-practices provision.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Remove the obstruction: add-ons should be off by default and any opt-out should be at least as easy as opting in (single click, at the same level of prominence, no hidden accordions).

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall design — pre-ticked paid add-ons, obscured deselection and a bundled total that conceals itemised costs until the final screen — is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer by causing them to pay for services they did not deliberately select. This backs the specific findings under Arts. 6-9 where any element falls outside them.
findings.evidence_quote: pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution'
findings.recommendation: Redesign the checkout so all optional paid items (including the carbon contribution) are opt-in, transparently priced and separately visible throughout, aligning the flow with professional diligence and consumer-choice standards.

verdicts.notes: The AeroFly checkout flow engages several UCPD prohibitions. Pre-selecting paid add-ons and hiding their itemised cost inside collapsible accordions with only a bundled total shown until the final screen constitutes a misleading omission of material price information (Art. 7). Advertising "Lisbon from €39" while pre-ticked extras inflate the amount actually payable is drip/partitioned pricing likely to mislead on price and its calculation (Art. 6). The obstructive deselection design (unticking each accordion) materially distorts consumer choice, engaging the aggressive-practices (undue influence) provision and the general fairness safety-net. The add-ons being "genuine services" does not cure the deceptive/obstructive design. No false-urgency or "free" claims are present, so those blacklist items do not apply.

report.executive_summary: Your AeroFly checkout campaign advertises a low headline fare ("Lisbon from €39") but then pre-ticks paid add-ons (Cancellation Cover €14.99, Priority Boarding €9.99, and a €2 carbon contribution) and hides both the itemised prices and the way to remove them behind collapsible accordions, showing only a bundled total until the final screen. This is the campaign's biggest problem: under EU consumer law (UCPD) it is likely to be an unfair commercial practice — misleading pricing (drip/partitioned pricing), a misleading omission of costs, and an aggressive/obstructive design that makes opting out harder than opting in. The add-ons being genuine services and the absence of pressure language do not fix this; the default-on selection and hidden costs are the issue. Two secondary issues need checking: your promo emails must have a valid marketing consent basis and a working unsubscribe link (GDPR/ePrivacy), and any AI-generated web/email copy should carry machine-readable "AI-generated" marking under the AI Act. The DSA does not apply here because this is your own first-party booking flow, not a third-party platform. Overall this campaign should not launch in its current form — the checkout design must be redesigned before going live in the EU.
recommendations: Make all paid add-ons opt-in (unticked by default), including the €2 carbon contribution — this is the single most important fix and addresses the core UCPD violations.
Show each add-on's price as a clearly itemised line in the running total from the moment it is offered, not just on the final screen; ensure the full breakdown is visible before the consumer commits.
Remove the obstructive accordion design so declining an add-on is at least as easy as accepting it (single click, same prominence, no hidden menus).
Ensure the advertised 'Lisbon from €39' fare is genuinely achievable through the default flow — do not pre-select paid extras that inflate the amount actually payable.

Confirm and document a valid lawful basis for the promo email list (prior opt-in consent or ePrivacy soft opt-in) and include a clear, one-click unsubscribe in every email that is honoured immediately.
Verify none of the pre-selected checkboxes double as consent to data processing, tracking or marketing; if they do, separate them out as pre-ticked/bundled consent is invalid under GDPR.
Identify which web/email assets are AI-generated and apply machine-readable provenance/watermark marking per AI Act Art. 50(2); retain documentation of the tooling used.
Confirm the checkout pre-selection logic is static UI and not AI-driven personalisation; if any AI dynamically steers defaults, re-assess against AI Act Art. 5(1)(a).

campaign.title: AeroFly checkout add-ons
campaign.text: An airline's own booking flow pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking. The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen. Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'. No pressure language is used and all add-ons are genuine services.

detected_practices: pre-ticked/pre-selected optional add-ons (opt-out defaults)
drip pricing / bundled total obscuring add-on costs until final screen
friction to deselect (accordions requiring individual unticking)
headline fare advertising excluding mandatory-appearing extras ('Lisbon from €39')

triage.summary: An airline booking flow pre-selects paid add-ons (cancellation cover, priority boarding, a carbon contribution) and hides the true total behind a bundled figure until the final screen, while promo emails advertise only the bare fare. The design uses opt-out defaults and deselection friction typical of drip-pricing and dark-pattern concerns, and generative AI is used in the campaign. Personalisation is declared as absent, but the email/web channels involve customer data, so GDPR should be sanity-checked.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares that generative AI is used to produce campaign content across web and email. Art. 50(2) requires that synthetic audio, image, video or text outputs be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The submission contains no indication that any AI-generated assets carry provenance marking, so the obligation is engaged and appears unaddressed. Severity is low because the content described (booking-flow UI, a 'from €39' fare email) is ordinary marketing copy with no deceptive synthetic element, and the gap is easily remedied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm which campaign assets (copy, imagery) are AI-generated and ensure the generation tooling embeds machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking metadata) on those outputs, and retain records demonstrating Art. 50(2) compliance.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's declared use of generative AI engages only the AI Act's transparency layer, not its prohibitions. Art. 50(2) (machine-readable marking of AI-generated content) applies to any AI-generated copy/visuals in the web and email assets, and the submission gives no indication such marking is in place. The dark-pattern tactics (pre-ticked add-ons, drip pricing, deselection friction) are not described as AI-driven, so the Art. 5(1)(a) manipulation prohibition is not engaged — those belong to UCPD/DSA. No deep fakes, synthetic likenesses, or public-interest text are present, so Art. 50(4) does not apply.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The campaign sends promotional emails, which constitute direct marketing and thus processing of personal data (email addresses) that requires a valid lawful basis. Email marketing generally requires prior consent (Art. 6(1) read with ePrivacy Art. 13), or a narrowly qualifying legitimate interest / existing-customer 'soft opt-in'. The campaign text does not state the lawful basis for the email list.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the promo email list: either GDPR-standard consent (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous) captured at sign-up, or the ePrivacy soft opt-in limited to existing customers for similar products with an opt-out offered at collection and in each message.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct-marketing emails must respect and actively facilitate the absolute right to object at any time. Every message must carry an easy, functioning opt-out/unsubscribe mechanism. The campaign description does not mention any unsubscribe facility.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure every promotional email contains a clear, one-click unsubscribe link, that objections are honoured immediately and permanently, and that the opt-out is at least as easy to use as the original opt-in.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is only lightly engaged by this campaign. Personalisation/targeting is declared absent and the text shows no profiling, special-category data, automated decision-making, or targeting of minors, so Arts. 4(4), 8, 9 and 22 are not triggered. The one genuine GDPR touchpoint is the promotional email channel, which constitutes direct marketing and therefore requires a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1), generally prior consent for email marketing under ePrivacy) and a facilitated right to object/opt-out in every message (Art. 21). The campaign text is silent on both, so these are flagged for verification rather than as established breaches. Note: the pre-ticked add-on checkboxes are pre-selections of paid services, not consent to personal-data processing, so they are a UCPD dark-pattern concern rather than a GDPR Art. 4(11) consent defect.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Presenting only a single bundled total and revealing the composition of the price (and the individual add-on charges) only on the final screen omits, hides or provides in an untimely manner the material information the average consumer needs to understand what they are paying and why. The total price and the fact that optional paid extras have been added are material information under Art. 7; drip-pricing that defers this disclosure to the last step is a classic misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen.
findings.recommendation: Show an itemised, transparent breakdown of the base fare plus each pre-selected add-on (Cancellation Cover €14.99, Priority Boarding €9.99, carbon contribution €2) and the running total from the first pricing screen onward, so the consumer sees the true payable price early and clearly rather than a single bundled figure disclosed only at checkout.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Advertising 'Lisbon from €39' while the booking flow then pre-adds ~€27 of opt-out extras risks deceiving the average consumer as to the price and the manner in which it is calculated (Art. 6(1)(d)). Because the extras are defaults the consumer must actively remove, the advertised entry price systematically understates the amount most consumers will actually pay, potentially causing a transactional decision (clicking through to book) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the advertised 'from' price is genuinely obtainable and reflects what a typical customer pays; either present add-ons as unticked opt-ins (so €39 is the real default price) or clearly signal in the ad that optional paid services are added by default in the booking flow.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Pre-selecting paid optional extras (opt-out defaults) and burying the deselect controls behind accordions that must each be opened and unticked is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer, who tends to accept defaults and may pay for services they did not want. This 'sneaking' default-setting combined with deselection friction is treated as an unfair dark pattern under the general fairness clause. (Note: pre-ticked boxes for additional payments are separately prohibited by the Consumer Rights Directive Art. 22; this finding addresses only the UCPD fairness dimension.)
findings.evidence_quote: pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Present all optional add-ons unticked by default (active opt-in), and make selection/deselection equally easy and equally prominent — visible checkboxes on the main summary rather than controls hidden inside individual accordions.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Imposing onerous barriers to removing charges the consumer never chose — requiring them to open each accordion individually and untick — can amount to undue influence that impairs the consumer's freedom of choice, one of the factors expressly relevant to aggressive practices (onerous barriers). While milder than high-pressure sales, the asymmetry between one-click acceptance (do nothing) and multi-step removal engages Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Remove the friction asymmetry: allow the consumer to decline all pre-added extras in a single, clearly visible action, and avoid designs where opting out is materially harder than accepting.

verdicts.notes: The AeroFly booking flow does not use blacklisted (Annex I) practices — there is no false urgency, no "free" misuse, and add-ons are genuine services. However, it raises real UCPD risks under the general clauses: the design pre-selects paid add-ons (opt-out defaults) with deliberate friction to remove them, and it presents a single bundled total while advertising a bare "from €39" fare, obscuring the price the consumer will actually pay until the final screen. These practices engage Art. 7 (misleading omission of material price information), Art. 6 (misleading action on price/manner of calculation), and Arts. 5/8-9 (distortion of economic behaviour via default-setting and onerous deselection). None reach "violation likely" as a blacklist match, but the drip-pricing and sneaked-in defaults are squarely the kind of practice the CJEU and 2021 UCPD Guidance treat as unfair.

report.executive_summary: Your AeroFly checkout campaign pre-selects three paid add-ons (Cancellation Cover €14.99, Priority Boarding €9.99, and a €2 carbon contribution) that customers must actively hunt down and untick, while showing only a single bundled total until the final screen and advertising a bare "Lisbon from €39" fare in emails. This combination — pre-ticked paid extras, deselection friction, and drip-pricing — is the core problem and drives a HIGH overall risk. Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive it engages misleading omissions (hiding the real price until checkout), misleading actions (the advertised €39 understates what most people actually pay), and unfair/aggressive design (defaults plus onerous opt-out). Separately, pre-ticked boxes for additional payments are directly prohibited by the Consumer Rights Directive (Art. 22), so this needs fixing regardless. Lower-level items to close out: confirm you have a valid lawful basis and a working unsubscribe link for the promo emails (GDPR/ePrivacy), and ensure any AI-generated copy or imagery carries machine-readable provenance marking (AI Act Art. 50(2)). The good news is there are no blacklisted practices, no false urgency, and the add-ons are genuine services — the risks are real but fixable through checkout redesign and transparency changes.
recommendations: Un-tick all add-ons by default. Present Cancellation Cover, Priority Boarding and the carbon contribution as active opt-ins, not opt-outs. This is the single most important fix and also resolves the Consumer Rights Directive Art. 22 prohibition on pre-ticked paid boxes.

Make declining as easy as accepting. Put visible checkboxes on the main summary and allow all extras to be removed in one click — eliminate the accordion-by-accordion friction that makes opting out harder than accepting.
Show an itemised running total from the first pricing screen. Break out base fare plus each add-on so the true payable price is clear early, not revealed only at the final screen.

Make the advertised 'from €39' genuinely obtainable. Either ensure €39 is the real default price (with add-ons unticked), or clearly disclose in the ad that optional paid services are otherwise added by default.

Verify the promo email lawful basis and opt-out. Confirm you hold valid consent or a qualifying soft opt-in for the email list, and ensure every message carries a working one-click unsubscribe that is honoured immediately.

Mark AI-generated assets. Identify which copy/imagery is AI-generated and ensure the tooling embeds machine-readable provenance (e.g. C2PA/watermark) metadata, retaining records to evidence AI Act Art. 50(2) compliance.

campaign.title: AeroFly checkout add-ons
campaign.text: An airline's own booking flow pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking. The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen. Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'. No pressure language is used and all add-ons are genuine services.

detected_practices: pre-ticked/pre-selected add-ons (opt-out defaults)
obscured deselection via collapsed accordions (dark pattern / friction)
bundled total hiding itemised costs until final screen
drip pricing / partitioned pricing ('Lisbon from €39' excluding mandatory-feeling add-ons)
generative AI use (declared)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult EU consumers. UCPD is the central concern here: pre-ticked boxes for optional services are prohibited under the Consumer Rights Directive, and drip pricing plus obscured opt-out mechanics may constitute misleading/aggressive or dark-pattern practices. AI Act included because generative AI is declared (transparency obligations may apply). GDPR included because email marketing processes personal data (contact details, consent for marketing). DSA plausibly engaged if the airline's platform/interface design implicates dark-pattern provisions; specialist review advised.
triage.summary: An airline booking flow pre-selects paid add-ons (cancellation cover, priority boarding, a carbon contribution) with deselection hidden behind collapsed accordions, and displays only a bundled total until the final screen, while promo emails advertise a bare fare of 'Lisbon from €39'. This pattern raises drip-pricing, pre-ticked box, and hidden-friction concerns even absent explicit pressure language. Generative AI is declared as used, and email channels imply processing of contact/personal data.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares use of generative AI. Where a generative AI system produces synthetic content used in the campaign (email creative, imagery, promotional copy), Art. 50(2) requires the provider to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The submission does not indicate whether any such marking is applied, so the obligation is engaged but unverified. Note this is a provider-side obligation; the marketer/deployer should confirm its AI tooling complies.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify which campaign assets are AI-generated and confirm the generative AI provider embeds machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) in outputs. Document this in the campaign's AI-use records. If AI is only used for ideation/drafting with no synthetic content published, record that Art. 50(2) does not apply.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The pre-selected add-ons and friction-laden deselection are potentially manipulative interface design, which Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits ONLY when deployed by an AI system and reaching the significant-harm threshold. The campaign attributes these mechanics to conventional booking-flow/UI design, not to any AI system, and uses no pressure language, so the AI Act prohibition is not made out. Flagged for awareness: if these defaults were driven or optimised by an AI system, Art. 5(1)(a) could be re-examined. The core assessment of these tactics belongs to UCPD (pre-ticked boxes, misleading omissions) and DSA (dark patterns).
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: No AI Act action required unless the checkout defaults or deselection friction are personalised/optimised by an AI system. If they are, reassess against Art. 5(1)(a) and ensure the interface does not materially distort consumer decisions. Otherwise defer to the UCPD/DSA assessments.

verdicts.notes: The substantive concerns in this campaign — pre-ticked add-ons, obscured deselection via accordions, bundled/drip pricing — are interface and pricing design tactics not attributed to any AI system, so they fall under UCPD/DSA rather than the AI Act. The AI Act is engaged only through the declared use of generative AI: where AI produces campaign assets (email creative, imagery, copy), Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking obligations apply and cannot be confirmed as met from the submission. No prohibited practices under Art. 5 are made out, since the manipulative mechanics are conventional design, not AI-driven, and there is no chatbot, deep fake, or synthetic likeness.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Sending promotional emails to EU consumers processes their personal data (email address, contact details) for direct marketing. This requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1); e-mail direct marketing generally requires prior consent (in conjunction with ePrivacy Art. 13) unless the narrow existing-customer 'soft opt-in' exemption is met. The campaign text does not evidence any lawful basis or how the recipient list was obtained, so compliance cannot be confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for the email list: either freely given, specific, informed prior consent, or the existing-customer soft opt-in (contact obtained during a sale, marketing only similar services, opt-out offered at collection and in every message). Maintain consent/basis records to demonstrate compliance.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct-marketing email must respect the absolute right to object and provide an easy, functioning opt-out in each message. The campaign material does not mention an unsubscribe/objection mechanism, so it cannot be confirmed that the obligation to facilitate opt-out at any time is met.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure every promo email contains a clear, one-click unsubscribe/objection link, honour objections immediately by suppressing the contact from marketing, and inform recipients of the right to object at the point of data collection (Art. 21(4)).

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data (email/contact details) is collected to run the email marketing programme, controllers must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights at the point of collection. The campaign does not reference any privacy information being provided at sign-up/booking.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email
findings.recommendation: Provide a concise Art. 13 privacy notice (or clear link to it) at every point where contact data is collected for marketing, covering purpose, legal basis, retention and the rights to object and withdraw consent.

verdicts.notes: The core problems in this campaign (pre-ticked add-ons, drip pricing, obscured deselection) are consumer-protection/dark-pattern issues under UCPD/DSA rather than data-protection breaches. GDPR is engaged only through the promotional email channel, which processes personal data (contact details) for direct marketing. The campaign text does not describe the lawful basis, consent origin, privacy notice or unsubscribe mechanism, so no violation is evidenced — but standing GDPR obligations apply and should be verified. No profiling/targeting is declared (Art. 4(4)/22 not engaged), no special-category data (Art. 9), and no minors (Art. 8), so those provisions are not applicable.

The campaign concerns an airline's own first-party booking flow and promotional emails. DSA obligations (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) apply to "providers of online platforms" — hosting services that store and disseminate third-party information to the public — and to VLOPs presenting advertising. An airline's own transactional checkout is not an online platform in this sense: it hosts no third-party content and presents no platform-served ads, and the submission declares no personalisation/targeting or recommender systems. While the pre-ticked add-ons, accordion-obscured deselection and bundled/drip pricing are textbook dark-pattern conduct, the applicable regime for a first-party trader is the UCPD/Consumer Rights Directive; DSA Art. 25 expressly operates "without prejudice to the UCPD," which covers the same conduct for all traders. No DSA provision is engaged on these facts.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Defaulting consumers into paid optional services and hiding the opt-out behind collapsed accordions is a 'sneaking into basket' dark pattern. It is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average consumer, who is steered into paying for services they did not actively choose. This is the general-fairness safety net catching the design pattern as a whole. (Note: pre-ticked boxes for optional payments are separately prohibited by the Consumer Rights Directive Art. 22.)
findings.evidence_quote: pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Present all optional add-ons unticked/opt-in by default. Make selecting and deselecting each add-on equally easy and visible on the same screen — no accordions required to remove an item. Do not treat the 'carbon contribution' as a default charge unless it is a genuinely unavoidable statutory cost.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Withholding an itemised breakdown of price components until the final screen provides material price information in an unclear and untimely manner. The average consumer needs to see, before committing, which charges are the fare and which are optional add-ons, and the amount of each. Presenting only a bundled total until the last step is a misleading omission of price information under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen.
findings.recommendation: Show a clear, itemised cost breakdown (base fare + each add-on + taxes) from the moment add-ons are presented, with the total updating live as items are added or removed. Clearly label optional versus unavoidable charges throughout the flow, not only on the final screen.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Advertising a headline fare of 'from €39' while the booking flow systematically steers consumers to a substantially higher total through pre-ticked add-ons (drip pricing) may deceive the average consumer as to the price and the manner in which it is calculated, causing a transactional decision (clicking through to book) they might not otherwise take. The mismatch between advertised and practically achievable price engages Art. 6(1)(d).
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the advertised 'from €39' price is genuinely obtainable without pre-selected paid extras, and that mandatory taxes/charges are reflected in advertised prices per pricing-transparency rules. Since add-ons are optional, they must not be pre-ticked, so the advertised fare remains the true achievable price.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Making removal of unwanted, pre-imposed charges deliberately burdensome (each item hidden behind a separate accordion requiring extra steps) can amount to undue influence / an onerous barrier that impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice, a factor expressly relevant to aggressive practices under Arts. 8-9. The asymmetry between easy default inclusion and effortful removal is the concern, even absent explicit pressure language.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Remove the friction asymmetry: deselecting an add-on should require no more effort than it takes to have it included (ideally a single visible tick on the main screen). Avoid burying opt-out controls inside collapsed elements.

verdicts.notes: The AeroFly checkout flow raises serious UCPD concerns even without pressure language. Two paid optional services and a "carbon contribution" are pre-selected by default, with deselection deliberately obstructed behind collapsed accordions, while an itemised cost breakdown is withheld until the final screen and promo emails headline a bare fare ("Lisbon from €39") that excludes these steered-in charges. This engages the general fairness clause (Art. 5), misleading omissions on price (Art. 7), misleading actions on price calculation (Art. 6) and, via the obstructive deselection design, aggressive-practice/undue-influence concerns (Arts. 8-9). The practices are true "sneaking into basket" and drip-pricing dark patterns.

report.executive_summary: The AeroFly checkout add-ons campaign advertises a low headline fare ("Lisbon from €39") but the booking flow pre-selects three paid extras — Cancellation Cover (€14.99), Priority Boarding (€9.99) and a €2 "carbon contribution" — and makes them hard to remove by hiding the opt-out inside collapsed accordions, showing only one bundled total until the final screen. This is the main problem: it is a classic "sneaking into basket" and drip-pricing dark pattern that likely breaches EU consumer law (UCPD Arts. 5, 6, 7 and 8-9) and separately the pre-ticked-box ban in the Consumer Rights Directive. Even without any pressure language, defaulting people into paid services and burying the way to opt out is treated as unfair. The promotional emails also carry standard data-protection obligations (GDPR): you must have a valid lawful basis/consent for the mailing list, a working one-click unsubscribe in every email, and a privacy notice at sign-up — none of which are evidenced in the submission. Because you declared use of generative AI, any published AI-generated creative must be machine-readable-marked under AI Act Art. 50(2), which should be confirmed with your AI tooling. The DSA does not apply to your own first-party checkout. Overall verdict: high risk, driven by the consumer-law dark-pattern issues, which are the priority to fix.
recommendations: Un-tick all optional add-ons by default (Cancellation Cover, Priority Boarding). Optional extras must be opt-in, not pre-selected — this addresses both the UCPD unfairness finding and the Consumer Rights Directive ban on pre-ticked boxes.
Only charge the €2 'carbon contribution' by default if it is a genuinely unavoidable statutory cost; otherwise present it as an unticked optional item too.

Make removing an add-on exactly as easy as adding one: put each control as a single visible tick on the main payment screen and stop burying opt-out inside collapsed accordions (fixes the misleading-omission and aggressive-practice concerns).
Show a live, itemised price breakdown (base fare + each add-on + taxes) from the moment add-ons appear, not just on the final screen, so consumers see what they are committing to before they commit.
Ensure the advertised 'from €39' fare is genuinely achievable with no pre-selected paid extras, so the headline price matches reality.

For the promo emails, document a valid GDPR/ePrivacy lawful basis for the recipient list (prior consent or the existing-customer soft opt-in), include a clear one-click unsubscribe in every message, and honour objections immediately.
Provide an Art. 13 privacy notice at every point contact data is collected for marketing (purpose, legal basis, retention, right to object/withdraw).

Confirm with your generative AI provider that any published AI-generated creative carries machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermark) per AI Act Art. 50(2), and record which assets are AI-generated; if AI was only used for drafting with no synthetic content published, document that the marking obligation does not apply.

campaign.title: ShoeVault 'we saw you looking' sequence
campaign.text: After a signed-in user abandons a cart, ShoeVault triggers: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days, three emails ('We saw you looking at the Air Runners — they're watching you back'), and an app push at 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.'). Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users. The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup; the preference centre works and unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes.

detected_practices: behavioural retargeting
cart-abandonment email sequence
app push notifications
late-night timing targeting (21:30)
disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users
cross-site display retargeting for 30 days
anthropomorphic/persuasive copy ('they're watching you back')
unsubscribe does not stop app pushes (partial opt-out)
consent-based marketing at signup
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is signed-in, adult shoppers in the EU; no indication minors are targeted or likely reached. Key concerns: consent scope and granularity under GDPR (broad 'marketing communications' consent, ePrivacy/tracking for cross-site retargeting, profiling), unsubscribe/opt-out failing to stop app pushes, disabled frequency caps enabling potentially aggressive/harassing repetition, late-night timing, and persuasive/potentially misleading anthropomorphic messaging under UCPD (aggressive commercial practices). DSA engaged for online advertising transparency and targeting rules on the display/news-site placements.
triage.summary: ShoeVault runs a cross-channel cart-abandonment retargeting sequence for signed-in adult EU shoppers, combining 30-day display retargeting, three emails, and a late-night app push, with frequency caps disabled for 'high-intent' users. Personalisation relies on user profiling and prior signup consent to 'marketing communications', but unsubscribing only halts emails and not the pushes. No generative AI is declared or apparent.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing (including profiling for such marketing) is absolute — once a user opts out, all direct-marketing processing for that person must stop. Here the user's opt-out via unsubscribe halts only the email channel while app-push marketing continues, meaning direct marketing continues after a clear objection. This is a direct failure to give effect to the absolute Art. 21 objection right across channels.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out effect global across all marketing channels (email, app-push, and display retargeting). When a user unsubscribes or objects, suppress them from all direct-marketing processing including push notifications and behavioural retargeting audiences, and provide a per-channel and an all-channel opt-out in the preference centre.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that withdrawing consent be as easy as giving it, and that the controller honour withdrawal. The signup covers 'marketing communications' generally, yet the withdrawal mechanism only partially works — pushes persist after the user acts to stop marketing. Withdrawal that is technically incomplete/ineffective for a channel does not satisfy Art. 7's easy-withdrawal condition.
findings.evidence_quote: the preference centre works and unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Ensure every marketing channel enabled by the consent can be withdrawn through the same preference centre with equal ease, and that withdrawal is technically propagated to the push system in a timely manner. Log and audit that opt-outs suppress all channels.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific, informed and unambiguous, and bundled consent does not qualify. A single blanket 'marketing communications' opt-in at signup is unlikely to constitute valid, granular consent covering materially different processing purposes — in particular cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling for 30 days, three-email sequences, and app-push notifications. These are distinct purposes/channels that generally require separately intelligible, granular consent.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Replace the single broad opt-in with granular, purpose- and channel-specific consent options (e.g., separate toggles for email, app-push, and cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling). Retain records demonstrating what each user consented to.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting relies on profiling personal data and requires a valid lawful basis — generally consent (also triggering ePrivacy for the tracking layer) or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment. If the only basis is the broad signup consent (which likely fails Art. 4(11) granularity for tracking), the cross-site retargeting lacks a demonstrably valid lawful basis for the profiling involved.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document a valid lawful basis specifically for cross-site retargeting/profiling (specific consent, and the corresponding ePrivacy consent for tracking technologies). Do not rely on the generic 'marketing communications' opt-in to cover behavioural tracking.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The retargeting sequence analyses each user's browsing/cart behaviour and 'high-intent' status to target tailored ads and messages, which meets the definition of profiling (automated processing to evaluate personal preferences/behaviour). This flags that the profiling-related GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) apply throughout the campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Treat the retargeting and 'high-intent' scoring as profiling and ensure all associated GDPR obligations (Arts. 6, 12-13, 21) are met; document the profiling logic.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that, at collection, the controller inform data subjects of the purposes and legal basis, recipients (e.g., ad networks used for cross-site retargeting), retention (the 30-day window), rights, and any profiling. A signup that only records consent to 'marketing communications' gives no indication these detailed disclosures — including behavioural scoring such as 'high-intent' segmentation and cross-site sharing — were provided at the point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered, accessible privacy notice at signup covering purposes, legal basis, the profiling/'high-intent' scoring, third-party ad recipients for retargeting, the 30-day retention window, and the right to object, in clear and plain language.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle prohibits processing that is unfair or that obscures how data is used. Continuing pushes after an unsubscribe, disabled frequency caps enabling relentless repetition for 'high-intent' users, and copy implying surveillance point to potentially unfair processing and insufficient transparency about how behavioural data drives the messaging intensity.
findings.evidence_quote: they're watching you back
findings.recommendation: Reinstate reasonable frequency caps for all users, align messaging intensity with fairness, and ensure users are transparently informed how their behavioural data determines targeting frequency and channel. Avoid copy that misleads users about the nature/extent of tracking.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data of signed-in EU adults for behavioural profiling and multi-channel direct marketing, relying on a single broad "marketing communications" consent captured at signup. Two issues stand out: (1) unsubscribing stops emails but NOT the late-night app pushes, which breaches the absolute right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21) and the requirement that withdrawal be as easy as giving consent (Art. 7); (2) the broad, bundled consent almost certainly fails the specific/granular standard for distinct purposes (cross-site retargeting profiling vs. email vs. push). Profiling and lawful-basis/transparency obligations are also engaged and appear inadequately satisfied as described.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The retargeting ads are presented on third-party online platforms (news sites). Under DSA Art. 26(1), each such ad must, in real time and unambiguously, be identifiable as an advertisement and disclose on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that this recipient sees it, plus how to change them. Because the ad is served through behavioural profiling of a cart-abandoning signed-in user, the targeting-parameter disclosure is squarely engaged, yet the campaign describes no such transparency or parameter-control mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Ensure creatives served on platforms carry clear 'advertisement' labelling with ShoeVault named as advertiser/payer, and that the platform's ad-transparency layer exposes the main targeting parameters (e.g. 'shown because you viewed items / abandoned a cart') with a link to change them. Confirm with the display/DSP partners that Art. 26(1) real-time disclosures are populated for this campaign.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Making a choice already exercised (opt-out) ineffective across channels, disabling frequency caps for 'high-intent' users, and nagging late-night repetition are textbook dark-pattern behaviours (obstruction, nagging, repeatedly overriding a choice already made) reflected in the dark-patterns concept behind DSA Art. 25. However, Art. 25 prohibits such design in a platform provider's own online interface; here the conduct occurs in ShoeVault's advertiser-controlled email/app channels, so it is primarily addressed by UCPD (aggressive practices) and GDPR (right to object). It is flagged for awareness in case any of this experience is operated within an online interface ShoeVault provides as a platform.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Treat unsubscribe/opt-out as global across all marketing channels including app pushes, do not disable frequency caps in a way that produces nagging, and avoid design that overrides a choice a user has already made. If any part of the retargeting runs in an interface ShoeVault itself operates as a platform, this becomes a direct Art. 25 exposure; otherwise resolve under the UCPD/GDPR findings.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is engaged mainly through the 30-day cross-site display retargeting placed on third-party news sites (online platforms), where Art. 26(1) requires per-ad transparency including advertiser identity, who paid, and the main targeting parameters with a way to change them — none of which the campaign describes. The behavioural-profiling nature of the targeting makes those parameter disclosures particularly relevant. Manipulative-design tactics (unsubscribe not stopping pushes, nagging repetition) map to the dark-patterns concept but sit largely in ShoeVault's own email/app channels, which are primarily UCPD/GDPR territory rather than DSA Art. 25 (a platform-interface prohibition); flagged for awareness. No sensitive-data targeting (Art. 26(3)) and no minor targeting (Art. 28) are engaged on the facts.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits, in all circumstances, making persistent and unwanted solicitations by e-mail or other remote media except to enforce a contractual obligation. Here the consumer's unsubscribe request is a clear expression that further marketing is unwanted, yet the app-push channel continues to solicit them (a win-back/cart-abandonment sequence, not enforcement of any contractual obligation). Continuing marketing contact after the consumer has opted out is exactly the scripted re-contact of unsubscribed users this blacklist point targets, and being blacklisted it is unfair per se with no need to show consumer detriment.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the unsubscribe / opt-out act as a global marketing suppression that stops ALL marketing channels — email, app push and display retargeting — not just email. Wire the preference centre and any in-app 'stop marketing' action into a single suppression list that gates every outbound channel, and provide a clear per-channel and all-channels opt-out for push notifications.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 make a practice aggressive where, by harassment or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice — with persistence and timing as express factors. Deliberately removing frequency limits for the users identified as most susceptible ('high-intent'), combining this with 30 days of cross-site display retargeting on news sites, three emails and app pushes deliberately timed to 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.'), amounts to relentless, uncapped repetition targeting vulnerable moments. findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing

findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(3) requires that withdrawing consent be as easy as giving it. If a user signed up once and consented generally, but withdrawal via the preference centre only removes emails while pushes and retargeting persist, withdrawal is materially harder and less effective than the original opt-in. Consent must also be demonstrable and clearly distinguishable, which a catch-all sign-up opt-in does not evidence for each processing purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Provide a granular preference centre where withdrawal of each processing purpose/channel is one clear action, and ensure withdrawal is as frictionless as the original opt-in. Keep records demonstrating consent was validly obtained for each purpose.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific and informed; bundled or generic consent does not qualify. A single 'marketing communications' opt-in at signup cannot validly cover distinct, more intrusive processing operations such as 30-day cross-site behavioural retargeting and behavioural profiling. The user was not given a specific, informed choice about behavioural tracking across third-party news sites versus receiving emails.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Unbundle consent so users can separately agree to (a) email marketing, (b) app-push marketing, and (c) behavioural/cross-site retargeting and profiling, each with clear, plain-language information about what it entails. findings.title: Lawful basis for processing

findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days

findings.title: Definition of profiling

findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault sequence engages UCPD primarily as an aggressive commercial practice. The most acute issue is that unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night app pushes — continuing to solicit a consumer after they have signalled refusal is a per-se prohibited persistent/unwanted solicitation (Annex I point 26). Independently, the overall design (disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users, 30-day relentless cross-site retargeting, deliberately timed 21:30 pushes, and anthropomorphic/pressuring copy) plausibly constitutes an aggressive practice through harassment and undue influence under Arts. 8-9, with Art. 5 as a fairness backstop. No blacklisted false-urgency or misleading claim is clearly made, so those are not cited.

report.executive_summary: The "we saw you looking" sequence targets signed-in EU shoppers who abandon carts with 30-day cross-site display retargeting, three emails, and late-night app pushes, using behavioural profiling to flag "high-intent" users. The single most serious problem is that unsubscribing only stops emails, not the 21:30 push notifications — continuing to message someone after they have opted out is a per-se banned practice under EU consumer law (UCPD blacklist) and also breaches the absolute right to object to marketing under GDPR. On top of that, the campaign relies on a vague one-off "marketing communications" sign-up consent that cannot lawfully cover cross-site behavioural tracking, so the legal basis for the retargeting is shaky. The disabled frequency caps for "high-intent" users, the deliberately timed late-night "Still up?" pushes, and the surveillance-styled "they're watching you back" copy together look like an aggressive, high-pressure practice. There are also transparency gaps: users were not clearly told at sign-up that their behaviour would be tracked across news sites, and the display ads need proper advertiser/targeting disclosures. In its current form the campaign carries critical legal exposure and should not launch as designed. The good news is that the core fixes are concrete and achievable without abandoning cart-recovery marketing altogether.
recommendations: Make one opt-out/unsubscribe stop ALL channels immediately — email, app-push and behavioural display retargeting. This fixes the most severe risk (UCPD Annex I per-se ban and GDPR Art. 21 right to object). Do this before any launch.
Remove the 'unsubscribe stops emails but not pushes' behaviour entirely; opting out must also stop the profiling that triggers the messages.

Reinstate reasonable frequency caps for every user segment — eliminate the 'disabled caps for high-intent users' tier — and stop the late-night (21:30) send times, which help make the sequence look aggressive under UCPD Arts. 8-9.

Unbundle consent: give users separate, specific, plain-language opt-ins for (a) email marketing, (b) app-push marketing, and (c) cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling. Do not rely on the generic 'marketing communications' sign-up tick for behavioural advertising (GDPR Arts. 4(11), 6, 7).
Establish and document a valid lawful basis for the 30-day cross-site retargeting (specific consent or a robust legitimate-interests assessment) and shorten/justify the retargeting window.

Revise the copy: drop the surveillance-themed 'they're watching you back' and pressuring 'Still up? Your cart is too' framing in favour of informative messaging (UCPD Art. 5 fairness; GDPR fairness/transparency).
Provide clear Art. 13 information at sign-up and in the privacy notice covering the profiling logic, cross-site tracking, ad-network recipients and retention/targeting windows.

Ensure the display placements pass accurate advertiser-identity and targeting metadata to hosting platforms so DSA Art. 26 ad-transparency disclosures can be populated, and confirm whether ShoeVault's app qualifies as an 'online platform' (which would add DSA dark-pattern obligations).
