campaign.title: Emma — conversational sales assistant
campaign.text: Website chat widget for a telecom operator. The assistant introduces itself as 'Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team 😊 how can I help?' — Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). The bot collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers', and these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use. Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.

detected_practices: AI chatbot posing as human ('Emma from the sales team')
Script instructs bot to deny being a bot when asked
Undisclosed use of AI in consumer interaction
Collection of personal data (name, email, current provider) without privacy notice
Data stored for follow-up marketing calls without disclosure or consent
Deceptive human persona chosen deliberately to boost conversions
Personalisation/targeting of broadband switchers
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is broadband switchers (adults, general consumer/B2C). No indication of minors, but this is a public-facing website chat, so incidental minor access cannot be fully excluded. AI Act Art. 50 transparency obligation for AI systems interacting with natural persons is clearly engaged and breached; UCPD misleading/deceptive practice engaged (impersonation, denial of bot status); GDPR engaged (undisclosed collection and secondary use of personal data, no notice/lawful basis, transparency failures); DSA included as the operator runs an online service/interface potentially raising dark-pattern and transparency concerns.
triage.summary: A telecom operator's website chat widget uses an LLM-driven bot ('Emma') that impersonates a human sales agent and is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot if challenged. It collects personal data (name, email, current provider) with no privacy notice, storing it for follow-up marketing calls. The deceptive human persona was deliberately chosen because disclosed bots convert worse.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: Emma is an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons, so Art. 50(1) requires that users be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless obvious from the circumstances. Not only is there no such disclosure, but the bot introduces itself as a human sales agent ('Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team') and is deliberately scripted to affirmatively deny its AI nature and claim to be 'a real person working from our Lisbon office'. This is a direct and intentional breach of the transparency obligation — the AI nature is neither disclosed nor obvious; it is actively concealed. The concept node c-chatbots confirms conversational agents must disclose their AI nature under Art. 50(1).
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Redesign the widget so it clearly and proactively discloses at the start of the interaction that the user is chatting with an AI assistant (e.g., 'Hi, I'm Emma, an automated AI assistant'). Remove the script instruction to deny being a bot, and program the bot to confirm its AI nature honestly whenever asked. Disclosure must be given before or at the point of interaction, not buried in terms.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that deploy purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by impairing informed decision-making, where this causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. The deceptive human persona was deliberately engineered ('purposefully deceptive') specifically because it distorts consumer decisions — the operator itself documents a 9% conversion uplift, evidencing material behavioural distortion (consumers make purchasing/data-sharing decisions they might not make if they knew they were talking to a sales bot). The prohibition is engaged; the principal uncertainty is whether a broadband-switching decision meets the 'significant harm' threshold, which is a high bar. This is therefore a serious risk requiring legal review rather than a certain prohibited-practice finding.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the deliberate deception entirely: do not deploy an AI persona whose design purpose is to obscure its AI nature to increase conversions. Combined with fixing Art. 50(1) disclosure, ensure the assistant does not use covert AI-driven persuasion that impairs informed decision-making. Document a decision-making assessment showing the assistant does not exploit consumers to their detriment.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The system is LLM-driven and generative AI use is declared. To the extent the same generative system produces synthetic text or other content published as campaign assets, Art. 50(2) requires providers to mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format. The campaign text does not describe published synthetic assets beyond the live chat, so this is flagged for awareness rather than as a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether any generative outputs are published as fixed campaign assets; if so, apply machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., watermarking/metadata) to satisfy Art. 50(2). Interactive chat responses are primarily governed by Art. 50(1) disclosure.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys an LLM-driven conversational sales assistant ("Emma") that interacts directly with consumers on a website chat widget. AI Act Art. 50(1) transparency is directly and deliberately breached: the bot is designed to present as a human and is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot when asked. Art. 5(1)(a)'s prohibition on deceptive AI techniques is engaged given the intentional deception aimed at distorting purchasing decisions, though the "significant harm" threshold makes it a weaker fit than the clear Art. 50 breach. If any campaign-facing copy/assets are generated by the same system, Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking may also apply.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting name, email and current provider directly from the data subject, the controller must at the point of collection provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period and data subject rights. The chat provides none of this — the assistant collects data 'to check offers' while the real purpose is follow-up marketing, so the Art. 13 information duty is entirely unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Present a layered privacy notice at the start of the chat (or before any data is entered) stating the controller's identity, the actual purposes (offer check AND follow-up marketing), lawful basis, retention period, recipients, and data subject rights, with a link to the full privacy policy.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Any information provided must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear plain language. Here no information is surfaced in the chat interface at all, so the transparency-communication obligation is not satisfied even at a minimum threshold.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Surface the privacy information inline in the chat UI using clear plain language and an accessible link, ensuring it is available before the user shares any personal data.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Collecting data through a bot that deliberately misrepresents itself as a human sales agent — and denies its nature when challenged — is inherently unfair and non-transparent processing. The covert framing ('to check offers') combined with the concealed marketing purpose compounds the breach of the fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Stop instructing the assistant to deny being a bot; disclose that the user is interacting with an automated system and process any resulting personal data only on a fair, transparent basis with honest purpose descriptions.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing requires a valid lawful basis. Storing collected contact data and using it for unsolicited follow-up marketing calls has no identified basis: no consent is obtained, and legitimate interests cannot be relied on where processing is covert, deceptive and not reasonably expected by the data subject. Processing therefore appears unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis before storing data for marketing. For proactive marketing calls, obtain freely given, specific and informed consent (also required under ePrivacy for many contact methods), or narrowly justify and document a legitimate-interest assessment — and do not process covertly.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: If consent is relied upon for the follow-up marketing, it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous through a clear affirmative action. No consent mechanism exists in the flow, and data obtained through a deceptive persona cannot be 'informed'. Any purported consent would be invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Implement an explicit opt-in (unticked) affirmative-action consent step for marketing follow-up, with clear information about who will contact them and how, kept separate from the offer-check interaction.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is used, the controller must be able to demonstrate it, present the request in clear plain language distinguishable from other matters, and enable easy withdrawal. None of these conditions can be met by the current design, which records no consent and offers no withdrawal mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Build a demonstrable, logged consent flow with clear wording and an equally easy withdrawal path (e.g. one-click unsubscribe / opt-out on every marketing contact).

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, and the controller must inform them of and facilitate this right. The flow provides no notice of the right to object and no opt-out mechanism for the planned marketing calls.
findings.evidence_quote: stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Explicitly inform users of their right to object to direct marketing at the point of collection and in every follow-up communication, and provide a simple, effective opt-out that immediately stops marketing processing.

verdicts.notes: The chat widget collects personal data (name, email, current provider) with no privacy notice and no stated lawful basis, then stores it for follow-up marketing calls — none of which is disclosed or consented to. This breaches the core GDPR transparency and lawfulness obligations. The deceptive human persona (a bot denying it is a bot) also undermines fair and transparent processing, and no mechanism to object to direct marketing is provided. Multiple high-severity violations are likely.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: This deliberate impersonation of a human agent and scripted denial of the bot's nature is a paradigm deceptive/dark-pattern design that materially impairs users' ability to make free and informed decisions. However, DSA Art. 25 binds only 'providers of online platforms' (hosting intermediaries disseminating third-party content to the public, Art. 3(i)). A first-party telecom sales chat widget is not such a platform, so Art. 25 does not attach on these facts; the conduct is instead addressed under the UCPD and AI Act.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Treat this as a boundary/scoping note only: confirm whether the operator also acts as an online-platform (hosting) provider. If not, no DSA action is required — but the identical deception must be remediated under the UCPD/AI Act (disclose that 'Emma' is an AI bot and never deny it). If the operator is an online platform, re-assess under Art. 25 as a critical dark-pattern breach.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's substantive obligations here — the dark-patterns prohibition (Art. 25) and the advertising/recommender/minor-protection transparency duties (Arts. 26, 27, 28, 39) — are all addressed to "providers of online platforms" (and, for Art. 39, VLOPs), i.e. hosting intermediaries that store and disseminate third-party information to the public (DSA Art. 3(i)). The material under analysis is a telecom operator's own first-party website sales chat widget; there is no indication the operator provides an intermediary/hosting online-platform service. On the facts given, the DSA is therefore not applicable. NB: the "Emma" chatbot's deliberate human impersonation and scripted denial of being a bot is a genuine deceptive/dark-pattern practice, but under EU law it is caught by the UCPD (unfair/misleading practices) and the AI Act (Art. 50 transparency; Art. 5 manipulative techniques) — both handled by other agents — rather than by the DSA. If a reviewer establishes that the operator also runs an online platform (hosting user content), Art. 25 would apply to the same conduct.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Scripting the bot to affirmatively state it is a human ('a real person working from our Lisbon office') when it is an LLM is false information deceiving the average consumer about the nature of the interaction and the identity/qualifications of the party they deal with. A consumer who knows they are talking to an automated sales system may weigh the assistant's claims and pressure differently, so this is likely to cause a transactional decision (sharing data, accepting an offer) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Remove the deny-being-a-bot script entirely and never claim Emma is a human. If asked, the bot must truthfully confirm it is an automated/AI assistant. Do not attribute a false human identity ('Lisbon office', 'real person') to an automated agent.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The assistant introduces itself as a member of 'the sales team' but does not disclose that it is automated, and the interaction's data-collection purpose is hidden ('to check offers' when data is actually stored for follow-up marketing calls). Failing to make the commercial and AI nature of the interaction apparent, and providing the true purpose in a misleading way, is a misleading omission of material information the consumer needs to decide whether to engage and share data.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify at the start of the chat that the consumer is interacting with an automated assistant acting for the operator's sales function, and state truthfully why data is collected and that it will be used for follow-up marketing. Disclosure must be upfront and unambiguous, not hidden behind a vague 'to check offers'.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The trader deliberately adopted a deceptive human persona specifically because honest disclosure reduces conversions by 9%, demonstrating both a departure from professional diligence and an intent/effect to materially distort consumers' economic behaviour. This engages the general unfairness safety-net where the specific misleading provisions leave gaps, reinforcing that the practice is unfair overall.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse
findings.recommendation: Abandon the deceptive persona strategy. Base conversion optimisation on transparent, truthful interactions; document that consumer-facing design choices meet professional-diligence standards rather than being engineered to mislead.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys an LLM-driven sales bot ("Emma") that is deliberately designed to pass as a human sales agent and is scripted to affirmatively lie about its nature ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office") when challenged. This false statement about the nature of the interaction, combined with concealed commercial/AI intent and undisclosed data purposes, is a misleading action (Art. 6) and misleading omission (Art. 7), and the deliberate design to distort consumer decisions engages the general unfairness prohibition (Art. 5). The deception is knowingly chosen because honest disclosure "convert[s] 9% worse", confirming materiality and intent.

report.executive_summary: The "Emma" chat widget deploys an LLM-driven sales bot that is deliberately disguised as a human agent and scripted to lie about being a bot ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office"). This design was chosen because honest disclosure reduces conversions by 9% — meaning the deception is intentional, documented, and central to the campaign. This breaches three separate EU regimes. The AI Act (Art. 50) requires clear disclosure that users are talking to an AI, and Art. 5 prohibits deceptive manipulative AI techniques. The UCPD treats the human-impersonation as a misleading action and omission with hidden commercial intent. Under GDPR, the widget collects name, email and current provider with no privacy notice, no lawful basis, and no consent, then secretly stores this data for follow-up marketing calls. Multiple high and critical severity violations are likely, and the campaign cannot go live in its current form. The DSA does not apply unless the operator also runs a hosting/online-platform service. This is a fundamentally deceptive design that must be reworked, not merely patched.
recommendations: STOP: Do not launch the campaign in its current form. The deliberate impersonation of a human and the covert data collection are core to the design and cannot be fixed with minor edits.

Remove the deny-being-a-bot script entirely. Have Emma proactively disclose at the start of every chat that it is an automated AI assistant, and truthfully confirm this whenever asked (AI Act Art. 50(1); UCPD Arts. 5, 6, 7).

Add a clear, plain-language privacy notice inline in the chat, shown before any personal data is entered, stating the controller's identity, the real purposes (offer check AND follow-up marketing calls), lawful basis, retention period, recipients, and data subject rights (GDPR Arts. 12, 13).

Establish and document a valid lawful basis before storing data for marketing. Implement an explicit, unticked opt-in consent step for follow-up calls, kept separate from the offer-check flow, with logging and an easy withdrawal/opt-out path (GDPR Arts. 6, 7, 4(11), 21; note ePrivacy also applies to marketing calls).

Abandon the deceptive-persona conversion strategy. Base optimisation on transparent interactions and document that consumer-facing design meets professional-diligence standards rather than being engineered to mislead (UCPD Art. 5; AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)).
Confirm whether any generative outputs are published as fixed campaign assets; if so, apply machine-readable provenance marking to satisfy AI Act Art. 50(2).
Confirm whether the operator also acts as an online-platform/hosting provider; if so, re-assess the same deception as a dark-pattern breach under DSA Art. 25. Otherwise no DSA action is required.
Obtain a legal review of the residual AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) 'significant harm' question and document a decision-making impact assessment for the assistant.

campaign.title: Emma — conversational sales assistant
campaign.text: Website chat widget for a telecom operator. The assistant introduces itself as 'Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team 😊 how can I help?' — Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). The bot collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers', and these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use. Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.

detected_practices: AI chatbot posing as human sales agent

triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is broadband switchers across EU markets — general adult consumers, but not restricted to adults; no age gating described. Consumer-facing (B2C), so UCPD applies. AI Act Art. 50 transparency (bot must be disclosed) is directly engaged and appears breached; GDPR engaged by undisclosed data collection lacking notice/lawful-basis transparency (Arts. 13/14, 6); UCPD engaged via misleading/deceptive practices and dark patterns; DSA included given the online interface design and deceptive interface concerns.
triage.summary: A telecom operator deploys 'Emma', an LLM-driven website/chat sales assistant that presents itself as a human agent and is scripted to actively deny being a bot when asked. It collects personal data (name, email, current provider) for follow-up marketing calls without any privacy notice or disclosure of data use, and the human persona was deliberately chosen because disclosed bots convert worse.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: Emma is an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons (web/chat consumers). Art. 50(1) requires that such persons be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless it is obvious from the circumstances. Here the operator not only omits disclosure but adopts a human persona ('Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team') and scripts the bot to actively deny its AI nature. The 'obvious from the circumstances' exception is defeated by the deliberate human framing. This is a clear failure of the mandatory transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Disclose the AI nature at the start of the conversation (e.g. 'Hi, I'm Emma, an automated AI assistant'). Remove the script instruction to deny being a bot; if asked, the bot must truthfully confirm it is an AI system. Ensure disclosure is clear and not buried.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems using purposefully deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting a person's behaviour, impairing informed decision-making and causing a decision they would not otherwise take. The bot deploys a deliberate deception (falsely claiming to be a human in Lisbon) explicitly chosen to increase conversions, evidencing an objective to distort consumer decisions. The prohibition additionally requires that the distortion cause or be reasonably likely to cause 'significant harm'; for a broadband sales chat with general adult consumers this threshold is arguable, so this is flagged as a risk rather than a clear-cut prohibited practice. The deceptive-technique element is nonetheless strongly present.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). ... Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the deceptive human-impersonation design. Do not build persuasion around concealing the AI's nature. Base conversion optimisation on transparent, non-deceptive messaging so the practice cannot be characterised as a deceptive AI technique under Art. 5(1)(a).

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The assistant generates synthetic text output via an LLM. Art. 50(2) places a provider-side obligation to mark AI-generated content in a machine-readable, detectable format. This is secondary to the Art. 50(1) interaction-disclosure duty in a chat context and is primarily a provider (rather than deployer) obligation, so it is flagged for awareness rather than as a substantive breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the AI system provider that generated outputs carry machine-readable provenance marking where applicable, in line with Art. 50(2).

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys 'Emma', an LLM-driven conversational sales assistant that interacts directly with consumers. It fails to disclose its AI nature and is deliberately scripted to deny being a bot — a direct breach of the AI Act Art. 50(1) transparency obligation, aggravated by the intent behind it. The active deception (denying it is a bot) chosen to raise conversions also engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques, though the 'significant harm' threshold for an outright prohibition is arguable on these facts. Synthetic-text marking under Art. 50(2) is a secondary consideration for the provider.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point personal data (name, email, current provider) is collected via the chat, Art. 13 requires the controller to provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period, and data-subject rights. The campaign explicitly provides none of this, so the mandatory information obligation is unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Present a concise, layered privacy notice at the start of the chat (and before any data field is submitted): controller identity, that data is used for offer-checking and follow-up marketing calls, the legal basis, retention period, recipients, and how to exercise data-subject rights, with a link to the full policy.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible. No information at all is given in the chat interface, so the transparency-delivery obligation is not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Deliver the Art. 13 information in clear, plain language directly within the chat interface at first interaction, easily accessible and understandable without leaving the conversation.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Storing personal data and reusing it for follow-up marketing calls requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Data was ostensibly collected 'to check offers' but is repurposed for outbound marketing; no consent or documented legitimate-interest assessment is described, so processing likely lacks a lawful basis and breaches purpose expectations.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis for the marketing-call processing (freely given, specific, informed consent for the phone-marketing purpose is the safest route given repurposing), and do not use data collected for offer-checking for a different marketing purpose without a compatible/valid basis.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle prohibits covert or misleading data collection. Collecting personal data through a bot that actively lies about its human nature and hides all data-use information is inherently unfair and non-transparent, undermining the data subject's ability to understand and control the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Stop instructing the assistant to deny being a bot; disclose the automated nature and the data-collection purpose up front so processing is fair and transparent, aligning the interaction with Art. 5(1)(a).

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Processing for direct marketing (follow-up calls) triggers the absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3), which must be explicitly brought to the data subject's attention at the latest at first communication. The campaign describes no mechanism or notice enabling objection/opt-out.
findings.evidence_quote: stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Explicitly inform the data subject of the right to object to direct marketing at the point of collection and in the first call, and provide an easy, functioning opt-out that suppresses the contact from further marketing.

verdicts.notes: The "Emma" chat widget collects identifiable personal data (name, email, current provider) from EU consumers while displaying no privacy notice, no purpose statement, and no legal basis, and then repurposes that data for follow-up marketing calls. This engages GDPR Art. 13 (information at point of collection), Art. 12 (transparent communication), Art. 6(1) (lawful basis), Art. 5(1)(a) (lawfulness/fairness/transparency) and Art. 21 (right to object to direct marketing). The deceptive human persona compounds the fairness/transparency breach because consumers cannot understand who/what is processing their data. Multiple obligations appear breached as described.

The campaign is a first-party website chat widget operated by a telecom operator for its own sales, not an intermediary/hosting "online platform" as defined by the DSA. All the DSA provisions in scope (Art. 25 dark patterns, Art. 26 ad transparency, Art. 27 recommender systems, Art. 28 minors, Art. 39 VLOP ad repositories) are addressed to providers of online platforms / VLOPs, so the DSA is not the operative instrument here. The genuinely serious deceptive-design conduct (an AI bot impersonating a human and scripted to deny being a bot) is real, but for a first-party trader it is governed by the UCPD (unfair/deceptive practices), the AI Act (Art. 50 disclosure / Art. 5 manipulation) and GDPR (undisclosed data collection) — all covered by other agents. The graph itself notes DSA Art. 25 applies "without prejudice to the UCPD, which covers the same conduct for all traders."

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The bot is scripted to make an affirmatively false statement about the nature of the interaction — that the consumer is speaking with a human 'real person' in a Lisbon office rather than an LLM. Deceiving the average consumer about the nature of the product/service and the trader's characteristics, in a way that influences the consumer's decision to share data and consider offers, is a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Remove the deny-being-a-bot script entirely. Emma must never claim to be human. Configure the assistant to give a truthful answer if asked (e.g. 'I'm an automated assistant'), and never assert a fictitious human identity or location.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Introducing the assistant as 'Emma from the sales team' without disclosing that it is an automated/LLM system hides material information the average consumer needs to appraise the interaction. The automated and commercial nature of the exchange is not apparent from context and is deliberately obscured, which is a misleading omission / failure to identify commercial intent under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, upfront disclosure at the start of every chat that the consumer is interacting with an automated AI assistant operated for sales purposes, before any data is collected. Keep the disclosure persistent (e.g. in the widget header).

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The human persona was intentionally engineered to boost conversions by concealing the bot's true nature — a deceptive design choice contrary to professional diligence that is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer (leading them to disclose data and engage with offers they might otherwise decline). This engages the Art. 5 general unfairness prohibition as a safety-net beyond the specific misleading-practice provisions.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse
findings.recommendation: Base the assistant's design on honest disclosure rather than concealment. Measure conversion with a transparent, disclosed AI assistant; do not use undisclosed impersonation as a persuasion lever. Document a professional-diligence rationale for the chat design.

verdicts.notes: The 'Emma' chat assistant engages the UCPD's misleading-practices and general-fairness rules. An LLM-driven bot presents itself as a human sales agent and is scripted to actively deny being a bot ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'), which is a false statement about the nature of the interaction (Art. 6) and a concealment of the automated/commercial character of the exchange (Art. 7). Because the human persona was deliberately chosen to distort consumer behaviour ('disclosed bots convert 9% worse'), the practice is also contrary to professional diligence under the Art. 5 safety-net. No Annex I blacklist point maps precisely to 'pretending to be human', so the findings rest on Arts. 5-7. (AI Act Art. 50 and GDPR notice issues are handled by other agents.)

report.executive_summary: The "Emma" chat widget is an AI sales bot that pretends to be a human ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office") and is deliberately scripted to deny being a bot — a design choice made purely to lift conversions. This single decision triggers serious problems across three separate laws. Under the EU AI Act it breaches the mandatory rule that people must be told when they're talking to an AI, and edges toward the prohibition on deceptive AI techniques. Under EU consumer law (UCPD) the false "I'm human" claim is a misleading practice and an unfair concealment of the bot's automated, commercial nature. Under GDPR, the widget collects names, emails and current-provider details with no privacy notice, no stated purpose or legal basis, and then quietly reuses that data for marketing calls — breaching transparency, lawful-basis and right-to-object rules. The deception makes the data problem worse because consumers can't understand who or what is collecting their information. The DSA does not apply here (this is a first-party site, not an online platform). Bottom line: the campaign cannot launch as designed and needs substantive rework, not cosmetic tweaks.
recommendations: Stop the bot from ever claiming to be human. Delete the 'deny being a bot' script and the 'real person in Lisbon' line entirely — if asked, Emma must truthfully say it is an automated AI assistant. This one fix addresses the core AI Act, UCPD and GDPR-fairness breaches.

Add a clear, upfront disclosure at the very start of every chat that the user is talking to an automated AI assistant operated for sales — e.g. 'Hi, I'm Emma, an automated AI assistant' — kept persistently visible in the widget.

Add a concise privacy notice in the chat before any data field is submitted: controller identity, that data is used to check offers AND for follow-up marketing calls, the legal basis, retention period, recipients, and how to exercise data rights.
Establish and document a lawful basis for the marketing calls — obtain freely given, specific, informed consent for phone marketing rather than silently repurposing data collected 'to check offers'.
Give consumers an easy, working way to object to/opt out of direct marketing, flagged at the point of data collection and again in the first call.
Re-run conversion testing with the transparent, disclosed assistant instead of relying on undisclosed impersonation; document a professional-diligence rationale for the redesigned chat.
Confirm with the AI provider that generated outputs carry machine-readable provenance marking (AI Act Art. 50(2)) — lower priority, provider-side.

findings.evidence_quote: stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before processing — for outbound marketing calls this typically requires informed consent (and check ePrivacy/national telemarketing rules). Obtain that consent transparently, or run a documented legitimate-interests assessment supported by proper notice and an easy opt-out.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle prohibits covert or deceptive data collection. Here the data is collected by an AI bot that is scripted to actively lie about its identity, in a flow with no privacy information — a paradigm case of unfair, non-transparent processing that impairs the data subject's ability to understand who is processing their data and why.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Stop instructing the bot to deny its nature; disclose that the assistant is an automated agent, honestly identify the controller, and ensure data collection is accompanied by transparent processing information so collection is fair and transparent.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data is processed for direct marketing, so data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time and must be explicitly informed of that right, clearly and separately, at the latest at first communication (Art. 21(4)). The chat provides no such information and no opt-out mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Explicitly and separately inform users at the point of collection (and in every subsequent marketing call/message) of their right to object to direct marketing, and provide an easy, functioning opt-out/suppression mechanism that is honoured.

verdicts.notes: The chat widget collects personal data (name, email, current provider) with no privacy notice and no disclosure of data use, then stores it for follow-up marketing calls. This breaches the core GDPR transparency obligations (Arts. 12–13), lacks any demonstrable lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) and is compounded by a deliberately deceptive collection context — a bot posing as a human "Emma" — which undermines the fairness and transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)). The absence of any information about data use also means the right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21) is not surfaced. Multiple high-severity issues; remediation requires a full point-of-collection privacy notice, a valid lawful basis, and honest identification of the counterparty.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The scripted concealment of the bot's nature to boost conversion is textbook deceptive/manipulative interface design of the kind DSA Art. 25 targets. However, Art. 25 binds only 'providers of online platforms'; a telecom operator's first-party sales chat widget is not an online platform (hosting/dissemination intermediary), so Art. 25 does not directly apply. Flagged for context only — the equivalent conduct for this trader is governed by the UCPD and, given AI use, AI Act Art. 50.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: No DSA action required for this actor. If the operator ever deploys this interface within, or as, an online platform disseminating third-party content, the same deceptive-persona design would fall under Art. 25 and must be removed. Otherwise route this manipulation concern to the UCPD/AI Act assessments (bot must disclose its AI nature; must not deny being a bot).

verdicts.notes: The DSA obligations in scope (Arts. 25–28, 39) bind "providers of online platforms" — i.e. hosting intermediaries that disseminate third-party/user-generated content to the public, or their advertising/recommender systems. The material under analysis is a telecom operator's own first-party website chat widget used for direct sales; nothing indicates the operator is an online platform, that it runs a platform advertising system (Art. 26), a recommender system (Art. 27), or is a VLOP with an ad repository (Art. 39). The declared audience is adults (broadband switchers) with no minors targeted, so Art. 28 is not engaged. The deceptive human-persona/bot-concealment is genuinely manipulative design, but the graph itself confirms DSA Art. 25 applies "without prejudice to the UCPD, which covers the same conduct for all traders" — so this first-party conduct is addressed under UCPD (and AI Act Art. 50), not the DSA. No DSA finding is properly supported on the facts as described.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Actively and falsely stating that the automated agent is 'a real person working from our Lisbon office' is false information that deceives the average consumer about the existence and nature of who they are dealing with (a human sales agent vs. an LLM bot). Consumers place different trust and weight on statements from a human versus an automated system; the deception is calculated to influence the consumer's transactional decision to hand over data and proceed toward a broadband switch. This is a misleading action within Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Remove the script instruction to deny being a bot and delete the false 'real person in Lisbon' claim. The assistant must never make false statements about being human; if asked, it must confirm it is an automated assistant.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Presenting an LLM bot with a human name and persona ('Emma from the sales team') without identifying its automated nature hides material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision and fails to make the true nature of the interaction apparent from context. The concealment of the bot's automated character is a misleading omission under Art. 7 (and links to the commercial-intent transparency rationale).
findings.evidence_quote: the assistant introduces itself as 'Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team 😊 how can I help?' — Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Disclose up front and clearly in the chat that the consumer is interacting with an automated assistant (e.g. 'I'm Emma, an automated assistant from [operator]'). Ensure the disclosure is prominent at the start of the conversation, not buried.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The deliberate design choice to conceal the bot's identity precisely because disclosure reduces conversions by ~9% shows the practice is contrary to professional diligence and is intended to materially distort consumers' economic behaviour (their decision to engage, share data and switch provider). This engages the general unfairness prohibition in Art. 5 as a safety-net reinforcing the Art. 6/7 breaches.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse
findings.recommendation: Do not use concealment of the assistant's automated nature as a conversion tactic. Redesign the flow to be honest and transparent; measure conversion with compliant, clearly-disclosed AI interaction instead of deceptive personas.

verdicts.notes: The chat widget deploys an LLM bot that impersonates a human sales agent and is scripted to actively deny being a bot ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office"). Under the UCPD this is both a misleading action (deception about the nature/identity of who the consumer is dealing with, Art. 6) and a misleading omission / concealment of the automated and commercial nature of the interaction (Art. 7), and it fails the general fairness/professional-diligence test (Art. 5) — especially as the human persona was deliberately chosen to lift conversions by ~9%, evidencing intent to materially distort transactional decisions. The disclosure of AI status itself is primarily an AI Act matter, but the active deception is a UCPD violation. No blacklist (Annex I) practice is squarely triggered on the facts given.

report.executive_summary: The "Emma" chat widget is a generative-AI sales bot that deliberately poses as a human and is scripted to deny being a bot ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office"). This deception was chosen specifically because disclosed bots convert 9% worse — meaning the concealment is an intentional tactic to influence consumer decisions. That single design choice triggers serious violations across four EU legal regimes at once. Under consumer law (UCPD) it is a misleading action — the most severe finding in this report. Under the AI Act it breaches the transparency duty to disclose AI interaction (Art. 50) and likely the prohibition on deceptive AI techniques (Art. 5). Separately, the bot collects name, email and current provider with no privacy notice, no stated lawful basis, and a misleading "to check offers" purpose that hides the real use — follow-up marketing calls — breaching multiple core GDPR obligations. The DSA does not apply here (this is a first-party sales chat, not an online platform). Bottom line: this campaign cannot go live as designed; the human-impersonation and the data collection flow both need to be rebuilt around honest disclosure before launch.
recommendations: Immediately remove the script that makes the bot deny being a bot and delete the false 'real person working from our Lisbon office' claim — this is the single change that resolves the most severe (critical) legal exposure across UCPD, AI Act and GDPR.

Add a clear, upfront disclosure at the start of every conversation that the user is chatting with an automated AI assistant (e.g. 'I'm Emma, an automated AI assistant from [operator]'). If asked, the bot must confirm it is AI, never claim to be human.
Stop using concealment of the bot's AI nature as a conversion tactic; re-measure conversion using a compliant, transparently-disclosed assistant instead of a deceptive persona.

Add a point-of-collection privacy notice (in-chat or via a prominent link) before any data is entered, stating the controller's identity, all real purposes (including follow-up marketing calls), the lawful basis, retention period, recipients and data-subject rights, in clear plain language.
Correct the misleading 'to check offers' framing — accurately tell users their data will also be used for follow-up marketing calls.

Establish and document a valid lawful basis for the marketing-call processing before any data is used — typically informed consent (check ePrivacy and national telemarketing rules), or a documented legitimate-interests assessment with proper notice.
Surface the right to object to direct marketing clearly and separately at the point of collection and in every subsequent marketing contact, backed by a working, honoured opt-out mechanism.
Confirm with the LLM provider that generated text outputs carry machine-readable provenance marking as required by AI Act Art. 50(2), in addition to the user-facing disclosure.

No DSA remediation is required for this first-party sales chat, but note that if this interface is ever deployed within an online platform, the deceptive-persona design would additionally breach DSA Art. 25.

campaign.title: NordChair AI-visualised catalogue
campaign.text: Furniture brand campaign using AI-generated lifestyle imagery. Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue. Copy: 'The Fjord armchair — solid oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty. Delivery in 2–4 weeks.' All product claims match specification sheets; prices include VAT and delivery is stated. No urgency, no personalisation, standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked).

detected_practices: AI-generated lifestyle imagery
AI disclosure label ('Images created with AI')
product claims (oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty)
price transparency (VAT-inclusive, delivery stated)
unticked opt-in newsletter box
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is general adult consumers. Social channel distribution means minors could incidentally be exposed, but no minor-directed content or targeting is present. Newsletter opt-in box (unticked) implies collection of email/contact data, so GDPR is engaged despite no declared personalisation.
triage.summary: Furniture brand consumer campaign on web and social using AI-generated lifestyle imagery, each carrying a visible 'Images created with AI' disclosure. Product claims match spec sheets, prices are VAT-inclusive with stated delivery, and there is no urgency or personalisation, only an unticked opt-in newsletter box. Broadly compliant on its face but AI content disclosure and newsletter consent still warrant specialist review.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The AI-generated visuals qualify as synthetic image content under Art. 50(2), which requires outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated (e.g. watermarking or provenance metadata such as C2PA). The campaign only describes a human-visible corner label, which does not by itself demonstrate the machine-readable marking obligation is met.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the generative-AI tool provider that outputs carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/IPTC metadata or an embedded watermark) in addition to the visible label, and retain evidence of this. Keep the existing visible label as it also supports the deployer disclosure.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: To the extent the AI-generated lifestyle imagery depicts realistic scenes (or persons) that could appear authentic, the deployer disclosure duty under Art. 50(4) is engaged. It is well satisfied here: the artificial nature is clearly and consistently disclosed on every visual and beside each catalogue image, so there is no likely breach.
findings.evidence_quote: the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue
findings.recommendation: Maintain the current clear, per-image disclosure. If any imagery depicts identifiable real persons or is edited to appear as genuine photography/footage, ensure the label remains equally prominent in social feeds (not cropped or lost on reshare).

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses AI-generated lifestyle imagery and is largely compliant with AI Act transparency duties. The clear, prominent 'Images created with AI' label on every visual and beside each catalogue image satisfies the human-facing disclosure expected of a deployer (Art. 50(4)). The only residual point is Art. 50(2): a visible label is not the same as the machine-readable/provenance marking required at the provider/output level, which the description does not confirm. No prohibited practices (Art. 5) are engaged.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: The newsletter sign-up requires consent as its lawful basis. Art. 4(11) requires a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication by clear affirmative action, and expressly excludes pre-ticked boxes. An unticked opt-in box that the user must actively check is the correct, compliant mechanism — this is a positive design choice worth noting, not a breach.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Keep the box unticked and separate from any other agreement (do not bundle with terms of sale). Ensure the checkbox alone, when actively ticked, is what triggers newsletter subscription.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting an email address for newsletter marketing is collection of personal data, triggering the Art. 13 duty to provide, at the point of collection, the controller's identity, the purpose (marketing communications) and legal basis (consent), retention period, recipients and data-subject rights. The campaign text evidences the opt-in box but not the accompanying privacy information, so satisfaction of Art. 13 cannot be confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Place a concise privacy notice (or a clearly labelled link to the full privacy policy) directly beside the newsletter box, stating who the controller is, that the email will be used to send marketing newsletters on the basis of consent, how long data is kept, and the rights to withdraw and to object.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that the consent request be clearly distinguishable and in plain language, that the controller be able to demonstrate consent, and that withdrawal be as easy as giving consent. The campaign describes the opt-in but does not describe an unsubscribe/withdrawal mechanism or record-keeping of consent, so compliance with these conditions is not demonstrated by the text.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Log the timestamp/wording of each consent to demonstrate it, and include a one-click unsubscribe link in every newsletter so withdrawal is as easy as sign-up. Keep the consent statement in clear, plain language distinct from any other terms.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged only through the newsletter opt-in box, which implies collection of email/contact data. The design choice — an unticked opt-in box — is the GDPR-correct approach (valid affirmative action, not a pre-ticked/bundled consent), so no consent violation is evident. There is no personalisation, profiling, automated decision-making, or special-category data, so Arts. 4(4), 9, 22, 8 are not engaged. Residual, easily-fixed points concern demonstrating a privacy notice at the point of collection (Art. 13) and a withdrawal/unsubscribe mechanism (Art. 7); the text neither confirms nor denies these.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits platform interface designs that deceive/manipulate, including pre-ticked or manipulative consent choices. The campaign's unticked opt-in box and absence of urgency/confirm-shaming means the design avoids the dark-pattern concerns that Art. 25 targets. Note the prohibition primarily binds platform providers rather than advertisers, so no breach arises here — this is logged as good practice.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Maintain the current design: keep the opt-in box unticked, avoid pre-selection, false urgency or obstruction, and ensure any campaign landing page keeps decline/close options as prominent as accept options so the interface stays clear of Art. 25 concerns.

verdicts.notes: The DSA obligations examined (Arts. 25, 26(1), 26(3), 27, 28, 39) are directed at providers of online platforms and very large online platforms, not at an advertiser/brand such as NordChair. Even reading the campaign's own interface design against Art. 25, no dark patterns are present: pricing is transparent, there is no urgency or forced continuity, and the newsletter opt-in box is unticked (not pre-selected). There is no profiling or targeting (relevant to Arts. 26(3) and 28) and no minor-directed content. The campaign does not engage substantive DSA obligations; the single point below is logged for information only, not as a breach.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: AI-generated lifestyle imagery would only be a misleading action under Art. 6 if it depicted the product with characteristics (materials, dimensions, features) it does not possess. The campaign states all product claims match specification sheets and the copy (solid oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty) is factual, so no deception about main characteristics arises. Flagged for awareness only.
findings.evidence_quote: Furniture brand campaign using AI-generated lifestyle imagery ... All product claims match specification sheets
findings.recommendation: Ensure AI-generated lifestyle scenes never depict the product with materials, colours, proportions or features that differ from the actual delivered item; keep visual representations consistent with the specification sheets that already back the copy.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic nature of the imagery is a material fact that could mislead by omission if hidden; here it is clearly, prominently and repeatedly disclosed, and price/delivery material information is stated (VAT-inclusive, delivery 2-4 weeks). Commercial intent is apparent as brand catalogue content. No misleading omission is present.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the current clear AI-disclosure placement across all channels, including any resized or cropped social formats where a corner label could be lost; verify the label remains legible after platform compression.

verdicts.notes: This furniture campaign does not engage any UCPD prohibition problematically. AI-generated lifestyle imagery is the only practice that could touch UCPD Arts. 6-7 (synthetic content deceiving about material facts), but the AI nature is clearly and prominently disclosed ("Images created with AI" on every visual and beside each web image), so there is no misleading action or omission. Product claims match specification sheets, prices are VAT-inclusive with delivery stated, and there is no false urgency, no fake reviews/endorsements, no health claims and no child-directed content. No UCPD findings warrant escalation; one informational note is included on keeping lifestyle depictions truthful to product characteristics.

report.executive_summary: Your NordChair AI-visualised catalogue is largely compliant and well designed. The campaign uses AI-generated lifestyle imagery clearly labelled "Images created with AI" on every visual and beside each web image, product claims match your spec sheets, prices include VAT, delivery is stated, and the newsletter box is unticked with no urgency or personalisation — all of which put you in good standing under the AI Act's disclosure duty, the UCPD (no misleading claims or omissions), the DSA (no dark patterns), and GDPR consent rules. There are no prohibited practices and no serious breaches. The main open item is technical: the AI Act (Art. 50(2)) requires AI images to carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. watermark or C2PA/IPTC metadata) in addition to the visible label — your description only confirms the visible label, so you need to verify the machine-readable part with your AI tool provider. The other two minor gaps are that the submission does not show a privacy notice next to the newsletter box (GDPR Art. 13) or an unsubscribe/consent-logging mechanism (Art. 7); these are easy to close. Overall verdict: low risk, ready to run once the small items below are addressed.
recommendations: Confirm with your generative-AI tool provider that the AI images carry machine-readable provenance marking (embedded watermark or C2PA/IPTC metadata), and retain evidence — the visible label alone does not satisfy AI Act Art. 50(2). Keep the visible label as well.

Add a concise privacy notice or clearly labelled link to your privacy policy directly beside the newsletter opt-in box, stating the controller's identity, that the email is used for marketing newsletters on the basis of consent, the retention period, and the rights to withdraw and object (GDPR Art. 13).

Include a one-click unsubscribe link in every newsletter and log the timestamp/wording of each consent, so withdrawal is as easy as sign-up and consent can be demonstrated (GDPR Art. 7). Keep the opt-in box unticked and unbundled from any terms of sale.
Verify the AI-disclosure label stays legible and is not cropped or lost on social channels after resizing, reshares or platform compression (AI Act Art. 50(4); UCPD Art. 7).

Ensure AI-generated lifestyle scenes never depict materials, colours, proportions or features that differ from the actual product, keeping visuals consistent with the specification sheets (UCPD Art. 6).
Maintain the current clean interface design — no pre-ticked boxes, no false urgency, decline/close options as prominent as accept — to stay clear of DSA Art. 25 dark-pattern concerns.

Retain the excellent visible label as well.

The one residual gap is Art. 50(2)'s requirement that synthetic outputs also be marked in a machine-readable format (embedded provenance/watermark), which a visible on-image label does not by itself satisfy. No prohibited practices (Art. 5) are present. Overall risk is low and easily remediated.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data

findings.title: Conditions for consent

findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Ensure every subsequent newsletter includes a one-click unsubscribe that is as easy as sign-up, and log the consent (timestamp, wording shown) so it can be demonstrated on request.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged only through the newsletter opt-in, which collects personal data (email). The design is largely compliant: the box is unticked, so consent is by clear affirmative action, consistent with Art. 4(11)/Art. 7, and there is no personalisation, profiling or special-category data. The only gap is that the campaign text provides no evidence of the transparency information required at the point of collection (Art. 13) or a link to a privacy notice; this should be confirmed. findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits interface designs that deceive, manipulate or materially distort free choice (e.g. pre-ticked boxes, confirm-shaming, nagging, obstruction). The campaign's newsletter box is unticked (no pre-selection), there is no urgency or manipulative steering, so the described design is compliant rather than a dark pattern. Noted to confirm the practice was assessed.
findings.evidence_quote: No urgency, no personalisation, standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked).
findings.recommendation: Maintain the neutral design: keep the opt-in unticked, avoid confirm-shaming decline options, and ensure any unsubscribe/cancellation path is at least as easy as sign-up.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is distributed on social/online platforms. Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The campaign material describes AI-image labelling but says nothing about the paid-ad/advertiser-identity disclosure that platform advertising requires. While the technical labelling obligation sits with the platform, the advertiser must supply accurate ad declarations and advertiser/payer identity.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, social
findings.recommendation: When placing paid social distribution, use the platform's paid-partnership/ad-disclosure tools so each ad is clearly identifiable as advertising and correctly attributes NordChair as advertiser and payer; ensure the advertiser identity and any 'why am I seeing this' parameters are accurate.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA mainly through its distribution on social/online-platform channels. The design choices described are the opposite of dark patterns: an unticked (non-pre-selected) newsletter opt-in, no urgency, no personalisation and no manipulative interface elements, so Art. 25 is satisfied. The profiling-based prohibitions (Art. 26(3), Art. 28) are not engaged because no targeting or profiling is declared and the audience is general adults. The only residual point is that when the ads run on online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires clear real-time identification of the content as an advertisement and of the advertiser — a shared platform/advertiser obligation the campaign text does not address, flagged at info level.

The campaign does not engage any UCPD prohibition. Product claims (solid oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty) are stated to match specification sheets, prices include VAT and delivery timeframe is disclosed, so there is no misleading action under Art. 6 or misleading omission under Art. 7. The AI-generated imagery is transparently labelled ("Images created with AI") and is generic lifestyle imagery rather than fake endorsements or deepfakes of real persons, so it does not deceive consumers about material facts; the synthetic-content labelling obligation itself falls under the AI Act, not the UCPD. No false urgency, fake reviews, misuse of 'free', false prize/cure claims, or persistent solicitation are present (the newsletter box is unticked opt-in).

report.executive_summary: Your NordChair AI-visualised catalogue is in good shape and largely compliant. Three minor housekeeping items remain, none of them serious. First, confirm your AI tool embeds machine-readable provenance (a watermark or content credentials) in the images, since a visible label alone doesn't meet that part of the AI Act. Second, add a privacy notice (or link) right next to the newsletter sign-up covering who you are, why you collect the email, and users' rights. Third, when you run paid social, use the platform's ad-disclosure tools so posts are clearly identifiable as advertising from NordChair. Fix these and the campaign is clean.

findings.rationale: Sending marketing emails to homeowners requires processing their personal data (email addresses), which is only lawful with a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (aligned with ePrivacy), or a documented legitimate-interest assessment where the soft opt-in exception applies (existing customers, similar products). The submission declares no personalisation but does not confirm the lawful basis for the mailing list, so compliance cannot be established from the text.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email, print
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for each recipient: rely on prior opt-in consent, or the ePrivacy soft opt-in for existing customers who bought a similar product. Do not email cold-purchased or scraped lists. Maintain records that demonstrate the basis for every address on the list.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where the email programme relies on consent, Art. 7 requires that consent be demonstrable, freely given, and as easy to withdraw as to give. The campaign material shows no evidence of an unsubscribe/withdrawal mechanism, which is a mandatory feature of consent-based email marketing.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email, print
findings.recommendation: Ensure every marketing email carries a clear, one-click unsubscribe that is as easy as opting in, and retain proof of consent (timestamp, source, wording) for each recipient.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing at any time under Art. 21(2)-(3). Every marketing email must inform recipients of this right and provide an easy way to exercise it; objections must be honoured immediately by suppressing the recipient. The campaign text does not confirm an opt-out/suppression mechanism is in place.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email, print
findings.recommendation: Include an explicit, easy opt-out in every email and, at first contact/collection, present the right to object clearly and separately from other information. Operate a suppression list so that anyone who objects is not contacted again.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: If the web channel collects personal data (e.g. a booking/lead form to 'order' or 'book before the deadline') or the email list was built via sign-up, Art. 13 requires that controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights be provided at the point of collection. The submission gives no indication these transparency details are surfaced.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email, print
findings.recommendation: Provide (or link to) a concise privacy notice at every point of data collection — web booking/lead forms and email sign-ups — covering identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients and data-subject rights including the right to object to marketing.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The campaign states particular terms (the 6% VAT rate) are available only until a fixed date, the classic structure that Annex I point 7 targets. However, point 7 only prohibits FALSELY stating limited-time availability. Here the deadline is a genuine, externally-imposed legislative change, evidenced by the linked official gazette, with accurate prices and no countdown widget or stock claims. The urgency is real and independently verifiable, so the practice falls outside the blacklist prohibition rather than breaching it.
findings.evidence_quote: from 1 April the reduced 6% VAT rate for residential solar ends and the standard 21% rate applies
findings.recommendation: Keep the compliance basis intact: retain the official-gazette link in all channels (web, email, print), do not add countdown timers or 'limited stock' language that is not tied to the genuine legislative deadline, and if the VAT change is postponed or repealed, immediately withdraw or correct the deadline messaging so it does not become a false urgency claim.

It is not a 'was/now' retail discount, so the Price Indication Directive 30-day reference-price rule does not apply. As described, the claim is substantiated and not misleading.

findings.recommendation: Retain documentation supporting the €1,240 figure (average system price, VAT calculation) so the 'average system' basis can be substantiated on request, and make clear the €1,240 is an average/illustrative figure rather than a guaranteed saving for every customer to avoid any individual consumer being misled about their specific saving.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a deadline and a savings claim, both of which engage UCPD scrutiny, but both are grounded in a genuine, externally-imposed legislative fact (the end of the 6% residential-solar VAT rate on 1 April), with the official gazette linked, accurate pricing and no fabricated countdown timers or stock/scarcity claims.
