report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes SolarHome solar panel installations by urging homeowners to book before 31 March to lock in the reduced 6% VAT rate before it reverts to 21% on 1 April, citing a €1,240 saving on an average system. The good news: the substance is solid. The urgency is based on a genuine, published legislative VAT change (with the official gazette linked), and there's no fake countdown or stock scarcity, so it does not fall foul of the EU ban on false urgency claims. The €1,240 saving is accurate and properly qualified as applying to the "average system." No AI, no personalisation, and no advertising-standards or platform (DSA) issues are engaged. The only real work is on the email channel: because you're emailing homeowners, GDPR and ePrivacy apply, and the submission doesn't confirm how the list was built, whether emails carry an unsubscribe option, or whether your booking form shows a privacy notice. None of these are breaches — they're verification gaps to close before you hit send. Overall this is a low-risk, defensible campaign that needs a short compliance checklist completed on the email side.
recommendations: Confirm and document the lawful basis for your email list before sending: rely on prior opt-in consent, or the ePrivacy 'soft opt-in' limited to existing customers who bought a similar product and were given an opt-out at collection. Never email purchased or rented lists.
Ensure every marketing email includes a clear, free, one-click unsubscribe link, and that opt-outs are actioned promptly and added to a suppression list so recipients are not re-contacted.

Add a concise privacy notice (or a clear link to one) at every data-collection point in the web booking flow and reference it in the email — covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention period and how to exercise data-subject rights.
Keep the official gazette link live and prominent across web, email and print so the factual basis for the 31 March deadline stays verifiable.

If the VAT change is postponed or extended, immediately update or withdraw the 'book by 31 March' urgency messaging — continuing it after a deferral would turn a true deadline into a false one and breach the ban on false urgency claims.

Retain the 'average system' qualifier on the €1,240 figure and add a short note that the actual saving varies with system size and that the reduced rate applies only where the installation is invoiced before the deadline. Keep dated records of the price/VAT calculation to substantiate the figure if challenged.

campaign.title: SolarHome pre-VAT-change offer
campaign.text: 'Order your SolarHome panel installation by 31 March: from 1 April the reduced 6% VAT rate for residential solar ends and the standard 21% rate applies — a €1,240 difference on the average system. Installations booked before the deadline are invoiced at the current rate.' The VAT change is a published legislative fact with the official gazette linked in the ad. Prices, savings calculations and the deadline are accurate; no countdown widget or stock claims are used.

detected_practices: deadline-based urgency (regulatory VAT change)
quantified savings claim (€1,240 difference)
price/tax rate comparison
sourced factual claim with official gazette link
email marketing
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults/homeowners, so minors are unlikely to be a primary concern. Although no personalisation is declared, email as a channel implies collection/processing of contact data, so GDPR is included for the email list and any lead data. UCPD applies as a standard consumer campaign; the urgency and savings claims appear substantiated but warrant verification that the VAT deadline and €1,240 figure remain accurate and non-misleading.
triage.summary: A multi-channel (web, email, print) B2C campaign for SolarHome solar panel installations aimed at adult homeowners in the EU, using a legislatively-grounded deadline (end of reduced 6% VAT rate on 1 April) and a quantified €1,240 savings claim to drive bookings before 31 March. The urgency is based on a verifiable published legislative fact linked in the ad, with accurate prices and no artificial countdown or stock-scarcity devices. No generative AI or personalised targeting is declared.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Sending marketing email requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1), and email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (aligned with ePrivacy). The campaign uses email but provides no information about how the recipient list was built or on what lawful basis contacts are being emailed. This obligation is engaged and cannot be confirmed satisfied from the material.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email, print
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the email list: either prior opt-in consent, or (for existing customers) the soft opt-in for similar products with a clear opt-out at collection and in every message. Retain records demonstrating the basis for each recipient.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct marketing communication must respect and facilitate the absolute right to object/opt out (Art. 21(2)-(3)). As an email marketing campaign this obligation is engaged, but the material does not show an unsubscribe/opt-out mechanism is present.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email, print
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, one-click unsubscribe link in every marketing email and ensure objections are actioned immediately and suppressed permanently. Reference the right to object in the privacy information.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The booking/lead flow collects personal data (contact and installation details). Art. 13 requires that identity of the controller, purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients and data-subject rights be provided at the point of collection. The campaign does not indicate a privacy notice is presented at sign-up or booking.
findings.evidence_quote: Installations booked before the deadline are invoiced at the current rate.
findings.recommendation: Ensure any web booking form, lead form or email sign-up links to a layered privacy notice meeting Art. 13 (and Art. 12 clarity requirements) at the point of data collection.

verdicts.notes: The campaign content is a substantiated, factual VAT-deadline offer with no personalisation, profiling, AI, or special-category data — so its substance does not breach GDPR. However, email is a declared channel and bookings generate lead/customer data, which engages baseline GDPR obligations (lawful basis for email direct marketing, transparency at point of collection, and facilitation of the right to object). The campaign text provides no evidence these are met or unmet, so findings are flagged for verification rather than as violations. No minors, profiling or Art. 9 data are in scope.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits only *falsely* stating that a product is available on particular terms for a very limited time. The deadline here reflects a real, published legislative change (the 6% VAT rate ending on 1 April), is externally verifiable via the linked official gazette, and uses no fake countdown timer or artificial stock claim. The urgency is therefore genuine and the per-se prohibition is not engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: no countdown widget or stock claims are used
findings.recommendation: No change required. To preserve compliance, monitor the legislative status: if the VAT change is postponed or repealed, immediately withdraw or update the deadline messaging, since a deadline tied to a cancelled change would become a false 'limited time on particular terms' claim.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 requires that price-advantage claims and the manner of price calculation not deceive the average consumer. The €1,240 figure is a comparison between the current 6% and future 21% VAT rate on an 'average system', stated to be accurate. As a factual, substantiated comparison it does not constitute a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: a €1,240 difference on the average system
findings.recommendation: Keep documentary substantiation for the €1,240 figure (basis of the 'average system', rate calculation) on file, and clearly present it as a VAT-difference on an average installation rather than a discount, so no individual consumer is misled about the saving on their specific system.

verdicts.notes: This is a deadline-driven B2C solar campaign whose urgency is grounded in a genuine, published legislative fact (the end of the reduced 6% residential VAT rate on 1 April), with the official gazette linked, accurate prices and quantified savings, and no artificial countdown or stock-scarcity devices. UCPD Annex I point 7 targets *false* urgency; here the time limit is true and externally verifiable, so the blacklist is not triggered and the €1,240 price-advantage claim is not a misleading action under Art. 6, provided the figures remain accurate at publication. The only residual risk is factual: if the VAT deadline is postponed/repealed or the €1,240 figure drifts from reality, the urgency and savings claims would become misleading.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes booking SolarHome installations before 31 March to lock in the current 6% VAT rate before it rises to 21%, quoting a €1,240 difference on an average system. The advertising substance is sound: the deadline is tied to a real, published legislative change (with the official gazette linked), prices and savings are accurate, and there is no fake countdown or scarcity gimmick — so it does not create false urgency or a misleading price claim under consumer law. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged, and the content itself does not breach GDPR (no profiling, targeting, minors, or sensitive data). The main open points are all baseline data-protection housekeeping triggered because email is a declared channel and bookings collect personal data: you must confirm a valid lawful basis for the email list, include a working unsubscribe mechanism, and present a privacy notice at the point of sign-up/booking. None of these are violations on the material shown — they are items to verify and document. The one thing to watch is that the whole offer rests on the VAT change actually happening: if it is postponed or repealed, the deadline and savings messaging must be pulled immediately or it becomes misleading.
recommendations: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the marketing email list (prior opt-in consent, or the soft opt-in for existing customers of similar products) and retain records for each recipient.
Ensure every marketing email contains a clear one-click unsubscribe link, and that opt-outs are actioned immediately and suppressed permanently.
Link a layered, Art. 13-compliant privacy notice at the point of data collection on any web booking form, lead form or email sign-up.

Keep documentary substantiation on file for the €1,240 figure (definition of the 'average system' and the 6%-vs-21% rate calculation), and present it clearly as a VAT difference rather than a discount.

Monitor the legislative status of the VAT change: if the 1 April change is postponed or repealed, immediately withdraw or update the deadline and savings messaging to avoid a false 'limited time' claim.

campaign.title: VitaBoost — Dr. Silva video series
campaign.text: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand. In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.' The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted. Media plan: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics.

detected_practices: AI voice-clone of real person (Dr. Rui Silva)
AI face-swap deepfake of a real physician
Unauthorised use of identity/likeness of a public figure
False endorsement/testimonial by a doctor
Health/immunity claim ('strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe')
Missing AI-generated content disclosure
Deletion of user comments flagging content as fake
Behavioural targeting on health interests
Targeting of a potentially vulnerable age group (55+)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults 55+ interested in health topics — an older cohort that may be more susceptible to false medical endorsements, raising vulnerability considerations under the UCPD. No indication minors are targeted, though social video placement carries some spillover risk. Health-interest targeting implies processing of potentially special-category (health) inferences under GDPR.
triage.summary: VitaBoost is running unlabelled deepfake video ads using an AI voice-clone and face-swap of a real, unaffiliated TV physician who falsely endorses the supplement with an unsubstantiated immunity health claim. The campaign uses interest/health-based behavioural targeting of users 55+ and suppresses comments that identify the content as fake.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The clips are AI-generated/manipulated audio-video depicting a real, identifiable person in a way that falsely appears authentic — a deep fake within Art. 50(4). As deployer, the brand must clearly disclose that the content is artificially generated/manipulated. Not only is disclosure absent, but users who flag the content as fake have their comments deleted, actively defeating the transparency the Article requires.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva ... The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted.
findings.recommendation: Immediately cease running the unlabelled deepfake, or add a clear, prominent disclosure on every clip stating it is AI-generated/manipulated and not real footage of Dr. Silva. Stop deleting comments that identify the content as synthetic. Note that lawful use also requires authorisation of the person's likeness; without that, mere disclosure will not cure the wider illegality.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The synthetic audio/video outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated/manipulated (provider obligation under Art. 50(2)). Nothing in the campaign indicates provenance marking/watermarking is applied; the assets are presented as authentic footage.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated assets carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., C2PA/SynthID-style watermarking) as generated, and verify the generative-AI provider embeds and preserves this marking through the production pipeline.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign uses AI (voice-clone/face-swap) to deploy a deceptive technique — fabricating the appearance of a real physician making a medical endorsement — with the effect of materially distorting consumers' behaviour by impairing informed decision-making and causing purchases they would not otherwise make. Because the false claim concerns immunity/health for an older audience, it is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (foregone medical care, health-based reliance on an unproven supplement).
findings.evidence_quote: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.'
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-generated fake authority figures or fabricated medical endorsements to persuade. Any endorsement must be genuine, authorised and substantiated; remove the synthetic physician entirely rather than merely labelling it.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The AI-generated deceptive endorsement is deliberately deployed via targeting to an older cohort (55+) with health concerns — a group whose age may make it more susceptible to false medical authority. Where AI exploits age-related vulnerability to materially distort behaviour and is reasonably likely to cause significant (health/financial) harm, Art. 5(1)(b) is engaged in addition to Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Discontinue targeting of an age-defined vulnerable cohort with deceptive medical claims. If the AI-produced deepfake and false endorsement are removed, this vulnerability concern is substantially mitigated; retain genuine, non-manipulative messaging only.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses an AI voice-clone and face-swap deepfake of a real, unaffiliated physician in unlabelled video ads — a textbook breach of the AI Act's deepfake transparency duty (Art. 50(4)), compounded by active suppression of comments identifying the content as fake. The synthetic assets also lack the machine-readable provenance marking required at the provider level (Art. 50(2)). Because a manipulative deepfake medical endorsement is deployed against an older cohort (55+) targeted on health interests and is reasonably likely to cause health/financial harm, the Art. 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(b) prohibitions are also credibly engaged. Overall this is a high/critical-risk campaign under the AI Act.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Targeting an audience segmented by 'interest in health topics' involves processing personal data that reveals or infers health status, a special category under Art. 9. Processing (including inferred health attributes for ad targeting) is prohibited unless a specific exception applies, and the only realistic marketing exception is the data subject's explicit consent. Nothing in the campaign indicates explicit consent has been obtained for health-based targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not build or use audience segments derived from health interests/conditions unless explicit, freely given, specific and informed consent under Art. 9(2)(a) has been obtained. Preferably remove health-interest targeting altogether and rely on non-sensitive criteria; note that platform ad targeting on Art. 9 categories is separately banned under DSA Art. 26(3).

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting users by age and inferred health interests is automated processing evaluating personal aspects (health, interests, behaviour) and therefore constitutes profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This brings the campaign's targeting squarely within GDPR profiling obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Document the targeting as profiling, complete a data protection impact assessment given the sensitive nature and the vulnerable 55+ cohort, and ensure all downstream GDPR profiling obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) are met.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Behavioural/personalised ad targeting generally requires consent or a rigorously documented legitimate-interest balancing test. The campaign describes no lawful basis, and where the targeting relies on health data (Art. 9) legitimate interest is not available — explicit consent is required.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis before running the targeting. For any health-based or otherwise sensitive targeting, obtain explicit consent; retain the record of consent and the balancing/LIA documentation for accountability.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires that personal data be processed fairly and transparently. Using personal data to deliver deceptive, undisclosed synthetic-endorsement ads to a targeted (and vulnerable) audience, while suppressing user comments that would reveal the deception, undermines fair processing: the data subjects are being profiled and targeted to receive content that manipulates them, without transparency about the nature of the advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the advertising delivered via profiled targeting is truthful and clearly disclosed (including AI-generated/deepfake labelling), stop deleting corrective user comments, and provide clear privacy transparency information so that the targeted processing meets the lawfulness, fairness and transparency standard.

verdicts.notes: The campaign explicitly declares behavioural targeting of "users 55+ interested in health topics" on social video platforms. Targeting on inferred health interests engages GDPR Art. 9 (special-category data), and the interest-based ad targeting is profiling under Art. 4(4) requiring a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis (and, for Art. 9 data, explicit consent). The deceptive, undisclosed deepfake context and deletion of "fake" comments also cut against the Art. 5(1)(a) fairness/transparency principle. No lawful basis, consent mechanism, or transparency information is described.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The media plan targets recipients by their interest in health topics. Under DSA Art. 26(3), online platforms may not present advertisements based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories of data, which include health data — inferred health interests count. This prohibition applies regardless of consent, so building the ad audience around a health-interest segment makes the campaign undeliverable on compliant platforms as designed.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove all health-related interest/segment criteria from the targeting. Rely only on non-sensitive parameters (e.g. broad contextual placement on general-interest video content) and do not use any proxy that infers health status or conditions. Document that no Art. 9 category is used, directly or by inference, to build the audience.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: As paid placement on social video platforms, each ad must be identifiable in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner as an advertisement, with the advertiser and payer disclosed and the main targeting parameters available (Art. 26(1)). The clips are presented as authentic statements by a real physician rather than as VitaBoost advertising, defeating ad-identifiability and advertiser-identity transparency.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ads carry the platform's clear 'advertisement/sponsored' marking, that VitaBoost is disclosed as the advertiser and payer, and that the creative does not masquerade as independent physician content. Supply accurate targeting-parameter metadata to the platform's ad-disclosure tools.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Systematically deleting user comments that identify the videos as fake, combined with presenting a synthetic endorsement disguised as genuine physician content, is designed to deceive and manipulate recipients and impair their ability to make free and informed decisions — the core harm targeted by the DSA Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition (which covers disguised advertisements and manipulative interface conduct on platforms).
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Stop suppressing comments that question the authenticity of the content; do not curate the ad's comment interface to hide truthful signals. Present the material honestly as advertising so the surrounding platform experience does not manipulate recipients.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If placed on Very Large Online Platforms, the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach will be archived in a public ad repository under Art. 39. The disguised deepfake creative and health-interest targeting will therefore be exposed to public and regulator scrutiny and cannot rely on obscurity.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms
findings.recommendation: Assume full public disclosure of the creative and targeting via VLOP ad repositories, and only run creative and targeting that can withstand that scrutiny — which the current deepfake/health-targeting design cannot.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as paid advertising on social video platforms and engages several DSA obligations that bind the platforms but are directly determined by the advertiser's campaign design. Most seriously, the media plan targets users interested in health topics, which relies on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special-category (health) inferences — a targeting basis flatly prohibited for platform advertising under DSA Art. 26(3). The undisclosed, disguised deepfake ads also cut against Art. 26(1) ad-identifiability requirements, and the deletion of comments flagging the content as fake plus the disguised-ad format engage the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition. (AI-labelling per AI Act and the misleading endorsement/health claim per UCPD are covered by other agents.)

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: The campaign fabricates and disseminates a false endorsement by a real physician who has no relationship with the brand, using AI to make it appear he personally recommends the product. This is a commissioned false endorsement misrepresenting an endorsement to promote the product — blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer effect. The related deletion of comments identifying the clips as fake also constitutes suppressing/misrepresenting genuine social endorsement covered by this point.
findings.evidence_quote: voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand ... 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily'
findings.recommendation: Cease all use of Dr. Silva's likeness/voice and remove any depiction implying his endorsement. Only feature endorsements from real, consenting individuals with a genuine, disclosed relationship to the brand. Do not delete or suppress genuine user comments; restore removed comments.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: The ad, voiced by a purported doctor, claims the supplement outperforms any prescribable treatment for strengthening immunity — an unsubstantiated therapeutic/curative-style claim about treating or preventing illness. Falsely claiming a product can cure or is superior to medical treatment is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances (and also engages the Health Claims Regulation).
findings.evidence_quote: it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe
findings.recommendation: Remove all disease/cure/immunity-superiority claims. Only use health claims authorised under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006, backed by evidence, and never present a food supplement as equivalent to or better than prescribed medical treatment.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The practice contains false information deceiving the average consumer about the product's main characteristics (benefits/results) and about the endorser's qualifications and approval — a real doctor's professional authority is falsely invoked. This is likely to cause consumers, especially the targeted 55+ health-interested cohort, to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Serves as the general misleading-action backstop to the blacklisted points.
findings.evidence_quote: In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily'
findings.recommendation: Ensure all product claims and any depicted qualifications/endorsements are truthful, substantiated and genuinely held. Do not attribute statements to real professionals who did not make them.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic/AI-generated and fictional nature of the videos is material information the average consumer needs to assess the authenticity of the 'doctor's' endorsement. Failing to disclose it, and actively removing user comments that would reveal it, hides material information and conceals the true nature of the content — a misleading omission. Commercial intent/authenticity is not apparent from context because the clip is designed to look like a genuine physician.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently label the content as AI-generated/fictional at the point of viewing, and disclose the advertising/commercial nature. Do not delete comments that accurately identify content as synthetic.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign deliberately targets an older cohort interested in health — a group more susceptible to false medical endorsements. Under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that vulnerable group, and a deceptive deepfake medical endorsement is highly likely to materially distort their economic behaviour, reinforcing the unfairness of the overall practice.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not exploit the credulity or health concerns of older audiences. Remove the deceptive elements; any legitimate health-product advertising to this group must be truthful, substantiated and clearly identifiable as advertising.

verdicts.notes: The VitaBoost campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including two blacklisted (per se unfair) practices. It uses an AI deepfake of a real, unaffiliated TV physician to fabricate a medical endorsement (Annex I point 23c; Art. 6) and makes a false curative/immunity claim (Annex I point 17). It also hides the synthetic nature of the content and suppresses comments flagging it as fake (Art. 7; Annex I point 23c). The targeting of adults 55+ interested in health topics engages the Art. 5(3) vulnerable-group standard, aggravating the deception. Overall: clear violation likely, with multiple blacklisted practices present.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses an AI deepfake (voice-clone and face-swap) of Dr. Rui Silva — a real TV physician with no relationship to the brand — to fabricate a medical endorsement claiming VitaBoost "strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe." As designed, the campaign breaches four separate EU regimes at the most serious levels. It triggers per se prohibited (blacklisted) practices under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (fake endorsement and false cure claim), an outright prohibited AI practice and a deepfake transparency failure under the AI Act, a flat ban on health-interest ad targeting under the DSA, and unlawful special-category data processing under the GDPR. The deletion of comments that flag the videos as fake compounds every one of these breaches. This is not fixable with a disclosure label: the fake endorsement, the false health claim, and the health-based targeting are each independently unlawful and must be removed entirely. In its current form the campaign cannot be run lawfully in the EU and exposes the brand to enforcement, fines, and likely litigation from Dr. Silva.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign. Immediately halt any live placements and pull all creative featuring the synthetic Dr. Silva.

Completely remove the AI deepfake and the fabricated physician endorsement — do not merely add an 'AI-generated' label. The fake endorsement of a real, non-consenting doctor is a blacklisted practice (UCPD Annex I 23c) and a prohibited manipulative AI practice (AI Act Art. 5), and neither disclosure nor consent cures it. Expect a likeness/rights claim from Dr. Silva.

Remove the claim that the product 'strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.' Presenting a supplement as equal or superior to medical treatment is a blacklisted false cure claim (UCPD Annex I 17). Only use health claims authorised under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 and backed by evidence.
Stop deleting user comments that identify the content as fake, and restore removed comments. This suppression aggravates the UCPD, AI Act transparency, and DSA dark-pattern breaches.

Remove all health-interest targeting. Targeting 'users 55+ interested in health topics' relies on inferred health data — banned outright for platform ads under DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of consent, and unlawful special-category processing under GDPR Art. 9. Use only broad, non-sensitive contextual placement.
Establish and document a valid GDPR lawful basis for any remaining personalisation, provide clear privacy transparency, and complete a DPIA given the vulnerable 55+ cohort.

For any future legitimate version: use only genuine, consenting, disclosed endorsers; mark any AI-generated assets with machine-readable provenance (AI Act Art. 50(2)); ensure ads are clearly identifiable as advertising with the advertiser disclosed (DSA Art. 26(1)); and assume full public exposure via VLOP ad repositories.

The campaign explicitly provides no such disclosure, and actively deletes comments identifying the content as fake, reinforcing the deception.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva ... The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Do not publish. If any AI-manipulated video is used at all, it must carry a clear, prominent disclosure that it is artificially generated/manipulated. However, cloning a real person's likeness without any relationship cannot be cured by a label alone (see also Art. 5(1)(a) and likeness/consent issues) — remove the deepfake of Dr. Silva entirely.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: As synthetic audio/video output of a generative AI system, the assets must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated under Art. 50(2). Nothing in the campaign indicates provenance marking is applied.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap
findings.recommendation: Ensure any AI-generated campaign asset embeds machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA / watermarking) so it is detectable as artificially generated. This is in addition to, not a substitute for, the Art. 50(4) human-facing disclosure.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI system is used to deploy a purposefully deceptive technique: a fabricated, hyper-realistic medical endorsement from a trusted TV physician. It is designed to materially distort consumers' purchasing decisions by impairing their ability to make an informed choice, and is reasonably likely to cause significant harm — consumers may substitute an unproven supplement for medical care based on a fake doctor's advice. Suppression of 'this is fake' comments removes the corrective signal, deepening the deception.
findings.evidence_quote: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.'
findings.recommendation: Cease the practice. A deceptive fabricated medical endorsement engineered to distort health decisions falls within the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition and cannot be remedied; base any campaign on genuine, substantiated claims and, if endorsements are used, only with the real, consenting person.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The deceptive AI-generated content is deliberately AI-targeted at older adults interested in health — a group more susceptible to health-authority persuasion and to deepfaked doctor endorsements. This exploits age-related vulnerability to materially distort behaviour in a way reasonably likely to cause significant harm (health and financial), engaging the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove age/health-vulnerability-based targeting of this deceptive content. Do not deploy AI-generated persuasion that leverages the heightened susceptibility of older audiences to fabricated medical authority.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses AI voice-cloning and face-swapping to fabricate a video endorsement of a real, unaffiliated physician (Dr. Rui Silva) — a textbook deep fake of a real person — with no AI-generation or manipulation disclosure. This directly breaches the AI Act's deep-fake transparency obligation (Art. 50(4)) and the synthetic-content marking obligation (Art. 50(2)). Because the deepfake is purposefully deceptive, engineered to distort purchasing decisions and directed at older adults through a false medical authority, it also engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques and, given the deliberate targeting of 55+ health-interested users, the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on exploiting age-related vulnerability.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting an audience by their interest in 'health topics' processes data revealing/inferring health status, which is a special category of personal data under Art. 9. Such processing — including inferred attributes — is prohibited unless an Art. 9 exception (notably explicit consent) applies. The campaign describes no explicit-consent mechanism for health-based targeting, so the processing is likely unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove health-interest targeting criteria and use non-sensitive parameters (e.g. broad age/geography without health inference), or obtain valid, granular explicit consent for health-based profiling. Note that for platform ad delivery this targeting is separately banned under DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of consent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural audience segmentation and interest-based targeting constitute profiling — automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (interests, health) of individuals. This brings the campaign within the profiling regime (lawful basis, transparency, objection, sensitive-data rules).
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Document that the targeting is profiling, complete a data protection assessment, and ensure a valid basis and transparency for the profiling operation before deployment.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised/behavioural advertising and profiling require a valid Art. 6 lawful basis (typically consent, or a documented and balanced legitimate-interests assessment). The campaign as described identifies no lawful basis for the targeting/profiling, and legitimate interest is difficult to sustain where health-interest inference is involved.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid Art. 6 lawful basis for the profiling; where consent is required (especially due to the Art. 9 health dimension), ensure it is obtained before targeting.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The synthetic clips process Dr. Silva's personal data — his likeness, face and voice — to generate a fabricated endorsement. He has no relationship with the brand and there is no indication of consent or any other lawful basis for processing his personal data, rendering the processing unlawful under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand
findings.recommendation: Cease using Dr. Silva's cloned likeness/voice. Do not process an identifiable person's image or voice for marketing without a valid lawful basis (here, his informed consent), which is absent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Fabricating statements attributed to a real, identifiable person via AI cloning, and presenting them as authentic, breaches the principle that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Using someone's identity to make claims they never made is inherently unfair and non-transparent processing of his personal data.
findings.evidence_quote: In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated attributed statements and any AI-generated depiction of Dr. Silva; only process personal data of identifiable persons in a lawful, fair and transparent manner.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Because the campaign relies on profiling for direct marketing, targeted individuals have an absolute right to object to that processing and profiling. The campaign describes no mechanism to facilitate objection/opt-out from the marketing profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Ensure recipients can easily exercise the absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling, and honour objections by suppressing the individuals from targeting.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages GDPR on two fronts. First, ad targeting of "users 55+ interested in health topics" segments the audience by inferred health interest — a special category under Art. 9 — meaning the profiling processes sensitive data that is prohibited absent explicit consent, on top of the general lawful-basis, fairness/transparency and right-to-object obligations for behavioural marketing. Second, the AI voice-clone and face-swap process the biometric/likeness (personal data) of a real, unaffiliated individual (Dr. Rui Silva) with no lawful basis and unfairly/deceptively. These are serious, likely violations rather than merely engaged obligations.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data under GDPR Art. 9, which include health. The declared media plan targets a paid ad audience by 'interested in health topics' — a health-related interest category that constitutes (directly or by inference) profiling on a special category of data. Such targeting is banned for platform advertising irrespective of any consent, so a campaign built around health-interest targeting cannot lawfully run as described.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove all health-related interest/affinity segments from the ad targeting. Target only on permissible, non-sensitive parameters (e.g. broad age/geography or contextual placement alongside general-interest content), and confirm with the ad platform that no health-based profiling proxies are used to deliver the ads.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: As paid placements on social video platforms, these are advertisements within DSA Art. 26(1), which requires recipients to be able to identify in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, plus meaningful information on the main targeting parameters. A synthetic 'doctor endorsement' video presented as if it were genuine editorial/testimonial content — with no advertiser attribution and no ad identification — defeats the ability of recipients to recognise it as paid advertising and to see who is behind it.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Ensure every placement carries the platform's clear 'ad/sponsored' label, discloses the paying advertiser (the VitaBoost brand) and the main targeting parameters via the platform's ad-disclosure tools, and does not disguise the paid, commercial nature of the video.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing, organising or operating online interfaces in ways that deceive or manipulate recipients or materially distort their ability to make free and informed decisions. Systematically deleting comments that flag the videos as fake curates the interface to suppress corrective information, reinforcing the deception created by the deepfake and impairing informed decision-making. Note: Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms; where the brand operates or controls the comment interface (e.g. its own channels/pages) it applies directly, otherwise the conduct is relevant context feeding platform-level obligations and UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Stop deleting user comments that identify the content as AI-generated or fake; suppressing truthful corrective feedback is manipulative interface conduct. Instead, correct the underlying deception by labelling the content and removing false endorsement claims.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If placed on very large online platforms (VLOPs), Art. 39 requires the ads — including content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach — to be published in a public ad repository. The deceptive deepfake endorsement and the health-interest targeting parameters would therefore be publicly archived and open to scrutiny by regulators, journalists and the impersonated physician.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms
findings.recommendation: Assume the ad, its advertiser identity and its targeting parameters will be publicly visible; only run creative and targeting that can withstand public and regulatory scrutiny — which the current deepfake endorsement and health targeting cannot.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as paid advertising on social video platforms and engages several DSA obligations. Most seriously, the media plan targets platform ads using health-interest profiling, which is flatly prohibited under Art. 26(3) regardless of consent. The synthetic, unlabelled doctor testimonial delivered as paid placement also raises Art. 26(1) ad-transparency concerns, and the deletion of comments flagging the content as fake touches on dark-pattern/manipulation concerns (Art. 25, though that provision binds platform operators rather than the advertiser directly). VLOP ad-repository archiving (Art. 39) means the targeting and deceptive claims will be publicly scrutinisable.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: The campaign commissions/creates a fabricated endorsement attributed to a real physician who has no relationship with the brand, and additionally suppresses negative social feedback ('comments calling them fake are deleted'). Submitting false endorsements and misrepresenting/suppressing social endorsements to promote products is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23c.
findings.evidence_quote: In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated Dr. Silva endorsement entirely; never present AI-fabricated or unauthorised endorsements as genuine. Stop deleting comments that flag content as fake — do not misrepresent or curate social feedback to hide the truth.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: Presenting a well-known physician as endorsing/recommending VitaBoost when he has not done so falsely claims approval/endorsement by an authority figure, a per se prohibited practice under Annex I point 4.
findings.evidence_quote: voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand
findings.recommendation: Do not claim or imply endorsement by any physician or body without genuine, documented authorisation complying with the terms of that approval.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: The claim frames the supplement as superior to prescription medicines for strengthening immunity, implying a curative/therapeutic effect on illness. Falsely claiming a product can cure/treat illness or dysfunction is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17 (and engages the Health Claims Regulation for food supplements).
findings.evidence_quote: it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe
findings.recommendation: Remove all curative and comparative-to-medicine health claims. Only use authorised health claims permitted under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 with proper substantiation.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The synthetic clip contains false information about the product's main characteristics (benefits, results) and the endorser's qualifications/relationship, deceiving the average consumer and likely causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.'
findings.recommendation: Base all product-benefit statements on substantiated evidence and genuine, disclosed sources; do not use invented expert testimony or exaggerated efficacy claims.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The campaign omits/hides material information — that the doctor and his statements are AI-generated fabrications and that the content is a paid advertisement — which the average consumer needs to make an informed decision. Failing to reveal the synthetic nature and commercial intent is a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose that content is a paid advertisement and (if any synthetic content were ever used legitimately) that it is AI-generated; ensure commercial intent is immediately apparent.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts economic behaviour. It deliberately targets older, health-interested consumers who may be more susceptible to a trusted doctor's authority; under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of that vulnerable group, aggravating the overall unfairness of the deepfake-doctor campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not design campaigns that exploit the trust or credulity of older audiences; the safety-net prohibition reinforces that the deepfake medical-endorsement approach must be abandoned rather than merely re-targeted.

verdicts.notes: The VitaBoost campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, several of them blacklisted (per se unfair in all circumstances). It fabricates a physician endorsement via AI deepfake of an unaffiliated real doctor (false endorsement + misleading action), makes an unsubstantiated immunity/comparative-cure claim, deletes 'this is fake' comments (misrepresenting social endorsements/suppressing negative reviews), and conceals the synthetic/commercial nature of the content. The deliberate targeting of health-interested adults 55+ with a false authority figure aggravates the assessment via the vulnerable-consumer standard. This is high/critical risk and should not run as described.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses AI to fake a video of a well-known TV doctor, Dr. Rui Silva, who has no connection to your brand, making him appear to say VitaBoost strengthens immunity "better than anything I can prescribe." All four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA, UCPD) returned "violation likely" findings, several at the most serious "critical" level. This is not a campaign that can be fixed with disclaimers or better labelling — its core elements are illegal. The main problems are: a deepfake of a real person used without consent, a fabricated medical endorsement, a false cure/immunity claim, deletion of comments that expose the videos as fake, and targeting older adults by their interest in health. The deepfake and fake doctor endorsement fall under outright prohibitions (AI Act Art. 5, UCPD blacklist), and the health-interest ad targeting is banned outright for platform advertising (DSA Art. 26(3)) regardless of consent. Running this as described would expose the brand to enforcement action, and the impersonated physician to legal claims. Verdict: do not launch — the campaign must be rebuilt from scratch.
recommendations: Do not publish this campaign. The deepfake of Dr. Silva and the fabricated medical endorsement are prohibited outright and cannot be cured by labels, disclaimers or re-targeting.

Remove the AI voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva entirely. Using a real, identifiable person's likeness and voice without consent breaches the AI Act, GDPR and the UCPD false-endorsement blacklist.

Delete the immunity/cure claim ('strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe'). Only use authorised, substantiated health claims permitted for food supplements — no comparisons to prescription medicine.
Stop deleting comments that flag the videos as fake. Suppressing corrective feedback compounds the deception and raises dark-pattern and unfair-practice concerns.

Remove all health-interest ad targeting. Targeting platform ads using health-related profiling is banned under DSA Art. 26(3) even with consent; use only broad, non-sensitive parameters such as general age/geography or contextual placement.
If any legitimate future campaign uses endorsements, use only the real, consenting person, and clearly label the content as a paid advertisement so its commercial nature is immediately obvious.
If AI-generated assets are ever used legitimately, apply both a clear human-facing disclosure and machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) per AI Act Art. 50.
Have any rebuilt campaign reviewed by legal/compliance before spend, given the older-adult audience triggers heightened vulnerable-consumer scrutiny.

campaign.title: VitaBoost — Dr. Silva video series
campaign.text: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand. In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.' The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted. Media plan: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics.

detected_practices: AI voice-clone of a real person
AI face-swap/deepfake of a real person
unauthorised use of a real physician's likeness
false endorsement / fake celebrity/expert testimonial
health claim ('strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe')
unlabelled AI-generated / synthetic media
deletion of user comments flagging content as fake
behavioural targeting by age and health interests
paid placement / advertising on social video platforms
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults 55+ interested in health topics — a potentially vulnerable group (older consumers, health-anxious) who may be especially susceptible to a fabricated doctor's endorsement, heightening UCPD misleading/aggressive-practice concerns.
triage.summary: Video/social campaign for VitaBoost using an unauthorised AI voice-clone and face-swap deepfake of a real TV physician, Dr. Rui Silva, who fabricates a medical endorsement and unsubstantiated immunity health claim. The synthetic clips are not labelled as AI-generated, critical comments are deleted, and placement is behaviourally targeted to health-interested users aged 55+ across EU markets.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The clips are a deep fake within Art. 50(4): AI-generated/manipulated video and audio depicting a real identifiable person (Dr. Rui Silva) in a manner that falsely appears authentic. As deployer of the deepfake, the brand must disclose that the content is artificially generated/manipulated. Not only is disclosure absent, the brand actively deletes user comments flagging the content as fake, defeating any organic signalling of its synthetic nature.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva ... The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted.
findings.recommendation: Do not run undisclosed deepfakes of real persons. If any AI-manipulated footage is used, apply a clear, prominent, and persistent on-screen/in-audio disclosure that the content is artificially generated. Stop deleting comments that identify content as AI-generated. (Note: fabricating a real doctor's endorsement without consent raises separate likeness/UCPD issues beyond this regulation.)

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI system is used to deploy a deceptive technique — a synthetic doctor who does not exist as depicted delivering a fabricated medical endorsement — with the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of viewers by impairing their ability to make an informed purchasing decision, causing them to buy VitaBoost they otherwise would not. Because the false claim concerns immunity/health and targets health-anxious older adults, it is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (financial loss and reliance on an unsubstantiated health product over prescribed care). This meets the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques.
findings.evidence_quote: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated AI endorsement and false health claim entirely. Do not use AI-generated personas to deliver deceptive medical claims that steer consumers toward a purchase. Any health messaging must be truthful, substantiated and delivered by genuine, consenting sources.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The deceptive AI content is deliberately targeted at a group vulnerable by reason of age (adults 55+) and health interest/anxiety, who are especially susceptible to a fabricated physician's endorsement. Directing the AI-generated deception at this group to materially distort their behaviour, in a way reasonably likely to cause significant (health and financial) harm, engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting age-based vulnerabilities.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting deceptive AI content to age/health-vulnerable audiences. Even after removing the deepfake, avoid AI-driven targeting designed to exploit the susceptibility of older, health-anxious consumers to endorsement-style medical claims.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign assets are synthetic audio/video generated by a generative AI system. Art. 50(2) requires that such outputs be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated/manipulated (e.g., provenance metadata/watermarking). There is no indication such marking is applied, and the clips are described as unlabelled.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets carry machine-readable provenance marking / watermarking identifying them as artificially generated, in addition to the human-facing disclosure required under Art. 50(4).

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses an AI voice-clone and face-swap deepfake of a real, identifiable physician to fabricate an endorsement, and is behaviourally targeted at a vulnerable audience (adults 55+ interested in health). This engages the AI Act's deepfake transparency obligation (Art. 50(4)), the synthetic-content marking obligation (Art. 50(2)), and — because the deceptive AI content is used to distort purchasing decisions and exploit an age-based vulnerability with likely health-related harm — the prohibitions in Art. 5(1)(a) and Art. 5(1)(b). The failure to label the clips and active deletion of comments identifying them as fake are aggravating factors. Overall this is a likely violation of the AI Act.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting an audience by 'interested in health topics' processes data revealing/inferring health status, a special category under Art. 9(1). Processing of such data (including inferred attributes used for ad targeting) is prohibited unless a specific exception — in the marketing context, the data subject's explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a) — applies. Nothing in the campaign indicates explicit consent was obtained for health-based targeting, so the processing is presumptively unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not target on health-related interest categories unless you can demonstrate freely-given, specific, informed and explicit consent for that specific purpose. In practice, remove the 'interested in health' targeting parameter and rely on non-sensitive criteria (e.g., contextual placement on general audiences), or restrict to platform interest segments that are not health-related.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Targeting by age and inferred health interest is automated processing to evaluate/predict personal aspects (health, interests) of natural persons, i.e. profiling within Art. 4(4). This classification triggers the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations for the campaign's targeting operations.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling activity, minimise the attributes used, and ensure each downstream obligation (lawful basis, information provision, opt-out) is met before running the targeted placement.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised/behavioural advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis. For non-sensitive personalisation this is generally consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment; where health data is involved, legitimate interest is unavailable and explicit consent is required. The campaign shows no established lawful basis for the profiling-based targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Media plan: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Establish and document the lawful basis for the targeting before launch. Given the health dimension, base targeting on explicit consent captured by the platform, or reconfigure the campaign to avoid profiling that requires a basis you cannot substantiate.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is the basis for health-based profiling (Art. 9(2)(a) and Art. 6(1)(a)), the controller must be able to demonstrate valid, specific, unbundled consent that is as easy to withdraw as to give. The campaign provides no evidence such consent conditions are satisfied for the sensitive targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Verify that the platform's consent mechanism captures specific, demonstrable, withdrawable consent covering health-interest targeting; retain records evidencing consent, and provide an equally easy withdrawal path.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that data-driven targeting not be conducted in a deceptive or covert manner. Targeting health-anxious older users with content built on a fabricated identity, while suppressing information that would let recipients recognise it as synthetic, undermines the fairness and transparency of the processing that delivers the ads to those individuals.
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Ensure targeting parameters and the commercial/synthetic nature of the content are transparent to recipients, and stop deleting comments that provide accuracy context; align the processing with the fairness principle.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The targeting constitutes profiling for direct marketing, so data subjects have an absolute right to object and to have processing for that purpose cease. The campaign as described does not indicate any mechanism to facilitate this opt-out.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Ensure recipients can easily object to the marketing profiling (e.g., via platform ad-preference/opt-out controls) and that objections are honoured and suppressed from future targeting.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's declared personalisation targets "users 55+ interested in health topics", which processes an inferred health-interest attribute — a special category of personal data under GDPR Art. 9 — to profile and target individuals. This engages the profiling definition (Art. 4(4)), requires a valid lawful basis and, for Art. 9 data, explicit consent (Arts. 6-7), and triggers transparency/fairness (Art. 5(1)(a)) and right-to-object (Art. 21) obligations that the campaign as described does not demonstrably satisfy. Note that the underlying ad targeting also engages DSA Art. 26(3) (handled by another agent); GDPR concerns here relate to the lawfulness of the processing itself.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Targeting users by 'interested in health topics' relies on health data, a special category under GDPR Art. 9. DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data, whether the attribute is provided directly or inferred, and regardless of consent. Selecting a health-interest audience for these paid ads squarely engages this ban.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove all health-related interest/affinity segments from the targeting for these platform ads. Target only on non-sensitive parameters (e.g. broad age/geography) and ensure no proxy segments effectively reconstruct a health-status audience. Confirm with the platform that no Art. 9 category is used to determine ad delivery.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters. These paid placements are disguised as genuine testimony from a real physician and are not identifiable as advertising, and no advertiser identity or targeting-parameter disclosure is described, defeating the transparency obligation for platform ads.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Ensure each placement carries the platform's clear 'ad/sponsored' label with the advertiser's identity, the payer, and accessible information on the main targeting parameters. The creative must be recognisable as advertising rather than independent editorial or personal testimony.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing, organising or operating online interfaces in ways that deceive or manipulate recipients or impair their ability to make free and informed decisions. Systematically deleting user comments that identify the ads as fake manipulates the interface to suppress signals that would let consumers assess the ad's authenticity, reinforcing the deception created by the deepfake. Where the advertiser operates or controls a platform interface (e.g. its own channel/page moderation), this deceptive-design conduct engages Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Stop deleting truthful user comments that flag the content as synthetic or fake; moderation must not be used to conceal the advertising or synthetic nature of the content. Combined with proper AI-generated labelling, allow the interface to convey accurate information to recipients.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA primarily through its advertising-targeting and transparency rules. Behavioural targeting of users "interested in health topics" uses a GDPR Art. 9 special category and is flatly prohibited for platform advertising under DSA Art. 26(3). The synthetic, unlabelled ads also fail the Art. 26(1) requirement that platform ads be clearly identifiable and disclose their main targeting parameters. Deletion of comments flagging the content as fake raises a DSA Art. 25 deceptive-interface concern where the campaign relies on platform interfaces it controls.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Annex I point 23c blacklists misrepresenting endorsements to promote a product. The campaign fabricates an endorsement from a real physician who has no relationship with the brand — a false/misrepresented endorsement created via AI. This is prohibited in all circumstances, without any need to assess consumer impact.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand.
findings.recommendation: Do not use Dr. Silva's likeness, voice or any fabricated endorsement. Remove all synthetic-physician content entirely. Only use genuine, authorised endorsements from persons who actually made the statements.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 17 blacklists falsely claiming a product can cure/treat illness. Presenting VitaBoost as superior to prescription medicine for strengthening immunity is an unsubstantiated curative/therapeutic claim delivered through a fake doctor, prohibited in all circumstances for a supplement.
findings.evidence_quote: it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe
findings.recommendation: Remove any claim that the product cures, treats, prevents illness or outperforms prescription medicine. Restrict messaging to claims that are substantiated and authorised under the Health Claims Regulation (EC) 1924/2006.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits misleading actions that deceive the average consumer about a product's main characteristics or about the trader's/endorser's qualifications. The ad presents a fabricated professional (deepfaked physician) making false benefit claims, deceiving consumers about both product benefits and the existence/authenticity of expert endorsement, and is likely to cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate false product-benefit and fabricated-qualification messaging; base all claims on verifiable evidence and genuine, disclosed spokespeople.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits misleading omissions and failure to identify commercial intent. Failing to disclose that the physician's endorsement is entirely AI-fabricated conceals material information the average consumer needs; the synthetic and fictional nature of the endorsement is material to whether they trust and act on it.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Where synthetic media is lawfully used at all, clearly and prominently label content as AI-generated/fictional and as advertising, so consumers are not deceived about its authenticity or commercial nature.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 (with Art. 5(3)) treats practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group from the perspective of that group. Older, health-anxious consumers are especially susceptible to a fabricated trusted-physician endorsement; deliberately targeting them with a deceptive fake-doctor health claim breaches professional diligence and materially distorts their behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not target vulnerable audiences with health endorsements; ensure all messaging meets professional-diligence standards and is assessed for its effect on the specific 55+ health-interested group being targeted.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Deleting comments that flag the content as fake is a form of misrepresenting/suppressing social endorsements and reviews — the marketing-relevance note for Annex I point 23c expressly covers suppressing negative reviews. It manipulates the social-proof signal consumers rely on to detect deception.
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Stop selectively deleting critical comments. Do not manipulate or suppress user feedback; moderation must not distort the authenticity of social endorsements around the campaign.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including at least two blacklisted (per se unfair) practices. It fabricates a medical endorsement from a real physician via an AI deepfake, makes a false immunity/cure-type claim, hides the synthetic and commercial nature of the content, and suppresses comments exposing it — all directed at older, health-interested consumers who are a vulnerable group under Art. 5(3). Several findings are critical because Annex I blacklist practices are unfair in all circumstances regardless of consumer effect.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses an AI voice-clone and face-swap to make a real, well-known TV physician (Dr. Rui Silva) appear to personally endorse VitaBoost — even though he has no relationship with the brand — and to claim the product "strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe." Across four separate legal regimes, this is one of the most serious types of violation possible. It fabricates the endorsement of a real doctor and makes a false cure-type health claim, both of which are outright banned practices under EU consumer law regardless of any impact assessment. The videos are not labelled as AI-generated, which breaches the AI Act's deepfake transparency rules, and the underlying deception may even fall under the AI Act's prohibited manipulative-AI provisions. Targeting "users 55+ interested in health topics" uses health data that is a special category — this is flatly prohibited for platform advertising under the DSA and lacks a lawful basis under GDPR. Deleting comments that flag the videos as fake compounds the deception and raises further DSA and consumer-law issues. In short: this campaign cannot be fixed with tweaks — the core concept is unlawful and must not run.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign in any form. Immediately halt production and pull any placements already live — the fabricated-doctor endorsement and the false immunity/cure claim are both per se illegal (blacklisted) practices under EU consumer law.

Remove all use of Dr. Silva's likeness, voice and any synthetic-physician content entirely. Only use genuine, authorised endorsements from people who actually made the statements and consented to their use.

Delete the claim that VitaBoost is superior to prescription medicine or strengthens immunity. Any health messaging must be limited to claims authorised under the EU Health Claims Regulation (EC 1924/2006) and be fully substantiated.
Stop deleting user comments that flag the videos as fake — this suppression aggravates the deception and creates additional DSA (dark-pattern) and consumer-law exposure.

Remove all health-related interest/affinity targeting segments. Targeting on inferred health interest is banned for platform ads under DSA Art. 26(3) and lacks a GDPR lawful basis; use only non-sensitive parameters and avoid proxy segments that reconstruct a health audience.

If AI-generated media is used in any future campaign, label it clearly and prominently as artificially generated/fictional (AI Act Art. 50(4)), apply machine-readable provenance/watermarking (Art. 50(2)), and ensure each placement carries a clear 'ad/sponsored' label with advertiser identity and targeting-parameter disclosure (DSA Art. 26(1)).

Have legal/compliance review any replacement concept before spend — given the vulnerable 55+ health-anxious audience, professional-diligence standards under UCPD Art. 5 apply and misuse of a real person's identity also raises likeness/publicity claims from Dr. Silva.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

detected_practices: emotion inference from behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history)
AI-based emotional state detection
behavioural targeting / personalisation
exploitation of inferred vulnerability (low-mood windows)
advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle
