targeting of vulnerable emotional states with betting/gambling ads
targeting with 'retail therapy' / impulse-purchase ads
undisclosed emotion-based ad delivery (users not informed)
standard sponsored labelling only
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users across the EU; minors declared excluded from the pilot. Key concern is the deliberate targeting of users in inferred vulnerable/distressed emotional states, which is relevant regardless of age.
triage.summary: A large EU social platform (28M users) pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house AI model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, with advertisers able to enable a 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed, and internal review already notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed. Minors are excluded, but the design raises serious concerns around exploiting emotional vulnerability, emotion recognition/manipulation, behavioural profiling and transparency.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: MoodMatch is an AI system deploying purposefully manipulative techniques operating beyond users' awareness: it covertly infers emotional state from behavioural signals and times manipulable-category ads (betting, impulse 'retail therapy', comfort food) to inferred low-mood moments. Users are not informed, so the technique operates beyond their consciousness and appreciably impairs their ability to make an informed decision, causing decisions (bets, impulse purchases) they would not otherwise take. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences the intended behavioural distortion, and gambling/impulse spending targeted at distressed users is reasonably likely to cause significant financial and psychological harm — satisfying the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition threshold.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy MoodMatch as designed. Discontinue any AI-driven timing or tailoring of advertising to inferred emotional/low-mood states. If mood inference is used at all, it must not drive ad delivery for harm-prone categories (gambling, impulse purchases); remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. Any emotion-aware feature must be redesigned so it cannot exploit inferred distress and cannot materially distort purchasing decisions.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI that exploits vulnerabilities to materially distort behaviour with likely significant harm. The system deliberately identifies and targets users in inferred distressed/low-mood states — a state of heightened susceptibility — and serves gambling and impulse-purchase advertising precisely at those moments, with internal data confirming higher conversion among distressed users. While Art. 5(1)(b)'s enumerated grounds are age, disability or a specific social or economic situation and a transient emotional state is an imperfect categorical fit, the deliberate exploitation of situational vulnerability for financially harmful ad categories places this practice squarely within the concern the provision addresses and creates substantial regulatory risk.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Treat inferred emotional vulnerability as an off-limits targeting signal. Exclude betting/gambling and other financially harmful ad categories from any emotion- or mood-derived delivery logic, and document a vulnerability-exploitation risk assessment demonstrating the system cannot direct such ads to users identified as distressed.

findings.title: Prohibition of emotion recognition in workplace and education
findings.rationale: The system performs emotion inference, but Art. 5(1)(f)'s prohibition is confined to the workplace and education-institution contexts. This campaign concerns consumer ad targeting on a social platform, so the Art. 5(1)(f) prohibition is not triggered. Flagged for completeness so the marketer understands the emotion-recognition risk here arises under Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) (and separately under GDPR), not Art. 5(1)(f).
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: No action required specifically under Art. 5(1)(f). Ensure the emotion-inference component is never repurposed into workplace or education settings, where it would be outright prohibited, and address the applicable Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) findings above.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI model to infer users' momentary emotional state and covertly time betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to inferred low-mood windows. This engages the AI Act's Article 5 prohibited-practices regime. It is a strong candidate for a prohibited manipulative AI technique (Art. 5(1)(a)) and plausibly for prohibited exploitation of vulnerability (Art. 5(1)(b)); the workplace/education emotion-recognition ban (Art. 5(1)(f)) does not apply to this consumer-advertising context. Given emotion inference is central and disclosure is absent, this is high-risk and likely unlawful under Art. 5.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's momentary emotional state — especially 'inferred as distressed' / 'low-mood' — produces data concerning the person's mental health, an Art. 9 special category. Art. 9 expressly covers inferred attributes. Processing such data is prohibited unless an exception (notably explicit consent) applies. Here users are not informed and no explicit consent is obtained, so there is no valid Art. 9 exception. This is a core, prohibited processing activity affecting up to 28M EU users.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Do not process inferred emotional/mental-health states for ad delivery. If any emotion inference is contemplated, it requires freely given, specific, informed, explicit opt-in consent under Art. 9(2)(a) with a clear ability to refuse; absent that, the MoodMatch inference and 'low-mood window' targeting must be discontinued.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle prohibits covert data collection and hidden processing. Inferring emotional state and exploiting inferred 'low-mood windows' — with internal notes of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' — while users are not informed is both covert and manifestly unfair (deliberately capitalising on vulnerability), breaching Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Cease the covert emotion-based targeting. Any behavioural processing must be disclosed and must not be designed to exploit users' vulnerable states; conduct a DPIA and fairness assessment before any similar processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: All personal-data processing needs a valid Art. 6 legal basis. No consent is obtained and consent would in any event be required given the sensitivity. Legitimate interests cannot be relied upon where the processing exploits inferred emotional vulnerability to drive conversions (esp. betting/gambling), because the balancing test tips decisively toward the data subjects' interests and fundamental rights. As described, no lawful basis is satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before processing; for this exploitative emotion-targeting use case, no basis is realistically available, so the processing should not proceed. If personalisation continues in a non-exploitative form, rely on properly obtained consent and complete a legitimate-interests/balancing assessment.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data are processed, Art. 13 requires controllers to inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling. Users are given no information about the emotional-state inference or its use to time ads, so the Art. 13 information duties (and the Art. 12 requirement to communicate transparently) are not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, layered privacy information disclosing the profiling logic, the emotion-inference purpose, the legal basis, and users' rights — though note that disclosure alone does not cure the underlying Art. 9/fairness problems.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The automated analysis of behavioural signals to evaluate and predict personal aspects (emotional state, behaviour, preferences) is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This classification triggers the connected obligations (lawful basis, transparency, Art. 21 objection, Art. 22 safeguards) that are not satisfied here.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Treat MoodMatch as profiling and apply the full set of GDPR profiling obligations, or discontinue it; document the profiling in the ROPA and DPIA.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct-marketing purposes triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3), and data subjects must be explicitly informed of that right. The campaign describes no mechanism for users to object to or opt out of the mood-based profiling and ad delivery.
findings.evidence_quote: Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'.
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy opt-out from profiling-based advertising, present the right to object explicitly at the latest at first communication, and stop mood-based processing for users who object.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Ad delivery is decided solely by automated profiling. While ordinary ad selection may not always 'similarly significantly affect' a person, deliberately targeting users inferred as distressed with gambling/betting and impulse-purchase ads, with documented 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed', can cross into similarly significant effects on vulnerable individuals, engaging Art. 22 and its safeguard requirements (which are absent).
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the solely-automated targeting of vulnerable states produces significant effects; if so, Art. 22 prohibits it absent a valid exception and safeguards. Given the exploitation of distress, the safer course is to exclude emotional-vulnerability signals from automated ad-delivery decisions entirely.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot infers users' momentary emotional/mental state (distress, low mood) from behavioural signals and uses it to time ad delivery — inferred mental-health data processed covertly, without consent or transparency. This engages several GDPR provisions, most seriously the Art. 9 prohibition on processing special-category (health) data, plus failures of lawful basis, fairness/transparency and profiling safeguards. Multiple likely violations are present; the design as described cannot be made compliant merely by tweaks — the core practice (exploiting inferred distress) is fundamentally problematic under GDPR fairness principles.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The platform designs and operates its ad-delivery interface to detect users' momentary emotional state and serve exploitative ad categories (betting, impulse 'retail therapy') precisely when users are inferred to be distressed. This deliberately distorts and impairs recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, and the internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences the manipulative effect. This is squarely the manipulation of online-interface operation prohibited by Art. 25, and the covert 'receptivity boost' toggle amplifies it.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Discontinue mood-based ad delivery. Do not use inferred emotional state (or the 'receptivity boost' toggle) as a signal for ad targeting or timing. If any emotion-adjacent personalisation is retained, redesign so it cannot exploit vulnerability, is opt-in and transparent, and never times commercial pressure to inferred distress.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Ad presentation is based on profiling of an inferred emotional/mental state. Inferred distress or low mood is a plausible proxy for mental-health data, which falls within the GDPR Art. 9 special categories referenced by Art. 26(3). Presenting advertisements based on profiling using such categories — including inferred attributes — is prohibited regardless of any consent. The 'receptivity boost' feature effectively lets advertisers piggy-back on this prohibited sensitive-data profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers ... ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Remove inferred emotional/mental-state signals from all ad-targeting and delivery logic. Ensure no ad presentation relies, directly or by inference, on GDPR Art. 9 categories. Audit the model to confirm distress/mood inferences are not used as a targeting parameter or proxy.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that, for each ad, recipients can identify in real time the main parameters used to determine that the ad is shown to them and how to change those parameters. Standard sponsored labelling discloses only that the item is an ad; it hides the decisive parameter (inferred low-mood window / 'receptivity boost'). Users are explicitly 'not informed', so the meaningful-parameters and how-to-change duty is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, real-time, per-ad disclosure of the main targeting parameters (including any behavioural/receptivity signals) and give users an accessible control to change or opt out of them. If mood-based delivery cannot be disclosed and controlled lawfully, it should not be used.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If the platform is designated a Very Large Online Platform, Art. 39 requires a public ad repository including targeting parameters and reach, meaning the MoodMatch mood-based delivery parameters would have to withstand public scrutiny. The stated 28M EU users is below the 45M VLOP threshold, so designation is uncertain and this is flagged for awareness rather than as a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP status. If designated, ensure any retained targeting parameters are lawful and accurately reflected in the public ad repository; the exploitative mood-based parameters described would not withstand such transparency and should be removed.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot engages several DSA obligations seriously. A large EU social platform operates its ad-delivery interface to exploit users' inferred emotional vulnerability, which is a prohibited manipulative design under Art. 25 and is corroborated by the platform's own note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Because ad delivery is driven by profiling on an inferred mental/emotional state (a likely GDPR Art. 9 health proxy), it also implicates the Art. 26(3) ban on sensitive-data ad targeting, and the failure to inform users breaches the Art. 26(1) real-time transparency duty on main targeting parameters. VLOP-specific repository duties (Art. 39) may also apply depending on designation.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Deliberately timing and selecting persuasive advertising to reach consumers precisely when an AI model infers they are in a distressed/low-mood state amounts to undue influence that exploits misfortune and impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Timing and exploitation of a weak emotional state are express Art. 8-9 factors. The advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises the exploitation, and the internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences that the practice causes transactional decisions consumers would not otherwise take. The inclusion of betting/gambling ads aimed at distressed users sharply aggravates the likelihood of significant consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue any ad delivery, timing or selection that is triggered by, weighted toward, or optimised for inferred negative emotional states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and prohibit emotion-conditioned delivery of high-risk categories (betting/gambling, impulse 'retail therapy'). Base ad delivery on lawful, non-exploitative signals only.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Even absent a specific prohibition, the practice is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts economic behaviour, engaging the Art. 5 fairness safety-net. Users in inferred distress are a clearly identifiable vulnerable group whose behaviour is assessed under Art. 5(3); the platform's own review confirms the practice materially distorts their purchasing decisions, which is the hallmark of an unfair practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Treat inferred-distress states as a vulnerability that must be protected rather than monetised. Adopt an internal policy barring targeting/optimisation on inferred emotional vulnerability and document a professional-diligence review before any behavioural-optimisation pilot launches.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: While the ads bear standard sponsored labels, users are not informed of the material fact that ad timing and selection are deliberately conditioned on their inferred emotional state. The commercial mechanism exploiting their mood is hidden, and this material information is omitted in a manner that impairs the consumer's ability to make an informed transactional decision under Art. 7. A generic 'sponsored' label does not disclose the emotion-based delivery basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: If any lawful form of personalised delivery is retained, provide clear, timely disclosure of the basis on which ads are selected/timed and offer users a genuine opt-out. Do not rely on a generic 'sponsored' label to cover an undisclosed emotion-inference targeting mechanism.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot deliberately times and selects ads (comfort-food, betting, 'retail therapy') to reach users during AI-inferred low-mood/distressed windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and internal evidence of elevated conversion among distressed users. This is a textbook aggressive commercial practice by undue influence exploiting consumers' emotional vulnerability/misfortune (UCPD Arts. 8-9), and independently breaches the general fairness/professional-diligence standard including the vulnerable-consumer test (Art. 5). The covert nature of the emotion-based delivery mechanism also engages the misleading-omission rules on hidden commercial practices (Art. 7). Exclusion of minors does not cure these adult-facing concerns.

report.executive_summary: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI to guess when your 28M EU users are in a low mood (from scrolling speed, dwell time and reactions) and then deliberately serves them betting, comfort-food and impulse 'retail therapy' ads at exactly those vulnerable moments, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and no disclosure to users. All four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA and UCPD) reached the same conclusion: this is very likely unlawful, and your own internal note about 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is direct evidence that it works by exploiting distress. The most serious problems are the AI Act's outright ban on manipulative AI (Art. 5), the GDPR ban on processing inferred mental-health data without consent (Art. 9), the DSA ban on both manipulative interface design and ads targeted using sensitive-data profiling (Arts. 25 and 26(3)), and the UCPD prohibition on aggressive practices that exploit consumers' emotional vulnerability (Arts. 8-9). This is not something that can be fixed with a disclaimer or a consent pop-up; the core concept — monetising inferred distress — is the violation. Excluding minors does not cure any of these adult-facing concerns. The clear verdict across the board is: do not launch this pilot as designed.
report.recommendations: ["Do not deploy MoodMatch as designed. Halt the pilot — the core mechanic (timing ads to inferred low-mood/distress) is prohibited under the AI Act Art. 5 and cannot be made compliant through tweaks or disclosures.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

detected_practices: emotion inference from behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history)
mood-based / emotional-state targeting of ads
exploitation of inferred low-mood/distress windows to boost conversion
targeting of vulnerable emotional states with betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads
behavioural profiling and personalised ad delivery
advertiser-facing 'receptivity boost' toggle
lack of transparency to users about mood inference
AI-generated / AI-driven ad delivery model
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users across the EU; minors explicitly excluded. However, the practice targets users in inferred emotionally vulnerable/distressed states, which raises heightened vulnerability concerns even among adults. Emotion-inference to influence behaviour of a natural person is a flagged AI Act concern (potential prohibited/high-risk manipulation and emotion-recognition-adjacent practices); non-transparent exploitation of distress engages UCPD unfair/aggressive practice rules and DSA obligations on VLOP-scale platforms regarding profiling-based advertising and transparency; behavioural/emotional profiling engages GDPR (special-category-adjacent inferences, transparency, lawful basis, DPIA).
triage.summary: A 28M-user EU social platform pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood/distress windows to raise conversion. Users are not informed of the mood inference, and advertisers can toggle a 'receptivity boost'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The AI system deliberately exploits users' momentary emotional distress — a specific adverse situation constituting vulnerability — by timing gambling and impulse-spend advertising to inferred low-mood windows, with the objective/effect of materially distorting purchasing behaviour. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences behavioural distortion, and betting/'retail therapy' ads to distressed individuals are reasonably likely to cause significant financial and psychological harm. Excluding minors does not cure the exploitation of adult emotional vulnerability, which Art. 5(1)(b) also covers.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the use of inferred emotional/mood state as a signal for timing or selecting ad delivery, especially for gambling, food and discretionary-spend categories. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. Do not deploy any AI feature whose purpose or effect is to serve commercial content preferentially during inferred distress.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: MoodMatch is a purposefully manipulative AI technique operating beyond users' awareness of the mechanism (users are not informed of the mood inference or exploitation). It materially distorts behaviour by appreciably impairing informed decision-making — serving offers precisely when users are least able to resist — causing decisions they would not otherwise take, as shown by 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. The likelihood of significant harm arises from the betting and impulse-spend content targeted at distressed users.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history ... Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Cease covert emotion-state inference used to influence commercial behaviour. If any mood/receptivity feature is retained, it must not be designed to distort decision-making; provide clear disclosure and user control, and prohibit exploitation-oriented ad categories. Legal review should treat this as a prohibited practice, not a fixable transparency gap.

findings.title: Prohibition of emotion recognition in workplace and education
findings.rationale: The system performs emotion inference on natural persons, which is the conduct Art. 5(1)(f) targets. However, that prohibition is limited to the workplace and education contexts; this is a consumer social platform, so Art. 5(1)(f) does not directly apply. Flagged for completeness because the emotion-inference conduct is squarely caught by Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) instead, and GDPR special-category concerns arise separately.
findings.evidence_quote: infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: No action under Art. 5(1)(f) specifically, but note that the same emotion-inference conduct is prohibited here under Art. 5(1)(a)/(b); ensure any workplace/education deployments of similar tech are separately assessed against 5(1)(f).

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch is an AI system that covertly infers users' momentary emotional state and times betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to inferred low-mood/distress windows to raise conversion. This engages two AI Act Article 5 prohibitions: Art. 5(1)(a) (purposefully manipulative AI technique distorting behaviour) and Art. 5(1)(b) (AI exploiting a vulnerability — here emotional distress / adverse situation) — both requiring reasonably likely significant harm, which betting and impulse-spend targeting of distressed users supports. Emotion recognition under Art. 5(1)(f) does not directly apply (not workplace/education). The generative-AI declaration does not clearly trigger Art. 50 transparency duties for the delivery model as described.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's momentary emotional/mental state — including 'distress' and 'low-mood' — produces data about a person's mental/psychological condition that is arguably health-related and, at minimum, sits within the special-category-adjacent scope Art. 9 protects (data revealing health). Art. 9 prohibits processing such inferred data unless a specific exception (notably explicit consent) applies. Here users are not informed at all, so no explicit consent exists and no other Art. 9(2) exception is engaged. Inferred attributes are expressly covered.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring emotional/mental-state categories for ad targeting unless you obtain freely-given, specific, informed EXPLICIT consent under Art. 9(2)(a) for that precise purpose; absent such consent, disable mood inference entirely. Document a lawful basis and Art. 9 condition before any resumption, and conduct a DPIA.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle prohibits covert data collection and hidden processing. Inferring emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history and using it to exploit 'inferred low-mood windows' — while telling users nothing and disguising the mechanism behind ordinary sponsored labels — is both non-transparent and manifestly unfair, especially given the internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Make the mood-inference processing transparent to users, and stop using inferences of vulnerability to increase ad receptivity; deploying a profiling technique specifically because it exploits distress cannot satisfy the fairness limb regardless of disclosure.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data (behavioural signals) is collected and used to infer emotional state and drive ad delivery, Art. 13 requires the controller to inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis, and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling with meaningful information about the logic involved. None of this is provided for the MoodMatch inference.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy notice and layered in-product disclosures at the point of data collection to describe the mood-inference profiling, its purpose, legal basis, and the profiling logic, in clear and plain language (Art. 12).

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: This profiling and personalised ad delivery is processing of personal data that requires a valid Art. 6 legal basis. Consent is absent (users not informed). Legitimate interests cannot succeed here: the balancing test fails where the purpose is to exploit users' inferred distress to boost conversion, and users would not reasonably expect covert emotional profiling. No contractual necessity applies.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any processing. Given the exploitative purpose, legitimate interests will not pass the balancing test; only informed opt-in consent could work — and for the emotional-state element that consent must be explicit (Art. 9).

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The MoodMatch model is automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (behaviour, emotional state, preferences) of natural persons and therefore squarely meets the definition of profiling, which triggers the associated obligations under Arts. 5, 6, 9, 13, 21 and 22.
findings.evidence_quote: infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Treat MoodMatch as profiling and apply the full set of profiling safeguards (transparency, lawful basis, DPIA, objection handling).

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: MoodMatch makes a solely automated decision about which ads (including betting) to serve to each user based on inferred distress. Where such automated targeting of vulnerable states materially affects the individual — steering distressed users toward gambling and impulse spending — it can amount to a decision producing a similarly significant effect under Art. 22, which is restricted absent a valid exception and safeguards.
findings.evidence_quote: Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'.
findings.recommendation: Assess whether MoodMatch produces similarly significant effects; if so, do not rely on it without an Art. 22 exception (explicit consent), and implement safeguards including human oversight and the right to contest. Excluding gambling/high-risk verticals from any receptivity-based delivery is strongly advised.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: This is direct-marketing-related profiling. Data subjects have an absolute right to object to processing (including profiling) for direct marketing, and Art. 21(4) requires this right to be brought to their attention clearly and separately at the latest at first communication. Because users are not informed of the mood-inference profiling, they cannot exercise this right and the notification duty is unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Present a clear, separate opt-out for direct-marketing profiling at first contact and honour objections immediately by ceasing mood-based ad targeting for that user.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch infers users' momentary emotional/mental state from behavioural signals and uses those inferences to time ad delivery — covert profiling of 28M EU users with no information, no lawful basis and no explicit consent. This engages the fairness/transparency principle, the Art. 13 information duties, the Art. 6 lawful-basis requirement, and — because inferred mental/emotional distress states are arguably health-adjacent special-category data — the Art. 9 prohibition. Automated exploitation of distress windows also engages Art. 22 and the Art. 21 right to object. Excluding minors does not cure any of these adult-user violations.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The platform operates its ad-delivery interface so as to detect and exploit users' inferred low-mood/distress and time commercial pressure to those moments, materially distorting or impairing recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions. Users 'are not informed', so the manipulation is covert. Internal review confirming higher conversion among distressed users evidences that the design exploits an impaired decision-making state — squarely the manipulation Art. 25 prohibits for online platforms.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Discontinue delivery logic that keys ad exposure or 'receptivity' to inferred negative emotional/distress states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. Ensure ad delivery does not exploit or amplify vulnerability, and document that the interface does not materially distort user decision-making.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) bans presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of GDPR Art. 9 data, including by inference. Inferred emotional/mental-health state (distress) is closely tied to health data under Art. 9, and the model profiles users on that inferred attribute to decide which ads to show. Presenting betting/comfort-food/'retail therapy' ads based on that inferred sensitive state is prohibited regardless of any consent.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed
findings.recommendation: Stop using inferred emotional/mental-state signals as an ad-targeting or delivery parameter. Confirm no ad selection relies, directly or via proxy, on inferences that fall within GDPR Art. 9 categories, and audit the model's features to exclude distress/mood as a targeting input.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that, for each ad, recipients receive in real time meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that they are shown the ad, and how to change them. 'Standard sponsored labels' identify that content is an ad but conceal the decisive targeting parameter here — the inferred emotional/mood state — so the transparency obligation on main parameters is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the main parameters that determine ad delivery (including any behaviour-derived receptivity/mood signals) in the per-ad transparency information, and provide a way for users to change or opt out of those parameters — or cease using undisclosed mood parameters entirely.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: The MoodMatch delivery model is a recommender system determining the order/selection of content presented to users. Art. 27 requires the main parameters of such systems, and options to modify them, to be set out in plain language. The mood-inference parameters are not disclosed to users, so the recommender-transparency obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers ... ads
findings.recommendation: Set out in plain language in the platform terms/settings the main parameters used by the delivery model (including behavioural mood-inference signals) and give users an option to influence or disable them.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 39 requires very large online platforms (>=45M average monthly EU active recipients) to maintain a public ad repository including targeting parameters and reach. The declared 28M EU users is below the VLOP threshold, so this obligation likely does not currently apply, but it would engage if the platform is designated a VLOP or exceeds the threshold; the covert mood-targeting parameters would then have to be publicly disclosed in the repository.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Monitor whether the platform meets/approaches the 45M VLOP threshold; if so, prepare an ad repository disclosing targeting parameters — noting that mood-based targeting would have to withstand public scrutiny and should be removed before designation.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch uses an in-house model to infer users' momentary emotional/low-mood state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred distress windows to raise conversion, without informing users. Under the DSA this most seriously engages Art. 25 (manipulative interface design impairing free/informed decisions) and Art. 26(3) (ban on presenting ads based on profiling using special-category/GDPR Art. 9 data, since inferred emotional/mental-health state is a proxy for a sensitive attribute). It also fails the Art. 26(1) requirement to disclose the main targeting parameters and, as a feed/delivery recommender, engages Art. 27 transparency. The platform's declared 28M EU users is below the 45M VLOP threshold, so the Art. 39 ad-repository obligation likely does not apply.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The system uses undue influence and exploits consumers' misfortune/emotional vulnerability by timing ad delivery to inferred distress in order to drive purchases. Timing and exploitation of the consumer's situation are express factors under Arts. 8-9. The internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' confirms the practice significantly impairs freedom of choice and causes transactional decisions users would not otherwise take. Serving betting ads to users inferred to be distressed is particularly harmful.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue any ad-delivery logic that keys targeting to inferred negative emotional states. Do not offer advertisers a 'receptivity boost' toggle tied to mood windows. If emotional/behavioural signals are used at all, they must never be used to intensify exposure during vulnerability, and high-risk verticals (betting, impulse purchases) must be excluded from any such optimisation.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of consumers. Under Art. 5(3), users in an inferred distressed/low-mood state form a clearly identifiable group whose vulnerability is being exploited; the practice must be assessed from the perspective of that vulnerable group, for whom the distortion is manifest. This acts as a fairness safety-net alongside the Arts. 8-9 finding.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Adopt a professional-diligence standard that prohibits exploiting inferred vulnerability; document a fairness assessment and remove distress-based optimisation entirely rather than merely excluding minors.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The fact that ad delivery is driven by inferred mood/distress is material information the average consumer needs to understand the nature and commercial intent of what they are seeing. A standard 'sponsored' label discloses that content is an advertisement but hides the material fact that its timing and selection are optimised to exploit the user's emotional state, constituting a misleading omission / concealment of the true nature of the commercial practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, timely disclosure that emotional-state inference influences ad delivery, and give users a meaningful ability to understand and refuse mood-based ad optimisation; do not rely on a generic 'sponsored' label to satisfy transparency about the targeting mechanism.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot is highly problematic under the UCPD. Its core mechanic — inferring users' momentary distress and preferentially delivering betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during those low-mood windows to raise conversion — is an aggressive commercial practice by undue influence and exploitation of consumers' emotional vulnerability (Arts. 8-9), reinforced by the general unfairness/vulnerable-group prohibition (Art. 5, incl. 5(3)). The concealment of the mood-inference mechanism from users also engages the misleading-omission/hidden-commercial-intent rule (Art. 7), since a standard 'sponsored' label does not reveal that delivery is optimised to exploit the user's emotional state. Excluding minors does not cure these issues, because the targeted adults are themselves rendered vulnerable by their inferred distressed state.

report.executive_summary: The 'MoodMatch' pilot uses an in-house AI model to secretly infer when your 28M EU users are feeling low or distressed (from scrolling speed, dwell time and reaction history) and then deliberately pushes gambling, comfort-food and impulse-spend ads at those exact moments to boost conversions. Your own internal review confirms this works — conversions rise among users the system flags as distressed — which is precisely the evidence that makes this legally indefensible. Four separate legal regimes all point the same way: this is a prohibited practice, not a fixable transparency gap. Under the EU AI Act it engages two outright bans (Art. 5 prohibitions on manipulative AI and AI that exploits vulnerability). Under the UCPD it is an aggressive commercial practice that exploits emotional vulnerability. Under the DSA it is a banned dark pattern and prohibited ad targeting on inferred sensitive (health-adjacent) data. Under the GDPR you are covertly profiling people's mental/emotional state with no notice, no lawful basis and no explicit consent. Excluding minors does not cure any of this — the harm is to the distressed adults being targeted. The clear verdict is: do not launch, and stop the pilot.
recommendations: Halt the MoodMatch pilot immediately. Do not use inferred emotional, mood or distress state as a signal to time, select or intensify any ad delivery — this is a prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) and (b), not something that disclosure or consent can rescue.
Remove the advertiser-facing 'receptivity boost' toggle entirely.

Permanently exclude high-risk ad verticals (betting/gambling, impulse and 'retail therapy' spend, comfort-food) from any behaviour-based delivery optimisation, and audit the model's input features to eliminate mood/distress and any proxies for it.

Stop the covert mental/emotional-state profiling: without freely-given, specific, informed EXPLICIT consent under GDPR Art. 9, and a documented Art. 6 lawful basis, disable mood inference completely. Note legitimate interests will fail the balancing test given the exploitative purpose.

Conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and treat MoodMatch as profiling with full safeguards (transparency, objection handling, human oversight) before any related feature is ever reconsidered.

Fix transparency and user-control obligations: provide clear Art. 13/Art. 12 notice at data collection, disclose the main ad-delivery parameters per-ad (DSA Art. 26(1)) and in recommender settings (DSA Art. 27), and offer a clear, separate direct-marketing opt-out at first contact (GDPR Art. 21).
Do not rely on the standard 'sponsored' label — it conceals the material fact that ad timing is optimised to exploit emotional state (UCPD Art. 7).

Have Legal/DPO document a fairness and professional-diligence assessment confirming the delivery interface does not distort user decision-making, and monitor the 45M VLOP threshold — mood-based targeting would have to withstand public ad-repository scrutiny and must be gone well before any VLOP designation.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

detected_practices: emotional state inference from behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history)
behavioural/psychological targeting
mood-based ad delivery during inferred low-mood windows
exploitation of inferred emotional vulnerability/distress
targeting of vulnerable emotional states with betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads
advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle
lack of user transparency about mood inference
generative AI in ad delivery/creation
measured 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users in the EU; minors declared excluded, but exclusion robustness should be verified given age-assurance limits on social platforms. The core concern is that adults inferred as 'distressed' constitute a situationally vulnerable audience being deliberately targeted.
triage.summary: A 28M-user EU social platform pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle. Users are not informed, and internal review notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed. Minors are declared excluded from the pilot.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The AI system deliberately exploits a vulnerability arising from a 'specific social or economic situation' — momentary emotional distress inferred by the model. It targets users precisely when inferred as distressed/low-mood and steers them toward betting, impulse ('retail therapy') and comfort-food spending. This has the objective and effect of materially distorting behaviour, and is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (financial harm, gambling harm, worsened wellbeing). The internal review noting 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences both the distortion effect and the exploitation of the low-mood state. This is a prohibited practice, not merely regulated.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy MoodMatch as designed. Cease inferring emotional/mood states to time or select advertising, and in particular never route betting or other high-harm categories based on inferred distress. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. If any mood signal is retained for non-exploitative purposes (e.g. wellbeing support), obtain a legal prohibition-review and hard-exclude high-harm ad categories.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The system deploys a purposefully manipulative AI technique operating beyond users' awareness: mood is inferred covertly, users are not informed, and ad timing is engineered to exploit a low-mood window to appreciably impair the user's ability to make an informed purchasing/betting decision. Combined with the measured conversion uplift among distressed users, this meets the Art. 5(1)(a) test of materially distorting behaviour causing a decision the user would not otherwise take, in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate covert mood-triggered targeting. Any AI-driven ad optimisation must not exploit undisclosed inferred psychological states; provide genuine transparency and user control, and ensure the technique cannot be characterised as covert behavioural distortion. Standard 'sponsored' labels are insufficient to cure this — the manipulative mechanism itself must be removed.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares generative AI use. If generative AI produces synthetic ad creatives (image/video/audio/text) served through MoodMatch, the provider must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The description does not confirm synthetic creatives (AI appears used for inference/delivery), so this obligation is only contingently engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Clarify whether generative AI produces any served ad assets. If so, ensure all AI-generated creatives carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) so they are detectable as artificially generated.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch is a strong candidate for a PROHIBITED AI practice under the AI Act. Its core function — using an in-house AI model to infer users' momentary emotional distress from behavioural signals and preferentially serving betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, without informing users — squarely engages Art. 5(1)(b) (exploitation of situational vulnerability) and Art. 5(1)(a) (covert manipulative technique). The platform's own finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is direct evidence of behavioural distortion and reasonably likely significant harm, especially given gambling ads. Art. 5(1)(f) does not apply (no workplace/education context); Art. 50 transparency obligations may apply if generative AI produces the ad creatives, but this is not clearly established.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's emotional/mental state — in particular flagging users as 'distressed' — produces data that reveals mental health. Under Art. 9, data concerning health includes inferred psychological/mental-health states, and the provision expressly covers inferred attributes. Such processing is prohibited unless a specific exception applies (typically explicit consent). None is present here: users are not even informed, so there is no explicit consent and no other Art. 9 exception. This is prohibited processing of special-category data.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history ... elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring and acting on emotional/mental-health states unless valid Art. 9(2) explicit, granular, freely-given consent is obtained specifically for emotional-state inference and mood-based ad delivery, or discontinue the mood-inference feature entirely. Explicit consent bundled into general terms will not suffice.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The mood-inference and mood-based ad delivery is processing of personal data that requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Given the intrusive, potentially manipulative nature of emotion inference targeting people at low-mood moments, legitimate interests would almost certainly fail the balancing test, and no consent has been obtained. The processing therefore lacks a lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Conduct a documented lawful-basis assessment and DPIA. For processing this intrusive, obtain valid consent (and explicit consent for the Art. 9 dimension); do not rely on legitimate interests to target users at inferred vulnerable moments.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Covertly inferring emotional state and deliberately serving betting/'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows is both non-transparent (users have no knowledge of the mood inference) and unfair (it exploits inferred vulnerability to increase conversion). This breaches the fairness and transparency principle at its core.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Disclose the emotional-state inference and its use in ad delivery clearly, and stop designing delivery to exploit low-mood/distress windows, which is inherently unfair processing even if disclosed.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data (behavioural signals, inferred mood) is collected and used, the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis, and the existence of profiling/automated decision-making. Users are given only standard sponsored labels and are not told their emotional state is inferred and used to time ads, so the Art. 13 information obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Provide layered, specific transparency information covering the emotion-inference purpose, the behavioural signals used, the legal basis, and the profiling logic before any such processing occurs.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The automated evaluation of users' emotional state and behaviour to tailor ad delivery is 'profiling' within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This definition anchors the applicability of the profiling-related obligations (Arts. 5, 6, 9, 13, 21, 22) to the campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Treat MoodMatch explicitly as profiling and apply the full set of profiling safeguards, notices and rights accordingly.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: MoodMatch is a solely automated profiling process that determines which users are served (or effectively steered toward) betting and 'retail therapy' ads based on inferred distress. Where such automated decisions similarly significantly affect individuals — plausible for vulnerability-based targeting of gambling to distressed users — Art. 22 restrictions and safeguards apply, and none are described.
findings.evidence_quote: Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the automated mood-based delivery produces significant effects on individuals; if so, ensure an Art. 22 legal basis (explicit consent) plus safeguards including human oversight, information, and the right to contest, or remove the automated targeting of vulnerable states.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Mood-based ad delivery is profiling for direct-marketing purposes, so users have an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2). Because users are unaware the processing exists, they cannot meaningfully exercise this right, and no opt-out mechanism is described.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easily accessible mechanism to object to profiling-based direct marketing (including mood inference), presented at the latest at first communication, and honour objections immediately.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch infers users' momentary emotional/mental state from behavioural signals and uses that inference to target them — squarely engaging GDPR. The inference of emotional distress/mood is very likely health-related special-category data (Art. 9) processed without any exception; there is no lawful basis, no transparency, and the profiling operates covertly. Several core GDPR obligations are engaged and, on the facts described, not satisfied.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits operating an online interface in a way that manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions. Deliberately timing betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to inferred low-mood/distressed windows to boost 'receptivity' is a design that exploits inferred emotional vulnerability to distort purchasing decisions. The internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences that the distortion is effective and intended.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue mood-inference-based ad timing entirely. Do not deliver advertising conditioned on inferred emotional/low-mood states; remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. Any personalisation must not exploit vulnerability and must preserve users' free and informed decision-making.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) bans presenting advertisements based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories. Inferred emotional distress / mental-health state is a health-related special category, and the ban applies whether the attribute is direct or inferred (per the c-sensitive-data-targeting concept). Serving ads based on inferred distress therefore falls within the prohibition regardless of any consent.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Cease any ad targeting or delivery decision that is based on inferred emotional or mental-health state. Exclude emotional-state inference from all advertising selection logic; sensitive-attribute-based ad targeting cannot be cured by consent under Art. 26(3).

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients receive, in real time, meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that they are shown the ad and how to change them. A key parameter here is the inferred low-mood window, yet users are not informed of it and only see a generic sponsored label. The main targeting parameter is concealed, so the transparency obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the actual main targeting parameters per ad and provide controls to change them. Since the true parameter (inferred mood) is itself unlawful under Arts. 25/26(3), remove it rather than disclose it; any lawful remaining parameters must be surfaced meaningfully and in real time.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: The platform uses a recommender/delivery system whose main parameters include behavioural signals and inferred mood. Art. 27 requires plain-language disclosure of the main parameters of recommender systems and options for users to influence them. The described system provides no such disclosure or user control over mood-based ranking.
findings.evidence_quote: infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers ... ads
findings.recommendation: Set out in plain language the main parameters governing ad/content ranking and give users options to modify or influence them; remove emotional-state inference from those parameters and reflect the change in the terms.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: At 28M EU users the platform is at/above the 45M VLOP threshold territory and, if designated a VLOP, Art. 39 requires a public ad repository capturing ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. Mood-based targeting parameters would have to be published and would not withstand public scrutiny, reinforcing the unlawfulness of the practice.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP designation status; if designated, ensure the ad repository accurately records targeting parameters and reach. Given repository transparency, do not deploy targeting parameters (inferred mood) that are themselves prohibited.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch runs on a 28M-EU-user social platform (VLOP-scale) and engages several DSA provisions. Most seriously, it manipulates users' decision-making by exploiting inferred emotional distress (Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition) and targets ads based on an inferred mental-health/emotional state that is a GDPR Art. 9 special category, which is flatly banned for platform advertising under Art. 26(3). The scheme also fails Art. 26(1) targeting-parameter transparency (users are not informed) and triggers Art. 27 recommender transparency and Art. 39 ad-repository obligations at VLOP scale.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive any practice that, through undue influence, significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise take; the guidance expressly lists 'exploitation of misfortune' and timing as aggravating factors. MoodMatch is engineered to identify each user's moment of emotional weakness (low mood inferred from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history) and to time the delivery of high-impulse categories (betting, comfort food, retail therapy) precisely to that window. This is a paradigmatic exploitation of the consumer's diminished capacity for rational choice through undue influence rather than persuasion on the merits.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the practice of timing or boosting ad delivery based on inferred negative emotional states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and the low-mood-window delivery logic entirely; ad delivery must not be conditioned on inferred distress. If mood/context signals are used at all, they must not be applied to exploit vulnerability for high-impulse categories such as gambling.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The materiality element of Arts. 8-9 (that the practice causes a transactional decision the consumer would not otherwise have taken) is directly evidenced by the platform's own internal finding of elevated conversion among distressed users. This is documentary proof that the mood-timed delivery materially distorts economic behaviour by exploiting the inferred emotional state, precisely the harm the aggressive-practices prohibition targets. The internal awareness also undermines any professional-diligence defence.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Treat the conversion-uplift-from-distress metric as evidence of consumer harm, not a success metric; cease optimising ad delivery toward it. Delete or repurpose the targeting so that conversion is not driven by inferred distress, and document the corrective decision for accountability.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The general prohibition (Art. 5) is the fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair where it is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts (or is likely to distort) consumers' economic behaviour, and Art. 5(3) requires assessment from the perspective of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group. Users inferred as being in a low-mood/distressed state are a situationally vulnerable group whose economic behaviour is predictably more easily distorted. Systematically detecting and monetising that vulnerability falls below the standard of professional diligence and independently engages Art. 5 even beyond the specific Arts. 8-9 analysis.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Adopt a fairness-by-design policy prohibiting targeting or delivery optimisation that relies on inferred emotional/mental states. Ensure any personalisation model cannot be steered toward exploiting situational vulnerability, and subject the model to an unfairness/vulnerability impact review before any rollout.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: While the 'sponsored' label discloses that the content is advertising (satisfying the basic hidden-commercial-intent concern), Art. 7 also captures the omission of material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision. Consumers are not told that the ads they see, and their timing, are selected on the basis of an inference about their momentary emotional/distressed state. This material fact about how and why the commercial practice reaches them is hidden, which is capable of affecting whether they engage with the ad. The standard sponsored label does not cure the omission of the mood-based selection mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: If any emotion- or mood-derived signal continues to influence ad selection (not recommended), provide clear, timely disclosure of that fact and a meaningful user control to opt out. Preferably, eliminate the mood-inference targeting so the omission issue does not arise.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot deliberately detects users' momentary emotional low points and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during those windows, with a measured effect of "elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed." Under the UCPD this is best characterised as an aggressive practice by undue influence (Arts. 8-9): exploiting a consumer's inferred emotional distress to impair their transactional decision-making and drive purchases they would not otherwise make, evidenced by the conversion uplift itself. It is compounded as an unfair practice under the general prohibition (Art. 5), including the vulnerable-consumer lens, since inferred-distressed users are a clearly identifiable situationally vulnerable group. The ads' standard sponsored labels disclose commercial intent, but the exploitative targeting mechanism engages the fairness rules regardless of labelling.

report.executive_summary: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI to infer when your users are emotionally low or distressed (from their scrolling speed, dwell time and reactions) and then deliberately serves them betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads at exactly those vulnerable moments — without telling them. All four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA and unfair commercial practices) independently conclude this is very likely unlawful, and several of the breaches are of the most serious "prohibited" kind, not fixable through tweaks or disclosures. In plain terms: this is not a targeting feature that needs adjusting, it is a practice that European law bans outright. The AI Act treats it as a prohibited AI practice (exploiting vulnerability and covert manipulation); GDPR treats inferred emotional/mental-health state as prohibited special-category data processed with no consent, notice or lawful basis; the DSA bans both dark-pattern manipulation and ad targeting based on such sensitive inferred data; and consumer law treats it as an aggressive practice exploiting misfortune. Your own internal note of "elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed" is direct evidence of consumer harm and intent, and would be highly damaging if regulators ever saw it. Excluding minors and using standard "sponsored" labels does not cure any of this. Do not launch this pilot as designed.
report.recommendations: Do not deploy MoodMatch. The core mechanism — inferring emotional/low-mood states and timing ads to those windows — is prohibited under the AI Act, DSA and consumer law, and cannot be fixed by consent or labelling. Halt the pilot immediately.

campaign.title: VoltRush energy drink stream sponsorships
campaign.text: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code. Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting; no profiling of minors is requested. Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
campaign.target_audience: declared 18+ gaming audience with substantial minor spillover

detected_practices: streaming sponsorship / influencer marketing
streamer shout-outs (potentially undisclosed advertising)
discount code promotion
animated brand overlays
interest-based ad targeting ('gaming interest, 18+')
audience analytics received by brand
