creatives (fast cuts, meme formats, teen-popular streamer) appealing to young audiences
triage.audience_notes: Declared 18+ gaming audience but with substantial and known minor spillover: brand-received analytics estimate 34% of viewers are 13-17, and a chosen streamer is popular with young teens. Targeting relies on platform declared-age data with no profiling of minors requested, but the known minor exposure heightens DSA (advertising to minors, no profiling-based ads to minors) and UCPD (vulnerable audience, aggressive/misleading practices, omission of high-caffeine warning) exposure. GDPR is engaged via interest-based targeting and receipt of audience analytics. No generative AI declared, so AI Act not flagged.
triage.summary: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams with branded overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, using interest-based '18+' age targeting in the EU. Despite an 18+ declared audience, brand-received analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and creatives (meme formats, a teen-popular streamer) plus omission of the high-caffeine warning from overlays raise minor-protection and fair-advertising concerns. Personalisation/targeting is used and audience data is received by the brand.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Interest-based ad targeting is profiling and constitutes processing of personal data that requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Personalised/behavioural advertising generally requires consent or a documented and balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign describes neither, so the processing has no demonstrated lawful basis as presented.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for the interest-based targeting: obtain valid consent via the platform's consent mechanism or complete and record a legitimate-interest assessment; ensure the chosen basis is reflected in the platform ad-buy configuration and privacy documentation.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting an audience by 'gaming interest' to serve tailored ads is automated processing to evaluate personal preferences/interests, meeting the definition of profiling. This characterisation is what pulls the practice into the Art. 6 lawful-basis and Art. 5 fairness obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Treat the interest-based audience build as profiling in your records of processing and DPIA screening, and ensure downstream GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights) are addressed accordingly.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that processing not be misleading or exploit data subjects. The brand has actual knowledge that a large share of the profiled/targeted audience are minors yet continues interest-based targeting relying only on platform-declared age. Processing personal data of an audience the controller knows is substantially composed of children, without addressing their heightened protection, is unfair and undermines the transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Act on the known 34% minor exposure: suppress or exclude the profiled targeting for the segments where minors are known to be reached, reassess the fairness of continuing interest-based ads on channels with known heavy minor viewership, and document the mitigation steps taken once the analytics revealed the spillover.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Where consent is the lawful basis for information-society-service processing reaching children, Art. 8 requires the child to be at or above the applicable age threshold (16, or 13-15 where a Member State has lowered it) and otherwise parental consent with reasonable verification. The brand knows minors under the relevant thresholds are within the audience being profiled/targeted, yet relies solely on platform declared-age data and takes no verification or child-specific measures, so any consent-based processing of these minors' data is not validly grounded.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Where consent underpins the targeting, implement age-assurance appropriate to the known minor exposure and exclude under-threshold minors from profiling; if adequate age verification/parental consent cannot be assured, do not process the personal data of the 13-17 cohort for targeted advertising.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The brand receives and processes audience analytics (personal data) derived from campaign delivery. Art. 13 requires that, when personal data is collected, data subjects be informed of the controller's identity, the purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention and their rights, including information about profiling. Nothing in the campaign indicates such information is provided to the audience whose data feeds the analytics and targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Ensure a transparent, accessible privacy notice covers the brand's role as recipient of audience analytics and as advertiser using interest-based targeting, specifying purposes, legal basis, profiling, retention and data-subject rights; coordinate with the platform on layered notices at the point of data collection.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Processing personal data for direct marketing, including related profiling, triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). The campaign as described does not indicate that an opt-out/objection route for the targeting is surfaced to the audience.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm and surface an easy opt-out from interest-based advertising (e.g. via platform ad-settings and privacy notice), and honour objections by ceasing targeting for those data subjects.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages GDPR through interest-based ad targeting (profiling under Art. 4(4)) and receipt of audience analytics by the brand, both of which are processing of personal data requiring a valid lawful basis, fair/transparent handling and proper information. The most serious GDPR risk arises from the brand's actual knowledge that ~34% of viewers are 13-17: relying only on the platform's declared-age targeting while profiling an audience known to include a large minor cohort undermines the lawful basis, fairness and the special protections children's data attracts. No consent flow, legitimate-interest assessment or privacy information is described, so key obligations appear unsatisfied as presented.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors, and requires age-appropriate protection where a service reaches minors. The campaign uses interest-based ('gaming interest') profiling for its ad placement, and the brand possesses analytics confirming ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, reinforced by deliberate selection of a streamer 'popular with young teens.' This constitutes awareness with reasonable certainty of large-scale minor exposure to profiling-based advertising, squarely engaging the prohibition and the high-level minor-protection duty — the '18+' declared target and 'no profiling of minors requested' label do not cure known actual minor reach.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Cease reliance on interest/behavioural profiling for placements with known substantial minor spillover; switch to contextual (non-profiled) placement, exclude creators with predominantly under-18 audiences, and set an actual-audience minor-share threshold (e.g. pause/redirect spend when under-18 viewership exceeds a defined low limit). Document that no profiling-based ads are served to identifiable minors.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Advertisements presented on online platforms must be identifiable in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time as advertising, on whose behalf they are presented and who paid, plus meaningful information on the main targeting parameters. Native streamer shout-outs and animated brand overlays blur editorial and commercial content; without a clear, real-time ad/sponsorship label and advertiser identification the transparency requirement is not met as described.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure every sponsored segment, overlay and shout-out is clearly and persistently labelled as advertising/sponsored, identifies VoltRush as the advertiser/payer, and that the platform surfaces the main targeting parameters and how to change them. Provide streamers with mandatory on-stream disclosure requirements.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs advertising on an online platform (streaming sponsorship with branded overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code) and uses interest-based targeting, engaging DSA advertising rules. The most serious DSA exposure is Art. 28: the brand relies on profiling-based ('gaming interest') targeting while receiving analytics showing ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17 and deliberately using a streamer popular with young teens — establishing awareness with reasonable certainty of substantial minor reach, which the profiling-ad-to-minors ban targets. Art. 26(1) transparency obligations for the sponsored/advertising nature and targeting parameters are also engaged. Art. 26(3) (special-category targeting) is not engaged on the facts, as targeting is interest/age-based only.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: The brand pays/incentivises streamers to promote the product via shout-outs and a discount code, but the campaign describes no clear disclosure that this content is paid/sponsored. Paid promotion presented within a streamer's ordinary editorial-style content without clear identification as advertising is an advertorial prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 11.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Require every participating streamer to give a clear, prominent and persistent ad disclosure (e.g. verbal 'this stream is sponsored by VoltRush' plus an on-screen 'Ad'/'Sponsored' label and platform paid-partnership tag) at the time of each shout-out and while the discount code is shown.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The high-caffeine warning is material safety-relevant information that a consumer needs to make an informed decision, especially given the promotional overlays are the point of exposure. Omitting it from the advertising creatives (while it exists only on-pack, seen only after purchase) is a misleading omission and provision of material information in an untimely manner under Art. 7. The same provision also captures the failure to make the commercial intent of the streamer shout-outs apparent.
findings.evidence_quote: The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
findings.recommendation: Include the high-caffeine warning (e.g. 'High caffeine content. Not recommended for children or pregnant/breastfeeding women') legibly within the animated overlays and any linked landing page, and ensure the paid nature of streamer content is clearly identified in-context.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The brand knows a substantial share of the actual audience is 13-17 and has chosen a streamer popular with young teens plus meme/fast-cut creatives that appeal to minors. Under Art. 5(3) the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of this clearly identifiable vulnerable group. Marketing a high-caffeine product to an audience it knows is largely minors, without the caffeine warning, risks materially distorting the economic behaviour of that vulnerable group and being contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Reduce known minor exposure (avoid streamers whose audience skews under-18, add stronger age gating), and design creatives and disclosures to the standard of the young-teen audience actually reached, including the caffeine warning. Document diligence steps taken once the 34% minor analytics were known.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Because the campaign reaches many minors through a teen-popular streamer, it is at material risk of the blacklisted practice of directly exhorting children to buy the product (or to get adults to buy it) if streamer scripts, the 'power your grind' overlays or the discount-code call-to-action are phrased as direct purchase urging. No verbatim exhortation is present in the submitted text, so this is flagged as a controllable risk rather than a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: a streamer popular with young teens
findings.recommendation: Prohibit in streamer briefs and creative copy any direct purchase exhortation aimed at the audience (e.g. 'buy it now', 'get yours', 'ask your parents'), and review scripts/overlays against Annex I point 28 before go-live given the known minor reach.

verdicts.notes: The VoltRush streaming campaign engages several UCPD provisions. The strongest issues are the apparent lack of ad disclosure on paid streamer shout-outs (advertorial/hidden commercial intent) and the omission of the high-caffeine warning from the advertising overlays (misleading omission of material safety information). The known ~34% minor viewership and use of a teen-popular streamer with meme/fast-cut creatives bring the campaign within the UCPD vulnerable-group standard (Art. 5(3)); no verbatim direct exhortation to children is present, so the Annex I point 28 blacklist is a risk to monitor rather than a confirmed breach.

report.executive_summary: This campaign sponsors live gaming streams for the VoltRush energy drink using branded overlays, paid streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with interest-based ad targeting nominally set to an 18+ gaming audience. The core problem is that your own audience analytics show roughly 34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and you deliberately chose a streamer popular with young teens — so the "18+" label does not reflect reality. This known minor exposure drives your most serious risks: the DSA bans profiling-based advertising to audiences you know with reasonable certainty include minors, and it undermines your lawful basis and fairness obligations for the data-driven targeting under GDPR. Separately, the paid streamer promotion appears to lack clear sponsorship disclosure (an outright prohibited practice under EU consumer law), and the high-caffeine warning appears only on-pack, not in the ad creatives that actually reach viewers — a misleading omission of material safety information. Marketing a high-caffeine product with meme-style creatives to an audience you know is largely minors also engages the consumer-protection "vulnerable audience" standard. The AI Act is not engaged. Overall this campaign carries high compliance risk and should not go live in its current form until the minor-targeting, disclosure and warning issues are fixed.
recommendations: Stop using interest/behavioural profiling on placements with known minor spillover. Switch to contextual (non-profiled) placement and set an actual-audience threshold that pauses spend when under-18 viewership exceeds a low limit (DSA Art. 28 — highest priority).</br>
Drop or replace streamers whose audiences skew under-18 (including the teen-popular streamer selected), since your own analytics establish 'reasonable certainty' of substantial minor reach.

Require every participating streamer to give a clear, prominent, persistent sponsorship disclosure — verbal 'this stream is sponsored by VoltRush' plus an on-screen 'Ad/Sponsored' label and the platform's paid-partnership tag — whenever the brand or discount code appears (UCPD Annex I point 11; DSA Art. 26).

Add the high-caffeine warning legibly into the animated overlays and any landing page (e.g. 'High caffeine content. Not recommended for children or pregnant/breastfeeding women'), not just on-pack (UCPD Art. 7).

Establish and document a valid lawful basis for the interest-based targeting: obtain valid consent or complete a legitimate-interest assessment, and reflect it in the ad-buy configuration and privacy documentation (GDPR Art. 6).

Where consent underpins targeting, implement age assurance and exclude under-threshold minors from profiling; if adequate age verification cannot be assured, do not process 13-17 data for targeted advertising (GDPR Art. 8).

Publish a transparent privacy notice covering the brand's role as recipient of audience analytics and advertiser, including purposes, legal basis, profiling, retention, objection rights, and surface an easy opt-out from interest-based ads (GDPR Arts. 13 & 21).

Review all streamer scripts and creative copy before go-live to remove any direct purchase exhortation aimed at the audience (e.g. 'buy it now', 'ask your parents'), given the known minor reach (UCPD Annex I point 28).
Formally document the diligence and mitigation steps taken once the 34% minor analytics became known — this evidence is relevant across DSA, GDPR and UCPD assessments.

The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.

High-caffeine product raises heightened concerns for minor exposure; DSA obligations re: targeting minors and profiling, and UCPD unfair/aggressive practices toward children, are engaged. Personalisation/targeting and audience analytics are in use.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Interest-based ad targeting ('gaming interest') and the behavioural audience analytics the brand receives constitute automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal preferences, interests and behaviour — i.e. profiling within Art. 4(4). This brings the campaign squarely within the GDPR profiling regime, triggering lawful-basis, transparency and (for minors) heightened obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting
findings.recommendation: Document that interest-based targeting and audience analytics are profiling, map the personal data flows (brand as controller/joint controller of received analytics), and complete a data protection impact assessment given the involvement of children and the scale of processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling-based advertising requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — typically consent or a properly documented legitimate-interest assessment. The submission declares personalisation/targeting and receipt of audience analytics but identifies no lawful basis, consent mechanism or LIA. For interest-based targeting via a platform, consent (via the platform) is generally required and cannot simply be presumed.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the targeting and analytics processing; obtain contractual assurance from the platform that valid consent (or another Art. 6 basis) is in place for behavioural targeting, and carry out and retain a legitimate-interests balancing test if relied upon.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The brand's own analytics confirm that roughly a third of the audience whose data is being processed for targeting/analytics are children (13-17). Where consent is the basis for processing children's data in information society services, Art. 8 requires the child to be at or above the applicable digital-consent age (13-16 depending on Member State) and, below it, parental consent with reasonable verification efforts. Relying solely on the platform's self-declared '18+' filter is inadequate given the controller knows, from its own data, that substantial numbers of under-16s are in scope — so processing of those children's data lacks a valid consent basis and required age assurance.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on a bare 'declared-age' platform filter that the brand's own data shows is failing. Implement proportionate age-assurance measures, exclude/suppress under-18 (and at minimum sub-digital-consent-age) audiences from profiling and analytics, and either obtain appropriate (parental) consent or cease processing minors' data for these purposes.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) is undermined where a controller processes personal data — including that of a large, known cohort of children — through targeting and analytics while asserting that minors are not profiled, despite its own analytics showing 34% are 13-17. Processing that the controller knows in practice sweeps in children's data, without corresponding transparency or safeguards, is not fair or transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: no profiling of minors is requested
findings.recommendation: Align actual processing with declared processing: acknowledge the known minor reach, provide clear and age-appropriate transparency about the targeting and analytics, and put in place measures so that the '18+' declaration reflects reality rather than a formal disclaimer contradicted by the brand's own data.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses interest-based ad targeting and receives audience analytics, both of which involve processing personal data and constitute profiling under GDPR. The most serious GDPR concern is that the brand's own analytics confirm ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, yet the campaign relies solely on the platform's "declared-age" filter — an approach that is demonstrably ineffective and means minors' personal data is being processed for behavioural targeting/analytics without an adequate lawful basis, age assurance, or child-appropriate safeguards. Lawful basis for the profiling, transparency, and children's-data protections (Art. 8) are engaged and appear unsatisfied as described. Note that DSA Art. 28 (profiling ads to minors) and UCPD are handled by other agents.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires a high level of protection for minors and prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign uses interest-based targeting ('gaming interest') and behavioural/audience analytics, and the brand's OWN analytics quantify that ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17. That constitutes actual awareness with reasonable certainty that a substantial minor audience is being reached with profiled/behaviourally-targeted advertising, which the 'declared 18+' targeting label does not cure. The heightened concern is amplified because the product is high-caffeine and the creatives (fast cuts, memes, a streamer popular with young teens) are demonstrably appealing to that under-18 segment.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17.
findings.recommendation: Stop relying on platform declared-age targeting alone. Because the brand's analytics establish substantial confirmed minor reach, disable profiling/behaviourally-targeted delivery for this placement and switch to contextual (non-profiled) buying, or exclude channels/streamers whose measured audience skews to 13-17. Introduce age-assurance/allowlisting of streamers with verified adult audiences, cap or drop placements where measured minor share exceeds a low threshold, and document these mitigation measures as 'appropriate measures' for minor protection.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that each advertisement on an online platform be identifiable in a clear, concise, unambiguous and real-time manner as an ad, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, plus meaningful information about the main targeting parameters. Sponsored animated overlays and paid streamer shout-outs are platform advertising whose commercial nature can blend into organic stream content; the submission does not indicate clear, real-time ad labelling or advertiser/payer identification, and since personalisation/targeting is in use the main targeting parameters must also be surfaced.
findings.evidence_quote: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure every sponsored overlay and streamer shout-out carries a clear, real-time advertising label (e.g. persistent 'Ad / Paid partnership with VoltRush' disclosure) identifying VoltRush as advertiser and payer, and confirm the platform surfaces the main targeting parameters and how to change them for these placements.

verdicts.notes: The campaign combines interest-based/behavioural ad targeting and audience analytics with a streaming environment where the brand's own data confirms ~34% of viewers are 13-17. This directly engages DSA Art. 28 (protection of minors / ban on profiling-based ads where minors are reached with reasonable certainty) — the brand cannot rely on 'declared-age, 18+' targeting when its own analytics establish substantial, quantified minor exposure. The sponsored overlays and streamer shout-outs also engage DSA Art. 26(1) advertising-transparency/labelling and targeting-parameter disclosure obligations. Art. 26(3) and Art. 39 are noted but not clearly triggered on the facts.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: UCPD Art. 5(3) requires practices likely to distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (here, minors, by reason of age and credulity) to be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. The brand's own audience analytics establish actual knowledge that roughly a third of the reached audience are 13-17, and the creative choices (fast-cut meme formats, a streamer popular with young teens) are calibrated to appeal to that group. Marketing a high-caffeine energy drink to a foreseeably and knowingly reached minor audience, while relying only on nominal 'declared-age' targeting despite contrary evidence, is contrary to professional diligence and likely to distort minors' economic behaviour. Continuing unchanged after seeing the analytics undermines any due-diligence defence.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens.
findings.recommendation: Do not treat platform 'declared-age' targeting as sufficient once analytics show material minor spillover. Introduce robust age-assurance/audience-verification, exclude channels/streamers with predominantly under-18 audiences, remove creative devices that disproportionately appeal to minors, and document a professional-diligence review responding to the 34% finding. If minor reach cannot be adequately controlled, do not run high-caffeine product ads on those placements.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 prohibits in all circumstances a direct exhortation to children to buy, or to persuade adults to buy for them. The campaign combines a teen-popular streamer, incentivising discount code and shout-outs directed at an audience the brand knows is substantially composed of 13-17 year-olds. The submitted text does not quote an explicit 'buy now' / 'ask your parents' exhortation, so this is not (yet) a clear-cut blacklist breach, but streamer shout-outs pushing a discount code to a known-minor audience sit very close to a direct exhortation and must be controlled to avoid crossing the line.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Prohibit and script-review any streamer copy that directly urges the audience to buy or redeem the code (e.g. 'grab yours now', 'go get it'), especially given the confirmed teen audience. Provide creators with mandatory do-not-say guidance and monitor live shout-outs; avoid discount-code calls to action on teen-heavy channels entirely.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Under Art. 7 a practice is a misleading omission where it omits, hides or provides untimely material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision. For a high-caffeine product, the caffeine/consumption warning is material safety information; presenting the promotional overlays without it means the information is not provided at the point and time of the marketing communication (only later, on pack after purchase). Given the audience skews younger, the omission at the decision-influencing stage is significant.
findings.evidence_quote: The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
findings.recommendation: Include the high-caffeine advisory prominently and legibly within the animated overlays and any streamer promotional segments, not solely on pack, so the material safety information reaches consumers at the point the commercial message is delivered.

verdicts.notes: The VoltRush stream sponsorship engages the UCPD chiefly through minor-protection and misleading-omission lenses. While no verbatim "direct exhortation to children" appears (so Annex I point 28 is a live risk rather than a clear breach), the brand's own analytics confirm ~34% of viewers are 13-17, the creatives are engineered to appeal to young teens, and the high-caffeine warning is dropped from the overlays. The strongest UCPD exposure is Art. 5(3) (practice distorting the behaviour of a foreseeably reached vulnerable group) and Art. 7 (omission of material safety information in the actual marketing communication).

report.executive_summary: This campaign sponsors live gaming streams for the VoltRush high-caffeine energy drink using animated overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with interest-based targeting nominally set to "18+". The core problem is that your own audience analytics show roughly 34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and the creative choices (fast-cut memes, a streamer popular with young teens) are clearly appealing to that group. Because you now have documented, actual knowledge of substantial minor reach, relying on the platform's "declared-age" filter alone is not defensible under three separate regimes. Under the DSA (Art. 28) this looks like profiling-based advertising served to recipients known with reasonable certainty to include minors — a prohibited practice. Under GDPR you lack a valid lawful basis, age assurance and child-appropriate safeguards for processing minors' data (Arts. 6, 8, 5(1)(a)), and your "no profiling of minors" declaration contradicts your own data. Under the UCPD, marketing a high-caffeine product to a knowingly-reached minor audience risks distorting a vulnerable group's behaviour (Art. 5(3)), sits close to a banned direct exhortation via the discount code (Annex I pt 28), and the missing on-screen caffeine warning is a misleading omission (Art. 7). The AI Act is not engaged. The overall verdict is high risk: the campaign should not run in its current form until minor exposure is controlled and disclosures fixed.
recommendations: Stop relying on the platform's 'declared-age 18+' filter alone — your own analytics prove it is failing. Switch these placements to contextual (non-profiled) buying and/or exclude streamers whose measured audience skews 13-17, capping placements where measured minor share exceeds a low threshold. (DSA Art. 28, GDPR Art. 8)

Disable profiling/behavioural targeting and audience analytics for any audience known to include minors, and implement proportionate age-assurance / streamer allowlisting with verified adult audiences. (DSA Art. 28, GDPR Arts. 6 & 8)

Add the high-caffeine advisory prominently and legibly inside the animated overlays and streamer promo segments — not just on pack — so the safety information reaches viewers at the point of the marketing message. (UCPD Art. 7)

Script-review and monitor all streamer shout-outs: prohibit any direct 'buy now / grab yours' call to action and avoid discount-code prompts entirely on teen-heavy channels to stay clear of the ban on direct exhortation to children. (UCPD Annex I pt 28, Art. 5(3))

Ensure every sponsored overlay and shout-out carries a clear, real-time 'Ad / Paid partnership with VoltRush' label identifying advertiser and payer, and confirm the platform surfaces the main targeting parameters. (DSA Art. 26(1))

Align your paperwork with reality: document that interest-based targeting and analytics are profiling, complete a DPIA covering children and scale, establish and record the lawful basis (consent or LIA), and update transparency notices to acknowledge actual minor reach. (GDPR Arts. 4(4), 5(1)(a), 6)
If minor reach on a given placement cannot be adequately controlled, do not run high-caffeine product ads on that placement at all.

campaign.title: VoltRush energy drink stream sponsorships
campaign.text: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code. Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting; no profiling of minors is requested. Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
campaign.target_audience: declared 18+ gaming audience with substantial minor spillover

detected_practices: streaming sponsorship with animated brand overlays
streamer shout-outs / influencer endorsement
discount code promotion
interest-based ad targeting ('gaming interest, 18+')
declared-age targeting via platform
use of streamer popular with young teens
meme-format and fast-cut creatives appealing to youth
high-caffeine warning present on pack but omitted from overlays
audience analytics showing substantial minor viewership (34% aged 13-17)
triage.audience_notes: Declared 18+ gaming audience but the brand's own analytics reveal ~34% of viewers are 13-17, i.e. substantial and known minor spillover. Streamer is popular with young teens and creatives use meme/fast-cut formats appealing to minors. GDPR is engaged by personalised interest/age targeting and processing of audience analytics; DSA is engaged by online advertising/targeting on a platform and heightened minor-protection duties; UCPD is engaged by potential omission of the caffeine warning in overlays and marketing that reaches vulnerable minors. AI Act excluded as no generative or AI-driven system is declared or apparent.
triage.summary: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams using animated overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with interest/age-based ad targeting in the EU. Although declared as 18+, analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17 and creatives use youth-appealing formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The high-caffeine warning appears on pack but not in the overlay creatives, and personalised targeting plus minor spillover raise data-protection and consumer-protection concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Interest-based ad targeting and audience segmentation by interest and age constitute automated processing of personal data to analyse/predict personal preferences and interests — i.e. profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This characterisation is the trigger for the downstream GDPR obligations below.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+'
findings.recommendation: Document the targeting/segmentation as profiling in the campaign's records of processing and confirm which party (brand or platform) acts as controller/joint controller for the interest-based targeting.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised/interest-based advertising and profiling require a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1) — generally consent or a documented, balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The submission declares personalisation/targeting but identifies no legal basis, LIA, or consent mechanism, so lawfulness of the profiling is not demonstrated.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the lawful basis for the interest/age targeting (obtain valid ePrivacy/GDPR consent for behavioural targeting where required, or complete a legitimate-interest assessment). Obtain joint-controller/DPA arrangements with the platform clarifying responsibility for the targeting data.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The brand holds analytics demonstrating it is aware that a substantial share of the audience reached by its interest-based targeting are minors, yet it continues to rely on nominal 'declared-age, 18+' targeting. Processing personal data for profiling/targeting while knowingly reaching children, without adjusting the operation, is difficult to reconcile with the lawfulness and fairness principle in Art. 5(1)(a), especially given children's heightened protection under GDPR.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Act on the analytics: stop treating the '18+' declared-age label as sufficient once the brand knows ~34% of actual reach is 13-17. Apply exclusion/frequency controls, adjust placement away from streamers with predominantly teen audiences, and document a fairness/DPIA-style assessment of the minor spillover before continuing.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Although the brand states it does not request profiling of minors, its analytics show minors are in fact reached by the interest-based targeting. Where consent is relied on for processing/targeting in connection with an information society service reaching children under the applicable age threshold (13-16), parental consent and reasonable verification are required; declared-age labelling alone does not satisfy this given the known minor spillover.
findings.evidence_quote: no profiling of minors is requested
findings.recommendation: Where consent underpins any targeting/tracking, implement genuine age-assurance rather than a self-declared '18+' flag, and ensure no consent-based profiling of users known or reasonably likely to be minors occurs without the Art. 8 parental-consent safeguards.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct-marketing/advertising purposes triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). The submission does not describe any mechanism enabling recipients to object to or opt out of the interest-based targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure recipients have a clear, accessible means to object to the profiling-based advertising (e.g. via the platform's ad-preferences/opt-out controls), and honour objections by suppressing further targeted delivery.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses interest- and age-based ad targeting ("gaming interest, 18+") and the brand receives audience analytics on viewer age composition — both engaging GDPR through profiling and the associated lawful-basis, fairness and transparency obligations. No user-facing data-collection form (lead gen, sign-up) is described, so transparency at point of collection (Art. 13) is only latently engaged. The most acute GDPR risk arises because the brand's own analytics show it knows ~34% of viewers are 13-17, undermining reliance on "declared-age" targeting and exposing the interest-based profiling to children's-data protections (Art. 8) and the fairness principle (Art. 5(1)(a)). Findings are risk-based rather than confirmed violations because the exact processing operations and legal basis are not fully specified in the submission.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28 requires platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of minor privacy/safety and prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The targeting here is interest/age-based (a form of profiling under GDPR Art. 4(4)), and the brand's own analytics establish it is aware with reasonable certainty that ~34% of the reached audience are 13-17. Continuing to run profiled sponsorship advertising into an audience known to be substantially minors — reinforced by a streamer popular with young teens and youth-appealing meme/fast-cut creatives — runs contrary to the Art. 28 minor-protection duty and the profiling-ad-to-minors ban.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on 'declared 18+' when your own analytics contradict it. Suspend profiling/interest-based delivery on placements with known high minor viewership, switch the sponsorship to contextual (non-profiled) placement, and require the platform to apply effective age assurance. Document that no profiling-based ads are served to identifiable minors, and reassess creative choices (streamer selection, meme/fast-cut formats) that heighten minor appeal.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, plus meaningful information on the main targeting parameters. Native influencer shout-outs and animated brand overlays embedded in live streams risk not being clearly identifiable as paid advertising, and the description gives no indication of an ad/sponsorship label or advertiser/payer disclosure or targeting-parameter information being surfaced to viewers.
findings.evidence_quote: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure every sponsored overlay and streamer shout-out is clearly and unambiguously labelled as advertising/sponsored in real time, identifies VoltRush as the advertiser and payer, and (for platform-served ad units) exposes the main targeting parameters and how to change them, per the platform's Art. 26 disclosure mechanisms.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs interest/age-based (profiling) advertising on a streaming platform, and the brand's own analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17 — i.e. it has reasonable certainty that a substantial minor audience is exposed to the profiled ads, engaging the DSA Art. 28 minor-protection duty and profiling-ad ban. The influencer overlay/shout-out format also engages Art. 26(1) advertising-identifiability obligations. Whether Art. 28 is a hard breach depends on platform-level classification and who "presents" the ad, but the advertiser's knowledge of the minor spillover creates clear DSA risk that must be addressed. Art. 26(3) (sensitive-data targeting) and Art. 39/27 do not appear engaged on the facts.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: For a high-caffeine energy drink, the caffeine warning is material safety/consumption information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision. Displaying it on pack but omitting it from the overlay creatives — which are the actual advertising touchpoint driving the discount-code purchase — is a misleading omission / untimely provision of material information under Art. 7. The concern is amplified because the creatives use fast cuts and meme formats and reach a large, known share of minors for whom caffeine risk is greater.
findings.evidence_quote: The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
findings.recommendation: Include the high-caffeine warning (e.g. 'High caffeine content. Not recommended for children...') clearly and legibly within the overlay creatives and any streamer read-outs, at a size/duration consumers can actually perceive, rather than relying only on the on-pack label.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (by reason of age or credulity) to be assessed from that group's perspective. The brand's own analytics show ~34% of viewers are 13-17, the chosen streamer is popular with young teens, and creatives use meme/fast-cut formats appealing to minors. Marketing a high-caffeine product to a known, substantial minor audience while omitting the caffeine warning is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to distort the economic behaviour of those minors, engaging the general unfairness prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Given known ~34% minor spillover, apply professional-diligence safeguards: suppress or re-cut youth-appealing creative elements, avoid streamers with a predominantly under-18 following, ensure caffeine warnings are prominent, and consider excluding this placement or adding age-gating rather than relying on nominal '18+' targeting that the brand knows is not achieved in practice.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: The shout-outs are paid/sponsored promotional content delivered through a creator's stream (editorial-style media). If the paid commercial nature is not made clear to viewers, this is an undisclosed advertorial, prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 11 (and a misleading omission of commercial intent under Art. 7). The submission describes the sponsorship but provides no evidence that the shout-outs are labelled as advertising/paid partnership.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure every streamer shout-out and the discount-code promotion is clearly and prominently disclosed as paid/sponsored content (e.g. verbal 'this is a paid sponsorship by VoltRush' plus persistent on-screen 'Ad/Sponsored' label), so the commercial intent is unmistakable to the audience, including younger viewers.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 bans direct exhortations to children to buy or to nag adults to buy. The current creatives ('power your grind', a discount code) and youth-appealing formats reach many minors, but the text discloses no verbatim direct 'buy now' exhortation aimed at children, so a blacklist breach is not established on the evidence. It is flagged as a watch-point because the combination of a minor-heavy audience, a teen-popular streamer and a purchase discount code creates a clear risk that any 'grab the code / buy now' phrasing would cross into a prohibited direct exhortation.
findings.evidence_quote: 'VoltRush — power your grind'
findings.recommendation: Audit the full creative and streamer scripts to confirm no direct call-to-purchase (e.g. 'grab yours now', 'get your code') is phrased as an exhortation to the child audience; keep any purchase prompts oriented to the verified-adult segment and avoid pester-power framing.

verdicts.notes: The VoltRush stream-sponsorship campaign engages the UCPD on several fronts. The most concrete issue is the omission of the high-caffeine warning from the overlay creatives (Art. 7 misleading omission), which is heightened because the brand's own analytics show ~34% of the actual audience are 13-17-year-olds — a clearly identifiable vulnerable group under Art. 5(3). The paid streamer shout-outs also require clear commercial-intent/sponsorship disclosure (Art. 7 / Annex I point 11), which the submission does not evidence. There is no verbatim direct exhortation to children, so Annex I point 28 is flagged only as a watch-point rather than a breach.

report.executive_summary: This campaign sponsors live gaming streams for the high-caffeine VoltRush energy drink using branded overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with interest/age-based ("gaming interest, 18+") ad targeting. The core problem is that your own audience analytics show roughly 34% of actual viewers are 13-17, so the "18+ declared-age" targeting does not reflect who you are actually reaching — and you know it. That single fact drives risk across three regulations at once. Under the DSA, serving profiling-based ads to an audience you know with reasonable certainty contains many minors runs against the minor-protection duty and the profiling-ad ban (Art. 28). Under the UCPD, marketing a high-caffeine product to this known minor-heavy audience while leaving the caffeine warning off the overlay creatives is a likely misleading omission and unfair practice, made worse by youth-appealing meme formats and a teen-popular streamer. Under GDPR, the interest/age targeting is "profiling," and knowingly reaching children undermines the fairness principle and needs a proper legal basis, real age assurance and an objection mechanism — none of which are evidenced. Separately, the paid streamer shout-outs must be clearly disclosed as advertising to avoid undisclosed-advertorial and ad-transparency breaches. The AI Act is not engaged. Overall verdict: high risk — the campaign should not run in its current form.
recommendations: Stop treating '18+ declared-age' as sufficient — your analytics show ~34% of viewers are 13-17. Switch to contextual (non-profiled) placement or suspend profiling-based delivery on any placement with known high minor viewership until effective age assurance is in place (addresses DSA Art. 28, GDPR Art. 5(1)(a)/Art. 8).
Move away from streamers with a predominantly under-18 following and re-cut or remove youth-appealing meme/fast-cut creative elements that heighten minor appeal (DSA Art. 28, UCPD Art. 5).

Add the high-caffeine warning ('High caffeine content. Not recommended for children...') clearly and legibly within the overlay creatives and streamer read-outs — do not rely on the on-pack label alone (UCPD Art. 7).

Clearly and persistently label every streamer shout-out, overlay and discount-code promotion as paid/sponsored advertising, identifying VoltRush as advertiser and payer, in real time (UCPD Annex I pt 11 / Art. 7; DSA Art. 26).

Establish and document a lawful basis for the interest/age targeting (valid ePrivacy/GDPR consent or a legitimate-interest assessment) and put joint-controller/DPA arrangements in place with the platform (GDPR Art. 6, Art. 4(4)).
Provide an accessible way for viewers to object to / opt out of profiling-based advertising and honour those objections (GDPR Art. 21).

Audit the full creative and streamer scripts to ensure no direct 'buy now / grab your code' exhortation is aimed at the child audience; keep purchase prompts oriented to verified adults (UCPD Annex I pt 28).
Document a fairness/DPIA-style assessment of the minor spillover before continuing, recording the mitigation controls applied.

campaign.title: VoltZ energy drink — teen engagement loop
campaign.text: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform. A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience. The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.

detected_practices: engagement quiz collecting personal data
custom audience creation from quiz completions
behavioural profiling ('gamer', 'late-night scroller')
behavioural targeting of minors
always-on retargeting loop
late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00)
energy drink marketing to teens
profiling based on watch behaviour
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is teens 13-17, i.e. minors. DSA Art. 28 prohibits targeted advertising to minors based on profiling; late-night scheduling and always-on retargeting raise aggressive-practice and vulnerable-audience concerns under UCPD, and energy-drink marketing to minors is itself sensitive.
triage.summary: VoltZ energy drink campaign on a short-video platform uses a branded quiz to collect minors' personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests), builds custom audiences, and behaviourally targets and retargets 13-17 year olds profiled as 'gamers' and 'late-night scrollers' with ads scheduled 22:00-01:00. Although generative AI is not declared, the ad system relies on algorithmic behavioural profiling and audience matching that likely implicates AI-based systems. The campaign engages sensitive concerns around targeting minors, profiling, and potentially unfair/aggressive commercial practices.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The platform's ad system is an AI system that uses algorithmic behavioural profiling to single out minors (13-17) — a group vulnerable due to age — and serves energy-drink advertising to them at late-night hours (22:00-01:00) reinforced by an always-on retargeting loop. This exploits age-related vulnerability with the objective or effect of materially distorting the minors' behaviour (driving repeated late-night consumption of a caffeinated energy drink) in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm (sleep disruption, excessive caffeine intake by children). This falls squarely within the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-based behavioural profiling to target the 13-17 age group at all. Disable age-based custom audiences for minors, remove the late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling that compounds the vulnerability, and switch to non-profiling contextual advertising that does not exploit age. Given energy-drink marketing to minors is inherently sensitive, exclude under-18 audiences entirely.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The quiz harvests 'mood' and other data to feed emotion-based, personalised targeting, and the always-on retargeting loop that re-serves ads on the basis of a 2-second watch signal operates as covert AI-driven nudging designed to distort behaviour. Combined with profiling users as 'late-night scroller', this constitutes purposefully manipulative AI technique that appreciably impairs the minor's ability to make an informed, autonomous decision and is reasonably likely to cause significant harm, engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience... An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Remove mood/emotional-state collection from the quiz and do not use inferred emotional or engagement signals to time or intensify ad delivery. Eliminate the always-on retargeting loop for this audience, and ensure any advertising to reachable users is transparent, non-manipulative and does not rely on covert behavioural nudging.

verdicts.notes: Although the submitter declared no generative AI, the campaign relies on the platform's algorithmic ad system for behavioural profiling and audience matching, which is an AI system within scope. The campaign engages the AI Act's prohibited-practices tier (Art. 5): it uses AI-driven profiling to target and retarget minors (13-17) with energy-drink ads scheduled late at night, exploiting age-related vulnerability (Art. 5(1)(b)) and deploying manipulative/emotion-based nudging via mood collection and an always-on retargeting loop (Art. 5(1)(a)). Transparency obligations (Art. 50) are not engaged — no chatbots, synthetic content or deepfakes are present.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The quiz is an information society service offered directly to children and collects their personal data. For under-16s (the default GDPR threshold, which Member States may lower to 13), consent is only valid with parental/guardian authorisation and reasonable verification efforts. The campaign targets the whole 13-17 band with no described parental consent or age-verification mechanism, so processing of the younger cohort's data likely lacks a valid legal basis.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests ... users aged 13-17
findings.recommendation: Determine the applicable digital-consent age per Member State; for users below that age obtain and verify parental consent before the quiz collects data, or exclude under-16s from data collection entirely. Implement robust, documented age-verification and parental-consent workflows.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A gamified quiz that quietly feeds completions into an advertising custom audience does not present a clear, specific, affirmative choice to be profiled for marketing, and minors are less able to give informed consent. Bundling data collection into quiz participation fails the freely-given/specific standard.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Separate the entertainment quiz from any marketing/profiling purpose; obtain a distinct, clearly-worded affirmative opt-in for advertising use of the data, using language a child can understand, with no reliance on quiz completion as implied consent.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: The controller must demonstrate consent, keep consent requests clearly distinguishable, and make withdrawal as easy as giving it. Deriving custom-audience membership from quiz completion, with no described consent record or withdrawal mechanism, does not meet Art. 7 conditions.
findings.evidence_quote: completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Maintain auditable consent records, present the consent request separately from the quiz, and provide an equally easy way for users to withdraw consent and be removed from the custom audience and retargeting loop.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Behavioural profiling and targeted advertising require a valid lawful basis. For minors, legitimate interest is very difficult to justify and consent (validly obtained, with parental consent where required) is effectively the only viable basis. No valid basis for profiling and retargeting minors is described.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Document a lawful basis for the profiling/targeting; given the audience are minors, rely only on valid (parental-backed) consent and cease profiling-based targeting of minors where such consent is absent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Segmenting individuals by inferred behavioural categories from watch behaviour and quiz responses is automated processing to evaluate personal preferences, interests and behaviour — i.e. profiling within Art. 4(4). This triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) which are not addressed in the campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Treat the segmentation as profiling and ensure the full profiling compliance stack (Art. 6 basis, Art. 13 transparency about profiling, Art. 21 objection) is in place — and avoid profiling minors for advertising.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting 'mood' and using it to time/tailor marketing risks processing inferred emotional/health-adjacent data. If mood is used to target teens (e.g. when low-energy or during late-night scrolling), this can engage the Art. 9 special-category regime, which prohibits processing absent explicit consent or another exception — a high bar with minors.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Do not collect or use mood/emotional-state data for targeting. If any emotional inference is retained, remove it from the targeting pipeline; only process special-category data with explicit consent and a valid Art. 9 exception, which is not appropriate for minors here.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection the controller must disclose identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and the existence of profiling. The quiz gives no indication these disclosures are provided, and the data is used for profiling and custom-audience building that must be disclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, child-friendly privacy notice at the quiz entry point covering all Art. 13 elements, expressly disclosing the profiling and advertising custom-audience use of the collected data.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information addressed to a child must be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear, plain language adapted to children. A gamified quiz aimed at 13-17 year-olds must present privacy information in age-appropriate form; nothing indicates this is done.
findings.evidence_quote: 'What's your energy type?' quiz
findings.recommendation: Adapt all privacy information and consent wording to a child audience — plain language, layered/visual formats — so 13-17 year-olds can genuinely understand what data is collected and why.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including profiling for it. An 'always-on' retargeting loop keyed to minimal engagement (2 seconds watched) provides no described opt-out, so the right to object is not facilitated as required.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy-to-use opt-out from retargeting/direct marketing in every ad and touchpoint, and immediately stop profiling/retargeting any user who objects; suppress objecting users from the always-on loop.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign collects personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) directly from minors aged 13-17 via a branded quiz and uses it to build custom audiences and behaviourally profile/retarget teens. This engages multiple GDPR obligations that are unlikely to be satisfied as described: child-consent rules (Art. 8), valid consent conditions (Arts. 4(11), 7), lawful basis for profiling (Art. 6(1)), the profiling regime (Art. 4(4)), transparency (Arts. 12-13) and the right to object (Art. 21). Collection of "mood" data to target minors also risks engaging Art. 9. No parental-consent, age-verification, transparency or opt-out mechanisms are described.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28 flatly prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients they are aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Here the declared target audience is explicitly teens 13-17 (minors), and the ads are served on the basis of behavioural profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') derived from watch behaviour and quiz data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests). This is precisely the prohibited practice: profiling-based advertising directed at known minors. Age is not inferred but declared (birthdate + school year captured by the quiz), so the 'reasonable certainty' threshold is met.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Stop all profiling/behaviourally-targeted ad delivery to the 13-17 audience. Ads reaching minors must not use profiling; switch to contextual (non-profiled) placement only, and configure the platform ad system to exclude profiling-based audiences for any segment known or likely to contain minors. Remove the custom audience built from quiz completions from any targeting affecting minors.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data (GDPR Art. 9) directly or by inference, regardless of consent. The quiz collects 'mood' and combines it with behavioural signals; mood/emotional-state data plus late-night ('late-night scroller') behavioural inference can amount to inferred data about mental/health state. If the custom audience or targeting parameters rely on this mood signal, the ad targeting is prohibited outright, irrespective of any consent obtained.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Exclude 'mood' and any emotional-state signal from all audience-building and ad-targeting parameters. Ensure the custom audience is not constructed using or inferring any GDPR Art. 9 special-category attribute; document the targeting parameters to demonstrate no sensitive-data profiling is used.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in ways that manipulate or materially distort recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, including repeatedly pressing choices/nagging. An 'always-on' loop that re-serves ads to minors after a mere 2-second view, combined with 22:00-01:00 scheduling, is an engagement design engineered to maximise repeated exposure of a vulnerable audience, which raises manipulative-design concerns, particularly as it targets minors.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on retargeting loop for the minor audience and set frequency caps / quiet-hours; do not treat a 2-second view as a retargeting trigger. Ensure the engagement 'loop' does not repeatedly re-surface content in a way that overrides informed choice, and drop the 22:00-01:00 late-night scheduling for teens.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that each advertisement on an online platform be clearly identifiable as an ad in real time, disclosing on whose behalf it is presented, who paid, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The campaign description does not indicate that the branded quiz and served creatives will carry clear ad labelling and targeting-parameter disclosure, so this obligation is engaged and should be verified.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform
findings.recommendation: Ensure every VoltZ creative and the branded quiz are clearly labelled as advertising, identify VoltZ as the advertiser/payer, and that the platform surfaces the main targeting parameters and opt-out controls to recipients.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on a short-video platform and deliberately serves profiling-based advertisements to a declared audience of minors (13-17), which is squarely prohibited by DSA Art. 28. This is a clear-cut violation: the ad system targets users known with reasonable certainty to be minors using watch-behaviour profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') plus quiz-derived data. Secondary concerns arise under Art. 26(3) (mood-based profiling potentially touching special-category data) and Art. 25 (manipulative always-on retargeting design). Art. 26(1) ad-transparency obligations are also engaged.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Persistent, always-on retargeting triggered by trivial engagement (2 seconds) and deliberately scheduled during late-night hours (22:00–01:00) to reach 13–17 year olds profiled by mood and 'late-night scroller' behaviour amounts to undue influence through persistence and exploitative timing. Because the audience is a clearly identifiable vulnerable group by age/credulity (Art. 5(3)), the impairment of freedom of choice is assessed from the perspective of the average teen, for whom relentless late-night pressure to consume an energy drink significantly distorts transactional behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds ... with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on retargeting loop for users under 18; do not schedule ads to minors during late-night hours (22:00–01:00); impose frequency caps and a meaningful engagement threshold, and drop mood-based timing of ads to minors.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: An 'always-on' loop that automatically and repeatedly re-serves ads via a remote medium (the video platform) to the same minors, triggered by a 2-second view, constitutes persistent solicitation. The campaign describes no opt-out or stopping condition, so it risks the blacklisted per se prohibition on persistent and unwanted solicitations by remote media.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Cap re-exposure frequency, provide and honour a clear opt-out/'stop showing me this' mechanism, and terminate the loop once a user signals disinterest; exclude minors from automated re-serving entirely.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a fairness safety-net, Art. 5 (with Art. 5(3)) captures the overall design: using mood, school year and interest data to behaviourally target energy-drink ads to 13–17 year olds — a group vulnerable by age and credulity — is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average member of that group, independent of any single blacklisted item.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Do not build the campaign around behavioural profiling of minors; adopt an age-appropriate, non-profiled contextual approach, and apply a professional-diligence standard that presumes heightened protection for under-18 audiences consuming stimulant products.

findings.title: Emotion-based AI targeting
findings.rationale: Collecting 'mood' and feeding it into targeting/custom audiences is emotion-based targeting: timing or tailoring marketing to inferred emotional states of minors reinforces the undue-influence analysis under UCPD Arts. 8–9 and the unfairness assessment under Art. 5(3). It amplifies the exploitation of an age-related vulnerability.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Stop collecting or using 'mood' for ad targeting; strip emotional-state signals from any audience segment, especially for minors.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The quiz is presented as an entertainment/engagement feature, but its real purpose is to harvest personal data and build a marketing custom audience for retargeting. If the data-collection and advertising purpose is not made clear and timely to the (minor) user, the commercial intent behind the quiz is hidden or provided in an untimely manner, engaging the misleading-omission / hidden-commercial-intent prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose, at the point of the quiz and in age-appropriate language, that it is advertising and that answers will be used to target ads; do not proceed without transparent, upfront notice of the commercial purpose.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Because the declared audience is children (13–17), any ad creative containing a direct exhortation to buy VoltZ (e.g. 'grab yours now', 'get one today') or to persuade parents to buy it would be a per se blacklisted practice. No verbatim creative text was supplied, so this cannot be confirmed, but it is a high-risk item to verify given the child-directed targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17
findings.recommendation: Before launch, review all creative copy directed at the 13–17 audience to ensure no direct call-to-purchase or pester-power messaging is present; document the review.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign targets minors (13–17) — a clearly identifiable vulnerable group under UCPD Art. 5(3) — with mood/interest-based behavioural profiling, late-night ad scheduling (22:00–01:00) and an always-on retargeting loop. These practices engage the UCPD aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8–9), the general unfairness safety-net (Art. 5), the blacklist on persistent solicitations (Annex I pt 26), and potentially hidden commercial intent (Art. 7). No verbatim ad creative was supplied, so the child-exhortation blacklist (Annex I pt 28) cannot be confirmed but should be checked before launch. Findings below are grounded in retrieved provisions; data-protection and platform-ban aspects fall to the GDPR/DSA agents.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs a branded "energy type" quiz that harvests teens' birthdate, school year, mood and interests, then uses the platform's ad system to profile 13-17 year-olds as "gamers" and "late-night scrollers" and repeatedly serve them energy-drink ads between 22:00 and 01:00 via an always-on retargeting loop. As designed, it is not fixable at the margins — it breaks the law on multiple fronts at once. The DSA flatly bans profiling-based advertising to known minors (Art. 28), and the AI Act treats AI that exploits the age-vulnerability of children to distort their behaviour as a prohibited practice (Art. 5). On top of that, you have no valid legal basis to collect and profile minors' data under GDPR (no parental consent, no age verification, sensitive "mood" data), and the late-night, always-on, mood-driven design is an aggressive/unfair practice toward a vulnerable audience under the UCPD. The overall verdict is critical: this campaign cannot launch in the EU in anything close to its current form. The core problems — targeting minors, behavioural profiling, mood data, late-night scheduling and relentless retargeting — must be removed, not merely tweaked.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as designed. Profiling-based advertising to a declared 13-17 audience is prohibited outright under DSA Art. 28 and cannot be cured by consent or disclaimers.</recommendations>

Stop all behavioural profiling and custom-audience targeting of minors. Switch to non-profiled contextual placement only, and configure the ad system to exclude any segment known or likely to contain under-18s.

Remove 'mood' and all emotional-state signals from the quiz and from every targeting/audience-building parameter — this touches special-category data (GDPR Art. 9) and is a per se banned targeting basis under DSA Art. 26(3).

Kill the always-on retargeting loop for minors and the 22:00-01:00 late-night scheduling. A 2-second view triggering endless re-serving to teens is manipulative design (DSA Art. 25) and an aggressive/persistent solicitation (UCPD Arts. 8-9, Annex I pt 26). At minimum apply frequency caps, quiet hours and a working opt-out.
Given this is stimulant/energy-drink marketing to children, the safest and recommended path is to exclude under-18 audiences entirely rather than attempt partial remediation.

If any data collection from minors is retained, establish the applicable digital-consent age per Member State and implement verified parental consent, plus a clear child-friendly privacy notice (GDPR Arts. 8, 12-13) and an easy withdrawal/opt-out mechanism (Arts. 7, 21).

Separate the quiz from any marketing purpose and disclose the commercial and data-harvesting intent upfront in age-appropriate language, so it is not a hidden-commercial-intent practice (UCPD Art. 7).

Before any launch, review all creative copy for direct calls-to-purchase or pester-power messaging aimed at children (UCPD Annex I pt 28), and ensure every ad is clearly labelled with advertiser, payer and targeting-parameter disclosures (DSA Art. 26(1)).
Note: although 'no generative AI' was declared, the platform's algorithmic profiling ad system is itself an in-scope AI system — reassess the campaign on that basis.

campaign.title: VoltZ energy drink — teen engagement loop
campaign.text: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform. A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience. The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00.
