An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.

detected_practices: engagement quiz collecting personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests)
custom audience creation from quiz completions
behavioural targeting on 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
always-on behavioural retargeting loop (re-serve after 2s watch)
late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00)
profiling of minors
energy drink marketing directed at teens (health-relevant product)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is teens 13-17; targeting and retargeting explicitly reach minors. DSA Art. 26/28 prohibit profiling-based advertising to minors, and GDPR requires heightened protections and valid consent basis for children's data. Energy-drink marketing to teens plus late-night scheduling and mood-based profiling amplifies UCPD vulnerability concerns.
triage.summary: A VoltZ energy-drink campaign on a short-video platform uses a branded quiz to collect sensitive-adjacent data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) from teens aged 13-17, feeding a custom audience for behavioural targeting and an always-on retargeting loop, with creatives scheduled late at night (22:00-01:00). Despite the 'no' declaration on generative AI, the platform's automated ad-serving and profiling system likely constitutes an AI/algorithmic decision-making component. The campaign explicitly targets and profiles minors, raising serious concerns across data protection, platform advertising rules, and unfair commercial practices.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The platform's automated ad-serving/profiling system is an AI system that targets a group vulnerable by reason of age (minors 13-17), and does so via mood signals and late-night scheduling designed to distort their consumption behaviour. Repeated retargeting of a caffeinated energy drink to children at night is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (excess caffeine intake, sleep disruption). The 'no generative AI' declaration does not exempt the automated profiling engine from Art. 5, which applies to any AI system.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Do not use behavioural/mood profiling or automated retargeting to target the 13-17 audience. Remove age-based targeting to minors entirely for this product, disable the always-on retargeting loop for under-18s, and drop the 22:00-01:00 late-night scheduling that compounds the exploitation of age-related vulnerability.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The combination of an always-on, low-threshold (2-second) retargeting loop, mood-derived audience signals from the quiz, and deliberate late-night scheduling constitutes an AI-driven, purposefully manipulative technique aimed at appreciably impairing minors' ability to make an informed decision and causing consumption decisions they would not otherwise take. Applied to minors and a health-relevant product, this is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Eliminate compulsive-loop mechanics: cap frequency, remove the 2-second retargeting trigger, and stop using inferred mood ('What's your energy type?') to time or intensify ad delivery. Ensure ad delivery does not exploit attention or emotional state, especially for minors.

findings.title: Prohibition of emotion recognition in workplace and education
findings.rationale: The quiz infers emotional state ('mood') for ad targeting. Art. 5(1)(f) only prohibits emotion recognition deployed within workplace or education institutions, so it is not squarely triggered here; however, the collection of 'school year' alongside mood inference in a minors-directed campaign is education-adjacent and worth flagging. The emotion inference itself is more relevant under Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) and GDPR.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Avoid inferring emotional/mood states for ad targeting, particularly in any context connected to schools or educational settings. Do not deploy the quiz or its outputs through school-linked channels.

verdicts.notes: Although the campaign declares no generative AI, the AI Act's Art. 5 prohibitions apply to any AI system, including the platform's automated profiling and ad-serving engine. The campaign uses that system to profile and repeatedly retarget minors aged 13-17 with an energy drink, exploiting age-related vulnerability with mood-based signals and late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling. This most likely engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting vulnerabilities and Art. 5(1)(a) on manipulative AI techniques. Emotion-recognition prohibition (Art. 5(1)(f)) is not squarely triggered since the inference is not deployed within an education institution.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The quiz is an information society service collecting personal data directly from children aged 13-17. Where consent is the legal basis, Art. 8 makes processing lawful only above the applicable age threshold (13-16 depending on Member State); below it parental consent and reasonable verification efforts are required. For an EU-wide campaign spanning all thresholds, no age-gating or parental-consent mechanism is described, so processing of under-16s' data is likely unlawful in Member States retaining the 16 threshold.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Implement robust age verification and, for users below the applicable Member-State threshold, obtain and verify parental/guardian consent before collecting quiz data. Apply the highest (16) threshold as a default across the EU unless per-market thresholds are configured, or exclude minors from the data-collection flow entirely.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting and profiling on 'mood', combined with late-night 'late-night scroller' targeting, involves inferring emotional/psychological state. Emotional-state data used to time and tailor marketing can reveal information about mental well-being that engages Art. 9 special-category protections, which require explicit consent and are prohibited absent an exception. Doing this to minors heightens the concern.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Stop collecting and profiling on 'mood'/emotional state, or obtain valid explicit consent under Art. 9 with a documented lawful basis. Given the audience is minors, remove mood as a targeting/profiling signal altogether.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Building a custom audience and behaviourally targeting/retargeting individuals is processing that requires a valid Art. 6 lawful basis. Consent is generally required for ad profiling; for minors legitimate interests is very hard to justify. No lawful basis is documented and the described flow does not evidence valid consent, so the profiling and audience creation likely lack a lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Document and secure a valid lawful basis before any profiling/audience use — for minors this means specific, granular consent (with parental consent below threshold), not repurposing quiz entries. Do not derive advertising audiences from quiz completions without a clearly stated, consent-based purpose.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and demonstrable, and clearly distinguishable. A gamified quiz that quietly repurposes entries into a custom audience does not show a distinct, informed, unbundled consent for profiling/marketing, nor an easy withdrawal mechanism, failing Arts. 7 and 4(11).
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Separate the quiz-participation purpose from any marketing/profiling purpose with a distinct, plain-language, opt-in consent request; keep records demonstrating consent; and provide an equally easy withdrawal path.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of watch behaviour and interests to evaluate personal aspects and build 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' segments is profiling under Art. 4(4). This confirms profiling of minors is occurring and triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Treat this segmentation as profiling and ensure the full GDPR profiling regime is satisfied; for minors, discontinue profiling-based ad targeting.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection the controller must disclose identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and the existence of profiling. The described quiz gives no indication that this information is provided, and the downstream custom-audience/retargeting purposes appear undisclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at the quiz entry point covering all Art. 13 elements, explicitly disclosing custom-audience creation, profiling and retargeting, in language a teenager can understand.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Where information is addressed to a child, Art. 12 requires it be concise, transparent and in clear, plain, age-appropriate language. Data collected from 13-17 year-olds via a branded quiz demands child-friendly transparency, which is not evidenced.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Design all privacy information and consent wording in clear, plain, age-appropriate language tailored to 13-17 year-olds and make it easily accessible within the quiz flow.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The always-on retargeting loop is direct-marketing profiling. Data subjects have an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, including related profiling, at any time; the described continuous loop provides no evident opt-out mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy, always-available opt-out from retargeting/direct-marketing profiling and honour objections immediately by ceasing processing and removing the individual from the retargeting audience.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign collects personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) directly from minors aged 13-17 via a branded quiz and feeds it into behavioural profiling, custom-audience targeting and an always-on retargeting loop. This engages multiple GDPR obligations with no described safeguards: children's consent (Art. 8), a valid lawful basis and GDPR-standard consent (Arts. 6, 7, 4(11)), special-category 'mood' data (Art. 9), transparency at collection (Arts. 12-13), and the right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). Because processing targets minors and includes emotional-state data, the risk profile is high and several requirements appear unmet as described.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling (as defined in GDPR Art. 4(4)) using personal data of recipients the platform is aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Here the declared target audience is teens 13-17, the quiz collects birthdate and school year (confirming minor status), and ads are then served based on behavioural profiles — this is squarely profiling-based advertising to known minors.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Disable all profiling/behavioural-based ad delivery and retargeting for the 13-17 audience. Any campaign reaching minors must use only non-profiling contextual targeting and age-appropriate design; remove the custom-audience and watch-behaviour targeting entirely for this cohort.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) bans presenting ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including where derived by inference. Collecting 'mood' and feeding it into a custom audience used for ad delivery risks profiling on mental/emotional-state data (a health-adjacent special category), which is prohibited for platform advertising regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Exclude 'mood' and any emotional/mental-state signal from audience building and ad-targeting parameters. Do not derive or use special-category inferences to determine ad recipients.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces that deceive, manipulate or materially distort recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, including repeatedly nagging users. A persistent, always-on loop that re-serves ads on a 2-second engagement trigger to minors is a manipulative engagement pattern that impairs free decision-making.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on retargeting loop for minors; impose strict frequency caps and an easy opt-out. Do not use minimal engagement (2s watch) as a trigger to relentlessly re-serve ads.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that platform ads be clearly identifiable as advertising in real time, disclose on whose behalf and who paid, and provide meaningful information on the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The campaign describes behavioural targeting parameters but no indication that ads are labelled or that targeting parameters are disclosed to recipients.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads
findings.recommendation: Ensure every VoltZ ad is clearly labelled as an advertisement identifying VoltZ as advertiser/payer, and that the platform surfaces the main targeting parameters and controls to change them for each ad.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on an online (short-video) platform and directs profiling-based advertising at an audience explicitly declared as minors aged 13-17, which is a direct prohibition under DSA Art. 28. Building a custom audience and targeting/retargeting on behavioural profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') using quiz-collected data — including 'mood' — also engages the Art. 26(3) ban on profiling with special-category data and the Art. 26(1) transparency obligation, while the always-on 2-second retargeting loop raises the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition. Multiple DSA prohibitions are likely breached as described.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Teens 13-17 are a clearly identifiable vulnerable group by reason of age and credulity, so the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group (Art. 5(3)). Targeting minors for an energy drink (a health-relevant, stimulant product) by exploiting inferred 'mood' and 'late-night scroller' profiling, timed to late-night hours when self-control and parental oversight are lowest, is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort their consumption behaviour. This is the fairness safety-net for the practice even where no single specific rule is triggered.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy age-, mood- or behaviour-based targeting/timing for this product to under-18s. Suppress the 13-17 age band from all VoltZ ad delivery, remove mood/interest signals from audience building, and stop late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling to minors. Restrict to an over-18 audience with age gating.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: An 'always-on' loop that relentlessly re-serves ads to minors after only a 2-second watch, combined with deliberate late-night timing and exploitation of inferred emotional 'mood' state, uses persistence and undue influence over a low-resilience audience. Under Arts. 8-9 the relevant factors expressly include timing, persistence and exploitation of the target's characteristics; applied to minors this significantly impairs their freedom of choice and pushes a transactional decision (purchasing/consuming VoltZ) they might not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on retargeting loop for under-18s, impose frequency caps and a minimum meaningful-engagement threshold well above 2 seconds, eliminate mood/emotion-based delivery, and do not schedule ads to minors during late-night hours.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The quiz is framed as fun entertainment ('What's your energy type?') but its material purpose is to harvest personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) to build an advertising custom audience. If the commercial and data-collection intent is not made clear to the teen user at the point of participation, this is a misleading omission / failure to identify commercial intent under Art. 7(2), which is especially serious given the audience are minors.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose at the start of the quiz that it is advertising for VoltZ and that responses will be used to target ads. Given the minor audience, avoid using quiz data for ad targeting at all; if retained, provide age-appropriate, transparent notice and a genuine choice.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: The blacklist prohibition on persistent and unwanted solicitations via remote media is engaged in spirit by an always-on loop that repeatedly re-contacts the same young users. The strict blacklist form typically bites where solicitation continues after an opt-out/objection; the campaign text does not evidence continuation after refusal, so this is a lower-confidence flag rather than a clear per-se breach, but the persistence design should be reviewed against any opt-out signals.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the retargeting system honours objections/opt-outs immediately and does not re-contact users who dismiss or block the ads; cap repetition so re-serving cannot become persistent and unwanted.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: This is a child/teen-directed advertisement, which is the exact context in which the per-se prohibition on direct exhortations to children to buy (or to pester adults to buy) applies. The supplied campaign text contains no verbatim call-to-action wording, so no breach is asserted; this is flagged so that any creative copy is screened before launch.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform ... serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17
findings.recommendation: Screen all VoltZ creative copy aimed at (or reaching) under-18s to ensure there is no direct 'buy now'-style exhortation to children or prompt to ask a parent to buy; document the review.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign targets a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (teens 13-17) for a health-relevant product using mood-based profiling, late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00) and an always-on retargeting loop. Under the UCPD this engages the vulnerable-consumer standard (Art. 5(3)), the aggressive-practice rules (Arts. 8-9, via timing/persistence/undue influence over minors) and the hidden-commercial-intent rule (Art. 7) for the branded quiz used as a data-harvesting/audience-building tool. No blacklisted "direct exhortation to children" (Annex I point 28) wording is present in the supplied text, so that prohibition is flagged only as a risk to watch rather than a confirmed breach. Overall the design is a serious fairness risk that likely breaches Arts. 5, 7 and 8-9 as described.

report.executive_summary: The VoltZ "teen engagement loop" campaign deliberately targets 13-17 year-olds with an energy drink using a quiz that harvests birthdate, school year, mood and interests, then profiles those minors and re-serves ads on an always-on loop scheduled for late night (22:00-01:00). As designed, this campaign hits some of the hardest legal walls in EU law: the DSA flatly bans profiling-based advertising to known minors and bans ads targeted using special-category (mood/emotional-state) data, and the AI Act's Article 5 prohibits AI systems that exploit the vulnerabilities of children — both of which this campaign appears to breach directly, not merely risk. On top of that, GDPR is engaged across the board (children's consent, lawful basis, special-category "mood" data, transparency, and the right to object), and the UCPD treats the late-night, mood-based, relentless retargeting of minors for a stimulant product as an unfair and aggressive practice. The "no generative AI" declaration does not help — Article 5 applies to the platform's automated profiling engine regardless. This is not fixable with disclaimers or consent tweaks: the core mechanic (profiling minors to sell an energy drink at night) is prohibited. The clear verdict is do not launch as designed; the campaign must be fundamentally rebuilt.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as designed — the central mechanic (profiling-based advertising to known 13-17 minors) is directly prohibited by DSA Art. 28 and cannot be cured by consent or disclosure.
Remove the 13-17 age band entirely from VoltZ ad delivery. If the product is to be advertised at all, gate it to an over-18 audience with proper age verification.

Eliminate 'mood'/emotional-state from all data collection, audience-building and targeting — it is banned as a targeting parameter under DSA Art. 26(3) and triggers GDPR Art. 9 special-category protections.

Disable the always-on retargeting loop and the 2-second re-serve trigger; this is a manipulative dark pattern (DSA Art. 25) and an aggressive practice (UCPD Arts. 8-9). Impose strict frequency caps and an immediate, easy opt-out.
Drop the 22:00-01:00 late-night scheduling to minors, which compounds the exploitation of age-related vulnerability under the AI Act and UCPD.

Stop deriving advertising custom audiences from quiz completions; if any minors' data is collected, secure a valid lawful basis with age-appropriate, unbundled consent and parental consent below the applicable Member-State threshold (default to 16 EU-wide).
Provide clear, child-friendly privacy notices and consent at the point of collection (GDPR Arts. 12-13), and clearly label all ads as advertising with disclosed targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26(1)).

Disclose the quiz's commercial and data-collection intent up front to avoid a hidden-commercial-intent breach (UCPD Art. 7), and screen all creative copy for any 'buy now' exhortation to children (UCPD Annex I point 28).

campaign.title: VoltZ energy drink — teen engagement loop
campaign.text: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform. A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience. The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.

detected_practices: branded quiz collecting personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests)
custom audience creation from quiz completions
behavioural targeting on 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
behavioural retargeting loop (re-serving ads after 2-second watch)
late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00)
profiling of minors
energy drink marketing to teens
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is teens 13-17 across the EU — this is explicitly a minors-directed campaign. DSA Art. 28 prohibits targeted advertising to minors based on profiling; GDPR requires heightened protections and lawful basis for processing children's data (Art. 8, birthdate/school year/mood profiling). Marketing an energy drink (high caffeine) to minors with late-night scheduling raises UCPD concerns around exploiting vulnerability. AI declaration ('no') should be independently verified since the targeting/retargeting engine appears to be an automated profiling system.
triage.summary: VoltZ energy drink campaign on a short-video platform explicitly targeting teens 13-17, using a quiz to collect sensitive-adjacent data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) to build custom audiences. The platform's ad system then profiles and behaviourally targets and retargets minors matching 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' patterns with late-night creatives (22:00-01:00). Despite the 'no' declaration on generative AI, the ad system's profiling/audience-matching engine likely constitutes an AI system, and personalisation of minors is central.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The platform's automated profiling/audience-matching and retargeting system is an AI system used to identify and target a group defined by age (minors 13-17) — an expressly named vulnerability under Art. 5(1)(b). It is built to materially distort their behaviour (drive consumption of a high-caffeine energy drink) by exploiting age-related vulnerability, amplified by an 'always-on retargeting loop' that re-serves ads after only a 2-second watch and by late-night scheduling when self-control is lowest. Marketing a high-caffeine product to children in this way is reasonably likely to cause significant harm to health/sleep, satisfying the harm element. The 'no generative AI' declaration is irrelevant: Art. 5 applies to any AI system, and an automated behavioural-targeting engine qualifies.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-driven profiling, custom audiences or behavioural retargeting to target the 13-17 age group at all. Disable age-based and behaviour-based ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') audience matching for minors, remove the late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling, and switch to non-profiled contextual placement only. Obtain a documented assessment confirming the campaign does not target an age-defined vulnerable group before launch.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI targeting system ingests inferred emotional/'mood' state and behavioural signals ('late-night scroller') and uses them to time and tailor ad delivery to minors — emotion-based AI targeting that is a purposefully manipulative technique under Art. 5(1)(a). Serving energy-drink ads to teens keyed to mood at 22:00-01:00 is designed to appreciably impair their ability to make an informed decision and cause them to consume in a way they otherwise would not, in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant (health/sleep) harm. The quiz collecting 'mood' as a targeting input, combined with a low-friction 2-second retargeting loop, evidences covert behavioural nudging rather than neutral advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Stop collecting and using 'mood' and emotional-state signals as targeting inputs, and remove mood/late-night-based ad timing. Eliminate the always-on 2-second retargeting loop directed at minors. Ensure any targeting logic cannot infer or exploit emotional states, and document that the campaign does not deploy manipulative techniques that distort minors' decisions.

verdicts.notes: Although the marketer declared "no" generative AI, the AI Act still applies: the platform's automated ad-targeting, custom-audience and always-on retargeting engine is an AI system that profiles individuals and materially shapes what they see. That system is being used to target and behaviourally lock-in minors aged 13-17 — an age-based vulnerability — with high-caffeine energy-drink creatives scheduled for late night (22:00-01:00) and keyed to "mood" and "late-night scroller" signals. This engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting age-related vulnerabilities and the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative AI techniques, both of which are prohibited practices. The Art. 50 transparency duties are not the main issue here since no chatbot, synthetic media or deep fake is described.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The quiz is an information society service offered directly to a declared audience of teens 13-17 and collects their personal data, feeding a custom audience for targeted advertising. Where consent is the legal basis, GDPR Art. 8 requires that the child be at least 16 (or the Member State's lowered threshold, minimum 13); below that age parental consent is needed and the controller must make reasonable verification efforts. The campaign describes no age gate, no parental-consent mechanism, and no verification — yet the declared range (13-17) spans below the 16 default in many Member States.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Implement robust age assurance and, for users below the applicable digital-consent age (13-16 depending on Member State), obtain and verify parental/guardian consent before collecting quiz data or building audiences. Do not run the quiz or profiling for users under the applicable threshold without verified parental consent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of watch behaviour to evaluate personal preferences, interests and behaviour and to segment users into 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' profiles is profiling within Art. 4(4). This confirms the processing is profiling and triggers the heightened requirements (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights) that follow, especially given the data subjects are minors.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, confirm it is not applied to minors without a valid basis, and align it with the stricter obligations that attach to profiling of children; prefer removing behavioural profiling of minors entirely.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Building a custom audience from quiz data and serving behaviourally targeted ads requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). For personalised advertising/profiling of individuals — especially children — this generally requires consent, and legitimate interests will rarely balance in favour of profiling minors for marketing. The campaign identifies no lawful basis and, given the audience, consent cannot be validly self-supplied by many of these minors.
findings.evidence_quote: completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6 lawful basis before any profiling; for advertising to minors, rely on properly obtained (and, where required, parent-verified) consent rather than legitimate interests, or cease the profiling.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent gathered via a fun quiz is unlikely to be 'freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous' as required by Art. 4(11). Bundling data collection into an engagement quiz whose real purpose is audience-building for retargeting means consent is neither specific nor informed, and minors' capacity to give valid consent is limited.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Separate the marketing/profiling purpose from the quiz, present a specific, granular, plain-language opt-in for profiling and custom-audience use, and avoid bundling. Ensure consent is a clear affirmative action and easily withdrawable.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting and processing 'mood' data, and using it in an engagement/targeting loop, risks processing data revealing emotional/mental state. Where mood is used to infer or act on health-adjacent or emotional vulnerability, it can engage Art. 9 special-category protection, which prohibits processing absent explicit consent or another exception. Combined with minors and late-night scheduling, this is high-risk emotion-linked processing.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Do not collect or use 'mood' data for targeting. If any emotional-state data is processed, treat it as potentially special-category, obtain explicit consent, and avoid using it to time or tailor ads to minors.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and information about profiling/automated decision-making (Art. 13). The described quiz gives no indication that any of this is disclosed to the teens whose data is collected and repurposed into a custom audience and retargeting loop.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear Art. 13 notice at the quiz entry point covering the profiling and custom-audience purposes, recipients (the ad platform), retention, and rights — written for the actual audience.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to be concise, transparent and in clear, plain language, particularly when addressed to a child. A campaign explicitly directed at 13-17-year-olds must present privacy information in child-appropriate language; nothing in the campaign indicates any such tailored transparency exists.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: teens 13-17
findings.recommendation: Deliver child-friendly, plain-language privacy information and consent flows appropriate to a 13-17 audience, avoiding legalistic or hidden disclosures.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct-marketing profiling triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). An 'always-on' retargeting loop must let data subjects object and stop the profiling immediately; the description gives no opt-out or suppression mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, effective opt-out from marketing profiling/retargeting, honour objections immediately by suppressing the user from the custom audience, and surface the right to object in the ad experience.

verdicts.notes: This campaign processes personal data of minors (13-17) at every stage: a quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; that data builds a custom audience; and an automated ad system profiles and behaviourally retargets teens. Under GDPR this engages Art. 8 (child consent), Art. 6/7 and Art. 4(11) (valid lawful basis/consent for profiling), Art. 4(4) (profiling), Art. 9 (mood/emotional data), Art. 12/13 (transparency to children) and Art. 21 (right to object to marketing profiling). Multiple obligations appear unmet as described, so a GDPR breach is likely; the mood-based profiling and absence of any verified parental-consent or lawful-basis mechanism are the most serious issues.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28 prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients they are aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Here the platform knows the audience is aged 13-17 (birthdate and school year are collected via the quiz, and the target is declared as teens 13-17), and the ads are served precisely on the basis of behavioural profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') plus an always-on retargeting loop. This is a knowing, profiling-based ad to identified minors — the core conduct the prohibition targets.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Cease all profiling-based ad delivery to the 13-17 audience. If VoltZ advertises on this platform at all, it must use only non-profiling contextual placement (no custom audiences, no behavioural interest/watch-history segments, no retargeting). Disable the custom-audience feed and the retargeting loop for any user known or reasonably likely to be a minor, and apply age-appropriate delivery controls.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) bans platform ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories. Collecting 'mood' and building profiles such as 'late-night scroller' can serve as proxies for mental/emotional health state, meaning the resulting ad targeting may be based — directly or by inference — on sensitive attributes. The prohibition applies regardless of any consent obtained via the quiz.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Remove 'mood' from the quiz data feeding the custom audience and exclude any emotional-state or wellbeing-related signals from ad targeting parameters. Do not use inferred sensitive attributes for audience creation; document that no Art. 9 category (or proxy) is used to determine ad recipients.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that manipulates recipients or materially impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions, including repeatedly pushing a choice. An always-on loop that re-serves ads to minors after only 2 seconds of incidental watching, combined with late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00), is a repetitive, engagement-maximising design that exploits the reduced resilience of minors and pressures continued exposure.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Disable the always-on retargeting loop for minors, remove the 2-second re-serve trigger, and stop late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling aimed at teens. Apply frequency caps and quiet hours, and ensure the ad experience does not nag or repeatedly re-expose users who have not chosen to engage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients can identify in real time that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is shown, who paid, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The campaign description does not indicate any ad labelling or disclosure of targeting parameters, so the transparency obligation is engaged and not evidently satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform.
findings.recommendation: Ensure every VoltZ placement is clearly and unambiguously labelled as an advertisement in real time, names VoltZ as advertiser/payer, and surfaces the main targeting parameters used and controls to change them, in line with the platform's Art. 26(1) mechanisms.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is explicitly a minors-directed campaign (teens 13-17) on a short-video platform that builds custom audiences from a data-collecting quiz and then behaviourally profiles and retargets those minors. This engages the DSA's strongest advertising prohibitions. DSA Art. 28 (no profiling-based ads to minors) is squarely and knowingly breached, and Art. 26(3) is likely engaged via 'mood' and behavioural profiling that acts as a proxy for sensitive/health data. The always-on retargeting loop also raises Art. 25 dark-pattern concerns, and Art. 26(1) transparency obligations are engaged but under-described.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Under Art. 5(3), practices likely to distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (here minors, by reason of age and credulity) are assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. Marketing a high-caffeine energy drink specifically to 13-17 year-olds, using their inferred profiles to maximise reach, is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the transactional decisions of an audience that lacks the maturity to critically evaluate such advertising. The safety-net prohibition is squarely engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Do not target energy-drink advertising to a declared 13-17 audience. Restrict the campaign to 18+, apply robust age-gating so minors are excluded from the custom audience, and document the professional-diligence assessment for marketing this product category to young people.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, through undue influence, it significantly impairs freedom of choice — with timing, persistence and exploitation of a susceptible state as express factors. Deliberately scheduling ads to minors late at night (a low-inhibition, fatigued window), combining this with mood-based targeting, and relentlessly re-serving ads via an always-on retargeting loop triggered by a mere 2-second view amounts to persistent, exploitative pressure on a vulnerable audience that is likely to distort their behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Remove late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling for any audience that may include minors, drop mood-derived signals from targeting, and cap/eliminate the always-on retargeting loop with clear frequency limits and easy opt-out. Ensure no aggressive persistence remains for younger viewers.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice where it is not apparent from context. The quiz is framed as a fun, engagement-driven personality test, but its actual purpose is to harvest personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) to build an advertising custom audience for retargeting. Teenage participants are unlikely to perceive that completing the quiz enrols them into a targeted advertising loop; this material commercial intent is hidden, engaging the misleading-omission prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose, before data is collected, that the quiz is advertising and that responses will be used to build audiences and serve/retarget VoltZ ads. Present the commercial and data-use intent in age-appropriate, unambiguous terms rather than as neutral entertainment.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: This is a child/minor-directed advertisement, so the per-se prohibition on including a direct exhortation to children to buy the product (or to pester adults to buy it) applies in all circumstances. The submitted material describes targeting mechanics but does not include the actual creative copy, so a direct exhortation ('grab yours', 'get VoltZ now', 'ask for it') cannot be confirmed or excluded from the text provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: teens 13-17
findings.recommendation: Review all creative copy and calls-to-action for any direct purchase exhortation aimed at children; remove imperative buy-now/pester-power messaging entirely. Given the 13-17 targeting, treat this as a per-se compliance checkpoint before launch.

verdicts.notes: This is an explicitly minors-directed campaign (teens 13-17) for a high-caffeine energy drink that combines mood/behaviour profiling, late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00) and an always-on retargeting loop. Under the UCPD this engages the vulnerable-consumer standard (Art. 5(3)), the aggressive-practices prohibition through exploitative timing and persistence (Arts. 8-9), and the hidden-commercial-intent rule for the data-harvesting quiz (Art. 7). No verbatim ad copy is supplied, so the Annex I point 28 blacklist (direct exhortation to children) cannot be confirmed but must be checked in the actual creatives.

report.executive_summary: This campaign targets a high-caffeine energy drink at 13-17 year-olds using a "personality quiz" to harvest their data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests), builds a behavioural custom audience, and then profiles and relentlessly retargets those teens — including late-night ads (22:00-01:00) and re-serving after just a 2-second view. As described, it breaches the strongest EU rules on multiple fronts and cannot launch in its current form. Most seriously, the DSA flatly bans profiling-based ads to known minors (Art. 28), and the AI Act treats behavioural targeting that exploits an age-based vulnerability and uses mood/emotional signals as a prohibited practice — the "no generative AI" declaration does not change this, because the platform's automated targeting engine is itself an AI system. On the data side, GDPR issues run through every stage: no age verification or parental consent, no valid lawful basis, sensitive "mood" data used for targeting, and no child-friendly transparency or opt-out. Under the UCPD, marketing this product to minors with late-night timing, mood targeting and a persistent retargeting loop is likely both an unfair and an aggressive practice, and the quiz hides its commercial intent. The verdict is critical: this campaign should not go live as designed, and the fixes required are structural, not cosmetic.
recommendations: STOP the campaign as designed — do not run profiling-based or retargeted advertising to the 13-17 audience at all. This is the single most important action: DSA Art. 28 prohibits profiling-based ads to known minors, and the AI Act prohibits behavioural targeting that exploits age-related vulnerability.

Remove 'mood' and all emotional-state signals from the quiz and from any targeting logic. Using inferred emotional/wellbeing data as a targeting proxy triggers AI Act Art. 5(1)(a), DSA Art. 26(3) (special-category ban) and GDPR Art. 9.

Disable the always-on retargeting loop and the 2-second re-serve trigger, and remove all late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling. This persistent, low-friction, late-night pressure drives the AI Act, DSA Art. 25 (dark patterns) and UCPD aggressive-practice findings.

Restrict energy-drink advertising to an 18+ audience with robust age assurance, so minors are excluded from custom audiences entirely. If any minors could be reached, switch to non-profiled contextual placement only — no custom audiences, no behavioural segments, no retargeting.

If any processing of teen data is retained, fix the GDPR foundations first: implement age verification and verified parental consent for users below the applicable digital-consent age (13-16 by Member State), establish and document a valid Art. 6 lawful basis, and unbundle marketing consent from the quiz with a specific, informed opt-in.

Rebuild the quiz so its commercial and data-use intent is disclosed up front in clear, child-appropriate language (GDPR Arts. 12-13, UCPD Art. 7), and provide an easy, immediately effective opt-out from marketing profiling/retargeting (GDPR Art. 21).

Before any launch, review all creative copy for direct purchase exhortations to children (UCPD Annex I, point 28) and ensure every placement is clearly labelled as advertising with disclosed targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26(1)).

Document a pre-launch compliance assessment covering AI Act prohibited-practice screening, DSA minors/ad obligations, a GDPR DPIA (profiling of children is high-risk), and the UCPD professional-diligence standard for marketing this product to young people.

campaign.title: GardenPro similar-products digest
campaign.text: A garden-tools retailer emails past purchasers (contact details obtained at sale, opt-out offered at collection and in every message) a quarterly digest of accessories for tools they bought: 'Blades and batteries for your GP-200 trimmer'. Legal basis is documented as legitimate interest with a balancing test on file; unsubscribe is one-click and immediate. One template footer, however, buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email.

detected_practices: personalised product recommendations based on prior purchases
behavioural/purchase-history targeting
email marketing to existing customers under legitimate interest
one-click unsubscribe (compliant)
obscured unsubscribe link buried below 14 lines of social icons
misleading unsubscribe labelling ('preferences' rather than stop email)
quarterly recurring digest
triage.summary: A garden-tools retailer emails past purchasers a personalised quarterly digest of accessories matched to tools they previously bought, relying on documented legitimate interest and offering one-click unsubscribe. While largely compliant, one email template buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and mislabels it as 'preferences', raising GDPR (soft opt-in/right to object, ePrivacy-adjacent) and UCPD (misleading omission / dark pattern) concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) grants an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, and the controller must respect and facilitate that objection. Burying the opt-out below 14 lines of social icons and labelling it 'preferences' instead of a clear stop-email option obstructs and obscures the exercise of that right in this template, even though the campaign otherwise offers a compliant one-click, immediate unsubscribe.
findings.evidence_quote: buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email
findings.recommendation: Correct the defective template so the opt-out is clearly presented near the top of the footer with unambiguous wording (e.g. 'Unsubscribe from these emails'), matching the one-click immediate mechanism used in other templates; avoid framing it merely as 'preferences'.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that data subjects can readily understand and control processing of their data. An obscured and mislabelled opt-out mechanism makes the ability to stop marketing processing less transparent and less fair, contrary to Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: One template footer, however, buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all templates present the opt-out transparently and consistently, using clear and plain language so recipients can immediately understand how to stop the marketing processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Emailing past purchasers about accessories for tools they bought is a recognised use case for the legitimate-interest basis (Art. 6(1)(f)) where a balancing test is performed and an opt-out is offered. The campaign documents this and offers opt-out at collection and in every message, so the lawful basis appears satisfied — flagged for completeness.
findings.evidence_quote: Legal basis is documented as legitimate interest with a balancing test on file
findings.recommendation: Keep the legitimate-interest assessment current and ensure the balancing test reflects the recurring quarterly cadence and the profiling of purchase history; retain evidence of opt-out being offered at collection.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Personalising content based on prior purchase history is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). campaign.title: RideLink surge notice
campaign.text: A ride-hailing app applies demand-based multipliers. Before booking, the screen shows: 'High demand — prices are 1.8x normal right now', the full fare estimate, and a 'wait for lower prices' option with a price alert. The multiplier is identical for all users in the zone (no individual profiling) and the promised fare is honoured. Marketing pushes announce 'weekend airport fares from €19' with the range and surge caveat in the same font size.

triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult app users; no indication minors are targeted or likely reached in significant numbers. Personal data is engaged because push notifications require device/account identifiers and location/zone data for surge determination, so GDPR review is warranted despite the absence of individual profiling. UCPD included to verify that 'from €19' anchor pricing and surge disclosures are not misleading (drip pricing / genuineness of headline price). AI Act and DSA not plausibly engaged: no AI system in use, and an app's own first-party price notices are not intermediary/platform advertising within DSA scope.

findings.rationale: Sending promotional push notifications to app users is direct marketing that processes personal data (device/account identifiers). The submission is silent on which basis is relied upon and whether consent was obtained, so lawfulness of the marketing pushes is not demonstrated as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes announce 'weekend airport fares from €19'

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: A 'from' headline price is a claim about the price and manner of price calculation under Art. 6. It is only misleading if the headline price is not genuinely obtainable or if surge/conditions are concealed. Here the range and surge caveat are disclosed with equal prominence (same font size), which addresses the drip-pricing concern. The only condition for continued compliance is that some genuine fares at or from €19 actually exist for the advertised weekend airport routes.

findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 blacklists FALSE statements of limited-time availability/terms used to force an immediate decision. The surge notice reflects a real, zone-uniform, non-personalised multiplier that is honoured, and the app offers a 'wait for lower prices' price-alert option that expressly gives consumers time to reflect. The urgency is genuine and not artificially manufactured, so the blacklist is not triggered.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages UCPD price-transparency and urgency/scarcity rules but, as described, satisfies them. The "1.8x high demand" surge notice reflects a genuine, zone-uniform multiplier that is honoured, so it is not a false urgency/scarcity claim under Annex I point 7 nor a misleading action under Art. 6. Full fare estimates are shown pre-booking with a "wait for lower prices" option, and the "from €19" headline is accompanied by the range and surge caveat in equal font size — actively meeting Art. 6/7 rather than concealing costs. No blacklisted practice is present; the only residual dependency (that €19 fares are genuinely available) is flagged for information.

report.executive_summary: Your RideLink surge notice campaign is fundamentally well-designed on the pricing and advertising side. The "1.8x high demand" surge message and the "from €19" airport push both clear EU consumer-protection rules (UCPD): the surge is genuine, applied uniformly to everyone in a zone (no individual profiling), honoured at booking, and the "from €19" claim carries the price range and surge caveat in equal font — so no misleading or false-urgency issues, as long as €19 fares are actually obtainable in practice. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. The real gaps are on data protection (GDPR), and they are procedural rather than substantive. The submission doesn't show what lawful basis you rely on to send marketing pushes, whether users can easily opt out of them, or whether your privacy notice properly covers both marketing pushes and location/zone processing. None of these are hard to fix — they are typically handled in app onboarding and notification settings — but they need to be documented and demonstrable before the marketing pushes go out. Overall risk is medium, driven entirely by the unaddressed GDPR/ePrivacy housekeeping.
recommendations: Secure and document a lawful basis for the marketing push notifications before sending: obtain granular opt-in consent to promotional pushes at onboarding (kept separate from transactional/service pushes like surge notices), or record a legitimate-interest assessment where appropriate.

Provide an always-available, easy way to turn off marketing pushes (e.g. an in-app notification-preferences toggle distinct from service messages), signpost this right at first contact, and suppress users from future marketing pushes immediately on objection.

report.executive_summary: This campaign launches a genuinely capped limited edition of 200 numbered watches, using a real scarcity claim and a hard pre-order deadline across web and email. The campaign does not state on what basis the email list was built.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing

findings.evidence_quote: Pre-orders close Friday 20:00 CET or when the 200 pieces are allocated, whichever comes first.

Preserve the manufacturer's attestation of the 200-unit cap and keep the live counter and deadline logic accurate for the whole campaign — this is what keeps the scarcity claim lawful.

Never reset the deadline, re-open allocations after 200 are sold, or reuse the 'only 200 ever made' claim for any future run of the same model — doing so would convert a truthful claim into prohibited false scarcity.
