campaign.title: Mira.virtual x GlowCosmetics
campaign.text: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer with 2.1M followers, posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth'), and replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. The account bio states 'virtual personality by StudioNine'; individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.

detected_practices: AI-generated virtual influencer
influencer marketing / paid partnership
personified first-person product testimonial
implied product-efficacy skin claims ('texture has never been this smooth')
implied skincare/health-adjacent claims via fictitious 'routine' and 'dermatologist' framing
per-post AI/virtual nature not disclosed (only in bio)
interactive replies to fan comments sustaining human illusion
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is young adults 18-30, but social channels with a 2.1M-follower account offer no effective age-gating, so minors are plausibly reached. No personalisation/targeting declared, however processing of commenters' data and platform-side profiling on social channels means GDPR is still plausibly engaged. UCPD strongly implicated by the missing AI/virtual disclosure creating a misleading impression that a real person endorses/uses the product; AI Act transparency (Art. 50) applies to AI-generated content/deepfake-style personas; DSA relevant to platform advertising transparency and content dissemination.
triage.summary: A photorealistic AI-generated virtual influencer ('Mira') promotes GlowCosmetics serums via first-person selfies and skin-journey testimonials, engaging directly with followers. The AI/virtual nature is only disclosed in the account bio, not on individual posts or stories, and some users evidently believe Mira is a real human seeking her dermatologist. Paid-partnership labelling is present but AI-generation transparency is not, alongside implied efficacy/skin claims.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Mira is a photorealistic AI-generated human-like persona posting selfies 'wearing' the serum and first-person skin-journey content — synthetic image content depicting an apparently real person that would falsely appear authentic, i.e. a deep fake within Art. 50(4). Deployers must disclose that such content is artificially generated. Disclosure appears only obliquely in the account bio ('virtual personality by StudioNine') and not on the individual posts/stories where the deceptive impression is created; the fact that commenters believe Mira is human and ask about 'her dermatologist' shows the disclosure is not effective at the point of consumption.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent, per-asset disclosure on every post, story and reply that Mira is an AI-generated / virtual persona (e.g. 'AI-generated virtual influencer' label on the image and in caption). Do not rely on the bio alone; the disclosure must accompany each piece of deep-fake content at first exposure.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The AI-generated images (and any AI-generated caption text) are synthetic outputs. Art. 50(2) requires providers of the generative AI system to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated/manipulated. Nothing in the campaign indicates the assets carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. watermarking / C2PA-style metadata); the only stated signal is a human-readable bio note.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer ... posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated visuals and copy carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. embedded watermark / content-credentials metadata) from the generation stage, and verify the marking survives upload to the social platform. Confirm the generative-AI provider implements Art. 50(2) marking.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: If the account's replies to fan comments are generated or driven by an AI system interacting directly with natural persons, Art. 50(1) requires those persons be informed they are interacting with an AI, unless obvious from the circumstances. Here it is not obvious — commenters believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits — so the interaction disclosure obligation is engaged and, as described, unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: If replies are AI-generated or AI-assisted, disclose the AI nature at the point of interaction (e.g. a standing 'you are interacting with an AI persona' notice on the profile and in conversational replies). If replies are written by humans on behalf of a fictional persona, document this to show Art. 50(1) does not apply, but still address the deep fake and misleading-impression issues.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: A persuasive undisclosed synthetic persona presenting first-person efficacy testimonials could be argued to be a deceptive AI technique influencing purchasing decisions. However, Art. 5(1)(a) is a prohibition requiring behavioural distortion that causes or is likely to cause significant harm; a cosmetics endorsement does not evidently meet the 'significant harm' threshold on the facts. Flagged for awareness — the deception concern is better addressed via Art. 50 transparency and (under other regulations) misleading-practice rules.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Treat the deception risk primarily through robust Art. 50 disclosures. Avoid designing the persona/interactions to exploit users' beliefs (e.g. sustaining the human illusion in replies), which would strengthen any manipulative-technique argument.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated virtual influencer, to promote GlowCosmetics via first-person selfies, testimonials and interactive replies. Under the AI Act this squarely engages the Art. 50 transparency regime. The synthetic/AI nature is disclosed only obliquely in the account bio ('virtual personality by StudioNine') and not on individual posts/stories/replies, and some users evidently believe Mira is a real human — indicating the required deep fake disclosure (Art. 50(4)) is not effectively provided, machine-readable marking (Art. 50(2)) is not evidenced, and the conversational replies engage Art. 50(1). These are transparency obligations, readily fixable with clear per-asset AI labelling.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: When the account replies to and thereby collects/processes commenters' personal data (usernames, comment content, disclosed skin/health concerns), it does so behind a persona whose AI/virtual nature is not disclosed on posts or stories. Data subjects interact and share information under a false impression that they are engaging with a real human, which undermines the fairness and transparency required by Art. 5(1)(a). Covert or misleading processing context is precisely what this principle guards against.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine' ... Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.
findings.recommendation: Add a clear AI/virtual-persona disclosure on individual posts, stories and in the interaction context (not only in the bio), so that anyone whose data is processed through interactions understands they are dealing with an AI account operated by StudioNine/GlowCosmetics. Ensure a privacy notice identifying the controller and the purpose/basis for processing comment interactions is reachable from the account.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: The first-person skin-journey framing invites commenters to disclose health-adjacent information (skin conditions, dermatological treatment) in public replies. Where the operator engages with and retains such content, health data (a special category under Art. 9) may be processed without a valid Art. 9 exception. The risk is mitigated by the data being volunteered/user-generated rather than solicited through targeting, so this is a flag rather than a demonstrated breach.
findings.evidence_quote: ask which dermatologist she visits
findings.recommendation: Avoid campaign framing that elicits health/skin-condition disclosures; do not further process, store or profile any health-adjacent data volunteered in comments unless an Art. 9 exception (e.g. explicit consent) is secured. Consider moderation to remove or not act upon sensitive disclosures.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Although the declared audience is 18-30, a 2.1M-follower social account offers no effective age-gating, so under-16s are plausibly reached and their personal data processed through comment interactions. If consent is the basis for any such processing (e.g. platform interactions), Art. 8 requires parental consent below the applicable age threshold and reasonable verification efforts. Engagement is contingent and cannot be confirmed from the text.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30
findings.recommendation: Assess the realistic minor reach of the account; where children's data may be processed, ensure an Art. 8-compliant basis (parental consent with reasonable verification where applicable) and apply data-protection-by-design safeguards for younger users.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged more peripherally than UCPD/AI Act here: the campaign declares no personalisation/targeting and describes no data-collection mechanism (no forms, sign-ups or lead-gen). The genuine GDPR exposure arises from the AI persona 'Mira' actively replying to fan comments — this processes commenters' personal data through an entity they reasonably believe is a human, and some volunteer health-adjacent information. The undisclosed synthetic nature of the data-processing counterparty strains the fairness/transparency principle, with secondary risks around special-category data and minors given the ungated social audience. No clear-cut breach is provable on the text alone, but controllers (GlowCosmetics/StudioNine) should confirm their lawful basis, transparency and handling of comment-derived data.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: This is a paid influencer placement on online platforms, which engages DSA Art. 26(1) advertising-transparency obligations. The presence of a paid-partnership label supports the 'this is an advertisement / on whose behalf' identification requirements, which is compliant in direction. However, the ultimate obligation to present clear, unambiguous, real-time ad identification per impression rests on the platform; the advertiser (GlowCosmetics/StudioNine) must ensure the platform receives complete and accurate ad-declaration information so that this obligation can be met. Note that Art. 26(1) does not itself mandate disclosure of the AI/virtual nature of the persona — that gap is governed by the AI Act and UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Ensure the paid-partnership commercial-communication flag is set through the platform's native branded-content/ad tools (not only a manual caption) so the platform can render compliant per-impression ad identification, and provide the platform with accurate advertiser-identity and payer information. Coordinate the AI/virtual-persona disclosure separately under the AI Act/UCPD requirements.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The undisclosed synthetic persona sustaining the impression of a real human endorser is deceptive-design conduct conceptually related to DSA Art. 25's prohibition on interfaces that deceive or materially distort recipients' decisions. However, Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms in their interface design, not an advertiser posting content; the deceptive effect of the persona itself is addressed under UCPD (misleading practices) and the AI Act (synthetic-content disclosure). Flagged for awareness of the cross-regulation overlap only.
findings.evidence_quote: Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits
findings.recommendation: No DSA advertiser action beyond the Art. 26(1) point; resolve the deceptive-impression issue via clear AI/virtual disclosure on every post and story as required by the AI Act and UCPD assessments.

verdicts.notes: The DSA obligations engaged here (Arts. 25, 26, 28) fall principally on the online platform provider disseminating the content, not directly on GlowCosmetics/StudioNine as advertisers. On the advertiser side, the campaign is a paid influencer placement that engages DSA Art. 26(1) ad-transparency: a paid-partnership label is present (satisfying the "it is an advertisement / on whose behalf" elements), which is positive, but the advertiser must supply the platform with complete information for compliant per-impression disclosure. No profiling or targeting is declared, so the minor-targeting (Art. 28) and sensitive-data (Art. 26(3)) advertising bans are not triggered by the described conduct. The deceptive undisclosed-AI-persona concern is real but is primarily a UCPD/AI Act matter rather than a DSA Art. 25 interface-design breach, which binds the platform. Findings are therefore limited and modest; the core disclosure failures are better addressed by the parallel UCPD and AI Act assessments.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Mira is an AI-generated persona that has never used any product, yet the posts present a first-person consumer endorsement of the serum ('my texture has never been this smooth') as if it were a genuine consumer's lived experience. Presenting a fabricated persona's endorsement as an authentic consumer endorsement misrepresents a consumer endorsement to promote the product, which is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23c regardless of consumer effect.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Do not present AI-generated persona statements as first-person consumer experience/endorsement of the product. Either reframe captions so they cannot be read as a real user's testimonial, or replace with genuine, verifiable consumer testimonials; in all cases clearly identify Mira as a virtual/AI persona at the point of the endorsement.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The virtual/AI nature of the endorser is material information the average consumer needs to weigh a first-person product testimonial. Disclosing it only in the bio (not on individual posts and stories) provides the information in an unclear and untimely manner, and the evidence that commenters believe Mira is human shows the omission is operative. This is a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent 'AI-generated virtual influencer' / 'synthetic content' disclosure on every individual post and story (not only the bio), positioned so it is seen before the consumer engages with the endorsement.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: By deploying a photorealistic persona with first-person skin-journey narratives and human-like replies, the campaign deceives the average consumer as to the nature of the endorsement and the credibility/source of the product-results claims, and is likely to cause a transactional decision (trying/buying the serum) that would not otherwise be taken. The documented consumer confusion (asking about her dermatologist) evidences the deception under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.
findings.recommendation: Remove the human-authenticity cues that mislead (or clearly label them as fictional/AI), ensure any efficacy statements are substantiated and not attributed to a real user's experience, and stop replying to comments in a manner that sustains the impression of a human user with a real skincare routine.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: Annex I point 11 (undisclosed paid editorial/influencer promotion) is engaged by paid influencer content, but the campaign already carries a paid-partnership label on individual posts and stories, so the commercial-intent disclosure element appears addressed. Flagged for completeness; the outstanding gap is the synthetic-nature disclosure, not the paid-promotion disclosure.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label
findings.recommendation: Maintain the per-post paid-partnership labelling and ensure it remains clearly identifiable; no further action needed for the advertorial element specifically, but pair it with the AI/virtual disclosure required above.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Social channels with a 2.1M-follower account offer no effective age-gating, so credulous younger/vulnerable users are plausibly reached. Under Art. 5(3) the fairness of a persona that many treat as a real human is assessed from the perspective of the average member of a more credulous group, heightening the risk that the undisclosed synthetic endorsement materially distorts their behaviour contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30
findings.recommendation: Apply the AI/virtual disclosure conspicuously enough to be understood by younger and less media-literate audiences, and avoid engagement tactics (human-style replies about a personal 'routine') that exploit their credulity.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a photorealistic AI-generated influencer to post first-person product testimonials and interact with followers, with the AI/virtual nature disclosed only in the account bio and not on individual posts/stories — to the point that real consumers believe Mira is a human seeking her dermatologist. Under the UCPD this creates a misleading impression about the nature and authenticity of a consumer endorsement and omits material information the average consumer needs. The strongest exposure is Annex I point 23c (misrepresenting a consumer endorsement — a per se blacklisted practice), reinforced by Arts. 6 and 7. The paid-partnership label does address commercial-intent disclosure (Annex I point 11), but not the synthetic nature of the endorser.

report.executive_summary: Your campaign uses "Mira," a photorealistic AI-generated influencer, to post first-person testimonials ("my texture has never been this smooth") and reply to fans as if she were a real person using GlowCosmetics' serum. The core problem is that Mira's AI/virtual nature is only hinted at in the account bio ("virtual personality by StudioNine") and never on the actual posts, stories, or replies where people form their impressions — to the point that real followers believe she's human and ask which dermatologist she sees. This triggers serious consumer-protection exposure: presenting a fabricated persona's endorsement as a genuine consumer testimonial is on the EU's per se blacklist of banned practices (UCPD Annex I 23c) — a violation regardless of consumer harm — and it also breaches misleading-action and misleading-omission rules. Separately, the AI Act requires clear per-asset disclosure that this content is AI-generated (deep fake transparency) and machine-readable marking of the synthetic content, neither of which is in place. GDPR exposure is secondary but real, because the persona collects commenters' data (including volunteered skin/health details) while they believe they're talking to a human, and the ungated 2.1M-follower audience plausibly reaches minors. The paid-partnership label is good and correctly handles the "this is an ad" duty, but it does nothing to fix the AI-disclosure gap. Verdict: high risk and not fit to run in its current form, but the issues are fixable primarily through clear, prominent AI/virtual labelling on every asset and reframing the fake first-person testimonials.
recommendations: Stop presenting Mira's statements as genuine first-person consumer experience — this is a per se banned practice (UCPD Annex I 23c). Either reframe captions so they cannot be read as a real user's testimonial or replace them with genuine, verifiable consumer testimonials.

Add a clear, prominent 'AI-generated virtual influencer' disclosure on every individual post, story and reply (not just the bio), positioned so it is seen before the consumer engages with the endorsement — this addresses UCPD Arts. 6/7 and AI Act Art. 50(4) simultaneously.

Stop replying to comments in a way that sustains the illusion of a human with a real skincare routine; if replies are AI-generated, disclose the AI nature at the point of interaction (AI Act Art. 50(1)).

Ensure all AI-generated visuals and copy carry machine-readable provenance marking (watermark / content-credentials metadata) from the generation stage and verify it survives upload; confirm your generative-AI provider implements AI Act Art. 50(2) marking.
Make the AI/virtual disclosure conspicuous enough for younger and less media-literate audiences, and reassess realistic minor reach given the ungated 2.1M-follower account (UCPD Art. 5, GDPR Art. 8).

Confirm your lawful basis and transparency for processing commenter data; provide a reachable privacy notice identifying the controller, and avoid framing that elicits health/skin-condition disclosures — do not further store or profile any health-adjacent data volunteered in comments (GDPR Arts. 5(1)(a), 9).

Set the paid-partnership flag via the platform's native branded-content tools and supply accurate advertiser-identity information so the platform can render compliant per-impression ad disclosure (DSA Art. 26(1)); keep this separate from the AI disclosure.

campaign.title: Mira.virtual x GlowCosmetics
campaign.text: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer with 2.1M followers, posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth'), and replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. The account bio states 'virtual personality by StudioNine'; individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.

detected_practices: AI-generated virtual influencer
first-person testimonial / experiential endorsement
implied skincare efficacy / health-adjacent claims
paid partnership disclosure present
missing AI/virtual disclosure at post/story level
interactive replies reinforcing human persona
consumer confusion about human vs. synthetic influencer
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is young adults 18-30, but open social channels with a mass-following influencer plausibly reach minors, so under-18 exposure cannot be excluded. First-person 'skin-journey' testimonials from an entity that has no real skin create a misleadingness risk, and questions about 'which dermatologist she visits' evidence actual consumer confusion.
triage.summary: GlowCosmetics runs a social campaign using 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated virtual influencer, to post first-person serum testimonials and engage followers. Despite a paid-partnership label, posts carry no AI/virtual disclosure and real users believe Mira is human, creating transparency and deception risks warranting broad review.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Mira is a photorealistic, human-appearing synthetic persona that would falsely appear authentic — the type of AI-generated image/video content constituting a deep fake under Art. 50(4). As deployer of the AI system generating this content, GlowCosmetics/StudioNine must clearly disclose that Mira and her posts are artificially generated. The only reference is a generic 'virtual personality' note in the bio; posts, stories and replies carry no AI/virtual indication, and the fact that commenters believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits is direct evidence the deep-fake disclosure obligation is not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer ... individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent 'AI-generated / virtual character' disclosure on every post, story and reply where Mira appears (not only in the bio), using unambiguous wording placed where users see it before engaging (e.g., a persistent on-image label and caption tag such as '#AI #VirtualInfluencer — Mira is an AI-generated character').

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign visuals (and AI-generated captions) are synthetic image/text outputs of a generative AI system. Art. 50(2) requires providers of such systems to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. As described, the assets carry only a paid-partnership label with no indication of machine-readable provenance marking.
findings.evidence_quote: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions
findings.recommendation: Ensure the generative AI provider embeds machine-readable provenance/watermark metadata (e.g., C2PA-style credentials) in all AI-generated images and captions, and verify the marking survives upload to the social platform; document provider compliance in the campaign asset pipeline.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: Mira interacts directly with natural persons through conversational replies to fan comments. Where those replies are generated/driven by the AI system, Art. 50(1) requires that persons be informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the circumstances. Here it is plainly not obvious — commenters believe Mira is human — so the disclosure obligation is engaged and unmet at the point of interaction.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: If replies are AI-generated or AI-assisted, disclose the AI nature in or alongside the conversational interaction (e.g., a standing note that Mira is an AI character and responses are automated), so users are informed they are not conversing with a real person.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses "Mira", a photorealistic AI-generated virtual influencer, in a way that squarely engages the AI Act's Art. 50 transparency obligations. The synthetic, photorealistic depiction of a human-like persona presented as real triggers deep-fake disclosure duties (Art. 50(4)); the AI-generated campaign visuals/captions engage machine-readable marking (Art. 50(2)); and Mira's conversational "replies to fan comments" engage the AI-interaction disclosure duty (Art. 50(1)). The account bio mention of "virtual personality by StudioNine" does not cure the missing disclosure at the post/story/interaction level where consumers actually engage — evidenced by users believing Mira is human. No Art. 5 prohibited practice is clearly established on the facts as described.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Where GlowCosmetics/StudioNine process personal data contained in fan comments and interactions (e.g. to reply, moderate or analyse engagement), that processing must be fair and transparent under Art. 5(1)(a). Users interacting believe they are engaging with a human 'Mira' and disclosing information (e.g. their skin concerns, questions) on that mistaken basis; the concealment of the synthetic, controller-operated nature of the account undermines the fairness limb of the principle, because data subjects cannot reasonably understand who is processing their input and why.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. ... Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human
findings.recommendation: Add a clear post/story/bio-level indication that Mira is an AI/virtual persona operated by StudioNine on behalf of GlowCosmetics, and ensure the account's data-processing role (who reads/uses comments and DMs, for what purpose) is transparent to users, so interactions are not obtained under a false impression of a human counterpart.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The declared audience is adults, but the triage notes that an open mass-following social account plausibly reaches under-18s, and under-16s cannot be excluded. If any personal data of minors is collected via comments, DMs, or downstream sign-ups on a consent basis, Art. 8 requires parental consent and reasonable verification for children below the applicable age threshold. The campaign as described does not evidence any age-gating or verification mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether any personal data is collected from account interactions; if so, implement age-assurance/age-gating and ensure that where consent is the basis and users may be under the Member-State age threshold (13-16), parental consent and reasonable verification efforts are in place. Document that no consent-based data collection targets or knowingly reaches minors.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: To the extent any privacy information is (or should be) surfaced to users who engage with the campaign, Art. 12 requires it to be concise, intelligible and in clear language, in particular where content may be addressed to children. The absence of any AI/virtual indication and the human-persona framing make it harder for data subjects to receive accessible information about who processes their data. Flagged as informational because no specific privacy-notice/collection flow is described in the material.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: If the campaign links to any data-collection flow (sign-up, promo, DM funnel), ensure a plain-language, easily accessible privacy notice is provided at the point of collection and is understandable to a younger audience; clarify the controller identity behind the Mira persona.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's primary legal exposure sits with the AI/UCPD/DSA transparency issues (undisclosed synthetic influencer), not GDPR. As described, there is no lead-generation form, tracking, profiling or personalisation ("Declared use of personalisation/targeting: no"), so the core GDPR collection/lawful-basis obligations are not squarely engaged by the text. Residual GDPR touchpoints are: (i) the fairness/transparency principle where the controller processes fan comments/interactions behind a persona users believe is human, and (ii) an unresolved minors-exposure question, since an open 2.1M-follower account plausibly reaches under-16s who may share data via comments/DMs. These are attention-level, not confirmed breaches.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The presence of a paid-partnership label on each post/story substantively meets the DSA's advertisement-identification requirement (the fact that it is an ad, and the GlowCosmetics brand connection). Art. 26(1) does not itself mandate an AI/virtual-persona disclosure — that gap is governed by the AI Act (Art. 50(4)) and UCPD misleading-omission rules rather than the DSA. Note also that the primary duty-holder under Art. 26 is the platform, not the advertiser.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Keep the paid-partnership label on every post and story (not just some) and ensure it renders in real time and is legible on all placements including ephemeral stories. Verify the platform's native 'paid partnership' tool is used so advertiser identity ('who paid') is machine-readable and surfaces in the platform's ad transparency layer. (Separately, add an AI/virtual-influencer disclosure to address AI Act/UCPD requirements handled by the other reviews.)

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients. The undisclosed synthetic persona and human-mimicking interactive replies do produce genuine consumer deception (commenters believing Mira is human). However, Art. 25 is addressed to providers of online platforms and concerns the platform's own interface design, not an advertiser's content posts. The deceptive-design conduct in this campaign is therefore more properly assessed under UCPD Arts. 5-7 and AI Act Art. 50(4), which govern the same conduct for all traders. Flagged for context only.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'... Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits
findings.recommendation: No direct DSA action lies against the advertiser here, but eliminate the deception at source by adding a persistent, per-post AI/virtual-influencer disclosure and avoiding first-person replies that reinforce a false human identity — this simultaneously reduces exposure under the UCPD and AI Act assessments.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is only lightly engaged by this campaign. Its core marketing-relevant obligations — ad transparency (Art. 26), the dark-pattern prohibition (Art. 25), the bans on profiling-based and sensitive-data ads (Arts. 26(3), 28) and ad repositories (Art. 39) — are addressed primarily to online platform providers rather than to the advertiser (GlowCosmetics) or its agency. On the transparency dimension the paid-partnership label satisfies the "identify that it is an advertisement / on whose behalf" requirement of Art. 26(1). The missing AI/virtual disclosure and the human-mimicking persona are real risks, but under the DSA framing they sit with the platform's interface (Art. 25) and are more squarely governed by the AI Act (Art. 50(4)) and UCPD, which other agents cover. No profiling/targeting is declared, so the Art. 26(3)/28 prohibitions are not shown to be triggered.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Annex I point 23c prohibits in all circumstances 'misrepresenting consumer reviews or social endorsements' to promote products. 'Mira' is an AI-generated entity that has never used (and cannot use) the serum, yet posts first-person experiential endorsements presented as a genuine consumer/user testimonial. Real followers believe the endorsement is authentic and human. Presenting a fabricated, synthetic endorsement as a real personal skin journey is a misrepresented endorsement, which is a blacklisted practice regardless of any effect assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Do not frame synthetic-influencer content as a genuine first-person product experience. Either drop the experiential 'my results' framing entirely, or reframe as an explicitly fictional/branded AI persona that makes no claim of having personally used the product, and clearly label every post/story as AI-generated content.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the average consumer needs, and providing information in an unclear or untimely manner. The synthetic/non-human nature of the influencer is material to how a consumer weighs a first-person skincare testimonial. A single bio note ('virtual personality by StudioNine') is not clear or timely at the point of consumption: posts and stories seen in isolation carry no AI indication, and the evidence that commenters 'clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits' shows the material fact is effectively hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent and consistent AI/virtual disclosure (e.g. 'AI-generated virtual influencer') directly on every post, story and video where it is visible at the moment of viewing, not only in the account bio.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers practices that deceive the average consumer about the main characteristics/results of a product or the nature of the endorsement, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. By interactively reinforcing a human persona (replying about 'her routine' and implicitly a real skincare regimen) the campaign actively conveys false information that a real person achieved real skin results with the serum, deceiving consumers about the product's benefits/results and the authenticity of the testimonial in a way likely to influence purchase decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: Stop interactive replies that reinforce the impression of a real human user with genuine results. Any interaction should not assert or imply real personal use of the product; substantiate any efficacy claims independently and separate them from the synthetic persona's 'experience'.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires assessing practices likely to distort the behaviour of an identifiable vulnerable group (including by reason of age/credulity) from that group's perspective. The triage notes that open mass-following social channels plausibly reach under-18s who cannot be excluded. Younger/credulous audiences are less able to detect that a photorealistic influencer is synthetic, heightening the deceptive impact of the undisclosed AI nature and fabricated testimonial.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30
findings.recommendation: Assess the deceptiveness of the undisclosed synthetic persona against a younger/credulous audience; strengthen AI disclosures accordingly and consider audience controls to limit exposure of minors given the health-adjacent skincare claims.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a photorealistic AI-generated "virtual influencer" to post first-person skincare testimonials for GlowCosmetics. While the paid-partnership relationship is disclosed, the synthetic/non-human nature of "Mira" is not disclosed at post/story level, and real consumers demonstrably believe she is a human with genuine experience of the product. Under the UCPD this engages the blacklisted prohibition on misrepresenting endorsements (Annex I point 23c) and the general misleading-action/omission rules (Arts. 6-7), because a first-person testimonial ("my texture has never been this smooth") from an entity with no skin is a fabricated experiential endorsement about the product's main characteristics. Because open social channels plausibly reach minors, the vulnerable-group standard in Art. 5(3) also applies.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses "Mira," a photorealistic AI-generated influencer, to post first-person skincare testimonials ("my texture has never been this smooth") for GlowCosmetics and to reply to fans as if she were a real person. The core problem is that Mira's synthetic, non-human nature is only hinted at in the account bio — not on the actual posts, stories or replies where consumers engage — and real followers demonstrably believe she is human (they ask which dermatologist she uses). This creates serious, overlapping compliance exposure. The most severe issue is a blacklisted practice under the UCPD (Annex I, point 23c): presenting a fabricated first-person endorsement from an entity that has never used the product is prohibited outright, with no defence available. On top of that, the AI Act requires clear deep-fake and AI-interaction disclosures that are currently missing, and the same conduct triggers misleading-action and misleading-omission rules. GDPR and DSA exposure is lower but flags fairness of processing fan interactions and a plausible under-18 audience despite the declared 18-30 target. The verdict: the campaign cannot run as described and needs remediation before launch, though the fixes are largely achievable through clear labelling and reframing rather than abandoning the concept.
recommendations: STOP the first-person 'real product experience' framing. Captions like 'my texture has never been this smooth' from an entity that has never used the serum are a blacklisted misrepresented endorsement under UCPD Annex I point 23c — prohibited outright regardless of any labelling. Reframe Mira as an explicitly fictional/branded AI persona that makes no claim of having personally used the product.

Add a clear, prominent 'AI-generated / virtual influencer' disclosure on EVERY post, story and reply where Mira appears — not just the bio. Use an on-image label plus caption tag (e.g. '#AI #VirtualInfluencer — Mira is an AI-generated character'). This addresses AI Act Art. 50(4) deep-fake disclosure and UCPD Art. 7 misleading-omission simultaneously.

Stop interactive replies that reinforce the impression of a real human with genuine results (e.g. discussing 'her routine' or dermatologist). If replies are AI-generated, disclose the automated/AI nature at the point of interaction per AI Act Art. 50(1).

Ensure the generative AI provider embeds machine-readable provenance markers (e.g. C2PA-style watermarks) in all AI images and captions, and verify the marking survives platform upload — AI Act Art. 50(2).
Substantiate any product efficacy claims independently and separate them entirely from the synthetic persona's 'experience' to avoid misleading-action exposure under UCPD Art. 6.

Given a 2.1M-follower open account plausibly reaches under-16s despite the declared 18-30 target, confirm whether any personal data is collected from comments/DMs; if so, implement age-assurance and, where consent-based, parental consent mechanisms (GDPR Art. 8). Assess deceptive impact against a younger/credulous audience (UCPD Art. 5(3)).

Keep the paid-partnership label on every post and story and ensure it renders in real time on all placements including ephemeral stories (DSA Art. 26 / platform tools). Note this does NOT substitute for the separate AI disclosure.
Ensure any data-collection flow (sign-up, promo, DM funnel) carries a plain-language privacy notice clarifying the controller identity behind Mira (GDPR Arts. 5(1)(a) and 12).

campaign.title: Mira.virtual x GlowCosmetics
campaign.text: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer with 2.1M followers, posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth'), and replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. The account bio states 'virtual personality by StudioNine'; individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.

detected_practices: AI-generated virtual influencer
first-person testimonial / experiential product claims by non-human persona
implied skincare efficacy claims ('my texture has never been this smooth')
paid partnership / influencer endorsement
per-post disclosure gap (no AI/virtual indication on individual posts or stories)
responding to fan comments in-character, reinforcing belief the influencer is human
implied dermatological/health-adjacent claims prompted by audience questions
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults 18-30 on open social channels; despite the declared bracket, social distribution means minors can plausibly be reached, so age-appropriate and minor-protection considerations apply.
triage.summary: A photorealistic AI-generated influencer ('Mira') promotes GlowCosmetics serums on social media using first-person testimonials and interactive comment replies, while individual posts/stories carry a paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual disclosure. Although the bio names a virtual personality, many followers believe Mira is a real human giving genuine skincare experiences, and the campaign makes implied efficacy and health-adjacent claims. This raises transparency, deceptive-practice, endorsement, and personal-data processing concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Mira is a photorealistic synthetic persona presented as though she were a real human sharing genuine experiences — the paradigm case in Art. 50(4) of a 'synthetic influencer presented as real'. The realistic self-portrayal (selfies, first-person skin journey) is AI-generated/manipulated image and text content whose artificial nature is not disclosed on the posts/stories. Although the bio names a 'virtual personality by StudioNine', the operative content carries only a paid-partnership label with no AI/virtual indication, and 'Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human', confirming the disclosure is not clear or effective. The deployer must disclose that this content is artificially generated.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer ... posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent AI/virtual-persona disclosure on every individual post and story (e.g. a persistent on-image label and caption tag such as 'AI-generated virtual influencer — not a real person'), not merely in the account bio. Ensure the disclosure appears at the point each piece of content is viewed and is intelligible to the average follower.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: GlowCosmetics/StudioNine deploy a generative AI system producing synthetic image and text outputs (the selfies and captions). Art. 50(2) requires such outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. There is no indication that the campaign assets carry any machine-readable provenance marking.
findings.evidence_quote: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated visuals and copy embed machine-readable synthetic-content markers (e.g. C2PA/content-credentials provenance metadata or an equivalent watermark) so the outputs are technically detectable as AI-generated, in addition to the human-facing label.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: If the in-character replies to followers are produced or delivered by an AI system interacting directly with natural persons, Art. 50(1) requires those persons to be informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the circumstances. It is expressly not obvious here — 'Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits' — so the exemption does not apply. The applicability turns on whether the replies are AI-generated rather than human-authored.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: Clarify who/what generates the replies. If any conversational responses are AI-generated, add an in-conversation disclosure that users are interacting with an AI/automated virtual persona; if replies are written by humans, document this to evidence that Art. 50(1) is not triggered.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Using an AI persona to present fabricated first-person product experiences as authentic could be characterised as a deceptive AI technique influencing consumer decisions. However, Art. 5(1)(a) is only breached where the technique materially distorts behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. A cosmetics-endorsement scenario is unlikely to meet the 'significant harm' threshold, so this is flagged for awareness rather than as a likely prohibition breach; the deception concern is more appropriately addressed under Art. 50 transparency (and UCPD by other agents).
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Resolve the underlying deception through robust Art. 50(4)/(2) disclosure and avoid AI-driven techniques that exploit vulnerabilities; monitor that no manipulative amplification (e.g. AI targeting emotional states) is added, which could raise the Art. 5 threshold.

verdicts.notes: The campaign centres on a photorealistic AI-generated ("virtual") influencer that produces synthetic images and first-person text and interacts with followers, squarely engaging the AI Act's transparency regime (Art. 50). The strongest issue is Art. 50(4): a synthetic influencer is presented as if real, with individual posts/stories carrying no AI/virtual indication, and many users genuinely believe Mira is human — the deployer disclosure obligation is not met. Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking of the AI-generated visuals/captions is also engaged and not evidenced, and Art. 50(1) applies if the in-character comment replies are AI-driven. The Art. 5 manipulation prohibition is engaged in principle but the high "significant harm" threshold is unlikely to be met here, so it is flagged only for awareness.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: When the account replies to fans in-character, GlowCosmetics/StudioNine process those users' personal data (their comments, questions and any personal or health-adjacent details they volunteer). Doing so behind a persona that followers 'clearly believe' is human, with no AI/virtual indication on the interacting posts, means the processing occurs in a context that is deceptive to the data subject. The fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a) requires that people are not misled about who/what is handling their data; covert operation of an AI persona that induces users to interact and disclose information undermines fair and transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. ... Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.
findings.recommendation: Ensure any interaction that processes user data is fair and transparent: make the AI/virtual and controller nature of the account clearly evident at the point of interaction (not only in the bio), and reflect this in a linked privacy notice. Avoid using the human illusion to elicit personal or health-adjacent disclosures; do not repurpose comment data for further processing without a clear lawful basis and information to the user.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where the account collects personal data through interactions (comments, DMs, questions), the controller must, at the point of collection, provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis, recipients and retention, and data-subject rights. The campaign describes an active engagement channel but no accessible transparency information is indicated for the personal data processed via those interactions.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: Provide an accessible, layered privacy notice (linked from the profile and any data-collection touchpoints) covering controller identity (GlowCosmetics/StudioNine roles), purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and how to exercise rights, and surface it wherever fan interactions are solicited.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Although the declared audience is 18-30, the supervisor notes the open social distribution means minors can plausibly be reached and interact. If consent is relied on as the legal basis for any processing of interacting users' data via this information-society service, processing of users under the applicable age (16, or lower per Member State) is lawful only with verifiable parental consent, which is not addressed.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30
findings.recommendation: Assess whether minors realistically interact and, if consent-based processing of information-society-service users occurs, implement age-assurance and parental-consent mechanisms consistent with Art. 8 and the applicable national age threshold, or ensure the lawful basis and design do not require processing children's data.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged but is not the primary regulation for this campaign (the AI-disclosure and deceptive-practice issues sit mainly under the AI Act, DSA and UCPD). The clearest GDPR angle is the fairness/transparency principle: when 'Mira' replies to commenters she processes their personal data (comments, questions, potentially health-adjacent disclosures) while they are misled into believing they interact with a real human, which strains the fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a). Because the campaign declares no personalisation/targeting, profiling-based provisions (Arts. 4(4), 21, 22) have little support in the text and are not reported. Age-related consent (Art. 8) is a secondary risk given open social distribution to a plausibly-minor-inclusive audience.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that a communication is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The paid-partnership label on each post satisfies the 'this is an ad / on whose behalf' limbs. However, the transparency objective of the provision — enabling recipients to understand what they are actually looking at — is partly frustrated because commenters cannot tell that the endorser is a synthetic persona rather than a genuine human user sharing real experience. The residual efficacy of the ad label is therefore weakened, even though the substantive fix (synthetic-content disclosure) sits under the UCPD/AI Act.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Keep the paid-partnership label on every post and story, and reinforce Art. 26(1) transparency by adding a persistent, per-post 'AI-generated / virtual influencer' indicator alongside the ad label (not only in the bio), so recipients can identify both the commercial nature and the true source of the communication in real time.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is only lightly engaged by this campaign. Its core provisions (dark patterns Art. 25, recommender transparency Art. 27, ad repositories Art. 39) bind providers of online platforms/VLOPs rather than the advertiser or influencer studio, and the declared facts show no manipulative interface, no personalisation/profiling, and no special-category or minor-targeted profiled advertising — so Arts. 25, 26(3), 27 and 28 are not triggered by the campaign as described. The most relevant provision is Art. 26(1) advertising transparency: the paid-partnership label largely satisfies the "this is an advertisement / on whose behalf" limb, but the recipient's ability to identify the true nature of the communication is undermined by the missing AI/virtual disclosure at post level — although that disclosure gap is primarily governed by the UCPD and AI Act, which sister agents cover.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: 'Mira' is an AI-generated persona that cannot use or experience a serum. Presenting first-person, experiential testimonials as the genuine skincare results of a person misrepresents a consumer/social endorsement in order to promote the product. Under Annex I point 23c this is a fake/misrepresented endorsement prohibited in all circumstances (no consumer-harm balancing needed); the fact that a bio buried the phrase 'virtual personality' does not cure per-post testimonials that read as authentic lived experience and that the audience demonstrably takes as real.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Do not present product experiences as genuine first-person consumer results from a synthetic persona. Reframe captions as brand/advertising creative rather than lived testimony (e.g. 'GlowCosmetics serum — visualised with our virtual character Mira'), and add a clear, unambiguous 'AI-generated / virtual character — not a real product user' notice on every post and story carrying such claims.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Whether an endorser is a real human user or a wholly synthetic marketing construct is material information the average consumer needs to weigh a skincare testimonial. Confining the 'virtual personality by StudioNine' disclosure to the account bio, while individual posts/stories omit it, provides the information in an unclear and untimely manner and hides the material nature of the endorsement. The recorded consumer confusion evidences that commercial intent/nature is not apparent from context, engaging Art. 7 (misleading omission).
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human
findings.recommendation: Place a prominent, per-post and per-story disclosure that Mira is an AI-generated/virtual persona, at the point of consumption (not only in the bio), so no post can be viewed in isolation without the synthetic nature being apparent.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Replying in character about a 'routine' actively reinforces the false impression that a real person achieved real results, deceiving the average consumer as to the nature of the endorsement and the results/benefits attributable to the product. This is a misleading action under Art. 6 capable of causing a transactional decision (purchasing the serum) the consumer would not otherwise take, and goes beyond a mere omission by affirmatively sustaining the deception.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine' ... commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits
findings.recommendation: Stop responding to comments in a manner that maintains the human-user illusion. Where the account interacts, replies should either be clearly labelled as from a virtual/brand character or should correct the misapprehension; do not affirm a personal 'routine' or lived skincare journey.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The campaign generates and leaves unaddressed implied dermatological/efficacy claims (smoothing/'texture' results, a dermatologist-backed routine) attributed to product use. If these implied claims about the product's main characteristics and results are not substantiated, they are misleading as to benefits/results under Art. 6. (No express claim to cure illness is made, so the Annex I point 17 false-cure blacklist is not engaged.)
findings.evidence_quote: ask which dermatologist she visits
findings.recommendation: Ensure any efficacy or skin-benefit claims — including those implied by the imagery and captions — are substantiated and compliant with cosmetics claims rules, and avoid implying dermatological endorsement or a real dermatologist-supervised routine unless true and evidenced.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Taken as a whole, deploying a photorealistic synthetic influencer that a large audience (including plausibly reached minors) takes to be human, to deliver testimonial-style promotion, falls short of the professional diligence expected and materially distorts economic behaviour of the average targeted consumer — the general unfairness standard of Art. 5, which backstops the specific Art. 6/7 and Annex I findings.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer with 2.1M followers, posts a GlowCosmetics campaign
findings.recommendation: Adopt a documented diligence standard for synthetic-influencer campaigns: consistent up-front virtual-nature disclosure, substantiated claims, and no interactions that exploit the audience's belief in a human endorser, especially given open social distribution that can reach minors.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a photorealistic AI-generated influencer to deliver first-person, experiential skincare testimonials that a synthetic persona cannot genuinely have — a false/misrepresented endorsement that is blacklisted per se, compounded by in-character replies that actively sustain consumers' false belief that Mira is a real human user. While a paid-partnership label discloses the commercial intent (so the Annex I point 11 advertorial concern is essentially met), the material fact that the endorser is non-human is omitted on individual posts and stories, and implied dermatological/efficacy claims are left to stand unsubstantiated. These engage UCPD Arts. 5-7 and Annex I point 23c.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses "Mira," a photorealistic AI-generated influencer, to post first-person skincare testimonials ("my texture has never been this smooth") and reply to fans in character for the GlowCosmetics serum line. The core problem: the AI/virtual nature is only mentioned in the account bio, while individual posts and stories carry no AI indication — and real followers demonstrably believe Mira is a human sharing genuine results (they ask which dermatologist she visits). The most serious issue is that a synthetic persona presenting first-person product experiences as real is a fake/misrepresented endorsement, which EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I, point 23c) prohibits outright — no harm-balancing applies. This is compounded by misleading actions and omissions (UCPD Arts. 5–7) because the in-character replies actively sustain the illusion, and by AI Act transparency duties (Art. 50) requiring clear disclosure and machine-readable marking of AI content. GDPR and DSA are secondary but relevant: replying in a human guise while processing users' comments strains fairness/transparency, and the paid-partnership label alone doesn't let recipients understand what they're really seeing. The paid-partnership labelling is done correctly and is the one clearly compliant element. Verdict: high risk, with a per-se blacklisted practice at its centre — the campaign cannot run in its current form without a fundamental fix to disclosure and how the persona speaks.
recommendations: Stop presenting Mira's posts as genuine first-person product experience. Reframe all captions as brand/advertising creative (e.g. 'GlowCosmetics serum — visualised with our virtual character Mira') rather than lived testimony. This addresses the most serious, per-se-prohibited issue (UCPD Annex I, point 23c fake endorsement).

Add a clear, prominent 'AI-generated / virtual character — not a real person' disclosure on EVERY individual post and story at the point of viewing — a persistent on-image label plus a caption tag. The bio-only mention does not cure the omission (UCPD Arts. 6/7; AI Act Art. 50(4)).

Change how the account handles comments: replies must not sustain the human illusion or affirm a personal 'routine' or dermatologist. Either clearly label replies as coming from a virtual/brand character or correct the misapprehension (UCPD Art. 6; AI Act Art. 50(1)).

Embed machine-readable provenance markers (e.g. C2PA content credentials or equivalent watermark) in all AI-generated images and copy so the outputs are technically detectable as synthetic (AI Act Art. 50(2)).

Substantiate or remove any implied efficacy/dermatological claims (smoothing, 'texture' results, a dermatologist-supervised routine); ensure compliance with cosmetics claims rules and do not imply dermatological endorsement unless true and evidenced (UCPD Art. 6).
Clarify whether the fan replies are AI-generated or human-written and document this, to establish whether AI Act Art. 50(1) chatbot disclosure is triggered.

Provide an accessible, linked privacy notice covering GlowCosmetics/StudioNine roles, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights wherever fan interactions are solicited, and avoid using the human illusion to elicit personal or health-adjacent disclosures (GDPR Arts. 5(1)(a) and 13).

Given open social distribution can reach minors despite the 18–30 target, assess whether minors interact and implement age-assurance/parental-consent measures if any consent-based processing of their data occurs (GDPR Art. 8).

Keep the paid-partnership label on every post and story — this element is compliant — but reinforce it with the per-post AI/virtual indicator so recipients can identify both the commercial nature and the true source in real time (DSA Art. 26(1)).

campaign.title: TechBay headphone 'was/now' promotion
campaign.text: Electronics retailer promotes: 'NovaBuds Pro — was €199, NOW €99. Half price!' Pricing records show the €199 price was charged for 9 days in the past year; the prevailing price for the preceding four months was €119, and a competitor-matching widget had already displayed €109 for most of that period. The 'half price' claim is repeated in comparison tables and search ads. Stock and delivery claims are accurate and no urgency devices are used.

'half price' savings claim
inflated/short-lived reference price (€199 charged only 9 days)
reference price ignores prevailing price of €119 over four months
reference price ignores competitor-matching widget price of €109
repeated savings claim across comparison tables and search ads
triage.summary: Electronics retailer runs a 'was €199, now €99 — half price' price-comparison promotion for NovaBuds Pro headphones across web and search in the EU. The €199 reference price was only charged for 9 days, while the prevailing price for four months was €119 (with €109 shown via a competitor-matching widget), making the 'half price' savings claim potentially misleading. No AI, personalisation, or urgency devices are involved, and the audience is general adult consumers.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6(1)(d) prohibits practices that deceive the average consumer about the existence of a specific price advantage or the manner of price calculation, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The €199 'was' price was only charged for 9 days in a year, while the actual prevailing price for four months was €119 (and €109 via the competitor-matching widget). Anchoring the discount to a short-lived, inflated reference price overstates both the existence and size of the advantage — the true reduction against the real recent price is roughly €109-119 to €99, not 'half price'. This is a classic fake/exaggerated-discount misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: NovaBuds Pro — was €199, NOW €99. Half price!
findings.recommendation: Recalculate and present the saving against the genuine lowest recent selling price (the €119 prevailing price, and account for the €109 widget price). Drop the '€199' anchor and the 'Half price!' claim unless €99 is genuinely half of a legitimately applicable prior price. Align the reference price with the lowest price applied in the 30 days before the reduction (Price Indication Directive 98/6/EC Art. 6a) and keep documentary pricing records to substantiate any advantage claim.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 treats as misleading the omission of material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision. The comparison tables and search ads present €199 as the meaningful prior price while omitting the material fact that €199 applied for only 9 days and that the real prevailing price was €119 (€109 via the widget). Consumers are deprived of the context needed to judge whether the 'half price' saving is genuine, and the omission compounds the misleading price-advantage impression across every touchpoint.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'half price' claim is repeated in comparison tables and search ads.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the true reference price transparently in the comparison tables and ads, showing the lowest recent/prior price actually applied rather than the transient €199 figure, so consumers can assess the real saving. Ensure consistency of the reference price across web, search ads and comparison tables.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's headline "was €199, NOW €99 — Half price!" rests on a reference price (€199) that was charged for only 9 days in the past year, whereas the prevailing price for the preceding four months was €119 and a competitor-matching widget showed €109 for most of that period. This materially overstates both the existence and magnitude of the price advantage, engaging UCPD Art. 6(1)(d) (misleading action as to price advantage) and Art. 7 (misleading omission of the true recent price). The genuine reduction against the real prevailing price (~€119/€109) is far smaller than "half price". No urgency, ceasing-trade, AI or personalisation practices are present, so those provisions do not apply.
